title: Writing a joint model
text:
Suppose several annotators give binary judgments about whether each event description is compatible with a proposed inference. A data-generating process says that each item has an unobserved propensity and that each response is drawn from the probability implied by that propensity. The process is interpretable, but it is not yet a probability model that can be fitted.
A joint probability model assigns one probability factor to every random step in the data-generating process. This is the product rule applied to the annotation process. The product states which quantities are conditionally independent and which observations share an unobserved item value.

title: Writing a joint model
section: Begin with the simplest response process
text:
Begin with the simplest response process
Let item i have an unobserved log-odds value \theta_i. For current purposes, all annotators use the same logistic response mapping. The probability of an affirmative response is

\pi_i=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\theta_i),

and each recorded response follows

Y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i).

As in the earlier account of random effects and partial pooling, the item values follow a population distribution,

\theta_i\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_\theta,\tau_\theta^2).

This population distribution has already been motivated in the grouped model sequence. Here it supplies the item generating step needed for the joint distribution. Stable annotator tendencies are introduced on the next page rather than hidden inside this first model.

title: Writing a joint model
text:
Translate steps into factors
Let \mathcal O be the set of observed item and annotator pairs. For observed responses \mathbf{y} and item values \boldsymbol\theta, the joint distribution is

p(\mathbf{y},\boldsymbol\theta
\mid\mu_\theta,\tau_\theta)
=
\prod_i p(\theta_i\mid\mu_\theta,\tau_\theta)
\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathcal O}p(y_{ij}\mid\theta_i).

The first product corresponds to generating each item value. The second corresponds to generating every recorded annotation conditional on its item’s value. Writing the product over \mathcal O allows different items to be seen by different annotators. The repeated occurrence of \theta_i in the response factors records the fact that responses to one item share that latent item value.
The order of the products does not describe temporal order. Multiplication is commutative. The conditional arguments inside each factor carry the dependency claim.

title: Writing a joint model
text:
Work through two items
Suppose item 1 has affirmative probability .75 and receives responses 1 and 1. Item 2 has affirmative probability .50 and receives responses 1 and 0. Conditional on the item probabilities, the response contribution is

\begin{aligned}
p(1,1,1,0\mid\pi_1=.75,\pi_2=.50)
&=(.75)(.75)(.50)(1-.50)\\
&=.140625.
\end{aligned}

The two responses to item 1 use the same .75 probability. The two responses to item 2 use the same .50 probability. This is how the joint expression records shared item structure without treating the item mean as another observation.
To complete the joint density, multiply this response contribution by the density assigned to each \theta_i. Since \theta_1=\operatorname{logit}(.75) and \theta_2=\operatorname{logit}(.50)=0, the item factors are

p(\theta_1\mid\mu_\theta,\tau_\theta)
p(\theta_2\mid\mu_\theta,\tau_\theta).

title: Writing a joint model
section: Compute the joint log density in base R
text:
Compute the joint log density in base R


Code
joint_log_density <- function(y, item, theta, mu_theta, tau_theta) {
  response_probability <- plogis(theta[item])

  response_terms <- dbinom(
    x = y,
    size = 1,
    prob = response_probability,
    log = TRUE
  )

  item_terms <- dnorm(
    x = theta,
    mean = mu_theta,
    sd = tau_theta,
    log = TRUE
  )

  sum(response_terms) + sum(item_terms)
}

y <- c(1, 1, 1, 0)
item <- c(1, 1, 2, 2)
theta <- qlogis(c(.75, .50))

joint_log_density(
  y = y,
  item = item,
  theta = theta,
  mu_theta = 0,
  tau_theta = 1
)


theta[item] repeats the appropriate item value for each response row. dbinom() calculates the four conditional response terms, while dnorm() calculates one population term for each item value. The function evaluates the joint density at supplied parameter values. It does not fit them.

title: Writing a joint model
text:
Separate observations from summaries
The raw annotations appear in the conditional response product. An item mean calculated from those same annotations is a deterministic summary of the responses, not a new independent measurement.
For item 1, the raw responses (1,1) determine the mean 1. Multiplying the joint model by a second likelihood term for that mean would count the same responses twice. The mean may be used in a descriptive or predictive check, but it should not reenter as independent data.

title: Writing a joint model
section: Do not count deterministic summaries twice
text:
Do not count deterministic summaries twice
Including a response and its deterministic summary as separate observations double counts the evidence. The resulting model appears to have more evidence than the annotation protocol produced. Its intervals may be too narrow, and its fit can be dominated by a summary already implied by the raw data.
The duplication can be detected by tracing each likelihood term to the random step and recorded event it represents. If two factors point to the same recorded responses without a second measurement process, one of them is duplicated.






NoteCheck the joint model




Which product generates latent item values?
Which term makes two responses to item 1 share information?
Why does the order of multiplication not state the dependency structure?
Why is an item mean not an additional response when the raw annotations already enter the likelihood?

title: Writing a joint model
text:
Summing up
A joint model translates each random step into one probability factor. Its conditional arguments state which observations share unobserved quantities. Tracing each factor to a recorded event prevents deterministic summaries from being counted twice. We next extend the response step with a stable annotator effect.

title: Parameter recovery
text:
Suppose a model for gated annotations fits without warnings and returns an estimate for every item and annotator quantity. Successful computation does not show that the data contain enough information to distinguish those quantities. Several parameter combinations may produce nearly identical response distributions.
A parameter recovery analysis tests the complete inference procedure on simulated data whose generating values are known. It asks whether the procedure can return those values under its own assumptions and under a design resembling the planned analysis.

title: Parameter recovery
text:
The recovery loop
One recovery replicate contains four steps.

Choose generating parameter values and a sample design.
Simulate latent quantities and recorded responses from the custom model.
Fit the planned model to the simulated responses.
Compare the fitted summaries with the generating values.

The fitting step is essential. Inspecting simulated observations alone tests the generator, not the ability of the inference procedure to recover its parameters.
Repeat the loop across many simulated datasets and across parameter settings that affect identifiability. The unit of evaluation is then a generating value paired with an estimate from one complete fit.

title: Parameter recovery
text:
Begin with one binary quantity
Consider a simple gate with true affirmative probability \pi=.75. Suppose 20 independent annotations produce 16 affirmatives. The estimated proportion is

\widehat\pi=\frac{16}{20}=.80,

so the estimation error in this replicate is

\widehat\pi-\pi=.80-.75=.05.

This one error does not estimate bias. It is one draw from the recovery procedure. Recall from estimator bias and mean squared error that repeated samples are needed to describe the distribution of estimation error.

title: Parameter recovery
Parameter recovery
text:
Implement a minimal recovery study
The following code uses the observed affirmative proportion as the estimator and an exact binomial interval. A custom model recovery study replaces these two lines with simulation from and fitting of the complete model.


Code
recover_gate_once <- function(probability, n_annotations) {
  response <- rbinom(
    n = n_annotations,
    size = 1,
    prob = probability
  )

  fit <- binom.test(sum(response), length(response))

  data.frame(
    generating = probability,
    estimate = mean(response),
    lower = fit$conf.int[1],
    upper = fit$conf.int[2]
  )
}

set.seed(731)

recovery <- do.call(
  rbind,
  replicate(
    n = 500,
    expr = recover_gate_once(
      probability = 0.75,
      n_annotations = 20
    ),
    simplify = FALSE
  )
)

recovery$error <- recovery$estimate - recovery$generating
recovery$covers <- with(
  recovery,
  lower <= generating & generating <= upper
)

c(
  bias = mean(recovery$error),
  rmse = sqrt(mean(recovery$error^2)),
  coverage = mean(recovery$covers)
)


The simulation fixes the gate probability and sample size, then repeats the generator and fitter 500 times. The resulting summaries are conditional on those choices. They do not describe recovery for rarer gates, fewer annotations, or a larger custom model.

title: Parameter recovery
text:
Test difficult regions
Recovery at one convenient setting provides narrow evidence. A gated model should be tested across gate rates, annotator counts, item counts, item variation, and annotator variation. Values near a boundary deserve particular attention because few responses may reach one branch of the instrument.
For latent item quantities, recovery should be checked under the identifying convention used during fitting. If only item contrasts or ranks are identified, evaluate those targets rather than demanding recovery of an arbitrary absolute origin.
Computation belongs in the record as well. Nonconvergence, divergent transitions, or excessive runtime at one parameter setting are failures of the planned procedure under that setting. Discarding failed fits can make recovery appear better than the procedure actually performs.

title: Parameter recovery
section: What recovery does and does not establish
text:
What recovery does and does not establish
Successful recovery shows that the fitter can retrieve parameters when data are generated by the same model. Real annotations may arise from a different response process. Posterior predictive checks and sensitivity analyses address parts of that mismatch.
Failed recovery is more decisive. If the procedure cannot recover a parameter under its own assumptions at the planned sample size, a precise interpretation of that parameter in real data is not supported. The model may need a narrower target, a stronger design, or fewer components. Conversely, successful parameter recovery does not validate the linguistic account. It establishes computational and design adequacy under the assumed generator, not that the generator describes annotators.
The appropriate conclusion is conditional. The procedure recovered a specific quantity over a stated range under a stated design. Any extension from that result to real annotation behavior requires separate evidence.






NoteCheck the recovery claim




Why must fitting occur inside every recovery replicate?
Can small average bias coexist with poor recovery in individual simulations?
Which parameter regions are likely to be difficult for a gated model?
What does failed recovery imply for interpretation of a real data estimate?
What does successful recovery fail to establish?

title: Parameter recovery
text:
Summing up
Parameter recovery pairs known generating values with estimates from the complete planned procedure. Bias, error, coverage, and computational failures describe different aspects of recovery. With this gate in place, the final page combines the preceding components in a narrow UDS measurement model.

title: Data-generating processes
text:
Suppose annotators judge the acceptability of a sentence on a four category scale. We observe the category, but the category alone does not say how sentence acceptability, response noise, and the scale boundaries combined to produce it. Writing code before answering that question can hide incompatible assumptions inside one function call.
A data-generating process is an ordered account of the random choices and deterministic mappings that could produce an observation. The threshold account below gives a latent-variable representation of the cumulative logit model introduced earlier. It is written before the joint distribution so that every later probability term has a stated role in the annotation process.

title: Data-generating processes
section: State one step at a time
text:
State one step at a time
For a first model of the ordered judgment, consider the following process.

Each sentence i has an unobserved acceptability value \theta_i.
A trial response Z_{ij} varies around that value.
Fixed ordered thresholds map Z_{ij} to the recorded category Y_{ij}.

This process intentionally omits stable annotator differences. Its purpose is to expose the item and observation rule before a later page extends the account.
To retain the earlier cumulative-logit response model, let trial variation follow a standard logistic distribution:

Z_{ij}=\theta_i+\varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\varepsilon_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Logistic}(0,1).

For four response categories, let c_1<c_2<c_3 be the thresholds. The recorded response is

Y_{ij}=k
\quad\text{when}\quad
c_{k-1}<Z_{ij}\leq c_k,

where c_0=-\infty and c_4=\infty. The dependence sequence is

\theta_i
\longrightarrow
Z_{ij}
\longrightarrow
Y_{ij}.

The arrows describe an order of generation, not a chronology in the annotator’s mind. They state which values are needed to generate each later value.

title: Data-generating processes
text:
Work through one response
Suppose one sentence has \theta_i=.8, and one trial receives noise \varepsilon_{ij}=-.2. Its latent response is

Z_{ij}=.8-.2=.6.

Let the thresholds be c_1=-1, c_2=0, and c_3=1. Since

0<.6\leq1,

the recorded category is Y_{ij}=3. The model interprets category 3 as the result of a latent response falling between the second and third thresholds. It does not interpret the numeral 3 as a direct measurement of \theta_i.
Different noise draws can yield different categories for the same sentence. If \varepsilon_{ij}=.5, then Z_{ij}=1.3 and the response becomes category 4. Trial variation is thus part of the measurement account rather than evidence that the sentence changed between presentations.

title: Data-generating processes
section: Implement the generation in base R
text:
Implement the generation in base R


Code
generate_ordered_response <- function(theta, noise, thresholds) {
  latent_response <- theta + noise
  response <- findInterval(latent_response, thresholds) + 1L

  data.frame(
    theta = theta,
    noise = noise,
    latent_response = latent_response,
    response = response
  )
}

generate_ordered_response(
  theta = 0.8,
  noise = -0.2,
  thresholds = c(-1, 0, 1)
)


The function accepts the random draw noise rather than generating it internally. This makes the hand calculation visible. A simulator would draw many noise values and then apply the same deterministic threshold mapping.

title: Data-generating processes
text:
A data-generating process makes commitments
The process says that noise enters before thresholding and that every response uses the same thresholds. If annotators differ in their scale use, common thresholds may fail. If a response is bounded and has meaningful endpoints, a latent ordered category process may not match the instrument. These are empirical and measurement commitments, not implementation details.
The process also brackets a question. It does not yet represent stable annotator tendencies. This omission is acceptable only because it is explicit and temporary. A later extension adds an annotator component after the joint distribution for the simpler process is clear.

title: Data-generating processes
text:
Account for every recorded variable
Every recorded variable should either appear in the data-generating process or be declared outside its scope. If confidence is recorded but omitted, the analysis should say that it does not model confidence. If a follow up question appears only after an affirmative gate, the display rule belongs in the process.
Conversely, every latent quantity needs a role. Adding an unobserved variable can make a model flexible while leaving its scale or meaning unidentified. A verbal label does not identify a latent variable.

title: Data-generating processes
section: Every variable needs a role in the model
text:
Every variable needs a role in the model
Every recorded or latent quantity must have a defined role in the generative process. An observed confidence score is omitted when the model silently ignores it while claiming to represent the complete instrument. A latent state is unidentified when it affects no observation or when several latent states make identical predictions.
The repair is a design decision. Give the variable a role in the data-generating process, narrow the model’s claim so the variable is explicitly omitted, or remove an unnecessary latent quantity. Writing the process before code exposes the choice.






NoteCheck the generative order




Which value is generated directly from \theta_i in the worked process?
Why can two responses to the same sentence differ under the model?
What model commitment is made by using one threshold vector for every response?
What happens when an observed variable has no defined role in the generative process?

title: Data-generating processes
text:
Summing up
A data-generating process orders the random choices and mappings that connect a linguistic quantity to a recorded annotation. The order exposes assumptions before they are compressed into software. The next page translates each step into a factor in one joint distribution.

title: Annotator effects
text:
Suppose two annotators judge the same set of event descriptions. One tends to affirm a proposed inference, while the other tends to reject it. If the model attributes every difference to the items, the first annotator’s responses may make every item appear more supportive of the inference.
The random-intercept model introduced earlier can also represent stable annotator variation. Here an annotator random intercept represents a stable upward or downward response tendency shared across one annotator’s judgments. It extends the item response model from the preceding page without changing the meaning of the item values.

title: Annotator effects
text:
Add one location term
Let \theta_i be the unobserved log odds for item i, and let a_j be annotator j’s random intercept. Define

\operatorname{logit}(\pi_{ij})=\theta_i+a_j,

with

Y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ij}).

To make a_j a random intercept, give the annotator deviations a population distribution centered at zero:

a_j\sim\operatorname{Normal}(0,\sigma_a^2).

A positive a_j raises the log odds of an affirmative response for every item judged by annotator j. A negative value lowers them. The effect is shared across responses, so it is not trial noise.
This equation is an extension of the earlier joint model. The item value still locates the item, and the annotator value shifts the response mapping for one person.

title: Annotator effects
text:
Work through two annotators
Suppose item 1 has \theta_1=-1 and item 2 has \theta_2=1. Annotator A has a_A=.5, while annotator B has a_B=-.5.
For item 1, the two linear predictors are

\eta_{1A}=-1+.5=-.5

and

\eta_{1B}=-1-.5=-1.5.

The corresponding probabilities are approximately .38 and .18. For item 2, the predictors are 1.5 and .5, giving probabilities of approximately .82 and .62.

title: Annotator effects
section: Compute the response surface in base R
text:
Compute the response surface in base R


Code
item_values <- c(item_1 = -1, item_2 = 1)
annotator_values <- c(A = 0.5, B = -0.5)

response_surface <- expand.grid(
  item = names(item_values),
  annotator = names(annotator_values)
)

response_surface$theta <- item_values[response_surface$item]
response_surface$a <- annotator_values[response_surface$annotator]
response_surface$linear_predictor <- with(response_surface, theta + a)
response_surface$probability <- plogis(response_surface$linear_predictor)

response_surface


The call to expand.grid() creates every item and annotator combination. This crossing is not merely convenient for the calculation. Overlap in the annotation design helps separate stable item values from stable annotator tendencies.

title: Annotator effects
text:
Fix the coordinate system
The decomposition into item and annotator locations is not identified without a reference. If every item value increases by a constant c and every annotator value decreases by the same c, then

(\theta_i+c)+(a_j-c)=\theta_i+a_j.

The response probabilities do not change. One possible identifying convention is

\sum_{j=1}^{J}a_j=0.

The population distribution used on this page instead fixes the population mean of the annotator random intercepts at zero. Either convention fixes the origin. Under the population-distribution convention, \theta_i is the item log odds for an annotator whose random intercept is zero. This conditional quantity is not the marginal probability obtained by averaging over the annotator distribution.
The constraint does not claim that an annotator with random intercept zero has no response behavior. It defines where zero lies on the latent log-odds scale.

title: Annotator effects
section: Location is not every annotator difference
text:
Location is not every annotator difference
Annotators may also differ in response variability or in how they use ordered category boundaries. A location effect cannot represent those patterns. It shifts all predictions in the same direction.
A more variable annotator is not automatically a lower quality annotator. Items may be genuinely ambiguous under that annotator’s grammar, or the response scale may interact with their interpretation. Scale or threshold variation should be added only when the response pattern and scientific target require it. This page does not introduce those extensions.

title: Annotator effects
section: Item and annotator effects must be identifiable
text:
Item and annotator effects must be identifiable
Item and annotator effects are perfectly confounded when each item is judged by only one annotator. If annotator A judges only item 1 and annotator B judges only item 2, a response difference can be assigned to \theta_1-\theta_2, to a_A-a_B, or to both. The two effects are thus not separately identifiable.
Crossing annotators with several items supplies overlap. A connected annotation design may still be sparse, but there must be a path of shared items or annotators tying the latent locations to one coordinate system. A fitted model cannot manufacture that overlap after collection.






NoteCheck the annotator location




What response pattern does a positive a_j represent?
Why does adding c to every \theta_i and subtracting it from every a_j leave predictions unchanged?
What does the zero sum convention identify?
Why can a location effect not represent endpoint avoidance?
Which annotation design makes item and annotator effects perfectly confounded?

title: Annotator effects
text:
Summing up
An annotator random intercept separates a stable response shift from an item value, subject to a coordinate constraint and sufficient overlap in the annotation design. The next page adds an instrument rule that determines whether a follow up annotation is observed.

title: Validating an imputation procedure
text:
The true values of naturally missing acoustic measurements are unavailable. If a third formant value was never recovered from the signal, no direct error can compare its imputation with the unseen truth. We can still ask a related question: when a measured value is hidden on purpose, how accurately does the complete procedure reconstruct it?
Holdout validation by artificial masking turns some observed cells into artificial missing cells, fits the imputation without those values, and compares the reconstructions with the values held aside. This applies the earlier training and test separation to matrix cells. The masking step creates known targets while preserving the rule that a target cannot guide its own prediction.

title: Validating an imputation procedure
text:
Define the validation error
Let O be the set of naturally observed cells, and choose a masked subset M\subset O. Construct a training matrix in which the cells in M are temporarily replaced by missing values. After fitting the imputation procedure to that matrix, let \widehat y_{ij}^{(-M)} be the reconstructed value for cell (i,j).
Using the mean squared error introduced earlier, mean squared reconstruction error is

\operatorname{MSE}(M)
=\frac{1}{|M|}
\sum_{(i,j)\in M}
\left(y_{ij}-\widehat y_{ij}^{(-M)}\right)^2.

The superscript (-M) records that the masked values were not available during fitting. Without this separation, the calculation would measure how well a procedure reproduces values it already saw.

title: Validating an imputation procedure
text:
Work through one masked cell
Consider four tokens with two standardized acoustic measurements.

\mathbf{Y}=
\begin{pmatrix}
1.0&1.2\\
2.0&2.1\\
3.0&2.9\\
4.0&4.2
\end{pmatrix}.

Mask the second measurement in row 3. As a simple reference procedure, impute the observed mean of that column. The training column contains 1.2, 2.1, and 4.2, so the imputation is

\widehat y_{32}^{(-M)}
=\frac{1.2+2.1+4.2}{3}=2.5.

The hidden value is 2.9, giving squared error

(2.9-2.5)^2=.16.

This calculation does not establish that mean imputation is adequate. It shows how masking produces an error whose target was unavailable to the fitting procedure.

title: Validating an imputation procedure
section: Implement the mask in base R
text:
Implement the mask in base R


Code
acoustic <- matrix(
  c(1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 1.2, 2.1, 2.9, 4.2),
  nrow = 4,
  ncol = 2
)

mask <- matrix(FALSE, nrow = nrow(acoustic), ncol = ncol(acoustic))
mask[3, 2] <- TRUE

truth <- acoustic[mask]
training <- acoustic
training[mask] <- NA

column_mean <- mean(training[, 2], na.rm = TRUE)
prediction <- column_mean
squared_error <- (truth - prediction)^2

c(truth = truth, prediction = prediction, squared_error = squared_error)


The same structure can evaluate the iterative PCA imputation from the preceding page. Replace the column mean calculation with the full iterative procedure, fit it to training, and retrieve its prediction at mask. Centering values, component directions, and every tuning decision must be estimated from training rather than from acoustic.

title: Validating an imputation procedure
text:
Repeat the masking
One masked cell may be unusually easy or difficult. Repeat the procedure across several masks so that every eligible observed cell can contribute an out of sample reconstruction error. The errors should be retained cell by cell before they are averaged.
For a small fully observed matrix, one cell can be masked at a time.


Code
mean_impute_cell <- function(x, row, column) {
  training <- x
  truth <- training[row, column]
  training[row, column] <- NA
  prediction <- mean(training[, column], na.rm = TRUE)

  data.frame(
    row = row,
    column = column,
    truth = truth,
    prediction = prediction,
    squared_error = (truth - prediction)^2
  )
}

errors <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(acoustic)), function(row) {
    mean_impute_cell(acoustic, row = row, column = 2)
  })
)

errors
mean(errors$squared_error)


This leave one cell out scheme is useful only when fitting after masking one cell resembles the intended imputation problem. A larger matrix may permit several cells to be masked at once, provided the masking does not remove all information needed to fit a column or row.

title: Validating an imputation procedure
text:
Match the natural missingness problem
Uniformly masking cells can create an easier task than natural missingness. Suppose F3 is usually absent for one vowel, one speaker group, or the highest values. A random mask dominated by common vowels and central values will mostly evaluate interpolation in well represented regions.
An imputation method may look artificially accurate when the masking scheme creates easier cases than the natural missingness process. To diagnose this problem, design several masking schemes that resemble plausible natural patterns. One scheme might mask F3 within the vowel category where tracking failures are common. Another might mask complete blocks that resemble session failures. The schemes should be stated before inspecting which one favors a preferred procedure.
Good performance under realistic artificial masks still does not prove that naturally missing entries are unbiased. The actual missing values may differ from all observed values available for masking. Holdout validation by artificial masking is thus a falsification tool. Poor reconstruction reveals a problem, while low error supports only the tested masking conditions.

title: Validating an imputation procedure
text:
Keep preprocessing inside the mask
Using the full matrix to calculate column means, scales, component directions, or the number of components gives the hidden values an indirect path into their predictions. This is data leakage, and it usually makes reconstruction error too optimistic.
Every estimated preprocessing operation belongs inside the masked training data. If the completed matrix later enters a predictive analysis, the imputation must also be fitted inside each training split of that analysis. This requirement follows the training and test separation introduced earlier in the course.

title: Validating an imputation procedure
section: Inspect errors at the level of the claim
text:
Inspect errors at the level of the claim
An overall mean can hide poor reconstruction for a minority vowel, speaker group, language, or measurement column. Retain the row and column identities attached to each masked error, then summarize error over the groups relevant to the linguistic target.
A low overall error does not compensate for systematic failure in the group that carries the theoretical contrast. The validation summary must use the same units and measurements that the later interpretation concerns.






NoteAudit the validation




Why can naturally missing values not provide a direct reconstruction error?
Which quantities must be estimated after the target cell is masked?
How can an unrealistically easy masking scheme make an imputation appear better than it is under natural missingness?
Why should cell level errors be retained before averaging?
What does low error under one masking scheme fail to establish?

title: Validating an imputation procedure
text:
Summing up
Holdout validation by artificial masking evaluates an imputation on observed values made unavailable during fitting. Its conclusions depend on the masking pattern, leakage prevention, and the linguistic groups over which errors are summarized. The result cannot reveal the true naturally missing values, but it can identify reconstruction failures before imputed cells are treated as measurements.

title: Missingness patterns
text:
Suppose an acoustic dataset has one row per vowel token and columns for duration, first formant, and third formant. Some third formant measurements are blank. Before deciding why they are blank or how to fill them, we need a representation of where the blanks occur.
For each potential measurement, a missingness indicator records whether the value was observed. The collection of these indicators is the missingness pattern. Unlike the missing measurements, the indicators are available for every cell. This notation extends the retention indicator used for exclusion rules, but it now records whether a measurement is available rather than whether an observed response is retained.

title: Missingness patterns
text:
Define the indicator
Let Y_{ij} be measurement j for token i. Define

R_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if }Y_{ij}\text{ is observed},\\
0 & \text{if }Y_{ij}\text{ is missing}.
\end{cases}

The measurement matrix \mathbf{Y} may contain blanks. The indicator matrix \mathbf{R} does not. It represents each blank as a zero and each observed value as a one.
This coding convention is arbitrary, so it must be stated. We use one for observed and zero for missing throughout the module.

1&1&1\\
1&0&0\\
1&1&1
\end{pmatrix}.

Read the matrix by column first. Duration has zero missing values, F1 has one, and F3 has two. Then read it by row. Token t4 has two absent measurements, while t2 has one. Finally, read entire row patterns. Three tokens have pattern (1,1,1), one has (1,1,0), and one has (1,0,0).
These summaries answer different questions. Column counts locate measurements with substantial loss. Row counts locate tokens with little observed information. Pattern counts show which measurements tend to be absent together.

title: Missingness patterns
section: Compute the same summaries in R
text:
Compute the same summaries in R


Code
acoustic <- data.frame(
  token = paste0("t", 1:5),
  duration = c(120, 135, 110, 160, 145),
  F1 = c(310, 325, 300, NA, 340),
  F3 = c(2450, NA, 2510, NA, 2380)
)

measurement_columns <- c("duration", "F1", "F3")
indicator <- 1L * !is.na(acoustic[measurement_columns])

indicator
colSums(1L - indicator)
rowSums(1L - indicator)


is.na() returns TRUE for a blank, so !is.na() returns TRUE for an observed cell. Multiplying by one changes the logical values into the stated zero and one coding. Subtracting the indicator from one then produces a count of missing values.
To count complete row patterns, combine each row of the indicator matrix into a label.


Code
pattern <- apply(indicator, 1, paste0, collapse = "")
table(pattern)


The labels 111, 110, and 100 correspond to the three patterns identified by hand. The column order belongs to the definition of each label, so a report should give that order.

title: Missingness patterns
section: Relate the indicator to observed information
text:
Relate the indicator to observed information
The indicator can be compared with measurements or labels that are observed. Suppose every token also has a vowel label and a recording session. We could tabulate whether F3 is observed within each vowel or session.


Code
acoustic$vowel <- c("i", "a", "i", "a", "i")
acoustic$session <- c("morning", "morning", "afternoon", "afternoon", "afternoon")
acoustic$F3_observed <- !is.na(acoustic$F3)

with(acoustic, table(vowel, F3_observed))
with(acoustic, table(session, F3_observed))


With five tokens, these tables are descriptive rather than stable estimates. Their role is to show which observed dimensions should receive attention in a larger dataset. If missingness differs by vowel, speaker, session, or an observed acoustic measurement, deletion may change the composition of the retained sample.

title: Missingness patterns
section: A pattern does not identify a missingness mechanism
text:
A pattern does not identify a missingness mechanism
An observed pattern does not identify the process that caused it. A table of missingness indicators thus cannot by itself establish a causal account of why values are missing.
For instance, F3 may be absent more often for vowel /a/. The tracker might fail because /a/ has acoustic properties that make tracking difficult. The recording session containing more /a/ tokens might instead have used a faulty microphone. Both processes can produce the same observed association between vowel and missingness.
Pattern analysis can rule out a claim that blanks are distributed evenly when strong structure is visible. It cannot establish that unobserved values are unrelated to their probability of being absent. That claim belongs to a missingness mechanism.






NoteInspect the pattern




What does R_{ij}=0 mean under the convention used here?
For the five token table, which token has the least observed acoustic information?
Why do column counts and pattern counts answer different questions?
Give two processes that could make F3 missing more often for one vowel category.

title: Missingness patterns
text:
Summing up
A missingness indicator turns the locations of absent measurements into fully observed data. Counts by column, row, and joint pattern describe different parts of that structure. The pattern cannot identify its own cause, so the next page states the assumptions made by different missingness mechanisms.

title: Missing data
text:
Suppose a vowel production study records duration and three formants for every token. The third formant tracker fails on some tokens, so the corresponding cells are blank. The blanks create a software problem because many functions expect a rectangular table. But filling or deleting the cells merely to satisfy the software would begin at the wrong place. As in the earlier discussion of exclusion rules, the process determining which observations enter an analysis can change the quantity being estimated.
Each blank records a measurement that could have been present but is absent. The reason for that absence may affect what an analysis estimates. A tracker that fails at random removes a different set of tokens from a tracker that fails on unusually high formant values. The visible table may not tell these cases apart.
The process that removes values determines which claims the retained data can support. An analysis thus requires two objects. The first is the linguistic measurement that might be absent. The second is an indicator recording whether that measurement was observed. Keeping the two objects separate prevents a blank from being treated as though it were a measured value.

title: Missing data
text:
Three questions precede imputation
Imputation replaces a missing value with one or more estimates. The replacement is produced by a model or rule. It is not a newly observed measurement.
Before choosing a procedure, ask three questions.

Which measurements are absent, and where do their absences occur?
What process could have made those measurements absent?
Which population or relation would an analysis of the observed subset estimate?

The first question concerns an observed pattern. The second concerns a data-generating process, some parts of which may be unobserved. The third concerns the estimand. These questions are connected, but they are not interchangeable. A visible association between vowel category and tracker failure does not prove why the tracker failed, and a plausible account of failure does not show how many rows an analysis will lose.

title: Missing data
text:
How the module proceeds
We begin with missingness patterns. That page defines a missingness indicator and uses it to count absent values by row, column, and pattern. Missingness mechanisms then distinguishes three claims about how that indicator depends on observed and unobserved measurements.
Complete case analysis studies the consequences of deleting any row with a missing analysis variable. This procedure is simple, but the retained rows may represent a selected population and can be far fewer than the missing percentage for any one column suggests.
Only then do we turn to iterative PCA imputation. This page depends on the earlier factorization sequence because the imputation repeatedly centers a matrix, fits a low rank representation, and reconstructs missing cells. The statistical object introduced here is the imputation iteration, not principal component analysis itself.
Finally, validating an imputation procedure hides observed values and checks whether the procedure reconstructs them without access to their true values during fitting. This validation cannot reveal the naturally missing values, but it can show where an imputation procedure fails on observed values made artificially unavailable.

title: Missing data
section: What the module does not assume
text:
What the module does not assume
No generic procedure makes missing data harmless. Complete case analysis may be adequate under a narrow selection claim. A low rank imputation may work when several measurements share stable linear structure. Neither procedure can establish its own assumptions from the completed table.
This limitation is useful. It forces the report to distinguish what was observed, what was assumed about absence, what was estimated from the retained or completed data, and what remains uncertain because the missing values were never measured.

title: Missing data
text:
What this module adds
By the end of the module, we should be able to encode missingness separately from a linguistic response, state what each missingness mechanism claims, determine how deletion changes the analysis set, and evaluate an imputation on values that were hidden on purpose. We begin by making the pattern of blank cells explicit.

Where are duration, F1, and F3 absent in the acoustic table?

A missingness indicator records whether a potential measurement was observed.

[Sources]
https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-MCAR.html

\[
R_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
1&\text{if }Y_{ij}\text{ is observed},\\
0&\text{if }Y_{ij}\text{ is missing}.
\end{cases}
\]

\[

\begin{pmatrix}
1&1&1\\
1&1&0\\
1&1&1\\

\end{pmatrix}
\]

Output
Column counts locate measurements with loss.
Row counts locate tokens with little information.

text:

An association between vowel and missing F3 does not identify the process that caused the association.

text:
Missingness mechanisms
Dependence on observed and unseen measurements

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Answer
A missingness mechanism states how observation depends on measured and missing values.

[Sources]
https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-MCAR.html

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Method
The object of interest is
\[
P(R=1\mid Y_{\mathrm{obs}},Y_{\mathrm{mis}}).
\]

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Answer
Values are missing completely at random (MCAR) when observation depends on neither observed nor missing measurements.
\[
P(R=1\mid Y_{\mathrm{obs}},Y_{\mathrm{mis}})=P(R=1)
\]

[Sources]
https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-MCAR.html

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Answer
Values are missing at random (MAR) when observation may depend on observed measurements but not additionally on the missing value.
\[
P(R=1\mid Y_{\mathrm{obs}},Y_{\mathrm{mis}})=P(R=1\mid Y_{\mathrm{obs}})
\]

[Sources]
https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-MCAR.html

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Answer
Values are missing not at random (MNAR) when observation still depends on the unseen value after observed measurements are considered.

[Sources]
https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-MCAR.html

text:

All three simple sentence trials are observed.
Only one of three complex sentence trials is observed.

The pattern is compatible with MAR through observed complexity and with MNAR through unseen reading time.

https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-MCAR.html

For required variables \(J\),
\[

\[

Hide measured values on purpose, fit without them, and compare their reconstructions with the held aside measurements.
This is the training and test separation applied to matrix cells.

title: Singular value decomposition
text:
A rank one matrix contains one common row by column pattern. Most linguistic matrices contain several such patterns. We need a rule that finds them in order, assigns each a strength, and reconstructs the original matrix when they are added together.
The singular value decomposition (SVD) provides that rule. It represents any real matrix as an ordered sum of mutually orthogonal rank one terms. The first term gives the closest rank one representation under squared reconstruction error, the second accounts for the strongest remaining orthogonal pattern, and the sequence continues through the matrix rank.
We will first state the decomposition and its dimensions. We will then work through a 2\times2 matrix for which every piece can be read by inspection. Finally, we will compute the same pieces in R and examine the sign and repeated-value ambiguities that constrain interpretation.

title: Singular value decomposition
text:
State the reduced decomposition
Let

\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}

have rank r. Its reduced SVD is

\mathbf{X}
=
\mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf T},

where

\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r},
\qquad
\mathbf{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r},
\qquad
\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times r}.

The columns of \mathbf{U} are the left singular vectors. They are orthonormal:

\mathbf{U}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{I}_r.

The columns of \mathbf{V} are the right singular vectors, and they are also orthonormal:

\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{I}_r.

The matrix \mathbf{D} is diagonal. Its nonnegative entries are the singular values:

\mathbf{D}
=
\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_r),
\qquad
d_1\geq d_2\geq\cdots\geq d_r>0.

The ordering fixes which pattern is called first, second, and so on.

title: Singular value decomposition
section: Turn the product into rank one terms

title: Singular value decomposition
text:
Work through a diagonal matrix
Consider

\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2&0\\
0&1
\end{bmatrix}.

The row and column axes already align with the matrix’s two patterns. We can choose

\mathbf{U}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0\\
0&1
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{D}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2&0\\
0&1
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{V}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0\\
0&1
\end{bmatrix}.

Multiplying the three matrices returns \mathbf{X}. The sum form makes the two patterns more visible:

\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{X}
&=
2
\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}1&0\end{bmatrix}
+
1
\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}0&1\end{bmatrix}\\
&=
\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}
+
\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}

The first rank one term reconstructs the upper-left entry of size 2. The second reconstructs the lower-right entry of size 1. Their sum reconstructs all four cells.
If we retain only the first term, the approximation is

\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_1
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2&0\\
0&0
\end{bmatrix}.

The omitted second term is smaller because d_2=1<d_1=2.

title: Singular value decomposition
section: Why the singular values measure strength
text:
Why the singular values measure strength
The squared size of the complete matrix under the Frobenius norm is

\lVert\mathbf{X}\rVert_F^2
=
\sum_i\sum_j x_{ij}^2.

For an SVD, orthogonality gives

\lVert\mathbf{X}\rVert_F^2
=
\sum_{k=1}^{r}d_k^2.

In the diagonal example,

\lVert\mathbf{X}\rVert_F^2
=
2^2+1^2
=
5.

The first term contributes d_1^2=4 of those 5 squared units, while the second contributes 1. This is why singular values quantify the magnitude of the ordered patterns.
The truncated sum through term K is also the closest rank K matrix to \mathbf{X} under the Frobenius norm. We will calculate its residual entries directly on the reconstruction page. For now, the important point is that the ordering is tied to squared reconstruction, not to a linguistic label.

title: Singular value decomposition
text:
Compute the decomposition in R
The R function svd() returns \mathbf{U}, the singular values, and \mathbf{V}.


Code
X_small <- matrix(
  c(
    2, 0,
    0, 1
  ),
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE
)

svd_fit <- svd(X_small)

svd_fit$u
svd_fit$d
svd_fit$v


The package returns the singular values as a vector rather than as the diagonal matrix \mathbf{D}. We can reconstruct that matrix and verify the product.


Code
D <- diag(svd_fit$d)
X_recovered <- svd_fit$u %*% D %*% t(svd_fit$v)

X_recovered
all.equal(X_small, X_recovered)


The transpose around svd_fit$v corresponds to \mathbf{V}^{\mathsf T} in the formal statement.

title: Singular value decomposition
text:
The signs are arbitrary
Suppose we replace both \mathbf{u}_k and \mathbf{v}_k with their negatives. Their outer product is unchanged:

(-\mathbf{u}_k)(-\mathbf{v}_k)^{\mathsf T}
=
\mathbf{u}_k\mathbf{v}_k^{\mathsf T}.

Software may thus return one singular direction with the opposite sign on a different system or after a numerically equivalent fit. Relative signs within a vector remain informative. The absolute choice of positive direction does not.
The SVD has sign indeterminacy. Any interpretation that depends on component 1 being positive rather than negative is not invariant to an equivalent decomposition.

title: Singular value decomposition
section: Repeated singular values weaken directional interpretation
text:
Repeated singular values weaken directional interpretation
A second issue arises when two singular values are equal. Suppose d_1=d_2. Any orthogonal rotation within their two-dimensional subspace can produce another valid pair of singular vectors with the same reconstruction.
Thus, the subspace is identified, but the individual directions within it are not uniquely fixed. Nearly equal singular values can likewise make individual vectors unstable under small changes to the matrix.
This instability does not make the SVD incorrect. The reconstructed subspace may remain stable even when one arbitrary basis for that subspace rotates. Interpretation should match what the decomposition identifies.






NoteProblem Set 5 connection



Problem Set 5, Tasks 6 and 7 use singular value decomposition to reconstruct masked inventory cells. The validation cells select the number of retained terms, while a separate test mask evaluates the selected representation. The separation is included because the factorization can otherwise choose its complexity from the same cells used for the final claim.

title: Singular value decomposition
text:
Check the ordered patterns

What are the dimensions of \mathbf{U}, \mathbf{D}, and \mathbf{V} in the reduced SVD of an n\times p rank r matrix?
Why is every term d_k\mathbf{u}_k\mathbf{v}_k^{\mathsf T} rank one?
In the diagonal example, how much squared matrix magnitude belongs to the first term?
Why can both singular vectors in one term be multiplied by -1 without changing the matrix?
If d_1=d_2, what is identified more securely: each individual vector or their shared subspace?

title: Singular value decomposition
text:
Before using variance directions
The SVD rewrites a real matrix as an ordered sum of orthogonal rank one patterns. Singular values measure their squared-reconstruction strength, while sign and repeated-value indeterminacies limit directional interpretation. The next page applies this decomposition to a centered linguistic matrix so that its directions describe observed variation around column means.

title: Reconstruction from components
text:
A low-dimensional representation is useful only because it leaves some details out. To understand what the representation preserves, we need to map it back into the original columns and measure the cellwise discrepancies that remain.
A rank-K approximation combines the first K terms of the singular value decomposition to approximate the original matrix. The residual matrix then records exactly what those terms did not represent.
We first derive the rank K reconstruction from the SVD. We then compute a two-component example by hand, implement the same calculation in R, and distinguish observed variance represented from predictive performance on observations excluded from fitting.

title: Reconstruction from components
section: Reconstruct with the first K terms
text:
Reconstruct with the first K terms
Let

\mathbf{X}
=
\mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf T}
=
\sum_{k=1}^{r}
d_k\mathbf{u}_k\mathbf{v}_k^{\mathsf T}.

Retaining the first K terms gives the rank K reconstruction

\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_K
=
\sum_{k=1}^{K}
d_k\mathbf{u}_k\mathbf{v}_k^{\mathsf T}.

Equivalently, let \mathbf{U}_K and \mathbf{V}_K contain the first K singular vectors, and let \mathbf{D}_K contain the first K singular values. Then

\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_K
=
\mathbf{U}_K
\mathbf{D}_K
\mathbf{V}_K^{\mathsf T}.

For PCA, the retained score matrix is

\mathbf{Z}_K
=
\mathbf{U}_K\mathbf{D}_K.

The same reconstruction can thus be written as

\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_{c,K}
=
\mathbf{Z}_K\mathbf{V}_K^{\mathsf T}.

This version makes the roles visible. Row scores say how strongly each observation expresses a component, and component directions distribute that expression back across the columns.

title: Reconstruction from components
section: Work through a rank one reconstruction
text:
Work through a rank one reconstruction
Return to the matrix

\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2&0\\
0&1
\end{bmatrix}.

Its two SVD terms are

2
\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}1&0\end{bmatrix}

and

1
\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}0&1\end{bmatrix}.

Keeping only the first term gives

\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_1
=
2
\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}1&0\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2&0\\
0&0
\end{bmatrix}.

The first component reconstructs the upper-left cell exactly. It predicts zero for the lower-right cell because the second pattern has been omitted.

title: Reconstruction from components
text:
Calculate the residual matrix
The rank K residual matrix is

\mathbf{E}_K
=
\mathbf{X}-\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_K.

For the rank one example,

\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{E}_1
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
2&0\\
0&1
\end{bmatrix}
-
\begin{bmatrix}
2&0\\
0&0
\end{bmatrix}\\
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
0&0\\
0&1
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}

A common summary is the squared Frobenius reconstruction error:

\lVert\mathbf{E}_K\rVert_F^2
=
\sum_i\sum_j e_{ij}^2.

Here,

\lVert\mathbf{E}_1\rVert_F^2
=
0^2+0^2+0^2+1^2
=
1.

If both components are retained, \widehat{\mathbf{X}}_2=\mathbf{X} and the observed reconstruction error is zero.

title: Reconstruction from components
text:
Derive variance represented
The total squared magnitude of \mathbf{X} is

\lVert\mathbf{X}\rVert_F^2
=
2^2+1^2
=
5.

The retained first component contributes d_1^2=4. Its proportion of represented squared variation is

\frac{d_1^2}{d_1^2+d_2^2}
=
\frac{4}{4+1}
=
0.8.

The residual proportion is 1/5=0.2, which matches the squared error divided by the total squared magnitude. More generally, the proportion represented by component k is

\frac{d_k^2}{\sum_{j=1}^{r}d_j^2}.

The cumulative proportion for the first K components is

\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K}d_k^2}
{\sum_{j=1}^{r}d_j^2}.

For centered data, this is the proportion of variance explained by the retained components. It describes the centered matrix used to fit the components, not performance on new observations.

title: Reconstruction from components
section: Return from transformed to original coordinates
text:
Return from transformed to original coordinates
PCA reconstructs the coordinates on which it was fit. If the matrix was only centered, the rank K reconstruction is \widehat{\mathbf{X}}_{c,K}. Add the training column means to recover the original origin:

\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_K
=
\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_{c,K}
+
\mathbf{1}_n\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\mathsf T}.

If the columns were standardized, first restore their units and then restore their means:

\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_K
=
\widehat{\mathbf{Z}}_K\mathbf{S}
+
\mathbf{1}_n\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\mathsf T}.

Forgetting either step yields predictions in centered or standardized coordinates rather than in the original measurements. The reconstruction may be algebraically correct and linguistically misreported because its units are wrong.

title: Reconstruction from components
text:
Implement reconstruction in R
The following code mirrors the matrix formula.


Code
X_scaled <- scale(
  X,
  center = TRUE,
  scale = TRUE
)

fit <- svd(X_scaled)
K <- 2

U_K <- fit$u[, seq_len(K), drop = FALSE]
D_K <- diag(fit$d[seq_len(K)], nrow = K)
V_K <- fit$v[, seq_len(K), drop = FALSE]

X_hat_scaled <- U_K %*% D_K %*% t(V_K)
E_K <- X_scaled - X_hat_scaled

sum(E_K^2)


The inverse transformation uses the means and scales stored by scale().


Code
column_means <- attr(X_scaled, "scaled:center")
column_sds <- attr(X_scaled, "scaled:scale")

X_hat <- sweep(
  X_hat_scaled,
  MARGIN = 2,
  STATS = column_sds,
  FUN = "*"
)

X_hat <- sweep(
  X_hat,
  MARGIN = 2,
  STATS = column_means,
  FUN = "+"
)


Every transformation used for reconstruction should be the one estimated during fitting. Recomputing a new origin or scale changes the representation being evaluated.

title: Reconstruction from components
section: Observed reconstruction is not held-out prediction
text:
Observed reconstruction is not held-out prediction
Adding a component cannot increase squared reconstruction error on the matrix used to fit the SVD. Each added term restores another orthogonal direction of observed variation. If all rank terms are retained, the observed error reaches zero apart from numerical precision.
Choosing the largest possible K will always look best on the fitted cells because observed reconstruction error decreases monotonically. Later terms may nevertheless represent sample-specific irregularities rather than structure that transfers to held-out cells.
To evaluate reconstruction as prediction, some cells or observations must be excluded from fitting and scored afterward under the training and test separation introduced earlier. The number of retained components must be chosen without consulting the final evaluation outcomes.

title: Reconstruction from components
section: Variance represented is not linguistic information
text:
Variance represented is not linguistic information
A component can account for substantial observed variance because it tracks recording source, sample composition, or a high-variance measurement. A low-variance component can encode a rare but systematic phonological contrast.
Thus, a statement that the first two components explain 80 percent of observed variance is a statement about squared reconstruction under a particular matrix design and transformation. It is not a statement that they preserve 80 percent of the linguistically relevant information.






NoteProblem Set 5 connection



Problem Set 5, Task 7 compares low rank reconstruction with a segment prevalence baseline on balanced hidden cells. Observed variance represented and held out reconstruction gain are different quantities. One describes the fitted matrix, while the other evaluates reconstruction on cells excluded from fitting.

title: Reconstruction from components
text:
Check the rebuilt cells

Which rank one term is omitted from \widehat{\mathbf{X}}_1 in the worked example?
Why is the squared Frobenius residual equal to 1?
How does d_k^2 enter the proportion of observed variation represented?
What must be restored after reconstructing standardized data?
Why can observed reconstruction error only decrease as K grows?
What additional separation is required before reconstruction error can support a held-out predictive claim?

title: Reconstruction from components
text:
Before choosing a dimension
Reconstruction maps retained scores and directions back to matrix cells, while the residual matrix shows what was discarded. Observed error measures compression of the fitted matrix and cannot select complexity without optimism. The next page uses held-out reconstruction to choose K before a separate final evaluation.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Suppose two acoustic measurements tend to rise together across vowel tokens. We could keep both coordinates, but much of their variation may run along one common direction. We would like to find that direction without choosing one of the measurements as a response variable.
Principal component analysis (PCA) finds orthogonal directions in a centered data matrix, ordered by the variance of the observations projected onto them. The first direction has the largest possible projected variance. Each later direction has the largest remaining projected variance subject to being orthogonal to the earlier directions.
We develop this idea from the singular value decomposition introduced on the previous page. We then solve a two-variable example by hand, reproduce it in R, and separate the variance criterion from claims about linguistic categories or processes.

title: Principal component analysis
section: Begin with variation around column means
text:
Begin with variation around column means
Let

\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}

be a linguistic data matrix, and let \mathbf{X}_c be its column-centered version. Centering matters because PCA is meant to describe variation around each observed column mean rather than distance from the numerical origin.
Take the SVD of the centered matrix:

\mathbf{X}_c
=
\mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf T}.

The columns of \mathbf{V} are the principal component directions. These directions live in the original p-variable coordinate space. The projected coordinates of the n observations are

\mathbf{Z}
=
\mathbf{X}_c\mathbf{V}
=
\mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}.

The matrix \mathbf{Z} is the score matrix. Its entry z_{ik} locates observation i along component k.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
State the variance criterion
Consider a unit-length direction \mathbf{v}, so that

\mathbf{v}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{v}=1.

Projecting every centered row onto this direction gives

\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{X}_c\mathbf{v}.

Since the columns of \mathbf{X}_c have mean zero, the projected scores also have mean zero. Their sample variance is

\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{z})
=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{z}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{z}
=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{v}^{\mathsf T}
\mathbf{X}_c^{\mathsf T}
\mathbf{X}_c
\mathbf{v}.

The first principal component direction solves

\mathbf{v}_1
=
\underset{\mathbf{v}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{v}=1}{\operatorname{argmax}}
\frac{1}{n-1}
\lVert\mathbf{X}_c\mathbf{v}\rVert^2.

The second solves the same maximization with the additional constraint

\mathbf{v}_2^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{v}_1=0.

Later directions remain orthogonal to all earlier directions. The right singular vectors provide exactly this ordered solution.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Work through two measurements
Suppose two centered acoustic measurements for two vowel tokens are

\mathbf{X}_c
=
\begin{bmatrix}
-1&-1\\
1&1
\end{bmatrix}.

Both measurements change together. Consider the unit direction

\mathbf{v}_1
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\1
\end{bmatrix}.

The scores are

\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{z}_1
&=
\mathbf{X}_c\mathbf{v}_1\\
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
-1&-1\\
1&1
\end{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\1
\end{bmatrix}\\
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
-\sqrt{2}\\
\sqrt{2}
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}

Because n=2, their sample variance is

\frac{(-\sqrt{2})^2+(\sqrt{2})^2}{2-1}
=
4.

Now consider the orthogonal unit direction

\mathbf{v}_2
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\-1
\end{bmatrix}.

Its scores are

\mathbf{X}_c\mathbf{v}_2
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0\\0
\end{bmatrix}.

There is no observed variation along the difference between the two measurements because the columns are identical. All observed variation lies along their common direction.
The first principal component is thus the direction of maximum sample variance.

title: Principal component analysis
section: Connect the scores to singular values
text:
Connect the scores to singular values
From

\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{D},

the score vector for component k is d_k\mathbf{u}_k. Since \mathbf{u}_k has squared length one, the sum of squared scores is d_k^2. The sample variance of component k is thus

\frac{d_k^2}{n-1}.

In the worked example, the first singular value is 2. Its component variance is

\frac{2^2}{2-1}=4,

which matches the direct score calculation. The second singular value is zero, so its component variance is zero.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Fit PCA in R
The function prcomp() centers the matrix and computes the SVD.


Code
X_two <- matrix(
  c(
    -1, -1,
     1,  1
  ),
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE
)

pca_two <- prcomp(
  X_two,
  center = TRUE,
  scale. = FALSE
)

pca_two$rotation
pca_two$x
pca_two$sdev


The rotation matrix contains the component directions \mathbf{V}. The x matrix contains the scores \mathbf{Z}. The sdev vector contains the score standard deviations

\frac{d_k}{\sqrt{n-1}}.

The sign of the printed first direction may be the reverse of the hand calculation. This is the sign indeterminacy inherited from the SVD, not a different solution.
For a general matrix X, the preprocessing decision should be stated explicitly.


Code
pca_fit <- prcomp(
  X,
  center = TRUE,
  scale. = TRUE
)


With scale. = FALSE, PCA describes the covariance structure of the centered variables. With scale. = TRUE, it describes the correlation structure of standardized variables. These coordinate systems can produce different directions because they assign different initial weights to the columns.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Interpret the variance criterion narrowly
The first component accounts for the largest observed projected variance under the chosen coordinate system. It is not automatically the direction most relevant to a linguistic theory.
A small-variance direction may separate two vowel categories. A large-variance direction may instead track microphone placement, speaker anatomy, or another source that dominates the measurements. PCA orders directions by observed variance, not by theoretical interest.
A component can explain the largest amount of sample variance without being linguistically central. Its substantive interpretation requires evidence beyond that variance criterion.

title: Principal component analysis
section: PCA does not use category labels
text:
PCA does not use category labels
PCA does not receive vowel labels, language families, experimental conditions, or other metadata when it computes its directions. If labeled groups separate in a score plot, that separation is a relation discovered after the representation was fit. It was not the criterion optimized by the algorithm.
A visible separation does not show that PCA recovered the category. The plot may omit later components, the label may correlate with a recording source, or a small number of observations may drive the appearance. The component scores need to be joined to metadata correctly and criticized with respect to the data construction.






NoteProblem Set 5 connection



Problem Set 5, Task 8 relates fitted component scores to inventory source, language family, and macroarea. A component that reconstructs inventories well need not correspond to a universal phonological dimension. Its association with database provenance and sampling structure is part of its interpretation.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Check the variance direction

Why is the matrix centered before PCA?
In the worked example, why does \mathbf{v}_2 produce only zero scores?
How is component variance related to the corresponding singular value?
What changes when scale. = TRUE rather than scale. = FALSE?
Why is the first component not automatically the most theoretically important direction?
What evidence would be needed before interpreting a score separation as a linguistic category distinction?

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Before reading observations and variables
PCA applies the SVD to a centered matrix and orders orthogonal directions by projected variance. The resulting criterion is exact, but its linguistic interpretation remains relative to the chosen rows, columns, and coordinate transformation. The next page separates the coordinates assigned to observations from the weights assigned to original variables.

title: Linguistic data matrices
text:
Suppose we have acoustic measurements for four vowel tokens. Each token has a first formant, a second formant, and a third formant. Before we can look for shared structure among those measurements, we need to decide what counts as one object and what information represents it.
A matrix representation places one kind of linguistic object in the rows and one kind of measured property in the columns. This is the earlier unit-of-analysis decision written in matrix form. We used the same matrix construction when representing objects for clustering. Here we retain it so that the row and column choices remain explicit before introducing factorization.
We begin by writing down the row and column maps. We then build a small matrix by hand and in R. Finally, we consider two representation failures that no factorization can repair after the matrix has been constructed.

title: Linguistic data matrices
section: Define the array and its indices

title: Linguistic data matrices
section: Build a vowel matrix by hand
text:
Build a vowel matrix by hand
Suppose the measurements are



token
F1
F2
F3




token 1
500
1500
2200


token 2
550
1450
2150


token 3
300
2300
3000


token 4
320
2250
2950



Placing tokens in rows and formants in columns gives

\mathbf{X}=
\begin{bmatrix}
500 & 1500 & 2200\\
550 & 1450 & 2150\\
300 & 2300 & 3000\\
320 & 2250 & 2950
\end{bmatrix}.

This is a 4\times 3 matrix because it represents four tokens using three measurements. The entry in row 3 and column 1 is

x_{31}=300.

Its interpretation comes from both index maps: token 3 has an F1 measurement of 300 Hz. The number 300 does not carry that interpretation on its own.
The third row is

\mathbf{x}_3^{\mathsf T}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
300 & 2300 & 3000
\end{bmatrix},

which is the acoustic representation of token 3 under this design. The first column is

\mathbf{x}_{\cdot 1}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
500 & 550 & 300 & 320
\end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf T},

which records how F1 varies across the four tokens.

title: Linguistic data matrices
text:
The rows define the objects
A row might instead represent a speaker. We could average all of a speaker’s token measurements and place those averages in one row. The resulting matrix would still have formant columns, but it would describe variation among speakers rather than variation among tokens.
This change is not a harmless rearrangement. Suppose one speaker produces two F1 values, 400 and 600. Their speaker mean is

\frac{400+600}{2}=500.

A speaker-level row retains the mean 500 but discards the fact that the two tokens differed by 200 Hz. A token-level analysis can represent that within-speaker difference. A speaker-level analysis cannot recover it from the average.
The row definition thus determines the observational unit. It also determines what kinds of variation the matrix still contains.

title: Linguistic data matrices
text:
The columns define the representation
Two tokens may appear similar when represented by formants and dissimilar when represented by duration and voice quality. Neither result is the similarity between the tokens in the abstract. Each is similarity with respect to a particular collection of measurements.
This point matters when columns repeat information. Suppose we include duration in milliseconds and a second column equal to twice duration. For two tokens with durations 100 and 120, the rows would contain

\begin{bmatrix}100&200\end{bmatrix}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}120&240\end{bmatrix}.

Both columns encode the same underlying measurement. A later matrix method will faithfully give that duplicated information two coordinates. It cannot infer that the analyst did not intend to count duration twice.
Thus, column selection is part of the linguistic representation rather than a neutral software step.

title: Linguistic data matrices
text:
Construct the matrix in R
The matrix can be entered row by row.


Code
X <- matrix(
  c(
    500, 1500, 2200,
    550, 1450, 2150,
    300, 2300, 3000,
    320, 2250, 2950
  ),
  nrow = 4,
  byrow = TRUE
)

rownames(X) <- paste0("token_", 1:4)
colnames(X) <- c("F1", "F2", "F3")

dim(X)
X["token_3", "F1"]
X["token_3", ]
X[, "F1"]


The matrix() call creates the numerical array. The row and column labels record the index maps that give its entries a linguistic interpretation. Stable identifiers are safer than relying on row positions after filtering or joining.

title: Linguistic data matrices
text:
Write a representation record
Before applying a matrix operation, write down the following information.

State what one row represents.
State how the represented objects were selected.
State what each column measures.
Identify columns derived from the same underlying measurement.
State the population or collection to which the represented objects belong.

This record prevents a later component plot from quietly changing its unit of interpretation. If rows are tokens, a component score locates tokens. If rows are languages, it locates languages. The algebra does not change that unit.

title: Linguistic data matrices
section: Information omitted from the matrix cannot be recovered
text:
Information omitted from the matrix cannot be recovered
A flexible factorization cannot determine which duplicated or poorly chosen columns are theoretically intended. It only represents the numerical relations supplied in \mathbf{X}.
The same limitation applies to premature aggregation. Once token measurements have been replaced by speaker means, no matrix decomposition can reconstruct the discarded token variation. The repair must occur when the matrix is designed.
Matrix operations can reorganize the information present in the array, but they cannot recover information removed before the array was built.






NoteData documentation: PHOIBLE 2.0



Read the PHOIBLE 2.0 download and citation page and the FAQ sections “Why do some languages have multiple entries in PHOIBLE?”, “Random sampling: one inventory per isocode/glottocode”, and “What are the different sources in PHOIBLE?”.
The download page identifies the release that should be cited. The three FAQ sections explain why one language may have several contributed inventories, how a one-inventory sampling rule changes the row set, and how source collections differ. The documentation is included because the row definition and source diagnostic must be fixed before a language by segment matrix can be interpreted.








NoteProblem Set 5 connection



Problem Set 5, Task 3 constructs a binary language by segment matrix from PHOIBLE inventories. A cell value can be interpreted only after the row selection, retained segment set, and meaning of absence have been fixed.

title: Linguistic data matrices
text:
Check the representation

In the vowel matrix, what does x_{42} measure?
How does the target of description change if rows are speakers rather than tokens?
Which information is lost when two token values are replaced by their speaker mean?
Why does including duration and twice duration give one measurement two coordinates?
What should be recorded before interpreting a row score from any later factorization?

title: Linguistic data matrices
text:
Before changing the coordinates
A linguistic data matrix maps objects to rows, measurements to columns, and individual measurements to cells. This representation fixes the unit and information available to every later operation. The next page changes the origin and unit of each column while keeping this row and column design fixed.

title: Centering and scaling
text:
A linguistic data matrix may combine variables with different origins and units. Formant frequencies may be measured in hertz, duration in milliseconds, and ratings on a seven point scale. We have already used centering to change a predictor’s reference point and used standardization before calculating distances. This page briefly recalls those operations and then expresses them for a complete matrix.
Centering changes a column’s origin. Scaling changes its unit. Together they define the coordinate system in which later matrix structure will be measured.
This page develops both operations as parts of one column transformation. We first calculate them for three durations, then express them for a complete matrix, and finally implement a training-based transformation that can be applied unchanged to new observations.

title: Centering and scaling
text:
Centering changes the origin
Let column j contain n observations. Its sample mean is

\bar{x}_j
=
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{ij}.

The centered entry is

x^c_{ij}=x_{ij}-\bar{x}_j.

Suppose a duration column contains 100, 120, and 140 milliseconds. Its mean is

\bar{x}
=
\frac{100+120+140}{3}
=
120.

Subtracting this mean gives

\begin{bmatrix}
100\\120\\140
\end{bmatrix}
-
\begin{bmatrix}
120\\120\\120
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
-20\\0\\20
\end{bmatrix}.

Zero now means the observed column mean. A value of -20 means 20 ms below that mean, and a value of 20 means 20 ms above it.
Centering does not reduce the differences among the observations. The original range was 140-100=40 ms, and the centered range is 20-(-20)=40 ms. The operation changes the reference point from zero milliseconds to the sample mean.

title: Centering and scaling
text:
Express centering for a matrix
Collect the p column means in

\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\mathsf T}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\bar{x}_1&\bar{x}_2&\cdots&\bar{x}_p
\end{bmatrix}.

Let \mathbf{1}_n be an n-element column vector of ones. Repeating the mean row n times gives \mathbf{1}_n\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\mathsf T}. The centered matrix is thus

\mathbf{X}_c
=
\mathbf{X}
-
\mathbf{1}_n\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\mathsf T}.

Every column of \mathbf{X}_c has sample mean zero. The row and column meanings remain unchanged. Only the column origins move.

title: Centering and scaling
Centering and scaling
text:
Express scaling for a matrix
Let \mathbf{S} be the diagonal matrix of column standard deviations:

\mathbf{S}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
s_1&0&\cdots&0\\
0&s_2&\cdots&0\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
0&0&\cdots&s_p
\end{bmatrix}.

When every s_j is positive, the standardized matrix is

\mathbf{Z}
=
\mathbf{X}_c\mathbf{S}^{-1}.

Right multiplication by \mathbf{S}^{-1} divides column j by s_j. This matrix expression is the same operation carried out in the hand calculation.

title: Centering and scaling
section: Decide whether equal variance is intended
text:
Decide whether equal variance is intended
Suppose one column ranges from 0 to 1 and another ranges from 0 to 3000. Without scaling, squared variation in the second column may dominate merely because its unit is numerically larger. Measuring the second column in kilohertz instead of hertz would change that dominance even though the acoustic observations were identical.
Standardization removes this unit dependence by giving every nonconstant column variance one. But equal variance is itself a modeling decision. If three columns are noisy measurements and one is reliable, standardization gives each noisy column the same initial variance as the reliable column.
Binary variables require similar care. A rare property has a smaller raw variance than a balanced property. Standardizing both gives them equal variance before factorization, which increases the relative weight of the rare property. That may be appropriate, but it should follow from the representation target rather than from a default setting.
Standardization gives every column unit sample variance before the factorization. This weighting decision should be stated explicitly because it determines how much each measured variable can contribute to the fitted components.

title: Centering and scaling
text:
Compute and store the transformation
The base R function scale() carries out both operations.


Code
X_centered <- scale(
  X,
  center = TRUE,
  scale = FALSE
)

X_standardized <- scale(
  X,
  center = TRUE,
  scale = TRUE
)

colMeans(X_centered)
apply(X_standardized, 2, sd)
