The fitted means and standard deviations are stored as attributes.


Code
training_means <- attr(X_standardized, "scaled:center")
training_sds <- attr(X_standardized, "scaled:scale")

training_means
training_sds


For a new matrix X_new, apply those same values.


Code
X_new_standardized <- sweep(
  X_new,
  MARGIN = 2,
  STATS = training_means,
  FUN = "-"
)

X_new_standardized <- sweep(
  X_new_standardized,
  MARGIN = 2,
  STATS = training_sds,
  FUN = "/"
)


Recomputing means and standard deviations on evaluation observations would put those observations in a different coordinate system. It would also create the data leakage discussed earlier by allowing evaluation observations to affect a fitted transformation. The training coordinate system must remain fixed.

title: Centering and scaling
text:
Handle a constant column deliberately
If a column is constant, then s_j=0. Division by zero is undefined, and standardization cannot be carried out for that column.
This is not merely a software inconvenience. A constant measurement supplies no variation among the represented objects. It cannot help distinguish their coordinates. The analysis should remove it or retain it under an explicitly different transformation, depending on the representational purpose.
Removing a constant column changes the linguistic representation, but the removed column contributes the same value to every object in the observed collection. Record that decision rather than letting nonfinite values propagate silently.






NoteProblem Set 5 connection



Problem Set 5, Task 6 centers each segment column by its observed training prevalence. A hidden centered cell is filled with zero, which corresponds to that prevalence on the original scale. Validation and test cells must not contribute to the centering values used to reconstruct them.

title: Centering and scaling
text:
Check the coordinate system

What does zero mean in the centered duration column?
Why does centering preserve the range in the worked calculation?
What measurement decision is made when every column is standardized to variance one?
Why must a new observation use the training means and standard deviations?
What happens when a constant column is divided by its sample standard deviation?

title: Centering and scaling
section: Before looking for one common pattern
text:
Before looking for one common pattern
Centering fixes a column’s origin, while scaling fixes its unit. The choices determine which variations later matrix operations treat as large. With the coordinate system now explicit, the next page asks when one shared row by column pattern is sufficient to generate a complete matrix.

title: Within-cluster loss
text:
K-means requires the number of centroids K before fitting. A small K may force distinct speaker profiles into one group. A large K may assign separate centroids to irregularities that do not recur. Recall from training and test data that training loss rewards flexibility on the observations used for fitting. It thus cannot identify a true group count.
Plotting the fitted within-cluster loss against K produces the standard elbow plot. The elbow method looks for a point after which another centroid produces a much smaller reduction than earlier centroids did.
We first show why the loss cannot increase with K. We then calculate the reductions in a small curve, implement the plot in R, and explain why a visual bend is a descriptive diagnostic rather than a discovery of the number of linguistic categories.

title: Within-cluster loss
section: Define the loss at each group count
text:
Define the loss at each group count
For a fitted K-means partition with K centroids, write

W_K
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\left\lVert
\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{z_i,K}
\right\rVert^2.

The subscript K records that both the assignments and centroids were fit under that candidate count. Lower W_K means that the rows lie closer to their assigned centroids on the training representation.
To measure what the next centroid adds, define the reduction

\Delta_K
=
W_{K-1}-W_K

for K\geq2. A larger \Delta_K means that moving from K-1 to K centroids substantially improves fitted compactness.

title: Within-cluster loss
section: Why the optimum curve cannot rise
text:
Why the optimum curve cannot rise
Suppose we have a fitted solution with K centroids. A model with K+1 centroids can reproduce that solution by placing the additional centroid on an existing centroid and leaving the assignments unchanged.
Since the K+1 model can do at least this well and may find a better partition,

W_{K+1}\leq W_K.

Thus, training loss cannot tell us to stop by reaching a minimum and then rising. Its minimum occurs at the largest permitted K, including the degenerate case of one centroid per distinct row.
The globally minimized within-cluster loss decreases monotonically as K increases because greater flexibility is evaluated on the same observations used to fit it. A reported K-means curve can still rise when the fitting algorithm reaches a poorer local minimum for one value of K. Multiple starts reduce that computational problem but do not change the monotonicity of the global optimum.

title: Within-cluster loss
text:
Calculate an elbow curve
Suppose repeated K-means fits give



K
W_K




1
500


2
280


3
190


4
165


5
148



The first reduction is

\Delta_2
=
500-280
=
220.

The remaining reductions are

\Delta_3=280-190=90,


\Delta_4=190-165=25,

and

\Delta_5=165-148=17.

The move from two to three centroids still removes 90 squared units. Later moves remove only 25 and 17. A reader might place the elbow near K=3 because the rate of improvement becomes much smaller after that point.
This interpretation is a judgment about the shape of the curve. The number 3 is not produced by a universal cutoff.

title: Within-cluster loss
section: Fit and plot the curve in R
text:
Fit and plot the curve in R
Fit every candidate with several initializations so that a poor start is less likely to distort one point on the curve.


Code
candidate_k <- 1:10

set.seed(214)

within_loss <- vapply(
  candidate_k,
  function(k) {
    kmeans(
      X_scaled,
      centers = k,
      nstart = 50
    )$tot.withinss
  },
  numeric(1)
)


Plot the loss rather than printing only the selected value.


Code
plot(
  candidate_k,
  within_loss,
  type = "b",
  xlab = "Number of centroids",
  ylab = "Within-cluster sum of squares"
)


The reductions can be displayed directly.


Code
data.frame(
  added_centroid = candidate_k[-1],
  loss_reduction = -diff(within_loss)
)


The code uses the same representation, scaling, starting policy, and fitting settings at every K. Changing these choices midway would make the points belong to different procedures.

title: Within-cluster loss
text:
The elbow may be ambiguous
Some curves decline smoothly without a visible bend. Two readers may also locate different elbows on the same curve. This is not a computational error. The elbow rule does not define how large the reduction ratio must be.
An elbow is often ambiguous. The plot can narrow attention to a range of plausible counts without selecting one mechanically.
A potential response is to search for a more elaborate curve transformation until a bend appears. That changes the rule after seeing the result. A better report shows the original loss curve, states the candidate range, and treats the elbow as one diagnostic.

title: Within-cluster loss
section: Loss values depend on the representation
text:
Loss values depend on the representation
Within-cluster loss depends on the feature units, number of columns, and number of rows. A loss of 190 has no standalone linguistic scale.
If formants are measured in hertz rather than kilohertz, raw squared distances change. If a feature is duplicated, it receives additional influence. If the sample contains more tokens, the sum has more terms.
Thus, loss curves from differently constructed representations should not be compared as though their vertical axes measured one common quantity. Refit and reinterpret the complete curve under each declared representation.

title: Within-cluster loss
section: Training compactness does not imply performance on held-out rows
text:
Training compactness does not imply performance on held-out rows
The elbow describes the rows used to estimate the centroids. It does not show that the partition is stable under another sample or that the centroids represent new speakers.
Increasing K can create a small cluster around one unusual training row. This reduces W_K but may not improve representation of any new row. Held-out validation later in the module will evaluate performance on rows excluded from fitting.
The elbow also says nothing about whether rows are closer to their assigned cluster than to an alternative. The next page adds that row-level comparison.

title: Within-cluster loss
text:
Check the loss curve

Why can W_{K+1} not exceed W_K for an optimally fit solution?
Which reduction in the worked table is largest?
Why might a reader place the elbow near K=3?
What makes the elbow rule judgment-dependent?
Why should losses from raw and standardized representations not be placed on one common scale?
What property of new rows is not measured by the fitted loss curve?

title: Within-cluster loss
text:
Before comparing nearest alternatives
The elbow plot shows how training compactness changes as centroids are added. Its monotonicity makes a visual elbow possible but prevents training loss from identifying a final group count by itself. The next page evaluates each row relative to both its assigned cluster and its nearest alternative cluster.

title: Validation without outcome labels
text:
The earlier chapters on predictive loss and cross-validation assumed an observed response. A clustering has no observed cluster label that the fitting procedure is meant to predict. We still need a quantity that learned structure can predict for rows excluded from fitting.
For K-means, the fitted centroids predict each held-out row by its nearest training centroid. The squared distance to that centroid is the held-out nearest-centroid loss. It asks whether centroids learned from training objects provide a compact representation of new objects under the same distance and scaling.
We first define one held-out prediction and calculate it by hand. We then place preprocessing and centroid fitting inside a validation loop, compare candidate group counts through paired row losses, and separate computational repetitions from linguistic sampling units.

title: Validation without outcome labels
text:
Predict a held-out row
Let

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\mathrm{train}}_1,
\ldots,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\mathrm{train}}_K

be centroids estimated from the training rows. A held-out row \mathbf{x}_i is assigned to the nearest fixed centroid:

\widehat{z}_i
=
\underset{k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}{\operatorname{argmin}}
\left\lVert
\mathbf{x}_i-
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\mathrm{train}}_k
\right\rVert^2.

Its loss is

L_i
=
\min_k
\left\lVert
\mathbf{x}_i-
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\mathrm{train}}_k
\right\rVert^2.

The row does not update the centroids before it is scored. It is represented by structure learned from other rows.

title: Validation without outcome labels
text:
Work through one new speaker
Suppose two training centroids are

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_1=(0,1)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_2=(5,5).

A held-out speaker has scaled profile

\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{test}}=(1,2).

Its squared distance to centroid 1 is

(1-0)^2+(2-1)^2
=
1+1
=
2.

Its squared distance to centroid 2 is

(1-5)^2+(2-5)^2
=
16+9
=
25.

The predicted assignment is cluster 1, and the held-out nearest-centroid loss is 2. The assignment is part of producing the prediction. The evaluation target is the numerical loss, since no observed cluster label is available.

title: Validation without outcome labels
section: Keep preprocessing inside the training fold

title: Validation without outcome labels
text:
Implement one validation split


Code
train_center <- colMeans(X[train, , drop = FALSE])
train_scale <- apply(
  X[train, , drop = FALSE],
  2,
  sd
)

X_train <- sweep(
  X[train, , drop = FALSE],
  2,
  train_center,
  "-"
)

X_train <- sweep(
  X_train,
  2,
  train_scale,
  "/"
)

X_test <- sweep(
  X[test, , drop = FALSE],
  2,
  train_center,
  "-"
)

X_test <- sweep(
  X_test,
  2,
  train_scale,
  "/"
)


Fit the K-means model on X_train.


Code
set.seed(214)

fit_train <- kmeans(
  X_train,
  centers = K,
  nstart = 50
)


Compute squared distance from every test row to every training centroid.


Code
squared_distance <- sapply(
  seq_len(K),
  function(k) {
    rowSums(
      sweep(
        X_test,
        2,
        fit_train$centers[k, ],
        "-"
      )^2
    )
  }
)

test_loss <- apply(
  squared_distance,
  1,
  min
)


The vector test_loss retains one held-out loss per row. Keeping these pointwise values allows paired model comparisons and group-level aggregation.

title: Validation without outcome labels
text:
Compare candidate values of K
The same held-out row can receive loss under K=2 and K=3. Define the paired difference

d_i
=
L_{i,K=3}-L_{i,K=2}.

A negative value favors three centroids for row i. A positive value favors two.
Suppose one row has loss 2.0 under K=2 and 1.5 under K=3. Its difference is

d_i=1.5-2.0=-0.5.

The third centroid reduces nearest-centroid loss for this row by half a squared unit. The aggregate comparison should summarize such paired differences at the sampling unit required by the claim.

title: Validation without outcome labels
section: Match the split to the new unit
text:
Match the split to the new unit
If each row is one independent participant and the target is another participant from the represented population, row-level folds may be appropriate. If several rows come from one household, site, or speaker, those related rows should move together whenever that group must be new.
Otherwise, training data may contain another record from the supposedly held-out group. The score then evaluates another record from a represented group.
The absence of response labels does not remove the need to define the unit that must be new at evaluation time.

title: Validation without outcome labels
section: Do not treat repeated folds as new samples
text:
Do not treat repeated folds as new samples
Repeating cross-validation across seeds can reveal sensitivity to the split. It does not create new speakers. The folds reuse rows, and their training sets overlap.
A t test over 100 seed-level mean losses would make uncertainty shrink because the analyst repeated the computation. It would not represent variation across newly sampled linguistic units.
Use repeated splits for algorithmic sensitivity. Use pointwise losses, aggregation at the declared group, a group bootstrap, or an explicit sampling model for inferential uncertainty.

title: Validation without outcome labels
section: Lower nearest-centroid loss is not category recovery
text:
Lower nearest-centroid loss is not category recovery
Lower held-out centroid loss means that training centroids represent new rows more compactly under the declared geometry. It does not show that the clusters correspond to natural speaker types or phonological categories.
External variables withheld from fitting may help interpret the learned assignments. Stability across samples may show that the representation recurs. These checks add evidence, but neither converts a centroid into a linguistic category by definition.
Clustering without a gold label cannot be validated against category truth. That does not make every form of validation impossible. The held-out nearest-centroid target evaluates a stated consequence of the centroids without assuming that the true categories are known.

title: Validation without outcome labels
text:
Check the held-out target

Which centroid predicts the held-out row (1,2) in the worked example?
Why is its loss 2 rather than 25?
Which means and standard deviations transform the test rows?
What does a negative paired difference d_i=L_{i,3}-L_{i,2} mean?
Why must all rows from one household move together when evaluating a household absent during fitting?
Why do 100 repeated splits not provide 100 independent samples of speakers?
What does lower held-out nearest-centroid loss establish, and what category claim does it not establish?

title: Validation without outcome labels
text:
Before introducing probability components
Held-out nearest-centroid loss evaluates whether K-means centroids learned from training rows place excluded rows near a training centroid. The calculation retains K-means geometry and assigns each row to its nearest center. The next page replaces that geometry with a probability model in which components can have different spreads and every observation receives density from every component.

title: Representing objects for clustering
text:
Suppose a survey records how often each participant speaks and reads two languages. A clustering algorithm receives numbers. It does not receive the interpretation that one row is a participant, that one column is speaking frequency, or that another column is meant only for later interpretation.
The rows of the input matrix define the objects that can be grouped. Its columns define the properties under which those objects can be similar. This is the unit-of-analysis choice from the opening module expressed as a matrix. The accompanying index maps connect those rows and columns to linguistic objects and measurements. A clustering cannot recover a distinction removed before this representation was constructed.
We first define the row by column matrix. We then build a small speaker representation by hand and in R. Finally, we separate clustering features from identifiers and external variables, since confusing those roles can build the intended interpretation into the groups themselves.

title: Representing objects for clustering
Representing objects for clustering
text:
Build a small speaker representation
Suppose three speakers report English and Spanish speaking frequency on a scale from 1 to 5.



speaker
English speaking
Spanish speaking




A
5
1


B
4
2


C
1
5



The clustering matrix is

\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
5&1\\
4&2\\
1&5
\end{bmatrix}.

The first row

\mathbf{x}_A=
\begin{bmatrix}5&1\end{bmatrix}

represents speaker A only in terms of the two selected speaking ratings. It contains no information about reading, age, community, or any other unrecorded or excluded property.
Speakers A and B differ by one rating point on each column. Speakers A and C differ by four points on each. A distance-based method will thus tend to regard A and B as more similar under this representation. The next page makes that comparison numerical.

title: Representing objects for clustering
text:
Assign each column a role
A useful representation record states how every available column is used.

Features included in the clustering define the learned groups.
Identifiers link rows to other records but do not define similarity.
Metadata withheld during fitting can be inspected afterward.
Sampling and grouping variables determine how rows are separated during evaluation.

These roles are not interchangeable. Suppose age is included as a clustering feature. A later finding that the groups differ in age partly restates how they were constructed. If age is withheld during fitting, its association with the groups is an external descriptive check.
The same issue applies to intended vowel labels. If a mixture is meant to find structure in formant measurements, the vowel labels should not enter the measurement matrix. They can be compared with the fitted components afterward.

title: Representing objects for clustering
section: Keep identifiers out of the geometry
text:
Keep identifiers out of the geometry
An identifier such as participant_id distinguishes records, but its numerical value has no measurement interpretation. Speaker 102 is not two units closer to speaker 104 than to speaker 108 in any linguistically meaningful sense.
Including such a column makes arbitrary differences among record numbers part of the distance calculation. The clustering may then produce groups driven by data-entry order.
The repair is simple: retain identifiers beside the matrix, not inside it. They remain necessary for joining assignments back to metadata and for keeping repeated records from the same sampling unit together during grouped validation.

title: Representing objects for clustering
section: Do not encode categories as ordered numbers
text:
Do not encode categories as ordered numbers
Suppose a language column is coded

\text{English}=1,
\qquad
\text{Spanish}=2,
\qquad
\text{Hindi}=3.

This coding places Spanish halfway between English and Hindi on a numerical line. The spacing comes from the labels rather than from a linguistic measurement.
If category identity should help define similarity, separate indicator columns may be used. But doing so states that shared category membership is part of the clustering target. If category is meant to interpret the groups, it should remain outside the fitted representation.
Thus, numerical storage does not guarantee numerical meaning.

title: Representing objects for clustering
section: Construct the feature matrix in R
text:
Construct the feature matrix in R
Keep row identifiers and external variables in a data frame.


Code
speaker_data <- data.frame(
  speaker_id = c("A", "B", "C"),
  english_speaking = c(5, 4, 1),
  spanish_speaking = c(1, 2, 5),
  age = c(26, 41, 33)
)


Select only the declared clustering features for the numerical matrix.


Code
feature_names <- c(
  "english_speaking",
  "spanish_speaking"
)

X <- as.matrix(speaker_data[, feature_names])
rownames(X) <- speaker_data$speaker_id

X


The age and speaker_id columns remain available, but neither can affect the fitted similarity. After clustering, assignments can be joined back using speaker_id.

title: Representing objects for clustering
section: Repeated records change the row target
text:
Repeated records change the row target
Suppose each participant completes the survey twice. Treating both surveys as separate rows creates a grouping of survey occasions. Treating their average as one row creates a grouping of participants but discards within-participant change.
Neither choice is universally correct. The representation should follow the intended object. If the goal is to describe stable participant profiles, repeated rows from one person should not be treated as unrelated participants.
The prose must refer to the same object that each matrix row represents. Otherwise the interpretation and the fitted grouping refer to different units.

title: Representing objects for clustering
section: A representation cannot discover what it already contains
text:
A representation cannot discover what it already contains
Excluding an interpretation variable does remove information from the grouping criterion. That exclusion is exactly what makes a later comparison with the variable informative.
If sex category enters a vowel clustering, an observed association between clusters and sex may be built into the geometry. If the aim is to ask whether formant-based components track sex category, the category must remain external to the fit.
This separation does not make the external variable ground truth. It makes the construction and interpretation steps distinguishable.

title: Representing objects for clustering
text:
Check the representation

What does one row represent in the three-speaker matrix?
How would the interpretation change if rows were households rather than speakers?
Why should participant_id remain outside the feature matrix?
What is learned by comparing clusters with age when age was withheld from fitting?
Why does coding three language names as 1, 2, and 3 create an unsupported geometry?
What grouping is obtained if repeated survey occasions, rather than participants, form the rows?

title: Representing objects for clustering
text:
Before measuring distance
The input matrix fixes the row object and the feature columns, while the analysis record states how external variables are used. These choices determine what a learned group can describe before an algorithm is selected. The next page defines how the declared feature values make two rows close or far apart.

title: K-means clustering
text:
Suppose each speaker is represented by two standardized language-use measures. We want to divide the speakers into K groups so that speakers assigned to the same group lie near a shared profile. The group labels are not observed in advance. The calculation uses the scaled Euclidean geometry fixed on the preceding page.
K-means clustering represents each group by a centroid and assigns every row to exactly one centroid. It alternates between assigning rows to the nearest centroid and replacing each centroid with the mean of its assigned rows.
We first state the loss optimized by the algorithm. We then carry out one full assignment and update cycle for four points, show why the mean is the correct update, and implement the same procedure in R. Finally, we identify the hard-membership geometry imposed by the method.

title: K-means clustering
text:
Define assignments and centroids
Let \mathbf{x}_i\in\mathbb{R}^p be row i. For a chosen number of groups K, let

z_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}

be the cluster assigned to row i, and let

\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\in\mathbb{R}^p

be the centroid of cluster k.
K-means minimizes the within-cluster sum of squared Euclidean distances:

W
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\left\lVert
\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{z_i}
\right\rVert^2.

Each row contributes its squared distance to the centroid of its assigned cluster. A smaller value means that the fitted clusters have a smaller within-cluster sum of squares under the chosen distance and scaling.

title: K-means clustering
section: Begin with four rows and two centroids
text:
Begin with four rows and two centroids
Consider four hypothetical speaker profiles:

\mathbf{x}_1=(0,0),
\qquad
\mathbf{x}_2=(0,2),


\mathbf{x}_3=(5,4),
\qquad
\mathbf{x}_4=(5,6).

Start with proposed centroids

\boldsymbol{\mu}_1=(0,0)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\boldsymbol{\mu}_2=(5,6).

These are initial values, not observed labels.

title: K-means clustering
text:
Carry out the assignment step
For each row, compare squared distances to both centroids. Squared distance is sufficient because the square root preserves the ordering.
For \mathbf{x}_1,

\lVert\mathbf{x}_1-\boldsymbol{\mu}_1\rVert^2=0

and

\lVert\mathbf{x}_1-\boldsymbol{\mu}_2\rVert^2
=
(0-5)^2+(0-6)^2
=
61.

Thus, \mathbf{x}_1 is assigned to cluster 1. The remaining comparisons are









row
squared distance to centroid 1
squared distance to centroid 2
assignment




\mathbf{x}_1
0
61
1


\mathbf{x}_2
4
41
1


\mathbf{x}_3
41
4
2


\mathbf{x}_4
61
0
2



The assignment step chooses the smaller value in each row of the table. For fixed centroids, this choice minimizes each observation’s contribution to W.

title: K-means clustering
text:
Carry out the update step
Replace each centroid with the coordinatewise mean of its assigned rows. Cluster 1 contains \mathbf{x}_1 and \mathbf{x}_2:

\boldsymbol{\mu}_1^{\mathrm{new}}
=
\frac{(0,0)+(0,2)}{2}
=
(0,1).

Cluster 2 contains \mathbf{x}_3 and \mathbf{x}_4:

\boldsymbol{\mu}_2^{\mathrm{new}}
=
\frac{(5,4)+(5,6)}{2}
=
(5,5).

Under the initial centroids, the total within-cluster loss is

W^{\mathrm{old}}
=
0+4+4+0
=
8.

Under the updated centroids, every row is one squared unit from its centroid:

W^{\mathrm{new}}
=
1+1+1+1
=
4.

The update has reduced the loss while keeping the assignments fixed.

title: K-means clustering
section: Why the centroid is a mean
text:
Why the centroid is a mean
Consider one coordinate of one fixed cluster with values x_1,\ldots,x_n. Its squared loss around a proposed center \mu is

Q(\mu)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu)^2.

Differentiate with respect to \mu:

\frac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}\mu}
=
-2\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu).

Setting the derivative to zero gives

\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i-n\mu=0,

so

\mu
=
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i.

The same argument applies to every coordinate. Thus, the coordinatewise mean minimizes squared distance for fixed assignments.

title: K-means clustering
text:
Alternate until the partition stabilizes
After the update, assign every row again using the new centroids. In the worked example, the assignments remain (1,1,2,2). Recomputing the means returns the same centroids, so the algorithm has converged.
Each assignment step cannot increase W because every row chooses its closest current centroid. Each update step cannot increase W because every centroid becomes the mean of its assigned rows. The loss decreases or stays fixed until the procedure reaches a local solution.
The K-means algorithm alternates these two steps until the assignments stop changing or the reduction in within-cluster loss falls below a specified tolerance.

title: K-means clustering
text:
Fit the procedure in R


Code
X_small <- matrix(
  c(
    0, 0,
    0, 2,
    5, 4,
    5, 6
  ),
  nrow = 4,
  byrow = TRUE
)

set.seed(214)

fit_k2 <- kmeans(
  X_small,
  centers = 2,
  nstart = 50
)

fit_k2$cluster
fit_k2$centers
fit_k2$tot.withinss


The cluster vector contains one hard assignment per row. The centers matrix contains one centroid per cluster. The tot.withinss value is W.
The argument nstart = 50 fits the algorithm from 50 initial centroid sets and keeps the solution with the smallest within-cluster loss. It addresses initialization sensitivity without changing the objective.

title: K-means clustering
section: Initial values can change the solution
text:
Initial values can change the solution
The K-means objective may have several local minima. Alternating updates cannot increase the loss, but they need not reach the smallest possible loss across every partition.
K-means can converge to a local minimum. A single initialization may yield a partition that another starting point improves. Several starts reduce the risk, and the final loss should be compared across starts.
A fixed random seed makes one computation reproducible. It does not make the selected start globally optimal. Reproducibility and optimization quality are different properties.

title: K-means clustering
text:
Know the imposed geometry
K-means assigns every row to exactly one group and measures fit by squared Euclidean distance to a centroid. It tends to favor compact groups with roughly similar spread in the chosen coordinate system.
Overlapping vowel categories or gradient speaker profiles may not have this structure. A poor K-means partition does not show that the linguistic objects lack organization. It shows that a hard centroid partition under this distance does not represent them well.
Cluster numbers are also arbitrary. Swapping labels 1 and 2 leaves the partition and loss unchanged. Interpret centroids and associated rows, not the numerical label itself.

title: K-means clustering
text:
Check the alternating updates

Which squared distances assign \mathbf{x}_3 to cluster 2 in the worked example?
Why does the update move centroid 1 from (0,0) to (0,1)?
What is the within-cluster loss after the update?
Why does the mean minimize squared loss for fixed assignments?
What does nstart = 50 protect against, and what does it not guarantee?
Which membership assumption is made by assigning every speaker to exactly one cluster?

title: K-means clustering
text:
Before comparing values of K
K-means alternates nearest-centroid assignments with mean updates to reduce within-cluster squared distance. The fitted partition depends on the representation, Euclidean geometry, group count, and initialization. The next page examines how fitted compactness changes as the declared number of centroids increases.

title: Gaussian mixtures
text:
Suppose we measure F1 and F2 for a collection of vowel tokens. The scatterplot may contain several overlapping dense regions. K-means assigns every token to one centroid and treats every direction around a centroid alike after scaling. Vowel clouds may instead differ in spread, orientation, and overlap.
A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) represents the observations as arising from several weighted Gaussian component distributions. Each component extends the earlier normal distribution to several jointly modeled measurements, with its own mean vector and covariance. Every component contributes some density to every observed token.
We first define one multivariate Gaussian component. We then combine several components into one observation density, calculate a two-component value by hand and in R, and separate a fitted distributional component from a phonological category.

title: Gaussian mixtures
Gaussian mixtures
text:
Read a two-dimensional covariance
For F1 and F2, write

\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\sigma^2_{F1,k}
&
\sigma_{F1,F2,k}\\
\sigma_{F1,F2,k}
&
\sigma^2_{F2,k}
\end{bmatrix}.

The diagonal entries describe marginal spread along F1 and F2. The off-diagonal covariance describes whether deviations from the component means tend to occur together.
A positive covariance tilts the ellipse toward joint increases. A negative covariance tilts it toward an increase in one formant and decrease in the other. Zero covariance aligns the ellipse with the measurement axes, though it does not imply that the complete vowel system is independent across formants.
This covariance geometry is one way a Gaussian component differs from the spherical groups favored by K-means.

title: Gaussian mixtures
text:
Combine components with weights
Let K be the number of components. Component k receives mixing weight

\pi_k\geq0,

and the weights satisfy

\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k=1.

Using the marginalization rule for a joint distribution, the mixture density for observation i is

p(\mathbf{x}_i)
=
\sum_{k=1}^{K}
\pi_k
\mathcal{N}
(\mathbf{x}_i;
\boldsymbol{\mu}_k,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k).

Every term is nonnegative, and the component weights determine their prior prevalence in the mixture. The model does not have to choose one hard group before assigning density to the observation.

title: Gaussian mixtures
text:
Calculate one mixture density
Suppose a one-dimensional mixture has two components. At a particular formant value, component 1 has density 0.08 and weight 0.60. Component 2 has density 0.02 and weight 0.40.
The weighted contribution from component 1 is

0.60(0.08)=0.048.

The weighted contribution from component 2 is

0.40(0.02)=0.008.

The mixture density is their sum:

p(x_i)
=
0.048+0.008
=
0.056.

Component 1 contributes more density at this observation, but component 2 still contributes. The next page normalizes these contributions into membership probabilities.

title: Gaussian mixtures
text:
Reproduce the density in R
For a one-dimensional Gaussian mixture with known parameters, dnorm() provides each component density.


Code
x_i <- 0
weight <- c(0.60, 0.40)

# Choose parameters that give densities 0.08 and 0.02
# at the same observation.
component_sd <- rep(
  1 / (0.08 * sqrt(2 * pi)),
  2
)

component_mean <- c(
  0,
  component_sd[2] * sqrt(2 * log(4))
)

component_density <- dnorm(
  x_i,
  mean = component_mean,
  sd = component_sd
)

weighted_contribution <- weight * component_density
mixture_density <- sum(weighted_contribution)

component_density
weighted_contribution
mixture_density


The printed component densities are 0.08 and 0.02 apart from numerical rounding. The computational structure matches the formal definition: evaluate each density, multiply by its weight, and sum.
For a real vowel analysis, \mathbf{x}_i contains F1 and F2, so each component evaluation uses a bivariate mean and covariance. Fitting those parameters comes later. This page only defines the observation model they must satisfy.

title: Gaussian mixtures
text:
Covariance restrictions state category geometry
A mixture must say which covariance parameters can differ across components. A restrictive model may give all components one shared spherical covariance. A flexible model may give every component its own unrestricted covariance matrix.
The shared spherical model says that every component has the same spread in all measured directions. That may be implausible for vowel formants. The unrestricted model can represent differently shaped and tilted clouds, but it estimates more parameters and may behave poorly for a sparsely represented component.
The covariance structure determines each component’s geometry. This modeling assumption is substantive, not merely computational.

title: Gaussian mixtures
section: Map the model to Peterson and Barney
text:
Map the model to Peterson and Barney
In the Peterson and Barney data, a row is a vowel token and the mixture features can be F1 and F2. Intended vowel is withheld from fitting and used afterward to describe component alignment.
Raw formants contain differences associated with speaker anatomy. A mixture of raw F1 and F2 may thus allocate components partly to speaker groups. Standardizing formants within speaker changes the target to a speaker-relative acoustic representation and may align components more closely with intended vowels.
Better alignment after normalization does not make each component identical to one phoneme, and a preferred component count need not equal the ten intended vowels. The fitted components and the linguistic categories remain different objects.

title: Gaussian mixtures
section: A component is not a phoneme
text:
A component is not a phoneme
A fitted Gaussian component is a distributional summary under the chosen measurements, transformations, component count, and covariance restrictions. It is not automatically a phonological category.
Several components may represent one vowel with internal speaker or contextual variation. One component may cover overlapping regions from several intended vowels. The mixture likelihood itself does not know which interpretation is linguistically correct.
Comparing fitted components with intended labels does not make the analysis supervised. The labels are external evidence used after fitting. They can diagnose alignment without determining the fitted objective.

title: Gaussian mixtures
text:
Guard against collapsing covariance
An unrestricted Gaussian component can concentrate around very few observations with a very small covariance. Its density may become extremely large, producing a degenerate likelihood fit.
This is a likelihood singularity: a component covariance can collapse around one observation as its likelihood grows without bound. Covariance restrictions, regularization, minimum component sizes, and careful fitting controls may be needed. A high likelihood is not trustworthy when it arises from a nearly singular component around one token.
The failure matters linguistically because an apparent tiny category may be a numerical collapse rather than a recurring vowel pattern.

title: Gaussian mixtures
text:
Check the observation model

What do \boldsymbol{\mu}_k and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k describe?
Why do the mixture weights sum to one?
How is the hand-calculated density 0.056 obtained?
What can an unrestricted covariance represent that a spherical covariance cannot?
Why should intended vowel labels remain outside the fitted formant mixture?
How can raw formants cause components to track speaker anatomy?
Why can covariance collapse create a misleading component?

title: Gaussian mixtures
text:
Before calculating membership
A Gaussian mixture assigns each observation the weighted sum of several component densities. Component means, covariances, and weights define a probability model whose geometry is more flexible than a hard centroid partition. The next page uses Bayes’ rule to calculate how the component contributions divide responsibility for one observed token.

title: Distance and scaling
text:
The input matrix tells us which measurements describe each linguistic object. It does not yet say how a difference of 100 Hz in F1 should be combined with a difference of 20 ms in duration. A distance calculation must turn those columnwise differences into one comparison. We have already used centering to change a predictor’s reference point. This page adds scaling because distance depends on both origins and units.
Euclidean distance and the scaling of the columns jointly determine the geometry of the feature space. Both are assumptions about which numerical differences should count as comparable.
We first calculate a raw Euclidean distance. We then show how one high-variance column can dominate it, standardize a small matrix by hand, and implement a training-based transformation in R. Finally, we state the linguistic assumptions built into the resulting geometry.

title: Distance and scaling
Distance and scaling
text:
Calculate one raw distance
Suppose two speakers have feature vectors

\mathbf{x}_A=(1,4)

and

\mathbf{x}_B=(3,5).

Their columnwise differences are 1-3=-2 and 4-5=-1. Thus,

\begin{aligned}
d(\mathbf{x}_A,\mathbf{x}_B)
&=
\sqrt{(1-3)^2+(4-5)^2}\\
&=
\sqrt{(-2)^2+(-1)^2}\\
&=
\sqrt{4+1}\\
&=
\sqrt{5}\\
&\approx2.24.
\end{aligned}

The first feature contributes four squared units, while the second contributes one. The first difference thus has four times the influence on squared distance.

title: Distance and scaling
text:
See the unit problem
Suppose one feature is a 1 to 5 speaking rating and another is an annual token count. Two speakers differ by one rating point and 1,000 tokens. Their squared contributions are

1^2=1

and

1000^2=1{,}000{,}000.

The token-count column dominates the distance. If the same counts were recorded in thousands of tokens, the numerical difference would be 1 and its squared contribution would also be 1. The learned geometry would change even though the speakers did not.
Raw Euclidean distance treats one numerical unit on every column as directly comparable. A variable measured on a numerically larger scale can thus dominate the distance.

title: Distance and scaling
text:
Standardize the columns
For feature m, let \bar{x}_m and s_m be its sample mean and sample standard deviation. The standardized value is

z_{im}
=
\frac{x_{im}-\bar{x}_m}{s_m}.

After this transformation, the observed column has sample mean zero and sample standard deviation one. A one-unit difference now means one observed sample standard deviation on that feature.
Consider three speaking ratings:

1,\ 3,\ 5.

Their mean is 3. Their sample standard deviation is 2, since

s
=
\sqrt{
\frac{(1-3)^2+(3-3)^2+(5-3)^2}{3-1}
}
=
2.

The standardized values are

\frac{1-3}{2}=-1,
\qquad
\frac{3-3}{2}=0,
\qquad
\frac{5-3}{2}=1.

The original four-point range has become a two-standard-deviation range. Relative position is retained, but the column unit has changed.

title: Distance and scaling
text:
Recalculate a comparison after scaling
Suppose two speakers differ by 1,000 tokens in a column whose sample standard deviation is 10,000. Their standardized difference is

\frac{1000}{10000}=0.1,

so its squared contribution is

0.1^2=0.01.

If the one-point rating difference is one full rating standard deviation, it contributes 1^2=1. After standardization, the rating difference contributes more to Euclidean distance than the token difference.
The underlying observations have not changed. The analysis has changed what counts as a comparable difference.

title: Distance and scaling
text:
Implement the transformation and distance
In R, scale() centers and standardizes each column.


Code
X_scaled <- scale(
  X,
  center = TRUE,
  scale = TRUE
)

colMeans(X_scaled)
apply(X_scaled, 2, sd)


The function dist() computes Euclidean distances among rows by default.


Code
distance_matrix <- dist(
  X_scaled,
  method = "euclidean"
)

as.matrix(distance_matrix)


The matrix is symmetric because d(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j)=d(\mathbf{x}_j,\mathbf{x}_i). Its diagonal is zero because every row has zero distance from itself.

title: Distance and scaling
Distance and scaling
section: Equal variance is not equal importance
text:
Equal variance is not equal importance
Standardization gives every column observed variance one. It does not make the columns equally reliable, theoretically important, or independent.
If two columns are near duplicates, their shared measurement effectively enters the distance twice. If one rating is noisy, standardization still gives it the same observed variance as a reliable acoustic measure. These are representation choices that scaling cannot diagnose.
Standardization is a defensible convention when differences of one sample standard deviation should be comparable across features. The analysis should state that convention and check whether its conclusions depend on it.

title: Distance and scaling
section: Euclidean distance makes a linguistic assumption
text:
Euclidean distance makes a linguistic assumption
Euclidean distance treats feature differences as continuous, symmetric, and additive after scaling. A difference of one unit has the same cost in either direction. Separate squared contributions are added across columns.
Ordinal ratings, binary grammatical properties, or strongly dependent acoustic measurements may not satisfy that interpretation. A poor clustering under Euclidean distance does not show that the objects lack structure. It may show that the declared geometry does not represent the relevant linguistic comparison.

title: Units of assignment
text:
Suppose an experiment compares word recognition after familiar accent training and unfamiliar accent training. Each participant completes 40 recognition trials, so a study with 24 participants produces 960 rows. What receives the training condition?
The answer is the participant, not the trial. Training happens once, before any of the 40 responses are collected. The unit of assignment is the entity that can independently receive a condition. Identifying this unit is the first step in reconstructing what was randomized and how many independent assignments the study contains.

title: Units of assignment
section: Assignment and observation are different maps
text:
Assignment and observation are different maps
Let r index rows in the recorded table. Each row belongs to an assignment unit g(r), and that unit receives condition Z_{g(r)}. The condition attached to row r is thus

Z_r=Z_{g(r)}.

When the participant is the unit of assignment, every row from the same participant has the same value of g(r) and the same assigned condition. If there are N=960 rows but G=24 participants, then there are 24 independent assignments, not 960. The rows remain useful because they measure each participant repeatedly. But they do not multiply the number of times training was assigned.
The unit of observation answers a different question. It is the entity represented by one measured response, such as a word recognition trial. The unit of analysis describes the entities compared by a particular statistical calculation. These three units can coincide, but they need not.

We can recover both counts from the table.


Code
trials <- data.frame(
  participant = rep(paste0("P", 1:4), each = 3),
  training = rep(c("familiar", "unfamiliar", "familiar", "unfamiliar"), each = 3),

nrow(trials)
participant_assignment <- unique(trials[c("participant", "training")])
nrow(participant_assignment)
table(participant_assignment$training)


The call to unique() implements the definition above. It retains one row for each distinct assignment unit and its condition. A design audit should perform this reduction before counting assignments.

title: Units of assignment
section: Ask what could have varied independently
text:
Ask what could have varied independently
The most reliable diagnostic is counterfactual and procedural: under the actual assignment procedure, what could have received a different condition? In the training study, one trial could not switch training while the other trials from the same participant remained unchanged. The participant is thus the assignment unit.
The same question applies at other levels. If an instructional intervention is assigned by classroom and responses are collected from individual students, the classroom is the unit of assignment. If an acoustic manipulation is applied once to an entire block, the block receives that manipulation. And if an item version is independently chosen for each presentation, the presentation may be the assignment unit, subject to any participant and item constraints.

title: Units of assignment
section: Response rows do not count assignments
text:
Response rows do not count assignments
Treating the unit represented by a row as an independent assignment unit would count 960 assignments rather than 24. The resulting uncertainty would appear too small because responses sharing one assignment are treated as if training had been assigned repeatedly. This is the same dependence problem developed for repeated linguistic observations, now stated in terms of the assignment procedure.
The number of response rows does not change the number of independent condition assignments. A model may represent the fact that responses share participants, but it cannot create assignment variation that the experiment did not produce.

title: Units of assignment
section: Write the design in three sentences
text:
Write the design in three sentences
Before collection, write one sentence for each unit.

One row of the raw data represents one word recognition trial.
Training condition is assigned once to each participant.
Responses are repeated within participants and words.

This compact description exposes the design before model notation obscures it. It also records which repeated units the earlier mixed effects models must preserve when they are applied to this study.






NoteAudit the assignment unit




A classroom receives a teaching method, and each student supplies five responses. What is the assignment unit, and what is the observation unit?
A participant hears 60 words, with accent independently selected for each word subject to equal condition counts. What could receive a different condition under the procedure?
Why can additional trials improve measurement without adding independent assignments?

title: Units of assignment
text:
Summing up
The unit of assignment is the entity whose condition could vary independently under the actual design. Separating it from the row of the data fixes the level at which assignment must operate. The next page turns from the receiving unit to the random assignment mechanism that selects its condition.

title: Power by simulation
text:
Suppose we plan a within-participant acceptability experiment. Each participant judges active and passive sentences, and the primary analysis compares each participant’s mean active rating with that participant’s mean passive rating. How many participants are needed?
There is no answer until we specify how large the condition difference might be, how much participant differences vary, and what decision the analysis must make. A simulation-based power analysis repeatedly generates data under those assumptions, fits the planned model, and applies the planned decision rule. It reuses the distinction between a null hypothesis and test statistic, but now evaluates the decision rule under a stated nonzero effect and complete design.

title: Power by simulation
section: Power is conditional on a data-generating process
text:
Power is conditional on a data-generating process
Let G denote an assumed data-generating process, and let A(Y) denote the decision returned by the planned analysis for simulated data Y. If A(Y)=1 means that the decision rule is met, power is

\operatorname{Power}(G)=P_G\{A(Y)=1\}.

The subscript G is essential. Power is not a fixed property of a sample size. It depends on the assumed effect, variation, design, exclusion process, analysis, and decision rule.
For the acceptability study, suppose the analysis will use one active minus passive difference D_i for each participant. A simple generating model is

D_i\sim\operatorname{Normal}(\delta,\sigma_D^2),

where \delta is the mean condition difference and \sigma_D is the standard deviation of participant differences. Both quantities must be supplied before simulation begins.

title: Power by simulation
section: Work through the simulation estimate by hand
text:
Work through the simulation estimate by hand
Imagine simulating 20 complete studies. The planned decision rule is met in 16 of them. The estimated power is

\widehat{\operatorname{Power}}=\frac{16}{20}=.80.

This estimate has Monte Carlo error because it is based on a finite number of simulated studies. As in the earlier discussion of Monte Carlo integration, the simulation average has its own numerical uncertainty. Its approximate Monte Carlo standard error is

\operatorname{MCSE}
=\sqrt{\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{Power}}(1-\widehat{\operatorname{Power}})}{S}},

where S is the number of simulations. With S=20 and estimated power .80,

\operatorname{MCSE}
=\sqrt{\frac{.8(.2)}{20}}
\approx .089.

An estimate of .80 with Monte Carlo standard error .089 is too imprecise for a fine distinction between candidate designs. If the same estimate came from 1,000 simulations, the standard error would be about .013.

title: Power by simulation
text:
Simulate the exact planned comparison
The following function simulates participant differences, runs the planned one sample test of those differences, and records whether the two sided decision rule is met.


Code
simulate_study <- function(n_participants, effect, sd_difference) {
  difference <- rnorm(
    n = n_participants,
    mean = effect,
    sd = sd_difference
  )

  test <- t.test(difference, mu = 0)

  data.frame(
    estimate = mean(difference),
    p_value = test$p.value,
    decision = test$p.value < .05
  )
}


Each argument corresponds to part of the formal statement. n_participants determines how many D_i values are drawn. effect supplies \delta, and sd_difference supplies \sigma_D. The analysis then operates on the same participant differences that the planned study would produce.
We estimate power by repeating the entire function.


Code
set.seed(903)

simulations <- replicate(
  n = 1000,
  expr = simulate_study(
    n_participants = 40,
    effect = 0.35,
    sd_difference = 0.80
  )$decision
)

estimated_power <- mean(simulations)
mcse <- sqrt(estimated_power * (1 - estimated_power) / length(simulations))

c(power = estimated_power, mcse = mcse)


The printed probability is conditional on a mean rating difference of .35 and a participant difference standard deviation of .80. It is not a claim that those assumptions are true. They should come from related evidence, a pilot, or a smallest difference that would matter for the linguistic argument.

title: Power by simulation
section: Power analysis is a curve, not one number
text:
Power analysis is a curve, not one number
A single assumed effect gives a single conditional answer. A more useful design analysis varies assumptions that remain uncertain. For instance, we can repeat the simulation across several participant counts and effect sizes while holding the decision rule fixed.


Code
set.seed(904)

designs <- expand.grid(
  n_participants = c(24, 32, 40, 48),
  effect = c(0.20, 0.35, 0.50)
)

designs$power <- mapply(
  FUN = function(n, delta) {
    mean(replicate(
      1000,
      simulate_study(n, delta, sd_difference = 0.80)$decision
    ))
  },
  n = designs$n_participants,
  delta = designs$effect
)

designs


This table describes a power curve across assumptions. A design that performs adequately only at the largest effect is more fragile than one that performs similarly across a plausible range. The decision should also consider whether the smaller effects would matter scientifically, not merely whether they would be difficult to detect.

title: Power by simulation
text:
Power follows the complete procedure
The simulated design and planned study must match. If the study will analyze participant differences, a simulation of unrelated trial values answers a different question. If the study will exclude participants below a prespecified accuracy threshold, the simulation should apply that rule and record how often it removes participants. If condition order can affect the response, plausible order effects should be included when they bear on the target.
The estimated power will not describe the planned study when the simulated analysis is simpler than the planned analysis or when the generated data omit a design feature that determines the comparison. The mixed effects models introduced earlier allow richer data generators for repeated participants and items. The principle does not change: simulate the design, fit the planned analysis, and apply the planned decision.
Power also does not guarantee a successful individual study. A study with power .80 still fails its decision rule with probability .20 under the assumed process. And power says nothing about bias when the data-generating assumptions are wrong. Simulation exposes assumptions; it does not certify them.






NoteAudit the design simulation




Which quantities define G in the participant difference simulation?
What uncertainty is measured by the Monte Carlo standard error?
Why does increasing the number of simulations not add participants to the planned study?
What target is changed if the simulation draws independent trials but the analysis compares participant averages?
Why should power be reported across plausible effect sizes?

title: Power by simulation
text:
Summing up
Simulation-based design analysis evaluates a complete planned procedure under a stated data-generating process. Estimated power is the proportion of simulated studies meeting the decision rule, and its Monte Carlo error depends on the number of simulations. The design pages have now fixed the comparison and its repeated units. That record tells us how to apply the earlier models for grouped linguistic data without confusing additional rows with additional assignments.

title: Exclusion rules
text:
Experiments sometimes produce observations that should not enter the target analysis. A microphone may fail during a production trial. A participant may press the same key throughout a judgment task. A response time may be long because the participant was interrupted. These cases differ in their causes, but each requires a decision about whether an enrolled participant or recorded trial belongs to the analyzed set.
The inclusion and exclusion criteria map enrolled observations to the retained analysis set. These criteria are part of the design because they determine which population of observations the final comparison represents. They should be stated before inspecting the condition effect whenever that is possible.

title: Exclusion rules
text:
Formalize retention as a variable
Let R_i=1 when observation i is retained and R_i=0 when it is excluded. An analysis of retained responses estimates a quantity conditional on R_i=1. This indicator anticipates the missingness indicators used later in the course, though exclusion and missing measurement are not the same event. For a two condition mean difference, the retained-sample quantity is

\Delta_{R=1}
=E[Y_i\mid Z_i=1,R_i=1]
-E[Y_i\mid Z_i=0,R_i=1].

This is not automatically the same as the condition difference over all enrolled trials. If retention is related to condition or to the unobserved response, the retained observations may represent different subsets of the two conditions.
The notation makes the role of the rule explicit. Exclusion is not merely a cleaning operation applied before the real analysis. It helps define the estimand.

title: Exclusion rules
text:
Separate measurement failure from behavior
A microphone dropout is a measurement failure. It may leave no usable acoustic response. A long response time is an observed behavior. It may reflect an interruption, but it may also be part of the phenomenon if the manipulation increases processing difficulty.
This distinction should be stated in terms of the measurement process. If a waveform contains no signal because the device did not record, the intended response is unavailable. If a participant takes 4,000 milliseconds to respond, a response was measured. Removing that value changes which behavior is represented.
A later response model may accommodate a long right tail without deleting valid observations. For current purposes, the design task is narrower: define which events count as technical failures, which values count as measured behavior, and which claim follows after either kind of removal.

title: Exclusion rules
text:
Work through condition dependent retention
Suppose five grammatical trials and five ungrammatical trials are planned in a small reading experiment. All grammatical trials produce a response. Two ungrammatical trials time out.



condition
retained response times
timeouts




grammatical
500, 510, 520, 530, 540
0


ungrammatical
520, 530, 540
2



Among retained trials, the mean grammatical response time is 520 milliseconds and the mean ungrammatical response time is 530 milliseconds. The retained difference is only 10 milliseconds. But 40 percent of the ungrammatical trials produced timeouts, compared with none of the grammatical trials.
The complete case mean thus answers a narrow question: among trials that produced a response before the timeout, how did mean response time differ? It cannot support the claim that the manipulation had little effect on processing. The missing responses are themselves condition dependent evidence about task difficulty.
We can retain the response and retention summaries separately.


Code
trials <- data.frame(
  condition = rep(c("grammatical", "ungrammatical"), each = 5),
  response_time = c(500, 510, 520, 530, 540, 520, 530, 540, NA, NA)
)

trials$retained <- !is.na(trials$response_time)

with(trials, table(condition, retained))
aggregate(
  response_time ~ condition,
  data = trials,
  FUN = mean,
  na.action = na.omit
)


The table of retained values should be interpreted before the retained means. It shows whether the analysis set is similarly constituted across conditions.

title: Exclusion rules
section: Define rules without using the desired effect
text:
Define rules without using the desired effect
Suppose response times above 2,000 milliseconds are removed only after the analyst notices that they weaken the expected condition difference. The observed outcome has then been used to select observations that support that outcome. A confidence interval or posterior interval from the final retained set does not include uncertainty introduced by trying multiple cutoffs.
Choosing an exclusion rule after inspecting its effect on the condition contrast biases the analysis toward a preferred result. Prespecification helps because the rule is chosen without knowledge of the realized contrast. When prior information is insufficient to justify one cutoff, the analysis can report a primary rule and a limited set of substantively defensible sensitivity analyses. The alternatives should be chosen because they represent different measurement assumptions, not because one produces the preferred result.

title: Exclusion rules
text:
Check every relevant margin
Exclusions should be tabulated by condition, participant, item, and relevant demographic or linguistic group. A participant rule may remove all observations from one speaker. A trial rule may remove particular words. Either can change the represented sample even if overall retention is high.
The exclusion rate can also be an outcome. Failure to produce a response may reflect task difficulty rather than missing measurement. Describing only the retained response distribution would hide that part of the manipulation’s effect.

title: Exclusion rules
text:
Report the observation flow
A reconstructible report gives counts at each stage.

State how many participants and trials were planned or recruited.
State how many completed the relevant procedure.
Give the count removed by each participant rule.
Give the count removed by each trial rule.
Give the final count by condition and repeated unit.

Each observation should have one recorded reason for its status, including retention. This record permits alternative rules to be evaluated without reconstructing decisions from an already filtered file.






NoteAudit the analysis set




What population of observations is described by \Delta_{R=1}?
Why is a microphone dropout different from a long but measured response time?
What does a higher timeout rate in one condition imply about a comparison of retained response times?
Why does trying several cutoffs create uncertainty that the final interval does not contain?

title: Exclusion rules
text:
Summing up
The inclusion and exclusion criteria map enrolled observations to the responses used in the comparison. Because retention can depend on condition and behavior, exclusion helps define the estimand rather than merely tidying the table. Once assignment, condition structure, counterbalancing, and retention have been specified, power by simulation can evaluate how the complete planned procedure behaves under explicit assumptions.

title: Between-participant designs
text:
Suppose an experiment tests whether two days of familiar accent training improves word recognition. Once a participant receives that training, the participant cannot return to the original untrained state. Asking the same person to complete an untrained condition afterward would compare two moments in a learning process, not trained and untrained versions of the same initial listener.
In a between-participant design, each participant contributes observations to only one condition. The condition effect is estimated by comparing groups rather than by subtracting two responses from the same participant. The resulting independence structure is the one used in the earlier chapter on comparing two independent means. This design preserves the meaning of a condition that has a lasting effect, though it also exposes the comparison to participant variation across groups.

title: Between-participant designs
text:
The comparison is across groups
Let Y_i be one participant level response, such as mean recognition accuracy after training, and let Z_i indicate the assigned condition. If Z_i=1 denotes familiar accent training and Z_i=0 denotes unfamiliar accent training, the estimated group difference is

\widehat\Delta=\bar Y_1-\bar Y_0,

where

\bar Y_z=\frac{1}{n_z}\sum_{i:Z_i=z}Y_i.

Each participant appears on only one side of this subtraction. Stable participant characteristics thus do not cancel within a difference score. Under the random assignment mechanism, preassignment characteristics and condition are independent, but realized groups can still differ by chance.

title: Between-participant designs
text:
Work through a small comparison
Suppose four participants receive familiar accent training and four receive unfamiliar accent training. Their recognition proportions are:



participant
training
proportion correct




P1
familiar
.82


P2
familiar
.74


P3
familiar
.79


P4
familiar
.85


P5
unfamiliar
.70


P6
unfamiliar
.68


P7
unfamiliar
.76


P8
unfamiliar
.72



The familiar group mean is

\bar Y_1=\frac{.82+.74+.79+.85}{4}=.80,

and the unfamiliar group mean is

\bar Y_0=\frac{.70+.68+.76+.72}{4}=.715.

Thus, the estimated difference is .80-.715=.085, or 8.5 percentage points. The estimate describes the difference between the two realized groups. Its uncertainty must include the fact that different participants appear in the two conditions.


Code
recognition <- data.frame(
  participant = paste0("P", 1:8),
  training = rep(c("familiar", "unfamiliar"), each = 4),
  proportion_correct = c(.82, .74, .79, .85, .70, .68, .76, .72)
)

group_means <- aggregate(
  proportion_correct ~ training,
  data = recognition,
  FUN = mean
)

group_means
with(recognition, t.test(
  proportion_correct[training == "familiar"],
  proportion_correct[training == "unfamiliar"]
))


The two vectors passed to t.test() contain different participants, so the call does not use paired = TRUE. Treating the values as paired would invent a relation between P1 and P5, P2 and P6, and so on that the design never created.

title: Between-participant designs
section: Trials improve measurement, not assignment replication
text:
Trials improve measurement, not assignment replication
Each participant may complete many recognition trials. Those trials can make that participant’s recognition proportion less sensitive to one unusually easy or difficult word. They do not replace additional independently assigned participants when the target is a population difference between training conditions.
Suppose P1 completes 400 trials while every other participant completes 40. The study still contains eight independently assigned participants. A trial weighted mean would allow P1 to contribute ten times as much as another participant, which changes the target toward a randomly selected recorded trial. A participant weighted mean gives each assigned participant one contribution, which matches a target over participants.
Items can vary within participants even when condition varies only between participants. The design record should thus state both that training is assigned between participants and that word responses repeat within participants and items. The earlier mixed effects model sequence uses that record to represent the shared variation.

title: Between-participant designs
text:
When this design is needed
Training, prolonged adaptation, and explicit instruction may have lasting effects. A between-participant design is appropriate when exposure to one condition changes how the participant would respond in another. It can also reduce demand effects when seeing multiple conditions would reveal the intended contrast.
The cost is that participant variation contributes directly to uncertainty. If a strong participant characteristic such as baseline proficiency is measured before assignment, the restricted randomization procedure introduced on the previous page can balance condition counts within proficiency groups. The same baseline measure should be retained in the analysis plan. This use is legitimate because the restriction is set before outcomes are observed.

title: Between-participant designs
text:
Do not invent pairs
A common failure is to arrange the two group vectors in some convenient order and run a paired analysis. The row positions then masquerade as pairs even though one participant has no natural counterpart in the other condition. The paired analysis usually understates uncertainty because it removes variation through an association that the design did not provide.
Another failure is to count trials as though condition were independently assigned to every trial. Both failures can be detected by writing the unit of assignment before writing the analysis.






NoteAudit the between-participant comparison




Why does a lasting training manipulation favor a between-participant design?
Which observations appear on both sides of \widehat\Delta?
Why do 100 trials from one participant not count as 100 training assignments?
Under what condition may a baseline proficiency measure be used to restrict assignment?

title: Between-participant designs
text:
Summing up
A between-participant design compares groups whose members received only one condition. It protects manipulations that cannot be reset, while participant differences remain part of the group comparison. Within either participant structure, sentence versions must still be distributed so that item identity is not confused with condition. That is the role of counterbalancing.

title: The widely applicable information criterion
text:
The PSIS-LOO page stored one log-likelihood contribution for every observation and posterior draw. The earlier chapter on predictive distributions explained why predictions average over posterior uncertainty. The widely applicable information criterion (WAIC) uses that pointwise matrix and posterior averaging to correct fitted posterior predictive density for optimism. Like the earlier information criteria, it reports a relative comparison rather than a standalone measure of linguistic adequacy. Unlike PSIS-LOO, it does not approximate omitted posteriors with importance ratios.
This page develops the WAIC correction one quantity at a time. We first calculate fitted posterior predictive density, then measure how much each pointwise log likelihood varies over the posterior, and finally subtract that variation as an optimism estimate.

title: The widely applicable information criterion
section: Begin with fitted posterior predictive density
text:
Begin with fitted posterior predictive density
For observation i, define the log pointwise predictive density (lppd)

\operatorname{lppd}_i
=
\log
\left[
\frac{1}{S}
\sum_{s=1}^{S}
p(y_i\mid\theta^{(s)})
\right].

The average inside the logarithm integrates the likelihood of y_i over posterior uncertainty. The observation helped determine that posterior, though. Thus, \operatorname{lppd}_i evaluates the fitted data under a posterior that has already seen the response being scored.
Summing the pointwise values gives

\operatorname{lppd}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}\operatorname{lppd}_i.

This is a fitted predictive summary, not an omitted-data evaluation.

title: The widely applicable information criterion
text:
Measure pointwise optimism
WAIC estimates effective flexibility using the posterior variance of each pointwise log likelihood:

p_{\mathrm{waic},i}
=
\operatorname{Var}_s
\left[
\log p(y_i\mid\theta^{(s)})
\right].

If the pointwise log likelihood changes little across posterior draws, this contribution is small. If it changes substantially, the observation contributes more to the estimated flexibility of the fitted model.
Summing gives the effective parameter estimate

p_{\mathrm{waic}}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{\mathrm{waic},i}.

The word effective matters. This quantity is not obtained by counting coefficients in a formula. It depends on the fitted posterior and the pointwise likelihood contributions.

title: The widely applicable information criterion
text:
Subtract the correction
WAIC’s expected log predictive density is

\operatorname{elpd}_{\mathrm{waic}}
=
\operatorname{lppd}
-
p_{\mathrm{waic}}.

Larger values are preferred. Some software also reports a deviance-scale value

\operatorname{WAIC}
=
-2\operatorname{elpd}_{\mathrm{waic}},

for which smaller values are preferred. Before comparing printed numbers, check which scale the software reports.
In R, the calculation uses the same pointwise log-likelihood matrix required by PSIS-LOO.


Code
waic_result <- loo::waic(log_lik_draws)
print(waic_result)


A single total log likelihood per posterior draw cannot recover the pointwise variances. The observation columns must remain separate.

title: The widely applicable information criterion
text:
Work a small correction
Suppose three observations have log pointwise posterior predictive densities

-1.0,\quad -0.8,\quad -1.2,

so that \operatorname{lppd}=-3.0. Suppose their posterior log-likelihood variances are

0.10,\quad 0.05,\quad 0.20.

The effective flexibility is

p_{\mathrm{waic}}
=
0.10+0.05+0.20
=
0.35.

Thus,

\operatorname{elpd}_{\mathrm{waic}}
=
-3.0-0.35
=
-3.35.

On the deviance scale, the corresponding value is 6.70. The calculation makes the correction visible: fitted predictive density is reduced because the fitted model has adapted to the same observations it scores.

title: The widely applicable information criterion
text:
Inspect the pointwise variances
A large posterior variance for one pointwise log likelihood warns that the WAIC approximation may be unreliable for that observation. The warning concerns the approximation, not merely the overall score.
This is one reason PSIS-LOO is usually easier to diagnose. PSIS-LOO reports a tail diagnostic connected directly to its importance-sampling approximation. WAIC remains useful pedagogically because its correction can be read from the posterior variance formula.
This comparison does not turn the page into a second PSIS lesson. The method developed here is WAIC. PSIS-LOO supplies a neighboring diagnostic standard against which the limits of WAIC can be stated.

title: The widely applicable information criterion
section: Keep the pointwise likelihood contributions fixed
text:
Keep the pointwise likelihood contributions fixed
WAIC is tied to the unit represented by one likelihood contribution. If one column describes one trial, the correction is pointwise at the trial level. It does not create prediction for a wholly new speaker, item, passage, or language.
Repeated observations from the same group may also share latent effects. The pointwise likelihood must be defined consistently with the fitted model, and the scientific claim must specify what information is available when a new response is predicted.

title: The widely applicable information criterion
text:
Check the correction

Why is \operatorname{lppd} a fitted predictive quantity?
What pointwise quantity supplies WAIC’s optimism correction?
Why is p_{\mathrm{waic}} not simply the number of regression coefficients?
Which direction is better for \operatorname{elpd}_{\mathrm{waic}}?
Which direction is better for the deviance-scale WAIC value?
Why must the log-likelihood matrix retain one observation per column?
Why does trial-level WAIC not estimate prediction for a new speaker?

title: The widely applicable information criterion
text:
What WAIC establishes
WAIC subtracts a posterior-variance estimate of optimism from fitted pointwise predictive density. Its effective flexibility depends on the fitted posterior rather than a raw coefficient count. The result remains an approximation tied to the pointwise likelihood unit and must be interpreted on the scale the software reports.

title: Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation
text:
The Bayesian chapters introduced posterior predictive distributions and importance sampling. The leave-one-out page then defined prediction for an omitted observation. PSIS-LOO combines these ideas to approximate Bayesian leave-one-out prediction without fitting every omitted-data posterior directly.
A Bayesian model supplies a posterior distribution over parameter values rather than one fitted parameter vector. If we want to predict an omitted judgment, we should average its predictive density over the posterior that would have been obtained without that judgment. Literal refitting carries out this instruction, but a model with N observations would require N additional posterior computations.
Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO) approximates those omitted-data posteriors using draws from the posterior fit to all observations. This page develops that single approximation. We first define exact Bayesian leave-one-out prediction, then derive the importance ratios, and finally interpret the resulting diagnostic.

title: Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation
section: Begin with exact Bayesian leave-one-out prediction
text:
Begin with exact Bayesian leave-one-out prediction
Let y_{-i} denote all observed responses except y_i. If the prior is p(\theta), the leave-one-out posterior is

p(\theta\mid y_{-i})
\propto
p(\theta)
\prod_{j\neq i}p(y_j\mid\theta).

The exact leave-one-out predictive density for the omitted response is

p(y_i\mid y_{-i})
=
\int
p(y_i\mid\theta)
p(\theta\mid y_{-i})
\,\mathrm{d}\theta.
