This expression averages the likelihood of the omitted response over uncertainty in \theta after fitting only the other responses. Taking logs and summing gives a leave-one-out estimate of the expected log pointwise predictive density (ELPD):

\operatorname{elpd}_{\mathrm{loo}}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\log p(y_i\mid y_{-i}).

Larger values indicate greater predictive density for the omitted observations. Since log densities are often negative, a value of -300 is larger than -320.

title: Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation
section: Relate the omitted posterior to the full posterior
text:
Relate the omitted posterior to the full posterior
Suppose we already have draws \theta^{(1)},\ldots,\theta^{(S)} from the full posterior

p(\theta\mid y)
\propto
p(\theta)
\prod_{j=1}^{N}p(y_j\mid\theta).

Removing the ith likelihood term gives

p(\theta\mid y_{-i})
\propto
\frac{p(\theta\mid y)}{p(y_i\mid\theta)}.

Thus, a full-posterior draw receives a large raw importance ratio for the leave-one-out posterior when p(y_i\mid\theta^{(s)}) is small:

r_i^{(s)}
\propto
\frac{1}{p(y_i\mid\theta^{(s)})}.

This inverse weighting is both the computational shortcut and its potential weakness. If a few draws receive extremely large ratios, the full posterior may represent the omitted posterior poorly.

title: Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation
text:
Smooth the largest ratios
PSIS fits a generalized Pareto distribution to the upper tail of the raw importance ratios and replaces the most extreme ratios with smoothed values. The approximation still uses the full-posterior draws, but no longer lets a few unstable raw values determine the estimate unchecked.
The Pareto k diagnostic reports the fitted tail-shape parameter for each omitted observation. A larger k suggests that the upper tail is heavy and that a few draws dominate the approximation. Thus, Pareto k evaluates the computation used to estimate the omitted predictive density. It is not an optional decoration on the final score.
A large value does not prove that the observation should be removed. The observation may identify a model failure, a data error, or a region with little training support. It may instead show only that full-posterior draws are a poor proposal for the omitted posterior. These possibilities require inspecting the observation and, when necessary, performing a more reliable refit.

title: Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation
text:
Preserve the pointwise log likelihood
The loo package expects a matrix with one row per posterior draw and one column per pointwise likelihood contribution.


Code
# Rows index posterior draws. Columns index observations.
dim(log_lik_draws)

loo_result <- loo::loo(log_lik_draws)
print(loo_result)

pareto_k <- loo::pareto_k_values(loo_result)
plot(pareto_k, ylab = "Pareto k")


Each matrix entry must be the log likelihood for one observation conditional on one posterior draw. A vector containing one total log likelihood per draw is not enough because omission operates one contribution at a time.
When a Pareto k value is problematic, possible responses include exact refitting for that observation, moment matching, or a validation design that better matches the predictive question. The choice depends on whether the difficulty lies in the approximation, the fitted model, or the prediction task.

title: Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation
section: Match the omitted unit to the claim
text:
Match the omitted unit to the claim
Default PSIS-LOO omits one likelihood contribution. In repeated linguistic data, that contribution is often one trial. Other trials from the same participant and item remain in the posterior fit.
This procedure may answer a new-trial question. It does not automatically estimate prediction for a wholly new participant, item, verb, passage, or language. If the scientific claim concerns a new passage, all positions in one passage must be omitted together or the model must be refit under an equivalent grouped scheme.
Summing row-level PSIS-LOO values within a passage does not retroactively remove that passage from training. The likelihood partition and validation procedure must already hold out the complete group required by the predictive question.

title: Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation
text:
Check the approximation

Which posterior appears in the exact predictive density p(y_i\mid y_{-i})?
Why are the raw importance ratios proportional to 1/p(y_i\mid\theta^{(s)})?
What does Pareto k diagnose?
What does a large Pareto k not establish about an observation?
Why must the log-likelihood matrix retain one column per pointwise contribution?
Why can row-level PSIS-LOO fail to answer a new-speaker question?

title: Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation
text:
What PSIS-LOO establishes
PSIS-LOO approximates omitted-observation predictive density while averaging over posterior uncertainty. The Pareto k diagnostic evaluates whether draws from the full posterior can represent each omitted posterior well enough for that approximation. The resulting score remains tied to the unit represented by one likelihood contribution.
The next page uses the same pointwise log-likelihood matrix to construct a different approximation based on posterior variation.

title: What must be new at prediction time
text:
The earlier page on populations and samples required an inferential claim to specify the population represented by a sample. Predictive evaluation requires a related decision. We must say which responses were unavailable during fitting and what information is available when those responses are predicted.
Out-of-sample prediction predicts responses that did not contribute to fitting the model. This definition leaves an important question open. Does the held-out response come from an observed participant and item, or does it come from a participant or item absent from the training data?
crumbs: What must be new at prediction time

title: What must be new at prediction time
text:
Specify the held-out observations
Suppose an acceptability experiment crosses participants with sentences. Several data separations are possible.








predictive question
participant during fitting
sentence during fitting




another response from an observed participant to an observed sentence
observed
observed


a response to a new sentence from an observed participant
observed
absent


a response from a new participant to an observed sentence
absent
observed


a response from a new participant to a new sentence
absent
absent



Every row concerns a response excluded from fitting. The rows nevertheless ask different scientific questions. A model can predict another response from represented participants and sentences while failing for a participant or sentence absent from the training data.
This is why the phrase new observation is incomplete. A new word might be a new token of an observed word type, a word type absent from fitting, or a word in a passage absent from fitting. The data split must encode the intended meaning of new.
crumbs: What must be new at prediction time

title: What must be new at prediction time
text:
State what information is available
Holding out a participant does not by itself determine which information about that participant may be used. Imagine a model with a participant-specific baseline. If five calibration trials are available before the sixth response is predicted, the baseline may be estimated from those five trials. If the intended use is prediction for the participant’s first trial, it may not.
Both procedures predict a response from a participant who was absent when the population-level model was fitted. They differ in the information available at prediction time. A report must state whether calibration responses were allowed.
The same issue arises with linguistic annotations. A model predicting an unseen verb’s acceptability profile may use corpus counts for that verb while withholding all of its acceptability judgments. A model predicting a language’s phonological inventory may use the language’s family and region while withholding its segment inventory. These predictors are permissible only if the corresponding information would be available in the intended use setting.
crumbs: What must be new at prediction time

title: What must be new at prediction time
section: Match the split to the question
text:
Match the split to the question
Suppose reading times are observed from readers s, word positions w, and passages p. A random row split can leave one reading-time response out while retaining other responses from the same reader and passage. This evaluates another response from the represented collection of readers and passages.
A new-reader question instead requires every response from one reader to be held out together. A new-passage question requires every word position from one passage to be held out together. The grouped cross-validation page develops these separations.
The held-out group also determines the replication relevant to the claim. Fifty-five passages provide 55 opportunities to examine prediction for an omitted passage. They do not provide thousands of independent omitted passages merely because the passages contain thousands of word positions.
crumbs: What must be new at prediction time

title: What must be new at prediction time
section: Theory determines what should be held out
text:
Theory determines what should be held out
The data separation should follow the theoretical contrast. Suppose one account claims that comprehenders preactivate full lexical forms, while another claims that context supplies graded syntactic and semantic information. Holding out word positions within observed passages asks whether those predictors help with other positions in the same collection of texts. Holding out complete passages asks whether the fitted relation generalizes to passages absent during fitting.
The second question may be scientifically preferable when the claim concerns connected texts. It also requires passage-level replication. The choice should be made from the claim and design, not from whichever split later produces the most favorable score.
crumbs: What must be new at prediction time

title: What must be new at prediction time
section: Write the predictive question in plain language
text:
Write the predictive question in plain language
A complete statement answers four questions.

What response is predicted?
Which observations or groups are excluded from fitting?
What predictors are available for the held-out observations?
To which population or use setting should the result generalize?

For instance:

The model predicts the mean log first-fixation duration of each content-word position in a passage omitted during fitting. Word length, word class, and independently collected predictability norms are available. No reading-time response from the held-out passage is used to fit the model. The score concerns omitted passages from the corpus, conditional on fixation and on the observed reader sample.

This statement is narrower than “predict natural reading.” It identifies the response, the held-out group, the permitted predictors, and the scope of the result.
crumbs: What must be new at prediction time

title: What must be new at prediction time
section: More than one predictive question may be useful
text:
More than one predictive question may be useful
A study may evaluate more than one data separation. For instance, it may report predictions for new responses from observed readers and predictions for readers absent during fitting. Each result needs its own split and interpretation.
The results should not be pooled into one score. They estimate performance under different information conditions. A secondary analysis should also not replace the analysis that motivated the study after the results are known.
The number of groups matters. A corpus with ten stories can use each story as a held-out group, but the resulting ten story-level scores may be unstable. Showing those scores makes the available replication visible.
crumbs: What must be new at prediction time

title: What must be new at prediction time
section: Match the question and the split
text:
Match the question and the split

State the required data separation for predicting another response from an observed participant and item.
State the required data separation for predicting an observed item for a participant absent during fitting.
A lexical model estimates a word-specific baseline using all corpus occurrences, then reports prediction for word types omitted during model fitting. What information leaked into the fitted procedure?
Why do 100,000 word observations from ten stories not provide 100,000 independent opportunities to evaluate prediction for an omitted story?
crumbs: What must be new at prediction time

title: What must be new at prediction time
text:
Before choosing a loss
Out-of-sample prediction requires a response excluded from fitting. A complete predictive question also states which groups are held out, which predictors remain available, and where the result should generalize. The next page defines the numerical consequence assigned to each prediction error.
crumbs: What must be new at prediction time

title: Leaving out one unit at a time
text:
The K-fold cross-validation page rotated several observations through each test fold. Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV) is the special case that makes one observation the test set at a time.
Suppose a small reading-time experiment contains too few observations to place a large portion of the data in a test set. We still want every observed response to be evaluated out of sample, and we would like each fitted model to use nearly all of the remaining data.
The word observation is doing important work. One observation may be one row, one participant, one sentence, or one passage, depending on how the data and predictive question are defined. The leave-one-out calculation is meaningful only after the analysis determines which of these counts as one observation.
This page first defines LOO-CV as a special case of cross-validation. It then works through a three-row regression by hand and implements the same procedure in R. Finally, it shows why row-level LOO does not automatically evaluate prediction for a speaker, item, or text absent during fitting.
crumbs: Leaving out one unit at a time

title: Leaving out one unit at a time
text:
Define the rotation
Begin with the simplest case in which rows are the observations left out. Let the data contain N observations. For each row i, fit the complete procedure to the data with row i removed. We write the resulting predictor as

\widehat{f}_{-i}.

The subscript -i means that observation i did not contribute to fitting. Its out-of-sample prediction is

\widehat{y}_{-i}=\widehat{f}_{-i}(x_i).

Given a previously chosen loss function L, the leave-one-out risk estimate is

\widehat{R}_{\mathrm{LOO}}
=
\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
L(y_i,\widehat{y}_{-i}).

LOO-CV is thus K-fold cross-validation with K=N when each row is one unit. Every row receives one prediction from a model that did not use that row’s response.
crumbs: Leaving out one unit at a time

title: Leaving out one unit at a time
text:
Follow three observations by hand
Consider three hypothetical word positions. Let x be word length on a simplified scale, and let y be log reading time.



row
x
y




1
1
1.0


2
2
2.0


3
3
2.5



We use a straight-line regression only because it lets us see each fit without software. Each training set contains two points, so its fitted line passes through those points.
First leave out row 1. The line through (2,2) and (3,2.5) has slope 0.5 and intercept 1. At x_1=1, it predicts

\widehat{y}_{-1}=1+0.5(1)=1.5.

The prediction error is 1.0-1.5=-0.5, so its squared loss is 0.25.
Next leave out row 2. The line through (1,1) and (3,2.5) has slope 0.75 and intercept 0.25. It predicts

\widehat{y}_{-2}=0.25+0.75(2)=1.75.

This error is 2.0-1.75=0.25, and its squared loss is 0.0625.
Finally leave out row 3. The line through (1,1) and (2,2) has slope 1 and intercept 0. It predicts

\widehat{y}_{-3}=0+1(3)=3.

The error is 2.5-3=-0.5, so the squared loss is again 0.25. Thus, the leave-one-out mean squared error is

\widehat{R}_{\mathrm{LOO}}
=
\frac{0.25+0.0625+0.25}{3}
=
0.1875.

The corresponding root mean squared error is \sqrt{0.1875}\approx 0.433. This number is on the scale of the response, which here is the simplified log-time scale.
crumbs: Leaving out one unit at a time

title: Leaving out one unit at a time
text:
Implement the same rotation
The R code follows the definition one row at a time.


Code
dat <- data.frame(
  word_length = c(1, 2, 3),
  log_time = c(1.0, 2.0, 2.5)
)

prediction <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(dat))

for (i in seq_len(nrow(dat))) {
  fit_i <- lm(
    log_time ~ word_length,
    data = dat[-i, ]
  )

  prediction[i] <- predict(
    fit_i,
    newdata = dat[i, , drop = FALSE]
  )
}

squared_loss <- (dat$log_time - prediction)^2
mean(squared_loss)
sqrt(mean(squared_loss))


The expression dat[-i, ] constructs the training data. The expression dat[i, , drop = FALSE] supplies the omitted predictor value at prediction time. No omitted response enters fit_i.
For an actual analysis, the loop must contain every fitted decision. If predictors are centered, the center is estimated from dat[-i, ]. If a penalty is tuned, the tuning procedure uses only dat[-i, ]. LOO-CV evaluates the complete procedure rather than a coefficient formula chosen using all of the responses.
crumbs: Leaving out one unit at a time

title: Leaving out one unit at a time
crumbs: Leaving out one unit at a time

title: Leaving out one unit at a time
text:
Understand the dependence among fits
In the three-row example, the fitted training sets overlap. With a larger dataset, any two row-level LOO fits share N-2 observations. The resulting prediction losses are not independent experiments, even though each response was individually withheld from its own fit.
This dependence does not invalidate the average in \widehat{R}_{\mathrm{LOO}}. It does rule out treating N fitted models as N independent repetitions of the study. The relevant uncertainty calculation still depends on the sampling units specified by the scientific claim.
crumbs: Leaving out one unit at a time

title: Leaving out one unit at a time
text:
Compare training size and computation
Each LOO model uses all but one observation. Its training set is thus very similar in size to the complete dataset. This may be useful when the dataset is small.
But the similarity comes at a computational cost. Row-level LOO with 10,000 observations requires 10,000 fits if carried out directly. A complex model may make that cost prohibitive. Five-fold or ten-fold cross-validation uses fewer fits, though each fit omits a larger portion of the observations.
LOO-CV can also be sensitive when one omitted observation has unusual predictor values. That observation may be difficult to predict because the training set supplies little nearby information. This is not automatically a flaw. It may reveal that the fitted relationship is being asked to extrapolate beyond predictor values well represented by the rest of the sample.
crumbs: Leaving out one unit at a time

title: Leaving out one unit at a time
section: Do not tune on the omitted response
text:
Do not tune on the omitted response
A common failure is to use all rows to choose a transformation, set of predictors, or tuning parameter and then report leave-one-out predictions from that fixed choice. The omitted response has already influenced the procedure, so the prediction is not fully out of sample.
The repair is the same separation used for any cross-validation procedure. Every response-adaptive decision must be repeated inside the training portion. If that decision itself needs held-out evaluation, it requires an inner validation step within the N-1 training rows.
This requirement can make literal LOO-CV unattractive for procedures with expensive tuning. In that case, fewer outer folds may provide a more practical evaluation without changing which observations or groups are held out.
crumbs: Leaving out one unit at a time

title: Leaving out one unit at a time
text:
Check the omitted unit

How many direct fits are required for row-level LOO with 250 rows?
In the three-row calculation, why is \widehat{y}_{-2} an out-of-sample prediction even though rows 1 and 3 appear in two different fits?
What must be omitted when predicting for an unadapted participant absent during fitting?
Why does row-level LOO usually evaluate another response from represented participants and items in a repeated participant by item experiment?
If a researcher chooses a penalty using all responses before running LOO-CV, which part of the separation has failed?
crumbs: Leaving out one unit at a time

title: Leaving out one unit at a time
text:
Before grouping folds
LOO-CV rotates a one-observation test set so that every observation receives a prediction from a fit that excluded it. The method uses nearly all available data for each fit, but the meaning of one observation must still match the scientific question. The next page shows how to keep complete speakers, items, passages, or languages together whenever those groups must be absent during fitting.
crumbs: Leaving out one unit at a time

title: Predicting observations the model did not see
text:
The linear-regression checks assessed how a fitted model reproduces the observations used to estimate it. Predictive evaluation asks a different question about responses that did not contribute to fitting.
Suppose a regression predicts reading time from word length, frequency, and contextual predictability. Its fitted residuals are small. This tells us how closely the fitted predictions track the responses used to estimate the model. It does not tell us how well the procedure predicts a response unavailable during fitting.
We must also say whether the omitted response comes from an observed passage, an omitted passage, an observed reader, or an omitted reader. A fitted description does not answer this question on its own.
crumbs: Predicting observations the model did not see

title: Predicting observations the model did not see
text:
Four decisions precede a score
A predictive evaluation makes four linked decisions.

The statement of what must be held out identifies which observations or groups are absent during fitting and what information is available about them.
The loss function determines how much each discrepancy between an observation and prediction costs.
The training and evaluation split ensures that the responses used for evaluation did not guide fitting or model choice.
The evaluation unit returns predictive differences to the speakers, items, passages, or languages represented by the claim.

These decisions cannot be made independently. If a complete passage must be absent during fitting, word positions from that passage must move together into the test set. If passage sizes differ, a position-weighted loss and a passage-weighted loss answer different questions. Uncertainty over predictive improvement should not treat arbitrary computational folds as independent passages.
crumbs: Predicting observations the model did not see

title: Predicting observations the model did not see
section: Three ways to hold out observations
text:
Three ways to hold out observations
Consider a corpus with 20 readers, 10 passages, and 100 word positions per passage. The same regression procedure may be evaluated with at least three data separations.








predictive question
what is omitted during fitting
what the result may describe




another trial
one observed response
another response from represented readers and passages


a new reader
every response from one reader
responses from readers absent during fitting


a new passage
every position in one passage
responses from passages absent during fitting



A random row split can evaluate the first question because other trials from the same readers and passages may remain in training. It cannot evaluate the second or third question, since the supposedly omitted group is partly observed during fitting.
This is why a report that one model predicts better is incomplete. Better for which response, under which loss, and with which observations or groups excluded from fitting?
crumbs: Predicting observations the model did not see

title: Predicting observations the model did not see
section: Use predictive comparison to test a theoretical contrast
text:
Use predictive comparison to test a theoretical contrast
The point of held-out prediction is not to generate a leaderboard of formulas. Predictive evaluation can test a theoretically motivated contrast. A control model may encode design and lexical variables. A second model may add full-form predictability. A third may add graded syntactic and semantic predictability. Each addition corresponds to a linguistic claim.
The held-out comparison asks whether that added information changes prediction for the specified observations. A coefficient and a predictive improvement answer related but distinct questions. The coefficient describes an estimated conditional association in the fitted model. The loss comparison describes the consequence of adding that information for responses excluded from fitting.
A model may fit on average while failing for long passages, rare words, one response range, or particular speakers. Retaining pointwise and groupwise losses allows us to locate such failures rather than hiding them inside one aggregate number.
crumbs: Predicting observations the model did not see

title: Predicting observations the model did not see
text:
How the module proceeds
We begin with what must be new at prediction time, which distinguishes an omitted trial from an omitted participant, item, passage, or language. Predictive loss then defines the numerical consequence assigned to each error. Prediction bias and prediction variance explain why closer training fit need not imply lower error on new responses.
Next, training and test data enforce the separation between fitting and evaluation. Cross-validation rotates that separation so that every observation receives a held-out prediction. Leave-one-out cross-validation uses one observation as the test set at a time. Grouped cross-validation keeps complete speakers, items, passages, or languages together whenever those groups must be absent during fitting.
We then turn to comparisons. Comparing predictive loss evaluates two procedures on the same held-out observations and shows why uncertainty should be summarized at the level specified by the scientific claim. Likelihood-ratio tests compare nested likelihood models in sample, and information criteria penalize in-sample fit. Finally, PSIS-LOO approximates leave-one-out prediction from posterior draws, while WAIC constructs a separate posterior-variance correction from the same pointwise log-likelihood matrix.
crumbs: Predicting observations the model did not see

title: Predicting observations the model did not see
text:
The assessment connection
PS2 applies the predictive sequence to reading-time data. It asks whether lexical, morphosyntactic, and semantic predictability measures improve prediction for passages omitted during fitting. Complete passages are held out, so the split, loss aggregation, and interpretation must all remain at the passage level.
The assessment is included here because it turns an underspecified predictive question into an analysis decision. A random row split would evaluate other positions from represented passages even if every printed score were computed correctly.
crumbs: Predicting observations the model did not see

title: Predicting observations the model did not see
text:
What this module adds
By the end of the module, we should be able to state what a predictive score estimates, reconstruct how each prediction was kept out of its own fit, and identify the units over which model differences vary. These capabilities let us replace the vague claim that a model predicts well with a narrower claim whose response, loss, and held-out observations are explicit.
crumbs: Predicting observations the model did not see

title: Cross-validation
text:
The preceding page separated one training set from one test set. K-fold cross-validation (CV) reduces dependence on a single partition by dividing the data into K folds and rotating which fold serves as the test set.
The output of CV is one out-of-fold prediction for every observation. Each prediction comes from a model that did not use that observation’s response.

title: Cross-validation
Cross-validation
text:
A base-R implementation
The following skeleton evaluates a linear model.


Code
set.seed(214)
fold <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(dat)))
prediction <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(dat))

for (k in 1:10) {
  test <- fold == k
  fit <- lm(response ~ predictor_1 + predictor_2, data = dat[!test, ])
  prediction[test] <- predict(fit, newdata = dat[test, ])
}

rmse <- sqrt(mean((dat$response - prediction)^2))


The vector prediction is more useful than ten fold scores. It permits inspection of error by response range, linguistic category, item, or another prespecified unit. It also makes paired comparisons between models possible.

title: Cross-validation
text:
What K changes
With larger K, each model is trained on a larger fraction of the data, while each test fold is smaller. Leave-one-out CV sets K=N: each fitted model omits one observation. This can be computationally expensive, and the resulting estimate of predictive performance can have high variance.
Five- or ten-fold CV is common because it balances training size and computation. These values are conventions, not probability laws. A dataset with 55 passages may instead use 55 folds when the predictive question requires one entire passage to be omitted at a time.
Randomly assigning observations to folds is part of the procedure. Different assignments can produce slightly different scores. Repeating random CV over several prespecified seeds reveals split sensitivity, but the repeated scores are not independent replications of the dataset. They reuse the same responses.

title: Cross-validation
section: Every fitted decision stays inside the loop
text:
Every fitted decision stays inside the loop
CV evaluates a procedure, not just its final coefficient formula. If a procedure selects predictors, centers variables, chooses a penalty, or imputes missing values, those steps are repeated using only the training portion of every fold.
For instance, a model with a tuning parameter \lambda cannot choose \lambda by comparing the outer test-fold responses. It requires an inner validation procedure within the outer training set. The outer prediction then evaluates the complete selection rule on data not consulted by either coefficient fitting or tuning.
This nested construction may be unnecessary when the model specification is fixed in advance. Avoiding an unneeded tuning layer keeps the lesson focused and the score interpretable.

title: Cross-validation
text:
What random row folds evaluate
Random row folds evaluate another row from the same mixture of represented units. In repeated linguistic data, the same speakers, items, passages, or languages may appear in both training and test folds. That can be appropriate when the question concerns another trial from represented groups.
It is not appropriate merely because random folds are easy to create. If the claim concerns a new speaker, all rows from each test speaker must be excluded from training. If it concerns a new passage, all positions in the passage must move together. The next page changes the fold construction while leaving the CV algorithm itself intact.

title: Cross-validation
section: Fold scores are not independent experiments
text:
Fold scores are not independent experiments
A common comparison computes one loss per fold and applies a t test to the K differences. This treats fold scores as independent observations even though their training sets overlap heavily. With ten-fold CV, any two fitted models share most of their training data.
The folds are computational partitions, not necessarily the sampling units of the scientific claim. Predictive differences should instead be returned to the independent groups specified by the claim. For prediction on omitted passages, that means passage-level losses, even if several passages were assigned to one computational fold.

title: Cross-validation
text:
Check the split

Why is each stored CV prediction out of sample for its own response?
What must happen to a training-estimated transformation in every fold?
Does repeating ten-fold CV 100 times create 1,000 independent estimates of performance on omitted corpora? Why not?
For which predictive question would random trial folds be reasonable in a repeated participant by item experiment?

title: Cross-validation
text:
Before grouping folds
K-fold CV rotates the training and test roles to obtain one held-out prediction per observation. Every adaptive decision belongs inside the fold, and random folds evaluate new rows from the observed mixture of groups. The next page specializes this rotation to one held-out observation per fit. Grouped cross-validation then changes the partition so that complete speakers, items, passages, or languages move together.

title: Prediction bias and prediction variance
text:
The earlier pages defined estimator bias, estimator variance, and their contribution to mean squared error. Here the estimator is a fitted prediction at a specified predictor value. The same decomposition thus concerns prediction bias and prediction variance across repeated training samples.
Suppose we use lexical frequency to predict reading time. A straight line may miss a real bend in the frequency effect. A very flexible curve may instead follow accidental bumps in the particular sample used to fit it. Both procedures can make poor predictions, but they fail for different reasons.
The bias-variance decomposition separates error that persists across repeated training samples from variation in the fitted prediction across those samples. It is useful because a model can reduce one source of error while increasing the other.
This page develops that decomposition in three steps. We first define the repetitions over which bias and variance are measured. We then derive the decomposition for squared loss and work through a small reading-time comparison. Finally, we consider what the decomposition does and does not allow us to infer from one observed dataset.

title: Prediction bias and prediction variance
text:
Begin with repeated training samples
Let x be a particular predictor value, such as a log frequency of 4. Suppose that the response for a word with that frequency is generated by

Y=f(x)+\varepsilon,

where f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x] is the true conditional mean and the noise term satisfies

\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\mid X=x]=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon\mid X=x)=\sigma^2.

Now imagine repeatedly drawing a comparable corpus and fitting the same complete analysis procedure to each corpus. The procedure produces a prediction \widehat{f}(x) from every training sample. Thus, \widehat{f}(x) is itself a random variable across training samples, even though any one fitted model returns a fixed number.
This repeated-sample interpretation is essential. Prediction variance does not describe variation among words with the same frequency. It describes variation among the predictions that would be learned from different training samples.

title: Prediction bias and prediction variance
text:
Define bias and prediction variance
The bias of the learning procedure at x is

\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat{f}(x))
=
\mathbb{E}[\widehat{f}(x)]-f(x).

The expectation averages the predictions across repeated training samples. If a straight line systematically predicts 20 ms too much at low-frequency words, its bias at that value is 20 ms.
The prediction variance at x is

\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{f}(x))
=
\mathbb{E}
\left[
\left(
\widehat{f}(x)-\mathbb{E}[\widehat{f}(x)]
\right)^2
\right].

A procedure has high prediction variance when small changes in the training corpus produce large changes in its fitted prediction. A highly flexible curve may have this property because each corpus contains different accidental bumps.

title: Prediction bias and prediction variance
text:
Derive the decomposition
We want the expected squared error for a new response Y at the fixed value x. This response is generated independently of the training sample, conditional on x:

\mathbb{E}
\left[
(Y-\widehat{f}(x))^2
\right].

Add and subtract both f(x) and \mathbb{E}[\widehat{f}(x)] inside the error:

Y-\widehat{f}(x)
=
\underbrace{Y-f(x)}_{\text{response noise}}
+
\underbrace{f(x)-\mathbb{E}[\widehat{f}(x)]}_{\text{negative bias}}
+
\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\widehat{f}(x)]-\widehat{f}(x)}_{\text{training-sample variation}}.

Squaring this sum produces three squared terms and three cross-products. The expected cross-products are zero. The response noise has mean zero, and the fitted prediction is centered around its own expectation. We are left with

\mathbb{E}
\left[
(Y-\widehat{f}(x))^2
\right]
=
\sigma^2
+
\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat{f}(x))^2
+
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{f}(x)).

The first term is the conditional response variance. In the bias-variance decomposition, it is often called irreducible error because even a procedure that knows f(x) exactly cannot predict which particular response noise will occur. The second and third terms arise from the learning procedure and may change when the model, fitting rule, or sample size changes.

title: Prediction bias and prediction variance
text:
Work through one frequency value
Suppose procedure A fits a straight line. At one frequency value, repeated samples show a bias of 20 ms and a prediction standard deviation of 15 ms. Its reducible expected squared error is

20^2+15^2
=
400+225
=
625\text{ ms}^2.

Procedure B fits a more flexible curve. Its bias is only 5 ms, but its prediction standard deviation is 30 ms:

5^2+30^2
=
25+900
=
925\text{ ms}^2.

Procedure B is closer to the true mean on average, so it has lower bias. But a particular fit from procedure B is much less stable across corpora. At this predictor value, the larger variance more than offsets the smaller bias.
Suppose the irreducible error is 40^2=1600\text{ ms}^2 for both procedures. Their complete expected squared errors are then 2225 and 2525. This term changes the total error but not the comparison, since both procedures predict the same response process at the same x.

title: Prediction bias and prediction variance
text:
Represent the calculation in R
The hand calculation can be represented directly.


Code
procedure <- data.frame(
  model = c("straight line", "flexible curve"),
  bias_ms = c(20, 5),
  prediction_sd_ms = c(15, 30)
)

procedure$bias_squared <- procedure$bias_ms^2
procedure$prediction_variance <- procedure$prediction_sd_ms^2
procedure$reducible_mse <-
  procedure$bias_squared + procedure$prediction_variance

procedure


The code does not estimate bias or variance from one corpus. It merely carries out the decomposition after those quantities have been supplied from a repeated-sampling argument, a simulation, or another justified source.

title: Prediction bias and prediction variance
section: Do not attach fixed labels to model classes
text:
Do not attach fixed labels to model classes
It is tempting to call simple models high bias and flexible models high variance. That slogan is sometimes useful, but it is not the definition. Bias and variance are properties of a complete learning procedure under a particular sequence of repeated samples.
Regularization may make a flexible curve stable. Partial pooling may reduce variation in predictions for sparsely observed verbs. A larger training sample may reduce the prediction variance of both procedures. Conversely, an unregularized model with only a few poorly identified parameters may be unstable.
Thus, coefficient count alone does not determine prediction variance. The sampling process, model, preprocessing, and fitting rule all matter.

title: Prediction bias and prediction variance
text:
What one dataset cannot reveal
We observe only one corpus, not the repeated corpora in the definitions. This limitation matters. The decomposition is an expectation over hypothetical training samples, so one observed dataset does not separately identify true bias and prediction variance.
Cross-validation can estimate their combined consequence for held-out prediction. Repeated cross-validation may also show that a model comparison is sensitive to the fold assignment. But neither procedure reveals the true bias term without additional assumptions about f(x) or a simulation in which the data-generating process is known.
This limitation affects interpretation. If a flexible model has worse held-out loss, we may say that its complete learning procedure predicts worse for the chosen data separation and loss. We should not claim that prediction variance caused the difference unless the design separately supports that diagnosis.

title: Prediction bias and prediction variance
text:
Check the decomposition

Across what repetitions is \operatorname{Var}(\widehat{f}(x)) defined?
In the numerical comparison, which procedure has lower bias and which has lower reducible expected squared error?
If procedure A and procedure B predict the same response process at the same x, why does irreducible error not affect which one has lower expected squared error?
Why can a flexible regularized model have lower prediction variance than a smaller unregularized model?
What can held-out loss establish that the separate bias and variance terms cannot be estimated to establish from one corpus?

title: Prediction bias and prediction variance
text:
Before separating the data
The bias and variance decomposition explains why a procedure that follows the training data more closely need not predict new responses better. It also makes the repetition explicit: prediction variance concerns new training samples, while irreducible error arises from new responses at a fixed predictor value. The next page turns this repeated-sample argument into an observable evaluation by separating fitting data from test data.

title: Zero-inflated counts
text:
The Poisson model already assigns positive probability to zero. A zero-inflated model is appropriate only when a second process is proposed to produce additional zeros.
Consider a corpus table that records how often each verb occurs in a particular syntactic frame. A zero may mean that the verb can occur in the frame but did not happen to occur in the finite corpus. It may instead mean that a separate grammatical or lexical process makes the frame unavailable for that verb.
A zero-inflated model represents these as two routes to an observed zero. The model is useful only when the research design or linguistic theory motivates both routes.

title: Zero-inflated counts
text:
Represent the two routes
Let q_i be the probability that observation i enters a structural zero state. If it does not enter that state, its count follows a Poisson distribution with mean \lambda_i. Thus the model contains a structural-zero component and a count component.
The structural-zero component always produces a zero. The count component can produce a zero or a positive count. Thus the probability of an observed zero is

P(Y_i=0)
=q_i+(1-q_i)e^{-\lambda_i}.

The first term is the structural-zero route. The second term is the probability of entering the count component and then receiving a Poisson zero.
For a positive count y_i, only the count component is available:

P(Y_i=y_i)
=(1-q_i)
\frac{e^{-\lambda_i}\lambda_i^{y_i}}{y_i!},
\qquad y_i>0.

This structure gives zero inflation its name. The model adds zero probability to the amount already supplied by the count distribution.

title: Zero-inflated counts
text:
Work through one probability
Suppose q_i=.60 and \lambda_i=2. The structural-zero component produces a zero with probability .60. The count component is entered with probability .40, and a Poisson distribution with mean 2 produces a zero with probability e^{-2}\approx .135.
The total zero probability is

.60+.40e^{-2}
\approx .654.

The observation has about a 65 percent chance of being zero. About 60 percentage points come from the structural-zero component. The remaining 5 percentage points come from a sampling zero in the count component.
This distinction is latent. When we observe a zero, the data do not label its route. The model infers the relative contribution of the two processes from their predictor relations and from the complete count distribution.

title: Zero-inflated counts
section: Give each process its own predictors
text:
Give each process its own predictors
The count component can use a log link:

\log\lambda_i
=\mathbf{x}_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\beta}.

Corpus size may enter this equation as an exposure offset. Lexical frequency or register may also predict the expected count among observations for which the frame is available.
The structural-zero component can use a logit link:

\operatorname{logit}(q_i)
=\mathbf{z}_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\gamma}.

A grammatical classification may enter this equation if it predicts that the frame is unavailable. The predictors need not be identical across the two processes because the processes answer different questions.
For instance, suppose a valency theory separates verbs that license a frame from verbs that do not. That classification may predict the structural-zero component. Among verbs that license the frame, corpus exposure and lemma frequency may predict the count component. Placing every predictor in both components would blur these theoretical roles.
fit <- glmmTMB(
  frame_count ~ log_frequency + offset(log(corpus_size)),
  ziformula = ~ valency_class,
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = verb_counts
)
The count formula describes the count component. The ziformula describes the probability of entering the structural-zero state. The signs have different meanings. A positive coefficient in the count formula raises the expected count among observations generated by the count component. A positive coefficient in the zero formula raises the probability of a structural zero.

title: Zero-inflated counts
text:
Require a process claim
An unusually large number of zeros does not by itself establish a structural-zero process. A misspecified mean, unrepresented grouping, or a count distribution with greater variance can also make a Poisson model underpredict zeros.
A two-component model requires a substantive account of why some observations enter a state that always returns zero. An excess of observed zeros alone does not supply that account.
In the verb frame case, a grammatical licensing theory may supply that account. In a production experiment, a technical failure that prevents a response from being recorded may supply another. By contrast, an unexplained histogram spike at zero supplies a diagnostic problem but not the required process interpretation.

title: Zero-inflated counts
text:
Check both components
A fitted zero-inflated model should reproduce the overall zero rate, the zero rate across theoretically relevant predictor values, and the distribution of positive counts. Reproducing only the total number of zeros is insufficient. The model may put the right amount of mass at zero for the wrong groups or distort the count component to compensate.
The interpretation should remain conditional. The structural-zero probability is a model-based estimate of a latent state. It is not an observed grammatical label for each zero. Its plausibility depends on whether the proposed predictors and study design distinguish the two routes.






NoteCheck the process claim



A corpus count table has 70 percent zeros. What additional linguistic or design evidence would justify a structural-zero component? Why is the zero percentage alone insufficient?

title: When ordinary linear regression cannot model the response
text:
The ordinary linear regression pages allowed the response to take any real value when its errors are normally distributed. Recall from the page on discrete random variables that a distribution’s support is the set of values its random variable can take. Real-valued support is suitable for some continuous measurements, but it conflicts with binary responses and counts.
The conflict has two parts. First, the response distribution assigns probability to values the measurement cannot take. Second, its constant conditional variance does not represent how variation changes with the conditional mean.
crumbs: When ordinary linear regression cannot model the response

title: When ordinary linear regression cannot model the response
section: Try a straight line for a binary response
text:
Try a straight line for a binary response
Suppose Y=1 marks an in completion and Y=0 marks a for completion. The conditional mean is a probability:

\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]
=\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid X=x)
=\pi(x).

Fit the straight-line mean

\pi(x)=.40+.15x.

At x=2, it gives .70. At x=5, it gives

.40+.15(5)=1.15.

A probability of 1.15 is impossible. The same line eventually predicts values below zero when x becomes sufficiently negative. Restricting the observed predictor range may hide these failures in one sample, but it does not change the fact that the mean function itself is unbounded.


Code
x <- c(-4, -2, 0, 2, 5)
linear_probability <- .40 + .15 * x

data.frame(x = x, predicted_probability = linear_probability)


At x=-4, the fitted value is -.20. At x=5, it is 1.15. Neither is a possible Bernoulli mean.
The constant-variance assumption of ordinary linear regression also conflicts with a binary response. For a Bernoulli variable,

\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X=x)
=\pi(x)[1-\pi(x)].

When the conditional mean changes, the conditional variance changes with it. One constant conditional variance cannot represent this relation. For instance, when \pi=.50,

\operatorname{Var}(Y)=.50(1-.50)=.25.

When \pi=.95,

\operatorname{Var}(Y)=.95(1-.95)=.0475.

Binary observations vary most when success and failure are equally likely. They vary less when one outcome is nearly certain. The mean and variance cannot be specified independently as they are in an ordinary linear regression with constant normally distributed errors.

title: When ordinary linear regression cannot model the response
section: Try ordinary linear regression for a count
text:
Try ordinary linear regression for a count
Suppose Y is the number of relative clauses in a document. Counts take values

0,1,2,3,\ldots

and cannot be negative.
A normal distribution assigns some probability below zero regardless of where its mean is placed. The mismatch is especially severe for small expected counts. Suppose the fitted mean is .4 clauses with residual standard deviation 1. The model assigns substantial probability to negative values and to noninteger values such as .6. Both are outside the response support.
Count variation also often grows with the expected count. A constant normal conditional variance does not encode that relationship. The Poisson distribution, for instance, has

\mathbb{E}[Y]=\lambda

and

\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\lambda.

An expected count of 2 has variance 2, while an expected count of 20 has variance 20. Whether this particular equality is adequate must be checked, but it begins with the right nonnegative integer support.
crumbs: When ordinary linear regression cannot model the response

title: When ordinary linear regression cannot model the response
section: Distinguish a response from an encoded number
text:
Distinguish a response from an encoded number
Encoding categories as numbers does not make them normally distributed measurements. If three response categories are coded 0, 1, and 2, the code does not establish that the distance from 0 to 1 equals the distance from 1 to 2. Nor does it allow the response to take values such as 1.4.
The storage format does not determine the measurement support. A response model must follow what the values mean, not merely how they are stored.
The same point applies to a binary response coded 0 and 1. Its mean is a probability, but individual observations remain two categories. A normal distribution over arbitrary real values does not become appropriate because the codes are numeric.
crumbs: When ordinary linear regression cannot model the response

title: When ordinary linear regression cannot model the response
text:
Identify the two repairs
We need a regression model that

uses a response distribution with the correct support; and
keeps the modeled conditional mean inside that support.

For a binary response, a Bernoulli distribution supplies the support \{0,1\}. For a count, a Poisson or negative-binomial distribution supplies nonnegative integers.
A transformation can connect the unconstrained linear predictor to a valid probability or positive expected count. The next page gives this transformation its standard name and develops it. The first repair addresses the possible observations. The second addresses the possible conditional means. These should not be collapsed.
crumbs: When ordinary linear regression cannot model the response

title: When ordinary linear regression cannot model the response
section: Choose the family from the measurement
text:
Choose the family from the measurement
The response family should be selected before looking for a significant coefficient. Ask what one observation is, which values it can take, and how its variation may depend on its mean.
For a binary choice, one observation is a success or failure. For a token count, one observation is a nonnegative integer attached to a declared exposure. For a continuous acoustic measurement, one observation may lie on a positive or real scale. These measurement statements constrain the model before predictors enter.
Choosing ordinary linear regression and then trying to make the response fit its assumptions reverses the required reasoning. The family should follow the response-generating claim.






NoteCheck the mismatch




Why is the problem with ordinary linear regression for a binary response more fundamental than a histogram that merely looks nonnormal?
Calculate Bernoulli variance at \pi=.10 and \pi=.50.
Why does coding ordered categories as 0, 1, and 2 not create a continuous response?
Explain why the possible response values and the relation between conditional mean and variance should be stated before choosing a familiar model family.



The next page develops the transformation that keeps a conditional mean inside its allowed range.

title: Sum coding
text:
The categorical-coding page used treatment coding to make the intercept equal the fitted mean of a reference category. Sometimes the relevant reference is the unweighted average of the modeled category means. Sum coding uses columns whose values sum to zero so that the intercept represents that average.
This choice answers a different intercept question without changing the fitted category means. The new reference is the category-weighted grand mean. It is the arithmetic mean of the model’s category-specific predictions, giving each category one equal contribution.
Consider three clause types: declarative, interrogative, and infinitival. One sum-coding matrix is
The model is
m_i
=
\beta_0+\beta_1C_{1i}+\beta_2C_{2i}.

title: Sum coding
text:
Substitute each category
For declaratives,

m_D=\beta_0+\beta_1.

For interrogatives,

m_Q=\beta_0+\beta_2.

For infinitivals,

m_I=\beta_0-\beta_1-\beta_2.

Add the three fitted means:

m_D+m_Q+m_I=3\beta_0.

Thus

\beta_0=\frac{m_D+m_Q+m_I}{3}.

The intercept is the unweighted average of the three modeled category means.
Suppose the fitted category means are

m_D=5.4,
\qquad
m_Q=6.0,
\qquad
m_I=5.7.

Then

\beta_0
=\frac{5.4+6.0+5.7}{3}
=5.7.

The intercept is not tied to one clause type. It is the category-weighted grand mean across the three types.

title: Sum coding
text:
Interpret the coefficients carefully
The coefficient \beta_1 is the declarative mean minus the grand mean. The coefficient \beta_2 is the interrogative mean minus the grand mean. The infinitival deviation is determined by the zero-sum constraint:

-(\beta_1+\beta_2).

These coefficients are not pairwise comparisons with the infinitival category. Treatment coding would provide those comparisons directly.
For the three means above,

\beta_1=5.4-5.7=-.3

and

\beta_2=6.0-5.7=.3.

The infinitival deviation is

-(\beta_1+\beta_2)=0,

which recovers m_I=5.7. The three deviations sum to zero, as the name sum coding suggests.

title: Sum coding
section: Distinguish the grand mean from the sample mean
text:
Distinguish the grand mean from the sample mean
Suppose a dataset contains 100 declaratives, 20 interrogatives, and 10 infinitivals. The raw sample mean gives the declarative category much more weight because it contributes more observations. The category-weighted grand mean gives each of the three fitted category means weight 1/3.
The two quantities coincide when the category counts are equal or when the category means happen to be equal. They need not coincide in an unbalanced sample. Calling \beta_0 simply “the overall sample mean” can thus be wrong.
A report should thus say whether a mean is observation-weighted or category-weighted. Sum coding supplies the latter reference in the displayed factor-only model.

title: Sum coding
text:
Set the contrasts in R


Code
dat <- data.frame(
  clause_type = factor(
    c("declarative", "interrogative", "infinitival"),
    levels = c("declarative", "interrogative", "infinitival")
  ),
  rating = c(5.4, 6.0, 5.7)
)

contrasts(dat$clause_type) <- contr.sum(3)

fit_sum <- lm(
  rating ~ clause_type,
  data = dat
)


Always inspect the actual contrast matrix:


Code
contrasts(dat$clause_type)
coef(fit_sum)


Factor level order determines which row receives which coding values.
The coefficient output should reproduce the hand calculation: an intercept of 5.7, a first deviation of -.3, and a second deviation of .3.

title: Sum coding
section: Coding does not change fitted category means
text:
Coding does not change fitted category means
Treatment and sum coding span the same two-dimensional contrast space for a three-level predictor. They produce the same fitted values, residuals, likelihood, and omnibus comparison when the model otherwise remains the same.
They change the coefficient meanings. Choose the coding whose coefficients express the comparisons required by the linguistic question.
For instance, a theory may predict that interrogative complements differ from the average selectional profile across clause types. Sum coding makes that deviation direct. A theory that instead predicts a difference between interrogatives and declaratives would be more directly represented by a coding whose column encodes that pairwise comparison.
The correct coding is thus not the one with the most symmetric matrix. It is the one whose rows and columns represent the comparisons required by the theory.






NoteReconstruct the coded means




What does \beta_0 represent under the displayed coding?
Which coefficient gives the interrogative deviation from that mean?
Why do treatment and sum coding have identical fitted values?
If the three fitted means are 4, 7, and 10, calculate the category-weighted grand mean and the two displayed sum-coded coefficients.
Distinguish the category-weighted grand mean from the observation-weighted sample mean in an unbalanced sample.

title: Repeated units in linguistic data
text:
The chapter on independent sampling separated the number of recorded observations from the assumptions that make those observations independent. Linguistic experiments often contain repeated participants and items, so the rows inherit dependence from the design.
Consider an acceptability experiment with 60 participants and 40 sentence items. Every participant judges several items, and every item is judged by several participants. The trial table may have 2,400 rows, but those rows are not 2,400 unrelated pieces of information.
A row records one response. It does not necessarily identify the unit that was independently sampled or the unit across which a claim should generalize.

title: Repeated units in linguistic data
text:
See repetition in the table



participant
item
condition
rating




p01
s01

7

Rows 1 and 2 share participant p01. Rows 1 and 3 share item s01. These links come from the design rather than from the numerical values of the ratings.
Responses from p01 may resemble one another because that participant uses the scale in a persistent way. Responses to s01 may resemble one another because that sentence has a persistent level of acceptability. Both sources can remain after the condition predictor has been included.
Thus the table contains at least three kinds of units:

2,400 response rows;
60 sampled participants;
40 sampled sentence items.

The counts answer different questions. The first tells us how many judgments were recorded. The second and third tell us how broadly the condition comparison was replicated across people and linguistic materials.

title: Repeated units in linguistic data
text:
Write the independence claim
A regression model without grouping terms often represents conditional independence with

p(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol\beta)
=\prod_i p(y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i,\boldsymbol\beta).

After the predictors are known, the joint probability is written as a product over rows. Under this model, learning the residual for one row gives no information about the residual for another.
Dependence arises when two rows share an unrepresented cause. If p01 tends to use higher ratings, observing one high response from p01 changes what we should expect for another response from p01. If s01 is persistently difficult, observing one low rating for s01 changes what we should expect from another participant on s01.
Treating these rows as unrelated can make uncertainty too small. It can also allow a few unusual participants or items to exert more influence than their number of independent units warrants.

title: Repeated units in linguistic data
text:
Distinguish crossed and nested units
Participant and item are crossed when participants encounter many items and items are encountered by many participants. The four row table above has this structure.
A nested structure has a different arrangement. Suppose a corpus contains utterances from interviews, and each interview records exactly one speaker. Utterances are nested within interviews, and interviews are nested within speakers. An interview cannot belong to two speakers under that design.
Nested grouping describes containment among observational units. It differs from one statistical model being nested within another, which means that a parameter restriction turns the larger model into the smaller model.
The distinction can be checked by asking two questions:

Can one level of unit A occur with several levels of unit B?
Can one level of unit B occur with several levels of unit A?

Two yes answers indicate crossing. If each level of B belongs to only one level of A, B is nested within A. Column order and identifier spelling do not determine this relation.

title: Repeated units in linguistic data
text:
Match dependence to the claim
A participant population claim requires replication across participants. An item population claim requires replication across items. A claim about both requires a design and analysis that preserve both sources.
For instance, a condition difference observed across 60 participants but built from only two target sentences has extensive participant replication and weak item replication. Adding more judgments of the same two sentences does not create new sentence evidence. The distinction among response, sampling, and generalization units thus concerns interpretation as well as standard errors.

title: Repeated units in linguistic data
text:
See why averaging is partial
Averaging all trials within each participant produces 60 rows. This representation preserves participant replication, but it removes item variation and any trial predictor that changes within the average. Averaging within each item produces 40 rows and loses participant variation.
Aggregation may answer a deliberately chosen question, but it cannot preserve both crossed sources in one ordinary row level analysis. Mixed effects models retain the trial responses while representing the shared participant and item variation.
Before writing such a model, record the possible sources of dependence:

State what one response row represents.
List every sampled unit that appears on more than one row.
State whether the units are crossed or nested.
State the populations across which the linguistic comparison should generalize.

This list describes the design. It should be possible to write it before deciding on software or a response distribution.






NoteCheck the row count



In a study with 50 participants, 30 items, and one judgment per participant and item pair, how many trial rows are possible? How many sampled units exist at each grouping level? Which count measures item replication?


The next page uses the recorded sources of dependence to separate population comparisons from sampled variation.

title: A straight-line mean
text:
The preceding page represented a regression through its conditional mean function m(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]. We now impose one restriction on that function.
Suppose we represent the conditional mean of log reading time as
m(x)=\beta_0+\beta_1x.
This is the mean function for simple linear regression. It contains one predictor and two coefficients.
The word simple refers to the number of predictors, not to the linguistic question or the difficulty of fitting the model. The word linear refers to the way the coefficients enter the mean function. With one predictor, that function is a straight line.

title: A straight-line mean
text:
Read the intercept
Set x=0:

m(0)=\beta_0+\beta_1(0)=\beta_0.

The intercept \beta_0 is the expected response when the predictor equals zero.
If \beta_0=5.70, the model assigns expected log reading time 5.70 to a word with surprisal 0 bits. Whether that reference point is linguistically informative depends on the observed predictor range.
An intercept remains part of the equation even when zero lies outside the observed range. It locates the line. But its linguistic interpretation may then depend on extrapolation. If the study contains words between 2 and 9 bits, the data do not directly show the response distribution at 0 bits.

title: A straight-line mean
text:
Read the slope
Compare the mean at x with the mean one unit higher:

\begin{aligned}
m(x+1)-m(x)
&=[\beta_0+\beta_1(x+1)]-[\beta_0+\beta_1x]\\
&=\beta_1.
\end{aligned}

The slope \beta_1 is the change in expected response for a one-unit increase in the predictor.
If \beta_1=.06, one additional bit of surprisal is associated with a .06 increase in expected log reading time.
The coefficient has units. Here it is measured in log milliseconds per bit. If surprisal were measured in nats instead of bits, the numerical coefficient would change because one unit on the predictor scale would represent a different amount of information.
The sign determines the direction:



slope
mean pattern




\beta_1>0
expected response increases with x


\beta_1=0
expected response does not change with x


\beta_1<0
expected response decreases with x



The slope also determines differences across larger predictor changes. For two values x_a and x_b,

m(x_b)-m(x_a)=\beta_1(x_b-x_a).

With \beta_1=.06, a four-bit contrast corresponds to an expected log-time difference of .24. This is the same result whether the comparison is from 3 to 7 bits or from 4 to 8 bits. The constant slope is the principal constraint of the straight-line mean.

title: A straight-line mean
text:
Calculate a small prediction table
Take \beta_0=5.70 and \beta_1=.06. Then



surprisal x
calculation
conditional mean m(x)




2
5.70+.06(2)
5.82


5
5.70+.06(5)
6.00


8
5.70+.06(8)
6.18



The three points lie on one line. The increase from 2 to 5 bits is .18, and the increase from 5 to 8 bits is also .18. A different pattern, such as a sharp increase only above 7 bits, cannot be represented by this mean function.

title: A straight-line mean
text:
Add observation-level variation
The line specifies only a conditional mean. Individual reading times still vary around it.
Ordinary linear regression adds a normally distributed error term:

Y_i\mid X_i=x_i
\sim
\mathcal{N}(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2).

Equivalently,

Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\varepsilon_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2).

The coefficients describe systematic change in the conditional mean. The parameter \sigma describes response variation around that mean, assumed constant across predictor values.
For a word with 5 bits of surprisal, the expected response is 6.00 under the worked model. The normal distribution says that an individual log reading time may fall above or below 6.00. If \sigma=.20, an observed value of 6.14 is not a contradiction. It is one possible realization from a distribution centered at 6.00.
We can simulate six responses at declared predictor values:


Code
set.seed(214)

x <- c(2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8)
conditional_mean <- 5.70 + .06 * x
y <- rnorm(length(x), mean = conditional_mean, sd = .20)

data.frame(
  surprisal = x,
  conditional_mean = conditional_mean,
  simulated_response = y
)


The conditional means lie exactly on the declared line. The simulated responses do not. Regression represents both facts: systematic change in the center and unexplained variation around that center.
Thus the complete model makes three commitments:

the conditional mean is linear;
responses around that mean are normally distributed; and
the conditional response variance is the same at every x.

It also inherits a sampling commitment from the earlier inference pages. The observations are treated as conditionally independent under this simple model. Repeated words from the same participant or repeated observations of the same item may violate that claim. The equation does not stop being linear, but the complete probability model is then missing the repeated structure.

title: A straight-line mean
section: Separate a line from a causal claim
text:
Separate a line from a causal claim
A positive \beta_1 describes a conditional association under the model. It does not by itself show that surprisal causes longer reading times. Word length, frequency, position, and other lexical or contextual properties may vary with surprisal.
Moving from a fitted association to a causal statement requires a design-based identification argument. Adding a normal response distribution or estimating the slope precisely does not supply that argument. A causal claim needs a design or identification argument that distinguishes the proposed cause from alternative sources of the association.






NoteCalculate two means




If \beta_0=5.70 and \beta_1=.06, calculate m(3) and m(7). How much does the expected response change across that four-bit difference?
Why does a conditional mean of 6.00 not require every observed response at that predictor value to equal 6.00?
Give one response pattern that a straight-line mean cannot represent.
Explain why the fitted surprisal association does not by itself license a causal interpretation.



The centering page changes the reference value for the intercept without changing this fitted line.

title: Transforming a response
text:
The straight-line mean does not determine the scale on which the response should be modeled. Reaction times are positive and often right skewed. Most responses cluster in a relatively narrow fast range, while a smaller number extend far into the slow tail. An ordinary linear regression fitted to raw milliseconds can consequently predict negative values and leave strongly skewed residuals.
One possible response is to transform the measurement before fitting the model. For a positive response Y_i, define
Z_i=\log Y_i.
The regression is then a model for the conditional mean of log response time:
Z_i
=
\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i,
\qquad
\epsilon_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2).
The logarithm is the new concept. The linear regression machinery is unchanged.
The transformation changes the scale on which the model treats effects as additive. On the raw scale, a linear model treats equal millisecond differences as comparable. On the log scale, it treats equal ratios as comparable.

title: Transforming a response
text:
See what the logarithm does
Compare three response times:



milliseconds
natural log




400
5.99


800
6.68


1600
7.38



Doubling from 400 to 800 milliseconds adds about .69 on the log scale. Doubling again from 800 to 1600 adds the same amount. Equal ratios on the original scale become equal differences on the log scale.
This property makes a linear coefficient multiplicative after back-transformation.
The reverse is also true. Equal differences on the log scale become equal ratios on the original scale. Since

\log(2y)-\log(y)=\log 2,

doubling any positive response produces the same log difference. But adding 400 milliseconds does not. The change from 400 to 800 is a doubling, while the change from 800 to 1200 is only a factor of 1.5.

title: Transforming a response
section: Interpret a coefficient as a ratio
text:
Interpret a coefficient as a ratio
Suppose x_i marks a high-surprisal word and

\beta_1=.08.

The expected log response differs by .08. Exponentiating gives

e^{.08}\approx1.083.

Thus the fitted geometric mean response is about 8.3 percent larger in the high-surprisal condition, under the model.
For a small coefficient, 100\beta_1 is a rough percentage approximation. Reporting 100(e^{\beta_1}-1) gives the exact multiplicative interpretation.
If \beta_1=-.10, then

e^{-.10}\approx.905.

The fitted geometric mean is multiplied by about .905, a decrease of about 9.5 percent. The approximation 100\beta_1=-10 percent is close but not exact.
For a two-unit predictor contrast, the ratio is

e^{2\beta_1}.

Coefficients remain expressed per predictor unit even after the response has been transformed.

title: Transforming a response
text:
Check the transformation in R


Code
response_time <- c(400, 800, 1600)

data.frame(
  response_time = response_time,
  log_response_time = log(response_time),
  recovered_response_time = exp(log(response_time))
)


Exponentiating recovers the original positive measurements up to numerical precision. The transformation is one-to-one on positive values, so no ordering information is lost. Its spacing changes.
The positivity restriction matters. A response of zero has log value -\infty, and a negative response has no real-valued logarithm. A log response model thus requires a measurement whose meaningful support is strictly positive.

title: Transforming a response
section: Do not back-transform the mean mechanically
text:
Do not back-transform the mean mechanically
If

\log Y\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),

then

\mathbb{E}[Y]=e^{\mu+\sigma^2/2},

not merely e^\mu. The quantity e^\mu is the median of the implied lognormal distribution.
Why does the mean differ? Exponentiation is nonlinear. Large positive log-scale deviations increase raw responses more than equally large negative deviations decrease them. The right tail thus pulls the raw-scale mean above e^\mu.
Suppose

\mu=6
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sigma=.30.

Then the raw-scale median is

e^6\approx403.4,

while the raw-scale mean is

e^{6+.30^2/2}
=e^{6.045}
\approx421.9.

The difference grows with \sigma. A single exponentiated fitted mean does not capture it.
This distinction matters when predictions are returned to milliseconds. A model for mean log time is not automatically a model for mean raw time.
The quantity e^{\widehat\mu} cannot automatically be interpreted as a raw-scale mean. That interpretation silently replaces a median-like quantity with a mean. The correction depends on the modeled residual distribution and its variance.

title: Transforming a response
section: Treat the transformation as part of the model
text:
Treat the transformation as part of the model
A transformation changes the response scale, residual pattern, coefficient interpretation, and predictive target. It should not be selected only because a histogram looks more symmetric.
The model should be checked on both scales. A satisfactory log-scale residual plot can coexist with poor predictions of the slow raw-time tail. Conversely, a raw-scale family such as a lognormal or shifted distribution may represent the measurement process more directly.
This is not a contest in which the most symmetric histogram wins. The scale of additivity should match the theoretical comparison and the response-generating process. If a processing account predicts proportional slowing, a log scale may state that claim directly. If it predicts an additive millisecond cost, a log response changes the target.

title: Transforming a response
text:
Report the modeled quantity
A complete coefficient interpretation states both scales. For instance: “A one-bit surprisal increase was associated with a .08 increase in expected log reading time, corresponding to an 8.3 percent multiplicative change in the fitted geometric mean.” This statement does not call the exponentiated value a raw-scale mean.
Predicted raw observations can instead be generated from the complete log-scale response model and summarized on the raw scale. That procedure retains residual variation rather than exponentiating only the conditional mean.






NoteTrack the response scale




What original-scale relationship becomes additive after taking logs?
If \beta_1=-.10, calculate the fitted multiplicative change.
Why is e^{\widehat{\mu}} not generally the predicted raw-scale mean?
What happens when a response equals zero?
Explain why exponentiating a fitted log-scale mean does not automatically give the raw-scale mean.

title: Residualizing a predictor
text:
The multiple-regression page introduced partial coefficients, and the residual page defined an observed minus fitted discrepancy. The process of residualization combines these two ideas, but it does not create a new directly observed linguistic variable.
Suppose surprisal and acceptability are correlated. One proposed response is to regress surprisal on acceptability and use the residual as a predictor of reading time.
The first regression is
S_i
=
\alpha_0+\alpha_1A_i+R_i,
where S_i is surprisal, A_i is acceptability, and R_i is the surprisal residual.
The residual satisfies
R_i
=
S_i-(\widehat{\alpha}_0+\widehat{\alpha}_1A_i).
It is the part of observed surprisal not linearly predicted by acceptability in the fitted sample.
The final phrase is essential. R_i is defined relative to one sample and one linear residualizer. A different sample, a nonlinear residualizer, or a different set of predictors would produce a different residualized variable.
The residual thus depends on the model used to residualize the predictor. It is a statistical construction, not a directly observed linguistic property.

title: Residualizing a predictor
text:
Interpret the new predictor
The second regression might be

Y_i
=
\beta_0+\beta_RR_i+\beta_AA_i+\epsilon_i.
