The coefficient \beta_R describes a change in reading time associated with residual surprisal while acceptability is held fixed. This is not the marginal association of the original surprisal variable.
In an ordinary linear regression containing the same acceptability term, the coefficient on R_i matches the partial coefficient on S_i. Residualization changes the parameterization, not the underlying fitted subspace.
This equivalence can be derived. Since

S_i=\widehat\alpha_0+\widehat\alpha_1A_i+R_i,

substitute this expression into the original response model:

\begin{aligned}
Y_i
&=\beta_0+\beta_SS_i+\beta_AA_i+\epsilon_i\\
&=\beta_0+\beta_S
(\widehat\alpha_0+\widehat\alpha_1A_i+R_i)
+\beta_AA_i+\epsilon_i\\
&=(\beta_0+\beta_S\widehat\alpha_0)
+(\beta_A+\beta_S\widehat\alpha_1)A_i
+\beta_SR_i+\epsilon_i.
\end{aligned}

The coefficient on R_i is the original partial surprisal coefficient \beta_S. The intercept and acceptability coefficient change because the coordinate system has changed.

title: Residualizing a predictor
text:
Verify the equivalence


Code
dat <- data.frame(
  acceptability = c(2.1, 2.8, 3.4, 4.2, 4.8, 5.5, 6.1, 6.7),
  surprisal = c(8.2, 7.4, 7.1, 6.0, 5.8, 4.9, 4.5, 3.7),
  log_rt = c(6.775, 6.712, 6.687, 6.609, 6.596,
             6.523, 6.501, 6.443)
)

fit_residualizer <- lm(surprisal ~ acceptability, data = dat)
dat$residual_surprisal <- residuals(fit_residualizer)

fit_original <- lm(log_rt ~ surprisal + acceptability, data = dat)
fit_residual <- lm(log_rt ~ residual_surprisal + acceptability, data = dat)

c(
  original_surprisal = coef(fit_original)["surprisal"],
  residual_surprisal = coef(fit_residual)["residual_surprisal"]
)


The coefficient on surprisal in the first response model equals the coefficient on residual_surprisal in the second, up to numerical precision.
The other coefficients are not equal. After residualization, the acceptability coefficient absorbs both its original response association and the part of surprisal that the residualizer assigned to acceptability. This is why the residualized fit must be interpreted as a reparameterized system, not as the original coefficient table with one purified predictor substituted.

title: Residualizing a predictor
section: Residualize both variables to expose the partial slope
text:
Residualize both variables to expose the partial slope
The same partial slope can be obtained by residualizing the response with respect to acceptability and regressing those response residuals on residual surprisal:


Code
outcome_residualizer <- lm(log_rt ~ acceptability, data = dat)
dat$residual_log_rt <- residuals(outcome_residualizer)

fit_residual_both <- lm(
  residual_log_rt ~ residual_surprisal,
  data = dat
)

coef(fit_residual_both)["residual_surprisal"]


This calculation reveals the comparison behind a partial coefficient. First remove the linear association with acceptability from both surprisal and the response. Then relate the two remaining quantities.

title: Residualizing a predictor
section: Do not treat residuals as purified constructs
text:
Do not treat residuals as purified constructs
Residual surprisal is not “pure processing difficulty.” It depends on the sample, the residualizer formula, measurement error in both variables, and the chosen functional form.
It is also directional. Residualizing surprisal against acceptability does not produce the same variable as residualizing acceptability against surprisal. The first preserves surprisal units and defines deviations from predicted surprisal. The second preserves acceptability units and defines deviations from predicted acceptability.
If acceptability is measured with error, subtracting its fitted association does not remove the underlying construct cleanly. It can also induce difficult interpretations when the residualizer is trained outside the predictive evaluation loop.
Interpreting that residual as a purified theoretical construct is not licensed. The linear algebra establishes coefficient equivalence. It does not establish that the residual corresponds to one causal or cognitive mechanism.

title: Residualizing a predictor
text:
Keep the residualizer inside cross-validation
For held-out prediction, estimate \widehat{\alpha}_0 and \widehat{\alpha}_1 using only the training fold. Then compute residual surprisal for the test fold from those training estimates.
Residualizing once on the complete dataset allows test-fold predictor relationships to influence the fitted transformation. That is leakage.
The same rule applies to centering constants, scaling constants, and any selected functional form when these are learned from data. The test observations may be transformed using training estimates, but they may not determine those estimates.
Residualization is often unnecessary for an explanatory multiple regression because the original two-predictor model already estimates the same partial surprisal coefficient. The explicit residualizer can still be pedagogically useful because it displays which surprisal variation identifies the coefficient.






NoteInterpret a residualized predictor




What does R_i measure relative to the residualizer model?
Does residualization eliminate uncertainty due to correlated constructs?
Where must the residualizer be fitted during cross-validation?
Which coefficients remain equal between the original and residualized response models, and which may change?
Explain why residualizing a predictor does not isolate a pure theoretical construct.

title: Random slope models
text:
The random-intercept model allowed group baselines to vary while holding one predictor association constant. A random-slope model also lets that association vary across groups.
Suppose every listener hears words in quiet and in noise. The average effect of noise may be positive, but listeners may differ in how strongly noise slows their responses.
A random-intercept model gives listeners different baselines while imposing one common noise association. A random-slope model allows that association to vary across listeners.

title: Random slope models
text:
Add a listener specific association
Let X_{ij}=1 mark noise and X_{ij}=0 mark quiet for trial i from listener j. Write

Y_{ij}
=\beta_0+b_{0j}
+(\beta_1+b_{1j})X_{ij}
+\varepsilon_{ij}.

The population noise association is \beta_1. Listener j has association

\beta_1+b_{1j}.

Model the slope deviations with

b_{1j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau_1^2).

The standard deviation \tau_1 describes between-listener variation in the noise association.

title: Random slope models
text:
Compare fitted listener lines
Suppose the population noise association is \beta_1=.20 on the log response time scale. Listener A has b_{1A}=-.05, while listener B has b_{1B}=.25. Their fitted associations are

.20-.05=.15

and

.20+.25=.45.

Both listeners are predicted to respond more slowly in noise, but the change is larger for listener B. The random intercepts can separately place their quiet baselines at different levels.
The population coefficient \beta_1 remains the average modeled association across the listener population. The random slope standard deviation states how incomplete that average is as a description of individual listeners.

title: Random slope models
section: Check that the design contains the contrast
text:
Check that the design contains the contrast
A listener specific noise association is a within listener comparison. Each listener must contribute information in both quiet and noise conditions. If listener A appears only in quiet and listener B appears only in noise, their baseline difference is inseparable from a listener specific noise difference.
The predictor may vary across the complete dataset and still fail to vary within listeners. A random slope for group j requires the relevant predictor contrast within enough levels of that group.
This within-group predictor variation can be checked before fitting:
with(
  word_recognition,
  table(listener, noise_condition)
)
For a binary condition, inspect whether listeners have observations in both columns. For a continuous predictor, inspect its within listener range. A population association estimated mostly from between listener differences does not support listener specific within listener slopes.

title: Random slope models
section: Fit slope variation without a new correlation
text:
Fit slope variation without a new correlation
In lme4, use separate intercept and slope terms to add slope variation while leaving its correlation with the intercept for the next page:
library(lme4)

fit_slopes <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ noise_condition +
    (1 | listener) +
    (0 + noise_condition | listener) +
    (1 | word),
  data = word_recognition
)
(1 | listener) adds listener baseline variation. (0 + noise_condition | listener) adds a listener deviation for the noise association without estimating its correlation with the intercept. (1 | word) represents repeated word items.
For a numeric predictor, (1 + predictor || listener) is a compact alternative that requests uncorrelated intercept and slope variation. Factor predictors can require explicit numeric contrasts for this syntax to produce the intended terms.

title: Random slope models
text:
See how the dependence changes
Two trials from listener j share b_{0j}. They also contain b_{1j}X_{ij} and b_{1j}X_{i'j}. The contribution of the slope deviation depends on the predictor values.
Two noise trials share both baseline and noise deviations. A quiet trial and a noise trial share the baseline, but only the noise trial receives the binary slope deviation under treatment coding. Thus one constant within listener correlation no longer describes every trial pair.
This dependence is the probabilistic consequence of random slope variation. A random-intercept-only model leaves persistent differences in listener condition associations in its residual structure.

title: Random slope models
text:
Match slope variation to generalization
If noise is manipulated within listeners and the claim concerns a population of listeners, listener slope variation is part of the target. If word types also appear in both quiet and noise, the noise association may vary across words as well. Each proposed random slope requires the relevant predictor contrast within levels of its grouping factor.
Adding a slope is not justified solely because software permits it. The design must supply the contrast, and the scientific claim must require generalization across that grouping population.






NoteCheck the design



Why can noise condition vary across the complete dataset while failing to vary within listeners? What table would reveal the problem before fitting?


The next page introduces a possible relation between group baselines and group slopes.

title: Random effects and partial pooling
text:
The preceding page separated planned population contrasts from variation across sampled groups. A random-effects model represents the latter through a shared group distribution and partial pooling.
Suppose three speakers have observed mean vowel durations of 90, 110, and 160 ms. The first two means are based on 20 tokens each. The third is based on only 2 tokens. Treating 160 ms as an equally stable speaker estimate ignores the difference in information.
A random effects model addresses this problem through partial pooling. Each speaker has a distinct deviation, but those deviations belong to one estimated population distribution.

title: Random effects and partial pooling
section: Model deviations from a shared center
text:
Model deviations from a shared center
Let \beta_0 be the population baseline. Give speaker j a deviation b_j:

\text{speaker baseline}_j
=\beta_0+b_j.

Model the deviations as draws from a common distribution:

b_j\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau^2).

The parameter \tau is the standard deviation of speaker baselines around the population baseline. The deviation b_j is the random effect introduced on the preceding page.
The zero center is not a claim that speakers do not differ. It defines \beta_0 as the population center and lets positive and negative deviations occur around it. The parameter \tau measures the extent of those differences.

title: Random effects and partial pooling
text:
Compare three pooling strategies
Complete pooling ignores persistent speaker differences. Every speaker receives the same baseline \beta_0.
No pooling estimates an unrelated baseline for every speaker. The two token speaker estimate relies only on two observations.
Partial pooling combines each speaker’s observations with the estimated population distribution. Speakers can differ, but the amount of evidence for each difference matters.
These strategies represent different claims. Complete pooling says the group labels add no persistent structure. No pooling says the observed groups share no informative population relation. Partial pooling says the groups vary and that their deviations arise from a common population.

title: Random effects and partial pooling
text:
See where shrinkage comes from
In a simple random-intercept model with known variances, the estimated speaker deviation has the form

\widehat b_j
=w_j(\overline y_j-\beta_0),

where

w_j
=\frac{n_j\tau^2}
{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2}.

The quantity w_j is between zero and one. It determines how much of the raw speaker difference is retained.
If n_j is small or the residual variance \sigma^2 is large, w_j is closer to zero. The estimate moves toward the population baseline. If n_j is large and the observations are consistent, w_j is closer to one. The estimate remains closer to the speaker’s raw mean.
This movement is called shrinkage or partial pooling. It is a consequence of the joint probability model, not a correction applied after unrelated speaker means have been estimated.

title: Random effects and partial pooling
text:
Keep two variances separate
The group standard deviation

\tau

describes stable between speaker baseline variation. The residual standard deviation

\sigma

describes token variation around a speaker’s baseline and the modeled predictor effects.
One cannot substitute for the other. A large residual variance does not represent persistent speaker differences. A large group variance does not represent token noise within a speaker.

title: Random effects and partial pooling
text:
Understand the exchangeability claim
The shared distribution treats speaker labels as exchangeable after conditioning on included predictors. Before observing the responses, swapping labels p01 and p02 does not change the model. The labels identify groups, but the model does not give one label a special distribution without a predictor that justifies it.
If speakers differ systematically by measured age or dialect, that structure should enter the population relation. The random effects then describe remaining speaker variation after those predictors are known.
Exchangeability is thus conditional rather than absolute. It asks whether the unexplained deviations can reasonably share one distribution. A model that pools speakers across known populations with very different variance structures may need a more specific group model.

title: Random effects and partial pooling
text:
Read a pooled estimate carefully
An estimated deviation near zero can have two sources. The speaker’s observations may lie close to the population relation, or the observations may provide little information and receive strong shrinkage. The estimate alone cannot distinguish these cases. Its uncertainty and the number of observations are part of the interpretation.






NoteCheck the pooling



Why should a speaker mean based on two tokens usually receive more shrinkage than a speaker mean based on two hundred consistent tokens? Which quantities in w_j express this difference?


The next page places one partially pooled baseline deviation in a regression equation.

title: Correlations among random effects
text:
The random-slope page gave each group a baseline deviation and an association deviation. The two deviations may themselves be related. Listeners with slower baselines may, for instance, show larger effects of background noise.
A random-effects correlation represents this population relation among deviations.

title: Correlations among random effects
Correlations among random effects
text:
Interpret the sign
Suppose the response is log response time and the predictor marks a difficult condition. A positive intercept-slope correlation means that participants with slower than average baselines tend to have larger than average difficulty associations. A negative correlation means that slower baselines tend to accompany smaller difficulty associations.
If \rho=0, the model treats baseline and association deviations as uncorrelated in the group population. It does not say that either variance is zero. Groups may still differ substantially in both quantities.
The sign must be interpreted with the predictor coding. If the difficulty predictor is reversed, every slope changes sign and the correlation changes sign. The underlying fitted lines can remain identical.

title: Correlations among random effects
section: Notice why the intercept definition matters
text:
Notice why the intercept definition matters
For a continuous predictor, the random intercept is the group deviation at X=0. If zero lies far outside the observed range, the intercept describes an extrapolated baseline. Its correlation with the slope may be difficult to interpret and weakly estimated.
Suppose observed speech rates range from 4 to 8 syllables per second. With the raw predictor, the intercept concerns a rate of zero. Centering at 6 changes the intercept to the fitted response at an observed, meaningful speech rate:

X_i^{c}=X_i-6.

The fitted response lines do not change, but the intercept deviations now refer to a different point on those lines. Their correlation with the slopes can change because the baseline itself has changed.
This is not a contradiction. The intercept-slope correlation is parameterization dependent. A report should state the predictor reference point before interpreting it.

title: Correlations among random effects
text:
Fit the joint covariance
In lme4, a single grouping term with an intercept and slope estimates their covariance:
fit_correlated <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ noise_condition +
    (1 + noise_condition | listener) +
    (1 | word),
  data = word_recognition
)
The listener term estimates \tau_0, \tau_1, and \rho. By contrast, the separate terms on the preceding page estimate both variances without \rho.
The correlated model is more flexible. It also requires enough listener levels and enough within listener contrasts to estimate an additional population parameter.

title: Correlations among random effects
text:
Recognize weak information
A fitted correlation near 1 or -1 can reflect a strong intercept-slope relation. It can also arise when the covariance structure is too rich for the available groups. Wide uncertainty, small group counts, sparse within group contrasts, or a singular fit make a substantive story premature.
The point estimate should thus be accompanied by the variance estimates and fitting diagnostics. If \tau_1 is nearly zero, a slope correlation has little stable variation to relate to the intercept.

title: Correlations among random effects
text:
Remove the correlation deliberately
An uncorrelated structure can be appropriate when the intercept-slope correlation is not part of the scientific target or cannot be estimated reliably:
fit_uncorrelated <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ noise_condition +
    (1 | listener) +
    (0 + noise_condition | listener) +
    (1 | word),
  data = word_recognition
)
This simplification changes the population model. It asserts zero correlation rather than merely hiding a printed value. The decision should follow the design, the target, and the available information.






NoteCheck the baseline



Why can centering a predictor change the intercept slope correlation without changing any fitted regression line? What does a correlation of zero leave free to vary?


The next page examines covariance structures that collapse to fewer effective dimensions than their formulas request.

title: Poisson regression
text:
The earlier chapters introduced the Poisson distribution, and the generalized-linear-model sequence introduced the log link. Poisson regression combines these components for count responses.
Suppose each row records a speaker turn, and the response counts filled pauses such as uh and um. Some turns contain no filled pause, others contain one, and a few contain several. A predictor records a centered measure of planning difficulty. The linguistic question is whether the expected number of filled pauses changes with that predictor.
The response is not continuous and cannot be negative. A straight line for the expected count can nevertheless cross below zero. Poisson regression avoids this problem by combining a Poisson response with a log link. The Poisson distribution describes the count variation. The log link keeps its expected value positive while retaining an additive linear predictor.

title: Poisson regression
text:
State the response model
Let Y_i be the number of filled pauses in turn i. Poisson regression begins with

Y_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_i),

where

\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid x_i]=\lambda_i
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid x_i)=\lambda_i.

The parameter \lambda_i is the conditional expected count. It is not required to be an integer. An expected value of 2.4 means that repeated turns with the represented predictor value would average 2.4 filled pauses under the model.
The equality between conditional mean and conditional variance is a substantive part of the Poisson model. Regression will let both quantities change with x_i, but it will not let them change independently.

title: Poisson regression
text:
Use the log link
The expected count must be positive, while a linear predictor can be any real number. Poisson regression writes

\log\lambda_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i.

Exponentiating both sides gives

\lambda_i=\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i).

The exponential is always positive. Thus every value of the linear predictor yields a valid expected count. As in logistic regression, the link applies to a conditional parameter rather than to the observed response. We do not take the logarithm of each observed count, so a recorded zero creates no special problem.

title: Poisson regression
text:
Work through a small change
Suppose

\beta_0=\log2
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\beta_1=.20.

At the centered predictor value x=0,

\lambda(0)=\exp(\log2)=2.

At x=1,

\lambda(1)
=\exp(\log2+.20)
=2e^{.20}
\approx2.44.

At x=2,

\lambda(2)
=\exp(\log2+.40)
=2e^{.40}
\approx2.98.

The expected count rises by about .44 in the first step and .54 in the second. The additive change is constant on the log scale, not the count scale.

title: Poisson regression
section: Interpret the slope as a rate ratio
text:
Interpret the slope as a rate ratio
Compare expected counts one predictor unit apart:

\begin{aligned}
\frac{\lambda(x+1)}{\lambda(x)}
&=\frac{\exp[\beta_0+\beta_1(x+1)]}
        {\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1x)}\\
&=e^{\beta_1}.
\end{aligned}

For \beta_1=.20,

e^{.20}\approx1.22.

A one unit increase in planning difficulty multiplies the expected filled pause count by about 1.22. Equivalently, it raises the expected count by about 22 percent. It does not add .20 filled pauses.
If \beta_1 is negative, the ratio lies between zero and one. For \beta_1=-.40,

e^{-.40}\approx.67.

The expected count is multiplied by .67, which is a decrease of about 33 percent. Describing this as a 67 percent decrease would confuse the remaining proportion with the amount lost.

title: Poisson regression
text:
Fit and predict in R
fit_pauses <- glm(
  filled_pauses ~ planning_difficulty,
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = speaker_turns
)
The formula supplies the linear predictor. poisson(link = "log") supplies the response distribution and link. The fitted coefficient table is on the log expected count scale.
Exponentiate the slope to obtain the rate ratio:
exp(coef(fit_pauses)["planning_difficulty"])
Then obtain expected counts at concrete predictor values:
new_turns <- data.frame(planning_difficulty = c(-1, 0, 1))

predict(
  fit_pauses,
  newdata = new_turns,
  type = "response"
)
These response scale predictions should accompany the ratio when the audience needs to understand the practical size of the association. A 22 percent increase can describe a change from .05 to .061 expected pauses or a change from 5 to 6.1. The ratio is the same, while the expected count difference is not.

title: Poisson regression
section: The observation window is part of the count
text:
The observation window is part of the count
Speaker turns can differ in duration. A five minute stretch of speech offers more opportunities for filled pauses than a five second turn. If the window varies, a count model without exposure can mistake opportunity for a linguistic association.
The present page assumes equal exposure so that the new technique remains Poisson regression with a log link. The next page adds known observation time to the linear predictor. This addition changes the target from an expected count in a common window to an expected rate.

title: Poisson regression
text:
Check the Poisson variation
Even with equal exposure, speakers may vary more than the Poisson distribution permits. Filled pauses may cluster within speakers or conversational episodes, and unmodeled turn types may create extra variation. A mean prediction can look reasonable while the fitted distribution produces too few zeros and too few large counts.
This is not repaired by interpreting the slope differently. It is a response distribution failure. Later pages introduce ways to detect extra Poisson variation and models that relax the equality of conditional mean and variance.






NoteCheck the ratio



If \beta_1=-.40, calculate e^{\beta_1}. State both the remaining proportion and the percentage decrease in the expected count. Then explain why neither number is an additive change in filled pauses.

title: Poisson regression
text:
What Poisson regression adds
Poisson regression models a nonnegative count with a Poisson distribution and keeps its expected value positive through a log link. Coefficients are additive on the log expected count scale and multiplicative on the count scale. The model also retains the Poisson mean and variance relation. The offset page next handles rows with different amounts of opportunity for the counted event.

title: Poisson mixed-effects models
text:
This page combines Poisson regression, an exposure offset, and a random intercept. The model answers a rate question while retaining repeated speaker structure.
Suppose a sociolinguistic corpus divides each interview into segments and counts filled pauses in each segment. Segments differ in duration, and several segments come from each speaker. A useful analysis must represent the response as a count, adjust for the amount of speech, and retain the repeated speaker structure.
A Poisson mixed-effects model combines these components. This page introduces no new distribution or grouping device. Its purpose is to show how the components work together in one linguistic analysis.

title: Poisson mixed-effects models
text:
State the observation and target
Let Y_{ij} be the number of filled pauses in segment i from speaker j. Let t_{ij} be the segment duration in minutes, and let x_{ij} be a centered measure of speech rate.
The target is the association between speech rate and the expected filled pause rate per minute. It is not the association between speech rate and raw counts. Longer segments create more opportunities for a filled pause even when the underlying rate is unchanged.
Speaker is the repeated unit. Several rows from the same speaker may share an unmeasured baseline tendency to produce filled pauses. This is the dependence that the random intercept will represent.

title: Poisson mixed-effects models
text:
Assemble the conditional model
Conditional on speaker j’s random intercept, use a Poisson response:

Y_{ij}\mid b_{0j}
\sim
\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_{ij}).

Place the exposure offset, fixed predictor, and random intercept in the log expected count:

\log\lambda_{ij}
=
\log t_{ij}
+
\beta_0
+
\beta_1x_{ij}
+
b_{0j},

where

b_{0j}\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_0^2).

Each term has one job. The offset \log t_{ij} accounts for known observation time. The coefficient \beta_1 describes the population association with speech rate. The deviation b_{0j} represents persistent speaker differences left after speech rate has been included.

title: Poisson mixed-effects models
text:
Move from counts to rates
Exponentiating the linear predictor gives

\lambda_{ij}
=
t_{ij}
\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1x_{ij}+b_{0j}).

Divide both sides by duration:

\frac{\lambda_{ij}}{t_{ij}}
=
\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1x_{ij}+b_{0j}).

The right side is the conditional expected filled pause rate per minute. This rate conditions on a particular speaker deviation. Multiplying it by duration returns the expected count for one segment.
Suppose \beta_0=\log 1.5, \beta_1=.25, x_{ij}=1, and b_{0j}=.30. The fitted rate is

1.5\exp(.25+.30)
\approx
2.60

filled pauses per minute. For a two minute segment, the expected count is

2(2.60)=5.20.

The fact that an expected count is not an integer causes no problem. Repeated segments with these properties would average about 5.20 filled pauses under the model.

title: Poisson mixed-effects models
text:
Interpret each multiplicative change
Holding speaker and duration fixed, a one unit increase in centered speech rate multiplies the expected rate by

\exp(\beta_1).

For \beta_1=.25,

\exp(.25)\approx1.28.

The fitted expected rate is thus about 28 percent higher. This comparison is conditional on the same speaker deviation. It should not be described as an additive increase of .25 filled pauses.
The speaker deviation also has a multiplicative interpretation. A speaker with b_{0j}=.30 has a fitted rate multiplied by

\exp(.30)\approx1.35

relative to a speaker at the center of the random effect distribution, with the other predictors held fixed. The standard deviation \tau_0 describes variation among speaker baselines on the log rate scale.

title: Poisson mixed-effects models
text:
Fit the assembled model
The data must contain one row per segment, a nonnegative integer count, a positive duration, the predictor, and a speaker identifier. The corresponding R model is
fit_pauses <- lme4::glmer(
  filled_pause_count ~ speech_rate_centered +
    offset(log(segment_minutes)) +
    (1 | speaker_id),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = speech_segments
)
The offset has a coefficient fixed at one. The speaker term groups rows that share a speaker. Replacing speaker_id with a unique segment identifier would not represent the repeated unit.
For two segments from the same speaker with the same speech rate, tripling duration triples the expected count. For two speakers with the same predictor value and duration, differences in fitted counts may reflect their estimated speaker deviations.

title: Poisson mixed-effects models
text:
Preserve the conditioning statement
Conditional on b_{0j}, the model retains the Poisson mean and variance relation:

\operatorname{Var}(Y_{ij}\mid b_{0j})
=
\operatorname{E}(Y_{ij}\mid b_{0j})
=
\lambda_{ij}.

This statement concerns segments from a speaker with a given deviation. A prediction for a new speaker must instead average over the speaker distribution. These conditional and population predictions need not have the same variance. The distinction is developed on the next page.






NoteCheck the assembled model




Which term changes expected counts when segment duration changes?
Which term represents persistent differences among speakers?
If \beta_1=.25, what is the expected rate ratio for a one unit predictor increase?
Why does the Poisson mean and variance equality above condition on b_{0j}?



The next page shows how speaker heterogeneity can produce extra Poisson variation when the random effects are averaged out.

title: Ordinal regression
text:
The earlier pages introduced categorical responses and the logit link. Ordinal regression uses those ideas when the response categories have a known order but no defensible numerical spacing. A commitment response of no, maybe, or yes places maybe between the two endpoints. It does not establish that the change from no to maybe is the same size as the change from maybe to yes.
Coding the categories as 1, 2, and 3 and fitting a linear regression adds that equal spacing assumption. Deleting maybe and fitting a binary logistic regression changes the response and discards the observations that may reveal uncertainty. Ordinal regression keeps the order while leaving the distance between adjacent categories unspecified.
This page introduces the cumulative logit model. It reuses the earlier probability, logit, linear-predictor, and categorical-response concepts.

title: Ordinal regression
section: Replace category scores with cumulative events
text:
Replace category scores with cumulative events
Let the ordered response be

Y_i\in\{\text{no},\text{maybe},\text{yes}\}.

The order creates two cumulative events:

Y_i\leq\text{no}

and

Y_i\leq\text{maybe}.

The first event contains only no. The second contains no and maybe. The remaining probability belongs to yes.
An ordinal model thus does not assign a numerical distance to the category labels. It models the probability of falling at or below each boundary in the ordered response.

title: Ordinal regression
text:
Introduce two ordered cutpoints
Let

\eta_i=\mathbf{x}_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta

be the linear predictor. Introduce cutpoints \kappa_1<\kappa_2. The cumulative logit model is

\operatorname{logit}\Pr(Y_i\leq c)
=\kappa_c-\eta_i,
\qquad c\in\{1,2\}.

The cutpoints divide an ordered latent location into the three recorded response regions. The ordering constraint matters. If \kappa_1 exceeded \kappa_2, the probability of being at or below no could exceed the probability of being at or below maybe.
Using the logistic cumulative distribution function F(z)=1/(1+e^{-z}), the category probabilities are

\Pr(Y_i=\text{no})=F(\kappa_1-\eta_i),


\Pr(Y_i=\text{maybe})
=F(\kappa_2-\eta_i)-F(\kappa_1-\eta_i),

and

\Pr(Y_i=\text{yes})=1-F(\kappa_2-\eta_i).

These probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one. Increasing \eta_i moves probability toward higher categories.

title: Ordinal regression
text:
Calculate one condition by hand
Suppose

\kappa_1=-.8,
\qquad
\kappa_2=1,
\qquad
\eta_i=0.

The probability of no is

F(-.8)\approx.310.

The cumulative probability through maybe is

F(1)\approx.731.

Thus the probability of maybe is

.731-.310=.421,

and the probability of yes is

1-.731=.269.

Now suppose a predictor raises the linear predictor from zero to one. The new probabilities are

\Pr(Y_i=\text{no})=F(-1.8)\approx.142,


\Pr(Y_i=\text{maybe})=F(0)-F(-1.8)\approx.358,

and

\Pr(Y_i=\text{yes})=1-F(0)=.500.

The one unit location shift reduces no probability, slightly reduces maybe probability, and raises yes probability. An ordinal coefficient is not a constant change in any one category probability. The complete response scale interpretation requires all three predicted probabilities.

title: Ordinal regression
section: Interpret one coefficient at both boundaries
text:
Interpret one coefficient at both boundaries
Suppose x_i increases by one and its coefficient is \beta. Because the model uses \kappa_c-\eta_i, a positive coefficient reduces the cumulative log odds at every cutpoint. Equivalently, it multiplies the odds of falling above each cutpoint by e^\beta.
For the three category response, the same coefficient describes both of these comparisons:

maybe or yes compared with no;
yes compared with no or maybe.

This shared coefficient is the proportional odds assumption. The model assumes that a predictor shifts the response upward through one common location change rather than having a separate effect at each boundary.
The assumption does not say that the category probabilities change by the same amount. They generally do not, as the hand calculation shows. It says that one log odds coefficient applies to both cumulative partitions.

title: Ordinal regression
text:
Fit the model in R
The response must be an ordered factor whose level order matches the linguistic scale:
judgments$commitment <- ordered(
  judgments$commitment,
  levels = c("no", "maybe", "yes")
)

fit_commitment <- ordinal::clm(
  commitment ~ embedding_environment,
  data = judgments,
  link = "logit"
)
The formula specifies the location predictor. The model estimates two cutpoints because the response has three categories. Reversing the factor levels reverses the direction of the fitted location scale, so the level order must be inspected before any coefficient is interpreted.
Predicted category probabilities provide the most direct summary:
new_environments <- data.frame(
  embedding_environment = levels(judgments$embedding_environment)
)

predict(
  fit_commitment,
  newdata = new_environments,
  type = "prob"
)
The output should be reported as a row of probabilities for each environment. A statement that one condition has a coefficient of 1.2 on an unnamed latent scale leaves the linguistic response implicit.

title: Ordinal regression
text:
Check the shared shift
A predictor may primarily distinguish no from the other responses while doing little to separate maybe from yes. In that case, a single shared coefficient can conceal a category specific pattern. The proportional odds assumption should thus be checked against predicted and observed category distributions at theoretically relevant predictor values.
Sparse categories create another limitation. If no responses are rare, the first boundary has little information. A model may estimate a broad upward shift while the data provide weak evidence about how that shift is divided between the two cumulative comparisons.
The present model also treats rows as conditionally independent. Repeated judgments from the same participant or repeated discourses require a dependence model introduced after the mixed effects foundation.






NoteCheck the order



If a predictor has a positive coefficient, which response direction receives more probability? Why does this sign depend on the order of the factor levels? What common restriction connects the two cumulative comparisons?

title: Ordinal regression
text:
What ordinal regression adds
Ordinal regression models ordered categories through cumulative events and ordered cutpoints. It preserves the category order without assuming equal numerical spacing. One location coefficient shifts every cumulative logit under the proportional odds assumption, so interpretation should return to the full set of category probabilities. After the mixed effects foundation, ordinal mixed models add repeated participant and item structure to this response model.

title: Ordered-beta regression
text:
A bounded response can combine three observable possibilities: the lower endpoint, an interior value, and the upper endpoint. Standard beta regression cannot represent this response space, and nudging endpoints inward makes an arbitrary constant part of the likelihood. Ordered-beta regression combines the ordered cutpoints introduced for ordinal regression with a beta distribution for interior responses.
We will construct the likelihood after rescaling the response to Y_i\in[0,1] and treating exact endpoints as genuine outcomes of the measurement process.

title: Ordered-beta regression
text:
One ordered location
Let

\eta_i=\beta_0+\mathbf{x}_i^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol\beta

be a linear predictor and let \kappa_0<\kappa_1 be two cutpoints. The model partitions the response into three ordered regions:

Y_i=0,\qquad 0<Y_i<1,\qquad Y_i=1.

Using the logistic CDF F, the region probabilities can be written as

\Pr(Y_i=0)=F(\kappa_0-\eta_i),


\Pr(0<Y_i<1)
=F(\kappa_1-\eta_i)-F(\kappa_0-\eta_i),

and

\Pr(Y_i=1)=1-F(\kappa_1-\eta_i).

These three probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one. Increasing \eta_i shifts probability upward: away from zero, through the interior, and toward one. The ordering connects endpoint use to the same latent location that organizes the interior response.

title: Ordered-beta regression
text:
The interior distribution
Conditional on falling inside the bounds, the response follows a beta distribution. One common parameterization uses

\mu_i=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\eta_i)

and a positive precision parameter \phi:

Y_i\mid 0<Y_i<1
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\mu_i\phi,(1-\mu_i)\phi).

The conditional interior mean is \mu_i. Larger \phi concentrates interior values near that mean; smaller \phi permits greater interior variation.
The full predictive distribution is thus mixed: discrete at zero and one, continuous between them. A histogram alone can obscure this structure because the endpoint bars and interior bins do not represent the same kind of probability.

title: Ordered-beta regression
section: Why the ordering is an assumption
text:
Why the ordering is an assumption
Ordered-beta regression is parsimonious because one predictor shifts the lower endpoint, interior location, and upper endpoint in an ordered way. This economy can also fail. Suppose some participants use 100 as a protest response unrelated to the latent continuum, or a floor response arises from a separate detection process. Then a model with distinct endpoint processes may fit better and may correspond more closely to the task.
Thus ordered-beta regression assumes that predictor effects on endpoint use and interior location arise through one ordered latent dimension. This ordering should be checked, not accepted merely because the model permits zeros and ones.

title: Ordered-beta regression
text:
Coefficients require predictions
An ordered-beta coefficient lives on the latent location scale. Its sign is often useful: a negative same-sense coefficient on a dissimilarity response shifts mass toward lower ratings. Its magnitude, however, does not equal a constant change in the observed mean. The change depends on the starting location, both cutpoints, and the precision.
Interpret the fitted model by comparing predictive distributions. For two conditions, report at least:

predicted probability of the lower endpoint;
predicted probability of the upper endpoint;
predicted mean or median on the recorded scale; and
an interval or plot showing interior variation.

These summaries reveal whether a predictor mainly shifts interior responses, changes endpoint use, or does both.

title: Ordered-beta regression
text:
Fitting the model
The ordbetareg package supplies a brms interface. A simple model has the same formula structure as other regressions:
ratings$dissimilarity_01 <- ratings$dissimilarity / 100

fit <- ordbetareg::ordbetareg(
  dissimilarity_01 ~ same_sense,
  data = ratings,
  chains = 4,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 20260825
)
Repeated participants or items require dependence terms already justified by the design. Adding them changes the conditional comparisons and the uncertainty; it is not an optional cosmetic repair.

title: Ordered-beta regression
text:
Predictive checks
An ordered-beta fit should reproduce more than the overall mean. Check the three parts separately:

compare observed and predicted mass at zero;
compare observed and predicted mass at one; and
compare the observed and predicted interior distribution.

Repeat these checks by theoretically relevant conditions and by major dependence units. A model can recover aggregate endpoint mass while missing that some participants never use endpoints and others use them on most trials.
Posterior computation requires the ordinary convergence checks as well. Endpoint flexibility does not rescue divergent transitions, low effective sample sizes, or an unidentified cutpoint.






NoteThe model licenses a distributional interpretation



Ordered-beta regression does not merely keep fitted means inside the scale. It assigns probability to each endpoint and density to every interior value. Interpret and check all three parts.

title: Ordered-beta regression
text:
Read the model

If a predictor has a negative coefficient for a 0 to 1 dissimilarity response, which direction should zero mass, the interior location, and one mass move?
Give one observation pattern that would challenge the ordered-boundary assumption.
Why is a good fit to the overall endpoint rate insufficient when participants contribute repeated responses?

title: Ordered-beta regression
text:
Before the application
Ordered-beta regression combines two ordered cutpoints with a beta interior distribution. The ordering makes the model economical, while separate checks of both endpoints and the interior make the assumption observable. The application page uses these tools to analyze event-description dissimilarity.

title: Negative binomial regression
text:
The earlier distribution chapter introduced the negative binomial distribution. In regression, its conditional mean is linked to predictors. Unlike the quasi-Poisson model, a negative binomial regression defines a complete response distribution whose variance can grow faster than its mean.
This page develops that single change and applies it to a theoretically motivated comparison from French liaison.

title: Negative binomial regression
text:
Change the mean variance relation
Let the expected count for observation i be \mu_i. In a common negative binomial parameterization,

Y_i\sim\operatorname{NegBin}(\mu_i,\kappa),


\operatorname{E}(Y_i)=\mu_i,


\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)
=\mu_i+\frac{\mu_i^2}{\kappa}.

The parameter \kappa controls response dispersion. A smaller value permits more variation. As \kappa grows, the quadratic term approaches zero and the variance approaches the Poisson variance.
Suppose \mu_i=5 and \kappa=2. The variance is

5+\frac{5^2}{2}=17.5.

A Poisson response with the same mean would have variance 5. If \kappa=100, the negative binomial variance becomes

5+\frac{25}{100}=5.25,

which is close to the Poisson value. The extra quadratic term allows the variance to exceed the mean.

title: Negative binomial regression
text:
Keep the log linked mean
The mean uses the same systematic relation as Poisson regression:

\log\mu_i
=\log t_i+
\mathbf{x}_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\beta},

where t_i is an optional exposure. The coefficient interpretation also remains multiplicative:

\frac{\mu(x+1)}{\mu(x)}
=e^{\beta_x}.

The negative binomial dispersion parameter changes the response variance. It does not change the theoretical comparison represented by \mathbf{x}_i.






NoteReading: Storme (2024), Sections 4.1 and 4.2.2



Storme, French liaison is allomorphy, not allophony: Evidence from lexical statistics.
Read Section 4.1, Dataset and coding, and Section 4.2.2, Token frequency analysis.
Why this reading? The paper asks whether French liaison is better analyzed as allomorphy or allophony. The morphological analysis predicts that liaison should be concentrated among comparatively frequent morphemes. The analysis thus supplies a theory bearing liaison predictor, and final consonant controls phonotactic differences in lexical frequency.
The paper motivates the negative binomial response by noting that the reconstructed response is an integer. That fact rules out some response models, but it does not distinguish a negative binomial distribution from a Poisson distribution. The analysis below first checks the Poisson variance restriction.

title: Negative binomial regression
section: Construct the response used in the paper
text:
Construct the response used in the paper
The released Study 1 data and code begin with frequency per million from Lexique 3.83. The code sums frequency over forms assigned to the same final morpheme, then multiplies by 100 to approximate a count in a corpus of 100 million tokens.
liaison_words <- read.csv(
  "https://zenodo.org/api/records/12733801/files/study1-data.csv/content"
)

liaison_counts <- aggregate(
  freqfilms2 ~ final_morph + FinalConsonant + Liaison,
  data = liaison_words,
  FUN = sum
)

liaison_counts$count <-
  as.integer(liaison_counts$freqfilms2 * 100)

dim(liaison_counts)
table(liaison_counts$Liaison)
The resulting table contains 11,195 final morphemes. Of these, 4,925 are coded as liaison morphemes and 6,270 as nonliaison morphemes. The response is highly variable. Its median is 11 among nonliaison morphemes and 14 among liaison morphemes, while a small number of very frequent morphemes produce much larger counts.
This response should be described precisely. It is an integer reconstruction from a normalized frequency measure, not a released table of independently observed token totals. The reconstruction may be useful for studying lexical frequency, but the integer conversion does not itself license a count distribution.

title: Negative binomial regression
text:
Diagnose the Poisson restriction
We first fit the theory bearing mean with a Poisson response. Liaison represents the morphological prediction. FinalConsonant controls the identity of the word final consonant.
poisson_fit <- glm(
  count ~ Liaison + FinalConsonant,
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = liaison_counts
)

poisson_dispersion <-
  sum(residuals(poisson_fit, type = "pearson")^2) /
  df.residual(poisson_fit)

poisson_dispersion
The Pearson dispersion ratio is about 1,365,928. This value is not a borderline judgment. The Poisson distribution represents far less conditional variation than the reconstructed counts contain. Its very small coefficient standard errors are thus not credible measures of uncertainty for this comparison.

title: Negative binomial regression
text:
Fit the negative binomial response
We now change only the response distribution:
library(MASS)

negative_binomial_fit <- glm.nb(
  count ~ Liaison + FinalConsonant,
  data = liaison_counts
)

coef(summary(negative_binomial_fit))
negative_binomial_fit$theta
The fitted dispersion parameter is about .119. This small value permits substantial count variation. The liaison coefficient is about 2.236 on the log mean scale. Exponentiating returns the adjusted mean ratio:
exp(coef(negative_binomial_fit)["Liaisonyes"])
The ratio is about 9.35. Conditional on final consonant, the fitted mean reconstructed count is about nine times as large for liaison morphemes as for nonliaison morphemes. The direction matches the morphological prediction in the reading.

title: Negative binomial regression
section: Keep the conclusion proportional to the design
text:
Keep the conclusion proportional to the design
The negative binomial fit addresses the failed Poisson variance restriction. It does not establish that every relevant source of dependence or heterogeneity has been represented. The response derives from frequency estimates and an integer conversion. Morphemes may also be related through lexemes, paradigms, and grammatical classes not represented in the present model.
Thus the defensible lesson has two parts. First, liaison status is associated with much greater reconstructed lexical frequency after final consonant is included. Second, the observed count variation is incompatible with Poisson uncertainty, while the negative binomial dispersion parameter lets the response variance exceed the mean. The second result supports use of the negative binomial over the Poisson for this table. It does not, on its own, settle the phonological analysis of liaison.






NoteCheck the repair



The negative binomial coefficient has the same linguistic interpretation as a log linked Poisson coefficient. Which new parameter changes the response variance? Which problem would remain if related morphemes were treated as independent?

title: Logistic regression
text:
The earlier pages introduced the Bernoulli distribution, the components of a generalized linear model, and log odds. Logistic regression combines those components for a binary response.
Suppose we ask which of two English complement forms a speaker chooses. A token is completed with in or for, and a predictor records a property of the surrounding context. The response has two possible values, but the scientific question still concerns graded variation. We want to know how the probability of an in completion changes with the context.
A linear regression does not respect this response. It can predict values below zero or above one, and it assumes a constant conditional variance around a continuous mean. A binary response instead has a variance determined by its probability. The variance is small near zero and one and largest near one half.
Logistic regression handles this problem by combining a Bernoulli response with a logit link between probabilities and an unrestricted linear predictor. This page assembles and interprets that model rather than introducing the Bernoulli distribution or link again.

title: Logistic regression
text:
Begin with the binary response
Let Y_i=1 mark an in completion and Y_i=0 mark a for completion. Each observed response has a Bernoulli distribution:

Y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i).

Its conditional mean and variance are

\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid x_i]=\pi_i
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid x_i)=\pi_i(1-\pi_i).

The parameter \pi_i is both the expected value of the zero and one response and the probability of an in completion. Regression must let this parameter vary with x_i while keeping it between zero and one.

title: Logistic regression
section: Put the straight line on the log odds scale
text:
Put the straight line on the log odds scale
Probabilities are bounded, while a linear predictor can be any real number. Logistic regression connects the two spaces with the logit link:

\operatorname{logit}(\pi_i)
=\log\left(\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}\right)
=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i.

The right side is an ordinary straight line. The left side converts a probability into log odds using the logit link. It does not transform the observed zeros and ones. It transforms the conditional probability that generates them.
To return to the probability scale, use the inverse logit:

\pi_i
=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)
=\frac{1}{1+\exp[-(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)]}.

The inverse logit maps every real linear predictor to a value strictly between zero and one. Thus the model can use a linear relation without producing an invalid probability.

title: Logistic regression
text:
Work through three predictor values
Suppose \beta_0=-1 and \beta_1=.5. At x=0, the linear predictor is

\eta(0)=-1+.5(0)=-1.

The predicted probability is

\pi(0)=\frac{1}{1+e^1}\approx.269.

At x=2,

\eta(2)=-1+.5(2)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\pi(2)=.50.

At x=4,

\eta(4)=-1+.5(4)=1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\pi(4)\approx.731.

The predictor increases by two units in both steps. The predicted probability rises by about .231 in each of these particular steps because the endpoints are symmetric around the point where \eta=0. That symmetry should not be mistaken for a constant probability slope. Moving two units farther into either tail produces a smaller probability change because the inverse logit flattens near zero and one.

title: Logistic regression
section: Interpret the coefficient on its native scale
text:
Interpret the coefficient on its native scale
The slope \beta_1=.5 is a .5 increase in log odds for a one unit predictor increase. Exponentiating gives the corresponding odds ratio:

e^{.5}\approx1.65.

Thus each one unit increase multiplies the odds of an in completion by about 1.65. This multiplier is constant when the model is additive on the log odds scale. The probability difference is not constant because the same odds multiplier acts on different starting odds.
For instance, consider one unit changes at two locations:









predictor change
starting probability
ending probability
probability change




0 to 1
.269
.378
.109


4 to 5
.731
.818
.087



Both rows represent the same .5 change in log odds and the same 1.65 odds multiplier. They do not represent the same change in probability. A results paragraph should thus state the scale. Saying that the outcome “increases by .5” is incomplete because a binary response cannot increase by .5 in the sense implied by a linear regression coefficient.

title: Logistic regression
text:
Fit the model in R
Suppose completion records in or for, and context_score is the predictor. First make the event coding visible:
completions$in_response <- as.integer(completions$completion == "in")

table(
  completion = completions$completion,
  coded_response = completions$in_response
)
Then fit the model:
fit_completion <- glm(
  in_response ~ context_score,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = completions
)
The formula defines the linear predictor. binomial(link = "logit") supplies the Bernoulli likelihood and the logit link. The model does not infer which category should count as one from the linguistic labels. That choice entered when in_response was constructed.
Response scale predictions make the coding and the nonlinear link concrete:
new_contexts <- data.frame(context_score = c(0, 2, 4))

predict(
  fit_completion,
  newdata = new_contexts,
  type = "response"
)
Without type = "response", predict() returns values on the link scale. Both outputs are useful, but they answer different questions. Link scale values show the additive model. Response scale values show the predicted linguistic choice probabilities.

title: Logistic regression
section: The event coding reverses every sign
text:
The event coding reverses every sign
Suppose we instead define Y_i=1 for a for completion. The fitted probabilities become complements of the original probabilities, and the coefficient signs reverse. No observation has changed. Only the modeled event has changed.
Every interpretation should state the event coded as one. A positive coefficient raises the probability of that category. It does not raise the probability of whichever category sounds linguistically prominent in the prose description.
The same issue affects reference levels for categorical predictors. The earlier coding pages make those numerical contrasts explicit before a categorical logistic model is fitted.

title: Logistic regression
section: A fitted association is not yet a causal effect
text:
A fitted association is not yet a causal effect
A logistic coefficient describes a conditional association under the fitted model. If context_score was observed in a corpus, tokens at different values may also differ in speaker, genre, lexical item, or other properties. The model does not create random assignment.
This limitation does not make the coefficient useless. It fixes the claim. The model estimates how the conditional probability varies across the represented contexts. A causal interpretation requires a design or a stronger identification argument introduced elsewhere.






NoteCheck the coefficient



If e^{\beta_1}=2, what doubles after a one unit increase: probability or odds? Calculate the probability change when the starting probability is .20, and then calculate it when the starting probability is .70.

title: Logistic regression
text:
What logistic regression adds
Logistic regression represents a binary linguistic response with a Bernoulli distribution and places an additive predictor on the log odds scale. Its coefficients describe log odds changes or odds ratios. Its response scale predictions describe changes in the probability of the event coded as one. The next page applies this model to a categorical verb-class predictor.

title: Verb type and temporal preposition choice
text:
The logistic-regression page assembled a Bernoulli response, logit link, and linear predictor. This page applies that model to a contrast represented through the categorical-predictor coding.
The SuperTelicity cloze experiment asked participants to complete event descriptions with temporal phrases. We will focus on whether a completion used in or for and compare manner verbs with result verbs.
The linguistic question is whether the two verb classes differ in the probability of an in completion.
The comparison bears on event structure. An in phrase tends to describe time to a culmination, while a for phrase tends to describe an event’s duration. Result verbs and manner verbs differ in how readily their lexical content supports a culmination. The model estimates the completion difference between the two verb classes.
crumbs: Verb type and temporal preposition choice

title: Verb type and temporal preposition choice
text:
Load and represent the response


Code
cloze <- read.csv("../slides/lecture11/supertelicity/data/data-cloze.csv")
cloze <- subset(cloze, verb_type %in% c("result", "manner") &
                        preposition %in% c("in", "for"))

cloze$in_response <- as.integer(cloze$preposition == "in")
cloze$verb_type <- relevel(factor(cloze$verb_type), ref = "result")


One observation represents one participant’s cloze response to one sentence. The binary response is 1 for in and 0 for for.
The filter yields 9,160 responses. The model treats the two selected prepositions as the complete outcome space for current purposes. Responses with other prepositions are outside this particular binary question rather than being recoded as for.
crumbs: Verb type and temporal preposition choice

title: Verb type and temporal preposition choice
text:
Inspect the observed response table


Code
with(cloze, table(verb_type, in_response))
aggregate(in_response ~ verb_type, data = cloze, FUN = mean)


The data contain 3,434 in responses and 1,446 for responses for result verbs. For manner verbs, they contain 1,442 in responses and 2,838 for responses. The observed in proportions are about .704 and .337.
These proportions show a large verb-class difference before regression. The model expresses that difference on the log odds scale and supplies a framework that can later be extended to repeated units.
crumbs: Verb type and temporal preposition choice

title: Verb type and temporal preposition choice
text:
State the model
Let X_i=1 mark a manner verb and X_i=0 a result verb:

Y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i)

and

\operatorname{logit}(\pi_i)
=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i.

The intercept is the log odds of an in completion for result verbs. The slope is the manner-minus-result log-odds difference.
crumbs: Verb type and temporal preposition choice

title: Verb type and temporal preposition choice
text:
Fit the model


Code
fit_cloze <- glm(
  in_response ~ verb_type,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = cloze
)

coef(fit_cloze)


The fitted intercept is about .865. Applying the inverse logit gives

\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(.865)\approx.704,

which is the fitted in probability for result verbs.
The manner coefficient is about -1.542. It is the manner-minus-result log odds difference. Exponentiating gives

e^{-1.542}\approx.214.

Thus the fitted odds of an in completion for manner verbs are about .214 times the fitted odds for result verbs. This is an odds ratio, not a probability ratio.
crumbs: Verb type and temporal preposition choice

title: Verb type and temporal preposition choice
text:
Return to probabilities
Create one row for each verb class:


Code
new_cloze <- data.frame(
  verb_type = factor(c("result", "manner"),
                     levels = levels(cloze$verb_type))
)

new_cloze$in_probability <- predict(
  fit_cloze,
  newdata = new_cloze,
  type = "response"
)

new_cloze


These fitted probabilities answer the modeled comparison more directly than the raw log-odds coefficients.
The two probabilities should be about .704 for result verbs and .337 for manner verbs. Their difference is

.337-.704=-.367.

The one-predictor model is saturated with respect to the two verb-class proportions, so it reproduces the observed proportion in each class. The coefficient and probability summaries are two parameterizations of the same group comparison.
crumbs: Verb type and temporal preposition choice

title: Verb type and temporal preposition choice
text:
State the licensed linguistic result
Within the selected in and for responses, result verbs have a substantially higher observed and fitted probability of an in completion than manner verbs. This pattern is consistent with the verb-class difference motivated by culmination structure.
The analysis does not show that lexical verb class alone caused each completion. Individual verbs differ within a class, participants differ in their completion preferences, and items differ in their temporal contexts. The present fit deliberately ignores those repeated sources to isolate one-predictor logistic regression.
The analysis is still incomplete as a final experiment model because participants and verbs repeat. For now, we isolate one-predictor logistic regression. The mixed-effects sequence will return to repeated units after their structure has been introduced.
The row-level standard errors incorrectly treat the 9,160 responses as independent. The point estimates reproduce the two class proportions, but the displayed model understates the sampling structure. This limitation is part of the result, not a reason to hide the descriptive verb-class difference.






NoteCheck the reference




If the reference is changed from result to manner, which coefficient signs change? Why do the two fitted probabilities remain the same?
Convert the fitted manner coefficient into an odds ratio.
Calculate the manner-minus-result probability difference.
What unsupported independence claim is added when the row-level standard errors treat all responses as independent?
crumbs: Verb type and temporal preposition choice

title: Uncertainty in a fitted slope
text:
The fitting page produced one estimated slope. As introduced in the chapters on estimators and standard errors, an estimate is one sample result, while its standard error describes variation across repeated samples.
The fitted slope \widehat{\beta}_1 is an estimator. A different sample of words and reading times would generally produce a different value.
Its sampling distribution describes this repeated-sample variation. The standard deviation of that distribution is the slope’s standard error.
The observed estimate must be distinguished from its repeated-sample distribution. The estimate is one number computed from one sample. The sampling distribution is a distribution of numbers we would obtain by repeating the entire sampling and fitting procedure. The standard error summarizes the spread of that second object.
We use the six constructed observations from the fitting page, but define them again so that every calculation on this page can be run on its own.
Code
reading_times <- data.frame(
  surprisal = 2:7,
  log_rt = c(5.78, 5.82, 5.93, 5.99, 6.05, 6.13)
)

fit <- lm(log_rt ~ surprisal, data = reading_times)

title: Uncertainty in a fitted slope
text:
Read the simple-regression formula
For ordinary simple linear regression with constant error variance,

\operatorname{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_1)
=\frac{\sigma}
{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2}}.

The numerator is response variation around the true conditional mean. More residual variation makes the slope harder to estimate.
The denominator measures how widely the predictor values are spread around their mean. A wider range of surprisal values supplies more information about the line’s change.
Sample size enters because adding observations usually adds terms to the denominator. But ten repetitions at nearly the same predictor value do not supply the same slope information as ten observations spread across the predictor range.
In practice, \sigma is unknown and replaced by an estimate.
The formula separates three sources of precision. First, smaller response variation produces a smaller numerator. Second, predictor values farther from their mean produce a larger denominator. Third, additional observations help only insofar as they add predictor spread and information about the response variation. This is why sample size alone does not determine slope precision.

title: Uncertainty in a fitted slope
text:
Compare two predictor designs
Suppose two studies each collect four observations and have the same residual standard deviation. Their predictor values are

\mathbf{x}_A=(4.9,5.0,5.0,5.1)

and

\mathbf{x}_B=(2,4,6,8).

Both means equal 5. The squared predictor deviations are

\sum_i(x_{Ai}-\bar x_A)^2
=(-.1)^2+0^2+0^2+.1^2
=.02

and

\sum_i(x_{Bi}-\bar x_B)^2
=(-3)^2+(-1)^2+1^2+3^2
=20.

If \sigma=.20, the idealized standard errors are

\operatorname{SE}_A
=\frac{.20}{\sqrt{.02}}
\approx1.414

and

\operatorname{SE}_B
=\frac{.20}{\sqrt{20}}
\approx.0447.

The second design is much more informative about change because it observes the response across a wider predictor range. This calculation does not license choosing implausible words merely to widen that range. It shows which feature of the design supplies information about the slope.

title: Uncertainty in a fitted slope
text:
Estimate residual variation
For a fitted simple linear regression, the usual residual variance estimate is

\widehat\sigma^2
=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2}{n-2}.

The denominator is n-2 because two coefficients, the intercept and slope, were estimated from the sample. Taking the square root gives \widehat\sigma, which is substituted into the standard-error formula. Thus the reported standard error depends both on the predictor design and on how far the observed responses fall from the fitted line.
The fitted-model summary performs these calculations:


Code
summary(fit)$coefficients


The slope row contains the estimate, its standard error, a test statistic, and a tail probability. On this page, the first two columns are the objects of interest. The estimate describes fitted change. The standard error describes the estimator’s precision under the model and sampling assumptions.

title: Uncertainty in a fitted slope
text:
Form a coefficient interval
For the constructed observations, the fitted slope is approximately

\widehat{\beta}_1=.07143

with standard error

\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat{\beta}_1)=.00361.

The finite-sample critical value for four residual degrees of freedom is about 2.776. This gives

.07143\mathbin{\pm}2.776(.00361)
\approx[.0614,.0815].

The interval is in log-reading-time units per bit of surprisal.
The endpoints preserve those units. They describe a set of slope values produced by a procedure whose long-run coverage is the declared confidence level, under the assumptions used to derive the procedure.
In R, the fitted model supplies the finite-sample t calculation:


Code
confint(fit, "surprisal", level = .95)


The interval has the repeated-sampling coverage interpretation developed earlier. It is not a posterior probability statement about this particular coefficient interval.
More specifically, imagine repeating the study and interval construction many times while holding the data-generating parameter fixed. About 95 percent of the constructed intervals would contain that fixed slope if the procedure’s assumptions held. After we observe one interval, frequentist probability does not assign a 95 percent probability to the fixed coefficient being inside it.
That reading reverses the roles of procedure and parameter. The procedure is random before data are collected; the parameter is not. Bayesian credible intervals support a different probability statement because the model represents uncertainty about the parameter directly.

title: Uncertainty in a fitted slope
text:
Distinguish coefficient and mean-response uncertainty
The slope interval concerns one coefficient. We may instead ask for uncertainty about the conditional mean at a particular predictor value. For

m(x_0)=\beta_0+\beta_1x_0,

uncertainty in the intercept and slope both contribute. The two coefficient estimates are also associated, so their uncertainties cannot be added as if they were unrelated.
R can construct an interval for the fitted conditional mean:


Code
predict(
  fit,
  newdata = data.frame(surprisal = c(3, 5, 7)),
  interval = "confidence",
  level = .95
)


These intervals are usually narrowest near the center of the observed predictor values and wider toward the edges. The data constrain the line most strongly where predictor observations are concentrated.
This mean-response interval is not an interval for a new individual’s reading time. A new response contains both uncertainty about the conditional mean and observation-level variation around that mean. The latter requires a prediction interval, which is wider. An interval for a new observation must thus remain distinct from an interval for the conditional mean.

title: Uncertainty in a fitted slope
text:
Distinguish precision from adequacy
A narrow interval says that the slope estimator is precise under the fitted model and sampling assumptions. It does not establish that a straight line, constant variance, independent observations, or the chosen predictor set adequately represents the data.
Those assumptions need separate checks. We first define residuals, then organize them into diagnostic plots.






NoteCheck the denominator




Holding residual variation and sample size fixed, which design estimates a slope more precisely: predictor values concentrated between 4.9 and 5.1, or values spread between 2 and 8? Use the standard-error formula.
Distinguish one observed slope estimate from its sampling distribution.
Why is a 95 percent confidence interval not a 95 percent posterior probability statement?
Distinguish an interval for a conditional mean from an interval for a new response.

title: The Laplace approximation
text:
A generalized linear mixed model contains random effects that are not observed directly. The model assigns those effects a population distribution, and the response likelihood is conditional on their values. To obtain a likelihood for the observed responses, we must average over every possible value of the random effects. This is the same marginalization operation introduced for marginal distributions, now applied to a likelihood.
This integral is part of the model definition, but it usually has no simple formula for a logistic or Poisson mixed model. The Laplace approximation replaces the difficult integrand with a simpler shape near its highest point.

title: The Laplace approximation
text:
See why the integral appears
Suppose a Poisson mixed model gives speaker j a random intercept b_j. Conditional on that intercept, the likelihood for the speaker’s responses is

p(\mathbf y_j\mid b_j,\boldsymbol\beta).

The group model assigns the intercept a density

p(b_j\mid\tau).

The speaker’s contribution to the observed data likelihood is thus

p(\mathbf y_j\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\tau)
=
\int
p(\mathbf y_j\mid b_j,\boldsymbol\beta)
p(b_j\mid\tau)
\,db_j.

The product inside the integral is large where two conditions coincide. First, the value of b_j must fit that speaker’s responses. Second, the value must remain plausible under the population distribution. Integration adds the area over all such values rather than selecting only one intercept.

title: The Laplace approximation
text:
Work on the log scale
Define the log integrand

h(b)
=
\log p(\mathbf y_j\mid b,\boldsymbol\beta)
+
\log p(b\mid\tau).

Let \widehat b be the value at which h(b) is largest. This is the conditional mode of the speaker effect for the current model parameters. At that point,

h'(\widehat b)=0.

Near the mode, a second order Taylor approximation gives

h(b)
\approx
h(\widehat b)
+
\frac{1}{2}h''(\widehat b)(b-\widehat b)^2.

The curvature h''(\widehat b) is negative because \widehat b is a maximum. We can write

H=-h''(\widehat b),

where H is positive. The approximation then becomes

h(b)
\approx
h(\widehat b)
-
\frac{H}{2}(b-\widehat b)^2.

This is a quadratic function of b. After exponentiation, it has the shape of a normal density centered at \widehat b.

title: The Laplace approximation
text:
Integrate the simpler shape
The normal-shaped approximation has a known area. In one dimension,

\int \exp[h(b)]\,db
\approx
\exp[h(\widehat b)]
\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{H}}.

Two local quantities determine this area. The height \exp[h(\widehat b)] records how well the best supported random effect fits. The curvature H records how quickly support falls as b moves away from that value. A narrow peak has large curvature and less area than a broad peak of the same height.
With several random effects, the same reasoning uses a mode vector and a curvature matrix. The calculation is larger, but the central move is unchanged. The integrand is replaced by a normal-shaped approximation around its joint mode.

title: The Laplace approximation
section: Keep computation separate from the model
text:
Keep computation separate from the model
The Laplace approximation does not add a predictor, change the response family, or alter the grouping structure. It is a way to calculate an approximate likelihood for a model whose likelihood already requires integration. Confusing the approximation used for computation with the model itself would thus be a mistake.
For instance, lme4::glmer() uses a Laplace approximation when nAGQ = 1:
fit <- lme4::glmer(
  response ~ condition + (1 | participant),
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = trials,
  nAGQ = 1
)
Changing the approximation can change estimated coefficients or variance components because the likelihood is calculated differently. But it does not repair a missing random slope, an inappropriate link, or an incorrect response distribution. Those are model specification problems.

title: The Laplace approximation
section: Know when the local shape may be inadequate
text:
Know when the local shape may be inadequate
The approximation tends to work best when the integrand is concentrated and roughly symmetric near its mode. It may be less accurate when groups contain little information, one response category is rare, variance estimates lie near a boundary, or the integrand is strongly asymmetric.
For an analysis whose conclusion might depend on small coefficient changes, fit a manageable version with a more accurate numerical integration setting and compare the quantities that support the conclusion. Agreement provides evidence that the local quadratic is adequate for those quantities. Disagreement identifies computational sensitivity. It does not by itself say which scientific model is preferable.






NoteCheck the approximation




Why must a generalized linear mixed model average over possible random effect values?
Why is the first derivative term absent at the conditional mode?
What do the height and curvature of the log integrand contribute to the approximated area?
Why can the Laplace approximation not repair a missing grouping term?



The next page uses the approximation behind the scenes while assembling a count model from components already introduced.

title: Earlier-versus-later Helmert contrasts
text:
The Helmert-coding page constructed a sequence in which each later level was compared with the average of earlier levels. We can reverse the grouping question. At each step, compare an earlier level with the average of the levels that follow it.
This contrast family is usually called reverse Helmert contrasts. Some sources use inverse Helmert contrasts. The displayed matrix, rather than the label alone, determines the interpretation.
Suppose a stress factor has three ordered levels: primary stress, secondary stress, and unstressed. A phonetic hypothesis might compare primary stress with the average of the two weaker categories, then compare secondary stress with unstressed.
One unscaled reverse Helmert matrix is
\begin{array}{c|rr}
&C_1&C_2\\\hline
\text{primary}&2&0\\
