\text{secondary}&-1&1\\
\text{unstressed}&-1&-1
\end{array}.
The first column compares primary stress with the average of secondary and unstressed. The second compares secondary stress with unstressed.

title: Earlier-versus-later Helmert contrasts
text:
Derive the coefficient meanings
The linear predictor is

\eta_i=\beta_0+\beta_1C_{1i}+\beta_2C_{2i}.

Substituting each row gives

\eta_{\text{primary}}=\beta_0+2\beta_1,


\eta_{\text{secondary}}=\beta_0-\beta_1+\beta_2,

and

\eta_{\text{unstressed}}=\beta_0-\beta_1-\beta_2.

The primary-minus-weaker-average comparison is

\begin{aligned}
\eta_{\text{primary}}
-\frac{\eta_{\text{secondary}}+\eta_{\text{unstressed}}}{2}
&=(\beta_0+2\beta_1)-(\beta_0-\beta_1)\\
&=3\beta_1.
\end{aligned}

The secondary-minus-unstressed comparison is

\eta_{\text{secondary}}-\eta_{\text{unstressed}}=2\beta_2.

The coefficients encode the reverse Helmert comparisons after accounting for column scaling. Dividing the first column by 3 and the second by 2 would make each coefficient equal the corresponding raw mean difference.

title: Earlier-versus-later Helmert contrasts
text:
When the comparisons are meaningful
ELCs are useful when a theory distinguishes one leading category from a set of categories ordered below it. For the stress example, the first hypothesis groups secondary and unstressed as weaker than primary stress. The second asks whether the two weaker categories are themselves different.
This interpretation requires more than a meaningful order. It requires the particular nested groupings encoded by the columns. Applying reverse Helmert contrasts to an unordered set of dialects would create arbitrary comparisons. Applying them to an ordered factor is also unmotivated if the theory asks for different groupings.
Ordering alone does not justify reverse Helmert contrasts. Order makes the comparison sequence possible. It does not make that sequence theoretically relevant.

title: Earlier-versus-later Helmert contrasts
text:
Inspect predictions as a check
No full-rank contrast matrix changes the fitted mean for each factor level when the same complete model is used. After fitting, reconstruct the level means and verify that the coefficient interpretation matches the matrix.


Code
stress_data <- data.frame(
  stress = factor(
    c("primary", "secondary", "unstressed"),
    levels = c("primary", "secondary", "unstressed")
  )
)

elc <- matrix(
  c(2, -1, -1,
    0,  1, -1),
  nrow = 3,
  ncol = 2
)

colnames(elc) <- c("primary_vs_weaker", "secondary_vs_unstressed")
rownames(elc) <- levels(stress_data$stress)

contrasts(stress_data$stress) <- elc
contrasts(stress_data$stress)


Constructing the matrix explicitly makes the sign and grouping visible. A package function may use the opposite sign, a different scaling, or the opposite naming convention. Do not infer the coefficient meaning from a function name alone.

title: Earlier-versus-later Helmert contrasts
text:
Reconstruct a numerical example
Suppose the fitted duration means are 120 milliseconds for primary stress, 92 for secondary stress, and 76 for unstressed syllables. The first reverse Helmert comparison is

120-\frac{92+76}{2}=36.

Under the unscaled matrix,

\beta_1=\frac{36}{3}=12.

The second reverse Helmert comparison is

92-76=16,

so

\beta_2=\frac{16}{2}=8.

The intercept is the unweighted average of the three means:

\beta_0=\frac{120+92+76}{3}=96.

Substituting (\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2)=(96,12,8) into the three design rows recovers 120, 92, and 76.

title: Earlier-versus-later Helmert contrasts
text:
Keep sign and grouping separate
Multiplying an entire contrast column by -1 reverses the sign of its coefficient. The fitted category means remain unchanged. Reordering factor levels, in contrast, can change which categories are grouped together. These are different operations.
For this reason, state the comparison in words and provide the matrix. “We used reverse Helmert contrasts” is not enough when the terminology and sign convention can vary.






NoteRecover the reverse Helmert coefficients




What does the second reverse Helmert contrast compare in the displayed three-level factor?
Why is the primary-minus-weaker-average difference equal to 3\beta_1?
Verify the three fitted means using (96,12,8).
Explain why an ordered factor does not by itself justify reverse Helmert contrasts.
Why should a report provide the matrix in addition to a contrast-family name?

title: Interaction terms
text:
The multiple-regression page held each predictor association constant across the values of the other predictors. An interaction term relaxes that restriction by allowing one modeled association to depend on another predictor.
Suppose a reading experiment manipulates an aspectual mismatch and measures verb surprisal. The theory predicts that surprisal has a larger reading-time association in mismatching contexts than in matched contexts.
An additive model cannot express this claim because it gives both conditions the same surprisal slope.
The theoretical claim concerns a difference between associations. The interaction term lets the conditional-mean model estimate that slope difference directly.

title: Interaction terms
text:
Begin with the additive model
Let C_i=0 mark the matched condition and C_i=1 the mismatch condition:

\eta_i
=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\beta_2C_i.

For C_i=0, the surprisal slope is \beta_1. For C_i=1, the coefficient on X_i is still \beta_1.
The condition changes the intercept only.
For instance, suppose \beta_1=.04 and \beta_2=.10. Increasing surprisal by one bit raises the fitted mean by .04 in both conditions. The mismatch line is shifted upward by .10, but the two lines remain parallel. A vertical shift is not a slope difference.

title: Interaction terms
text:
Add a product term
The interaction model is

\eta_i
=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\beta_2C_i
+\beta_3X_iC_i.

Substitute C_i=0:

\eta_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i.

The matched-condition slope is \beta_1.
Substitute C_i=1:

\eta_i
=(\beta_0+\beta_2)
+(\beta_1+\beta_3)X_i.

The mismatch-condition slope is \beta_1+\beta_3.
Thus \beta_3 is the difference between the two slopes on the linear-predictor scale.
More explicitly,

\begin{aligned}
\text{slope}_{\text{mismatch}}
-\text{slope}_{\text{matched}}
&=(\beta_1+\beta_3)-\beta_1\\
&=\beta_3.
\end{aligned}

If \beta_1=.04 and \beta_3=.03, the matched slope is .04 and the mismatch slope is .07. The interaction coefficient is .03, not .07.

title: Interaction terms
section: Read the condition difference at two surprisal values
text:
Read the condition difference at two surprisal values
The mismatch-minus-matched difference at surprisal x is

\begin{aligned}
\Delta(x)
&=\eta(x,C=1)-\eta(x,C=0)\\
&=\beta_2+\beta_3x.
\end{aligned}

Thus the condition difference itself changes with surprisal. At x=0, the difference is \beta_2. At x=4, it is \beta_2+4\beta_3.
This makes the reference point for x important. If surprisal is centered at 5 bits, x=0 means 5 bits on the original scale. The coefficient \beta_2 is then the condition difference at 5 bits, not at zero original bits.

title: Interaction terms
text:
Derive the difference in differences
An interaction can also be written as a difference in differences. Compare each condition at surprisal values x_a and x_b:

\begin{aligned}
&[\eta(x_b,1)-\eta(x_a,1)]
-[\eta(x_b,0)-\eta(x_a,0)]\\
&\qquad=\beta_3(x_b-x_a).
\end{aligned}

For a one-bit contrast, this quantity is \beta_3. For a four-bit contrast, it is 4\beta_3. The comparison should state the predictor interval because the interaction coefficient is expressed per predictor unit.

title: Interaction terms
text:
Fit the product in R


Code
reading_times <- expand.grid(
  surprisal_centered = c(-2, 0, 2),
  condition = factor(c("matched", "mismatch"),
                     levels = c("matched", "mismatch"))
)

reading_times$log_rt <- with(
  reading_times,
  6.00 +
    .04 * surprisal_centered +
    .10 * (condition == "mismatch") +
    .03 * surprisal_centered * (condition == "mismatch")
)

fit_interaction <- lm(
  log_rt ~ surprisal_centered * condition,
  data = reading_times
)

coef(fit_interaction)


The * expands to the two lower-order terms and their product:


Code
terms(log_rt ~ surprisal_centered * condition)


Keeping the lower-order terms makes the coefficients correspond to the lines derived above.
The constructed responses follow the interaction equation exactly, so the fit recovers coefficients 6.00, .04, .10, and .03 up to numerical precision. Real observations would vary around these conditional means.

title: Interaction terms
text:
Calculate response-scale predictions
The fitted lines are easier to check in a prediction table:


Code
prediction_grid <- expand.grid(
  surprisal_centered = c(-2, 0, 2),
  condition = levels(reading_times$condition)
)

prediction_grid$predicted_log_rt <- predict(
  fit_interaction,
  newdata = prediction_grid
)

prediction_grid


At centered surprisal -2, the matched prediction is 5.92 and the mismatch prediction is 5.96, a difference of .04. At centered surprisal 2, the matched prediction is 6.08 and the mismatch prediction is 6.24, a difference of .16. The condition contrast has increased by .12 across four surprisal units, which equals 4(.03).

title: Interaction terms
text:
Keep the lower-order terms
Removing surprisal_centered while retaining its product with condition would force the matched-condition slope to zero. Removing condition would force the two lines to have the same intercept at centered surprisal zero. These are substantive constraints, not cosmetic simplifications.
Lower-order terms should not be removed merely because their coefficient tests are not of interest. The product coefficient is interpreted relative to the two lower-order terms. Removing them changes the lines and the slope difference being estimated.

title: Interaction terms
text:
Separate interaction from causation
An interaction states that a modeled association differs across conditions. It does not by itself show that the condition causes the slope difference. If condition was experimentally assigned while surprisal was measured, the two parts of the claim may have different identification support. The coefficient equation does not supply that design argument.
Thus the interaction should be reported as the comparison it answers: how much the fitted surprisal slope differs between mismatch and matched contexts, on the log-reading-time scale, over a declared predictor interval.






NoteCheck the second slope




If \beta_1=.04 and \beta_3=.03, what is the surprisal slope in each condition? Which coefficient is the slope difference?
If \beta_2=.10, calculate the mismatch-minus-matched difference at centered surprisal values 0 and 3.
Express the interaction over a five-bit surprisal contrast as a difference in differences.
Explain why lower-order terms should ordinarily remain when their interaction is included.

title: Regression as a sequence of extensions
text:
A regression model describes how a response distribution changes with predictors. We will not introduce the full architecture at once.
The linear-regression sequence begins with one question: how does a conditional mean change with one numerical predictor? We then add a response distribution, fit the line, quantify coefficient uncertainty, calculate residuals, and check whether the fitted model reproduces relevant patterns. Multiple predictors appear only after every part of the one-predictor model is in place.
Generalized linear models retain this regression structure for responses whose support is not the real line. We introduce the link-function architecture before treating binary responses, counts, and bounded responses separately.
Mixed-effects models address another problem: repeated speakers, items, verbs, documents, or languages. We first identify the repeated units and the desired generalization, then add random intercepts, random slopes, and nonnormal response families one step at a time.
The pages use distinct linguistic examples where possible. A dataset appears again only when several pages are successive steps of one analysis, such as inspecting a response, fitting its model, and checking its predictions.
Begin with conditional means. After the linear sequence, follow the separate generalized linear model and structured data branches shown on the chapter dependency graph.
crumbs: Regression as a sequence of extensions

title: Helmert coding
text:
The categorical-coding page showed that a contrast matrix determines the coefficient comparisons. An ordered categorical predictor may support comparisons among successive groups of levels. Suppose a visual-world experiment presents a preview for 0, 100, 300, or 600 milliseconds. A processing account may ask whether each longer preview differs from the average response at the shorter previews.
Helmert coding constructs those comparisons as orthogonal contrast columns.
The first Helmert contrast column compares 100 with 0 milliseconds, the second compares 300 milliseconds with the average of 0 and 100, and the third compares 600 milliseconds with the average of the three shorter previews.
One common matrix is
The columns encode distinct comparisons:
The numerical scale of each column matters for coefficient magnitude. For instance, substituting the first two rows gives
\begin{aligned}
m_{100}-m_0
&=(\beta_0+\beta_1-\beta_2-\beta_3)\\
&\quad-(\beta_0-\beta_1-\beta_2-\beta_3)\\
&=2\beta_1.
\end{aligned}
Thus \beta_1 is half the difference between 100 and 0 under this unscaled matrix. The column represents the intended direction, but the coefficient is scaled by the contrast values.
For the second column,
m_{300}-\frac{m_0+m_{100}}{2}=3\beta_2.
And for the third,
m_{600}-\frac{m_0+m_{100}+m_{300}}{3}=4\beta_3.
These factors of 2, 3, and 4 are why a report should include the matrix rather than only the contrast name.

title: Helmert coding
text:
Check orthogonality
Take the dot product of the first two columns:

(-1)(-1)+(1)(-1)+(0)(2)+(0)(0)=0.

The other column pairs also have dot product zero. This orthogonality means the columns encode nonoverlapping directions in the balanced design matrix.
It does not make the empirical questions theoretically appropriate. The ordering and grouping of levels must come from the linguistic analysis.
Orthogonality is a property of the columns, not evidence for the processing account. If the scientific hypothesis compares 600 with 0 milliseconds directly, this Helmert coding makes that hypothesis a combination of several coefficients. A purpose-built contrast could make the direct comparison easier to read.

title: Helmert coding
text:
Set and inspect the matrix


Code
preview_data <- data.frame(
  preview = factor(
    c("0 ms", "100 ms", "300 ms", "600 ms"),
    levels = c("0 ms", "100 ms", "300 ms", "600 ms")
  )
)

contrasts(preview_data$preview) <- contr.helmert(4)
contrasts(preview_data$preview)


R’s sign convention may be the reverse of a textbook matrix. Reversing an entire column reverses the corresponding coefficient sign but leaves fitted values unchanged.
Contrast terminology also varies across sources. Some sources reserve Helmert for earlier-versus-later comparisons and describe the displayed Helmert sequence reverse Helmert. The name does not settle the interpretation. The printed matrix does.

title: Helmert coding
text:
Recover fitted means
Let

m_i
=
\beta_0+\beta_1H_{1i}+\beta_2H_{2i}+\beta_3H_{3i}.

Substituting each row recovers the four category means. Response-scale predictions remain the safest way to communicate results, especially in logistic regression where the inverse link is nonlinear.
Suppose the four fitted means are 700, 660, 610, and 600 milliseconds. The encoded comparisons are then:

660-700=-40,


610-\frac{700+660}{2}=-70,

and

600-\frac{700+660+610}{3}\approx-56.7.

Under the unscaled matrix, the corresponding coefficients are -20, -70/3, and -56.7/4. These coefficients encode the same comparisons after accounting for column scaling.

title: Helmert coding
text:
Distinguish Helmert from polynomial coding
Helmert coding compares grouped levels. Polynomial coding represents linear, quadratic, and higher-order trends across equally meaningful ordered positions. The preview durations here are ordered, but their numerical gaps are not equal. If the theory predicts change per millisecond, a numeric duration predictor may represent that claim more directly.






NoteRead the displayed contrast matrix




What comparison does H_2 encode in the displayed matrix?
Why is the comparison involving 300 milliseconds equal to 3\beta_2 rather than \beta_2 under the unscaled matrix?
What does a zero dot product between two columns establish?
Why must a contrast matrix be reported when naming conventions vary?
When might numeric preview duration be preferable to four ordered categories?

title: Generalized linear mixed models
text:
This page combines the logistic response model with the group deviations introduced for random-intercept models. Neither component is new; their combination is a generalized linear mixed model.
Suppose an experiment records whether a participant chooses a pronoun on each trial. The response is binary, so logistic regression supplies the response distribution and link. But each participant contributes several choices. A model that treats those choices as unrelated observations loses the repeated participant structure.
A linear mixed-effects model represents repeated observations through group-specific deviations, but its normally distributed response does not represent a binary choice. A generalized linear mixed model, or GLMM, combines the two structures already introduced. It uses a generalized linear model response family and link, then places random effects inside the linear predictor.
The principal concept on this page is the combination. No new response distribution or random effect distribution is required.

title: Generalized linear mixed models
section: Begin with the logistic response model
text:
Begin with the logistic response model
Let Y_{ij}=1 when participant j chooses a pronoun on trial i. Let X_{ij}=1 when the antecedent was the preceding subject and X_{ij}=0 otherwise. A logistic regression without random effects writes

Y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ij})

and

\operatorname{logit}(\pi_{ij})
=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{ij}.

The model has one baseline log odds value, \beta_0, and one subject status contrast, \beta_1. Participants with the same predictor value receive the same fitted probability. Any remaining participant variation is forced into the Bernoulli trial variation.
That last assumption is often implausible. Some participants may prefer pronouns across conditions, while others may avoid them. Repeated responses from one participant then share a baseline tendency.

title: Generalized linear mixed models
text:
Add participant baselines
Insert a participant random intercept into the linear predictor:

\operatorname{logit}(\pi_{ij})
=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{ij}+b_{0j},

where

b_{0j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau_0^2).

The fixed intercept \beta_0 describes the population center on the log odds scale. The deviation b_{0j} moves participant j above or below that center. The parameter \tau_0 describes how much participant baselines vary in the modeled population.
The Bernoulli distribution remains attached to each response. The logit link still maps the linear predictor to a valid probability. The random intercept changes only the participant specific location of that linear predictor.

title: Generalized linear mixed models
text:
Calculate two conditional probabilities
Suppose

\beta_0=-.5,
\qquad
\beta_1=1,
\qquad
b_{0j}=.4.

For a nonsubject antecedent, X=0:

\eta_{j,0}=-.5+1(0)+.4=-.1

and

\pi_{j,0}=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(-.1)\approx.475.

For a subject antecedent, X=1:

\eta_{j,1}=-.5+1(1)+.4=.9

and

\pi_{j,1}=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(.9)\approx.711.

These are probabilities conditional on participant j having deviation .4. A participant with deviation -.6 receives lower fitted probabilities in both conditions, even though the population coefficient \beta_1 is unchanged.

title: Generalized linear mixed models
text:
Fit the model in R
fit_pronoun_glmm <- lme4::glmer(
  pronoun ~ subject_status +
    (1 | participant_id),
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = reference_choices
)
The fixed part of the formula is the same as a logistic regression. (1 | participant_id) adds one random intercept for each participant and a population variance parameter for those intercepts.
The grouping column identifies the source of dependence. Replacing it with a row identifier would give each observation its own group and would not represent repeated participants. Omitting the term would assert that any participant variation beyond subject_status is adequately described by Bernoulli trial variation.
If experimental items also repeat, the design may require a second grouping term:
fit_crossed_glmm <- lme4::glmer(
  pronoun ~ subject_status +
    (1 | participant_id) +
    (1 | item_id),
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = reference_choices
)
This formula has crossed participant and item intercepts. It does not average the responses by participant or by item. Each binary response remains in the likelihood, while the linear predictor records both shared sources of variation.

title: Generalized linear mixed models
text:
Distinguish conditional and population predictions
The hand calculation conditioned on one participant deviation. A different question concerns a new participant drawn from the modeled population. That prediction must average over the random effect distribution:

\mathbb{E}_{b}
\left[
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\eta+b)
\right].

Because the inverse logit is nonlinear,

\mathbb{E}_{b}
\left[
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\eta+b)
\right]
\ne
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\eta)

in general. Setting the random effect to zero describes a participant at the population center on the link scale. It does not necessarily equal the probability obtained by averaging over the population of participants.
A report should state whether its predicted probabilities condition on estimated groups, set group deviations to zero, or average over a group population. The appropriate calculation follows from the claim. Prediction for a returning participant can condition on that participant’s estimated deviation. Prediction for a new participant cannot.

title: Generalized linear mixed models
section: Fixed effects retain a conditional interpretation
text:
Fixed effects retain a conditional interpretation
In the random intercept logistic model, e^{\beta_1} is the subject status odds ratio for observations with the same participant deviation. With crossed item intercepts, the contrast also conditions on the same item deviation. This is sometimes called a subject specific or cluster conditional interpretation.
The coefficient should not be described as the marginal odds ratio across the population unless that quantity has been computed. Nonlinearity means that averaging probabilities over random effects does not preserve the same odds ratio.
This distinction is easy to miss when software prints one coefficient table. The model contains more than one useful scale: the additive link scale, the group conditional response scale, and the population averaged response scale.

title: Generalized linear mixed models
section: A random intercept does not represent every dependence pattern
text:
A random intercept does not represent every dependence pattern
The model above lets participants differ in baseline pronoun use. It assumes that the subject status contrast \beta_1 is common across participants. If participants vary in that contrast, a random intercept alone can still understate uncertainty about the experimental comparison.
The repair is not to add every possible random term without reference to the design. It is to ask which manipulated or repeated contrasts vary across which sampled units. The earlier random slopes page develops that design question.
GLMMs can also face weakly estimated variance components, separation, and computational warnings. A successful optimizer message does not establish that the response family, link, and dependence structure reproduce the relevant features of the data. Those checks remain part of model criticism.






NoteCheck the components



Which part of the model prevents invalid probabilities? Which part represents repeated responses from one participant? For a prediction about a new participant, why is inserting an estimated deviation from an observed participant inappropriate?

title: Generalized linear mixed models
text:
What the combination adds
A GLMM retains the response distribution and link of a generalized linear model while adding group specific variation to its linear predictor. This combination keeps individual binary responses in the likelihood and represents dependence among responses from the same participant or item. Its predictions must specify how the random effects are handled. The next page applies the same construction to an ordered response.

title: Population comparisons and sampled variation
text:
The preceding page identified participants and items as repeated units before introducing a mixed-model formula. We now distinguish the planned population comparisons from variation across those sampled units.
Suppose an experiment compares two constructions across sampled participants and sentence items. The construction contrast is the quantity of theoretical interest. We want one population coefficient describing the difference between those two conditions.
Participants and items play another role. The observed people represent possible people who could have taken part, and the observed sentences represent possible items that could instantiate the constructions. Mixed-effects terminology distinguishes population-level coefficients, called fixed effects, from group-level deviations modeled as draws from a population distribution, called random effects.

title: Population comparisons and sampled variation
text:
Begin with the scientific target
Let C_i=1 mark the target construction and C_i=0 mark the control. A coefficient \beta_C represents the population comparison between those declared conditions:

\operatorname{E}(Y_i\mid C_i=1)
-\operatorname{E}(Y_i\mid C_i=0)
=\beta_C

for a linear model without other changing predictors.
The labels target and control are not treated as a random sample from a population of arbitrary condition names. They define the comparison targeted by the hypothesis.
A fixed effect is a coefficient that the model does not itself treat as varying across levels of a grouping factor. In this example, it represents the construction comparison in the population relation. The word fixed does not mean that the coefficient is known, constant across every conceivable population, or measured without uncertainty.

title: Population comparisons and sampled variation
text:
Represent sampled variation
Participants may differ in baseline ratings, and items may differ in baseline acceptability. The analysis usually does not seek 60 unrelated participant coefficients and 40 unrelated item coefficients as its primary result. It seeks population distributions that describe how sampled levels vary.
For participant j, write a deviation b_j. A random effects model treats

b_j\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau^2).

The standard deviation \tau describes participant to participant variation. Each observed participant receives an estimated deviation under that shared distribution.
The same logic can apply to sentence items. A separate distribution describes how item baselines vary around the population relation. These distributions connect the observed levels to the broader populations identified from the sampling design.

title: Population comparisons and sampled variation
section: Do not use storage type as the criterion
text:
Do not use storage type as the criterion
Condition, participant, item, and dialect region may all be stored as categorical columns. Their storage type does not determine their modeling role.
Ask instead:

Are coefficients for these particular levels the scientific target?
Or are the observed levels sampled instances from a population across which the claim should generalize?

Five declared experimental conditions are usually represented by fixed contrasts because those contrasts state the hypothesis. Fifty participant identifiers usually index random effects because the claim is not restricted to those fifty people.
Context can change the answer. A study may compare exactly five dialect regions because their historical differences are the target. That analysis needs fixed contrasts among those regions. Another study may sample many communities to estimate broader regional variation. A group distribution may then match the target better.

title: Population comparisons and sampled variation
section: Separate a predictor from a grouping index
text:
Separate a predictor from a grouping index
Participant age is a measured predictor. Participant identifier is a grouping index. Adding a participant random effect does not replace the age coefficient. The random effect represents remaining participant variation after the modeled predictors have been included.
Likewise, an item’s construction condition is a predictor, while item identifier indexes persistent item variation. One row can contain both roles because the roles answer different questions.
This distinction prevents a common mistake: treating every source of variation as an unnamed group deviation. If a measured property encodes a theoretical contrast, place that contrast in the population relation. Let the group distribution represent remaining variation around it.

title: Population comparisons and sampled variation
text:
State the populations in words
For the construction experiment, a useful target statement is:

The fixed condition coefficient represents the target minus control comparison. Participant and item effects represent variation across the participant and sentence populations sampled by the design.

This sentence identifies the target comparison and the two generalization populations. Without those statements, the labels fixed and random provide little information.
The distinction also limits the conclusion. If the study samples many participants but uses one item, a participant random effect cannot create evidence across items. The model can represent only populations for which the design supplies levels.






NoteCheck the target



A study compares three writing systems and aims to report those three specific differences. Should writing system identity be random because it is categorical? State the exact comparison before choosing the model term.


The next page shows how a shared group distribution produces partial pooling.

title: The exponential family
text:
The generalized-linear-model page stated that a standard generalized linear model uses an exponential-family response. We now define that family. Normal, Bernoulli, and Poisson distributions look different, but they can all be written in a common form.
The exponential-family form lets us separate the observed response, a transformed parameter, and any dispersion term. This representation does not make the distributions identical. It shows which mathematical roles they share.

title: The exponential family
text:
The common form
A distribution belongs to the exponential family if its density or mass function can be written as

p(y\mid\theta,\phi)
=
\exp\left(
\frac{y\theta-b(\theta)}{a(\phi)}+c(y,\phi)
\right).

The symbols have specific jobs:

y is the observed response.
\theta is the natural parameter.
\phi is a dispersion parameter when the family has one.
b(\theta) determines the mean and variance.
c(y,\phi) contains terms that do not involve \theta.

This notation is abstract because it must cover several distributions. We will make it concrete with the Bernoulli distribution.
The natural parameter \theta need not equal a familiar mean parameter. It is the parameter value that makes the observed response enter linearly in the exponent. The function b(\theta) then provides the normalization needed for the probabilities or density to sum or integrate to one.

title: The exponential family
text:
Rewrite the Bernoulli distribution
For y\in\{0,1\},

p(y\mid\pi)=\pi^y(1-\pi)^{1-y}.

Taking logs gives

\log p(y\mid\pi)
=
y\log\pi+(1-y)\log(1-\pi).

Collect the terms involving y:

\log p(y\mid\pi)
=
y\log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}+\log(1-\pi).

Thus the natural parameter is

\theta=\log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi},

which is the log odds. The Bernoulli canonical link will arise from this same quantity.
To identify the remaining pieces, solve for \pi in terms of \theta:

\pi=\frac{e^\theta}{1+e^\theta}.

Then

\log(1-\pi)=-\log(1+e^\theta),

so

\log p(y\mid\theta)
=y\theta-\log(1+e^\theta).

For the Bernoulli family,

b(\theta)=\log(1+e^\theta),

there is no separately estimated dispersion parameter, and c(y)=0 under this representation.

title: The exponential family
text:
Why this family is useful
For this form,

\mathbb{E}[Y]=b'(\theta)

and

\mathrm{Var}(Y)=a(\phi)b''(\theta).

The conditional variance is thus tied to the conditional mean in a family-specific way. The function that expresses this relation is the variance function. Bernoulli variance is \pi(1-\pi). Poisson variance is \lambda. Normal variance is governed by a separate dispersion parameter.
For the Bernoulli form,

b'(\theta)
=\frac{e^\theta}{1+e^\theta}
=\pi.

The first derivative recovers the mean. The second derivative is

b''(\theta)
=\frac{e^\theta}{(1+e^\theta)^2}
=\pi(1-\pi),

which recovers the variance. The mean-variance relation is thus encoded in the same b function.
This relation is one reason the response distribution matters. Choosing a family is not merely choosing the range of possible outcomes. It also chooses a mean variance relation.

title: The exponential family
text:
Write the Poisson exponential-family form
For count y\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\},

p(y\mid\lambda)
=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^y}{y!}.

Taking logs gives

\log p(y\mid\lambda)
=y\log\lambda-\lambda-\log(y!).

Set

\theta=\log\lambda.

Since \lambda=e^\theta, the log mass becomes

\log p(y\mid\theta)
=y\theta-e^\theta-\log(y!).

Thus

b(\theta)=e^\theta

and

c(y)=-\log(y!).

Both the first and second derivatives of b(\theta) equal e^\theta=\lambda. This yields the Poisson equality of mean and variance.

title: The exponential family
section: Connect natural parameters to canonical links
text:
Connect natural parameters to canonical links
A canonical link sets the linear predictor equal to the natural parameter. For the Bernoulli family,

\eta=\theta=\log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi},

so the canonical link is the logit. For the Poisson family,

\eta=\theta=\log\lambda,

so the canonical link is the log link.
Canonical links make the predictor enter the exponential-family form through its natural parameter. They are not required by the response support. Another monotone link can map to the same allowed mean range while producing a noncanonical model.
Not every generalized linear model must use its canonical link. Canonical links often simplify estimation and interpretation, but the model choice remains separate.

title: The exponential family
section: The family does not include every useful distribution
text:
The family does not include every useful distribution
The negative binomial is often represented in an exponential family form under a fixed dispersion parameter, but regression practice usually estimates that dispersion. Mixtures, zero inflated models, and ordered beta models require additional structure. Thus, generalized linear modeling provides a useful architecture, not a catalog of every model linguists may need.
Membership in the exponential family also does not establish that a family is adequate for a particular response. A Poisson likelihood has count support, but a linguistic count can still have more variation than its mean. Mathematical convenience does not replace measurement and predictive checks.

title: The exponential family
text:
Verify the derivatives numerically
At \theta=0, the Bernoulli mean is .5 and variance is .25. At \theta=\log4, the mean is .8 and variance is .16:


Code
theta <- c(0, log(4))
bernoulli_mean <- exp(theta) / (1 + exp(theta))
bernoulli_variance <- bernoulli_mean * (1 - bernoulli_mean)

data.frame(
  theta = theta,
  mean = bernoulli_mean,
  variance = bernoulli_variance
)


This calculation makes the mean-variance coupling concrete before any regression predictors are added.






NoteRecover the exponential-family form




Which term determines the mean and variance through its derivatives?
What is the Bernoulli natural parameter?
Why does choosing a response family also choose a variance relation?
Identify b(\theta) for the Poisson family.
Explain why a generalized linear model need not use the canonical link.

title: Deviance
text:
The earlier maximum-likelihood page defined the likelihood as a function of the parameter with the observed data held fixed. For ordinary linear regression, residual sums of squares provide a natural measure of mismatch. Generalized linear models use deviance to compare a fitted model with a model that reproduces the observed responses as closely as the response family allows.
This likelihood comparison defines the model deviance. The saturated model is not a theoretically plausible model. It is a likelihood benchmark that gives each observation enough freedom to attain the best family-specific fit.

title: Deviance
text:
The saturated model
A saturated model has enough parameters to fit every observation’s response. Its likelihood is L_{\mathrm{sat}}. The fitted candidate model has likelihood L_{\mathrm{fit}}.
The deviance is

D
=
2\left[
\log L_{\mathrm{sat}}
-
\log L_{\mathrm{fit}}
\right].

The saturated model cannot fit worse than the candidate. The deviance is thus nonnegative. Smaller values indicate that the candidate is closer to the saturated fit.
The factor 2 places likelihood differences on the conventional deviance scale. A deviance of zero means that the candidate attains the saturated likelihood. It does not mean that the candidate is the true data-generating model.

title: Deviance
text:
Calculate Bernoulli deviance
Suppose five binary responses contain three successes and two failures, and an intercept-only model fits probability

\widehat\pi=.6.

The fitted log likelihood is

\begin{aligned}
\log L_{\text{fit}}
&=3\log(.6)+2\log(.4)\\
&\approx-3.365.
\end{aligned}

The saturated Bernoulli model assigns fitted probability 1 to each observed success and 0 to each observed failure. Its log likelihood is 0 because every observed response receives probability 1. Thus

\begin{aligned}
D
&=2[0-(-3.365)]\\
&\approx6.730.
\end{aligned}



Code
y <- c(1, 1, 0, 1, 0)
pi_hat <- mean(y)
log_lik_fit <- sum(dbinom(y, size = 1, prob = pi_hat, log = TRUE))
deviance_by_hand <- 2 * (0 - log_lik_fit)

fit <- glm(y ~ 1, family = binomial())

c(
  by_hand = deviance_by_hand,
  from_model = deviance(fit)
)


The two values agree. The calculation compares the fitted common probability with observation-specific saturated probabilities.

title: Deviance
section: Residual deviance is not meaningful alone
text:
Residual deviance is not meaningful alone
A deviance value has no universal good cutoff. Its scale depends on the family, sample size, and observed responses. Use it through comparisons, dispersion checks, and residual contributions.
For instance, doubling a dataset by duplicating every observation can roughly double a deviance while leaving fitted response proportions unchanged. A raw value cannot be interpreted independently of the number and form of observations.
One decontextualized cutoff cannot interpret every deviance value. Deviance becomes informative through a declared model comparison or a family-specific diagnostic.

title: Deviance
text:
Compare nested models
Suppose model 0 is nested within model 1. The difference in deviance is

D_0-D_1
=
2\left[
\log L_1-\log L_0
\right].

This is the likelihood ratio statistic. Under regularity conditions and a null hypothesis that the smaller model is correct, it has an approximate chi squared distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the difference in parameter counts.
The approximation can fail at parameter boundaries, with small samples, or for irregular mixture models. The test also answers a fit question. It does not directly estimate held out prediction.
The models must be nested for this subtraction to have the usual likelihood ratio interpretation. Model 0 is nested in model 1 when a constraint on the larger model’s parameters reproduces the smaller model. Setting one added slope to zero is a common case.
If the two models use different response families or different observations, their saturated references may not be comparable. Subtracting the displayed deviances can then answer no clean nested-model question.

title: Deviance
text:
Deviance and overdispersion
For a Poisson model, a residual deviance much larger than its residual degrees of freedom can be evidence that the conditional variation exceeds the Poisson mean variance relation. This ratio is a diagnostic, not a proof of one particular cause. Omitted grouping, excess zeros, and a negative binomial response can all produce related patterns.
The numerator and denominator should not be treated as an exact test without checking the setting. A large ratio says that the fitted Poisson model leaves more likelihood discrepancy than its parameter count would lead us to expect under a rough reference. It does not identify which alternative model will fix the discrepancy.

title: Deviance
text:
In R


Code
deviance(fit)
df.residual(fit)

# For two fitted nested models on identical rows:
# anova(smaller_fit, larger_fit, test = "Chisq")


The models must be fit to the same observations and with comparable likelihoods. A difference caused by different missing value deletion is not a clean nested model comparison.
Thus a comparison should begin with a row check. The number and identity of modeled observations must agree. The commented code records the operation without assuming that two comparison models exist on this page.






NoteInterpret deviance relative to the saturated model




What does the saturated model do?
How is a nested model deviance difference related to a likelihood ratio statistic?
Why is a large Poisson deviance ratio a clue rather than a diagnosis?
Recalculate the Bernoulli deviance for four successes and one failure under fitted probability .8.
Explain why one decontextualized deviance cutoff cannot apply to every model.

title: Design matrices
text:
The multiple-regression page wrote one linear predictor for each observation. A design matrix collects those observation-specific equations into one matrix equation.
A regression formula is converted into a numeric matrix before the model is fit. This design matrix places one observation on each row and one coefficient contribution on each column.
The model matrix is the numeric representation produced from the formula. Inspecting this representation is useful because coefficient meaning comes from the numbers in the matrix, not from the surface form of a variable name.
Suppose three words have centered log frequencies -1.2, .4, and .8, along with centered neighborhood densities 3, -2, and 1. The additive model is
Code
log_rt ~ log_frequency + neighborhood_density
Its design matrix is
\mathbf{X}=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -1.2 & 3\\
1 & 0.4 & -2\\
1 & 0.8 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
The first column represents the intercept. The second contains centered frequency values. The third contains centered neighborhood-density values. All three rows contain 1 in the first column because every observation receives the intercept.

title: Design matrices
section: The linear predictor is a matrix product
text:
The linear predictor is a matrix product
With coefficient vector

\boldsymbol\beta=
\begin{bmatrix}
\beta_0\\\beta_1\\\beta_2
\end{bmatrix},

all linear predictors are

\boldsymbol\eta=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta.

For the second row,

\eta_2=1\beta_0+.4\beta_1-2\beta_2.

The row shows exactly which coefficients contribute to that observation’s fitted value.
Suppose

\boldsymbol\beta
=
\begin{bmatrix}
6.2\\
-.08\\
.015
\end{bmatrix}.

Then the second fitted conditional mean is

\begin{aligned}
\eta_2
&=1(6.2)+.4(-.08)-2(.015)\\
&=6.138.
\end{aligned}

The matrix product repeats this calculation for all three observations at once.

title: Design matrices
text:
Multiply the matrix by hand
Matrix multiplication takes the dot product of each design row with the coefficient vector:

\begin{aligned}
\eta_1&=6.2+(-1.2)(-.08)+3(.015)=6.341,\\
\eta_2&=6.2+.4(-.08)-2(.015)=6.138,\\
\eta_3&=6.2+.8(-.08)+1(.015)=6.151.
\end{aligned}

Thus

\boldsymbol\eta
=
\begin{bmatrix}
6.341\\
6.138\\
6.151
\end{bmatrix}.

These are three conditional means. The design matrix does not contain the responses, and the multiplication does not add residual variation.

title: Design matrices
text:
Construct the matrix in R


Code
lexical_rows <- data.frame(
  log_frequency = c(-1.2, .4, .8),
  neighborhood_density = c(3, -2, 1)
)

X <- model.matrix(
  ~ log_frequency + neighborhood_density,
  data = lexical_rows
)

beta <- c(6.2, -.08, .015)

X
as.vector(X %*% beta)


The first command exposes the model matrix. The second verifies the three hand calculations. %*% is R’s matrix-multiplication operator.
The column names provide another check:


Code
colnames(X)


Their order must match the order of the coefficients in beta. Swapping the two slope values without swapping the columns would calculate a different model.

title: Design matrices
text:
Interpret columns through row changes
To read a coefficient, compare two hypothetical rows that differ in one column. For instance,

\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\end{bmatrix}

and

\begin{bmatrix}1&1&0\end{bmatrix}

differ only by one frequency unit. Their fitted values differ by \beta_1. The same logic gives \beta_2 when only the third column changes by one unit.
This row-comparison method generalizes beyond numeric predictors. Later pages show how categorical comparisons and products become columns, but their coefficients are still read by comparing design rows.

title: Design matrices
text:
Keep rows and variables separate
The matrix has one row per modeled observation, not one row per distinct word type unless the dataset itself has one observation per word type. Repeated tokens generate repeated rows, possibly with identical predictor values but different responses.
Similarly, one original variable need not always become one matrix column. The The formula and contrast coding determine the actual columns. On this page, each numeric predictor supplies one column, so the correspondence happens to be one-to-one.
One formula variable does not always produce one model-matrix column. That correspondence holds for these two numeric predictors but will fail for categorical predictors. Inspecting model.matrix() prevents the assumption from being carried into settings where it is false.






NoteReconstruct the matrix product




Calculate the fitted value for the first row using the displayed coefficient vector.
What changes in a design row when centered frequency increases by one unit and centered neighborhood density stays fixed?
Why does the design matrix not contain the response?
Explain why one formula variable does not always produce one model-matrix column and why that correspondence holds only for the current example.

title: Correlated predictors
text:
The multiple-regression page interpreted each coefficient through a comparison that holds the other predictors fixed. Word length and lexical frequency often vary together. Very frequent words tend to be short. If both enter a reading-time regression, the model must learn their separate coefficients from words that break this usual association.
The problem is easiest to see with an extreme example.

title: Correlated predictors
text:
Begin with perfect overlap
Suppose every word in a dataset satisfies

\text{length}=10-\text{frequency}.

The fitted mean is

m
=\beta_0+\beta_F\text{frequency}
+\beta_L\text{length}.

Substitute the exact relation:

\begin{aligned}
m
&=\beta_0+\beta_F\text{frequency}
+\beta_L(10-\text{frequency})\\
&=(\beta_0+10\beta_L)
+(\beta_F-\beta_L)\text{frequency}.
\end{aligned}

Only the combinations \beta_0+10\beta_L and \beta_F-\beta_L are identified. Many separate coefficient triples produce the same fitted means.
With perfect collinearity, unique partial coefficients do not exist.

title: Correlated predictors
section: Move to strong but imperfect overlap
text:
Move to strong but imperfect overlap
Real predictors are rarely exact transformations of one another. But when they are strongly correlated, the data contain few comparisons between words of different length at similar frequency.
The coefficients are then learned from a narrow and possibly unusual subset of predictor combinations. Their sampling uncertainty grows, and small changes in the sample can move the separate estimates substantially.
This predictor overlap is collinearity.
Strong predictor association also limits the directly observed comparisons. A partial frequency coefficient requires words that differ in frequency while remaining similar in length. If almost every frequent word is short and almost every rare word is long, the sample supplies few such comparisons.

title: Correlated predictors
text:
Construct a nearly collinear sample
Consider ten constructed word observations with centered log frequency and centered length. The two predictors are almost perfectly negatively correlated.


Code
frequency <- seq(-2, 2, length.out = 10)
centered_length <-
  -1.8 * frequency + c(.2, -.1, .1, -.2, .15, -.15, .2, -.1, .1, -.2)

log_rt <-
  6 - .08 * frequency + .02 * centered_length +
  c(.01, -.005, .004, -.008, .006, -.004, .008, -.006, .005, -.01)

lexical_sample <- data.frame(
  frequency = frequency,
  centered_length = centered_length,
  log_rt = log_rt
)

cor(lexical_sample$frequency, lexical_sample$centered_length)


The correlation is about -.998. The sample contains almost no independent movement in frequency and length.
Fit the additive model:


Code
fit_collinear <- lm(
  log_rt ~ frequency + centered_length,
  data = lexical_sample
)

coef(fit_collinear)
confint(fit_collinear)


The separate slope estimates need not resemble the coefficients used to construct the responses. Many pairs of frequency and length slopes produce nearly the same fitted values over this narrow diagonal band of predictor space.

title: Correlated predictors
text:
Perturb one response
Now increase the final log response by .03 and refit:


Code
perturbed_sample <- lexical_sample
perturbed_sample$log_rt[10] <- perturbed_sample$log_rt[10] + .03

fit_perturbed <- lm(
  log_rt ~ frequency + centered_length,
  data = perturbed_sample
)

rbind(
  original = coef(fit_collinear),
  perturbed = coef(fit_perturbed)
)


The frequency slope changes from about -.003 to -.032, and the length slope changes from about .063 to .045. The one-response perturbation is small on the response scale, but it moves the allocation of association across the two predictors.
The fitted values move much less:


Code
max(abs(fitted(fit_collinear) - fitted(fit_perturbed)))


The largest change is about .013. This is the distinction between unstable attribution and relatively stable interpolation.

title: Correlated predictors
section: Look at the comparison, not a threshold
text:
Look at the comparison, not a threshold
A correlation of .70 is not automatically acceptable or unacceptable. Ask which observations identify each theoretical contrast.
If a theory distinguishes exposure from form complexity, we may need both frequency and length even when their separate estimates are uncertain. That uncertainty may be the correct reflection of the data.
Removing length would make the frequency coefficient describe the joint pattern in which frequency and length vary together. Keeping both asks for a partial frequency comparison at fixed modeled length. These are different estimands. Neither choice repairs missing comparison support.
If two columns are alternate noisy measurements of one construct, a measurement model or a prespecified composite may better represent the theory.
Dropping or residualizing a predictor changes the coefficient target. Regularization may stabilize predictions, but it cannot create predictor combinations that were not observed.

title: Correlated predictors
text:
Prediction can remain stable
Different coefficient combinations may make similar predictions within the observed predictor region. Thus collinearity can strongly affect attribution to separate coefficients while having less effect on interpolation.
Extrapolation remains risky because the fitted model has not learned what happens when the correlated predictors take novel combinations.
For instance, the constructed sample contains no word that is simultaneously high in centered frequency and high in centered length. A prediction in that corner depends on how the model divided the diagonal association between its two slopes. Since multiple divisions fit the observed band similarly, the novel combination can receive very different predictions.

title: Correlated predictors
text:
Report what the data distinguish
A useful analysis states the observed predictor relation, shows the support for the theoretically relevant comparison, and reports uncertainty in the partial coefficients. A correlation threshold alone cannot perform this argument.
The next page summarizes the precision loss with a variance inflation factor. It does not replace the analysis of predictor support because the numerical factor cannot say whether the scarce comparisons answer the linguistic question.






NoteFind the supporting observations




If length and frequency are negatively correlated, which words are most informative about a length coefficient holding frequency fixed?
Why can the separate slopes change while fitted values remain similar in the observed predictor band?
Explain how strong predictor correlation limits the comparisons that directly support a partial coefficient.
Why is prediction for a frequent long word especially uncertain in the constructed sample?

title: Coding a categorical predictor
text:
The design-matrix page used numeric predictor columns. A categorical predictor must first be represented by numeric columns whose row patterns determine the coefficient comparisons.
Suppose a verb-type predictor has three levels:
\{\text{result},\text{manner},\text{stative}\}.
A regression equation needs numerical columns. A contrast coding turns the levels into columns whose coefficients represent declared comparisons.
The categories themselves have no numerical distance. We cannot subtract manner from stative in the way we subtract two frequency values. The coding supplies numeric rows that make particular comparisons estimable.

title: Coding a categorical predictor
text:
Choose a reference level
Use result verbs as the reference and create two indicator columns:



verb type
manner column M
stative column S




result
0
0


manner
1
0


stative
0
1



The linear predictor is

\eta
=\beta_0+\beta_M M+\beta_S S.

title: Coding a categorical predictor
text:
Substitute each row
For a result verb, both indicators are zero:

\eta_{\text{result}}=\beta_0.

For a manner verb,

\eta_{\text{manner}}=\beta_0+\beta_M.

For a stative verb,

\eta_{\text{stative}}=\beta_0+\beta_S.

Thus \beta_M is the manner-minus-result difference on the linear-predictor scale, and \beta_S is the stative-minus-result difference.
The intercept is the result-verb mean because the result row contains zeros in both contrast columns. The two slope coefficients each compare another category with that same reference.

title: Coding a categorical predictor
text:
Reconstruct coefficients from category means
Suppose the fitted mean ratings are



verb type
fitted mean




result
5.8


manner
5.2


stative
6.1



Under the displayed reference coding,

\beta_0=5.8.

The manner coefficient is

\begin{aligned}
\beta_M
&=\eta_{\text{manner}}-\eta_{\text{result}}\\
&=5.2-5.8\\
&=-.6.
\end{aligned}

The stative coefficient is

\begin{aligned}
\beta_S
&=\eta_{\text{stative}}-\eta_{\text{result}}\\
&=6.1-5.8\\
&=.3.
\end{aligned}

Substituting these coefficients recovers all three means:

\begin{aligned}
\eta_{\text{result}}&=5.8,\\
\eta_{\text{manner}}&=5.8-.6=5.2,\\
\eta_{\text{stative}}&=5.8+.3=6.1.
\end{aligned}

This reconstruction is the safest check on a contrast interpretation.

title: Coding a categorical predictor
text:
Set the reference in R


Code
cloze <- data.frame(
  verb_type = c("result", "manner", "stative")
)

cloze$verb_type <- relevel(
  factor(cloze$verb_type),
  ref = "result"
)

model.matrix(~ verb_type, data = cloze)


Software otherwise may choose a reference alphabetically. That default can make the coefficient table answer a comparison different from the theoretical question.
The column names printed by model.matrix() identify the represented comparisons. The order of rows follows the observations, while factor level order determines the reference and the contrast columns.

title: Coding a categorical predictor
text:
Why use only two columns?
With an intercept and three unrestricted indicators, the three indicators sum to the intercept column of ones. This exact dependency prevents unique coefficient estimates.
Two columns suffice to represent three group locations relative to a reference.
More specifically, the intercept supplies the result location. The manner column supplies the change needed to reach the manner location, and the stative column supplies the change needed to reach the stative location. A third indicator would duplicate information already present in the intercept and two contrasts.

title: Coding a categorical predictor
section: Coding changes coefficients, not fitted group means
text:
Coding changes coefficients, not fitted group means
If we make manner the reference, the intercept and comparison coefficients change. The model can still produce the same fitted value for result, manner, and stative verbs.
For the three means above, making manner the reference yields

\beta_0^*=5.2,


\beta_R^*=5.8-5.2=.6,

and

\beta_S^*=6.1-5.2=.9.

The numbers differ from the result-reference coefficients, but the category means remain 5.8, 5.2, and 6.1. Coding changes the coordinate system used to describe the same fitted values.
Choose coding to make the theoretically relevant comparison direct. If the hypothesis concerns manner versus result, treatment coding with one of those levels as reference makes the coefficient immediately readable.
The stative-minus-manner comparison is not a single displayed coefficient under result reference coding. It is

\begin{aligned}
\eta_{\text{stative}}-\eta_{\text{manner}}
&=(\beta_0+\beta_S)-(\beta_0+\beta_M)\\
&=\beta_S-\beta_M.
\end{aligned}

With the example values, this difference is .3-(-.6)=.9. The comparison is fully represented even though it does not appear in one coefficient row.
The displayed coefficient rows are not the only available comparisons. Predictions and linear combinations can recover any comparison represented by the fitted category means.






NoteCheck one comparison




Using the table above, express the stative-minus-manner difference in terms of \beta_S and \beta_M.
Reconstruct the three fitted means from \beta_0=5.8, \beta_M=-.6, and \beta_S=.3.
Why do three category means require only an intercept and two contrast columns?
Explain why the displayed coefficient rows are not the only comparisons available from the fitted model.

title: Centering a predictor
text:
In a simple linear regression, the intercept is the conditional mean at predictor value zero. Suppose observed surprisal values range from 2 to 9 bits. The intercept in
m(x)=\beta_0+\beta_1x
describes a word with surprisal 0, outside the observed range.
We can make a more useful reference point by centering the predictor.
Centering is a reparameterization. It changes which predictor value receives the label zero and thus changes the intercept attached to that label. It does not change the distances among observations.

title: Centering a predictor
text:
Subtract a declared reference
Let 5 bits be the reference value and define

X_i^c=X_i-5.

The conversion is



original surprisal X
centered surprisal X^c




2
-3


5
0


9
4



Zero on the centered scale now represents 5 bits on the original scale.
Negative centered values do not represent negative surprisal. A value of x^c=-3 means three bits below the declared reference, which is 2 bits on the original scale. Centered values must be interpreted together with the subtracted reference.

title: Centering a predictor
text:
Rewrite the line
Use

m(x^c)=\beta_0^c+\beta_1^c x^c.

At x^c=0,

m(0)=\beta_0^c.

Thus the centered intercept is the expected response at 5 bits.
Substitute x^c=x-5 into the centered line:

m(x)=\beta_0^c+\beta_1^c(x-5).

For this to describe the same line as \beta_0+\beta_1x, the slope remains

\beta_1^c=\beta_1,

while the intercept becomes

\beta_0^c=\beta_0+5\beta_1.

title: Centering a predictor
text:
Check that predictions remain unchanged
Let \beta_0=5.70 and \beta_1=.06. The original prediction at 7 bits is

5.70+.06(7)=6.12.

The centered intercept is

5.70+5(.06)=6.00.

At 7 bits, x^c=2, so the centered prediction is

6.00+.06(2)=6.12.

The fitted mean is identical. Centering changes coefficient interpretation, not the line.
We can verify the equality over all three values in the table:


Code
x <- c(2, 5, 9)
x_centered <- x - 5

beta_0 <- 5.70
beta_1 <- .06
beta_0_centered <- beta_0 + 5 * beta_1

original_prediction <- beta_0 + beta_1 * x
centered_prediction <- beta_0_centered + beta_1 * x_centered

data.frame(
  x = x,
  x_centered = x_centered,
  original_prediction = original_prediction,
  centered_prediction = centered_prediction
)


Every row contains the same two predictions. This equality is the diagnostic for a correct reparameterization.

title: Centering a predictor
section: Choose the reference from the question
text:
Choose the reference from the question
Several references may be defensible.

A theoretical baseline makes the intercept describe a linguistically specified predictor value.
A conventional value, such as 5 bits, may make the intercept easy to state.
The sample mean makes centered predictor values sum to zero in the observed sample.

These choices do not alter the slope in simple linear regression, but they alter the question answered by the intercept. Centering at 5 bits asks for the expected response at 5 bits. Centering at the sample mean asks for the expected response at the average predictor value in that sample.
The sample mean is not automatically the most theoretically useful reference. If two experiments have different surprisal distributions, their mean-centered intercepts refer to different original values. A common declared reference can make comparisons across experiments easier to interpret.

title: Centering a predictor
text:
Distinguish centering from scaling
Centering subtracts a reference:

x^c=x-a.

Scaling divides by a positive constant:

x^s=\frac{x}{b}.

Centering changes the intercept but preserves a one-unit difference. Scaling changes what one unit means and thus changes the numerical slope. If surprisal is divided by 2, a one-unit increase on the new scale corresponds to a two-bit increase on the old scale.
The two operations can be combined, but they answer different interpretive needs. A report should state both the subtracted reference and any divisor.

title: Centering a predictor
text:
Report the reference value
Centering at the sample mean, a theoretical baseline, and a conventional value produce different intercepts. The analysis must state which value was subtracted.

title: Centering a predictor
text:
Interpret the centered reference value
An interpretation must not silently treat the centered zero as the original zero. Suppose x^c=x-5 and the centered intercept is 6.00. An incorrect interpretation would describe 6.00 as the expected response at zero bits. The correct description is the expected response at 5 bits.
This error can survive a technically correct fit because predictions remain unchanged. It is an interpretive failure, not an optimization failure. Reporting the centering constant beside the coefficient prevents it.






NoteCheck the slope




Why does subtracting 5 from every predictor value preserve every one-unit difference between observations?
If the original intercept is 4.2 and the slope is .3, what is the intercept after centering at 10?
What original surprisal does x^c=-2 represent when the centering constant is 5?
Explain why mean centering can make intercepts across two samples refer to different original predictor values.

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
The earlier Bayesian chapters introduced posterior distributions and prior predictive distributions. This page applies those ideas to the same ordinary linear regression likelihood used on the frequentist fitting page.
The ordinary linear regression model is
Y_i\mid x_i,\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma
\sim
\mathcal{N}(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2).
Frequentist fitting treated \beta_0, \beta_1, and \sigma as fixed unknown parameters. Bayesian linear regression adds prior distributions for them.
The conditional response model has not changed. The new step is to represent uncertainty about the coefficients and conditional standard deviation before observing the responses. Instead of starting with one unknown line, the model starts with a distribution over lines.

title: Bayesian linear regression
section: Assign a prior to each coefficient
text:
Assign a prior to each coefficient
Suppose the response is log reading time and surprisal has been centered at 5 bits. One possible specification is

\beta_0\sim\mathcal{N}(6,.25^2)

and

\beta_1\sim\mathcal{N}(0,.10^2).

The intercept prior places most prior density on expected log reading times near 6 at the reference surprisal.
Since surprisal was centered at 5 bits, \beta_0 is the expected log reading time at 5 bits. The prior is thus attached to a specific linguistic reference point. If we had not centered the predictor, the same numerical prior would describe expected log reading time at 0 bits, which may be outside the observed range.
The slope prior is centered at no association and represents most plausible changes per bit as modest on the log-time scale.
About 95 percent of a normal distribution lies within roughly two standard deviations of its mean. Thus this prior places about 95 percent of its mass between -.20 and .20 log-time units per bit. Across a four-bit surprisal contrast, those endpoints imply conditional-mean changes of -.80 and .80. The four-bit implication is often easier to assess than a one-bit coefficient.
The conditional standard deviation also needs a prior that assigns probability only to positive values:

\sigma\sim p_+(\sigma).

For current purposes, suppose p_+ is a half-normal distribution with scale .25:

\sigma\sim\operatorname{Normal}^+(0,.25^2).

The superscript + means that negative draws are excluded. This prior assigns its greatest density near zero while allowing progressively less density for larger response variation.

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
Priors inherit measurement units
A prior standard deviation of .10 for a log-time slope is not automatically suitable for a raw-millisecond slope. The coefficient’s units combine response units per predictor unit.
Centering changes the intercept’s reference point, and rescaling a predictor changes the numerical slope. Prior choices must be interpreted after those transformations are declared.
Suppose we replace surprisal in bits, x, with half-bit units,

x^*=2x.

A one-unit increase in x^* is only a half-bit increase. To represent the same line, the new slope must be

\beta_1^*=\frac{\beta_1}{2}.

The prior standard deviation must likewise change from .10 to .05 if the prior is meant to represent the same response-scale changes. Copying a numerical prior across predictor units would change the model.

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
Inspect prior predictions
Draw parameter values from the priors, calculate conditional means across the observed surprisal range, and draw possible reading times:

\widetilde{Y}_i
\sim
\mathcal{N}(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2).

If the prior model routinely predicts impossible or implausible reading times, the coefficient priors need revision. Prior predictive checking is more informative than calling a normal prior “weak” without examining its response-scale implications.
We can sample prior conditional means without fitting the data:


Code
set.seed(214)

n_draws <- 1000
beta_0 <- rnorm(n_draws, mean = 6, sd = .25)
beta_1 <- rnorm(n_draws, mean = 0, sd = .10)
sigma <- abs(rnorm(n_draws, mean = 0, sd = .25))

centered_surprisal <- c(-3, 0, 4)

prior_means <- sapply(
  centered_surprisal,
  function(x) beta_0 + beta_1 * x
)

apply(prior_means, 2, quantile, probs = c(.025, .5, .975))


The three columns summarize prior expected log reading times at 2, 5, and 9 bits on the original scale. The intervals widen away from the centered reference because uncertainty about the slope contributes more strongly at larger distances from zero.
To inspect possible observations rather than conditional means, we would also draw residual variation using sigma. This produces a wider distribution because individual responses vary around each sampled line.

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
Update to a posterior
Bayes’ rule combines the prior model and normal likelihood:

p(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma\mid\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x})
\propto
p(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{x},\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma)
p(\beta_0)p(\beta_1)p(\sigma).

Posterior draws represent joint uncertainty in the line and conditional standard deviation.
The word joint is load-bearing. A posterior draw contains one compatible value of the intercept, slope, and conditional standard deviation. Combining an intercept from one draw with a slope from another would break the dependencies learned from the data.
For posterior draw s, the conditional mean at predictor value x is

m^{(s)}(x)
=\beta_0^{(s)}+\beta_1^{(s)}x.

Repeating this calculation across draws gives a posterior distribution over the conditional mean at that predictor value.
A 95% credible interval for \beta_1 contains 95% of that coefficient’s posterior probability. This is a posterior statement, not the repeated-sampling statement attached to a confidence interval.

title: Bayesian linear regression
Bayesian linear regression
section: Evaluate priors on the response scale
text:
Evaluate priors on the response scale
Terms such as weakly informative do not determine a prior independently of the measurement scale and predictor range. A verbal label such as weakly informative does not by itself justify an unexamined numerical prior.
A normal slope prior with standard deviation 1 may be modest for one response scale and extreme for another. The response-scale predictions decide. A distribution over regression lines is useful precisely because it lets us inspect those predictions before the data pull the model toward an observed line.






NoteCheck the scale




If surprisal is changed from bits to half-bit units, how does the numerical slope change? Why must the slope prior change with it?
What reference point does the displayed intercept prior describe?
Why must a posterior contrast be calculated within each joint draw?
Explain why a label such as weakly informative does not justify a numerical prior without a scale check.

title: Standard errors
text:
The preceding page defined the sampling distribution of an estimator. Its standard error is the standard deviation of that sampling distribution:
\operatorname{SE}(\widehat{\Theta})
=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\Theta})}.
This definition concerns an estimator, not an individual response. Keeping those two objects separate is the main task on this page.

title: Standard errors
text:
Begin with response variation
Suppose vowel duration in a population has mean \mu and standard deviation

\sigma=30\text{ ms}.

The standard deviation says how far individual vowel durations tend to fall from \mu. If we draw another vowel, its duration may differ substantially from the first one. This is variation among responses.
Now suppose that we repeatedly draw independent samples of 25 vowels. We calculate the sample mean in every sample. Those sample means also vary, but they vary less than the individual durations. This is variation among estimates across samples.








quantity
object that varies
question answered




response standard deviation
individual vowel duration X_i
How dispersed are durations?


standard error
sample mean \overline{X}
How dispersed are mean estimates?



Both quantities have units of milliseconds. Their shared units do not make them interchangeable.

title: Standard errors
section: Derive the standard error of a mean
text:
Derive the standard error of a mean
The estimator of the population mean is

\overline{X}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.

We first move the constant 1/n outside the variance:

\operatorname{Var}(\overline{X})
=\frac{1}{n^2}\operatorname{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right).

If the observations are independent, their variances add. If they also have a common variance \sigma^2, then

\operatorname{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right)
=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(X_i)
=n\sigma^2.

Substitution gives

\operatorname{Var}(\overline{X})
=\frac{n\sigma^2}{n^2}
=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}.

Taking the square root yields the standard error:

\operatorname{SE}(\overline{X})
=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.

For 25 vowels with \sigma=30 ms, the calculation is

\operatorname{SE}(\overline{X})
=\frac{30}{\sqrt{25}}
=6\text{ ms}.

The individual durations have a standard deviation of 30 ms, while means based on 25 independent durations have a standard error of 6 ms.

title: Standard errors
text:
Change the sample size
The square root in the denominator determines how precision changes with sample size.



n
calculation
standard error




25
30/\sqrt{25}
6 ms


100
30/\sqrt{100}
3 ms


400
30/\sqrt{400}
1.5 ms



Multiplying the sample size by four divides the standard error by two. Merely doubling the sample size does not halve it.


Code
sigma <- 30
n <- c(25, 100, 400)
se <- sigma / sqrt(n)

stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(se, c(6, 3, 1.5))))
data.frame(n, se)

title: Standard errors
text:
Estimate an unknown standard error
The population standard deviation \sigma is usually unknown. We replace it with the sample standard deviation s:

\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\overline{X})
=\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}.

Suppose 25 observed vowels have s=32 ms. The estimated standard error is

\frac{32}{\sqrt{25}}=6.4\text{ ms}.

This number is an estimate of estimator spread. It is not a revised estimate of response spread. The response standard deviation remains 32 ms in the sample.

title: Standard errors
text:
Recognize the independence failure
The derivation used independence when it added n separate variances. Repeated tokens from one speaker may be correlated. Counting 400 such tokens as 400 independent observations can thus produce an estimated standard error that is much too small.
The calculation treats the number of rows as the amount of independent information. The relevant n is instead determined by the sampling design and the dependence structure. A large file can contain little independent information.

title: Standard errors
text:
Check your understanding

If \sigma=40 ms and n=16, what is \operatorname{SE}(\overline{X})?
What sample size gives a standard error of 5 ms when \sigma=40 ms?
Why can response standard deviation and standard error have the same units but different interpretations?
Which step of the derivation fails when observations are positively correlated?

The next page asks where the center of the sampling distribution falls. That property is estimator bias.

title: Cross-chain agreement
text:
The trace plot page used visual overlap to assess cross chain agreement. The \widehat{R} statistic summarizes that comparison numerically. Suppose four MCMC chains target a parameter \Theta representing a syntactic complexity effect in a reading time model.
The \widehat{R} statistic compares between-chain variation with within-chain variation. Values near one are consistent with chain agreement. Values above one indicate that chain identity still predicts the sampled value.

title: Cross-chain agreement
text:
Build the basic variance comparison
Let there be M chains with N draws each. Write \overline{\beta}_m for the mean of chain m and s_m^2 for its sample variance.
The average within-chain variance is

W
=
\frac{1}{M}
\sum_{m=1}^Ms_m^2.

The scaled between-chain variance is

B
=
N
\operatorname{Var}
(\overline{\beta}_1,\ldots,\overline{\beta}_M).

A combined variance estimate is

\widehat{V}
=
\frac{N-1}{N}W
+
\frac{1}{N}B.

The basic variance-ratio diagnostic is

\widehat{R}
=
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat{V}}{W}}.

When chain means are separated, B increases and so does \widehat{R}.

title: Cross-chain agreement
text:
Calculate two cases
The following function implements this basic calculation for a matrix with one chain per column.


Code
basic_rhat <- function(draw_matrix) {
  n <- nrow(draw_matrix)
  m <- ncol(draw_matrix)
  within <- mean(apply(draw_matrix, 2, var))
  between <- n * var(colMeans(draw_matrix))
  variance_plus <- ((n - 1) / n) * within + between / n
  sqrt(variance_plus / within)
}

set.seed(556)
n <- 1000
agreeing <- matrix(rnorm(4 * n), nrow = n, ncol = 4)
separated <- sweep(
  matrix(rnorm(4 * n), nrow = n, ncol = 4),
  2,
  c(-2, -2, 2, 2),
  "+"
)

rhat_agreeing <- basic_rhat(agreeing)
rhat_separated <- basic_rhat(separated)

stopifnot(abs(rhat_agreeing - 1) < .01)
stopifnot(rhat_separated > 2)
c(agreeing = rhat_agreeing,
  separated = rhat_separated)


The calculation makes the comparison visible. Current software uses improved versions rather than this elementary formula.

title: Cross-chain agreement
text:
Understand splitting and ranking
A chain can drift from low to high values while retaining the same overall mean as another drifting chain. Splitting each chain into an early half and a late half turns that within-chain change into disagreement among sequences.
Modern \widehat{R} also rank-normalizes the draws before forming the comparison. Ranking improves behavior for skewed and heavy-tailed distributions. The reported diagnostic is commonly called rank-normalized split \widehat{R}.
Students should use the software diagnostic for fitted models. The hand calculation above supplies the logic that the modern procedure refines.

title: Cross-chain agreement
text:
Interpret a failure narrowly
A high \widehat{R} supports a focused conclusion: the chains do not provide mutually consistent draws for that quantity. It does not identify one guaranteed repair. More iterations may help slow exploration, while difficult posterior geometry or weak identification may require a different parameterization or model.
An \widehat{R} value near one is not a convergence certificate. Chains can agree in the same incomplete region, and agreement says little about information lost to dependence. The statistic must be considered with traces and later efficiency diagnostics.
