title: Effective sample size
text:
The autocorrelation page showed why dependent draws contain less information about some summaries than the same number of independent draws. For the basic calculation, suppose one stationary chain contains
S=3{,}000
saved draws for a tone height contrast. If those draws are strongly dependent, they do not estimate posterior summaries as precisely as 3,000 independent target draws. Modern software extends the calculation across multiple chains.
The effective sample size (ESS) is the approximate number of independent draws that would provide comparable Monte Carlo precision.

title: Effective sample size
text:
Connect ESS to autocorrelation
For a stationary scalar sequence, a basic expression is

\operatorname{ESS}
\approx
\frac{S}
{1+2\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\rho_t},

where \rho_t is the autocorrelation at lag t. The denominator is the integrated autocorrelation time. Positive dependence increases this denominator and reduces ESS.

title: Effective sample size
text:
Calculate a geometric case
Suppose

\rho_t=.5^t.

The sum of this geometric series is

\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}.5^t
=1.

Thus

1+2\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\rho_t
=1+2(1)
=3.

The effective sample size is

\operatorname{ESS}
\approx
\frac{3000}{3}
=1000.

The chain output has roughly the mean-estimation precision of 1,000 independent target draws.


Code
saved_draws <- 3000
rho_sum <- sum(.5^(1:100))
integrated_time <- 1 + 2 * rho_sum
ess <- saved_draws / integrated_time

stopifnot(abs(rho_sum - 1) < 1e-12)
stopifnot(abs(ess - 1000) < 1e-8)
c(raw_draws = saved_draws,
  integrated_time = integrated_time,
  ESS = ess)

title: Effective sample size
section: Connect ESS to Monte Carlo error
text:
Connect ESS to Monte Carlo error
If a posterior quantity has standard deviation \sigma_g, the Monte Carlo standard error of its estimated mean is approximately

\operatorname{MCSE}
\approx
\frac{\sigma_g}{\sqrt{\operatorname{ESS}}}.

Suppose the posterior standard deviation of the tone contrast is .30. With ESS equal to 1,000,

\operatorname{MCSE}
\approx
\frac{.30}{\sqrt{1000}}
\approx.0095.

This is numerical uncertainty in the estimated posterior mean. It is not the posterior standard deviation .30 and does not describe uncertainty about the linguistic parameter.

title: Effective sample size
text:
Distinguish bulk and tail information
Bulk ESS measures information relevant to central summaries such as means and medians. Tail ESS measures information relevant to tail probabilities and interval endpoints.
A chain may move adequately through the center while rarely reaching a posterior tail. Its mean can then be estimated precisely while a 2.5% quantile remains unstable. The required ESS depends on the quantity being reported.
Modern ESS estimates combine multiple chains and stabilize the estimated autocorrelation sequence before summing it. The infinite-series formula is the conceptual target, while software must estimate it from finite draws.

title: Effective sample size
section: Effective sample size does not count participants
text:
Effective sample size does not count participants
ESS counts simulation information, not participants, speakers, items, or tokens. An ESS of 1,000 thus does not mean that the study has 1,000 observations.
Running longer can increase ESS and reduce Monte Carlo error. It cannot add information to the posterior target. Low ESS calls the numerical summary into question, while wide posterior uncertainty may remain even after ESS is excellent.
Raw draw count is thus a storage fact. ESS is a summary-specific estimate of computational information. Neither is a measure of linguistic sample size.






NoteProblem Set 4 connection



Problem Set 4, Task 3 reports both bulk and tail effective sample sizes for the model quantities used in the projection analysis. A stable posterior center does not establish that interval endpoints are estimated with comparable simulation information, so both summaries are required.

title: Effective sample size
text:
Check your understanding

Why does positive autocorrelation usually reduce ESS?
If the integrated autocorrelation time is five and S=10{,}000, what is ESS?
Why can bulk ESS and tail ESS differ?
Which quantity changes when the sampler runs longer, posterior spread or Monte Carlo error?

The next page studies an algorithm-specific failure reported as divergent transitions.

title: Conjugate priors
text:
The posterior distribution page normalized a finite update by summing over the parameter values. A conjugate prior allows some continuous updates to be normalized by recognizing a familiar distribution family. Suppose a phonological study records whether a word-final coronal stop is deleted.
X_i\mid\Pi=\pi
\sim
\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi).
The parameter \Pi is the deletion probability for the population and sampling context defined by the study. This page introduces a prior family that makes the posterior update algebraic.

title: Conjugate priors
text:
Write the beta prior
Recall the beta distribution on the unit interval. Choose

\Pi\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,2).

The beta density is

p(\pi)
=
\frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\pi^{\alpha-1}(1-\pi)^{\beta-1},
\qquad 0<\pi<1.

For \alpha=2 and \beta=2, the density is symmetric around .50 and has less density near zero and one. Its mean is

\mathbb{E}[\Pi]
=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}
=\frac{2}{4}
=.50.

When deriving the posterior, terms that do not depend on \pi can be absorbed into a proportionality constant:

p(\pi)\propto\pi^{2-1}(1-\pi)^{2-1}.

title: Conjugate priors
text:
Write the likelihood from counts
Suppose the sample contains s=14 deletions and f=6 realized stops. The Bernoulli likelihood is

p(\mathbf{x}\mid\pi)
=\prod_{i=1}^{20}
\pi^{x_i}(1-\pi)^{1-x_i}.

Collecting equal powers gives the likelihood kernel

p(\mathbf{x}\mid\pi)
\propto
\pi^{14}(1-\pi)^6.

The sequence order does not enter this model. Only the number of deletions and realizations enters the kernel.

title: Conjugate priors
section: Multiply and recognize the posterior family
text:
Multiply and recognize the posterior family
Bayes’ rule gives

\begin{aligned}
p(\pi\mid\mathbf{x})
&\propto
p(\mathbf{x}\mid\pi)p(\pi)\\
&\propto
\pi^{14}(1-\pi)^6
\pi^{2-1}(1-\pi)^{2-1}\\
&=
\pi^{16-1}(1-\pi)^{8-1}.
\end{aligned}

This is the kernel of a beta density. Thus

\Pi\mid\mathbf{x}
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}(16,8).

In general, a \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) prior and Bernoulli data with s successes and f failures produce

\Pi\mid\mathbf{x}
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+s,\beta+f).

The beta distribution is a conjugate prior for the Bernoulli likelihood because the posterior remains in the beta family.

title: Conjugate priors
text:
Calculate posterior summaries
The posterior mean is

\mathbb{E}[\Pi\mid\mathbf{x}]
=\frac{16}{16+8}
=\frac{2}{3}
\approx.667.

The observed proportion is 14/20=.70. The posterior mean lies between the prior mean .50 and the observed proportion. The posterior interval is also available directly from beta quantiles.


Code
alpha_prior <- 2
beta_prior <- 2
successes <- 14
failures <- 6

alpha_posterior <- alpha_prior + successes
beta_posterior <- beta_prior + failures
posterior_mean <- alpha_posterior /
  (alpha_posterior + beta_posterior)
posterior_interval <- qbeta(
  c(.025, .975),
  alpha_posterior,
  beta_posterior
)

stopifnot(alpha_posterior == 16)
stopifnot(beta_posterior == 8)
stopifnot(abs(posterior_mean - 2 / 3) < 1e-12)

c(mean = posterior_mean,
  lower = posterior_interval[1],
  upper = posterior_interval[2])

title: Conjugate priors
section: Do not treat the shapes as literal observations
text:
Do not treat the shapes as literal observations
The update resembles adding two prior successes and two prior failures. This pseudocount interpretation is useful for the algebra, but \alpha and \beta are not literal unobserved tokens. The beta shape parameters determine a density. Their substantive interpretation comes from the probabilities and predictions that density implies.
Conjugacy is likewise a computational property, not a reason to choose the prior. A beta prior may be easy to update while placing implausible mass on deletion rates. Prior predictive simulation, introduced on the next page in the sequence, checks that implication on the observation scale.
The posterior remains conditional on the Bernoulli model. If deletion probabilities vary by speaker or segmental context, the simple update does not represent that structure.

title: Conjugate priors
text:
Check your understanding

Begin with \operatorname{Beta}(3,7) and observe eight deletions and two realizations. What is the posterior?
What is the mean of that posterior?
What property makes the beta prior conjugate here?
Why does conjugacy not establish that a prior is linguistically appropriate?

The next page in the sequence checks priors with prior predictive distributions.

title: The chi-squared test of independence
text:
The Fisher’s exact test page constructed a finite conditional reference distribution for a two by two table. The chi squared test of independence instead uses a large sample reference approximation. Suppose a corpus classifies 300 referring expressions by grammatical role and form.
The chi-squared test of independence compares each observed cell count with the count expected if grammatical role and referring-expression form were independent.

title: The chi-squared test of independence
text:
Construct one expected count
Under independence,

\mathbb{P}(\text{subject and pronoun})
=
\mathbb{P}(\text{subject})
\mathbb{P}(\text{pronoun}).

The marginal probabilities estimated from the table are

\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(\text{subject})
=\frac{150}{300}=.5

and

\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(\text{pronoun})
=\frac{200}{300}=\frac{2}{3}.

Multiplying this joint probability by the grand total gives the expected subject-pronoun count:

E_{11}
=300(.5)\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)
=100.

The same calculation can be written directly from the margins:

E_{ij}
=
\frac{
(\text{row }i\text{ total})
\times
(\text{column }j\text{ total})
}{
\text{grand total}
}.

The expected table under independence is




pronoun
full noun phrase
total




subject
100
50
150


object
100
50
150


total
200
100
300



The expected table has the same margins as the observed table. Only the allocation within rows differs.

title: The chi-squared test of independence
text:
Add the cell discrepancies
Pearson’s statistic is

X^2
=
\sum_i\sum_j
\frac{(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}.

Every cell contributes a nonnegative quantity. For the subject-pronoun cell,

\frac{(120-100)^2}{100}=4.

For the subject-full-noun-phrase cell,

\frac{(30-50)^2}{50}=8.

The object row contributes the same two values:

\frac{(80-100)^2}{100}=4

and

\frac{(70-50)^2}{50}=8.

Thus

X^2=4+8+4+8=24.

Larger values record larger aggregate discrepancies from the independence table.

title: The chi-squared test of independence
text:
Determine the reference distribution
For a table with r rows and c columns, the chi-squared reference distribution has

\nu=(r-1)(c-1)

degrees of freedom. Here,

\nu=(2-1)(2-1)=1.

Once the margins are fixed, only one cell can vary freely. Its value determines the other three counts, which gives the same one degree of freedom seen in the formula.
The upper-tail probability is


Code
reference_table <- matrix(
  c(120, 30,
     80, 70),
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE
)

result <- chisq.test(reference_table, correct = FALSE)
expected <- result$expected
contributions <- (reference_table - expected)^2 / expected
p_value <- pchisq(24, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)

stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(expected), c(100, 100, 50, 50))))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sum(contributions), 24)))
stopifnot(abs(p_value - 9.63357e-07) < 0.000000000001)

expected
contributions
c(chisq = unname(result$statistic), p = p_value)


The p value is approximately 9.63\times10^{-7}. The observed allocation would be highly unusual under the approximate independence reference model.

title: The chi-squared test of independence
text:
Localize the discrepancy
The total statistic is omnibus. It shows that the complete table departs from independence, but it does not say that every imaginable comparison differs.
The signed differences reveal the pattern. Subjects have 20 more pronouns and 20 fewer full noun phrases than expected. Objects show the reverse. Because each deviation is squared in X^2, the total statistic itself discards direction.
An omnibus rejection does not identify which cells produce the association. Inspect observed counts, expected counts, and signed residuals to state where the association lies.

title: The chi-squared test of independence
text:
Check the approximation and independence
The chi-squared reference distribution is a large-sample approximation. It tends to work better when expected cell counts are not sparse. Every expected count here is at least 50, so sparsity is not the main concern.
Observation independence is separate. Repeated expressions from the same speaker or document can be dependent even when all expected counts are large. Large counts do not repair clustered sampling.
For a sparse two-by-two table, Fisher’s exact test supplies a finite-sample conditional calculation. If multiple predictors, interactions, or repeated units matter, a regression model can represent more of the linguistic structure than either table test.

title: The chi-squared test of independence
text:
Check your understanding

Calculate the expected object-pronoun count from the margins.
Why does a two-by-two table have one degree of freedom once its margins are fixed?
Which cells contribute most to X^2, and why?
Why can document clustering invalidate the test even when every expected count is large?

The next section develops posterior distributions, which represent uncertainty about parameter values using a different inferential framework.

title: Bootstrap confidence intervals
text:
The sampling distribution page described how an estimator varies across possible samples, and the confidence interval page used that variation to construct an interval. The bootstrap approximates the same sampling distribution by resampling. Suppose we observe median fundamental frequency for twelve speakers:
Code
f0 <- c(182, 195, 201, 176, 188, 210, 193, 184, 205, 199, 180, 191)
median(f0)
The sample median is 192 Hz. An analytic sampling distribution for the median is less familiar than the sampling distribution of a mean. The nonparametric bootstrap approximates it by resampling the observed units.
The target is the population median of the speaker-level summaries. The estimator is the median of the twelve observed summaries. We would like to know how much that estimator might change if the sampling process produced another set of twelve speakers from the same target population.
If the population distribution were known, we could repeatedly sample from it and calculate a median after each sample. But the population distribution is the object we do not know. The nonparametric bootstrap replaces it with the empirical distribution, which assigns probability 1/12 to each observed speaker summary. This replacement is the bootstrap’s central approximation.

title: Bootstrap confidence intervals
text:
Draw one bootstrap sample
Sample twelve values from the observed twelve, with replacement:


Code
set.seed(414)
f0_star <- sample(f0, size = length(f0), replace = TRUE)
f0_star
median(f0_star)


Because sampling is with replacement, some speakers appear more than once and others do not appear in this bootstrap sample.
For instance, one bootstrap sample might contain

176,180,180,184,188,191,193,193,199,201,205,210.

The value 180 occurs twice, the value 193 occurs twice, and several observed values do not occur. Its median is 192. Another resample will generally contain a different pattern of repetitions and omissions, so its median may differ.
Sampling with replacement is essential. If every bootstrap sample contained each original speaker exactly once, every sample would merely reorder the same twelve numbers. The median would always remain 192, and the resulting distribution would contain no information about sampling variation.

title: Bootstrap confidence intervals
text:
Repeat the procedure
For bootstrap replicate b:

draw a sample of size n from the observed units with replacement;
calculate the estimator on that resample; and
store the resulting estimate \widehat{\theta}^{*(b)}.

Repeat these steps many times:


Code
set.seed(414)

bootstrap_medians <- replicate(
  10000,
  median(sample(f0, size = length(f0), replace = TRUE))
)

hist(bootstrap_medians, xlab = "bootstrap median", main = "")


The empirical distribution of bootstrap estimates approximates the estimator’s sampling distribution, using the observed empirical distribution in place of the unknown population distribution.
The two distributions involved here should not be conflated. The empirical distribution of the twelve f_0 values approximates the population distribution of speaker summaries. The distribution of the 10,000 bootstrap medians approximates the sampling distribution of the median estimator. We resample observations from the first distribution to construct the second.
The following summary makes that separation visible:


Code
c(
  observed_median = median(f0),
  bootstrap_mean = mean(bootstrap_medians),
  bootstrap_standard_error = sd(bootstrap_medians)
)


The standard deviation of the bootstrap medians is a bootstrap estimate of the standard error. It describes variation in the estimator across bootstrap samples. It is not the standard deviation of speaker fundamental frequency.

title: Bootstrap confidence intervals
text:
Form a percentile interval
A 95% percentile bootstrap confidence interval takes the .025 and .975 quantiles of the bootstrap estimates:


Code
quantile(bootstrap_medians, c(.025, .975))


The calculation is simple, but the percentile interval is not always the most accurate bootstrap construction. Its purpose here is to make the resampling logic visible.
Suppose the resulting interval is [182,201] Hz. The repeated-sampling claim is about the procedure. If we could repeatedly sample twelve speakers from the target population and construct an interval in this way, the method is intended to cover the population median in about 95 percent of those repetitions under conditions where the bootstrap approximation works well. The endpoints are not probabilities for the fixed population median.
The percentile method uses the quantiles of the bootstrap estimates directly. It tends to work best when the bootstrap distribution is reasonably centered on the observed estimate and not strongly skewed. With only twelve observations, the sample may give a poor approximation to the population, especially in its tails. The interval can also have coarse endpoints because a median from a small sample can take only a limited set of values.

title: Bootstrap confidence intervals
text:
Choose the resampling unit
The example has one summary per speaker, so resampling speakers matches the proposed independent unit.
If the raw table instead contained many vowel tokens per speaker, resampling individual rows would treat those tokens as exchangeable across speakers and destroy the within-speaker structure. A suitable bootstrap might resample speakers and retain each selected speaker’s observations together.
Consider a table with 20 speakers and 30 vowel tokens per speaker. The table has 600 rows, but it does not necessarily contain 600 independent units. If the scientific claim concerns speakers, one speaker should enter or leave a bootstrap sample as a block. A selected speaker may appear twice, along with both copies of that speaker’s complete token set. An omitted speaker contributes no tokens to that replicate.
The statistic must also be recomputed from the resampled data. If the analysis first averages tokens within speaker and then compares vowel categories within speaker, each bootstrap replicate must repeat those operations. Resampling a finished list of token-level residuals would correspond to a different procedure.
The bootstrap reproduces the sampling assumptions encoded by the resampling design. It does not decide which units are independent.

title: Bootstrap confidence intervals
text:
Check simulation error
The earlier random seed page separated reproducibility from validity. Here the number of bootstrap replicates B controls Monte Carlo precision. With a small B, the estimated quantiles may move appreciably when the random seed changes. We can check this source of variation by running the same procedure with several values of B.


Code
bootstrap_interval <- function(B, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  estimates <- replicate(
    B,
    median(sample(f0, size = length(f0), replace = TRUE))
  )
  quantile(estimates, c(.025, .975))
}

bootstrap_interval(500, 214)
bootstrap_interval(5000, 214)
bootstrap_interval(5000, 414)


If the 5,000-replicate intervals agree closely while the 500-replicate interval moves, more simulation has reduced Monte Carlo error. If large bootstrap runs still produce an unstable scientific conclusion, the issue may lie in the small original sample or the resampling design. Increasing B cannot create new speakers.






NoteCheck one replicate




Why must a nonparametric bootstrap sample contain n draws rather than every original case exactly once? Explain what would happen to the estimate if no cases were repeated or omitted.
Distinguish the empirical distribution of the observations from the bootstrap distribution of the estimates.
If a dataset contains repeated tokens from each speaker, state which rows should move together when speakers are the intended independent units.
Explain why increasing B reduces simulation error but does not repair a sample containing too few speakers.

title: Autocorrelation in a Markov chain
text:
The \widehat{R} page compared different chains. We now use the correlation concept introduced earlier to describe dependence across iterations within one Markov chain. Suppose one chain contains saved draws for a consonant duration parameter:
.10,.12,.13,.15,.14,.18,\ldots
Adjacent values are similar because the sampler moves through the posterior gradually. The autocorrelation measures the association between a sequence and a shifted copy of itself.

title: Autocorrelation in a Markov chain
text:
Construct lagged pairs
At lag one, align every draw except the last with the following draw:



draw at s
draw at s+1




.10
.12


.12
.13


.13
.15


.15
.14


.14
.18



The correlation between these columns is the empirical lag-one autocorrelation.
For a stationary chain, the population autocorrelation at lag t is

\rho_t
=
\operatorname{Cor}
(\Theta^{(s)},\Theta^{(s+t)}).

Lag one compares adjacent draws. Lag ten compares draws separated by ten transitions. A chain of length 1,000 supplies 999 lag-one pairs and 990 lag-ten pairs.

title: Autocorrelation in a Markov chain
text:
Read the autocorrelation function
The sequence

\rho_1,\rho_2,\rho_3,\ldots

is the autocorrelation function (ACF). Rapid decay toward zero suggests that dependence weakens over a small number of transitions. Slow decay means that information about one draw persists across many later draws.
An autoregressive sequence supplies a controlled illustration:

X_s=.85X_{s-1}+\varepsilon_s.

Its theoretical autocorrelation is \rho_t=.85^t.


Code
set.seed(829)
draws <- as.numeric(
  arima.sim(model = list(ar = .85), n = 5000)
)
empirical_acf <- as.numeric(
  acf(draws, lag.max = 10, plot = FALSE)$acf
)

stopifnot(abs(empirical_acf[2] - .85) < .05)
data.frame(
  lag = 0:10,
  empirical = empirical_acf,
  theoretical = .85^(0:10)
)


The entry at lag zero is one because a sequence is perfectly correlated with itself. The following entries estimate dependence across increasing separation.

title: Autocorrelation in a Markov chain
text:
Separate target correctness from efficiency
High autocorrelation does not by itself imply the wrong stationary distribution. A transition can preserve the correct posterior while moving through it slowly. The problem is efficiency for a finite run.
When adjacent draws are nearly repetitions, 5,000 saved values contain less information about a posterior mean than 5,000 independent target draws. Strong positive autocorrelation thus increases Monte Carlo error for a fixed raw draw count.
Negative autocorrelation can instead make alternating draws offset one another and may improve precision for some averages. The complete autocorrelation pattern matters, not only the lag-one value.
Autocorrelation does not by itself make a stationary chain invalid or a Monte Carlo estimate biased. It primarily changes the variance of Monte Carlo estimates when the chain explores the target. Failure to reach a target region is a different problem.

title: Autocorrelation in a Markov chain
text:
Do not thin by default
Keeping every tenth draw reduces visible autocorrelation in the stored sequence, but it also discards information. Unless storage or downstream computation is limiting, retaining draws and accounting for their dependence is usually more informative than routine thinning.

title: Autocorrelation in a Markov chain
text:
Check your understanding

How many aligned pairs enter lag 25 for a chain of length 1,000?
What does slow ACF decay show about saved draws?
Why can a correct chain still have high autocorrelation?
Why does thinning not create new information?
Why can two chains with the same lag-one autocorrelation still have different long-lag efficiency?

The effective-sample-size page translates the dependence pattern into an information-equivalent draw count.

title: Why use random variables?
text:
The foundations chapter defined outcomes, events, and probability measures. Suppose one outcome in a phonetics study is a complete vowel token. The stored record includes the speaker, word, waveform, vowel label, and measured duration, but the research question may concern only duration.
We need a principled way to move from the complete token to the property used in the analysis. A random variable provides that mapping.
Let \Omega contain the complete vowel token outcomes. Define a mapping D that returns the duration of each outcome in milliseconds:
D(\omega)=\text{duration of vowel token }\omega.
For three constructed outcomes, the mapping might look like this.
The outcomes remain complete tokens. The mapping returns one numerical value from each token.

title: Why use random variables?
text:
Values give us new events
Suppose we want the event that vowel duration exceeds 100 ms. Using D, we can write

D>100.

This expression is shorthand for the set of outcomes whose mapped values exceed 100:

\{\omega\in\Omega:D(\omega)>100\}.

In the table, that event contains \omega_1 and \omega_3. The event still consists of vowel token outcomes, not bare duration values.
This connection is the main reason to introduce a random variable. A random variable maps each outcome to a value while retaining the event in the original sample space that produced any selected set of values.

title: Why use random variables?
section: One outcome can support several questions
text:
One outcome can support several questions
Duration is not the only property of the token. Define another mapping H by

H(\omega)=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if the vowel is high},\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}

The same outcome \omega_1 may satisfy D(\omega_1)=112 and H(\omega_1)=1. The two mappings do not compete. They encode different questions about the same represented token.
This separation is useful because the stored record is usually richer than any single analysis response. We can define one variable for duration, another for vowel height, and another for speaker identity without pretending that the record itself is a single number.

title: Why use random variables?
section: Work through the mapping in base R
text:
Work through the mapping in base R


Code
tokens <- data.frame(
  outcome = c("omega1", "omega2", "omega3"),
  word = c("heed", "hid", "heed"),
  speaker = c("s01", "s01", "s02"),
  duration = c(112, 83, 126)
)

tokens$outcome[tokens$duration > 100]


The result contains omega1 and omega3. The code returns outcome identifiers after selecting on the mapped duration values.

title: Why use random variables?
section: Retain the outcomes as well as the extracted values
text:
Retain the outcomes as well as the extracted values
Extracting a property does not make the original outcome dispensable. If the table keeps only the values 112, 83, and 126, then speaker and word identity disappear. A later analysis can no longer ask whether durations repeat within speakers or differ across words.
A random variable does not require this deletion. It is a mapping defined on outcomes. Retaining the outcome identifier and other design identifiers keeps the extracted value connected to the observation process.

title: Why use random variables?
text:
Check your understanding

Let W(\omega) return the word produced in token \omega. Which outcomes in the table belong to the event W=\textit{heed}?
Explain why D>100 describes a set of vowel tokens rather than a set containing only the numbers 112 and 126.
Define a mapping that records whether the speaker is s01. What are its possible values?
Which information is lost if duration values replace the complete outcomes rather than being attached to them?

This page motivated the mapping. The next page states the formal condition that makes such a mapping compatible with the probability model.

title: Variance
text:
The expected value page summarized the center of a distribution. Suppose D records the dependency length of a selected syntactic relation. Two probability models may have the same mean dependency length while differing in how tightly their mass is concentrated around that mean.
Consider these constructed PMFs.
Both variables have mean 2:
\mathbb{E}[D_1]=2
and
\mathbb{E}[D_2]=1(.50)+3(.50)=2.
The means do not capture the fact that D_1 always equals 2 while D_2 is always one word away from 2.
The variance summarizes expected squared distance from the mean:
\operatorname{Var}(X)
=\mathbb{E}\!\left[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^2\right].

title: Variance
text:
Compute deviations before averaging
For D_2, subtract the mean from each support value.



d
d-2
(d-2)^2
mass
weighted squared deviation




1
-1
1
.50
.50


3
1
1
.50
.50



Add the final column:

\operatorname{Var}(D_2)=.50+.50=1.

For D_1, the only value equals its mean. Its squared deviation is zero, so

\operatorname{Var}(D_1)=0.

The two variables have equal means but different variances.

title: Variance
text:
Why square the deviations?
If we averaged the signed deviations from the mean, the result would be zero:

(-1)(.50)+(1)(.50)=0.

This cancellation occurs for any variable with a finite mean. Squaring makes deviations on both sides contribute positively.
Squaring also gives greater weight to larger departures. A deviation of 2 contributes 2^2=4, while a deviation of 1 contributes 1^2=1. Variance is thus sensitive to probability placed far from the mean.

title: Variance
text:
Compute variance in base R


Code
dependency_length <- c(1, 3)
dependency_mass <- c(.50, .50)

mean_length <- sum(dependency_length * dependency_mass)
variance_length <- sum((dependency_length - mean_length)^2 * dependency_mass)

c(mean = mean_length, variance = variance_length)


The results are 2 and 1. The code follows the definition directly: find the mean, compute squared deviations, weight them, and add.

title: Variance
text:
Keep the units visible
If dependency length is measured in words, then each deviation is measured in words. Squaring produces squared words. The variance of D_2 is thus 1 squared word.
Squared units make variance useful for algebra but less direct as a descriptive distance. The next page takes a square root to return to the original measurement units.
Variance also requires the expected squared deviation to be finite. A variable can have a finite mean but place enough probability far from that mean for its variance to be infinite.

title: Variance
text:
Signed deviations cancel
The mean signed deviation cannot summarize spread. The positive and negative deviations cancel, producing zero even for the dispersed variable D_2.
Variance repairs the cancellation by squaring before averaging. This choice defines a particular spread summary; it should not be confused with an average absolute distance.

title: Variance
text:
Check your understanding

Compute the variance of a variable that takes 0 and 4 with equal probability.
Why is the average signed deviation from the mean always zero when the expectation exists?
What units does variance have when the variable is measured in milliseconds?
Can a variable have variance zero while taking two different values with positive probability? Justify your answer from the definition.

Variance measures spread in squared units. The next page expresses the same spread scale in the units of the original variable.

title: Student’s t distribution
text:
The normal distribution page introduced standardization when the population scale is fixed. Suppose instead that a sample mean is centered at a reference value and divided by a scale estimated from the same finite normal sample. The resulting statistic has more tail uncertainty than a standard normal variable.
Student’s t distribution is the heavier tailed symmetric reference family for that statistic. We write
T\sim t(\nu),
where \nu>0 is the degrees of freedom.
The distribution is centered at zero and symmetric:
f_T(-t)=f_T(t).
Its tails contain more probability than the standard normal tails when \nu is finite.

title: Student’s t distribution
text:
Compare central intervals
The middle 95 percent of a standard normal distribution lies between approximately -1.96 and 1.96. For t(5), the middle 95 percent lies between approximately

-2.57\text{ and }2.57.

The wider interval reflects heavier tails. A value of 2.2 is outside the central normal interval but inside the central t(5) interval.
As the degrees of freedom increase, the t family approaches the standard normal family.



reference
lower .025 quantile
upper .975 quantile




t(5)
about -2.57
about 2.57


t(10)
about -2.23
about 2.23


t(30)
about -2.04
about 2.04


standard normal
about -1.96
about 1.96



The table makes the limiting pattern visible without treating degrees of freedom as a generic scale parameter.

title: Student’s t distribution
text:
Calculate a two-sided tail probability
Suppose the observed standardized value is |t|=2.5 with 5 degrees of freedom. Symmetry gives

\mathbb{P}(|T|\geq2.5)
=2\mathbb{P}(T\geq2.5).

In R,


Code
2 * pt(2.5, df = 5, lower.tail = FALSE)


The probability is approximately .0545. Under the standard normal reference, the corresponding two-sided tail probability is about .0124. Scale uncertainty changes the reference probability substantially.

title: Student’s t distribution
text:
Interpret degrees of freedom
Degrees of freedom record how much independent information remains for estimating variation after constraints have been imposed. In the simple case of estimating one mean from n observations, deviations from that estimated mean must sum to zero. Only n-1 deviations can vary freely, giving

\nu=n-1.

Other designs and estimators create different constraints. Thus \nu should not be treated as another name for sample size.
Smaller \nu represents greater uncertainty about the scale used in the standardized quantity. The reference distribution then places more probability in the tails. Larger \nu reduces that extra tail mass.

title: Student’s t distribution
section: Inspect several references in base R
text:
Inspect several references in base R


Code
degrees_freedom <- c(5, 10, 30)

data.frame(
  df = degrees_freedom,
  lower = qt(.025, df = degrees_freedom),
  upper = qt(.975, df = degrees_freedom)
)


These quantiles are properties of the reference distributions, not estimates of the lexical decision effect itself.

title: Student’s t distribution
text:
Keep two uses separate
The t family may be used as a reference distribution for a standardized estimator. It may also be used as a model for response deviations with heavier tails. These are different statistical roles.
Choosing a t reference for an estimator does not change the observed response values or make the sample mean resistant to an extreme measurement. A robust response model requires an explicit likelihood choice.

title: Student’s t distribution
section: Heavy tails do not repair the measurement model
text:
Heavy tails do not repair the measurement model
A heavier tailed reference distribution does not automatically make the underlying measurement analysis robust. The reference describes uncertainty in a standardized quantity. It does not rewrite the measurement model that produced that quantity.
Specify which object follows the t distribution: a reference statistic, an error term, or another standardized variable.

title: Student’s t distribution
text:
Check your understanding

Which central 95 percent interval is wider, t(5) or t(30)? Explain using scale uncertainty.
Why does estimating one mean from n values leave n-1 freely varying deviations?
Would |t|=2.5 have more upper tail probability under t(5) or the standard normal reference?
What must be specified before claiming that a t family makes a response model robust?

The t family represents a signed standardized quantity. The next page represents nonnegative sums of squared standardized quantities.

title: Reproducing a simulation
text:
The preceding page introduced simulation from a target distribution. Suppose we simulate ten choices between two word orders under a target probability of .60 for order A. Running the simulation twice usually gives different sequences because the pseudorandom number generator advances after each draw.
A random seed sets that generator to a known initial state. It makes the computational sequence reproducible.
Code
set.seed(214)
sample(c("A", "B"), size = 10, replace = TRUE,
       prob = c(.60, .40))

set.seed(214)
sample(c("A", "B"), size = 10, replace = TRUE,
       prob = c(.60, .40))
The two simulated vectors are identical. The seed does not change the target probabilities. It restarts the generator from the same state.

title: Reproducing a simulation
section: Separate the procedure from one realization
text:
Separate the procedure from one realization
The sampling procedure is the instruction to draw ten independent labels with probabilities .60 and .40. A seed determines which particular ten labels appear in one computational run.
Another seed gives another valid realization from the same procedure. Neither realization must contain exactly six A outcomes. The target proportion concerns repeated simulation, not a requirement imposed on each small sample.
This distinction is useful when a simulated summary enters an analysis. A stable result should not depend materially on the accidental choice of seed once enough simulation draws have been used.

title: Reproducing a simulation
section: Set the seed once before related draws
text:
Set the seed once before related draws
Consider this incorrect loop:


Code
simulated_count <- numeric(100)

for (b in 1:100) {
  set.seed(214)
  simulated_count[b] <- sum(runif(10) <= .60)
}


Every iteration resets the generator. The loop repeats the same simulated count 100 times.
Set the seed once instead:


Code
set.seed(214)
simulated_count <- numeric(100)

for (b in 1:100) {
  simulated_count[b] <- sum(runif(10) <= .60)
}


Now the complete sequence is reproducible while individual iterations differ.

title: Reproducing a simulation
text:
Check simulation stability during development
Suppose we estimate the expected A count by averaging many simulated counts. We can compare several seeds:


Code
estimate_mean_count <- function(seed, draws) {
  set.seed(seed)
  mean(replicate(draws, sum(runif(10) <= .60)))
}

sapply(c(11, 29, 47), estimate_mean_count, draws = 10000)


Each result should be near the theoretical expectation 10(.60)=6. If conclusions change across seeds, the simulation may use too few draws or contain an implementation error.
Increasing draws reduces Monte Carlo variation. It does not repair a wrong target distribution.

title: Reproducing a simulation
section: Place the seed at the right scope
text:
Place the seed at the right scope
One analysis may contain several related random operations. Setting one seed before the complete block makes the whole sequence reproducible. Resetting before every individual call can create unintended repetition or dependence.
The seed should be recorded with the code and set before the first random draw that affects the reported result.

title: Reproducing a simulation
text:
Reproducibility is not validity
A reproducible simulation is not necessarily statistically valid. A fixed seed cannot make dependent tokens independent, correct an incorrect PMF, or make a convenience sample representative.
Reproducibility answers whether another analyst can regenerate the same computation. Adequacy answers whether the computation represents the intended linguistic process. These questions require separate checks.

title: Reproducing a simulation
text:
Check your understanding

What object does set.seed() hold fixed?
Why does resetting the same seed inside a loop repeat outcomes?
If a simulated estimate changes substantially across seeds, what should be checked?
Why can a perfectly reproducible simulation still use an inadequate linguistic model?

Simulation draws one variable at a time or several together. The next page begins the multivariable sequence by assigning probability to value combinations.

title: Probability density functions
text:
The preceding page explained why a continuous distribution assigns zero probability to an exact value. Suppose R is the speaking rate of an utterance in syllables per second. A table of point masses thus cannot describe how probability is arranged across its support.
A probability density function, abbreviated PDF, assigns a density height f_R(r) to each possible rate r. Probability is obtained from area under this function, not from the height at one point.
The distinction is visible in the statement
\mathbb{P}(R=4)=0
even when f_R(4) is positive. The height describes how quickly probability accumulates near 4 syllables per second.

title: Probability density functions
text:
Begin with a simple density
Consider the constructed function

f_R(r)=
\begin{cases}
\frac{1}{4} & \text{if }2\leq r\leq6,\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}

The density has height 1/4 across an interval of width 6-2=4. Its total area is

4\times\frac{1}{4}=1.

Thus the function allocates one unit of total probability across its support.

title: Probability density functions
section: Find an interval probability by hand
text:
Find an interval probability by hand
What is the probability that speaking rate falls between 3 and 5 syllables per second? The interval has width 2 and density height 1/4, so its area is

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(3\leq R\leq5)
&=2\times\frac{1}{4}\\
&=.50.
\end{aligned}

Integral notation expresses the same area calculation:

\mathbb{P}(3\leq R\leq5)
=\int_3^5 f_R(r)\,\mathrm{d}r.

The integral adds the areas of narrow strips across the selected interval. In this constant height example, it reduces to width times height.

title: Probability density functions
text:
Check the two PDF requirements
A density must be nonnegative:

f_R(r)\geq0
\qquad\text{for every }r.

Its total area must equal one:

\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_R(r)\,\mathrm{d}r=1.

These conditions concern area. A density height may exceed one when it is concentrated on a narrow interval. For instance, height 2 across an interval of width .5 gives area 2\times.5=1.

title: Probability density functions
section: Check the area in base R
text:
Check the area in base R


Code
rate_density <- function(r) {
  ifelse(r >= 2 & r <= 6, 1 / 4, 0)
}

integrate(rate_density, lower = 2, upper = 6)$value
integrate(rate_density, lower = 3, upper = 5)$value


The returned values are one for the complete support and .5 for the selected interval.

title: Probability density functions
text:
Interpret density in measurement units
The density f_R(r) has units inverse to the units of R. Here the height is measured per syllable per second. Multiplying by interval width cancels those units and produces a unitless probability.
This unit check is another reason not to interpret density height as probability. The two objects have different units as well as different mathematical roles.

title: Probability density functions
section: Density height is not point probability
text:
Density height is not point probability
The value f_R(r) is not \mathbb{P}(R=r). If f_R(4)=.25, it is incorrect to say that the probability of exactly 4 syllables per second is .25. The point probability is zero under the continuous model.
The valid interpretation concerns a region: probability near 4 accumulates at a rate described by the density height, and an interval probability is the area across that region.

title: Probability density functions
text:
Check your understanding

Under the constructed density, compute \mathbb{P}(2\leq R\leq3) by width times height.
Why may a density height exceed one without producing a probability larger than one?
Explain what f_R(4)=.25 says and what it does not say.
A candidate density has height .2 from 0 to 4 and zero elsewhere. Does it have total area one?

Mass and density represent probability differently. The next page gives one threshold function that applies to both representations.

title: The normal distribution
text:
The preceding pages introduced continuous distributions through their probability density functions. Suppose a phonetic model represents an F1 measurement as varying symmetrically around 550 Hz. Values near 550 receive the most density, and values become less dense as their distance from 550 grows in either direction.
The normal distribution is a continuous location and scale family with this symmetric shape. We write
X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2).
The first parameter is the mean:
\mathbb{E}[X]=\mu.
The second parameter is the variance:
\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.
Thus the standard deviation is \sigma, not \sigma^2.

title: The normal distribution
section: Read the density from the center outward
text:
Read the density from the center outward
The density is

f_X(x)
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}
\exp\!\left[-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right].

At x=\mu, the centered distance x-\mu is zero, so the density reaches its maximum. Moving the same distance above or below \mu produces the same squared distance and thus the same density.
This equality gives the family’s symmetry:

f_X(\mu-d)=f_X(\mu+d).

The density decreases smoothly as |d| grows.

title: The normal distribution
section: Change location while holding scale fixed
text:
Change location while holding scale fixed
Increasing \mu shifts the full density to larger values. Decreasing \mu shifts it to smaller values. The spread and symmetric shape remain unchanged when \sigma is held fixed.
For instance, moving from \mathcal{N}(550,40^2) to \mathcal{N}(600,40^2) adds 50 Hz to the center without changing the standard deviation.

title: The normal distribution
section: Change scale while holding location fixed
text:
Change scale while holding location fixed
Increasing \sigma spreads probability across a wider range. The density peak becomes lower because the total area must remain one. Decreasing \sigma concentrates probability nearer \mu.
Compare \mathcal{N}(550,40^2) with \mathcal{N}(550,80^2). Both have mean 550 Hz, but the second standard deviation is twice as large.


Code
f1 <- seq(300, 800, length.out = 400)

plot(f1, dnorm(f1, mean = 550, sd = 40), type = "l",
     xlab = "F1 in Hz", ylab = "density")
lines(f1, dnorm(f1, mean = 600, sd = 40), lty = 2)
lines(f1, dnorm(f1, mean = 550, sd = 80), lty = 3)


The first comparison isolates location; the second isolates scale.

title: The normal distribution
text:
Standardize one value
Standardization subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation. The resulting z-score

Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}

records signed distance from the mean in standard deviation units. Under the normal model,

Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).

For X\sim\mathcal{N}(550,40^2), the values 510 and 590 are one standard deviation below and above the mean:

\frac{510-550}{40}=-1

and

\frac{590-550}{40}=1.

The probability between them is

\mathbb{P}(510\leq X\leq590)
=\mathbb{P}(-1\leq Z\leq1)
\approx.683.

In R,


Code
pnorm(590, mean = 550, sd = 40) -
  pnorm(510, mean = 550, sd = 40)


This interval calculation is a property of the normal family. It is not a universal rule for every distribution with mean 550 and standard deviation 40.

title: The normal distribution
text:
Check support against the measurement
A normal variable has support across the full real line. It assigns some density to negative values even when the measurement, such as F1, cannot be negative.
The approximation may still be useful when the mean is many standard deviations from the boundary and the modeled density below zero is negligible. It may be poor for a strongly right skewed response or one concentrated near a hard boundary.

title: The normal distribution
text:
A histogram is not enough
A roughly bell shaped histogram does not by itself justify a normal model. A finite histogram may hide tail asymmetry, boundary problems, or repeated structure across speakers and items.
Check the support, the symmetry claim, and the deviations relevant to the linguistic analysis. Visual familiarity alone does not establish those properties.

title: The normal distribution
text:
Check your understanding

In \mathcal{N}(100,225), what are the mean, variance, and standard deviation?
Standardize X=130 under the model in the first question.
Which parameter changes when a density shifts right without changing shape?
Give one linguistic response for which support on the full real line may be a poor direct choice.

The normal family fixes a particular tail shape. The next page retains symmetry while allowing more probability far from the center.

title: Marginal distributions
text:
The preceding page retained the paired values of two random variables. A marginal distribution removes one variable by summing or integrating over all of its values. Suppose a morphological analysis records tense T and number N for one sampled verb token.
The joint table preserves both distinctions. If our question concerns tense without retaining number, we must add over all number values.
The resulting one variable PMF is the marginal distribution of tense.

title: Marginal distributions
section: Sum one row at a time
text:
Sum one row at a time
The past tense mass is

\begin{aligned}
p_T(\mathrm{past})
&=p_{T,N}(\mathrm{past},\mathrm{sg})
+p_{T,N}(\mathrm{past},\mathrm{pl})\\
&=.30+.20\\
&=.50.
\end{aligned}

The present tense mass is

p_T(\mathrm{pres})=.15+.35=.50.

Thus the marginal tense PMF is (.50,.50).
The same operation down columns gives the marginal number PMF:

p_N(\mathrm{sg})=.30+.15=.45

and

p_N(\mathrm{pl})=.20+.35=.55.

title: Marginal distributions
section: Add the margins to the table
text:
Add the margins to the table




singular
plural
p_T(t)




past
.30
.20
.50


present
.15
.35
.50


p_N(n)
.45
.55
1



The term marginal comes from writing the resulting probabilities at the margins of a joint table.

title: Marginal distributions
text:
State the general operation
For discrete variables,

p_T(t)=\sum_n p_{T,N}(t,n).

Hold T at the selected value t and sum over every possible value of N.
For continuous variables,

f_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}y.

The integral accumulates joint density across all y while holding x fixed.
Both operations remove one represented distinction while retaining a probability distribution over the other variable.

title: Marginal distributions
section: Compute the margins in base R
text:
Compute the margins in base R


Code
joint_tense_number <- matrix(
  c(.30, .15, .20, .35),
  nrow = 2,
  dimnames = list(
    tense = c("past", "present"),
    number = c("singular", "plural")
  )
)

rowSums(joint_tense_number)
colSums(joint_tense_number)


The row sums give the tense margin; the column sums give the number margin.

title: Marginal distributions
text:
What marginalization changes
Marginalizing number answers how tense probability is allocated when number is not distinguished. It does not claim that number has no relationship with tense.
In the joint table, plural tokens are more often present than past, while singular tokens are more often past than present. Those pairings disappear from the tense margin (.50,.50).
Marginalization is thus a deliberate loss of information. It is appropriate when the target question averages across the removed variable.

title: Marginal distributions
section: Marginalizing does not make a variable irrelevant
text:
Marginalizing does not make a variable irrelevant
Summing over a variable for one calculation does not make it scientifically irrelevant. Number was summed out to answer one tense question, but the joint table still shows a tense and number association.
State the target. The marginal distribution averages across N; a conditional or joint question retains it.

title: Marginal distributions
text:
Check your understanding

Compute p_N(\mathrm{pl}) from the joint cells.
Verify that each marginal PMF sums to one.
Which joint information is lost when number is marginalized?
For continuous variables, which variable disappears in f_X(x)=\int f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy?

Marginalization removes a distinction. The next page asks whether two variables remain associated after a third distinction is held fixed.

title: Joint distributions
text:
The foundations chapter introduced the joint probability of two events. A joint distribution extends that idea to pairs of random variable values. Suppose each dialogue turn is annotated for two properties. Let P record whether the turn contains a politeness marker, and let R record whether it ends in a final pitch rise:
P=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{politeness marker present},\\
0 & \text{politeness marker absent},
\end{cases}
and
R=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{final rise present},\\
0 & \text{final rise absent}.
\end{cases}
One sampled turn produces a pair (P,R). The possible pairs are
(0,0),\ (0,1),\ (1,0),\ (1,1).
A joint distribution assigns probability to these value combinations.

title: Joint distributions
text:
Read a joint PMF table
Consider this constructed joint PMF.




no rise R=0
rise R=1




no marker P=0
.25
.15


marker P=1
.20
.40



The lower right cell says

p_{P,R}(1,1)
=\mathbb{P}(P=1,R=1)
=.40.

It is the probability that one turn contains both a politeness marker and a final rise.
The upper right cell says

p_{P,R}(0,1)=.15,

the probability of a final rise without a politeness marker.
The subscript on p_{P,R} identifies the two variables in the joint PMF. The comma inside the probability event means that both value statements hold for the same outcome.

title: Joint distributions
text:
Check the joint PMF requirements
Every cell is nonnegative. The cells also sum to one:

.25+.15+.20+.40=1.

The four value pairs are mutually exclusive and exhaustive under the two binary annotations. One turn belongs to exactly one cell.
A single row or column does not need to sum to one. It represents only part of the complete pair space. The whole table is the PMF.

title: Joint distributions
section: Ask about a set of pairs
text:
Ask about a set of pairs
The event that at least one annotation is present contains three pairs:

\{(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)\}.

Its probability is

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(P=1\text{ or }R=1)
&=.15+.20+.40\\
&=.75.
\end{aligned}

The remaining pair (0,0) has probability .25, so the complement check gives 1-.25=.75.

title: Joint distributions
section: Store and inspect the table in base R
text:
Store and inspect the table in base R


Code
joint_pr <- matrix(
  c(.25, .20, .15, .40),
  nrow = 2,
  dimnames = list(
    politeness = c("absent", "present"),
    rise = c("absent", "present")
  )
)

joint_pr
sum(joint_pr)
joint_pr["present", "present"]


R fills matrices by columns, so the vector order must match the declared row and column labels. The final indexing call checks the linguistic interpretation of one cell.

title: Joint distributions
section: Why separate PMFs do not recover pairing
text:
Why separate PMFs do not recover pairing
Suppose we know how often politeness markers occur and how often final rises occur. Those two separate summaries do not tell us which turns contain both.
Many joint tables can have the same separate probabilities while placing different amounts of mass on (1,1). The pairing information lives in the joint distribution.
This fact is central for linguistic association. If a final rise and a politeness marker tend to cooccur, the pattern concerns how their values are paired on the same turns, not only how frequent each annotation is separately.

title: Joint distributions
text:
The continuous version
For continuous X and Y, a joint density f_{X,Y}(x,y) allocates density across a two dimensional support. A single point (x,y) has probability zero. Probabilities are volumes over regions of value pairs.
The representation changes from a table of masses to a surface of density, but the object remains a distribution over paired values.

title: Joint distributions
text:
Preserve the pairing
Paired observations cannot be replaced with two separate lists. Shuffling the rise labels across turns leaves the separate frequencies unchanged while changing which turns occupy each joint cell.
Retain the observation key connecting both measurements to the same turn. A joint distribution requires that pairing.

title: Joint distributions
text:
Check your understanding

Translate p_{P,R}(1,0) into a linguistic event and read its probability from the table.
Compute the probability that exactly one annotation is present.
Why can a row sum be less than one in a valid joint PMF?
Explain how shuffling one annotation changes the joint distribution without changing either separate frequency table.

The joint table retains both variables. The next page removes one distinction by adding over all of its values.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
The foundations module assigned probabilities to events in a sample space. Linguistic analyses often need a further step. The outcomes may be recordings, annotated sentences, or complete experimental trials, while the analysis concerns one property of those outcomes.
This module develops the mapping from a linguistic outcome to a value and then asks how probability is arranged across the resulting values.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
The representation sequence
The first group of pages introduces the relevant objects in a fixed order.

Why use random variables? begins with the problem of extracting one property from a complex linguistic outcome.
Defining random variables states the mapping formally and explains why preimages must be measurable events.
Discrete random variables have values that can be listed.
Probability mass functions assign probability to the separate values of a discrete variable.
Continuous random variables take values throughout an interval under the model.
Probability density functions represent continuous probability as area.
Cumulative distribution functions accumulate probability through a threshold for either kind of variable.

The discrete and continuous pages form two branches. The cumulative distribution function brings them back together.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
The summary sequence
Once a distribution over values has been represented, we can summarize particular features of it.

Expected values summarize center with a probability weighted average.
Expectations of functions average a transformed value under the original distribution.
Linearity of expectation gives the expectation of a sum.
When expectations fail asks whether the weighted average is finite.
Variance summarizes expected squared distance from the mean.
Standard deviation returns that spread summary to the original units.
Central moments place variance within a larger family of summaries around the mean.

These pages introduce no named distribution family. A family becomes useful only after its shared representation and summaries have been developed separately.
The chapter dependency graph shows which earlier chapters this chapter assumes. Begin with why we use random variables.

title: The geometric distribution
text:
The binomial page counted targets in a fixed number of independent Bernoulli draws. The geometric distribution instead counts how long sampling continues before the first target. Suppose we sample word tokens from a declared corpus population until we encounter a loanword.
\pi=.20.
Define T as the draw number on which the first loanword appears. The geometric distribution represents this waiting time when draws are independent and share the same target probability.
We write
T\sim\operatorname{Geometric}(\pi).
Under the draw number convention,
\operatorname{supp}(T)=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}.
The smallest possible value is 1 because the first draw might already be a loanword.

title: The geometric distribution
section: Build the first probabilities from sequences
text:
Build the first probabilities from sequences
For T=1, the first token must be a loanword:

\mathbb{P}(T=1)=.20.

For T=2, the first token must be a nonloanword and the second a loanword:

\mathbb{P}(T=2)=.80(.20)=.16.

For T=3, two nonloanwords must be followed by a loanword:

\mathbb{P}(T=3)=.80^2(.20)=.128.

The sequence requirement has one form for every value of T: failures first, then one target outcome.

title: The geometric distribution
text:
Write the general PMF
For the first loanword to appear on draw t, the process must produce

t-1 nonloanwords, each with probability 1-\pi;
one loanword, with probability \pi.

Independence lets us multiply these probabilities:

p_T(t)
=(1-\pi)^{t-1}\pi,
\qquad t\in\{1,2,3,\ldots\}.

For t=4 and \pi=.20,

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(T=4)
&=(.80)^3(.20)\\
&=.1024.
\end{aligned}

The mass decreases with t because every additional step requires another preceding nonloanword.

title: The geometric distribution
text:
Calculate cumulative waiting probabilities
The event T>4 means that the first four draws are all nonloanwords. Thus

\mathbb{P}(T>4)
=(1-\pi)^4
=.80^4
=.4096.

The complement gives

\mathbb{P}(T\leq4)
=1-.4096
=.5904.

This calculation avoids adding the first four PMF values separately.

title: The geometric distribution
text:
Read the center and spread
Under the draw number convention,

\mathbb{E}[T]=\frac{1}{\pi}

and

\operatorname{Var}(T)=\frac{1-\pi}{\pi^2}.

With \pi=.20, the expected draw number is 5 and the variance is 20. The expected wait is not a claim that the fifth draw is the most likely first target. In fact, the PMF is largest at 1 and decreases thereafter.

title: The geometric distribution
section: Use R with the convention visible
text:
Use R with the convention visible
R’s geometric functions count failures before the first success, so dgeom(3, .20) gives the probability of three failures followed by success. That event corresponds to T=4 under our draw number convention.


Code
pi_loanword <- .20

dgeom(3, prob = pi_loanword)
(1 - pi_loanword)^3 * pi_loanword
1 - (1 - pi_loanword)^4


The first two calls return .1024. The final call returns the probability that the first loanword appears by draw 4.

title: The geometric distribution
text:
Make the linguistic assumptions visible
The geometric family assumes that the target probability stays fixed and that one draw does not change another. Sequential corpus tokens may violate both claims. Loanwords may cluster by topic, and documents may have different borrowing rates.
The model can still serve as a baseline, but a mismatch should be traced to the sampling representation rather than hidden inside the word waiting.

title: The geometric distribution
text:
Check the support convention
A geometric random variable can count the draw on which the first success occurs or the failures before that success. The same waiting process has support beginning at 1 under the first convention and at 0 under the second, so the two conventions cannot be mixed.
The two variables differ by one:

T=F+1.

Writing what the variable counts prevents an off by one interpretation.

title: The geometric distribution
text:
Check your understanding

With \pi=.25, compute the probability that the first target occurs on draw 3.
Under R’s failures convention, which value represents a target on draw 3?
Derive \mathbb{P}(T>k) by describing the required first k outcomes.
Give one corpus property that could make the target probability change across draws.

The geometric family stops at the first target. The next page extends the same waiting process to a specified later target.

title: Expectations of functions
text:
The preceding page defined expectation as a probability weighted average. We now apply the same operation after transforming each possible value. Suppose L records the length of a word in phonological units, with this constructed PMF.
An account of lexical access might propose that processing cost grows with squared length rather than length itself. Define the transformation
g(l)=l^2.
The quantity of interest is now the expected transformed value \mathbb{E}[g(L)].

title: Expectations of functions
text:
Transform first, then average
Apply g to each support value and retain its original probability.



l
g(l)=l^2
p_L(l)
g(l)p_L(l)




1
1
.50
.50


2
4
.30
1.20


3
9
.20
1.80



Adding the last column gives

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[g(L)]
&=1(.50)+4(.30)+9(.20)\\
&=3.50.
\end{aligned}

For a discrete random variable,

\mathbb{E}[g(X)]
=\sum_x g(x)p_X(x).

For a continuous random variable,

\mathbb{E}[g(X)]
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}g(x)f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x.

We can use the distribution of X directly. We do not need to derive a separate distribution for g(X) before computing the expectation.

title: Expectations of functions
text:
Compare two orders of operation
The expected word length is

\mathbb{E}[L]
=1(.50)+2(.30)+3(.20)
=1.70.

Squaring this mean gives

g(\mathbb{E}[L])=1.70^2=2.89.

This differs from the expected squared length:

\mathbb{E}[g(L)]=3.50.

The two operations answer different questions. g(\mathbb{E}[L]) transforms the center of the original values. \mathbb{E}[g(L)] transforms every possible value and then averages the transformed results.

title: Expectations of functions
section: Check the calculation in base R
text:
Check the calculation in base R


Code
word_length <- 1:3
word_mass <- c(.50, .30, .20)
cost <- function(length) length^2

expected_cost <- sum(cost(word_length) * word_mass)
cost_of_expected_length <- sum(word_length * word_mass)^2

c(expected_cost, cost_of_expected_length)


The results are 3.5 and 2.89.

title: Expectations of functions
text:
Interpret the transformed expectation
The value 3.5 is expressed in squared length units because the transformation squares the input. Its scientific interpretation depends on the proposed cost function. If the theory does not motivate g(l)=l^2, the calculation remains mathematically valid but does not become a theoretically useful processing summary.
This is why the transformation should be stated before the expectation is computed. The function encodes the property being averaged.

title: Expectations of functions
section: Transforming an expectation is not taking the expectation of a transformation
text:
Transforming an expectation is not taking the expectation of a transformation
The quantity g(\mathbb{E}[X]) cannot generally be substituted for \mathbb{E}[g(X)]. The equality fails for nonlinear functions because values on opposite sides of the mean are changed by different amounts before averaging.
The safe procedure is literal: apply g to each possible value, weight by the probability of that value, and add or integrate.

title: Expectations of functions
text:
Check your understanding

Using the word length PMF, compute \mathbb{E}[2L+1] from the definition.
Compute (2\mathbb{E}[L]+1) and compare the result with your first answer.
Explain why \mathbb{E}[L^2] differs from \mathbb{E}[L]^2 here.
What theoretical claim is encoded by choosing g(l)=l^2 as the processing cost?

This page averaged one transformed variable. The next page identifies the special simplification available when the transformation is a sum of terms.

title: Defining random variables
text:
The preceding page introduced a random variable as a function from complete outcomes to values. We now add the measurability condition that makes probability statements about those values well defined.
Suppose the outcomes in a syntax study are fully annotated sentence trees. The analysis concerns embedding depth, so we define
H(\omega)=\text{maximum embedding depth in tree }\omega.
The function takes a complex outcome and returns a value. To use that value in probability statements, every measurable set of values must lead back to an event that the original model can measure.
This measurability requirement completes the formal definition of the random variable introduced on the preceding page.

title: Defining random variables
text:
Distinguish the two spaces
Let \langle\Omega,\mathcal{F}\rangle be the measurable space of sentence tree outcomes, using the sigma-algebra introduced earlier. Let \langle A,\mathcal{G}\rangle be the measurable space of depth values. The function has the form

H:\Omega\longrightarrow A.

For a small finite study, the value set might be

A=\{0,1,2,3\}.

The sigma-algebra \mathcal{G} contains the measurable sets of depth values. If every subset is measurable, then \{2\} and \{2,3\} both belong to \mathcal{G}.

title: Defining random variables
text:
Work backward with a preimage
Suppose three outcomes receive these values.



sentence tree outcome
H(\omega)




\omega_1
1


\omega_2
2


\omega_3
2



Select the value set \{2\}. The outcomes mapped into that set are

H^{-1}(\{2\})
=\{\omega\in\Omega:H(\omega)\in\{2\}\}
=\{\omega_2,\omega_3\}.

This set is the preimage of \{2\} under H.
The superscript -1 does not say that H has an inverse function. Both \omega_2 and \omega_3 map to 2, so the depth value does not recover one unique tree. The preimage collects every outcome whose mapped value belongs to the selected set.
For the set \{1,2\},

H^{-1}(\{1,2\})=\{\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3\}.

The operation always moves from values back to outcomes.

title: Defining random variables
text:
State measurability
The function H is a random variable when

E\in\mathcal{G}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
H^{-1}(E)\in\mathcal{F}.

This condition is called measurability. It says that every measurable question about the value corresponds to a measurable event in the original outcome space.
If \{2\}\in\mathcal{G}, then the event \{\omega_2,\omega_3\} must belong to \mathcal{F}. Otherwise the expression “the probability that embedding depth is 2” would refer to an event to which the model assigns no probability.
In a finite model with \mathcal{F}=2^\Omega, every preimage is measurable because every subset of outcomes belongs to \mathcal{F}. The requirement becomes more substantive for larger outcome spaces, but its interpretation remains the same.

title: Defining random variables
section: Read probability notation through the preimage
text:
Read probability notation through the preimage
Once H is defined, we write

\mathbb{P}(H=2)

as shorthand for

\mathbb{P}\bigl(H^{-1}(\{2\})\bigr)
=\mathbb{P}(\{\omega_2,\omega_3\}).

Similarly,

\mathbb{P}(H\leq2)

means the probability of the preimage of all depth values at or below 2. The notation is compact, but the probability measure still acts on an event of outcomes.

title: Defining random variables
section: Check the preimage in base R
text:
Check the preimage in base R


Code
depth <- c(omega1 = 1, omega2 = 2, omega3 = 2)

names(depth)[depth == 2]
names(depth)[depth <= 2]


The first result encodes H^{-1}(\{2\}). The second encodes the preimage of the set of values at or below 2.

title: Defining random variables
section: A many to one mapping has no inverse function
text:
A many to one mapping has no inverse function
One outcome cannot be recovered from a many to one mapping. The value 2 does not determine whether \omega_2 or \omega_3 occurred. The notation H^{-1}(\{2\}) denotes the preimage containing both outcomes rather than selecting one.
This distinction matters whenever many linguistic records share a value. A duration, rating, or word count rarely identifies the full token from which it was extracted.

title: Defining random variables
text:
Check your understanding

Using the table, compute H^{-1}(\{1\}) and H^{-1}(\{1,2\}).
Why is a preimage a set of sentence tree outcomes rather than a set of depth values?
State the measurability condition in words.
If \{\omega_2,\omega_3\}\notin\mathcal{F}, which probability statement about H becomes unavailable?

We now know what a random variable must preserve. The next page considers variables whose possible values can be listed.

title: Covariance
text:
The variance page averaged a squared deviation for one variable. Covariance instead averages the product of paired deviations from a joint distribution. Suppose a constructed probability model places equal mass on four word tokens with contextual surprisal X and reading time Y.
We want to know whether values above the surprisal mean tend to occur with values above the reading time mean.
The covariance is the expected product of paired deviations:
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)
=\mathbb{E}\!\left[
(X-\mathbb{E}[X])(Y-\mathbb{E}[Y])
\right].

title: Covariance
text:
Compute the two means
The surprisal mean is

\mathbb{E}[X]
=.25(1+1+3+3)
=2\text{ bits}.

The reading time mean is

\mathbb{E}[Y]
=.25(200+250+350+400)
=300\text{ ms}.

These means center each variable before their paired deviations are multiplied.

title: Covariance
text:
Multiply paired deviations



outcome
X-2
Y-300
product




\omega_1
-1
-100
100


\omega_2
-1
-50

\omega_3

\omega_4
