These pages establish the ordinal link and its multilevel extension before this problem set applies them to CommitmentBank.

title: Problem Set 4: Commitment in naturally occurring discourse
text:
Begin with the measurement
The response scale has seven ordered categories:







Rating
Interpretation




-3
the speaker is certain that the complement is false


0
the speaker is uncertain whether the complement is true or false


3
the speaker is certain that the complement is true



The intermediate categories express intermediate ordered judgments. The difference between -3 and -2 need not equal the difference between 1 and 2. Thus a normal linear model would add a spacing assumption that the task did not establish.
Recall from ordinal regression that an ordinal model asks whether a response falls at or below each boundary. With seven categories, there are six boundaries. For boundary k, the cumulative logit model is

\operatorname{logit}\left[\Pr(Y_i \leq k)\right]
= \theta_k - \eta_i,
\qquad k \in \{-3,-2,-1,0,1,2\}.

The ordered thresholds \theta_k divide a latent commitment scale into the seven observed categories. The linear predictor \eta_i moves an observation along that scale. Because \eta_i is subtracted, a positive coefficient lowers the probability of falling at or below every boundary and shifts probability toward higher ratings.
One coefficient is shared across all six cumulative logits. This is the proportional-odds assumption introduced earlier. It says that a predictor shifts location on the latent scale rather than having a separate effect at every response boundary. We will retain this assumption throughout the assignment so that the model sequence changes only the linguistic predictors.

title: Problem Set 4: Commitment in naturally occurring discourse
section: Put the repeated observations into the model
text:
Put the repeated observations into the model
Let rating i come from annotator a[i], discourse d[i], and predicate v[i]. The linear predictor for the larger model is

\eta_i
= \beta_F F_i
+ \boldsymbol{x}_{E_i}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\beta}_E
+ u_{a[i]} + w_{d[i]} + z_{v[i]},

with

u_a \sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,\sigma_a^2),
\qquad
w_d \sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,\sigma_d^2),
\qquad
z_v \sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,\sigma_v^2).

The annotator intercept represents a person’s general tendency to use higher or lower categories. The discourse intercept represents properties of a particular passage that every annotator saw. The predicate intercept represents lexical differences that remain after the binary factivity classification.
Including factivity and predicate variation is not redundant. The factivity coefficient estimates the average difference between the two lexical classes. The predicate distribution asks how far individual predicates depart from that class average. This distinction makes the inadequacy of a class-only account estimable.

title: Problem Set 4: Commitment in naturally occurring discourse
text:
Prepare the data
The official repository contains corpus passages from three source corpora and does not state a separate data license. The course repository thus supplies a retrieval script rather than a copy of the data. From the repository root, run:
Rscript problem-sets/ps4/scripts/prepare-commitmentbank.R
The script downloads the official participant-level CSV, checks a fixed SHA-256 checksum, and creates a local analysis table without the passage or prompt text.


Code
library(brms)
library(loo)
library(posterior)
library(ggplot2)

ratings <- read.csv("data/commitmentbank-model.csv")

primary <- ratings[ratings$modal_type %in% c("none", "EP"), ]
primary$rating <- ordered(primary$rating, levels = -3:3)
primary$factive <- factor(primary$factive, levels = c("no", "yes"))
primary$embedding <- factor(
  primary$embedding,
  levels = c("conditional", "modal", "negation", "question")
)
primary$annotator <- factor(primary$annotator)
primary$discourse <- factor(primary$discourse)
primary$predicate <- factor(primary$predicate)
primary$cell <- interaction(
  primary$factive,
  primary$embedding,
  sep = ": "
)
primary <- droplevels(primary)

stopifnot(
  nrow(primary) == 9599L,
  nlevels(primary$discourse) == 982L,
  nlevels(primary$annotator) == 496L,
  nlevels(primary$predicate) == 45L
)


The filter follows the paper. Weak epistemic modals can diagnose projection because they remove the matrix entailment without adding a non-epistemic interpretation. Ability, circumstantial, and deontic modals do not provide the same diagnostic. We will restore them only in the predeclared sensitivity analysis.

title: Problem Set 4: Commitment in naturally occurring discourse
text:
Task 1: reconstruct the design (10 points)
Create one table of rating counts and a second table of discourse counts by factive and embedding. Then answer the following questions.

Why is the rating an ordered response rather than a continuous response?
What is repeated within an annotator?
What is repeated within a discourse?
Why can the predicate effect not replace the discourse effect?
Which factivity by environment cells have the weakest discourse support?

State the target of the conditional predictions used later. They describe a rating with the annotator, discourse, and predicate random intercepts set to zero. They are not probabilities averaged over those random-effect distributions, and they do not describe every English speaker or every clause-embedding predicate.

title: Problem Set 4: Commitment in naturally occurring discourse
section: Task 2: check the priors before fitting the data (15 points)
text:
Task 2: check the priors before fitting the data (15 points)
Use the prespecified priors:


Code
prior_set <- c(
  prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b"),
  prior(exponential(1), class = "sd")
)


The Intercept class names the six ordered thresholds in this model. The b class names the factivity and embedding coefficients. The sd class names the three group standard deviations.
Define the larger formula now because a prior predictive check should use the model whose posterior will later be interpreted.


Code
environment_formula <- bf(
  rating ~ factive + embedding +
    (1 | annotator) + (1 | discourse) + (1 | predicate),
  family = cumulative("logit")
)

# Fit with sample_prior = "only".


Draw 500 replicated datasets from the prior predictive distribution. Plot the overall proportion in each category for every replicate, then place the observed proportions on the same plot. Answer three questions.

Do the priors permit all seven response categories?
Do they routinely imply that nearly every response occupies one category?
Would you revise the priors before seeing the posterior? Explain the proposed revision or explain why no revision is needed.

Do not choose a prior because it recreates the observed distribution closely. Prior predictive checking rules out implications that were unreasonable before the outcomes were used for fitting.

title: Problem Set 4: Commitment in naturally occurring discourse
section: Task 3: fit the factivity model (20 points)
text:
Task 3: fit the factivity model (20 points)
The first model asks whether the traditional lexical classification predicts the ordered commitment response while partially pooling the three grouping units.


Code
factivity_formula <- bf(
  rating ~ factive +
    (1 | annotator) + (1 | discourse) + (1 | predicate),
  family = cumulative("logit")
)

# Fit the factivity-only model with four chains, 1,000 warmup iterations, and 1,000 retained
# iterations per chain. Use the prespecified priors, adapt_delta = 0.95, and a
# fixed seed.


Before interpreting the model, report:

the number of divergent transitions;
the largest split R-hat;
the smallest bulk effective sample size among reported population and group-scale parameters; and
the smallest tail effective sample size among those parameters.

Then report the median and 95 percent posterior interval for factiveyes. Explain its sign using the cumulative probability equation. Finally, report the three group standard deviations and inspect the predicate deviations for know, realize, accept, and tell.
The factivity coefficient and predicate deviations answer different questions. A positive class coefficient can coexist with substantial lexical departures. Explain how that combination bears on the limits of a class-only account.

title: Problem Set 4: Commitment in naturally occurring discourse
text:
Task 4: add embedding environment (20 points)
Fit the model that adds embedding environment using environment_formula. Use the same data, priors, random structure, chains, iterations, and seed as the factivity-only model. This is a prespecified comparison: the only formula change is the addition of embedding.
Perform the same diagnostic audit used for the factivity-only model. Then summarize the three embedding coefficients. Conditional antecedents are the reference level, so each coefficient compares one environment with a conditional antecedent while holding factivity fixed and setting the grouping deviations to their modeled values.
Environment is constant within a discourse. This fact determines how the two models must be compared. If we leave out one rating, the remaining ratings of that discourse still estimate its discourse intercept. The intercept can then carry information that the environment predictor would otherwise supply. A rating-level comparison would answer the wrong question.
The prespecified comparison instead uses five folds grouped by discourse and stratified by factivity and environment. Every rating of a discourse enters the same fold. Each held-out discourse receives one new discourse intercept drawn from the fitted group distribution, and that intercept is shared across its ratings. The ten model fits across five folds are slow, so you will audit the supplied discourse-level output instead of refitting them.
Download the grouped comparison results, then read them into R.


Code
grouped_cv <- read.csv("data/commitmentbank-grouped-cv.csv")

stopifnot(
  nrow(grouped_cv) == 982L,
  length(unique(grouped_cv$case)) == 982L,
  setequal(grouped_cv$fold, 1:5)
)


First verify that each fold contains all eight factivity by environment cells and between 194 and 200 discourses. Each value \ell_{d,m} in the supplied file is the log predictive density for all ratings in discourse d under model m. This is the group-level pointwise quantity required by the new-discourse target. Then compute

\Delta = \sum_d \left(\ell_{d,\mathrm{environment}} -
\ell_{d,\mathrm{factivity}}\right)

and its discourse-level standard error,

\operatorname{SE}(\Delta)
= \sqrt{D\operatorname{Var}\left(\ell_{d,\mathrm{environment}} -
\ell_{d,\mathrm{factivity}}\right)}.

Report the difference, its standard error, and their ratio. Explain why one row is one discourse rather than one rating. State whether the difference exceeds the prespecified two-standard-error threshold. Finally, explain one limitation of the standard error: the discourse is the pointwise unit, but the five training sets overlap.

title: Problem Set 4: Commitment in naturally occurring discourse
section: Task 5: return to response categories (20 points)
text:
Task 5: return to response categories (20 points)
Create the eight combinations of factivity and embedding environment. Use posterior_epred() with re_formula = NA to obtain conditional category probabilities from the model that includes embedding environment, with every random intercept set to zero. Do not call these population-averaged probabilities, because they do not integrate over the fitted random-effect distributions.
For each combination, report:

the posterior mean and 95 percent interval for each of the seven category probabilities;
the probability of a high commitment response, defined before fitting as \Pr(Y \geq 2); and
the posterior expected rating, used only as a compact summary of the seven probabilities.

Plot the seven category probabilities rather than only the expected ratings. Then answer three substantive questions.

Does factivity shift probability toward stronger commitment in every environment?
Which environment has the largest probability of negative commitment responses?
Does any environment make the factive and nonfactive distributions identical?

The additive model builds in a common latent factivity shift. It does not build in identical response probabilities, because the inverse link and thresholds make the probability differences depend on position along the scale.

title: Problem Set 4: Commitment in naturally occurring discourse
text:
Task 6: criticize the model (10 points)
Generate posterior predictive datasets from the model that includes embedding environment. Compare observed and replicated category proportions overall, by factivity, by embedding environment, and within the eight factivity by environment cells. Identify one feature the model reproduces and one feature it misses. A fitted coefficient is not a substitute for checking the response distribution that the model generates.
Next perform the prespecified sensitivity analysis. Restore all modal types, rebuild the factors in the same order, and refit the model that includes embedding environment without changing its formula or priors. Compare the factivity and embedding summaries with the primary fit. Focus on the modal prediction because every restored item contains a non-epistemic modal.
Explain whether the sensitivity result supports the paper’s decision to restrict the projection diagnostic to epistemic modals. Do not select whichever fit gives a more dramatic coefficient. The two fits answer questions about different inclusion rules.

title: Problem Set 4: Commitment in naturally occurring discourse
Problem Set 4: Commitment in naturally occurring discourse
text:
Submission checklist

The data checksum passes and no corpus text is submitted.
The response remains an ordered factor with levels -3 through 3.
The factivity-only model and the model that adds embedding environment use identical priors and random structures.
Every fitted model receives a diagnostic audit before interpretation.
The grouped comparison uses discourse as its pointwise unit and reports the uncertainty of the difference.
Posterior predictions show category probabilities, not only latent coefficients.
The sensitivity analysis changes only the modal inclusion rule.
The final paragraph states what the corpus sampling does not license.

title: Problem Set 2: Prediction across passages
text:
Accounts of prediction in comprehension differ in what they take readers to anticipate. One view emphasizes a particular upcoming word form. Another allows context to support partial information, such as the upcoming word’s syntactic class or semantic content, even when its full form is uncertain.
Luke and Christianson tested these accounts using the Provo Corpus. Their coefficient analyses suggest that orthographic, morphosyntactic, and semantic predictability are associated with eye movements. We will ask a different question: do these predictor sets improve first-fixation prediction for a passage omitted during model fitting?
The focal method is grouped cross-validation. The models are linear regressions already introduced in the notes.






NoteReading



Read Luke and Christianson (2016), “Limits on lexical prediction during reading”, together with the Provo Corpus data description in Luke and Christianson (2018), “The Provo Corpus”. The first reading supplies the lexical and graded prediction contrast. The second explains how the passages, readers, eye movements, and predictability norms were collected. Both are included because a passage-held-out score is interpretable only after the theoretical predictors and the sampling units have been named.

The helper below fits a linear model from a fixed design matrix and returns test predictions.

fit_predict <- function(design, response, train, test) {
  coefficients <- qr.coef(qr(design[train, , drop = FALSE]), response[train])
  coefficients[is.na(coefficients)] <- 0
  drop(design[test, , drop = FALSE] %*% coefficients)
}

score <- function(observed, predicted) {

    RMSE = sqrt(mean((observed - predicted)^2)),

title: About
text: This site contains materials for Statistical Methods in Linguistics, a course taught by Aaron Steven White at the University of Rochester.

title: About
text:
About the course
The course develops the probability-theoretic and statistical tools used to analyze linguistic data. We begin by asking how linguistic observations can be represented as outcomes in a probability space; we then develop random variables and probability distributions; finally, we use those objects to motivate frequentist and Bayesian inference, regression, generalized linear models, and mixed-effects models.
The notes are organized by topic rather than class meeting. Each substantive page introduces one principal concept and uses only earlier prerequisites. The chapter dependency graph shows which chapters supply concepts used in later chapters.

title: Problem Set 1: Paired acoustic measurements
text:
The first formant (F1) is an acoustic correlate of vowel height: higher vowels tend to have lower F1. We will ask whether F1 differs between /i/ as in heed and /ɪ/ as in hid in the Hillenbrand vowel sample.
Every recorded speaker produced both vowels. Thus the theoretically relevant predictor is vowel category, while speaker identifies which two measurements form a pair. The focal method is inference for a paired mean difference: construct one within-speaker difference and estimate its population mean.
By the end of the assignment, you should be able to (i) identify a contrast-bearing unit from a repeated design, (ii) compute and interpret a paired t interval, and (iii) explain why an analysis that ignores the pairing answers the question less efficiently.






NoteReading



Read Hillenbrand, Getty, Clark, and Wheeler (1995), “Acoustic characteristics of American English vowels”. Focus on the speaker sample, recording procedure, and formant measurements. The reading is included because the paired analysis follows from the recording design: each speaker contributes both vowel measurements, and the within-speaker contrast is the unit that bears on vowel category.


Before beginning, review turning linguistic records into data, paired observations, and inference for a paired mean difference. These pages establish the unit of analysis, the pairing relation, and the confidence interval used below.

title: Problem Set 3: Harmonic alignment in the dative alternation
text:
English speakers can describe a transfer using a double-object dative, as in Kim gave Lee the book, or a prepositional dative, as in Kim gave the book to Lee. The recipient occurs before the theme in the first variant and after the theme in the second. The alternatives thus let us ask which properties make an argument more likely to occur early.
Bresnan, Cueni, Nikitina, and Baayen connect this ordering to harmonic alignment. Accessible, pronominal, animate, and short arguments tend to precede less accessible, nonpronominal, inanimate, and long arguments. Harmonic alignment is a probabilistic constraint, not a categorical ban. It predicts a direction of change in construction probability when an argument property changes.
The focal method is logistic regression with multiple predictors. The response is PP = 1, so a positive coefficient raises the modeled probability that the recipient follows the theme. A negative coefficient raises the modeled probability that the recipient immediately follows the verb. Keeping this coding in view will be necessary in every interpretation.
Earlier methods supply two secondary checks. First, response-scale predictions show what a collection of log-odds coefficients implies for concrete dative profiles. Second, grouped evaluation asks whether the alignment pattern improves prediction for tokens headed by a verb omitted during fitting. Neither check introduces a second model family.






NoteReading



Read Bresnan, Cueni, Nikitina, and Baayen (2007), “Predicting the Dative Alternation”, in Cognitive Foundations of Interpretation, pages 69 to 94. Focus on the discussion of harmonic alignment and the move to a multiple-predictor logistic model. The reading is included because it supplies the linguistic hypothesis, explains why the predictors are correlated, and treats lexical conditioning as a possible limit on a broad alignment account. This problem set uses a smaller prespecified model, so it is not a reproduction of every analysis in the chapter.


Before beginning, review odds and log odds, logistic regression with multiple predictors, predictive loss, and grouped cross-validation. The first two pages establish the focal method. The latter two establish the evaluation procedure used in Task 4.

title: Problem Set 3: Harmonic alignment in the dative alternation
section: From ordering claims to coefficient signs
text:
From ordering claims to coefficient signs
Let p_i be the probability that token i has a PP recipient. An additive logistic model has the form

\operatorname{logit}(p_i)
= \log\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)
= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_K x_{Ki}.

Each coefficient describes a conditional change in PP log odds. “Conditional” matters because argument properties are correlated. Pronouns tend to be short, animate referents tend to be discourse accessible, and discourse accessible expressions tend to occur early. A multiple-predictor model asks whether one property carries a directional association while the remaining modeled properties are fixed.
Exponentiating a coefficient gives an odds ratio. An odds ratio above one raises the PP odds, while an odds ratio below one lowers them. Odds are not probabilities. Task 3 thus returns the fitted model to the response scale before you write the main substantive comparison.
crumbs: PS3: Dative alternation and logistic regression

title: Problem Set 3: Harmonic alignment in the dative alternation
text:
Data and source
The data come from the dative table in languageR 1.5.0, which adapts the corpus annotations analyzed in Bresnan et al. (2007). The package documentation describes 3,263 dative tokens from spoken Switchboard and the written Wall Street Journal Treebank. The teaching table contains annotations but no corpus sentence text.


Code
items <- read.csv("data/dative-alternation.csv")
dim(items)
head(items)


One row is one annotated dative token. The response recipient_realization is NP when the recipient immediately follows the verb and PP when it follows the theme. The principal predictors describe the two arguments:

recipient_accessibility and theme_accessibility: accessible, given, or new
recipient_pronominality and theme_pronominality: pronominal or nonpronominal
recipient_animacy: animate or inanimate
recipient_length_words and theme_length_words: length in graphemic words

The columns modality and semantic_class supply controls. The semantic class codes are a for abstract, c for communication, f for future transfer, p for prevented possession, and t for transfer of possession. These controls matter because the written and spoken samples differ, and different transfer meanings have different construction distributions. They are not substitutes for the alignment predictors.
The table contains 75 verb types. Some are common, while many occur only once or twice. This imbalance will matter when you evaluate transfer across verbs. A change in average token loss and a count of improved verb types answer different descriptive questions.

text:
Task 2: fit the prespecified model sequence (25 points)
Set the factor levels below. These baselines make every coefficient in Task 1 interpretable without changing the observed data.


Code
factor_levels <- list(
  modality = c("spoken", "written"),
  semantic_class = c("a", "c", "f", "p", "t"),
  recipient_accessibility = c("accessible", "given", "new"),
  theme_accessibility = c("accessible", "given", "new"),
  recipient_pronominality = c("nonpronominal", "pronominal"),
  theme_pronominality = c("nonpronominal", "pronominal"),
  recipient_animacy = c("animate", "inanimate")
)

for (variable in names(factor_levels)) {
  items[[variable]] <- factor(items[[variable]], levels = factor_levels[[variable]])
}


Fit two models whose formulas are fixed before you inspect the fitted coefficients.

The first model contains relative log length, modality, and semantic class.
The second model adds recipient accessibility, theme accessibility, recipient pronominality, theme pronominality, and recipient animacy.

The first model is a comparison baseline, not a claim that length, modality, and semantic class exhaust dative choice. The second asks whether the discourse and referential properties add the directional pattern predicted by harmonic alignment.


Code
baseline_formula <- pp ~
  relative_log_length + modality + semantic_class

alignment_formula <- update(
  baseline_formula,
  . ~ . + recipient_accessibility + theme_accessibility +
    recipient_pronominality + theme_pronominality + recipient_animacy
)

# Fit both formulas with glm(..., family = binomial()).


Construct a table containing the second model’s coefficient, its exponentiated value, and a Wald 95 percent interval on the odds-ratio scale. Interpret relative length and one recipient property in words. Name the reference level, the direction of the contrast, and the fact that the remaining predictors are held fixed by the model.
Then compare every focal coefficient sign with your predictions from Task 1. This comparison is the primary result here. Do not reduce it to a count of p values. A matching sign supports the predicted direction in this fitted corpus model, while a mismatching sign identifies a part of the alignment account that the model does not recover.

title: Problem Set 3: Harmonic alignment in the dative alternation
section: Task 3: interpret probabilities, not only coefficients (25 points)
text:
Task 3: interpret probabilities, not only coefficients (25 points)
A coefficient is local to the log-odds scale. Several coefficients can combine nonlinearly on the probability scale, so we now compare predeclared profiles. Predeclaring the profiles prevents the fitted model from choosing its own most dramatic contrast.
Create the two predeclared profiles below. Both describe a spoken transfer event with equal-length arguments.

The first profile has a given, pronominal, animate recipient and a new, nonpronominal theme.
The second profile has a new, nonpronominal, inanimate recipient and a given, pronominal theme.

Use transfer of possession (semantic_class = "t") for both profiles. Predict the probability of a PP recipient for each profile using the second model. Report the probability difference and explain why the direction follows from harmonic alignment.
Then inspect data support. Count exact corpus matches for each profile and count matches after ignoring modality, semantic class, and equal length. An extreme model prediction supported by very few matching tokens should be reported as an extrapolation toward a sparse corner of the predictor space, not as a categorical construction rule.
Then start from the first profile and change only recipient accessibility from given to new. Report the two model predictions and their difference. Why is this comparison easier to interpret than comparing two observed token subsets that also differ in pronominality, animacy, length, and verb?
This is a model-based predictive contrast. The corpus does not randomly assign accessibility, so the contrast does not by itself identify a causal effect.

title: Problem Set 3: Harmonic alignment in the dative alternation
section: Task 4: test transfer to omitted verbs (25 points)
text:
Task 4: test transfer to omitted verbs (25 points)
The second model may predict the observed tokens partly because it learns associations carried by common verbs. Leaving out a complete verb type asks a stricter question: do the alignment predictors help on tokens whose verb type was absent during fitting? This is why the grouping variable is verb, not a random row label.
For a binary response, the Brier loss for token i is

(y_i-\widehat p_i)^2.

Smaller values are better. A confident wrong prediction receives a large loss, while a well calibrated probability receives a small loss. Average the token losses within each held-out verb before constructing the requested verb plot.
Use leave-one-verb-out evaluation. For each of the 75 verb types:

hold out every token of that verb;
fit both models to the remaining verb types;
predict the held-out responses; and
compute Brier loss for each model.



Code
verb_levels <- unique(items$verb)

# Return one row per held-out verb with its token count and both Brier losses.


Report token-weighted Brier loss for each model and the proportion of verb types on which the second model improves. Plot the per-verb difference first model loss - second model loss against held-out token count, with a horizontal line at zero.

title: Problem Set 5: Structure in phoneme inventories
text:
Languages do not assemble their phoneme inventories by choosing each segment in isolation. A language with one series of voiced stops may be more likely to have other members of that series. Vowel length may recur across several vowel qualities. Place contrasts may likewise extend across several manners of articulation. These examples suggest that segment presence has structure.
The comparison baseline predicts whether a segment occurs in an inventory using only the overall prevalence of that segment. It does not use the other segments in the inventory. A low rank representation can improve on this prevalence-only baseline only if recurring configurations of segments contain information about a cell that we deliberately hide.
The focal technique is a low-rank approximation based on the singular value decomposition. We will represent languages by segments, hide a balanced set of present and absent cells, select the rank on validation cells, and evaluate the selected representation on separate test cells. Following the earlier definition of predictive loss, the improvement in reconstruction is the baseline Brier loss minus the low-rank Brier loss:

\operatorname{improvement}
=
\operatorname{Brier}_{\text{prevalence}}
-
\operatorname{Brier}_{\text{low rank}}.

A positive improvement means that the low rank representation reconstructs held out cells better than segment prevalence alone. It does not show that the components are universal phonological dimensions. We will need the inventory source, language family, and macroarea diagnostics to determine how much structure those labels carry.






NoteData documentation



Consult the PHOIBLE 2.0 download and citation page and the FAQ sections “Why do some languages have multiple entries in PHOIBLE?”, “Random sampling: one inventory per isocode/glottocode”, and “What are the different sources in PHOIBLE?”. This documentation is included because the row selection and source diagnostic depend on how PHOIBLE combines inventories from different descriptions and collections. The factorization cannot be interpreted before those sampling decisions are understood.


Before beginning, review linguistic data matrices, centering and scaling, rank one structure, singular value decomposition, principal component analysis, scores and loadings, reconstruction, and choosing components. Each page supplies one part of the analysis below. The low-rank approximation is the only focal technique introduced here. Masking and scoring apply the training, validation, and test separation used earlier in the course.

title: Problem Set 5: Structure in phoneme inventories
text:
Prepare the data
The archived release is Moran and McCloy’s (2019) PHOIBLE 2.0, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.2593234. The PHOIBLE site licenses the data under Creative Commons Attribution ShareAlike 3.0 Unported. The course does not commit a copy of the archive.
From the repository root, run:
Rscript problem-sets/ps5/scripts/prepare-phoible.R
The script downloads the pinned CLDF archive, checks its MD5 and SHA 256 values, and creates data/phoible-pilot.rds inside the PS5 directory. It retains consonants and vowels, removes tones, and removes rows explicitly marked as marginal. A blank marginality field remains because it means that the source did not state whether the segment is marginal.
Load the prepared object and the audited functions.


Code
phoible <- readRDS("data/phoible-pilot.rds")
source("scripts/phoible-svd-functions.R")

names(phoible)
phoible$provenance


The object contains three linked tables.

memberships: one row states that one segment occurs in one contributed inventory.
inventories: one row describes one contributed inventory and its Glottocode, source collection, top level family, and macroarea.
segments: one row describes one PHOIBLE segment parameter.

The inventory source is the PHOIBLE collection that contributed a description, not the language’s family or location. Several collections have restricted geographic coverage. Thus source, family, and macroarea may be associated with one another.

title: Problem Set 5: Structure in phoneme inventories
section: Task 1: establish the recorded and sampling units (10 points)
text:
Task 1: establish the recorded and sampling units (10 points)
Use the provenance record and the three tables to answer the following questions.

How many rows, contributed inventories, and Glottocodes occur in the original CLDF release?
What does one row of memberships represent?
Why can one Glottocode have more than one inventory?
Why would treating all 3,020 inventories as independent language samples give heavily described Glottocodes extra weight?
What claim does the exclusion of tones make about the matrix studied here?
What claim does it not make about tone as a phonological property?

Create a frequency table for the number of contributed inventories per Glottocode. Report how many Glottocodes have more than one inventory and the largest number attached to one Glottocode.


Code
# Count contributed inventories within each Glottocode.


Piloted checkpoint: the archived release contains 105,462 value rows, 3,020 inventories, and 2,186 Glottocodes. The later matrix must have one row for each of those 2,186 Glottocodes.

title: Problem Set 5: Structure in phoneme inventories
section: Task 2: select one inventory per Glottocode (10 points)
text:
Task 2: select one inventory per Glottocode (10 points)
There is no uniquely correct way to choose among several descriptions of the same Glottocode. We will compare two declared rules.

Randomly select one inventory per Glottocode with seed 20260827.
Select the inventory with the most retained nonmarginal consonants and vowels. Break ties by choosing the smaller inventory ID.

The seeded rule follows the random sampling option in the PHOIBLE FAQ. The largest rule follows its suggested option for an analyst who prefers more inclusive segment inventories. The second rule will tend to prefer descriptions that split contrasts more finely, so it is a sensitivity condition rather than a neutral gold standard.


Code
seeded_inventories <- select_inventories(
  phoible$inventories,
  rule = "seeded_random"
)
largest_inventories <- select_inventories(
  phoible$inventories,
  rule = "largest_inventory"
)

# Verify one row per Glottocode under each rule.


Join the two selections by glottocode. Report the count and proportion for which the rules choose the same inventory. Then make a source frequency table under each rule.


Code
# Compare selected inventory IDs and source frequencies.


Explain why agreement between the rules does not show that the selected inventory is the true inventory for a language. It shows only that the two operational rules often make the same choice.
Piloted checkpoint: each rule selects 2,186 inventories. The rules choose the same inventory for 1,887 Glottocodes, or .8632 of the sample.

title: Problem Set 5: Structure in phoneme inventories
section: Task 3: construct the language by segment matrix (10 points)
text:
Task 3: construct the language by segment matrix (10 points)
We now turn the membership table into a binary matrix. A row is a selected inventory. A column is a PHOIBLE segment. A cell equals one when that segment occurs in the selected inventory and zero otherwise.
Very rare segment columns create two problems for this exercise. First, a segment seen only once or twice supplies too little information for held out reconstruction. Second, a large set of nearly empty columns makes the result depend on many source specific transcription decisions. The primary analysis thus retains a segment only if it occurs in at least 20 selected inventories.


Code
primary_data <- build_inventory_matrix(
  prepared = phoible,
  selected = seeded_inventories,
  minimum_count = 20L
)
X <- primary_data$matrix

dim(X)
summary(rowSums(X))
summary(colMeans(X))
mean(X)


Answer four questions.

What do the row and column counts mean linguistically?
What does a row sum mean?
What does a column mean estimate?
Why does a zero mean absence from the selected description rather than articulatory impossibility?

Make a histogram of segment prevalence. Label the horizontal axis as a proportion of selected inventories, not as a probability for the world’s languages.


Code
# Plot colMeans(X).


Piloted checkpoint: the primary matrix has 2,186 rows and 293 columns. Its mean cell value is .1045, so approximately .8955 of its cells are zeros.

title: Problem Set 5: Structure in phoneme inventories
section: Task 4: hide balanced present and absent cells (10 points)
text:
Task 4: hide balanced present and absent cells (10 points)
If we scored every cell, an algorithm that always predicts zero would appear accurate because almost 90 percent of the matrix is zero. Such a score would say little about recovering segments that are actually present. We will thus mask equal numbers of present and absent cells.
For every eligible inventory, reserve three present and three absent cells for validation. Then reserve a disjoint set of three present and three absent cells for testing. An inventory is eligible when it has at least ten present and ten absent cells. The cells are known in the source data. They are hidden only to evaluate reconstruction.


Code
masks <- make_balanced_masks(X, seed = 20260847L)

sum(masks$eligible)
sum(masks$validation)
sum(masks$test)
sum(masks$validation & masks$test)
table(X[masks$validation])
table(X[masks$test])


Explain why the following properties matter.

Present and absent cells occur equally often in each scoring set.
Validation and test cells do not overlap.
At least four present cells remain observed in every eligible row after both sets are hidden.
Test cells remain hidden while rank is selected.

Piloted checkpoint: all 2,186 inventories are eligible. Validation and test each contain 13,116 cells, split equally between presence and absence, with no overlap.

title: Problem Set 5: Structure in phoneme inventories
section: Task 5: define the prevalence baseline (10 points)
text:
Task 5: define the prevalence baseline (10 points)
The baseline uses the observed training prevalence of segment j,

\widehat p_j
=
\frac{\text{observed inventories containing segment }j}
{\text{inventories observed for segment }j}.

The same value is predicted for every hidden cell in column j. Thus the baseline knows that /m/ is common and a rarer segment is rare, but it cannot use the rest of a particular inventory.
Hide both validation and test cells. Estimate the column means from the remaining cells, and predict each validation cell with its column mean.


Code
validation_training <- X
validation_training[masks$validation | masks$test] <- NA_real_

segment_prevalence <- colMeans(validation_training, na.rm = TRUE)
validation_cells <- which(masks$validation, arr.ind = TRUE)
validation_baseline <- segment_prevalence[validation_cells[, "col"]]
validation_truth <- X[masks$validation]

balanced_score(validation_truth, validation_baseline, loss = "brier")


For a binary cell with observed value y and prediction p, Brier loss is (y-p)^2. The balanced score takes the mean loss for present cells and absent cells separately, then averages those two means. Write out this calculation using the validation vectors and verify that it matches balanced_score().
Explain why column prevalence is a more informative baseline than the constant value .5, even though the evaluation set is balanced.
Piloted checkpoint: validation balanced Brier loss for the prevalence-only baseline is .2168.

title: Problem Set 5: Structure in phoneme inventories
section: Task 6: select the rank on validation cells (15 points)
text:
Task 6: select the rank on validation cells (15 points)
The low rank model begins with the same column means. After centering, a hidden cell is filled with zero on the centered scale, which is equivalent to filling it with its column mean on the original scale. We then compute

\mathbf{X}_{c}
=
\mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf T}.

At rank K, the reconstruction for cell (i,j) is

\widehat x_{ij,K}
=
\widehat p_j
+
\sum_{k=1}^{K}d_k u_{ik}v_{jk}.

The first term is the prevalence-only baseline. Each additional term uses a row score and a segment loading to adjust that baseline. Predictions below zero or above one are clipped to the unit interval because the cells are binary.
We center each segment column but do not divide it by its standard deviation. Standardizing a binary column would give a rare segment a different weight from the one it has in cellwise Brier loss. The unscaled factorization thus matches the reconstruction target stated above. This is a modeling decision, not a general prohibition against scaling binary variables.
Fit up to rank 40 while both validation and test cells are hidden. Score the declared candidate ranks on validation cells.


Code
candidate_ranks <- c(1L, 2L, 3L, 5L, 8L, 12L, 16L, 24L, 32L, 40L)

validation_fit <- fit_low_rank(
  inventory_matrix = X,
  mask = masks$validation | masks$test,
  maximum_rank = max(candidate_ranks)
)

validation_brier <- vapply(candidate_ranks, function(rank) {
  prediction <- predict_masked(validation_fit, masks$validation, rank)
  balanced_score(validation_truth, prediction, loss = "brier")
}, numeric(1))

rank_curve <- data.frame(
  rank = c(0L, candidate_ranks),
  validation_brier = c(
    balanced_score(validation_truth, validation_baseline, "brier"),
    validation_brier
  )
)
rank_curve


Plot the curve and select the rank with the smallest validation loss. Report the reduction in validation Brier loss at that rank.


Code
# Plot validation_brier by rank and identify the minimizing rank.


Explain why the selected rank need not be the first bend in a scree plot. Then explain why choosing the rank from observed reconstruction error would favor larger ranks even when they do not reconstruct hidden cells better.
Piloted checkpoint: validation selects rank 32. Balanced Brier loss falls from .2168 under the prevalence-only baseline to .1242, a reduction of .0925.

title: Problem Set 5: Structure in phoneme inventories
section: Task 7: evaluate once on the test cells (10 points)
text:
Task 7: evaluate once on the test cells (10 points)
The rank is now fixed. Restore the validation cells, keep only the test cells hidden, and recompute the factorization. This refit uses the validation values as training information without allowing the test values to determine the component directions.


Code
selected_rank <- rank_curve$rank[which.min(rank_curve$validation_brier)]

test_fit <- fit_low_rank(
  inventory_matrix = X,
  mask = masks$test,
  maximum_rank = max(candidate_ranks)
)
test_truth <- X[masks$test]
test_baseline <- predict_masked(test_fit, masks$test, rank = 0L)
test_low_rank <- predict_masked(test_fit, masks$test, rank = selected_rank)

test_results <- data.frame(
  model = c("prevalence", paste("rank", selected_rank)),
  balanced_brier = c(
    balanced_score(test_truth, test_baseline, "brier"),
    balanced_score(test_truth, test_low_rank, "brier")
  ),
  balanced_log_loss = c(
    balanced_score(test_truth, test_baseline, "log"),
    balanced_score(test_truth, test_low_rank, "log")
  )
)
test_results


Compute the reduction in test Brier loss. Then interpret it as a change in mean squared probability error under the balanced scoring target. Do not describe it as a percentage increase in accuracy.
Calculate the fraction of centered squared variation represented by the first 32 singular values. Why is this quantity not interchangeable with the reduction in test Brier loss?
Piloted checkpoint: test balanced Brier loss falls from .2123 to .1106, a reduction of .1017. Balanced log loss falls from .6877 to .3830. The selected components represent .6476 of centered squared variation in the test fit.

title: Problem Set 5: Structure in phoneme inventories
section: Task 8: inspect phonological and database structure (15 points)
text:
Task 8: inspect phonological and database structure (15 points)
Good reconstruction establishes cooccurrence structure. It does not tell us what generated that structure. We will inspect segment loadings and three labels attached to each selected inventory.
First, list the ten largest positive and negative loadings for components 1 and 2.


Code
top_loadings(
  test_fit,
  phoible,
  colnames(X),
  component = 1L,
  n = 10L
)

top_loadings(
  test_fit,
  phoible,
  colnames(X),
  component = 2L,
  n = 10L
)


Describe one recurring phonological pattern in each table. For component 1, attend to the contrast between several plain obstruents and several retroflex or dental segments. For component 2, attend to long vowels. Because component signs are arbitrary, write about segments loading on the same or opposite sides, not about an inherently positive component.
Next, calculate component scores and their association with source, top level family, and macroarea. For a score vector z and grouping g, the squared correlation ratio, also called eta squared in a one-way analysis, is

\eta^2(z,g)
=
\frac{\sum_h n_h(\overline z_h-\overline z)^2}
{\sum_i(z_i-\overline z)^2}.

It measures the proportion of observed score variation lying between the named groups. For the family calculation, families with fewer than 15 selected inventories are combined into Other small families. Without this grouping, a family represented by one inventory would place all of that inventory’s score variation between families by construction. The ratio is not a causal effect, and it does not identify which of the three associated labels generated the pattern.


Code
associations <- score_associations(
  test_fit,
  selected_rank,
  primary_data$metadata
)

associations[associations$component <= 5L, ]


Finally, compute the reduction in Brier loss for each inventory and summarize it by source, family, and macroarea.


Code
inventory_scores <- score_by_inventory(
  X,
  masks$test,
  test_baseline,
  test_low_rank
)
group_results <- summarize_groups(inventory_scores, primary_data$metadata)

# Inspect groups with at least 50 inventories for source and macroarea.
# Inspect families with at least 15 inventories.


Answer three questions.

Is reconstruction gain confined to one large source, family, or macroarea?
Why do strong component associations block a universal interpretation of the loadings?
Why does a positive group mean not show that every inventory in that group is well reconstructed?

Piloted checkpoint: component 1 association ratios are .72 for source, .67 for grouped family, and .74 for macroarea. The mean reduction in Brier loss is positive for all six macroareas with at least 50 inventories, all nine sources with at least 50 inventories, and all 25 families with at least 15 inventories.

text:
Submission checklist
