title: Conditional probability
text:
The joint probability \mathbb{P}(P\cap A)=.40 tells us how much of the full pronoun probability belongs to forms that are both plural and accusative. A different linguistic question asks: among plural forms, how much of the probability belongs to accusative forms?
The phrase among plural forms changes the reference set. We no longer compare the plural accusative mass with the entire sample space. We compare it with the plural event.
This restricted comparison is a conditional probability. We write
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)
and read the expression as “the probability of A given P.” The event to the right of the vertical bar states the condition. The event to the left states what we want to measure within that condition.

title: Conditional probability
text:
Rescale the plural event
The plural event contains two outcomes:

P=\{\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.

Their original probabilities are .10 and .40. Those values sum to .50, because the plural event receives half of the mass in the full space.



plural outcome
probability in \Omega_4
probability within P




they
.10
.10/.50=.20


them
.40
.40/.50=.80



Dividing each plural probability by .50 makes the two restricted values sum to one. Within the plural event, them receives probability .80. Since them is the only plural accusative outcome,

\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)=.80.

title: Conditional probability
text:
Derive the definition
The part of P that also belongs to A is the intersection

A\cap P=\{\textit{them}\}.

Its original probability is .40. The full conditioning event has probability .50. Dividing the relevant part by the conditioning whole gives

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)}{\mathbb{P}(P)}\\
&=\frac{.40}{.50}\\
&=.80.
\end{aligned}

In general, for \mathbb{P}(C)>0,

\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}.

The numerator finds the part of the condition where B also occurs. The denominator rescales that part relative to all mass in the condition.
This rescaling makes the conditioning event certain within itself:

\mathbb{P}(C\mid C)
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(C\cap C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}
=1.

title: Conditional probability
text:
Reverse the condition
Now ask for the probability of plurality among accusative forms. The numerator is still the same intersection, since P\cap A=A\cap P. The denominator changes:

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(P\cap A)}{\mathbb{P}(A)}\\
&=\frac{.40}{.70}\\
&\approx .57.
\end{aligned}

Thus \mathbb{P}(A\mid P)=.80, while \mathbb{P}(P\mid A)\approx.57. The two expressions use the same overlap but different reference events.
Base R makes the denominator visible.


Code
p_plural_and_acc <- .40
p_plural <- .50
p_acc <- .70

p_acc_given_plural <- p_plural_and_acc / p_plural
p_plural_given_acc <- p_plural_and_acc / p_acc

c(p_acc_given_plural, p_plural_given_acc)


The output is .8 and approximately .571.

title: Conditional probability
section: Why the condition must have positive probability
text:
Why the condition must have positive probability
If \mathbb{P}(C)=0, the original measure places no mass inside C to rescale. The problem is not only arithmetic division by zero. This definition cannot construct a within C probability measure from an event that has no mass.
We will later encounter settings in which conditioning on exact continuous values requires a more careful construction. Nothing from those settings is needed for the finite event calculation here.

title: Conditional probability
section: A common failure: transposing conditional probabilities
text:
A common failure: transposing conditional probabilities
Swapping the target event and conditioning event transposes the conditional probability. A corpus may show that most passive clauses contain an animate subject. This is a claim about

\mathbb{P}(\text{animate subject}\mid\text{passive}).

It does not by itself show that most clauses with animate subjects are passive, which concerns the reversed conditional.
The safest reading procedure is verbal: read the expression from the condition outward. First restrict to the event on the right of the bar. Then ask what portion also belongs to the event on the left.

title: Conditional probability
text:
Check your understanding

Compute \mathbb{P}(A^c\mid P) from the table and verify that it sums with \mathbb{P}(A\mid P) to one.
Compute \mathbb{P}(P\mid A^c) and describe the reference event in words.
Explain why \mathbb{P}(A\mid P) and \mathbb{P}(P\mid A) share a numerator but need not be equal.
Give a linguistic pair of events for which reversing the condition changes the scientific question.

Conditional probability turns an overlap and a reference event into a probability within the conditioning event. The next page rearranges this definition to obtain the product rule.

title: Events
text:
The pronoun sample space lists individual forms, but most linguistic questions concern properties shared by several forms. If we ask whether a recorded pronoun is third person, he, her, and them all give the same answer. We need an object that groups those outcomes without erasing the fact that they are different forms.
An event is a set of outcomes. Let T be the event that the recorded pronoun is third person:
T
=\{\textit{he},\textit{him},\textit{she},\textit{her},\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.
The event T occurs whenever the realized outcome belongs to this set. If the outcome is him, then T occurs. If the outcome is we, then T does not occur.
This definition separates two objects.
The same outcome may belong to many events. That fact lets us represent several properties of one token.

title: Events
section: Translate a linguistic question into a set
text:
Translate a linguistic question into a set
Let A be the event that the pronoun has accusative form:

A
=\{\textit{me},\textit{him},\textit{her},\textit{us},\textit{them}\}.

The forms him, her, and them belong to both T and A. We can represent the question “is the pronoun both third person and accusative?” by keeping only those shared outcomes. The relevant operation is intersection:

T\cap A
=\{\textit{him},\textit{her},\textit{them}\}.

Read T\cap A as “T and A.” The intersection is narrower than either starting event because an outcome must satisfy both descriptions.
Now ask whether the pronoun is third person or accusative. We keep every outcome that belongs to at least one of the events. The relevant operation is union:

T\cup A
=\{\textit{me},\textit{he},\textit{him},\textit{she},\textit{her},
\textit{us},\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.

Read T\cup A as “T or A.” This or is inclusive. The outcome him belongs to the union even though it belongs to both starting events.
Finally, suppose we ask whether the pronoun is not third person. The complement T^c contains every outcome in \Omega that is not in T:

T^c
=\{\textit{I},\textit{me},\textit{you},\textit{we},\textit{us}\}.

The complement is always relative to the declared sample space. If \Omega included reflexive pronouns, then T^c might include additional forms.

title: Events
text:
Work through one outcome
Take the outcome them.

them belongs to T, so the third person event occurs.
them belongs to A, so the accusative event occurs.
them belongs to T\cap A, since both events occur.
them does not belong to T^c, since the third person event occurs.

Now take me. It belongs to A but not T. It thus belongs to T\cup A, but not to T\cap A.
Base R supplies operations with the same interpretation.


Code
omega <- c("I", "me", "you", "he", "him", "she", "her",
           "we", "us", "they", "them")
third <- c("he", "him", "she", "her", "they", "them")
accusative <- c("me", "him", "her", "us", "them")

intersect(third, accusative)
union(third, accusative)
setdiff(omega, third)


The final expression computes T^c by removing the members of T from \Omega.

title: Events
text:
The two limiting events
The empty event \varnothing contains no outcomes. It cannot occur under the current representation. The full event \Omega contains every outcome, so it occurs whenever the observation process produces a represented result.
These are events because both are subsets of \Omega. They will provide the lower and upper endpoints when we assign probabilities.

title: Events
text:
Translating connectives into set operations
A linguistic connective must be translated into the corresponding set operation. The most common error is translating and with a union or translating inclusive or with an intersection.
Consider the claim “the pronoun is plural and accusative.” A union would include plural nominative they and singular accusative him. Those forms satisfy only half of the claim. The intersection retains only them, which satisfies both parts.
A second source of error is a moving sample space. If T^c is first computed relative to personal pronouns and later interpreted relative to all noun phrases, its meaning has changed. Writing \Omega before computing a complement prevents that shift.

title: Events
text:
Check your understanding

Write T\setminus A, the third person outcomes that are not accusative. Then verify that (T\cap A)\cup(T\setminus A)=T.
Let P=\{\textit{we},\textit{us},\textit{they},\textit{them}\} be the plural event. List P\cap A and P\cup A.
Explain why them can make both T and A occur without being two outcomes.
Suppose reflexives are added to \Omega. Which part of the definition of T^c must be recomputed?

Events give us the questions we might ask. A probability model must also state which of those questions it is prepared to measure. The next page introduces that collection.

title: Independence
text:
Suppose that we learn a pronoun is plural. Does that information change how likely the pronoun is to have accusative form? Conditional probability lets us state the question precisely:
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)\stackrel{?}{=}\mathbb{P}(A).
In the toy pronoun measure,
\mathbb{P}(A)=.70
but
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)=.80.
Restricting attention to plural forms changes the probability of accusative form. The two events are associated under this measure.
Events B and C are independent when
\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)
=\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C).
This definition compares the observed mass in the intersection with the mass that would result from multiplying the two margins.

title: Independence
section: Check the pronoun events by hand
text:
Check the pronoun events by hand
The marginal probabilities are

\mathbb{P}(P)=.50
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathbb{P}(A)=.70.

Their product is

\mathbb{P}(P)\mathbb{P}(A)
=.50\times.70
=.35.

The observed joint probability is

\mathbb{P}(P\cap A)=.40.

Since .40\neq.35, the events are not independent under this measure.
The same conclusion follows from conditioning. The probability of A changes from .70 in the full space to .80 within P.

title: Independence
text:
Connect the two statements
When \mathbb{P}(C)>0, the product rule gives

\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)
=\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C).

If B and C are independent, the definition also gives

\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)
=\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C).

Equate the right sides and divide by \mathbb{P}(C):

\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)=\mathbb{P}(B).

Thus independence has a conditional interpretation: learning that C occurred does not change the probability of B.

title: Independence
text:
Build an independent comparison measure
Keep the same outcome labels and margins, but change how the mass is arranged inside the table.




accusative A
nominative A^c
total




plural P
.35
.15
.50


singular P^c
.35
.15
.50


total
.70
.30
1



Now the upper left cell equals the product of its margins:

\mathbb{P}(P\cap A)
=.35
=.50\times.70.

Conditioning gives the same result:

\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)
=\frac{.35}{.50}
=.70
=\mathbb{P}(A).

The accusative proportion is also .70 in the singular row. Knowing the number category provides no information about case under this new measure.


Code
joint_independent <- matrix(
  c(.35, .35, .15, .15),
  nrow = 2,
  dimnames = list(
    number = c("plural", "singular"),
    case = c("accusative", "nominative")
  )
)

p_joint <- joint_independent["plural", "accusative"]
p_plural <- sum(joint_independent["plural", ])
p_acc <- sum(joint_independent[, "accusative"])

c(observed = p_joint, product = p_plural * p_acc)


Both returned values are .35.

title: Independence
text:
Independence belongs to the measure
The two tables use the same outcome labels and the same events. The original table makes P and A dependent; the comparison table makes them independent. Independence is thus a property of events under a probability measure, not a property of the linguistic labels alone.
This matters when interpreting corpus data. A construction choice and an animacy feature may appear independent in one genre but associated in another. The sample space may represent the same categories in both cases, while the probability measure changes with the population of tokens.

title: Independence
text:
Independence is not mutual exclusivity
Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together. If two mutually exclusive events B and C both have positive probability, then

\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)=0

while

\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C)>0.

They are not independent. Observing C tells us that B did not occur, which is strong information.
Mutual exclusivity concerns whether the intersection is empty. Independence concerns whether the intersection receives the product of the marginal probabilities.

title: Independence
section: A common failure: no difference means independence
text:
A common failure: no difference means independence
A small difference in a finite sample does not establish independence. Independence is an exact claim about a probability measure. Estimated proportions from finite data will rarely match exactly, even when an independence model is useful, and they may match by chance when the underlying events are associated.
Later chapters introduce statistical models for uncertainty about such claims. At this stage, we can determine only whether a fully specified probability measure satisfies the independence equation.

title: Independence
text:
Check your understanding

Verify independence in the comparison table using both the product definition and the conditional interpretation.
Change the upper left cell from .35 to .40 and the lower left cell from .35 to .30, leaving the margins fixed. Does independence still hold?
Explain why two mutually exclusive events with positive probability cannot be independent.
Give a linguistic setting in which the same two event labels might be independent in one represented population but dependent in another.

This completes the foundations sequence. We have built probability claims from represented outcomes, measurable events, and a coherent measure. Continue to the next module when you are ready to add the next object in the dependency sequence.

title: Joint probability of events
text:
Suppose that we want to know how often a pronoun is both plural and accusative. The word both tells us to find an intersection before doing any probability calculation.
Return to the four form sample space
\Omega_4=\{\textit{he},\textit{him},\textit{they},\textit{them}\}
with the probability measure below.
Let P be the plural event and A the accusative event:
P=\{\textit{they},\textit{them}\}
and
A=\{\textit{him},\textit{them}\}.
The joint probability of P and A is the probability assigned to their intersection:
\mathbb{P}(P\cap A).
We will sometimes abbreviate this quantity as \mathbb{P}(P,A). The comma is shorthand for the intersection. It does not introduce another probability operation.

title: Joint probability of events
section: Compute the joint probability by hand
text:
Compute the joint probability by hand
Begin with the set operation:

P\cap A=\{\textit{them}\}.

Then apply the probability measure:

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(P\cap A)
&=\mathbb{P}(\{\textit{them}\})\\
&=.40.
\end{aligned}

The result says that .40 of the probability mass falls on outcomes that are simultaneously plural and accusative. It does not say that .40 of plural forms are accusative. That second statement restricts the comparison to plural forms and will require conditional probability.

title: Joint probability of events
section: Arrange all joint events in a table
text:
Arrange all joint events in a table
The number distinction P versus P^c and the case distinction A versus A^c divide the sample space into four nonoverlapping intersections.




accusative A
nominative A^c
total




plural P
them: .40
they: .10
.50


singular P^c
him: .30
he: .20
.50


total
.70
.30
1



Read one cell at a time. The upper right cell represents

P\cap A^c=\{\textit{they}\},

so its probability is .10. The lower left cell represents

P^c\cap A=\{\textit{him}\},

so its probability is .30.
The four interior cells are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Their probabilities must sum to one:

.40+.10+.30+.20=1.

The row and column totals are called marginal probabilities because they appear at the margins of the joint table. For instance,

\mathbb{P}(P)=.40+.10=.50.

The marginal probability adds across all case values. It answers how much mass belongs to the plural event without requiring one particular case.

title: Joint probability of events
section: Reconstruct the table in base R
text:
Reconstruct the table in base R
The following code stores the four joint probabilities in a matrix and computes its margins.


Code
joint <- matrix(
  c(.40, .30, .10, .20),
  nrow = 2,
  dimnames = list(
    number = c("plural", "singular"),
    case = c("accusative", "nominative")
  )
)

joint
rowSums(joint)
colSums(joint)
sum(joint)


The row sums are .50 and .50, the column sums are .70 and .30, and the full sum is one. These checks expose a transposed or omitted cell before it affects later calculations.

title: Joint probability of events
text:
Interpret the joint object
A joint probability preserves two distinctions at once. This makes the table more informative than either margin alone. Two corpora can both have \mathbb{P}(P)=.50 and \mathbb{P}(A)=.70 while placing different amounts of mass in P\cap A.
For a linguistic analysis, the joint table is often the first place to inspect whether a proposed association is even present. If plural forms are much more often accusative than singular forms, the relevant difference must appear in how mass is arranged across the four cells, not merely in the two margins.

title: Joint probability of events
section: Using a marginal probability for an intersection
text:
Using a marginal probability for an intersection
A marginal probability cannot replace an intersection probability. In the toy model, \mathbb{P}(A)=.70 includes both him and them. It cannot answer the question about forms that are both plural and accusative because it also includes singular accusative mass.
The repair is grammatical as much as mathematical. Translate and into an intersection, list the outcomes in that intersection, and only then apply \mathbb{P}.

title: Joint probability of events
text:
Check your understanding

Write the event represented by each of the four interior cells in the table.
Compute \mathbb{P}(P^c\cap A^c) by listing the outcomes first.
Explain why \mathbb{P}(P\cap A)=.40 does not mean that 40\% of plural forms are accusative.
Construct a different four cell table with the same row and column margins but with \mathbb{P}(P\cap A)=.35.

Joint probability measures the overlap in the full sample space. The next page restricts the relevant space to one event and rescales the mass within it.

title: Turning a question into a comparison
text:
Suppose we want to know whether an aspectual mismatch makes a sentence harder to process. We design two conditions and observe the following average reading times at a critical verb:
The mismatch condition is 45 ms slower. What does that difference tell us?
By itself, not very much. Perhaps mismatch caused additional processing. Perhaps the mismatch sentences contained less frequent verbs. Perhaps a small number of participants produced the difference. The subtraction is correct, but its linguistic interpretation depends on how the observations and comparison were constructed.
We will work from the research question to the numerical comparison one step at a time.
crumbs: Turning a question into a comparison

title: Turning a question into a comparison
text:
Step 1: identify the response
The response is the measurement whose variation we want to understand. In this experiment, it might be reading time at the critical verb.
We need to say more than “reading time.” Is the measurement the first-pass time, total time, or time from a particular reading procedure? Is it recorded in milliseconds or transformed before analysis? Which region supplies it?
A precise statement is:

The response is the total reading time in milliseconds at the critical verb on one participant and sentence trial.

This sentence also identifies the unit of analysis.
crumbs: Turning a question into a comparison

title: Turning a question into a comparison
text:
Step 2: identify the linguistic contrast
The main predictor distinguishes the observations that the theory says should differ. Here it records whether a trial contains an aspectually matched or mismatched context.
The values must correspond to an actual design contrast. If all matched sentences contain one set of verbs and all mismatched sentences contain another, the predictor does not isolate aspectual mismatch. It also separates the two verb sets.
This is why theoretically interesting predictors are more than available columns. Their values should encode a linguistic distinction for which an account predicts a change in the response.
For a dative-choice study, predictors might encode whether the recipient is pronominal, whether the theme is discourse-new, and how the lengths of the two arguments compare. These variables express proposals about accessibility, information structure, and production difficulty. Trial number or recording channel may also matter, but for a different reason: they describe the design or measurement process.
crumbs: Turning a question into a comparison

title: Turning a question into a comparison
section: Step 3: say which observations are being compared
text:
Step 3: say which observations are being compared
Imagine that every participant sees both conditions and every sentence appears in both conditions across participants. The comparison then occurs within participants and within sentence items.
This structure matters. A comparison between different groups of participants may reflect preexisting group differences. A comparison between different item sets may reflect lexical differences. A within-participant and within-item design rules out some of these alternative descriptions by construction.
We can now expand the analysis statement:

The response is total reading time at the critical verb on one participant and sentence trial. The comparison is between aspectually matched and mismatched trials, with both conditions represented within participants and sentence items.
crumbs: Turning a question into a comparison

title: Turning a question into a comparison
text:
Step 4: state the estimand
The estimand is the population quantity we want to learn about. Let \mu_{\mathrm{mismatch}} be the mean reading time for mismatch trials in the target population, and let \mu_{\mathrm{match}} be the corresponding mean for match trials. One possible estimand is

\tau
=\mu_{\mathrm{mismatch}}
-\mu_{\mathrm{match}}.

In words, \tau is the difference in mean reading time between the mismatch and match conditions.
The population still needs to be specified. Do we mean only these participants and sentences, or new readers and new sentence items from populations represented by the experiment? The design must contain the relevant replication if the broader target is to be plausible.
Our complete statement is now:

One observation is a participant’s reading of the critical verb in one sentence. The response is total reading time in milliseconds. The comparison is the within-participant and within-item contrast between aspectually matched and mismatched contexts. The target is the difference in mean reading time for readers and items from the populations represented by the design.

Writing this statement takes only a few sentences. It prevents the fitted coefficient from acquiring a broader interpretation than the data and design support.
crumbs: Turning a question into a comparison

title: Turning a question into a comparison
section: The same records can answer a different question
text:
The same records can answer a different question
Suppose the experiment also asks participants to choose an interpretation after each sentence. We can now ask at least three questions:

Does mismatch change reading time?
Does mismatch change the probability of choosing one interpretation?
Do participants with larger reading-time differences also show larger interpretation differences?

These questions use overlapping records, but their responses and estimands differ. The first has a time response. The second has a categorical response. The third compares participant-level contrasts.
Thus a dataset does not come with one inevitable analysis. The research question determines which observations, response, comparison, and target are relevant.
crumbs: Turning a question into a comparison

title: Turning a question into a comparison
text:
What can go wrong?

The unit does not match the claim
Suppose a corpus contains thousands of tokens from one speaker. Those data may describe that speaker’s production precisely. They do not show how speakers vary because only one speaker was observed.


The predictor does not isolate the contrast
Suppose every mismatch sentence uses one set of verbs and every match sentence uses another. The condition difference combines mismatch and lexical identity. Collecting more observations will estimate that combined difference more precisely, but it will not separate the two sources.


The evaluation answers a different question
Suppose a model is meant to predict responses for new readers, but its training and test sets contain trials from the same readers. The evaluation measures prediction of additional trials from observed readers. It does not measure transfer to new readers.
These problems arise before the choice of estimator. A more elaborate model cannot recover a comparison that the data never contained.
crumbs: Turning a question into a comparison

title: Turning a question into a comparison
text:
Exploration can change the question
Exploratory analysis may show that the original target was poorly chosen. A slider response, for instance, may contain many observations at both endpoints. A target concerned only with average slider position may miss a theoretically important distinction between endpoint and interior responses.
The right response is to write a revised question and target. Exploration is allowed to change the analysis. The change should be explicit so that the new result is not presented as if it answered the original question unchanged.
crumbs: Turning a question into a comparison

title: Turning a question into a comparison
text:
Test the distinction

A corpus study asks whether discourse-new themes favor the prepositional dative. State the unit, response, predictor, comparison, and target.
A study averages acceptability judgments by sentence before analysis but interprets its result as variation among participants. Which variation has already been removed?
A word-recognition model is evaluated by randomly splitting trials, but the intended target is performance on new word types. How should the split change?

On the next page, we apply the same discipline to a famous word-frequency pattern.
crumbs: Turning a question into a comparison

title: Mutually exclusive events
text:
Suppose that one observed token is either nominative or accusative under our four form pronoun representation. A single form cannot have both surface cases. We need to distinguish this structural fact about the events from any claim about how frequent the cases are.
Let
N=\{\textit{he},\textit{they}\}
be the nominative event and let
A=\{\textit{him},\textit{them}\}
be the accusative event. The two sets share no outcomes:
N\cap A=\varnothing.
Events whose intersection is empty are mutually exclusive. They cannot both occur on one realization of the outcome represented by \Omega.
The definition concerns set membership:
B\text{ and }C\text{ are mutually exclusive}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
B\cap C=\varnothing.
No probability appears in this definition. We can establish mutual exclusivity before assigning any numerical mass.

title: Mutually exclusive events
text:
Add probabilities across exclusive events
Under the toy probability measure,

\mathbb{P}(N)=.20+.10=.30

and

\mathbb{P}(A)=.30+.40=.70.

Since N and A are mutually exclusive, their union contains two nonoverlapping parts. The probability measure thus gives

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(N\cup A)
&=\mathbb{P}(N)+\mathbb{P}(A)\\
&=.30+.70\\
&=1.
\end{aligned}

In this representation, N\cup A=\Omega_4. The sum equals one because the two events are both exclusive and exhaustive.
Exclusivity and exhaustivity are separate properties. Consider the singleton events \{\textit{he}\} and \{\textit{them}\}. They are mutually exclusive because they share no outcome. Their union does not equal \Omega_4, so their probabilities sum to .20+.40=.60, not to one.

title: Mutually exclusive events
text:
Work through a nonexclusive pair
Let

P=\{\textit{they},\textit{them}\}

be the plural event. Compare P with the accusative event A. Their intersection is

P\cap A=\{\textit{them}\}.

The pair is not mutually exclusive because them makes both events occur. Directly adding \mathbb{P}(P)=.50 and \mathbb{P}(A)=.70 would count the mass on them twice. The result 1.20 is a warning that the nonoverlap condition has failed.
The base R set check should come before the arithmetic.


Code
nominative <- c("he", "they")
accusative <- c("him", "them")
plural <- c("they", "them")

length(intersect(nominative, accusative)) == 0
length(intersect(plural, accusative)) == 0


The first expression returns TRUE; the second returns FALSE.

title: Mutually exclusive events
text:
The represented outcome matters
Mutual exclusivity is always relative to what happens once. If one outcome is one pronoun token, nominative and accusative forms are mutually exclusive in the toy representation. If one outcome is a sentence containing two pronouns, the event “the sentence contains a nominative pronoun” and the event “the sentence contains an accusative pronoun” may occur together.
The linguistic labels have not changed. The unit represented by one outcome has changed, and that change alters the intersection.

title: Mutually exclusive events
section: Labels do not guarantee mutual exclusivity
text:
Labels do not guarantee mutual exclusivity
Contrasting linguistic labels do not by themselves imply an empty intersection. Terms such as singular and plural often denote mutually exclusive values of one annotation. But terms such as plural and accusative denote values on different dimensions and may overlap.
The safe procedure is to write the events as sets and compute their intersection. If the intersection is empty, the events are mutually exclusive under the declared sample space. The labels alone do not establish the result.

title: Mutually exclusive events
text:
Check your understanding

Are \{\textit{he},\textit{him}\} and \{\textit{they},\textit{them}\} mutually exclusive? Are they exhaustive?
Let F be the first person event and P the plural event in the larger pronoun sample space. Write F\cap P and decide whether the events are mutually exclusive.
Give two mutually exclusive events that are not exhaustive in \Omega_4.
Explain why changing the outcome from one token to one sentence can change whether two linguistic events are mutually exclusive.

Mutual exclusivity tells us when two events cannot occur together. The next page assigns a probability to the event in which two properties do occur together.

title: Probability measures
text:
The sample space \Omega tells us which outcomes the model represents. The sigma-algebra \mathcal{F} tells us which groupings of those outcomes the model can measure. Neither object says that one pronoun form is more common than another.
We add that information with a probability measure. A probability measure assigns a number to each event in \mathcal{F}. We write it as
\mathbb{P}:\mathcal{F}\rightarrow[0,1].
Read this notation from left to right. The function \mathbb{P} takes an event from \mathcal{F} as its input and returns a number between zero and one.
The three objects
\langle\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}\rangle
together form a probability space: represented outcomes, measurable events, and numerical probabilities.

title: Probability measures
text:
Assign mass to individual outcomes
Return to the four pronoun forms

\Omega_4
=\{\textit{he},\textit{him},\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.

For this finite example, let \mathcal{F}=2^{\Omega_4} so that every subset is measurable. Suppose a toy corpus motivates these assignments.



outcome
assigned probability




he
.20


him
.30


they
.10


them
.40



The table gives probabilities to singleton events. Larger events receive probabilities by adding the values of their nonoverlapping outcomes.
Let

A=\{\textit{him},\textit{them}\}

be the accusative event. Its probability is

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(A)
&=\mathbb{P}(\{\textit{him}\})
+\mathbb{P}(\{\textit{them}\})\\
&=.30+.40\\
&=.70.
\end{aligned}

The number .70 concerns the event A under this particular measure. It is not a property of the label “accusative” in isolation.

title: Probability measures
text:
The three requirements
Not every numerical assignment is a probability measure. The assignment must satisfy three requirements.
First, every event has nonnegative probability:

\mathbb{P}(B)\geq 0
\qquad\text{for every }B\in\mathcal{F}.

Second, the full sample space has probability one:

\mathbb{P}(\Omega)=1.

Third, probabilities add across a countable collection of events that share no outcomes. If B_1,B_2,\ldots are pairwise disjoint, then

\mathbb{P}\!\left(\bigcup_i B_i\right)
=\sum_i\mathbb{P}(B_i).

The first requirement rules out negative probability. The second says that some represented outcome occurs. The third keeps the probability of a combined event consistent with the probabilities of its nonoverlapping parts.

title: Probability measures
section: Check the toy measure by hand
text:
Check the toy measure by hand
Each value in the table is nonnegative, so the first requirement holds for the singleton events. The singleton events divide \Omega_4 into nonoverlapping parts. Their values sum to

.20+.30+.10+.40=1,

so the probability of \Omega_4 is one.
Now combine he and him. Since the two singleton events share no outcomes,

\mathbb{P}(\{\textit{he},\textit{him}\})
=.20+.30
=.50.

This calculation uses the third requirement. We are not estimating another number from the corpus. We are extending a coherent assignment from individual outcomes to a larger event.
A few base R checks reproduce the arithmetic.


Code
pronoun_mass <- c(he = .20, him = .30, they = .10, them = .40)

all(pronoun_mass >= 0)
sum(pronoun_mass)
sum(pronoun_mass[c("him", "them")])


The three results are TRUE, 1, and .7.

title: Probability measures
text:
Derive two useful consequences
The impossible event has probability zero. Since \Omega and \varnothing are disjoint and \Omega\cup\varnothing=\Omega,

\mathbb{P}(\Omega)
=\mathbb{P}(\Omega)+\mathbb{P}(\varnothing).

Subtracting \mathbb{P}(\Omega) from both sides gives

\mathbb{P}(\varnothing)=0.

The probability of a complement also follows from the requirements. Since B and B^c are disjoint and their union is \Omega,

\mathbb{P}(B)+\mathbb{P}(B^c)=1.

Thus

\mathbb{P}(B^c)=1-\mathbb{P}(B).

For the accusative event, this gives \mathbb{P}(A^c)=1-.70=.30, which agrees with the mass assigned to he and they.

title: Probability measures
section: Assignments that violate the probability axioms
text:
Assignments that violate the probability axioms
An assignment that violates any of the three requirements is not a probability measure. Suppose the four pronoun values were .20, .30, .10, and .50. Each value would lie between zero and one, but their sum would be 1.10. The assignment would give the complete sample space more than unit probability.
Renormalizing the values might produce a probability measure, but it changes every numerical claim. Before doing so, we should ask why the original values did not sum to one. They may be raw corpus counts, percentages computed from different denominators, or model scores that were never intended as probabilities.

title: Probability measures
text:
Check your understanding

Using the toy measure, compute the probability of the plural event P=\{\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.
Compute \mathbb{P}(P^c) in two ways: by adding singleton probabilities and by using the complement rule.
Explain why four nonnegative values that sum to one define a coherent assignment to the singleton events in this finite space.
A table reports values .40, .35, .20, and .10 for four exhaustive outcomes. Which requirement fails?

The next question concerns events that cannot occur together. On the next page, we use the probability measure to characterize mutual exclusivity.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Big Question
What does a probability model say about a linguistic measurement extracted from a complete observation?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Data
One vowel token contains a waveform, a word, a speaker, a vowel label, and a duration.
Which part enters the analysis?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Challenge
Probability is assigned to outcomes, but an analysis usually concerns one property of those outcomes.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
This Module

Map outcomes to values.
Represent probability across those values.
Summarize the resulting distribution.
Use standard distribution families for particular observation processes.
Extend the representation to several variables.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Random variables
From complete outcomes to measured values

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can one vowel token support questions about duration, vowel height, and speaker identity?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Idea
A random variable maps each outcome to a value.
The outcome remains the object to which probability is assigned.

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Introduction to Bayesian Data Analysis for Cognitive Science, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Data



outcome
word
speaker
duration




\(\omega_1\)
heed
s01
112


\(\omega_2\)
hid
s01
83


\(\omega_3\)
heed
s02
126

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
Define \(D(\omega)\) as the duration of token \(\omega\).
Then \(D>100\) names the vowel tokens whose durations exceed 100 ms.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #1
The event \(D>100\) contains \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_3\).
It does not contain the bare numbers 112 and 126.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What must the mapping preserve so that probability statements about its values are defined?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
Every measurable set of values must lead back to a measurable event of outcomes.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The preimage of a value set \(E\) is
\[H^{-1}(E)=\{\omega:H(\omega)\in E\}.\]

[Sources]
Siegrist, Probability, Mathematical Statistics, and Stochastic Processes, Section 2.9: https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
A mapping is measurable when
\[E\in\mathcal G\quad\Longrightarrow\quad H^{-1}(E)\in\mathcal F.\]

[Sources]
Siegrist, Probability, Mathematical Statistics, and Stochastic Processes, Section 2.9: https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
If \(H(\omega_1)=1\) and \(H(\omega_2)=H(\omega_3)=2\), what is \(H^{-1}(\{2\})\)?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
\[H^{-1}(\{2\})=\{\omega_2,\omega_3\}.\]
The superscript denotes a preimage, not an inverse function.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Upshot
A random variable extracts a value without severing that value from the observation process.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Separate values and continuous regions
How probability is arranged over support

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
Can the possible values be listed one by one?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
A discrete random variable has finite or countably infinite support.

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Data
Grammatical person has finite support.
Utterance length has support \(\{0,1,2,3,\ldots\}\).
Both variables are discrete.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #1
Discrete does not mean unordered.
It means that the support values are separate and listable.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
A probability mass function, or PMF, assigns probability to each support value:
\[p_S(s)=\mathbb P(S=s).\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question



syllables \(s\)
1
2
3
4




\(p_S(s)\)
.42
.33
.17
.08



What is \(\mathbb P(S\geq3)\)?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
\[\mathbb P(S\geq3)=.17+.08=.25.\]
The masses are added across disjoint value events.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What changes when a measurement can take any value throughout an interval?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
A random variable with a density is absolutely continuous.
A point and an interval are different events.

[Sources]
Pfeiffer, Applied Probability, Distribution and Density Functions: https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Applied_Probability_%28Pfeiffer%29/07%3A_Distribution_and_Density_Functions/7.01%3A_Distribution_and_Density_Functions

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #2
Rounding a duration to whole milliseconds does not make its modeled support discrete.
Storage precision and modeled support answer different questions.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
A probability density function, or PDF, represents probability as area:
\[\mathbb P(a\leq X\leq b)=\int_a^b f_X(x)\,dx.\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
Suppose \(f_D(d)=1/100\) on \([50,150]\).
What is \(\mathbb P(80\leq D\leq100)\)?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #3
Density height is not point probability.
For a continuous variable, \(\mathbb P(D=100)=0\) even when \(f_D(100)>0\).

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can one representation describe threshold probabilities for either kind of variable?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The cumulative distribution function, or CDF, is
\[F_X(x)=\mathbb P(X\leq x).\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Interpretation
For a discrete variable, the CDF is a step function.
For a continuous variable, it accumulates area under the density through \(x\).

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Upshot
Mass belongs to separate values. Density becomes probability only after integration. The CDF accumulates either representation.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Summaries of a distribution
Center, spread, and shape

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can we summarize the center of a distribution while respecting unequal probabilities?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The expected value of a discrete variable is
\[\mathbb E[X]=\sum_x x\,p_X(x).\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
If word length is 1, 2, or 4 with masses .25, .50, and .25, what is \(\mathbb E[L]\)?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
\[\mathbb E[L]=1(.25)+2(.50)+4(.25)=2.25.\]
An expectation need not be a possible observation.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What if the theoretical quantity is a transformation of the measurement?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
Transform first, then average:
\[\mathbb E[g(X)]=\sum_x g(x)p_X(x).\]

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #1
In general,
\[\mathbb E[g(X)]\neq g(\mathbb E[X]).\]
The two operations answer different questions.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
Must we derive the complete distribution of a sum before finding its expectation?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
Linearity of expectation gives
\[\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_i a_iX_i\right]=\sum_i a_i\mathbb E[X_i].\]

[Sources]
Siegrist, Probability, Mathematical Statistics, and Stochastic Processes, Section 4.1: https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/04%3A_Expected_Value/4.01%3A_Definitions_and_Basic_Properties

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #2
Linearity of expectation does not require independence.
Dependence changes the distribution of the sum, not this equality.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Challenge
A valid PMF may place enough probability on large values that its expected value is not finite.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Data
For \(p_L(l)=6/(\pi^2l^2)\) on \(l=1,2,\ldots\),
\[\mathbb E[L]=\frac{6}{\pi^2}\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{l}.\]

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Result #1
The harmonic series diverges.
Every finite sample mean is finite, but the model expectation does not exist as a finite number.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can two distributions have the same mean but different dispersion?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The variance is expected squared distance from the mean:
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Data
\(D_1\) always equals 2.
\(D_2\) equals 1 or 3 with equal probability.
Both means are 2, but their variances are 0 and 1.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can spread be returned to the units of the measurement?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The standard deviation is
\[\operatorname{SD}(X)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #3
Standard deviation is a root mean squared distance.
It does not determine how much probability lies within one standard deviation of the mean.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How do variance and directional asymmetry fit within one family of summaries?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The \(k\)th central moment is
\[\mu_k=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^k].\]

[Sources]
Siegrist, Probability, Mathematical Statistics, and Stochastic Processes, Section 4.1: https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/04%3A_Expected_Value/4.01%3A_Definitions_and_Basic_Properties

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Interpretation
\(\mu_1=0\). The second central moment is variance. Odd orders retain direction, while even orders do not.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Upshot
Expectations summarize specified functions of a distribution. Their interpretation depends on existence, units, and the function being averaged.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Discrete distribution families
Models for categories, totals, waiting times, and counts

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can a model assign probabilities to several unordered linguistic categories?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The categorical distribution assigns a probability vector \(\boldsymbol\pi\) to \(K\) labels.
\[\pi_k\geq0,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k=1.\]

[Sources]
Stan Functions Reference, Categorical Distribution: https://mc-stan.org/docs/functions-reference/categorical-distribution.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #1
Reordering labels without reordering their probabilities changes the model.
The labels and probability vector must remain aligned.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What is the corresponding model when there are exactly two coded outcomes?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The Bernoulli distribution has support \(\{0,1\}\) and
\[p_Y(y)=\pi^y(1-\pi)^{1-y}.\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
If 1 means a passive response and \(\pi=.30\), what are \(\mathbb P(Y=1)\) and \(\mathbb P(Y=0)\)?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
\[\mathbb P(Y=1)=.30,\qquad \mathbb P(Y=0)=.70.\]
Reversing the coding changes which event \(\pi\) names.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How do we model a total number of successes across a fixed number of independent opportunities?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The binomial distribution gives
\[\mathbb P(Y=y)={n\choose y}\pi^y(1-\pi)^{n-y}.\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #2
The model requires a fixed number of opportunities, a common success probability, and independent trials conditional on \(\pi\).

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What changes when tokens are sampled without replacement from a finite corpus list?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The hypergeometric distribution counts samples without replacement from a finite population.

[Sources]
OpenStax, Introductory Statistics, Hypergeometric Distribution: https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/4-5-hypergeometric-distribution

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #3
Without replacement, one draw changes the composition available for later draws.
The binomial independence assumption no longer applies.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How many opportunities occur before the first target token?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The geometric distribution models a waiting time to the first success.
Its support convention must be stated.

[Sources]
OpenStax, Introductory Statistics, Geometric Distribution: https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/4-4-geometric-distribution

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
If \(Y\) counts trials through the first success, what is \(\mathbb P(Y=3)\)?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
\[\mathbb P(Y=3)=(1-\pi)^2\pi.\]
Two failures must occur before the success on trial 3.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How many trials occur before the \(r\)th success?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The negative binomial distribution extends the waiting time to a specified success count.
The parameterization must be stated.

[Sources]
Penn State STAT 414, Negative Binomial Distribution: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/lesson/11/11.4

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can we model the number of events observed in a declared amount of exposure?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The Poisson distribution has
\[\mathbb P(Y=y)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^y}{y!}.\]

[Sources]
Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Count Models: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=234

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #4
Exposure is part of the count definition.
Ten events in ten minutes and ten events in ten hours do not express the same rate.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Challenge
The Poisson model makes the mean and variance equal to \(\lambda\).
Observed extra variation signals a model mismatch, not a different calculation of \(\lambda\).

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Upshot
Each discrete family corresponds to a different observation process. The support and sampling assumptions identify the relevant family.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Continuous distribution families
Models for bounded and unbounded measurements

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What density assigns equal probability to equal width intervals within fixed bounds?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The continuous uniform distribution on \([a,b]\) has density
\[f_X(x)=\frac{1}{b-a}.\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #1
A density height may exceed one.
The total area, not the height, must equal one.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What family can represent different shapes over the open unit interval?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The beta distribution has support \((0,1)\) and shape parameters \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Bayesian Data Analysis: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introBDA.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Interpretation
\[\mathbb E[X]=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}.\]
Holding the ratio fixed while increasing \(\alpha+\beta\) concentrates density around the same mean.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What family describes a symmetric bell shaped density over the real line?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The normal distribution is determined by location \(\mu\) and scale \(\sigma\).

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Method
Standardize one value with
\[z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}.\]
The resulting value measures distance from the mean in standard deviation units.

[Sources]
Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Standardization: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=102

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Challenge
The normal distribution has support on the complete real line.
It is not automatically appropriate for positive or bounded measurements.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What symmetric reference distribution allows more probability in the tails?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
Student’s \(t\) distribution is indexed by degrees of freedom and approaches the normal distribution as they increase.

[Sources]
Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Student’s t Distribution: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=173

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #2
Heavy tails can represent occasional large deviations.
They do not repair an inappropriate response support or measurement model.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What distribution results from adding squared independent standard normal variables?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The chi-squared distribution is indexed by degrees of freedom and has nonnegative support.

[Sources]
OpenStax, Introductory Statistics, Chi-Square Distribution: https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/11-1-facts-about-the-chi-square-distribution

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Interpretation
With \(
u\) degrees of freedom,
\[\mathbb E[X]=
u,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=2
u.\]

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #3
An upper tail probability under a reference distribution is not the probability that a hypothesis is true.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Upshot
Continuous families differ in support, shape, and tail behavior. Those properties must match the linguistic measurement and observation process.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Simulation
Turning a distribution into reproducible draws

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can one uniform draw select a value from a target distribution?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
Inverse transform sampling applies the inverse CDF to \(U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\).

[Sources]
Peng, Advanced Statistical Computing, Inverse Transform Sampling: https://bookdown.org/rdpeng/advstatcomp/inverse-transform-sampling.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Implementation

Compute cumulative probabilities.
Draw \(u\) from the unit interval.
Return the first value whose cumulative probability is at least \(u\).

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What does a random seed reproduce?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
A random seed fixes the initial state of a pseudorandom number generator.
It reproduces one sequence of draws from a procedure.

[Sources]
R base documentation, Random Number Generation: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/Random.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #1
Reproducibility is not validity.
A fixed seed can reproduce a simulation from a poorly specified model.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Upshot
Simulation implements a probability model. The seed makes the implementation repeatable, while the model determines what the draws mean.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Joint distributions
Probability for paired linguistic measurements

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can a model preserve which duration occurred with which predictability value?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
A joint distribution assigns probability to pairs or tuples of random variable values.

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #1
Separate marginal distributions do not recover pairing.
Different joint tables can have the same row and column totals.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How do we recover the distribution of one variable from the joint table?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
A marginal distribution sums over the other variable:
\[p_X(x)=\sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y).\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
Can two variables be independent within each clause type but associated after clause types are pooled?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
Yes. Conditional independence states independence after conditioning on a third variable.

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
\[X\perp Y\mid Z\]
means
\[p(x,y\mid z)=p(x\mid z)p(y\mid z).\]

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #2
Conditional and unconditional claims differ.
Always state the conditioning set.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How does the expected response change with a specified predictor value?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The conditional expectation is
\[\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x].\]
It is a function of the conditioning value \(x\).

[Sources]
Siegrist, Probability, Mathematical Statistics, and Stochastic Processes, Conditional Expected Value: https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/04%3A_Expected_Value/4.07%3A_Conditional_Expected_Value

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #3
The marginal mean combines conditional means using the distribution of the conditioning variable.
Changing that mixture can change the marginal mean without changing either conditional mean.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can paired deviations summarize whether two measurements vary together?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The covariance is
\[\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Interpretation
Positive covariance means that above mean values tend to pair with above mean values.
Its magnitude depends on both measurement units.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can this paired association be expressed without measurement units?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The Pearson correlation coefficient is
\[\rho_{XY}=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{SD}(X)\operatorname{SD}(Y)}.\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #4
Correlation summarizes linear association.
It does not identify a causal direction.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Interim Discussion
Joint distributions preserve pairing. Marginalization removes one coordinate. Conditioning restricts attention to a specified value or stratum.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Conclusion
From observations to probability models

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Big Question
What does a probability model say about a linguistic measurement extracted from a complete observation?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer

Random variables map outcomes to values while preserving measurable events.
PMFs and PDFs represent probability on different kinds of support.
Expectations summarize declared functions when the relevant expectation exists.
Distribution families encode particular observation processes.
Joint distributions retain relations among several measurements.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
Before choosing a distribution, what are the outcome, the measured value, its support, and the process that generated it?

title: The Bernoulli distribution
text:
The categorical distribution permits any finite number of unordered labels. Its binary case can be coded with zero and one. Suppose an elicited wh dependency either contains a resumptive pronoun or contains a gap.
X=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if the response contains a resumptive pronoun},\\
0 & \text{if the response contains a gap}.
\end{cases}
The Bernoulli distribution represents one draw with two possible values, 0 and 1.
Let
\pi=\mathbb{P}(X=1).
Since the two masses must sum to one,
\mathbb{P}(X=0)=1-\pi.
We write
X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi).
The single parameter \pi is the probability of the outcome coded as 1. The coding statement must thus be part of the model description.

title: The Bernoulli distribution
section: Write one PMF for both values
text:
Write one PMF for both values
The two row PMF can be written as

p_X(x)=\pi^x(1-\pi)^{1-x},
\qquad x\in\{0,1\}.

Substitute x=1:

\begin{aligned}
p_X(1)
&=\pi^1(1-\pi)^0\\
&=\pi.
\end{aligned}

Substitute x=0:

\begin{aligned}
p_X(0)
&=\pi^0(1-\pi)^1\\
&=1-\pi.
\end{aligned}

The exponents select the appropriate factor. Any nonzero number raised to the zeroth power is one, so the unused factor drops out.

title: The Bernoulli distribution
text:
Calculate a concrete Bernoulli model
Suppose resumptive pronouns occur with probability .35 in the represented elicitation context. Then

\pi=.35

and

1-\pi=.65.

The complete PMF is



x
linguistic outcome
p_X(x)




0
gap
.65


1
resumptive pronoun
.35



The table concerns one response. It does not say that exactly 35 of every 100 finite samples must contain a resumptive pronoun.

title: The Bernoulli distribution
text:
Derive the mean and variance
The expected value is

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X]
&=0(1-\pi)+1(\pi)\\
&=\pi.
\end{aligned}

For a zero and one variable, the mean is the probability of 1.
The variance is

\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(X)
&=(0-\pi)^2(1-\pi)+(1-\pi)^2\pi\\
&=\pi(1-\pi).
\end{aligned}

With \pi=.35, the variance is

.35(.65)=.2275.

The variance approaches zero as \pi approaches either endpoint because the outcome becomes increasingly predictable.

title: The Bernoulli distribution
section: Check the PMF in base R
text:
Check the PMF in base R


Code
pi_resumptive <- .35
bernoulli_mass <- c(
  gap = 1 - pi_resumptive,
  resumptive = pi_resumptive
)

sum(bernoulli_mass)
sum(c(0, 1) * bernoulli_mass)
pi_resumptive * (1 - pi_resumptive)


The results are 1, .35, and .2275.

title: The Bernoulli distribution
text:
Reverse the coding
We could define 1 to mean gap and 0 to mean resumptive pronoun. The new Bernoulli parameter would be .65. The underlying probabilities of the two linguistic outcomes would not change.
Coefficient signs in later binary regression models depend on this coding. Reversing the event marked by 1 reverses which probability the model describes.

title: The Bernoulli distribution
section: Check which event is coded as 1
text:
Check which event is coded as 1
The interpretation of \pi depends on which event is coded as 1. The number .35 is not a free standing “Bernoulli probability.” It is the probability of the declared target event.
Write the coding definition immediately before the parameter statement. Then \pi=\mathbb{P}(X=1) can be translated back into the linguistic event without guessing.

title: The Bernoulli distribution
text:
Check your understanding

Let 1 mark a passive clause. If 18 percent of clauses are passive, write both PMF values.
Reverse the coding in the first question. What is the new value of \pi?
Derive \mathbb{E}[X]=\pi from the two support values.
Why is Bernoulli variance small when \pi is close to zero or one?

The Bernoulli family represents one binary draw. The next page represents the number of target outcomes across a fixed number of comparable draws.

title: The binomial distribution
text:
The Bernoulli distribution represents one binary observation. The binomial distribution represents a sum of Bernoulli observations under additional assumptions. Suppose a bilingual production task gives a participant six positions at which a code switch could occur.
X_i=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if position }i\text{ contains a code switch},\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
The response of interest is not one position. It is the total number of switched positions:
K=\sum_{i=1}^{6}X_i.
If the six indicators are independent and share one switch probability \pi, then K has a binomial distribution:
K\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(6,\pi).
More generally, the family has a fixed number of opportunities n and one target probability \pi.

title: The binomial distribution
text:
Establish the support
The smallest possible count is zero and the largest is the number of opportunities. Thus

\operatorname{supp}(K)=\{0,1,2,3,4,5,6\}.

The upper bound is part of the model. A count of 7 is impossible because only six positions were observed.
This denominator distinguishes a binomial count from an unbounded count. Recording 2 switches without recording 6 eligible positions discards part of the response.

title: The binomial distribution
section: Count the sequences that give one total
text:
Count the sequences that give one total
Take K=2. One sequence of position outcomes is

1,1,0,0,0,0.

Under the shared probability and independence assumptions, this sequence has probability

\pi^2(1-\pi)^4.

The two switches can occupy any two of the six positions. The number of such sequences is

{6\choose2}
=\frac{6!}{2!4!}
=15.

Since the sequences are mutually exclusive, their probabilities add:

\mathbb{P}(K=2)
={6\choose2}\pi^2(1-\pi)^4.

The general PMF is

p_K(k)
={n\choose k}\pi^k(1-\pi)^{n-k},
\qquad k\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\}.

The binomial coefficient counts arrangements. The remaining factors give the probability of any one arrangement.

title: The binomial distribution
text:
Calculate one probability by hand
Let \pi=.25. Then

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(K=2)
&={6\choose2}(.25)^2(.75)^4\\
&=15(.0625)(.31640625)\\
&\approx.297.
\end{aligned}

Thus about .297 of the modeled probability lies on exactly two switches among six positions.
In base R,


Code
dbinom(2, size = 6, prob = .25)
pbinom(2, size = 6, prob = .25)


The first call returns the mass at exactly 2. The second returns cumulative probability through 2, so the two calls answer different questions.

title: The binomial distribution
text:
Derive center and spread
Since K is a sum of six indicators, linearity of expectation gives

\mathbb{E}[K]=6\pi.

With \pi=.25,

\mathbb{E}[K]=1.5.

Under independence, the variance is

\operatorname{Var}(K)=6\pi(1-\pi)=1.125.

The expected value 1.5 is an average across repeated groups of six. One observed group still has an integer count.

title: The binomial distribution
text:
Make the assumptions linguistic
The model requires three linked claims.

The number of eligible positions is fixed at six.
Every position has the same switch probability \pi.
Conditional on \pi, knowing one position’s outcome does not change another position’s probability.

Repeated positions from one discourse may violate the third claim because switching can cluster. Different syntactic environments may violate the second because they offer different switch constraints.

title: The binomial distribution
text:
Retain the number of opportunities
A binomial model requires both the number of target events and the number of opportunities. Two speakers with 2 switches have different response proportions if one had 6 opportunities and the other had 60.
Retain both K and n. The family models the target count relative to its fixed opportunity count.

title: The binomial distribution
text:
Check your understanding

If twelve positions are observed, list the support of K.
Explain why {12\choose4} appears in the mass for four switches.
With n=10 and \pi=.20, compute the expected count and variance.
Give one linguistic reason that positions in the same conversation might not be independent.

The binomial model keeps one target probability across comparable opportunities. The next page considers a finite population whose target probability changes when an object is sampled without replacement.

title: The chi-squared distribution
text:
The normal distribution page introduced standard normal variables. Suppose three independent annotation discrepancies have been standardized relative to a reference model. Their values are
Z_1=1,
\qquad
Z_2=-.5,
\qquad
Z_3=2.
If discrepancy direction is not relevant, we can square each value and add:
Q=Z_1^2+Z_2^2+Z_3^2.
When Z_1,\ldots,Z_\nu are independent standard normal variables, this sum has a chi-squared distribution with \nu degrees of freedom:
Q\sim\chi^2_\nu.
The support is [0,\infty) because a sum of squares cannot be negative.

title: The chi-squared distribution
text:
Calculate one squared discrepancy
For the three constructed values,

\begin{aligned}
Q
&=1^2+(-.5)^2+2^2\\
&=1+.25+4\\
&=5.25.
\end{aligned}

The value 2 makes the largest contribution because squaring gives greater weight to larger standardized departures.
If these were three independent standard normal discrepancies, the reference distribution would have \nu=3.

title: The chi-squared distribution
section: Read center and spread from degrees of freedom
text:
Read center and spread from degrees of freedom
For Q\sim\chi^2_\nu,

\mathbb{E}[Q]=\nu

and

\operatorname{Var}(Q)=2\nu.

With three degrees of freedom, the mean is 3 and the variance is 6. The observed value 5.25 lies above the reference mean, but a tail probability is needed to state how much reference mass lies at least that far right.

title: The chi-squared distribution
text:
Calculate the upper tail
The upper tail probability is

\mathbb{P}(Q\geq5.25).

In R,


Code
pchisq(5.25, df = 3, lower.tail = FALSE)


The result is approximately .154. Under the reference assumptions, about .154 of the probability lies on values at least as large as 5.25.
This is a statement about the statistic’s reference distribution. It is not the probability that a null hypothesis is true.

title: The chi-squared distribution
section: See what changing degrees of freedom does
text:
See what changing degrees of freedom does
With one degree of freedom, the distribution is strongly right skewed because one squared value often lies near zero but can occasionally be large. Adding more independent squared terms moves the center right and makes the shape less sharply skewed.


Code
q <- seq(0, 20, length.out = 300)

plot(q, dchisq(q, df = 1), type = "l",
     xlab = "squared discrepancy", ylab = "density")
lines(q, dchisq(q, df = 4), lty = 2)
lines(q, dchisq(q, df = 10), lty = 3)


Degrees of freedom determine both center and spread for this family.

title: The chi-squared distribution
section: Degrees of freedom count unconstrained variation
text:
Degrees of freedom count unconstrained variation
The symbol \nu does not always count observations directly. It counts independent pieces of variation remaining after constraints.
In an r by c contingency table with row and column totals treated as fixed, the final row and column values are determined by the earlier cells. The number of free cell comparisons is

\nu=(r-1)(c-1).

The chi-squared test page later derives this count for a small linguistic table.

title: The chi-squared distribution
section: A tail probability is not a hypothesis probability
text:
A tail probability is not a hypothesis probability
An upper tail probability is not the probability that a hypothesis is true. The tail calculation conditions on a reference model and asks how often the statistic would be at least as large.
It does not reverse that conditional statement. Interpreting hypotheses requires a separate inferential framework developed later.

title: The chi-squared distribution
text:
Check your understanding

Why can a chi-squared value not be negative?
If \nu=8, what are the mean and variance?
Which constructed discrepancy contributes most to Q=5.25, and why?
State the upper tail probability in words without treating it as a hypothesis probability.

The family pages define target distributions. The next page gives a general procedure for turning cumulative probability into simulated values.

title: Conditional independence
text:
The foundations chapter defined independence for events, and the preceding pages extended probability to joint distributions. We now ask whether two variables are independent after conditioning on a third. Suppose a corpus records subject omission O, verb final order V, and clause type C.
Conditional independence states that two variables are independent within every relevant value of a conditioning variable.
We write
O\perp\!\!\!\perp V\mid C
and read the statement as “O is independent of V given C.”

title: Conditional independence
section: Build an independent table for main clauses
text:
Build an independent table for main clauses
Within main clauses, suppose

\mathbb{P}(O=1\mid C=\mathrm{main})=.80

and

\mathbb{P}(V=1\mid C=\mathrm{main})=.75.

If O and V are independent within this clause type, the joint target probability is

.80(.75)=.60.

The full conditional joint PMF is

section: Build an independent table for subordinate clauses
text:
Build an independent table for subordinate clauses
Within subordinate clauses, suppose

\mathbb{P}(O=1\mid C=\mathrm{sub})=.20

and

\mathbb{P}(V=1\mid C=\mathrm{sub})=.25.

The joint target probability under conditional independence is .20(.25)=.05.

Again, every cell factors into the corresponding conditional margins.

title: Conditional independence
text:
State the conditional factorization
For every relevant clause type c, conditional independence requires

p_{O,V\mid C}(o,v\mid c)
=p_{O\mid C}(o\mid c)p_{V\mid C}(v\mid c).

An equivalent statement is

p_{O\mid V,C}(o\mid v,c)
=p_{O\mid C}(o\mid c).

Once clause type is known, learning verb order does not change the conditional distribution of subject omission.

title: Conditional independence
text:
Pool the clause types
Suppose main and subordinate clauses each receive probability .50. Averaging corresponding cells across the two tables gives



pooled clauses

V=1
