In the pooled table,

\mathbb{P}(O=1,V=1)=.325.

The product of the pooled margins is

\mathbb{P}(O=1)\mathbb{P}(V=1)
=.50(.50)
=.25.

Since .325\neq.25, the variables are dependent before conditioning on clause type.
Main clauses have high probabilities for both properties, while subordinate clauses have low probabilities for both. Mixing clause types produces a pooled association even though the properties are independent within each type.

title: Conditional independence
section: Verify one stratum in base R
text:
Verify one stratum in base R


Code
main <- matrix(c(.05, .20, .15, .60), nrow = 2)
subordinate <- matrix(c(.60, .15, .20, .05), nrow = 2)
pooled <- .50 * main + .50 * subordinate

main[2, 2]
sum(main[2, ]) * sum(main[, 2])
pooled


The first two results both equal .60, verifying one main clause cell. The pooled matrix shows the induced association.

title: Conditional independence
text:
Conditional and unconditional claims differ
The example establishes that

O\perp\!\!\!\perp V\mid C

does not imply

O\perp\!\!\!\perp V.

The reverse implication also need not hold. An independence claim is incomplete unless it states which variables are conditioned on.

title: Conditional independence
text:
State the conditioning set
A conditional independence claim must state its conditioning set. Saying “subject omission is independent of verb order” erases the fact that the equality holds only within clause types in this model.
Include the vertical bar in notation and prose: independent given clause type.

title: Conditional independence
text:
Check your understanding

Verify the cell \mathbb{P}(O=0,V=1\mid C=\mathrm{main})=.15 from its margins.
Compute \mathbb{P}(O=1\mid V=1,C=\mathrm{sub}) and compare it with \mathbb{P}(O=1\mid C=\mathrm{sub}).
Why are O and V dependent in the pooled table?
State precisely which independence claim the two stratum tables support.

Conditional independence concerns complete distributions within groups. The next page summarizes the center of a response distribution within each condition.

title: Correlation
text:
The preceding page showed that covariance depends on both association and measurement scale. Correlation divides covariance by the standard deviations of the two variables. Suppose X records whether a dative recipient is pronominal and Y records whether the double object construction is used:
X=1\text{ for a pronominal recipient}
and
Y=1\text{ for a double object construction}.
Consider this constructed joint PMF.
The table suggests a positive linear association, but covariance depends on the numerical scales. Correlation standardizes covariance by the two standard deviations:
\operatorname{Cor}(X,Y)
=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}
{\operatorname{SD}(X)\operatorname{SD}(Y)}.
The quantity is defined when both standard deviations are positive and finite.

title: Correlation
text:
Compute the means and covariance
The target probabilities are

\mathbb{E}[X]=\mathbb{P}(X=1)=.50

and

\mathbb{E}[Y]=\mathbb{P}(Y=1)=.60.

Since XY=1 only in the lower right cell,

\mathbb{E}[XY]=.40.

An equivalent covariance formula is

\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)
=\mathbb{E}[XY]-\mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y].

Thus

\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)
=.40-.50(.60)
=.10.

title: Correlation
text:
Compute the two standard deviations
For a zero and one variable with target probability \pi, the variance is \pi(1-\pi). Thus

\operatorname{Var}(X)=.50(.50)=.25

and

\operatorname{Var}(Y)=.60(.40)=.24.

The standard deviations are

\operatorname{SD}(X)=.50

and

\operatorname{SD}(Y)=\sqrt{.24}\approx.490.

The correlation is

\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Cor}(X,Y)
&=\frac{.10}{.50\sqrt{.24}}\\
&\approx.408.
\end{aligned}

The positive value reflects the concentration of mass in the two matching cells, especially X=1,Y=1.

title: Correlation
section: Verify the calculation in base R
text:
Verify the calculation in base R


Code
x <- c(0, 0, 1, 1)
y <- c(0, 1, 0, 1)
mass <- c(.30, .20, .10, .40)

mean_x <- sum(x * mass)
mean_y <- sum(y * mass)
cov_xy <- sum((x - mean_x) * (y - mean_y) * mass)
sd_x <- sqrt(sum((x - mean_x)^2 * mass))
sd_y <- sqrt(sum((y - mean_y)^2 * mass))

cov_xy / (sd_x * sd_y)


The result is approximately .408.

title: Correlation
text:
Read the scale
Correlation lies between -1 and 1.



value
linear pattern




1
perfect increasing linear relation


0
no linear relation


-1
perfect decreasing linear relation



Intermediate values summarize direction and degree of linear association. A value of zero does not rule out a nonlinear relationship.

title: Correlation
section: See why positive unit changes cancel
text:
See why positive unit changes cancel
If X^*=a+bX with b>0, then the covariance with Y is multiplied by b and the standard deviation of X is also multiplied by b. The factor cancels in the correlation.
Adding a constant changes the mean but not the centered deviations. Thus converting a measurement by a positive linear unit transformation does not change correlation.
Reversing a binary coding uses a negative slope and flips the sign. The interpretation must remain tied to the outcome coded as 1.

title: Correlation
section: Correlation does not identify a causal direction
text:
Correlation does not identify a causal direction
A correlation is not a directional causal effect. Correlation is symmetric:

\operatorname{Cor}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Cor}(Y,X).

It does not select a response, adjust for other variables, or identify what would happen under an intervention. Those claims need a design and model that represent direction.

title: Correlation
text:
Check your understanding

Recompute the covariance if the lower right cell changes to .30 and the lower left changes to .20 while the margins are allowed to change.
Why does adding 100 to every value of a continuous X leave correlation unchanged?
What happens to the sign if the coding of Y is reversed?
Give one nonlinear relationship that could have correlation near zero.

This completes the random variables and distributions module. The next module begins the distinction between population quantities, samples, and estimators.

title: Cumulative distribution functions
text:
The earlier pages represented discrete probability with a probability mass function and continuous probability with a probability density function. A cumulative distribution function provides one representation that applies to both. Suppose M records the number of morphemes in a sampled word token.
A cumulative distribution function, abbreviated CDF, records the probability at or below every threshold:
F_X(x)=\mathbb{P}(X\leq x).
The function accumulates probability from the lower end of the support through the threshold x.

title: Cumulative distribution functions
section: Build a discrete CDF by hand
text:
Build a discrete CDF by hand
Consider this constructed PMF.



morpheme count m
p_M(m)




1
.55


2
.30


3
.10


4
.05



At threshold 1, the CDF contains only the first mass:

F_M(1)=.55.

At threshold 2, it contains the first two masses:

F_M(2)=.55+.30=.85.

Continuing gives the full CDF table.



threshold m
F_M(m)

For a discrete variable,

F_X(x)=\sum_{x'\leq x}p_X(x').

The CDF increases in jumps when a support value has positive mass.

title: Cumulative distribution functions
text:
Accumulate a continuous density
For a continuous variable with density f_X, the same definition is represented by area:

F_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}f_X(x')\,\mathrm{d}x'.

The operation changes from summing masses to integrating density, but the interpretation remains \mathbb{P}(X\leq x).
Suppose a boundary duration variable B has

F_B(120)=.25

and

F_B(180)=.72.

Then the probability in the interval above 120 and at or below 180 is

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(120<B\leq180)
&=F_B(180)-F_B(120)\\
&=.72-.25\\
&=.47.
\end{aligned}

The subtraction removes the probability already accumulated through 120.

title: Cumulative distribution functions
section: Compute the discrete CDF in base R
text:
Compute the discrete CDF in base R


Code
morpheme_value <- 1:4
morpheme_mass <- c(.55, .30, .10, .05)
morpheme_cdf <- cumsum(morpheme_mass)

data.frame(morpheme_value, morpheme_mass, morpheme_cdf)


The CDF must be nondecreasing and approach one at the upper end of the support. The cumsum() result lets us check both properties.

title: Cumulative distribution functions
text:
Read the threshold direction
The definition always uses the lower tail:

F_X(x)=\mathbb{P}(X\leq x).

An upper tail probability follows by complementation:

\mathbb{P}(X>x)=1-F_X(x).

For the morpheme count variable,

\mathbb{P}(M>2)=1-.85=.15,

which agrees with adding the masses at 3 and 4.

title: Cumulative distribution functions
section: Reading the direction of the threshold
text:
Reading the direction of the threshold
The cumulative distribution function gives a lower tail probability, not an upper tail probability. The value F_B(180)=.72 places .72 of the mass at or below 180, not above it.
Writing the defining event next to the function usually repairs the error:

F_B(180)=\mathbb{P}(B\leq180).

title: Cumulative distribution functions
text:
Check your understanding

Use the morpheme PMF to compute F_M(3).
Compute \mathbb{P}(M>1) from the CDF and verify it from the PMF.
If F_B(200)=.81, what is \mathbb{P}(B>200)?
Explain why a discrete CDF has jumps while a continuous variable cannot add positive mass at one point.

The CDF describes probability through every threshold. The next page compresses a complete distribution into one probability weighted center.

title: Discrete random variables
text:
The formal definition of a random variable requires a measurable mapping from outcomes to values. We now classify that variable by the possible values in its distribution.
Suppose L maps each utterance outcome to its number of word tokens. The possible values begin
0,1,2,3,\ldots
There may be no fixed largest utterance length in the model, but the possible values can be placed in a list. This property makes L a discrete random variable.
For a discrete random variable, the set of values assigned positive probability is its support. We write the support of this utterance length variable as
\operatorname{supp}(L)=\{0,1,2,3,\ldots\}.
A random variable is discrete when its support is finite or countably infinite. Countably infinite means that every support value can be assigned a position in a sequence, even though the sequence has no final value.

title: Discrete random variables
section: Compare finite and countably infinite support
text:
Compare finite and countably infinite support
An annotation variable P might record grammatical person:

\operatorname{supp}(P)
=\{\textsc{first},\textsc{second},\textsc{third}\}.

This support is finite. The utterance length support is countably infinite. Both variables are discrete because their values occur as separate, listable possibilities.
The support values need not be numerical. Grammatical person is discrete even when represented with linguistic labels. Numerical coding may be convenient in software, but it does not create discreteness.

title: Discrete random variables
text:
Values define separate events
The statement L=5 corresponds to the event

\{\omega\in\Omega:L(\omega)=5\},

which contains every five word utterance outcome. The statement L\geq5 corresponds to

\{\omega\in\Omega:L(\omega)\in\{5,6,7,\ldots\}\}.

For a discrete variable, each support value can be considered separately. A single value such as L=5 may receive positive probability.

title: Discrete random variables
text:
Work through a finite sample
Suppose a conversation excerpt contains utterance lengths

2,5,1,5,3.

The observed values are \{1,2,3,5\}, but the modeled support may still include 0, 4, 6, and larger integers. An observed sample does not determine the full support.
The event L\geq3 contains the third, fifth, and larger support values, but in this sample it selects the observed lengths 5, 5, and 3.


Code
utterance_length <- c(2, 5, 1, 5, 3)

sort(unique(utterance_length))
utterance_length[utterance_length >= 3]


The first line reports observed distinct values. It should not be interpreted as a complete statement of modeled support.

title: Discrete random variables
section: Discrete is not the same as unordered
text:
Discrete is not the same as unordered
Grammatical person is often treated as a set of categories without a numerical distance between them. Utterance length is ordered, and differences such as 5-3=2 have an interpretation in words. Both variables are discrete.
Thus discreteness concerns whether the support values are separate and listable. It does not determine whether they are ordered or whether arithmetic on their labels is meaningful.

title: Discrete random variables
section: Observed values do not determine the complete support
text:
Observed values do not determine the complete support
The distinct values in one sample need not exhaust the modeled support. If the longest utterance in a small sample contains five words, that fact does not imply that \operatorname{supp}(L)=\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}.
The support is a modeling statement about possible values. The sample reports which of those values happened to occur in the observed records.

title: Discrete random variables
text:
Check your understanding

Is the number of relative clauses in a sentence finite or countably infinite under a model with no fixed sentence length limit?
Why is a part of speech variable discrete even when its values are not numbers?
Give one discrete ordered variable and one discrete unordered variable from linguistics.
Explain why the largest observed value does not automatically determine the upper end of the support.

The support lists the separate values. The next page assigns probability to those values.

title: Expected values
text:
The earlier pages introduced probability mass functions and probability density functions. We can now summarize the center of either distribution. Suppose R records the number of self repairs in a sampled dialogue turn.
We want one number that summarizes the center of this probability distribution. Averaging the four support values would give (0+1+2+3)/4=1.5, but that calculation gives equal weight to values with unequal probabilities.
The expected value weights each value by its probability. It is also called the mean of the distribution when the weighted average exists.

title: Expected values
text:
Weight and add by hand
Multiply each support value by its mass.



r
p_R(r)
r p_R(r)




0
.50
0


1
.30
.30


2
.15
.30


3
.05
.15



Add the weighted contributions:

0+.30+.30+.15=.75.

In notation,

\mathbb{E}[R]
=\sum_r r\,p_R(r)
=.75.

The symbol \mathbb{E} denotes the expectation operation. It takes the full probability distribution of R and returns its probability weighted average.

title: Expected values
section: Interpret a value outside the support
text:
Interpret a value outside the support
The support contains only whole repair counts, so no dialogue turn has exactly .75 repairs. The expected value need not be a possible observed value.
One useful interpretation concerns repeated sampling. If many turns are sampled under the same probability model, the average number of repairs per turn tends to approach .75. The expectation describes the long run center of the modeled process, not the outcome of one turn.

title: Expected values
section: Compute the expectation in base R
text:
Compute the expectation in base R


Code
repair_count <- 0:3
repair_mass <- c(.50, .30, .15, .05)

sum(repair_count * repair_mass)


The result is .75. The multiplication is elementwise, so each support value is paired with its own probability before the products are summed.

title: Expected values
text:
The continuous form
For a continuous variable X with density f_X, separate point masses are replaced by density area. The expected value is

\mathbb{E}[X]
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,

when the integral exists. The value x weights each narrow region, and f_X(x) states how densely probability is allocated there.
The discrete sum and continuous integral implement the same idea: values receiving more modeled probability contribute more to the center.

title: Expected values
section: Weight each support value by its probability
text:
Weight each support value by its probability
The expectation is not the arithmetic average of the distinct support values. For the repair example, that calculation gives 1.5 rather than .75 because it treats the rare value 3 as if it were as common as 0.
Identify the probability attached to each value. The expectation averages outcomes under the distribution, not labels in the support set.

title: Expected values
text:
Check your understanding

Recompute \mathbb{E}[R] after moving .10 of mass from R=0 to R=2.
Why can .75 be the expected repair count when no turn has .75 repairs?
What quantity provides the weights in a discrete expectation?
Explain the shared logic of the discrete sum and the continuous integral.

Expected value averages the original values. The next page asks how to average a transformed property of those values.

title: The hypergeometric distribution
text:
The binomial model used independent draws with a shared target probability. Suppose instead that an annotation archive contains 30 distinct clauses, nine passive and 21 active, and we choose five distinct clauses without replacement.
The clauses are sampled without replacement. Once a passive clause is selected, only eight passive clauses remain in the archive. The target probability thus changes across draws.
Let
K=\text{the number of passive clauses among the five selected clauses}.
This count has a hypergeometric distribution.

title: The hypergeometric distribution
text:
Specify the finite population
We need three collection sizes.

The archive contains N=30 clauses.
The target set contains M=9 passive clauses.
The audit draws n=5 clauses.

The remaining N-M=21 clauses are active. The support of K contains counts that are compatible with these finite totals. Here

K\in\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}.

title: The hypergeometric distribution
section: Count samples rather than ordered sequences
text:
Count samples rather than ordered sequences
To obtain exactly k passive clauses, choose k of the 9 passives and 5-k of the 21 active clauses. The number of favorable samples is

{9\choose k}{21\choose5-k}.

The total number of five clause samples is

{30\choose5}.

Every five clause subset is equally likely under simple sampling without replacement. Thus

\mathbb{P}(K=k)
=\frac{{9\choose k}{21\choose5-k}}
       {{30\choose5}}.

title: The hypergeometric distribution
section: Calculate the probability of two passives
text:
Calculate the probability of two passives
Set k=2:

\mathbb{P}(K=2)
=\frac{{9\choose2}{21\choose3}}
       {{30\choose5}}.

The combinations are

{9\choose2}=36,
\qquad
{21\choose3}=1330,
\qquad
{30\choose5}=142506.

Thus

\mathbb{P}(K=2)
=\frac{36\times1330}{142506}
\approx.336.

R computes the same mass with


Code
dhyper(2, m = 9, n = 21, k = 5)


Here m is the number of target objects, n is the number of other objects, and k is the sample size. The first argument is the observed target count.

title: The hypergeometric distribution
section: Read the mean and finite population correction
text:
Read the mean and finite population correction
The target proportion in the archive is

\frac{M}{N}=\frac{9}{30}=.30.

The expected target count in five draws is

\mathbb{E}[K]
=n\frac{M}{N}
=5(.30)
=1.5.

The variance is

\operatorname{Var}(K)
=n\frac{M}{N}\left(1-\frac{M}{N}\right)
\frac{N-n}{N-1}.

The final factor is the finite population correction. Here it is 25/29, which reduces the variance because removing one clause constrains later draws.

title: The hypergeometric distribution
text:
Compare with independent sampling
If each draw instead came independently from a very large population with passive probability .30, the target count would be binomial. Both models would have mean 1.5, but the without replacement model has smaller variance.
The distinction is not about which curve looks better. It follows from whether the same finite clauses remain available after each draw.

title: The hypergeometric distribution
section: Sampling without replacement changes later probabilities
text:
Sampling without replacement changes later probabilities
Draws are not independent after sampled objects have been removed. The passive probability on the second draw depends on what happened on the first draw.
Specify the finite population and sampling rule. If every selected clause is unavailable to later draws, the hypergeometric calculation represents that dependence directly.
The same finite sampling calculation appears when margins of a contingency table are fixed. The Fisher’s exact test page later uses this connection for inference.

title: The hypergeometric distribution
text:
Check your understanding

In the PMF, what does {21\choose5-k} count?
Compute the expected passive count when 8 clauses are drawn from the same archive.
Why is the variance smaller than under independent sampling with probability .30?
When would the binomial model become a close approximation to this sampling process?

Sampling without replacement changes probability after each draw. The next page returns to repeated comparable draws and models the wait to the first target outcome.

title: Sampling with cumulative probability
text:
The cumulative distribution function records the probability accumulated through each threshold. Inverse transform sampling uses those thresholds to generate values. Suppose a prosodic annotator assigns one of three boundary strengths with probabilities
The PMF tells us the target frequencies across repeated draws. To simulate one label, we need a rule that converts a basic pseudorandom value into one of these outcomes.
Inverse transform sampling uses a uniform draw on (0,1) and the target CDF to make that conversion.

title: Sampling with cumulative probability
text:
Turn probabilities into intervals
Accumulate the category masses in their declared order.



boundary label
mass
cumulative endpoint
uniform interval




weak
.50
.50
(0,.50]


intermediate
.30
.80
(.50,.80]


strong
.20
1
(.80,1)



Draw

U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1).

If U=.74, it falls in (.50,.80], so the simulated label is intermediate. If U=.92, it falls in (.80,1), so the label is strong.
The interval widths match the target masses. A uniform draw thus lands in each interval with the required probability.

title: Sampling with cumulative probability
text:
State the discrete rule
Let the cumulative endpoints be

c_1=.50,
\qquad
c_2=.80,
\qquad
c_3=1.

Choose the first category k for which

U\leq c_k.

The rule maps one uniform value to one target outcome. It also makes the category order part of the implementation, just as it was for a categorical parameter vector.

title: Sampling with cumulative probability
section: Implement the rule in base R

title: Sampling with cumulative probability
section: Extend the rule to a continuous target
text:
Extend the rule to a continuous target
Let F be a continuous CDF and let

F^{-1}(u)=\inf\{x:F(x)\geq u\}

be its quantile function. If U is uniform on (0,1), then

X=F^{-1}(U)

has CDF F.
Consider a constructed target CDF on (0,1):

F(x)=x^2.

Solve u=x^2 for x:

F^{-1}(u)=\sqrt{u}.

If U=.36, the transformed draw is

X=\sqrt{.36}=.60.

The transformation stretches and compresses parts of the uniform interval so that the resulting values have the target cumulative probabilities.


Code
u <- runif(1000)
x <- sqrt(u)

mean(x <= .5)


The target CDF gives F(.5)=.25, so the simulated proportion at or below .5 should be near .25 when the number of draws is large.

title: Sampling with cumulative probability
text:
What the procedure requires
The target CDF must be valid, and its inverse or generalized inverse must be available. Some families have no convenient analytic inverse, so software may use numerical inversion or another sampling method.
The procedure guarantees the target distribution only when the uniform generator and mapping are implemented correctly. It does not guarantee that the target distribution is a good linguistic model.

title: Sampling with cumulative probability
text:
Check the implemented cutpoints
The implemented cumulative endpoints must match the target probability masses. If the first endpoint were coded as .40 instead of .50, the weak category would be simulated too rarely and the other intervals would change.
Compute cumulative endpoints from the probability vector and check simulated proportions against the target masses.

title: Sampling with cumulative probability
text:
Check your understanding

Which boundary label is selected by U=.80 under the stated endpoint rule?
Why must the final cumulative endpoint equal one?
If F(x)=x^2, what value is produced by U=.81?
What diagnostic would reveal incorrectly implemented cutpoints in a large discrete simulation?

The mapping produces a pseudorandom realization. The next page explains how to reproduce that realization without confusing reproducibility with model adequacy.

title: Linearity of expectation
text:
The preceding page showed that a transformation is ordinarily applied before its expectation is taken. A linear combination has an additional simplification. Suppose a corpus sample contains three clause positions, and I_i records whether position i contains a resumptive pronoun.
T=I_1+I_2+I_3.
We want the expected total count. Deriving every possible value of T would require tracking all combinations of the three indicators. Linearity of expectation lets us work term by term instead.

title: Linearity of expectation
text:
Begin with one indicator
An indicator I_i takes value 1 when the target event occurs and 0 otherwise. If the target probability at position i is \pi_i, then

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[I_i]
&=0\times\mathbb{P}(I_i=0)
+1\times\mathbb{P}(I_i=1)\\
&=\pi_i.
\end{aligned}

The expected value of an indicator is the probability of the event it marks.
Suppose the three target probabilities are

\pi_1=.20,
\qquad
\pi_2=.50,
\qquad
\pi_3=.80.

Then the expected total is

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[T]
&=\mathbb{E}[I_1+I_2+I_3]\\
&=\mathbb{E}[I_1]+\mathbb{E}[I_2]+\mathbb{E}[I_3]\\
&=.20+.50+.80\\
&=1.50.
\end{aligned}

The value 1.50 need not be an observed count. It is the probability weighted average count under repeated realizations of the three positions.

title: Linearity of expectation
text:
State the general rule
For random variables X_1,\ldots,X_n and constants a_1,\ldots,a_n,

\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n a_iX_i\right]
=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\mathbb{E}[X_i].

For two variables and an added constant, this gives

\mathbb{E}[aX+bY+c]
=a\mathbb{E}[X]+b\mathbb{E}[Y]+c.

The expectation operation passes through sums and constant multiples.

title: Linearity of expectation
text:
Independence is not required
The three clause positions may be dependent. A speaker who uses a resumptive pronoun in one position might be more likely to use another later in the same discourse. Linearity of expectation still gives

\mathbb{E}[T]=\pi_1+\pi_2+\pi_3.

Dependence affects how probability is arranged across the possible total counts. It does not change the expected sum when the three marginal event probabilities remain fixed.
A smaller hand check makes this point visible. Suppose exactly one of two variants is selected, so I_1+I_2=1 on every outcome. If

\mathbb{P}(I_1=1)=.70

and

\mathbb{P}(I_2=1)=.30,

then

\mathbb{E}[I_1+I_2]=.70+.30=1.

The indicators are constrained by one another, but linearity still holds.

title: Linearity of expectation
section: Compute the expected total in base R
text:
Compute the expected total in base R


Code
resumptive_probability <- c(.20, .50, .80)

expected_total <- sum(resumptive_probability)
expected_total


The result is 1.5. The calculation can use unequal probabilities for different linguistic contexts.

title: Linearity of expectation
text:
Linearity does not require independence
Summands need not be independent for expectation to move through a sum.
The linear rule should not, however, be extended to nonlinear operations. In general,

\mathbb{E}[XY]
\neq\mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y].

That product equality needs additional conditions. Linearity concerns sums and constant multiples only.

title: Linearity of expectation
text:
Check your understanding

If four token positions have target probabilities .10, .25, .40, and .60, what is the expected total count?
Why does the expected count calculation not require independent positions?
Show from the two possible indicator values that \mathbb{E}[I]=\mathbb{P}(I=1).
Which operation in \mathbb{E}[XY] prevents direct use of linearity?

Linearity simplifies expectations that exist. The next page asks what must be checked before treating an expectation as a finite summary.

title: The negative binomial distribution
text:
The geometric distribution counted failures before the first target. Suppose we continue sampling corpus tokens until we encounter the third loanword. Let F record the number of nonloanwords observed before that third target.
The negative binomial distribution represents this waiting count when each draw is independent and has the same target probability \pi.
Let r be the target number of loanwords. We write
F\sim\operatorname{NegBin}(r,\pi).
Under the failures convention,
\operatorname{supp}(F)=\{0,1,2,3,\ldots\}.
The value zero is possible because the first r draws might all be targets.

title: The negative binomial distribution
section: See why the final draw is fixed
text:
See why the final draw is fixed
Take r=3 and F=2. Every qualifying sequence contains three target outcomes, written S, and two failures, written F. The final draw must be the third target. The earlier four positions contain two targets and two failures.
The possible sequences are

FFSSS,
\quad
FSFSS,
\quad
FSSFS,
\quad
SFFSS,
\quad
SFSFS,
\quad
SSFFS.

There are six sequences. This count equals

{2+3-1\choose2}={4\choose2}=6.

The final target is reserved, and the failures can occupy any two of the first four positions.

title: The negative binomial distribution
text:
Derive the PMF
For general r and f, every qualifying sequence has r targets and f failures. Its probability is

\pi^r(1-\pi)^f.

The number of sequences is

{f+r-1\choose f}.

Multiplying arrangement count by sequence probability gives

p_F(f)
={f+r-1\choose f}(1-\pi)^f\pi^r,
\qquad f\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.

title: The negative binomial distribution
text:
Calculate one waiting probability
Let r=3, \pi=.20, and f=4. Then

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(F=4)
&={6\choose4}(.80)^4(.20)^3\\
&=15(.4096)(.008)\\
&=.049152.
\end{aligned}

This is the probability of observing exactly four nonloanwords before the third loanword.
Base R uses the same failures convention:


Code
dnbinom(4, size = 3, prob = .20)


The argument size specifies the target number of successes, and the first argument specifies failures before that target.

title: The negative binomial distribution
text:
Read the mean and variance
For this parameterization,

\mathbb{E}[F]
=r\frac{1-\pi}{\pi}

and

\operatorname{Var}(F)
=r\frac{1-\pi}{\pi^2}.

With r=3 and \pi=.20,

\mathbb{E}[F]
=3\frac{.80}{.20}
=12

and

\operatorname{Var}(F)
=3\frac{.80}{.20^2}
=60.

The family allows a long right tail because many failures may occur before the required target count is reached.

title: The negative binomial distribution
text:
Recover the first target case
Set r=1. The arrangement count becomes one:

{f\choose f}=1.

The PMF reduces to

p_F(f)=(1-\pi)^f\pi,

which is the geometric waiting process under the failures before first target convention.

title: The negative binomial distribution
text:
Check the parameterization
Negative binomial distributions can count failures, total draws, or target events. These parameterizations cannot be mixed. If F counts failures before target r, then the total number of draws is

T=F+r.

Some texts or software model T instead. Others use a mean and dispersion parameter for the same family. A numerical parameter is interpretable only after the counted quantity and convention have been declared.

title: The negative binomial distribution
text:
Check your understanding

List every sequence with one failure before the third target.
With r=2 and \pi=.25, calculate \mathbb{P}(F=3).
What total draw count corresponds to F=4 and r=3?
Explain why setting r=1 recovers the geometric waiting process.

The negative binomial family models a count generated by waiting for a fixed target number. The next page models event counts in a declared unit of exposure.

title: The Poisson distribution
text:
Suppose we divide a conversation into one-minute intervals and count filled pauses in each interval. One observation may contain 0 filled pauses, another 2, and another 5.
The response is a nonnegative count:
X\in\{0,1,2,3,\ldots\}.
A common baseline model for such counts is the Poisson distribution:
X\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda),
where \lambda>0 is the expected count in one specified unit of exposure.
The probability mass function of a Poisson random variable specifies the distribution of one count. A homogeneous Poisson process provides one possible generative account for that distribution. Under that process, events occur at a constant rate and increments in nonoverlapping intervals are independent. The Poisson count distribution itself can also be used as an observation model without claiming that the full event sequence follows this process.

title: The Poisson distribution
section: Exposure is part of the definition
text:
Exposure is part of the definition
The statement \lambda=2 is incomplete until the opportunity for events to occur is stated. It might mean two filled pauses per minute, per hundred words, or per speaker turn.
Here one observation is a one-minute interval, so

\mathbb{E}[X]=\lambda=2

means two filled pauses per minute on average under the model.
The expected count scales with exposure when the modeled event rate stays fixed. A thirty-second interval has half the exposure of a one-minute interval, so its expected count is

2\left(\frac{30}{60}\right)=1.

A five-minute interval has five times the exposure, so its expected count is

2(5)=10.

This scaling does not claim that every five-minute stretch contains exactly ten filled pauses. It changes the Poisson mean for the larger opportunity window.

title: The Poisson distribution
text:
Calculate point probabilities
The Poisson PMF is

p_X(x)
=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!},
\qquad x\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.

For \lambda=2, the probability of no filled pauses is

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(X=0)
&=\frac{e^{-2}2^0}{0!}\\
&=e^{-2}\\
&\approx.135.
\end{aligned}

The probability of exactly two is

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(X=2)
&=\frac{e^{-2}2^2}{2!}\\
&=2e^{-2}\\
&\approx.271.
\end{aligned}

These are probabilities of individual counts. We can also ask for the probability of a range of counts. The probability of at most two filled pauses is

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(X\leq 2)
&=\mathbb{P}(X=0)+\mathbb{P}(X=1)+\mathbb{P}(X=2)\\
&\approx .135+.271+.271\\
&\approx .677.
\end{aligned}

The distinction between exactly two and at most two is the distinction between a probability mass function and a cumulative distribution function. The first selects one point in the support. The second adds the mass at every point up to and including the requested count.

title: The Poisson distribution
section: Ask four kinds of question in R
text:
Ask four kinds of question in R
R uses the same four prefixes for every named distribution family. For the Poisson family, they are dpois, ppois, qpois, and rpois.








function
statistical question
result when \lambda=2




dpois(2, 2)
What is \mathbb{P}(X=2)?
approximately .271


ppois(2, 2)
What is \mathbb{P}(X\leq2)?
approximately .677


qpois(.90, 2)
What is the smallest x with \mathbb{P}(X\leq x)\geq.90?
4


rpois(6, 2)
What might six new observations look like?
six simulated counts



The first three calls are deterministic. They return the same answer whenever their arguments are unchanged. The last call is a simulation. Its result may change from one call to the next because it draws new values from the specified distribution.


Code
dpois(2, lambda = 2)
ppois(2, lambda = 2)
qpois(.90, lambda = 2)
rpois(6, lambda = 2)


The quantile call deserves a slower reading. Counts are discrete, so there may be no count whose cumulative probability is exactly .90. R returns the smallest count at which the cumulative probability reaches or passes .90. For \lambda=2, the cumulative probability through 3 is about .857, while the cumulative probability through 4 is about .947. Thus the requested quantile is 4.

title: The Poisson distribution
text:
Draw the whole distribution
A probability mass function is easier to interpret when we look at all of its values together. The following code evaluates the PMF from 0 through 10.


Code
counts <- 0:10
mass <- dpois(counts, lambda = 2)

plot(
  counts, mass,
  type = "h", lwd = 4,
  xlab = "filled pauses in one minute",
  ylab = "probability"
)
points(counts, mass, pch = 16)


The distribution places its greatest mass near 2, which is also its expected value. But an expected value is not a promise about the next observation. Zero, one, three, and larger counts remain possible. The parameter describes a distribution over repeated observations, not the value that each observation must take.

title: The Poisson distribution
section: One parameter controls center and spread
text:
One parameter controls center and spread
For a Poisson variable,

\mathbb{E}[X]=\lambda

and

\operatorname{Var}(X)=\lambda.

Thus a Poisson distribution with mean 2 must also have variance 2. The model cannot hold the mean fixed while increasing the variance.
This restriction may be too strong for linguistic counts. If speakers, documents, genres, or lexical items have different rates, the observed variance may be much larger than the mean. The negative-binomial page introduces one distribution that relaxes this equality.

title: The Poisson distribution
text:
Diagnose the first failure mode
Suppose 100 one-minute intervals have a sample mean of 2.1 filled pauses and a sample variance of 9.4. A Poisson model fitted to the center would use a value of \lambda near 2.1. It would then require a variance near 2.1 as well. The gap between 2.1 and 9.4 is evidence that the one-parameter family misses some structure in the observations.
This pattern is called overdispersion relative to the Poisson model. It does not by itself tell us why the extra variation occurs. Speakers may have different pause rates. Speech tasks may differ. Pauses may cluster after moments of planning difficulty. Each possibility suggests a different analysis. The mean to variance comparison is thus a diagnostic, not an explanation.






NoteCheck the exposure




Two documents contain 3 target constructions each, but one has 500 words and the other 5,000. Explain why the raw counts do not represent the same rate.
With X\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(2), explain the difference between dpois(2, 2) and ppois(2, 2) without referring to the R function names.
A corpus count has a mean of 4.3 and a variance of 18.7. State the Poisson restriction that this summary appears to violate. Then identify one linguistic source of the extra variation.

title: Probability mass functions
text:
The preceding page used support to list the possible values of a discrete random variable. Suppose S records the number of syllables in a sampled word token. Knowing that S is discrete does not tell us how likely its support values are.
Consider this constructed probability table.
The function assigning a probability to each support value is a probability mass function, abbreviated PMF. We write
p_S(s)=\mathbb{P}(S=s).
The capital S denotes the random variable. The lowercase s stands for one possible value. Thus
p_S(2)=\mathbb{P}(S=2)=.33.
This statement assigns .33 of the total probability to the event containing two syllable word outcomes. In this constructed model, \operatorname{supp}(S)=\{1,2,3,4\}.

title: Probability mass functions
text:
Check the two PMF requirements
First, a PMF must assign nonnegative mass:

p_S(s)\geq0
\qquad\text{for every support value }s.

Second, the masses across the complete support must sum to one:

\sum_s p_S(s)=1.

For the constructed table,

.42+.33+.17+.08=1.

The rows represent mutually exclusive and exhaustive value events. One word token falls in one syllable count row, and the table includes every value in the modeled support.

title: Probability mass functions
text:
Add mass across selected values
What is the probability of a token with at least three syllables? The relevant event contains the rows for 3 and 4:

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(S\geq3)
&=p_S(3)+p_S(4)\\
&=.17+.08\\
&=.25.
\end{aligned}

The calculation adds masses because the two value events do not overlap. A token cannot have exactly three syllables and at least four syllables under this representation.

title: Probability mass functions
section: Represent the PMF in base R
text:
Represent the PMF in base R


Code
syllable_value <- c("1", "2", "3", "4")
syllable_mass <- c(.42, .33, .17, .08)

all(syllable_mass >= 0)
sum(syllable_mass)
sum(syllable_mass[syllable_value %in% c("3", "4")])


The three results are TRUE, 1, and .25. These checks establish that the entered table satisfies the PMF requirements and recover the selected event probability.

title: Probability mass functions
text:
Interpret zero mass carefully
If p_S(7)=0, then the event S=7 has zero probability under the stated model. This may reflect a deliberately restricted support or a model that treats the value as impossible. It need not mean that no seven syllable word can exist in every linguistic population.
The PMF belongs to a represented sampling process. A lexicon weighted by word types and a corpus weighted by word tokens can assign different masses to the same syllable counts.

title: Probability mass functions
section: The masses must cover the complete support
text:
The masses must cover the complete support
A probability mass function cannot omit possible values without accounting for their probability. Suppose the first three rows above were retained but the final row were dropped. The remaining masses would sum to .92, so the table would not define a PMF on the declared support.
Renormalizing the three values would define a different model conditional on at most three syllables. That change may be useful, but it must be stated as a new reference event rather than treated as harmless deletion.

title: Probability mass functions
text:
Check your understanding

Verify that the values .50, .30, and .20 define a PMF over a three value support.
Under the syllable PMF, compute \mathbb{P}(S\leq2).
Explain why the support must be declared before interpreting a mass of zero for a count above 4.
What model change occurs if the final row is dropped and the remaining masses are renormalized?

A PMF assigns mass to separate support values. The next page considers a model whose values instead fill an interval.

title: Standard deviation
text:
The preceding page defined variance as an expected squared deviation from the mean. Suppose the modeled voice onset time variable V has variance
\operatorname{Var}(V)=625\text{ ms}^2.
The value 625 is measured in squared milliseconds. A phonetician cannot compare it directly with a 10 ms difference between two category means because the units differ.
The standard deviation is the nonnegative square root of the variance:
\operatorname{SD}(X)
=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.
For the voice onset time variable,
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{SD}(V)
&=\sqrt{625\text{ ms}^2}\\
&=25\text{ ms}.
\end{aligned}
Taking the square root returns the spread summary to the measurement units of V.

title: Standard deviation
text:
Compare two category spreads
Suppose a second stop category has variance

900\text{ ms}^2.

Its standard deviation is

\sqrt{900\text{ ms}^2}=30\text{ ms}.

The second variable has greater spread whether we compare variance or standard deviation. The square root preserves the ordering of nonnegative values.
The difference between 25 ms and 30 ms is easier to interpret than the difference between 625 and 900 squared milliseconds because it is on the original voice onset time scale.

title: Standard deviation
section: Compute and report in base R
text:
Compute and report in base R


Code
vot_variance <- c(category_a = 625, category_b = 900)
vot_sd <- sqrt(vot_variance)

vot_sd


The results are 25 and 30. The code assumes that the input variances have already been computed on the millisecond scale.

title: Standard deviation
text:
What standard deviation summarizes
Standard deviation is the square root of the expected squared distance from the mean. It is not the average absolute distance from the mean.
This distinction matters because squaring weights large deviations more strongly. Two distributions may have the same average absolute distance and different standard deviations if one places more probability far from its center.
Standard deviation is also not a complete description of distribution shape. Equal means and standard deviations do not guarantee equal tails, symmetry, or modality.

title: Standard deviation
section: Standard deviation does not determine coverage
text:
Standard deviation does not determine coverage
A fixed proportion of observations need not fall within one standard deviation of the mean. A mean and standard deviation alone do not determine that proportion.
Coverage statements require additional information about the distribution’s shape. Until a particular shape has been justified, standard deviation should be interpreted as a root mean squared distance, not as a guaranteed interval containing a fixed percentage of outcomes.

title: Standard deviation
text:
Check your understanding

A duration variable has variance 144\text{ ms}^2. What is its standard deviation?
If a log duration variable has variance .16 in squared log units, what is its standard deviation and in which units should it be reported?
Why do variance and standard deviation order two distributions by spread in the same way?
What additional information would be needed before interpreting one standard deviation as a particular coverage interval?

Standard deviation rescales the second central moment. The next page shows how changing the exponent summarizes other features of deviations from the mean.

title: The uniform distribution
text:
The earlier density page represented continuous probability by area. Suppose a psycholinguistic experiment places an auditory cue at a randomized time between 200 and 800 ms after word onset, with equal width intervals inside this window equally probable.
The continuous uniform distribution represents a constant density across a bounded interval. Write
X\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(a,b),
\qquad a<b.
For the cue procedure, a=200 and b=800.

title: The uniform distribution
text:
Derive the density height
The support width is

b-a.

If the constant density height is h, the rectangular area must equal one:

h(b-a)=1.

Solving gives

h=\frac{1}{b-a}.

Thus the PDF is

f_X(x)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{b-a} & \text{if }a\leq x\leq b,\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}

For the 200 to 800 ms window, the width is 600 ms and the density height is

\frac{1}{600}

per millisecond.

title: The uniform distribution
text:
Calculate an interval probability
What is the probability that the cue occurs between 350 and 500 ms? The selected interval has width

500-350=150\text{ ms}.

Its probability is the rectangular area

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(350\leq X\leq500)
&=150\left(\frac{1}{600}\right)\\
&=.25.
\end{aligned}

Every 150 ms interval fully contained in the support has the same probability. This equal area property is the meaning of uniformity.
An individual point still has probability zero:

\mathbb{P}(X=350)=0.

The family is uniform over interval widths, not positive point masses.

title: The uniform distribution
text:
Read the mean and variance
The mean lies at the midpoint:

\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{a+b}{2}.

For the cue window,

\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{200+800}{2}=500\text{ ms}.

The variance is

\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{(b-a)^2}{12}.

Here

\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{600^2}{12}=30{,}000\text{ ms}^2.

The mean describes the center of repeated random cue placements. It does not make 500 ms more likely than another exact value in the window.

title: The uniform distribution
section: Check the calculations in base R
text:
Check the calculations in base R


Code
dunif(400, min = 200, max = 800)
punif(500, min = 200, max = 800) -
  punif(350, min = 200, max = 800)
(200 + 800) / 2
(800 - 200)^2 / 12


The four results are the density height, interval probability, mean, and variance.

title: The uniform distribution
section: A density height may exceed one
text:
A density height may exceed one
If the support is (0,.5), its width is .5 and its density height is 2. The total area remains

.5(2)=1.

The height exceeds one because it is measured per unit of X. It is not itself a probability.

title: The uniform distribution
section: Uniform density does not give positive point probabilities
text:
Uniform density does not give positive point probabilities
Under a continuous uniform model, every point has probability zero. Equal width intervals, not individual points, have equal positive probability.
The distinction matters when a randomization program uses a finite set of integer millisecond times. That implementation is discrete, even if a continuous uniform family is a useful approximation.

title: The uniform distribution
text:
Check your understanding

For a cue window from 100 to 400 ms, compute the density height.
In that window, what is the probability of an onset between 175 and 250 ms?
Why is the density at 200 ms not the probability of exactly 200 ms?
How would a program restricted to the integer values 100 through 400 change the support?

The uniform family fixes density height across a bounded interval. The next page retains a bounded support while allowing density to change across it.

title: When an expectation does not exist
text:
The expected value page defined the mean of a distribution only when the required sum or integral exists. Suppose L records utterance length in words. Every observed utterance has a finite length, and every finite sample has an ordinary arithmetic mean. It does not follow that every probability model over possible utterance lengths has a finite expected value.
An expectation exists as a finite summary only when its probability weighted contributions converge to a finite number.
For a discrete nonnegative variable,
\mathbb{E}[L]=\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}l\,p_L(l).
The masses may sum to one while the value weighted masses fail to have a finite sum.
crumbs: When an expectation does not exist

title: When an expectation does not exist
text:
Construct a heavy tailed PMF
Consider the following toy model for positive utterance lengths:

p_L(l)=\frac{6}{\pi^2l^2},
\qquad l=1,2,3,\ldots

The masses are nonnegative. They also sum to one because

\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{l^2}=\frac{\pi^2}{6}.

Thus this assignment is a valid PMF over positive integer lengths.
Now compute the expectation:

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[L]
&=\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}l\frac{6}{\pi^2l^2}\\
&=\frac{6}{\pi^2}\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{l}.
\end{aligned}

The final series does not converge. The model assigns progressively less probability to long utterances, but length grows quickly enough that the weighted contributions have no finite sum.
crumbs: When an expectation does not exist

title: When an expectation does not exist
text:
Inspect partial contributions
If we add contributions only through a finite cutoff K, we obtain

m_K=\frac{6}{\pi^2}\sum_{l=1}^{K}\frac{1}{l}.

These partial contributions keep increasing:



cutoff K
m_K




10
about 1.78


100
about 3.15


1,000
about 4.55



No finite cutoff reveals a value at which the contributions settle. The increase becomes slow, but it does not stop.


Code
partial_mean <- function(cutoff) {
  (6 / pi^2) * sum(1 / seq_len(cutoff))
}

sapply(c(10, 100, 1000), partial_mean)


The code evaluates finite partial sums. It illustrates divergence; it does not turn the infinite expectation into a finite mean.
crumbs: When an expectation does not exist

title: When an expectation does not exist
text:
A useful existence condition
For a variable that may take positive and negative values, a standard finite mean condition is

\mathbb{E}[|X|]<\infty.

This condition requires the expected absolute magnitude to be finite. It prevents positive and negative infinite contributions from being treated as if they cancel to a meaningful center.
Algebraic manipulations of expectation assume that the relevant expectations exist. Before splitting an expectation into terms or reporting a mean from a model, the weighted sum or integral should be checked.
crumbs: When an expectation does not exist

title: When an expectation does not exist
section: What a finite sample can and cannot show
text:
What a finite sample can and cannot show
A sample from the utterance length model contains only finite values, so its arithmetic mean is finite. Increasing the sample size may bring occasional very large observations that move the sample mean substantially. The absence of such an observation in one dataset does not establish a finite model expectation.
Other summaries may remain defined. A threshold with half of the probability below it can exist even when the probability weighted mean does not.
crumbs: When an expectation does not exist

title: When an expectation does not exist
section: A finite sample mean does not imply a finite expectation
text:
A finite sample mean does not imply a finite expectation
The sample mean of finitely many observations is finite even when the expectation under the model is not. The sample calculation uses finitely many observed values. The model expectation ranges over the complete support, including values beyond the sample maximum.
Inspect the weighted sum or integral under the model rather than only the observed arithmetic mean.
crumbs: When an expectation does not exist

title: When an expectation does not exist
text:
Check your understanding

Why do the masses p_L(l) define a valid PMF even though \mathbb{E}[L] is not finite?
Which series appears after multiplying l by p_L(l)?
What does the condition \mathbb{E}[|X|]<\infty guarantee?
Why can every finite sample have a finite mean while the model expectation fails to exist?

The next spread summary also depends on a finite expectation of a transformed value. The next page introduces variance and keeps its existence requirement visible.

The file proportion, the average speaker proportion, and a population proportion are different quantities.

text:
Challenge
One dataset is only one possible result of a sampling process.

text:
Possibility
Write the population quantity first, define the estimation rule second, and study that rule under a stated model third.

This Module

Construct posterior and predictive distributions.
Approximate posterior quantities by simulation.
Diagnose the resulting Markov chains and fitted model.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Populations and samples
Naming the target units

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
Thirty Rochester speakers each produce twenty vowel tokens.
The table has 600 rows and 30 sampled speakers.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Approach
Buchstaller and Khattab ask how a sample of speakers can support a claim about a speech community.
Buchstaller and Khattab 2013

[Sources]
https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139013734.006

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A target population contains the units about which we want to make a claim.
A sample contains the units observed through a particular selection process.

[Sources]
https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-1-definitions-of-statistics-probability-and-key-terms

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Goal
A parameter is a fixed numerical feature of the modeled population.
The realized sample mean is an estimate.

[Sources]
https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-1-definitions-of-statistics-probability-and-key-terms

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Upshot
Six hundred tokens can sharpen summaries for 30 observed speakers. They do not create 600 independently sampled speakers.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Independent sampling
Connecting observations to a parameter

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
Four clauses are coded for whether each contains an overt subject.
\[
(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=(1,0,1,1)
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
Observations are independent and identically distributed (IID) when they share one distribution and their joint probability factors.

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
\[
X_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi),\qquad
p(x_1,\ldots,x_n\mid\pi)=\prod_i p(x_i\mid\pi).
\]
Recall the Bernoulli distribution.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Output
For the observed sequence,
\[
p(1,0,1,1\mid\pi)=\pi^3(1-\pi).
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Distinct rows need not be independent. Clauses can share speakers, documents, genre, and discourse context.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
A corpus proportion
Making the sampling statement concrete

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
The Universal Dependencies English Web Treebank teaching extract contains 12,280 personal pronoun tokens.
UD English EWT

[Sources]
https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/en_ewt/

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Output
Accusative tokens: \(3{,}327\)
Nonaccusative tokens: \(8{,}953\)
\[
\widehat\pi=\frac{3327}{12280}\approx.271
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
The estimate describes the coded extract. It does not explain case licensing or justify independence across repeated documents and forms.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Maximum likelihood
Comparing parameter values for fixed data

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Question
Which accusative probability makes the observed token sequence most probable under the working model?

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The likelihood function holds the observed data fixed and varies the parameter.
\[
L(\pi;\mathbf x)=\pi^{3327}(1-\pi)^{8953}
\]

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
\(p(x\mid\pi)\) is a distribution over possible observations for fixed \(\pi\).
\(L(\pi;\mathbf x)\) compares parameter values for fixed observations.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
The log likelihood turns a product into a sum.
\[
\ell(\pi)=k\log\pi+(n-k)\log(1-\pi)
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The maximum-likelihood estimate maximizes the likelihood.
\[
\widehat\pi_{\mathrm{MLE}}=\frac{k}{n}=.271
\]

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Upshot
Maximum likelihood selects a parameter value under the declared model. It does not establish that the model is adequate.

title: Learning from a sample
section: Maximum likelihood for a Poisson mean
text:
Maximum likelihood for a Poisson mean
A count response

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
The English Web Treebank teaching extract contains 2,594 wh expressions and their linear distances to annotated heads.
Silveira et al. 2014

[Sources]
https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/en_ewt/index.html
https://aclanthology.org/L14-1067/

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
For \(X_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\),
\[
\ell(\lambda)=\left(\sum_i x_i\right)\log\lambda-n\lambda-\sum_i\log(x_i!).
\]
Recall the Poisson distribution.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Output
Setting the derivative to zero gives
\[
\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{MLE}}=\bar x\approx3.007.
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
The distance data exclude zero, and the Poisson mean variance equality may fail.
Estimation and adequacy are separate questions.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Sampling distributions
An estimation rule across possible samples

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
A lexical decision task has population accuracy \(\pi=.75\).
Each possible sample produces a different sample proportion.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The sampling distribution is the probability distribution of an estimator across possible samples.

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=173

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
The parameter is fixed, the estimator is a rule, and the estimate is that rule’s value for one realized sample.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Result #1
Larger independent samples concentrate the sampling distribution around the same parameter.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Upshot
A sampling distribution contains possible estimates, not possible population parameters.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Standard errors
The spread of a sampling distribution

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Question
How much would an estimate vary across repeated samples under the model?

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The standard error is the standard deviation of an estimator’s sampling distribution.

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=173

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
For an IID sample mean,
\[
\operatorname{SE}(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Result #1
Doubling \(n\) does not halve the standard error. Multiplying \(n\) by four does.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Replacing the true independent unit with the row count makes the standard error too small.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Estimator bias
Average error across possible samples

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The bias of an estimator is
\[
\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat\theta)=E[\widehat\theta]-\theta.
\]

[Sources]
https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/07%3A_Point_Estimation/7.01%3A_Estimators

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
An unbiased estimator may miss the parameter in one realized sample.
Realized error is not estimator bias.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Unbiasedness alone does not rank estimators. Their sampling variation may differ.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Mean squared error
Combining bias and sampling variance

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
Mean squared error averages squared estimation error.
\[
\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat\theta)=E[(\widehat\theta-\theta)^2]
\]

[Sources]
https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/07%3A_Point_Estimation/7.01%3A_Estimators

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
\[
\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat\theta)
=\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\theta)
+\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat\theta)^2.
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Surprising Fact
A slightly biased estimator can have lower MSE if its sampling variance is sufficiently smaller.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Upshot
Bias and variance answer different questions. MSE evaluates their combined squared error.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Confidence intervals
Coverage across repeated samples

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Goal
Estimate a population prominence contrast \(\tau\) from one realized study.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A confidence interval is produced by a procedure with a declared repeated sampling coverage probability.

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=173

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
An approximate normal interval is
\[
\widehat\tau\pm1.96\operatorname{SE}(\widehat\tau).
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The coverage probability is the probability that the interval procedure contains the fixed parameter across repeated samples.

[Sources]
https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat100/Lesson09

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
Confidence is a property of the interval procedure. It is not a posterior probability attached to the fixed parameter.

title: Learning from a sample
section: Exact intervals for a binomial probability
text:
Exact intervals for a binomial probability
When the normal interval is unreliable

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
A Wald interval can extend outside zero and one and can have poor coverage for small samples or probabilities near a boundary.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The Wald interval uses a normal approximation around the sample proportion.

[Sources]
https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat504/Lesson02

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Approach
The Clopper-Pearson confidence interval inverts exact binomial tail tests.

[Sources]
https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/binom.test.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
“Exact” refers to the finite sample binomial calculation. It does not establish independence, a shared probability, or representative sampling.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Bootstrap confidence intervals
Approximating a sampling distribution by resampling

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
Twelve speakers supply median fundamental frequency measurements.
The target is the population median.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The nonparametric bootstrap resamples observations with replacement from the empirical distribution.

[Sources]
https://openintro-ims.netlify.app/foundations-bootstrapping.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method

Sample twelve speakers with replacement.
Calculate the bootstrap median.
Repeat the resampling procedure.
Use the distribution of bootstrap medians.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A percentile bootstrap confidence interval uses quantiles of the bootstrap estimates.

[Sources]
https://openintro-ims.netlify.app/foundations-bootstrapping.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
If tokens repeat within speakers, resample speakers and retain each selected speaker’s tokens together.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Upshot
The resampling unit must match the independent unit in the population claim.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Null hypotheses and test statistics
Comparing a discrepancy with a reference distribution

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A null hypothesis states a parameter claim. An alternative hypothesis states the competing parameter values.

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=173

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
A test statistic standardizes the observed discrepancy.
\[
T=\frac{\widehat\theta-\theta_0}{\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat\theta)}
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The null distribution is the reference distribution of the test statistic under the null model.

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=173

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
A p value measures tail compatibility with the declared null model. It is not an effect size or the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Inference for one mean
Unknown response variance

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
Each independent speaker supplies one acoustic contrast.
The target is the population mean contrast \(\mu\).

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The one-sample t-test uses the estimated standard error of the sample mean.

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=308

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
\[
t=\frac{\bar X-\mu_0}{S/\sqrt n},
\qquad df=n-1.
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Output
A t confidence interval replaces the normal critical value with the corresponding t quantile.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Many tokens from one speaker do not provide many independent speaker contrasts.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Paired observations
Constructing a within pair response

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
Every speaker produces two vowel categories.
The measurements share vocal tract anatomy and recording conditions.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A paired design forms one within pair difference for each independent pair.

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=173

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
\[
D_s=Y_{sA}-Y_{sB}.
\]
Shared additive speaker shifts cancel inside \(D_s\).

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
Covariance determines the precision gained by pairing.
Positive within pair covariance reduces the variance of the difference.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Sorting the two response vectors independently destroys the pairing and can create invalid differences.

title: Learning from a sample
section: Inference for a paired mean difference
text:
Inference for a paired mean difference
Applying the one sample procedure to differences

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Goal
Estimate the population mean of the speaker differences, \(\mu_D\).

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
The paired t-test is a one-sample t-test applied to \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\).
\[
t=\frac{\bar D-\mu_{D,0}}{S_D/\sqrt n}
\]

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=308

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
Speaker F1 differences use the vowel measurements of Hillenbrand et al.
Hillenbrand et al. 1995

[Sources]
https://doi.org/10.1121/1.411872

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Upshot
The interval describes the mean within speaker vowel contrast, not the distribution of individual vowel measurements.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Comparing two independent means
Different units in each group

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Question
How does uncertainty change when the two condition means come from different speakers?

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
Welch’s two-sample t-test allows the two groups to have different variances.

[Sources]
https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/t.test.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
\[
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\bar X_1-\bar X_2)
=\sqrt{\frac{S_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{S_2^2}{n_2}}.
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Do not use an equal variance assumption merely because a software default or familiar formula includes it.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Upshot
Paired and independent designs use different sources of variation. The test must match the design.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Fisher’s exact test
A conditional comparison for a two by two table

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
A morphological sample classifies nouns by stem type and plural allomorph.
The question is whether the two classifications are independent.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
Fisher’s exact test constructs a conditional null distribution over tables with the observed margins fixed.

[Sources]
https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/fisher.test.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
The free cell follows a hypergeometric distribution under the conditional independence model.
The two sided p value sums tables at least as improbable as the observed table.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Output
The two sided p value is approximately \(.0391\).
The observed table probability is only one term in that sum.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The sample odds ratio describes the direction and magnitude of association in the observed table.

[Sources]
https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/fisher.test.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Association between stem type and allomorph does not identify a causal or linguistic mechanism.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
The chi-squared test of independence
An approximate reference distribution

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
A corpus classifies 300 referring expressions by grammatical role and form.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The chi-squared test of independence compares observed cell counts with counts expected under independence.

[Sources]
https://openstax.org/books/introductory-business-statistics-2e/pages/11-4-test-of-independence

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
For cell \(r,c\),
\[
E_{rc}=\frac{(\text{row total})(\text{column total})}{\text{grand total}}.
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Output
\[
X^2=\sum_{r,c}\frac{(O_{rc}-E_{rc})^2}{E_{rc}},
\qquad df=(r-1)(c-1).
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Interpretation
The omnibus statistic records aggregate discrepancy. Signed cell differences locate its direction.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Small expected counts weaken the approximation. Repeated speakers or documents also violate the independent row assumption.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Posterior distributions
Updating uncertainty about a parameter

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
A listener chooses a collective or distributive interpretation for an ambiguous reciprocal sentence.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A prior distribution assigns probability to parameter values before the present data are observed.

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introBDA.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
Multiply prior support by likelihood support and normalize.
\[
p(\theta\mid y)=\frac{p(y\mid\theta)p(\theta)}{p(y)}
\]
Recall Bayes’ rule.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The posterior distribution represents parameter uncertainty after conditioning on the observed data.

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introBDA.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
The posterior is a probability distribution over the parameter. The likelihood alone is not.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Summarizing posterior draws
Claims from a posterior distribution

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A posterior summary is a numerical description calculated from the posterior distribution or its draws.

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introBDA.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Output
Posterior means and medians locate the center.
Credible intervals retain a declared posterior probability mass.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
For a directional claim, estimate
\[
P(\theta>0\mid y)\approx\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mathbf 1(\theta^{(s)}>0).
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
Transform and contrast parameters inside each draw before summarizing. This preserves joint posterior uncertainty.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Conjugate priors
An analytic beta Bernoulli update

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
A phonological study observes 14 word final coronal stop deletions and 6 realized stops.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A conjugate prior yields a posterior in the same distribution family after multiplication by the likelihood.

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introBDA.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
\[
\Pi\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),\qquad
Y\mid\Pi=\pi\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,\pi).
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Output
\[
\Pi\mid y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+s,\beta+f).
\]

Prior predictive distributions
Checking implications before observing the present data

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Question
What response counts does the complete prior model expect for ten ambiguous sentences?

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The prior predictive distribution averages the observation model over the prior.
\[
p(\widetilde y)=\int p(\widetilde y\mid\theta)p(\theta)\,d\theta
\]

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introBDA.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
Draw one parameter value for a complete simulated dataset, then generate the responses conditional on that value.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Interpretation
Inspect predictions on the response scale. Ask whether the implied counts are plausible before using the present responses.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Drawing a new response probability for every trial represents a different sampling structure from drawing one for the complete ten trial dataset.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Posterior predictive distributions
Predicting after the update

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The posterior predictive distribution averages the observation model over posterior uncertainty.
\[
p(\widetilde y\mid y)=\int p(\widetilde y\mid\theta)p(\theta\mid y)\,d\theta
\]

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introBDA.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
Draw \(\theta^{(s)}\) from the posterior, then draw \(\widetilde y^{(s)}\) from the observation model conditional on \(\theta^{(s)}\).

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
Predictive spread contains parameter uncertainty and future response variation.
These are distinct sources of variation.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #2
Prediction asks what future observations may look like. Model checking compares replicated observations with the observed data.
