.00234375


.50
.0625
.50
.03125


.75
.10546875
.30
.031640625



The normalizing constant is

Z
=.00234375+.03125+.031640625
=.065234375.

Dividing each product by Z gives posterior probabilities of approximately .0359, .4791, and .4850.


Code
theta <- c(.25, .50, .75)
prior <- c(.20, .50, .30)
likelihood_kernel <- theta^3 * (1 - theta)
unnormalized <- prior * likelihood_kernel
posterior <- unnormalized / sum(unnormalized)

stopifnot(abs(sum(posterior) - 1) < 1e-12)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  posterior,
  c(0.03592814, 0.47904192, 0.48502994),
  tolerance = 1e-7
)))

data.frame(theta, prior, likelihood_kernel, posterior)


The data favor larger values because three of four responses were collective. The prior gives substantial mass to .50, so the posterior probabilities for .50 and .75 are nearly equal. This result is an update from a particular prior through a particular likelihood.

title: Posterior distributions
text:
Understand the normalizer
The denominator

p(\mathbf{x})
=
\sum_{\theta}
p(\mathbf{x}\mid\theta)p(\theta)

is the prior predictive probability of the observed data, up to any likelihood factor that is common to all parameter values. It does not depend on which \theta is being evaluated. Dividing by it makes the posterior probabilities sum to one.
For a continuous parameter, the sum becomes an integral:

p(\mathbf{x})
=
\int
p(\mathbf{x}\mid\theta)p(\theta)
\,\mathrm{d}\theta.

We often write

p(\theta\mid\mathbf{x})
\propto
p(\mathbf{x}\mid\theta)p(\theta)

when we first care about posterior shape. A normalized density is still required before assigning posterior probabilities or calculating expectations.

title: Posterior distributions
text:
Interpret a continuous density
For a continuous parameter, p(\theta\mid\mathbf{x}) is a density rather than the probability that \Theta equals exactly \theta. The probability of any single point is zero. Posterior probability is assigned to an interval by integrating:

\mathbb{P}(a<\Theta<b\mid\mathbf{x})
=
\int_a^b
p(\theta\mid\mathbf{x})
\,\mathrm{d}\theta.

A higher density at .75 than at .50 says that a small neighborhood around .75 receives more posterior mass per unit width. It does not assign positive probability to the exact point .75 in a continuous model.

title: Posterior distributions
text:
Keep the conditioning direction visible
The error of transposing a conditional probability also applies here. The likelihood evaluates the observed data as a function of a candidate parameter. The posterior distributes uncertainty over parameter values after conditioning on those data. Bayes’ rule connects the two quantities, but it does not make them interchangeable.
Posterior uncertainty is also not computational error. In the hand calculation, the posterior probabilities are exact under the model. Later simulation methods will approximate posterior summaries and add Monte Carlo error, but that error is not part of the posterior itself.

title: Posterior distributions
text:
Check your understanding

Which quantity is fixed when evaluating p(\mathbf{x}\mid\theta)?
Why do the unnormalized posterior values not sum to one?
What role does p(\mathbf{x}) play in Bayes’ rule?
If the prior put all its probability on \theta=.25, could these data create posterior support at .75 under this model?
Why is a continuous posterior density at one point not a point probability?

The posterior-summaries page shows how a posterior distribution supports probability statements, expectations, and intervals.

title: Summarizing posterior draws
text:
The posterior distribution page represented uncertainty over parameter values. Suppose an analysis produces 4,000 draws of a difference \Delta between two response probabilities:
\Delta^{(1)},\ldots,\Delta^{(4000)}.
The draws approximate the posterior distribution of \Delta. They retain more information than one estimate and one interval, but a results paragraph still needs a small set of interpretable quantities.
A posterior summary is a calculation performed on the posterior distribution. It is not an additional model and does not create new evidence. The summary selects one aspect of the uncertainty already represented by the draws.

title: Summarizing posterior draws
text:
Locate the posterior center
The posterior mean is approximated by

\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[\Delta\mid y]
=
\frac{1}{S}
\sum_{s=1}^{S}\Delta^{(s)}.

The posterior median is the middle draw after sorting. In R:
mean(draws$delta)
median(draws$delta)
Suppose five equally weighted illustrative draws are

-.09,\;-.07,\;-.06,\;-.05,\;.02.

Their mean is

\frac{-.09-.07-.06-.05+.02}{5}=-.05,

while their median is -.06. The positive tail pulls the mean upward. With a symmetric posterior, the two centers will tend to be similar. With a skewed posterior, their difference records the different way each summary treats the tail.
Neither quantity is automatically the “Bayesian estimate.” The mean minimizes posterior expected squared error, while the median minimizes posterior expected absolute error. A course report can often use the median or mean consistently, provided the choice is stated and the full uncertainty is not hidden.

title: Summarizing posterior draws
text:
Construct a credible interval
An equal-tailed 95 percent credible interval uses the .025 and .975 posterior quantiles:
quantile(draws$delta, c(.025, .975))
The earlier confidence interval page attached a coverage interpretation to a repeated sampling procedure. A credible interval has a different interpretation. If the posterior quantiles are

[-.08,-.02],

then 95 percent of the represented posterior probability lies between those values. Conditional on the likelihood, prior, observed data, and computational approximation, this is a probability statement about \Delta.
The conditioning clause matters. A credible interval does not guarantee that the model represents the linguistic sampling process or that the prior was appropriate. It describes uncertainty inside the fitted model.
A 95 percent confidence interval has a different interpretation. Its 95 percent refers to long run coverage of an interval procedure across repeated samples. The two intervals can have similar numerical endpoints while licensing different probability statements.

title: Summarizing posterior draws
text:
Calculate a directional probability
If the linguistic hypothesis predicts a negative response probability difference, estimate

\Pr(\Delta<0\mid y)

with the proportion of posterior draws below zero:
mean(draws$delta < 0)
If 3,800 of 4,000 draws are negative, the estimate is

\frac{3800}{4000}=.95.

This quantity answers a directional posterior question. It is not a p value because it does not describe a tail probability for a test statistic under a null sampling distribution. It also does not describe the size of the association. A posterior probability of .95 can accompany a very small negative difference.
Thus report direction together with a magnitude and interval on a meaningful scale. Replacing every posterior with a new verbal evidence label would discard the quantities that the analysis was designed to estimate.

title: Summarizing posterior draws
text:
Transform each draw before summarizing
Suppose \Theta is a response probability. Its odds are \Theta/(1-\Theta). Transform every posterior draw:
odds <- draws$theta / (1 - draws$theta)
quantile(odds, c(.025, .5, .975))
Transforming the endpoints of an equal-tailed interval with this monotonic function gives the same interval endpoints as transforming every draw and taking the corresponding quantiles. But the mean of transformed draws is generally not the transformation of the posterior mean:

\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\Theta}{1-\Theta}\mid y\right]
\ne
\frac{\mathbb{E}[\Theta\mid y]}{1-\mathbb{E}[\Theta\mid y]}.

Compute the estimand within every posterior draw, then summarize the resulting distribution. This procedure is necessary when an estimand combines several parameters or uses a nonlinear transformation.

title: Summarizing posterior draws
section: Preserve joint uncertainty in a contrast
text:
Preserve joint uncertainty in a contrast
Suppose a model contains response probabilities \Theta_A and \Theta_B for two linguistic conditions. Separate summaries do not retain which values occurred together in one posterior draw.
For each draw s, compute the condition difference:

\Delta^{(s)}
=\Theta_A^{(s)}-\Theta_B^{(s)}.

The collection of \Delta^{(s)} values is the posterior distribution of the probability difference. Subtracting separate summaries of \Theta_A and \Theta_B would ignore posterior dependence between them.
probability_difference <- draws$theta_a - draws$theta_b

quantile(probability_difference, c(.025, .5, .975))
mean(probability_difference > 0)
This calculation also fixes the comparison. The output is a probability difference for two declared conditions, not two unrelated marginal summaries.

title: Summarizing posterior draws
section: Match the summary to the claim
text:
Match the summary to the claim
A parameter summary answers a parameter question. A response probability contrast answers a question about predicted outcomes. A directional probability answers a sign question. These targets overlap, but they are not interchangeable.
For instance, a claim that one embedding environment produces more yes judgments should be supported by category probabilities or their contrast. A parameter on another scale may explain how the model generates that change, but it is not itself a change in the observed response category.
Selecting response scale summaries after inspecting many predictor profiles can exaggerate a dramatic pattern. Predeclare the theoretically diagnostic profiles or show a complete small grid of conditions. Posterior computation does not remove researcher choice from reporting.






NoteProblem Set 4 connection



Problem Set 4, Task 3 summarizes posterior parameters. Task 4 compares predicted responses across embedding environments. These tasks are included here because parameter summaries and response scale comparisons support different parts of the projection claim.








NoteCheck the inferential claim



What probability statement does a 95 percent credible interval support? How would you estimate \Pr(\Delta>0\mid y) from draws? Why should a multi parameter predicted contrast be calculated within each draw?

title: Summarizing posterior draws
text:
What posterior summaries add
Posterior means, medians, intervals, directional probabilities, and derived contrasts describe different features of one fitted posterior distribution. The appropriate summary follows from the estimand. Nonlinear or multi parameter targets must be computed within each draw before they are summarized. Later predictive pages use the same draw by draw rule to generate complete replicated observations.

title: Prior predictive distributions
text:
The conjugate prior page updated a prior after observing data. A prior predictive distribution instead propagates the prior through the observation model before the present data are observed. Suppose a study will present 10 ambiguous sentences and record how often one modeled response process yields an instrument interpretation. Let Y be that count.
We propose a prior on the participant’s interpretation probability:
\Pi\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,2).
Conditional on \Pi=\pi, the ten binary choices define a count distribution. Before observing the participant, what values of Y does the complete model expect?
The prior predictive distribution answers this question. It averages possible observations over parameter values under the prior:
p(\widetilde{y})
=\int p(\widetilde{y}\mid\pi)p(\pi)\,\mathrm{d}\pi.
The tilde marks \widetilde{Y} as a possible observation generated from the model rather than a response already observed.
The expression combines two claims. The binomial observation model says how a fixed value of \pi generates a count. The beta prior says which values of \pi receive substantial probability before the present participant’s data are observed. The integral propagates the second claim through the first.
We can read the integral as a weighted average. For each possible \pi, compute the binomial probability of \widetilde{y}. Then weight that probability by the prior density at \pi and add across the unit interval. Values of \pi that are more plausible under the prior contribute more to the resulting predictive probability.

title: Prior predictive distributions
text:
Simulate one possible dataset
First draw a probability from the prior:

\pi^{(s)}\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,2).

Then draw ten choices using that probability and count the successes:

\widetilde{y}^{(s)}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(10,\pi^{(s)}).

Repeat the two steps to approximate the full prior predictive distribution.
One simulation draw makes the averaging concrete. Suppose the prior draw is \pi^{(1)}=.68. We keep that value fixed while generating all ten responses in prior predictive dataset 1. If the simulated count is \widetilde{y}^{(1)}=8, the pair (.68,8) is one draw from the joint prior model. A second prior predictive dataset receives a new draw from the prior because the integral averages predictions over our prior uncertainty about \pi.


Code
set.seed(414)

pi_prior <- rbeta(10000, shape1 = 2, shape2 = 2)
y_prior <- rbinom(10000, size = 10, prob = pi_prior)

plot(prop.table(table(y_prior)),
     xlab = "instrument choices out of 10",
     ylab = "prior predictive probability")

title: Prior predictive distributions
section: Inspect predictions on the response scale
text:
Inspect predictions on the response scale
The beta density describes an abstract probability parameter. The simulated values are counts that the experiment could record. They are often easier to evaluate.
If a prior and likelihood predict that nearly every ten trial dataset must contain either 0 or 10 instrument readings, but comparable experiments show substantial interior counts, the prior predictive distribution reveals a mismatch before the present responses are used.
The opposite failure can occur as well. A prior concentrated tightly around \pi=.50 may imply that almost every ten-trial count lies near 5. Such a model would rule out a strong preference for either interpretation before the experiment begins. If the linguistic theory permits the modeled response probability to lie far from .50, that prior is too restrictive even if its center appears neutral.
We can also inspect summaries:


Code
quantile(y_prior, c(.025, .25, .5, .75, .975))
mean(y_prior == 0 | y_prior == 10)


The quantiles describe the central spread of possible recorded counts. The boundary proportion describes how often the model expects categorical response patterns. Neither quantity is a universal diagnostic. We choose summaries that express the parts of the measurement we care about.

title: Prior predictive distributions
text:
Compare priors through predictions
Parameter-scale language can conceal how strongly two priors differ. Consider three beta priors:

\operatorname{Beta}(2,2),
\qquad
\operatorname{Beta}(20,20),
\qquad
\operatorname{Beta}(.5,.5).

All three are symmetric around .50. But symmetry does not make them equivalent. The first permits moderate variation, the second concentrates near .50, and the third favors values near the boundaries.


Code
set.seed(414)

simulate_prior_counts <- function(alpha, beta, draws = 10000) {
  pi_draw <- rbeta(draws, alpha, beta)
  rbinom(draws, size = 10, prob = pi_draw)
}

y_moderate <- simulate_prior_counts(2, 2)
y_concentrated <- simulate_prior_counts(20, 20)
y_boundary <- simulate_prior_counts(.5, .5)

rbind(
  moderate = quantile(y_moderate, c(.05, .50, .95)),
  concentrated = quantile(y_concentrated, c(.05, .50, .95)),
  boundary = quantile(y_boundary, c(.05, .50, .95))
)


The predictive counts state the practical commitments of each prior in the units the experiment records. We can ask whether each commitment is compatible with the design, earlier studies, and the range of behavior the theory leaves open.

title: Prior predictive distributions
section: Match the simulation to the sampling structure
text:
Match the simulation to the sampling structure
The current simulation draws one \pi per complete ten trial dataset and then ten choices conditional on that value. It represents prior uncertainty about one shared probability in this model. It does not by itself define a population distribution of participant preferences.
To represent several participants with different underlying probabilities, we would need an additional population distribution and one participant probability drawn from it for each participant. That structure is not part of the current model. Drawing a new \pi before every trial would instead put the beta variation at the trial level. These are different generative claims, even if every version uses the same beta and binomial functions.
A prior predictive check is only as informative as this generative structure. Simulating the correct response range while ignoring the grouping in the study can make a poorly specified model appear plausible.

title: Prior predictive distributions
section: Keep prior checking prior to the update
text:
Keep prior checking prior to the update
Prior predictive checks use the prior and observation model. They do not use the posterior.
If we repeatedly tune the prior until it reproduces the present observed outcome, that outcome has already influenced the prior. Any such data-dependent choice should be acknowledged rather than described as information supplied before the data.
Prior predictive checking does not require a prior to predict the observed data closely. Before observing the current sample, a useful prior may allow many outcomes that did not happen. The narrower question is whether it places substantial probability on impossible or theoretically indefensible data, or rules out outcomes that the design and existing knowledge make plausible.






NoteProblem Set 4 connection



Problem Set 4, Task 2 uses prior predictive category proportions for a seven category commitment response. Students must thus simulate the response scale before any observed commitment rating updates the model.








NoteCheck the simulation order




Why must each predictive count use the same sampled \pi^{(s)} for all ten choices?
What different model would result from drawing a new \pi before every choice?
Two priors have the same mean. Explain why their prior predictive distributions can still differ.
Give one response scale summary that would detect a prior predicting too many categorical response patterns.

title: Sampling distributions
text:
The maximum likelihood page produced one estimate from one observed sample. We now study an estimator as a rule that could be applied to every possible sample. Suppose a lexical decision task has population response accuracy
\pi=.75.
We sample 20 independent trials and estimate accuracy with the sample proportion. One sample might give .70, another .80, and another .75. The population parameter is unchanged while the sample summary varies.
The distribution of an estimation rule across possible samples is its sampling distribution.

title: Sampling distributions
text:
Keep three objects distinct
The estimand is the target population quantity:

\pi=.75.

The estimator is the rule applied before we know which sample will occur:

\widehat{\Pi}
=\frac{1}{20}\sum_{i=1}^{20}X_i.

The capital notation emphasizes that \widehat{\Pi} varies across possible samples.
After one sample is observed, the estimator produces an estimate, perhaps

\widehat{\pi}=.70.









object
varies across repeated samples?
role




estimand \pi
no
fixed target under the model


estimator \widehat{\Pi}
yes
rule applied to any possible sample


estimate \widehat{\pi}
already realized
output for one observed sample



Calling the estimate an estimator hides the repeated-sampling object whose properties we want to study.

title: Sampling distributions
section: Enumerate a very small sampling distribution
text:
Enumerate a very small sampling distribution
Before simulating 20 trials, take n=2 and \pi=.75. The possible ordered samples and proportion estimates are



sample
probability
estimate




(0,0)
.25^2=.0625
0


(0,1)
.25(.75)=.1875
.5


(1,0)
.75(.25)=.1875
.5


(1,1)
.75^2=.5625
1



Combine samples that produce the same estimate:



possible \widehat{\Pi}
probability




0
.0625


.5
.375


1
.5625



This PMF is the sampling distribution for the sample proportion when n=2 and \pi=.75.
Its expected value is

0(.0625)+.5(.375)+1(.5625)=.75.

The center equals the estimand.

title: Sampling distributions
text:
Simulate the larger case
For n=20, enumeration is possible but tedious. Simulation gives an approximation.


Code
set.seed(414)

accuracy_estimates <- replicate(
  10000,
  mean(rbinom(20, size = 1, prob = .75))
)

mean(accuracy_estimates)
sd(accuracy_estimates)


The simulated center should be near .75. The simulated standard deviation should be near the analytic value derived below.

title: Sampling distributions
text:
Calculate center and spread
Under IID Bernoulli sampling,

\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\Pi}]=\pi

and

\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\Pi})
=\frac{\pi(1-\pi)}{n}.

For \pi=.75 and n=20,

\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\Pi})
=\frac{.75(.25)}{20}
=.009375.

The sampling standard deviation is

\sqrt{.009375}\approx.0968.

Estimates from samples of 20 can thus differ from the target by several percentage points under the model.

title: Sampling distributions
text:
Change the sample size
If n increases to 100, the variance becomes

\frac{.75(.25)}{100}=.001875,

and the sampling standard deviation becomes approximately .0433. The population parameter has not changed. The estimator has become more stable because each estimate averages more independent observations.

title: Sampling distributions
text:
A sampling distribution contains estimates
The sampling distribution here contains possible sample proportions, not zero and one trial responses. It is a distribution of estimates across possible samples, not a distribution of individual response values.
State what repeats. Entire samples repeat, and one estimate is computed from each sample.

title: Sampling distributions
text:
Check your understanding

For n=2 and \pi=.50, enumerate the sampling distribution of the sample proportion.
Which object is fixed in the repeated-sampling model, \pi or \widehat{\Pi}?
Why does increasing n narrow the sampling distribution without changing the population accuracy?
Distinguish an estimator from its realized estimate in one sentence.

The next pages use this distribution in two ways. Standard errors summarize its spread, while estimator bias compares its center with the target.

title: Implementing a model in Stan
text:
The preceding pages developed Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and the No-U-Turn Sampler. Stan is a probabilistic programming language that uses these methods after the analyst declares observed data, unknown parameters, and density contributions.
Consider a constructed study of overt subject pronouns. Code y_i=1 when a sampled clause contains an overt subject pronoun and y_i=0 otherwise. The statistical model is
Y_i\mid\Pi=\pi
\sim
\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi)
with prior
\Pi\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,2).
The Stan program is

title: Implementing a model in Stan
Implementing a model in Stan
Implementing a model in Stan
Implementing a model in Stan
text:
Prepare a matching data object
Suppose the constructed sample has 12 overt pronouns among 20 clauses.


Code
y <- c(rep(1L, 12), rep(0L, 8))
stan_data <- list(n = length(y), y = y)

stopifnot(stan_data$n == 20L)
stopifnot(sum(stan_data$y) == 12L)
stopifnot(all(stan_data$y %in% 0:1))

analytic_posterior <- c(alpha = 2 + sum(y),
                        beta = 2 + length(y) - sum(y))
analytic_posterior


The conjugate update derived earlier gives a \operatorname{Beta}(14,10) benchmark. A successful Stan fit should approximate this posterior within Monte Carlo error. The benchmark checks the implementation for this simple model; most Stan models will not have an analytic comparison.

title: Implementing a model in Stan
text:
Match code to factorization
Stan vectorizes y ~ bernoulli(pi), but the statement still represents

\sum_{i=1}^n
\log p(y_i\mid\pi).

If several clauses come from one speaker, concise vectorization does not remove that dependence. The program has asserted conditional independence by adding separate Bernoulli terms with one common probability.
Translate each density statement back into the product or sum it represents, then ask whether that factorization matches the linguistic sampling process.

title: Implementing a model in Stan
section: Separate program validity from model adequacy
text:
Separate program validity from model adequacy
Stan can parse a program, calculate gradients, and return draws from the declared posterior. None of those outcomes establishes that independent Bernoulli observations are a suitable model for the clauses.
A completed sampling run is not a validated analysis. The analyst still must check computational behavior, prior implications, posterior predictions, and the linguistic correspondence between data rows and modeled units.
Stan supplies the sampling machinery. The analyst supplies the model and the inferential target.
The program should be stored with the exact data transformation and interface call used to fit it. Identical Stan code can target a different posterior when variables are recoded or rows are filtered.

title: Implementing a model in Stan
text:
Check your understanding

Why does y belong in the data block rather than the parameters block?
What is the difference between <lower=0, upper=1> and pi ~ beta(2, 2)?
What does a tilde statement add in the model block?
Why can a program run without representing speaker or document dependence?

The next page begins the computational audit by reading trace plots.

title: Bounded similarity judgments
text:
White, Grimm, and Glass’s Experiment 2 asks whether two event descriptions that instantiate the same PropBank sense are judged more similar than descriptions that instantiate different senses. Participants rated within-verb pairs on an integer slider from 0, completely identical, to 100, extremely different. Lower values thus indicate greater perceived similarity.
We will first identify one contrast in the released data, then inspect the response support as on the bounded-response page, fit a linear mixed model as a benchmark, and replace that benchmark with ordered-beta regression. The random-intercept page introduced the repeated-participant and repeated-item structure used by both models.

title: Bounded similarity judgments
text:
Construct a within-verb teaching extract
The full study contains 10,800 test judgments. The preparation script constructs the teaching extract from that release. We retain test trials whose two descriptions are contentful, then restrict the data to verbs with both same-sense and different-sense pairs. This restriction ensures that the same-sense contrast is represented within every retained verb.
ratings <- read.csv(
  "../data/aspectual-similarity/within-verb-similarity.csv"
)

c(
  ratings = nrow(ratings),
  participants = length(unique(ratings$participant_id)),
  verbs = length(unique(ratings$verb)),
  pairs = length(unique(ratings$sentence_pair_id))
)
The result contains 4,405 ratings from 202 participants, 14 verbs, and 218 sentence pairs. One row is a participant by pair judgment. Participants and sentence pairs repeat, so neither the ratings nor the pair-level predictor are independently replicated 4,405 times.
The deterministic preparation script asserts these counts and verifies that every retained verb has both predictor values. The adapted CSV has SHA-256 checksum b19edbb7463a6767274e3dde78e902b0e8777424a21d7fdf231ea1e6d0e25f35.

title: Bounded similarity judgments
text:
Inspect the response before fitting
hist(
  ratings$dissimilarity,
  breaks = seq(-.5, 100.5, by = 1),
  xlab = "Dissimilarity rating",
  main = "Within-verb similarity judgments"
)

mean(ratings$dissimilarity %in% c(0, 100))
aggregate(dissimilarity ~ same_sense, ratings, mean)
Every integer value from 0 through 100 occurs. Exact endpoints account for 20.8% of the teaching extract, so standard beta regression cannot use the observed responses without altering them. Nudging one fifth of the observations inward would also make the arbitrary nudge part of one fifth of the pointwise likelihood contributions. Endpoint use varies across participants: some never use an endpoint, while others use one on every retained trial.
Same-sense pairs have a mean dissimilarity of 55.9; different-sense pairs have a mean of 76.4. This 20.4-point raw difference is theoretically relevant, but it does not yet account for repeated participants or pairs.

title: Bounded similarity judgments
text:
A linear mixed model benchmark
Fit a linear mixed-effects benchmark with normally distributed errors and participant and sentence-pair intercepts:
linear_fit <- lme4::lmer(
  dissimilarity ~ factor(same_sense) + verb_type +
    (1 | participant_id) + (1 | sentence_pair_id),
  data = ratings,
  REML = FALSE
)
The fit estimates a -20.1-point same-sense contrast. Its participant, sentence-pair, and residual standard deviations are 13.5, 14.7, and 21.3 points, respectively. Thus the contrast survives a basic dependence repair.
But the likelihood fails the support check. For fixed-effect predictions \widehat\mu_i and residual scale \widehat\sigma, compute
mu <- predict(linear_fit, re.form = NA)
sigma <- sigma(linear_fit)

illegal_mass <- mean(
  pnorm(0, mu, sigma) + 1 - pnorm(100, mu, sigma)
)
The result is 10.1%. The benchmark places about one tenth of its fixed-effect predictive mass outside a scale that participants could not leave. The coefficient answers the intended contrast, while the response distribution makes predictions the task cannot produce.
This is why model criticism should identify the specific discrepancy. “The residuals are nonnormal” would not tell us whether the problem is skew, tail weight, dependence, or support. Here the model assigns positive probability to values outside the response support, and that discrepancy is exact and measurable.

title: Bounded similarity judgments
text:
Replace the response distribution
Use the same predictor and dependence structure with an ordered-beta likelihood:
ratings$dissimilarity_01 <- ratings$dissimilarity / 100

ordered_beta_fit <- ordbetareg::ordbetareg(
  dissimilarity_01 ~ factor(same_sense) + verb_type +
    (1 | participant_id) + (1 | sentence_pair_id),
  data = ratings,
  chains = 4,
  cores = 4,
  warmup = 1000,
  iter = 3000,
  control = list(adapt_delta = .99),
  seed = 20260825
)
The audited teaching pilot estimates a same-sense coefficient of -.870 on the latent scale, with a 95% interval of [-1.052, -.692]. This coefficient is not measured in slider points.
We next check the endpoint predictions. The median predicted endpoint mass is 20.78%, with a 95% interval of [19.35%, 22.33%], compared with 20.82% in the observed data. The released full Experiment 2 model also recovers the zero mass, one mass, mean, and standard deviation in its complete data. Its reported convergence diagnostics do not show a computational warning.
The latent coefficient is not an 87-point response change. Its negative sign shifts the entire predictive distribution toward greater similarity: more probability near zero, lower interior values, and less probability at 100. The interpretation thus comes from predicted response distributions, not from multiplying the coefficient by 100.

title: Bounded similarity judgments
text:
Read the comparison in stages
The raw means show the expected direction: same-sense pairs receive lower dissimilarity ratings. The linear mixed model shows that the direction remains after accounting for repeated participants and sentence pairs. Its predictive distribution then reveals a separate problem, since about one tenth of its probability lies outside the response scale. Ordered-beta regression removes that support failure and reproduces the observed endpoint proportion.
The restricted extract answers a narrower question than the full paper. Exact PropBank label equality is directly observed here, while the paper’s full analysis propagates probabilistic sense, telicity, and durativity measures and permits richer by-verb variation. The teaching extract supports a comparison of same-sense and different-sense contentful pairs among verbs represented by both pair types. It does not show that one 20-point contrast applies to every English verb.

title: Bounded similarity judgments
text:
LING 414 extension
Return to the full released analysis and replace exact same-sense with its probabilistic score. Then compare a fixed-effects-only fit with the dependence-aware model for the telicity-by-same-sense and durativity-by-same-sense interactions. The telicity interaction disappears after participant and sentence-pair structure enters, while the durativity interaction shows the reverse pattern. This contrast supplies a concrete pseudoreplication diagnosis, but it should follow the simpler bounded-response lesson rather than serve as its entry point.

title: Bounded similarity judgments
text:
Data, license, and citation
The source paper is White, Grimm, and Glass (2026), Aspectual similarity predicts sense similarity. The companion repository records the analysis code, current paper source, and cleaned data. The data are licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; the teaching extract is shared under the same terms. Ordered-beta regression follows Kubinec.






NoteTwo recurring questions



What counts as a new observation? For the narrow fitted model, a new judgment may come from an observed participant and pair; a stronger claim requires new participants, new pairs, or new verbs and a validation design that holds out the corresponding unit.
What breaks the simpler model? Exact endpoints and 10.1% predictive probability outside the permitted response range break the response model even though the mean same-sense contrast is stable.

title: Bounded responses
text:
The generalized-linear-model sequence introduced support as the set of values to which a response distribution assigns probability. A similarity slider from completely identical to extremely different cannot produce a value below its left endpoint or above its right endpoint. The bounds are part of the measurement, not incidental features of one sample. A probability model for the response should represent that fact.
A response whose possible values lie in a known interval [L,U] is a bounded response. Percentages, visual-analog scales, proportions, and normalized annotation scores can all be bounded. The concept concerns support: which values the measurement process can produce. It does not yet select a particular likelihood.

title: Bounded responses
section: Bounds come from the measurement process
text:
Bounds come from the measurement process
Suppose a participant rates dissimilarity on an integer slider from 0 to 100. The response satisfies

Y_i\in\{0,1,\ldots,100\}.

A coarser analysis might treat the slider as approximately continuous and record only

Y_i\in[0,100].

The approximation discards the one-point spacing but preserves the legal range. Rescaling produces

Z_i=\frac{Y_i-L}{U-L}\in[0,1].

Rescaling does not remove the bounds. It simply expresses them as zero and one.
This distinction matters because an observed zero may have substantive meaning. A participant who selects completely identical has used the measurement scale exactly as designed. Replacing that value with .001 to satisfy software changes the recorded response and makes an arbitrary constant part of the analysis.

title: Bounded responses
text:
Boundary values are outcomes
A bounded response can have no observations at its endpoints, occasional observations there, or large piles at one or both endpoints. We can begin by calculating the proportion of observations equal to L or U:

\widehat{p}_{\partial}
=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\mathbb{I}(Y_i\in\{L,U\}).

This proportion describes the response distribution. It is not automatically evidence for a special cognitive state. A high endpoint rate might arise because the scale labels make the endpoints attractive, because some stimuli genuinely elicit categorical responses, or because particular participants use the scale coarsely. Those explanations require design information and conditional checks.
At minimum, inspect endpoint use overall, separately at each endpoint, and by repeated measurement units such as participant and item. An overall rate can hide one participant who responds almost entirely at the endpoints and another who never uses them.
boundary <- ratings$dissimilarity %in% c(0, 100)
mean(boundary)

participant_boundary <- aggregate(
  boundary,
  list(participant = ratings$participant_id),
  mean
)

title: Bounded responses
text:
What a normal distribution licenses
A normally distributed response has support on the entire real line:

Y_i\mid\mu_i,\sigma
\sim\operatorname{Normal}(\mu_i,\sigma).

For a bounded response, its probability of an impossible value is

p_{\text{illegal},i}
=\Phi\left(\frac{L-\mu_i}{\sigma}\right)
+1-\Phi\left(\frac{U-\mu_i}{\sigma}\right),

where \Phi is the standard-normal CDF. This probability may be negligible when the fitted mean is far from both endpoints and residual variation is small. It may be substantial for a wide response distribution or for means near a boundary. Thus “the scale is roughly continuous” does not by itself justify a normal likelihood. The relevant question is what the fitted distribution predicts.
This illegal-mass calculation checks a particular way the model can fail. It is more informative than asking whether a histogram looks normal. A model that assigns 10% of its predictive mass outside the legal scale has made a visible claim about outcomes that the experiment cannot record.

title: Bounded responses
text:
Bounded is not censored
Bounds and censoring are distinct measurement stories.

A bounded slider records a response whose scale ends at L and U.
A censored measure records only that an underlying value fell below or above a detection threshold.

If a voice-onset-time tracker reports every negative estimate as zero, zero may represent censored latent values. If a participant intentionally chooses the left endpoint of a similarity scale, zero is an observed category at the bound. The same number can thus require different likelihoods because it arose through a different observation process.

title: Bounded responses
text:
What boundedness does not decide
Knowing that the response is bounded narrows the model space, but several choices remain.

If all observations lie strictly inside (0,1), beta regression may represent the interior distribution.
If exact zeros and ones occur, the likelihood needs to assign them positive probability.
If a small number of ordered categories were shown, an ordinal model may better preserve the task.
If the response is a count of successes out of known trials, a binomial likelihood may represent the generating process more directly than a generic bounded model.

These options are not interchangeable fixes. They describe different measurement processes. The next page shows why moving endpoints inward does not make standard beta regression a neutral analysis of slider responses.






WarningDo not repair the data before stating the model



Transforming zeros and ones into interior values makes ordinary beta software run, but it removes the empirical question of why participants used the endpoints. State the response support and endpoint process first.

title: Bounded responses
text:
Read the model

A study reports the proportion of trials on which each child produced a plural. Is the response merely bounded, or does the known number of trials suggest a more specific likelihood?
A confidence slider ranges from 0 to 100, but the interface never permits exactly 0 or 100. Which support should the model use?
An ordinary linear regression fit to a 1 to 7 judgment scale assigns .2% probability outside the scale under its normality assumption. Is that enough to approve the model? Identify one other feature of the measurement process that remains untested.

title: Bounded responses
text:
Before moving on
A bounded response has known support, and values at its bounds are observed outcomes rather than automatic outliers. Endpoint proportions describe how the bounds were used, while the normal-distribution calculation quantifies one specific support failure. The next page traces an inward endpoint transformation through the ordinary beta likelihood.

title: Checking a linear regression
text:
The residual page distinguished an observed residual from an unobserved error term. An ordinary linear regression with normally distributed errors makes predictions about patterns that should remain after subtracting the fitted conditional mean. Residual diagnostics compare those predictions with the observed residuals.
The aim is not to certify that a model is true. A finite dataset cannot establish that every assumption holds. The aim is to find consequential ways in which the model fails to reproduce the data.
Each check needs three parts: a model prediction, an observable discrepancy, and a consequence for the linguistic analysis. A generic statement that a plot “looks bad” omits the first and third parts.

title: Checking a linear regression
text:
Construct a diagnostic example
Suppose a phonetic study relates a speaker’s local articulation rate to a segment duration. We construct observations with a slight bend in the mean and greater duration variation at faster rates, then fit a straight line with constant variance.


Code
set.seed(214)

duration_data <- data.frame(
  rate = seq(2, 7, length.out = 80)
)

duration_data$mean_duration <-
  175 - 15 * duration_data$rate +
  3 * (duration_data$rate - 4.5)^2

duration_data$duration <- rnorm(
  nrow(duration_data),
  mean = duration_data$mean_duration,
  sd = 3 + duration_data$rate
)

fit <- lm(duration ~ rate, data = duration_data)


The fitted model is intentionally incomplete. This lets us connect visible residual patterns to the exact commitments the line fails to represent.

title: Checking a linear regression
text:
Check the mean shape
Plot residuals against fitted values:


Code
plot(fitted(fit), residuals(fit),
     xlab = "fitted conditional mean", ylab = "residual")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)


If the linear mean is adequate, the residual center should stay near zero across the fitted range.
A U-shaped pattern suggests that the mean bends while the model forces a straight line. A systematic rise suggests that the fitted slope misses part of the association.
Why does a U shape diagnose curvature? At the low and high ends, the observations fall systematically above the line, so residuals tend to be positive. Near the middle, they fall below the line, so residuals tend to be negative. The residual sign changes in an ordered way across fitted values. Random scatter around zero would not have this systematic sequence.
This is evidence about the conditional mean. It does not yet identify which alternative mean function should replace the line. A theoretical account of articulation rate should guide that choice.

title: Checking a linear regression
text:
Check constant variance
The ordinary linear regression model assumes one conditional response variance \sigma^2 at every predictor value.
If the residual cloud is narrow at low fitted values and wide at high fitted values, the variance changes with the mean. This fan shape is evidence against the constant-variance assumption.
The constructed durations should show this pattern because their standard deviation was set to 3+\text{rate}. The fitted line uses one residual standard deviation for all observations. It may consequently understate uncertainty for fast speech and overstate it for slow speech.
We should also plot residuals against theoretically relevant predictors or groups. A speaker-specific residual shift can be invisible when all speakers are pooled against fitted values.
The predictor on a residual plot need not appear in the fitted formula. Plotting residuals against an omitted variable can reveal structure left in the data. For instance, if residuals for phrase-final segments are mostly positive, the model may have omitted phrase-final lengthening. The pattern is theory-bearing because it isolates a particular linguistic contrast the fitted mean does not represent.

title: Checking a linear regression
text:
Check distributional shape
A normal quantile plot compares ordered residuals with the quantiles expected from a normal distribution:


Code
qqnorm(residuals(fit))
qqline(residuals(fit))


Systematic tail departures indicate that extreme residuals occur differently from the prediction under normally distributed errors. Skew creates an asymmetric pattern.
The quantile plot pairs each ordered residual with the corresponding theoretical normal quantile. If the empirical and theoretical distributions differ mainly in the upper tail, the largest observed durations will bend away from the line while most middle residuals remain near it. This location matters if the analysis uses predictions for unusually long segments.
The goal is not to demand a perfect diagonal. We ask whether the departure is large enough to affect the quantities the analysis uses, such as coefficient intervals or predictions for slow responses.
Treating every departure from a diagonal as a binary violation, and every nearly diagonal plot as approval, gives the plot too much authority. Instead ask what feature differs, where it differs, and which inferential quantity may change.

title: Checking a linear regression
text:
Check observation order
Conditional independence also makes a prediction. Once the modeled predictors are accounted for, residuals should not retain an ordered pattern induced by the sampling process.


Code
plot(
  seq_along(residuals(fit)),
  residuals(fit),
  xlab = "observation order",
  ylab = "residual"
)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)


A sequence of positive residuals followed by negative residuals might reflect drift over an experimental session. Alternation between positive and negative values might reflect a counterbalancing or trial-order pattern. The plot does not prove a particular source, but it locates dependence the fitted model does not represent.
For repeated linguistic data, row order may not be the most informative order. We may instead group or order residuals by participant, item, recording session, or corpus document. The choice should follow the sampling structure.

title: Checking a linear regression
text:
Check the right discrepancy
A reading-time model should be checked for right skew and condition-specific spread. A phonetic model may need speaker-specific residual patterns. A lexical model may need item or frequency structure.
Generic normality tests compress all departures into one number and become sensitive to negligible deviations in large datasets. Diagnostic plots are more useful when they identify the form and location of a mismatch.

title: Checking a linear regression
section: Turn a pattern into an analysis decision
text:
Turn a pattern into an analysis decision
Finding a mismatch begins a model revision. It does not automatically license deleting observations or trying transformations until a plot appears tidy. The revision should target the observed discrepancy.
For instance, curvature in the residual center motivates reconsidering the mean function. A fan shape motivates reconsidering constant variance. A speaker shift motivates representing speaker structure. These responses differ because the checks diagnose different commitments.
Report the observed pattern and its consequence. “Residual spread increased with fitted duration, so the constant-variance model may understate uncertainty at the upper end” is more informative than “assumptions were checked.”






NoteKeep two checks separate



MCMC diagnostics ask whether an algorithm represented a posterior. Residual checks ask whether the statistical model reproduces relevant patterns in the observations.








NoteDiagnose the discrepancy




What residual pattern would a mean function that bends upward tend to produce under a fitted straight line?
What model prediction does a fan-shaped residual cloud challenge?
Why might plotting residuals by participant reveal a pattern hidden in a residual-versus-fitted plot?
State the model prediction, observed discrepancy, and inferential consequence for one pattern on this page.

title: The coefficient of determination
text:
The least-squares fit minimizes the sum of squared residuals. The coefficient of determination compares that fitted sum with the sum obtained from an intercept-only model.
If we ignored surprisal, we could assign every word the sample mean log reading time. The coefficient of determination, written R^2, measures the proportional reduction in squared error obtained by replacing that mean-only prediction with the fitted line.
Thus, R^2 compares the fitted line with a mean-only baseline based on the same observed responses.

title: The coefficient of determination
text:
Define the baseline error
The mean-only prediction for every observation is \bar y. Its total sum of squares (SST) is

\mathrm{SST}=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\bar y)^2.

The word total refers to observed variation around the sample mean. It does not refer to all variation that could occur in the population.
For the six constructed log reading times used on the fitting page,

\bar y=5.95.

The first response contributes

(5.78-5.95)^2=.0289

to the baseline error. Adding the six contributions gives

\mathrm{SST}=.0902.

title: The coefficient of determination
text:
Define the fitted-line error
The fitted line assigns observation i the conditional mean \widehat y_i. Its sum of squared errors (SSE) is

\mathrm{SSE}=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\widehat y_i)^2.

Since the line was chosen to minimize this quantity, its value cannot exceed the squared error of the mean-only line. For the six observations,

\mathrm{SSE}\approx.000914.

The fitted line thus leaves much less squared error than the mean-only prediction. We can express this reduction as

R^2
=1-\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{\mathrm{SST}}.

Substituting the two values gives

R^2
=1-\frac{.000914}{.0902}
\approx.9899.

The fitted line reduces observed squared error by about 98.99 percent relative to predicting the sample mean for every word.

title: The coefficient of determination
text:
Verify the calculation in R
We define the observations again so that the page can be executed on its own.


Code
reading_times <- data.frame(
  surprisal = 2:7,
  log_rt = c(5.78, 5.82, 5.93, 5.99, 6.05, 6.13)
)

fit <- lm(log_rt ~ surprisal, data = reading_times)

sst <- sum((reading_times$log_rt - mean(reading_times$log_rt))^2)
sse <- sum(residuals(fit)^2)
r_squared <- 1 - sse / sst

c(sst = sst, sse = sse, r_squared = r_squared)
summary(fit)$r.squared


The two calculations of R^2 agree. The first exposes the comparison, while the second retrieves the value stored by the fitted-model summary.

title: The coefficient of determination
text:
Interpret the baseline precisely
An R^2 of .60 would mean that the fitted line reduces squared error by 60 percent relative to the observed sample mean. It would not mean that 60 percent of each reading time has been explained. Nor would it mean that 60 percent of the causes of reading-time variation have been identified.
That stronger causal reading is not licensed. R^2 compares two collections of sample predictions. The comparison does not identify why the association occurs.
The baseline also matters. If the sample contains only a narrow range of surprisal values, total variation around the sample mean may be small. The same amount of residual error can then produce a lower R^2 than it would in a sample with a wider response range. Values from studies with different sampling designs are thus not automatically comparable.

title: The coefficient of determination
section: Understand why adding predictors raises sample R^2
text:
Understand why adding predictors raises sample R^2
Suppose we add another predictor to an ordinary least-squares model. The larger model could assign that new coefficient a value of zero and reproduce every fitted value from the smaller model. Thus its minimized squared error can stay the same or decrease, but it cannot increase. Since SST is unchanged, sample R^2 can stay the same or increase.
This mathematical property is not evidence that every added predictor supplies a useful generalization. It says only that a more flexible model can match the responses used to fit it at least as well. Later model-comparison pages develop separate tools for questions about predictions beyond those responses.

title: The coefficient of determination
text:
Keep the claim narrow
A large sample R^2 does not establish that the line is straight enough, that the conditional response variance is constant, that the observations are independent, or that the predictor has a causal effect. Each claim requires its own evidence.
The constructed data have R^2\approx.99 because the six responses were chosen to lie very close to a line. This makes the arithmetic easy to inspect. It should not set an expectation for the proportion of reading-time variation that a single lexical predictor will account for in real data.






NoteReconstruct the comparison




If SST is 100 and SSE is 40, calculate R^2 and state the baseline.
Why can adding a predictor never lower ordinary sample R^2?
Explain the variance-to-cause substitution.
What would R^2=0 say about the fitted line relative to the mean-only prediction?

title: Checking Poisson dispersion
text:
The Poisson-regression page imposed equality between the conditional mean and conditional variance. The deviance-residual page then showed why count discrepancies should be scaled relative to their fitted means. We now use that scaling to check the Poisson variance restriction.
A Poisson regression specifies both a conditional mean and a conditional variance. If an observation has expected count \lambda_i, then
\operatorname{E}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i)=\lambda_i
and
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i)=\lambda_i.
The equality of the mean and variance is not a general fact about counts. It is a restriction imposed by the Poisson distribution. The Poisson-distribution page introduced overdispersion for variation beyond this restriction. Here we diagnose it after predictors have supplied a different fitted mean for each observation.
This page introduces one diagnostic question: does the fitted Poisson distribution represent the amount of conditional variation in the observations?

title: Checking Poisson dispersion
text:
Focus on conditional variation
Suppose several comparable corpus samples each have an expected count of 4. A Poisson model also assigns those samples a variance of 4 and a standard deviation of 2. Counts close to 4 should be common. Counts such as 0 and 12 should be much less common.
Now suppose the observed samples contain many zeros alongside several counts above 15. Their unconditional variance may be large because the samples differ in genre, length, or predictor values. That fact alone does not diagnose the model. We must first compare each observation with the mean predicted for its own covariate values.
Overdispersion occurs when the conditional count variation is systematically larger than the fitted Poisson distributions allow.

title: Checking Poisson dispersion
text:
Scale each discrepancy
The raw residual is

y_i-\widehat{\lambda}_i.

Its size is hard to compare across observations. A discrepancy of 4 is large when the expected count is 1, but modest when the expected count is 100. The Pearson residual divides the raw discrepancy by the Poisson standard deviation:

r_{P,i}
=\frac{y_i-\widehat{\lambda}_i}
{\sqrt{\widehat{\lambda}_i}}.

Consider two observations. The first has observed count 5 and fitted mean 1. The second has observed count 104 and fitted mean 100. Both raw residuals equal 4. Their Pearson residuals differ:

r_{P,1}=\frac{5-1}{\sqrt{1}}=4,


r_{P,2}=\frac{104-100}{\sqrt{100}}=.4.

The first observation is four fitted standard deviations above its mean. The second is less than one half of a fitted standard deviation above its mean. Scaling reveals which discrepancy is surprising under the model.

title: Checking Poisson dispersion
text:
Summarize the residual variation
A common descriptive summary is the Pearson estimate of dispersion:

\widehat{\phi}
=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{P,i}^{2}}{n-p},

where p is the number of fitted coefficients. The denominator is the residual degrees of freedom.
If the Poisson variance is a reasonable description and the sample is sufficiently informative, the ratio should be near one. A value much larger than one means that the squared standardized discrepancies are collectively too large. A value below one indicates less residual variation than the Poisson model assigns.
pearson_residual <- residuals(fit, type = "pearson")

dispersion_ratio <-
  sum(pearson_residual^2) / df.residual(fit)

dispersion_ratio
There is no universal cutoff separating adequate and inadequate models. An estimate of 1.05 and an estimate of 8 do not raise the same concern, but their evidential meaning also depends on the number of observations, the fitted means, and the dependence among observations. Treat the Pearson estimate of dispersion as a diagnostic summary rather than an automatic decision rule.

title: Checking Poisson dispersion
text:
Locate the mismatch
One ratio cannot show where the mismatch occurs. A model may fit most observations well while failing for one register or one range of expected counts. We should inspect the Pearson residuals against fitted values and against the predictors already in the model.
plot(
  fitted(fit),
  residuals(fit, type = "pearson"),
  xlab = "Fitted count",
  ylab = "Pearson residual"
)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
A widening band suggests that the variance grows faster than the Poisson mean. A systematic curve suggests that the conditional mean is misspecified. A cluster of large residuals attached to one known subset suggests that the subset needs separate investigation.
These patterns matter because overdispersion describes a failure of the fitted variance relation, not its cause. Omitted predictors, an incorrect functional relation, dependence among observations, a different count distribution, or a second process that generates zeros may all produce excess conditional variation. The Pearson estimate of dispersion does not choose among those explanations.

title: Checking Poisson dispersion
text:
Keep diagnosis separate from repair
The appropriate conclusion from a large Pearson estimate of dispersion is narrow: the fitted Poisson variance appears too small for the observed conditional variation. We should then inspect the location of the mismatch and ask which part of the data-generating process the model omitted.
The next pages introduce possible repairs one at a time. A quasi-Poisson model changes the variance multiplier. A negative binomial model changes the response distribution. A zero-inflated model represents two routes to zero. None is licensed by a large Pearson estimate of dispersion alone.






NoteCheck the diagnosis



A Poisson model has a dispersion ratio of 6. What has the diagnostic established? What has it not established about the source of the extra variation?

title: Deviance residuals
text:
The deviance page defined total deviance relative to a saturated model, while the earlier residual page defined observation-level discrepancies. Deviance residuals divide total deviance into signed observation-level contributions.
Let d_i be observation i’s contribution to the deviance. The deviance residual is
r_i^{D}
=
\operatorname{sign}(y_i-\widehat\mu_i)
\sqrt{d_i}.
The sign tells us whether the observation lies above or below its fitted mean. The magnitude tells us how much it contributes to the total deviance.
This residual is scaled by the fitted response family because d_i is calculated from the likelihood for the declared response family.

title: Deviance residuals
section: Why raw residuals are not enough
text:
Why raw residuals are not enough
A raw residual is

y_i-\widehat\mu_i.

Under a Poisson model, a difference of three counts has a different meaning when the fitted count is one than when it is one hundred. Deviance residuals account for the response distribution when measuring mismatch.
For a Poisson response, the contribution is

d_i
=2\left[
y_i\log\frac{y_i}{\widehat\mu_i}
-(y_i-\widehat\mu_i)
\right],

with the first term treated as zero when y_i=0.
Suppose y_i=4 and \widehat\mu_i=1. The raw residual is 3, and

d_i
=2[4\log4-3]
\approx5.090.

The deviance residual is

r_i^D=\sqrt{5.090}\approx2.256.

Now suppose y_i=103 and \widehat\mu_i=100. The raw residual is again 3, but

d_i
=2\left[103\log\frac{103}{100}-3\right]
\approx.089.

The deviance residual is only about .299. A difference of three counts is much more surprising relative to a fitted mean of 1 than a fitted mean of 100 under the Poisson mean-variance relation.


Code
y <- c(4, 103)
mu <- c(1, 100)

contribution <- 2 * (y * log(y / mu) - (y - mu))
deviance_residual <- sign(y - mu) * sqrt(contribution)

data.frame(
  y = y,
  fitted_mean = mu,
  raw_residual = y - mu,
  deviance_residual = deviance_residual
)

title: Deviance residuals
section: Use residuals to locate model failure
text:
Use residuals to locate model failure
Plot deviance residuals against fitted values and theoretically relevant predictors. Also summarize them by speaker, item, lexical class, or other repeated units.


Code
count_data <- data.frame(
  predictor = 0:5,
  count = c(0, 1, 1, 3, 7, 11)
)

fit <- glm(count ~ predictor, family = poisson(), data = count_data)
dev_resid <- residuals(fit, type = "deviance")

plot(fitted(fit), dev_resid)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)


A curved center suggests a missing mean relation. A changing spread suggests that the family variance relation is inadequate. A cluster of large residuals in one group suggests omitted group structure.
The plot should be connected to a specific discrepancy. If large positive FSRs occur mainly in phrase-final positions, the model may underpredict counts there. If their spread grows with the fitted mean, the Poisson variance relation may be too restrictive.

title: Deviance residuals
text:
Do not expect perfect normality
Deviance residuals are constructed to be more symmetric than raw residuals, but they are not automatically independent standard normal observations. This is especially visible with binary data, where each response can take only two values.
Thus, a normality test on deviance residuals is not a general goodness of fit test for a generalized linear model. Use checks that reproduce the actual response and the discrepancy relevant to the scientific claim.
Using residual normality as a universal GLM approval criterion imports a familiar ordinary-linear-regression diagnostic without asking whether it follows from the fitted discrete response model.

title: Deviance residuals
text:
Connect local and global checks
The squared deviance residuals sum to the model deviance:

\sum_i (r_i^D)^2=D.

The total says how much discrepancy there is under this measure. The residual plot says where that discrepancy occurs. Both are needed for a useful diagnosis.
Squaring removes the signs. Two models can thus have similar total deviance while placing their positive and negative discrepancies in different linguistic conditions. The observation-level plot retains information that the sum discards.
The signed square root of a deviance contribution remains a model diagnostic, not a deletion rule. A large residual may identify miscoding, an omitted predictor, a rare but valid observation, or an inadequate family. Its source must be investigated.






NoteInterpret a deviance residual




What determines the sign of a deviance residual?
Why can the same raw count residual have different importance at different fitted means?
Why is a normality test on deviance residuals not a general model check?
Which information is lost when signed residuals are squared and summed?
Explain why residual normality is not a universal approval criterion for generalized linear models.

title: Modeling conditional scale
text:
The heteroscedasticity page diagnosed changes in conditional variance. Distributional regression represents such changes directly by giving more than one parameter of the response distribution its own predictor equation.
Ordinary linear regression usually gives predictors to the conditional mean and holds the conditional standard deviation fixed. If response variability is theoretically relevant, we can give the scale parameter its own predictor model.
Let
Y_i\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2).
Model the mean as usual:
\mu_i
=
\beta_0+\beta_1x_i.
Now model the log standard deviation:
\log\sigma_i
=
\gamma_0+\gamma_1x_i.
This is distributional regression. Different parameters of the response distribution receive separate predictor equations.
On this page, the new step is narrow: the conditional standard deviation receives one predictor. The mean and spread equations remain distinct, even when they use the same predictor.

title: Modeling conditional scale
text:
Keep the scale positive
The standard deviation must be positive. A straight line can be negative, so we model its logarithm and exponentiate:

\sigma_i
=
\exp(\gamma_0+\gamma_1x_i).

Suppose

\gamma_0=\log100
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\gamma_1=-.20.

At x=0,

\sigma(0)=100.

At x=1,

\sigma(1)=100e^{-.20}\approx81.9.

A one-unit predictor increase multiplies the conditional standard deviation by e^{-.20}\approx.819, an 18.1% decrease.
For a two-unit increase, the multiplier is

e^{2(-.20)}=e^{-.40}\approx.670.

The conditional standard deviation decreases by about 33.0 percent across that two-unit contrast. The change is multiplicative because the scale equation is additive on \log\sigma_i.
The coefficient \gamma_1 is not a change in the response mean. The mean coefficient remains \beta_1.
This gives two separate questions:

Does the center of the response distribution change with x?
Does the spread around that center change with x?

\beta_1 answers the first, while \gamma_1 answers the second. Interpreting one as the other confuses location with scale.

title: Modeling conditional scale
text:
Calculate two conditional distributions
Suppose the mean model has

\beta_0=6.2
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\beta_1=-.08,

while the scale model has

\gamma_0=\log(.20)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\gamma_1=-.20.

At x=0,

Y\mid x=0\sim\mathcal{N}(6.2,.20^2).

At x=2, the conditional mean is

6.2-.08(2)=6.04,

and the conditional standard deviation is

.20e^{-.20(2)}\approx.134.

Thus

Y\mid x=2\sim\mathcal{N}(6.04,.134^2).

The second distribution has both a lower center and a narrower spread. One equation does not stand in for the other.
We can verify the calculations directly:


Code
x <- c(0, 2)

conditional_mean <- 6.2 - .08 * x
conditional_sd <- .20 * exp(-.20 * x)

data.frame(
  x = x,
  conditional_mean = conditional_mean,
  conditional_sd = conditional_sd
)

title: Modeling conditional scale
text:
Fit separate formulas
In brms, the mean and scale formulas can be written explicitly:
fit_distributional <- brm(
  bf(
    log_rt ~ frequency + duration,
    sigma ~ frequency
  ),
  family = gaussian(),
  data = lexical_data
)
The second formula predicts the conditional standard deviation on its log scale. A custom Stan model writes the same two equations before the observation statement.
In brms, the scale formula is interpreted on the log scale for a Gaussian family. Thus a positive frequency coefficient in the sigma formula multiplies residual spread upward, while a negative coefficient multiplies it downward. The coefficient table should be translated into values of \sigma_i at theoretically relevant predictor values.
The mean and scale formulas need priors in a Bayesian fit. A prior on \gamma_1 can be inspected by drawing scale curves across the observed frequency range. Priors that routinely imply residual standard deviations near zero or many times the response range need reconsideration.

title: Modeling conditional scale
text:
Read predictions as distributions
Distributional regression should be checked by simulating complete responses, not only by plotting fitted means. At low and high frequency, compare the observed and predicted center, spread, and tails.
predicted <- posterior_predict(
  fit_distributional,
  newdata = prediction_grid
)
A successful scale model should reproduce the change in conditional spread that motivated it. A lower information criterion without the intended variance pattern would not establish that the model solved the scientific problem.
Useful checks compare observations and replicated responses within predictor regions. For low and high frequency, calculate a spread statistic such as the standard deviation or an interquantile range. Then ask whether the observed contrast falls within the distribution produced by the model.
The mean model must be checked at the same time. A curved mean that is forced to be linear can make residual spread appear to change because some predictor regions have larger systematic misses. Adding a predictor to the scale equation of a misspecified mean can absorb those misses without representing the intended source of variability.
The scale equation may then absorb systematic errors in the mean equation. Model criticism should first ask whether the residual center remains near zero, then ask whether its spread changes.

title: Modeling conditional scale
section: Avoid giving every parameter every predictor
text:
Avoid giving every parameter every predictor
The scale formula needs a linguistic or measurement rationale. Adding all mean predictors to all distributional parameters can make the model weakly identified and difficult to interpret.
For a frequency hypothesis, compare a constant-scale model with one prespecified frequency term. Later extensions can add participant or item variation when the design supports it.
The predictor also needs enough observations across its range to estimate spread. A mean can be estimated from relatively few observations at a predictor value, but local variance is harder to learn. Sparse edges of the range may leave \gamma_1 strongly dependent on its prior.






NoteRead the scale equation




Why is a log link used for \sigma_i?
Which coefficient describes the change in the conditional mean?
What posterior predictive pattern would show that the scale model is useful?
Calculate the multiplier on \sigma for a three-unit increase when \gamma_1=.10.
Explain how a scale equation can absorb systematic errors in a misspecified mean equation.

title: Exposure offsets
text:
The Poisson-regression page interpreted coefficients for counts observed over a common window. When observation windows differ, an exposure offset separates the expected rate from the number of opportunities.
Two corpus documents each contain 10 relative clauses. The first has 1,000 words and the second has 10,000 words.
Their counts are equal, but their rates differ:
10/1000=.010
and
10/10000=.001.
The longer document supplied ten times as many opportunities for a construction to occur.
A count combines how often an event occurs per opportunity with how many opportunities were observed. A rate separates those quantities.

title: Exposure offsets
text:
Separate rate from exposure
Let t_i>0 be the exposure for observation i. Let r_i be the expected event rate per exposure unit. Then the expected count is

\lambda_i=t_ir_i.

Take logarithms:

\log\lambda_i
=\log t_i+\log r_i.

Model the log rate with predictors:

\log r_i
=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i.

Substitution gives

\log\lambda_i
=\log t_i+\beta_0+\beta_1x_i.

The term \log t_i is the exposure offset.
The offset is known from the observation design. It enters the linear predictor without an estimated coefficient. The remaining coefficients describe expected rates after exposure has been accounted for.

title: Exposure offsets
text:
Reconstruct two expected counts
Suppose the expected relative-clause rate is .002 per word. For a 1,000-word document,

\lambda_1=1000(.002)=2.

For a 10,000-word document,

\lambda_2=10000(.002)=20.

The expected counts differ by a factor of 10 even though the expected rates are identical. The offset lets the Poisson mean represent that difference.
On the log scale,

\log\lambda_2-\log\lambda_1
=\log10000-\log1000
=\log10.

Exponentiating returns the expected-count ratio 10.

title: Exposure offsets
section: Why its coefficient is fixed at one
text:
Why its coefficient is fixed at one
The equation assumes that doubling exposure doubles the expected count while leaving the expected rate unchanged:

\lambda_i
=t_i\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i).

The coefficient on \log t_i is fixed at 1 because exposure defines the rate denominator.
If we estimated a free coefficient instead, we would ask whether counts scale proportionally with exposure. That is a different model and a different scientific question.
The fixed coefficient does not say that every document with twice the word count must contain exactly twice the observed clauses. It says that the expected count doubles when the modeled rate is held fixed. Poisson variation still produces different observed counts around that expectation.
Interpreting proportional expected counts as deterministic observed counts is an error.

title: Exposure offsets
text:
Fit an offset in R


Code
documents <- data.frame(
  genre = factor(c("conversation", "conversation",
                   "news", "news")),
  word_count = c(500, 2000, 1000, 4000),
  relative_clause_count = c(2, 5, 7, 21)
)

fit_rate <- glm(
  relative_clause_count ~ genre + offset(log(word_count)),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = documents
)

coef(fit_rate)


The genre coefficient now compares expected relative-clause rates per word, not raw document counts.
To obtain rates, predict for an exposure of one word:


Code
genre_rates <- data.frame(
  genre = levels(documents$genre),
  word_count = 1
)

genre_rates$rate_per_word <- predict(
  fit_rate,
  newdata = genre_rates,
  type = "response"
)

genre_rates$rate_per_1000_words <-
  1000 * genre_rates$rate_per_word

genre_rates


Setting exposure to one returns the fitted rate per exposure unit. Multiplying by 1,000 changes only the reporting unit.

title: Exposure offsets
text:
Define the opportunity carefully
Word count is one possible exposure for document-level construction counts. It assumes every word contributes proportionally to the opportunity for a relative clause. A theory may instead define opportunities as noun phrases, clauses, or positions that license a particular dependency.
These denominators answer different questions. A rate per word describes corpus density. A rate per noun phrase may describe the probability that a noun phrase is modified by a relative clause. The most convenient denominator is not automatically the theoretically relevant one.
Substituting an available denominator for the theoretically intended opportunity can change the target rate. The offset can be numerically correct and still answer the wrong rate question.

title: Exposure offsets
section: Distinguish an offset from a predictor
text:
Distinguish an offset from a predictor
A predictor receives an estimated coefficient because the analysis asks how the rate changes with that variable. An offset receives a fixed coefficient because it defines how the count scales with known opportunity.
Adding log(word_count) as an ordinary predictor would estimate a scaling exponent:

\log\lambda_i
=\beta_0+\gamma\log t_i+\beta_1x_i.

The offset model fixes \gamma=1. Estimating \gamma asks whether expected counts scale sublinearly or superlinearly with document length. That may be a useful hypothesis, but it no longer defines a simple rate per word.
Exposure units must be meaningful and reported. Rates per word, minute, speaker turn, or opportunity defined by a syntactic context answer different questions.
Zero exposure is not allowed because \log0 is undefined and no event can occur without an opportunity. Such rows usually indicate that the observation unit or denominator needs to be reconsidered.






NoteCheck proportional exposure




If two observations have the same predictors but one has three times the exposure, what ratio of expected counts does the offset model impose?
Why does this claim concern expected counts rather than observed counts?
Distinguish an exposure offset from an estimated exposure predictor.
Explain how an available denominator can define the wrong target rate.

title: Fitting a linear regression
text:
The straight-line mean specifies what the coefficients mean. The earlier page on maximum likelihood supplied a general fitting principle. This page shows how least squares and maximum likelihood select the same coefficient estimates when errors are normally distributed with constant variance.
Consider six constructed word observations:
We want values of \beta_0 and \beta_1 that place a line near these points. The mean function tells us what a candidate line means, but it does not yet tell us which candidate to choose. We need a rule that compares whole lines against the observed responses.

title: Fitting a linear regression
text:
Define each fitted value
For observation i, a candidate line gives

\widehat{y}_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i.

The vertical discrepancy between the observed and fitted response is

y_i-\widehat{y}_i
=y_i-(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i).

title: Fitting a linear regression
text:
Add squared discrepancies
Least squares chooses the line that minimizes

\operatorname{SSE}(\beta_0,\beta_1)
=\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[y_i-(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)\right]^2.

Squaring prevents positive and negative discrepancies from canceling and gives greater weight to larger misses.
For instance, residuals of .2 and -.2 sum to zero even though neither observation lies on the line. Their squared values sum to .08. The squared error objective thus records both misses without allowing one direction to erase the other.
The objective evaluates a complete candidate line. Moving the intercept or slope changes several fitted values at once, so the coefficient estimates must be chosen jointly.
When errors are normally distributed with constant variance, the coefficient values that minimize this sum also maximize the likelihood.
To see the connection, the normal log likelihood for fixed \sigma can be written as

\ell(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma)
=C-n\log\sigma
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[y_i-(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)\right]^2,

where C does not depend on the coefficients. For a fixed positive value of \sigma, increasing the squared-error sum lowers the log likelihood. Thus the coefficient values with the smallest sum also have the largest normal likelihood.
This equivalence does not say that squared error is a universally appropriate fitting rule. It follows from the normal likelihood. A binary response or a count response requires a different probability model, and later pages derive the fitting objectives implied by those models.

title: Fitting a linear regression
text:
Derive the two coefficient estimates
The least-squares slope for one predictor is

\widehat\beta_1
=\frac{
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)
}{
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar x)^2
}.
