The numerator measures how predictor and response deviations move together. The denominator measures the spread of the predictor. Their ratio gives response change per predictor unit.
This expression also explains why the slope is not obtained by averaging the ratios y_i/x_i. Both variables must first be expressed relative to their own means. Otherwise the calculation confounds the line’s vertical location with its change across the predictor.
For the six observations,

\bar x=4.5,
\qquad
\bar y=5.95,


\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)=1.25,

and

\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2=17.5.

Thus

\widehat\beta_1
=\frac{1.25}{17.5}
\approx.0714.

The fitted line passes through the point (\bar x,\bar y), so the intercept is

\begin{aligned}
\widehat\beta_0
&=\bar y-\widehat\beta_1\bar x\\
&=5.95-.0714(4.5)\\
&\approx5.629.
\end{aligned}

Thus the fitted conditional mean is

\widehat m(x)=5.629+.0714x.

title: Fitting a linear regression
text:
Fit the line in R


Code
reading_times <- data.frame(
  surprisal = 2:7,
  log_rt = c(5.78, 5.82, 5.93, 5.99, 6.05, 6.13)
)

fit <- lm(log_rt ~ surprisal, data = reading_times)
coef(fit)


The formula has three parts:



syntax
role




log_rt
response


~
“is modeled as a function of”


surprisal
predictor



The fitted coefficients define

\widehat{m}(x)
=\widehat{\beta}_0+\widehat{\beta}_1x.

For this fit, the output should return an intercept near 5.629 and a slope near .0714. The slope says that the fitted conditional mean increases by about .0714 log-time units for each one-unit increase in surprisal. It does not say that every observed response increases by that amount, since individual responses vary around the line.
The software result is useful as a check on the hand derivation. But the hand derivation supplies the interpretation: lm() has selected the same line that minimizes the squared residuals.

title: Fitting a linear regression
text:
Obtain fitted conditional means


Code
reading_times$fitted <- fitted(fit)
reading_times


Each fitted value is the model’s estimated conditional mean at that observation’s surprisal. It is not a claim that the individual response must equal the line.

title: Fitting a linear regression
text:
Calculate the residuals
The residual for observation i is the observed response minus its fitted conditional mean:

e_i=y_i-\widehat m(x_i).

The first word has fitted mean

5.629+.0714(2)\approx5.7718,

so its residual is approximately

5.78-5.7718=.0082.

A positive residual places the observed response above the line. A negative residual places it below the line. With an intercept in the fitted model, the residuals sum to zero up to numerical precision. This zero sum is a consequence of the fitting rule, not evidence that the model is adequate.


Code
sum(residuals(fit))
sum(residuals(fit)^2)


The second value is the minimized squared-error sum. Any other intercept and slope produce a sum that is at least as large for these observations.

title: Fitting a linear regression
text:
Separate fitting from evaluation
The fitted line is the best line under the declared squared-error rule. This is a narrow claim. It does not establish that a line is a good representation of the conditional mean, that the conditional response variance is constant, or that the observations are conditionally independent.
The best-fitting line within a model family is not necessarily an adequate model. Optimization answers which member of the chosen model family fits best. Adequacy asks whether that family captures the patterns needed for the linguistic question. Residual checks later provide evidence about the second question.
The coefficient estimates summarize this one sample. The next page studies how such estimates vary across possible samples.






NoteCheck the objective




If a candidate line produces residuals -.1, .2, and -.3, calculate its sum of squared errors for those three observations.
Why would the unsquared residual sum be a poor fitting objective?
Use the fitted equation to calculate the conditional mean at 6 bits of surprisal.
Explain the optimization-adequacy substitution in this example.

title: Components of a generalized linear model
text:
A generalized linear model, or GLM, combines a response distribution from the exponential family, a linear predictor, and a link function. The preceding page introduced the link and inverse link. The next page on the exponential family states the formal restriction on the response distribution. For now, normal, Bernoulli, and Poisson distributions supply the examples.
Build the model in three steps. The response family states what one response can be and how its variance relates to its mean, the linear predictor states how predictors combine, and the inverse link maps that combination to a valid conditional mean.
crumbs: Components of a generalized linear model

title: Components of a generalized linear model
text:
Step 1: choose the response family
The response family must match the possible values of Y.



response
possible family




continuous real-valued measurement
normal


binary choice
Bernoulli


nonnegative count
Poisson



The family also specifies how the conditional variance relates to the conditional mean.
For a Bernoulli response, the mean is a probability \pi_i and the variance is \pi_i(1-\pi_i). For a Poisson response, the mean and variance are both \lambda_i. The family thus contributes more than the range of possible observations.
crumbs: Components of a generalized linear model

title: Components of a generalized linear model
text:
Step 2: recall the linear predictor
As introduced on the design-matrix page, the linear predictor is

\eta_i
=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_px_{ip}.

Because the coefficients and predictor values are real numbers, \eta_i can take any value on the real line.
The coefficients are additive on this scale. Increasing x_{i1} by one changes \eta_i by \beta_1 while other predictors are held fixed.
The linear predictor does not itself need to satisfy the response constraints. It is an intermediate representation. A value of \eta_i=3 is neither a probability nor an expected count until an inverse link interprets it.
crumbs: Components of a generalized linear model

title: Components of a generalized linear model
text:
Step 3: use the inverse link
Let

\mu_i=\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i].

The inverse-link function maps the unconstrained linear predictor into the mean values allowed by the response family:

\mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i).

Equivalently,

g(\mu_i)=\eta_i.

For ordinary linear regression, the identity inverse link gives

g^{-1}(\eta)=\eta.

The conditional mean can be any real value, so no transformation is needed.
For a Bernoulli response, the inverse link must map the real line into (0,1). For a count response, it must map into positive expected counts.
crumbs: Components of a generalized linear model

title: Components of a generalized linear model
text:
Assemble a Bernoulli GLM
Suppose Y_i=1 marks an in completion and Y_i=0 marks a for completion. Let x_i be a centered duration measure. A Bernoulli GLM with an inverse-logit mapping is

Y_i\mid x_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i),


\eta_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,

and

\pi_i=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta_i}}.

Take \beta_0=-.40 and \beta_1=.70. At x=0,

\eta(0)=-.40

and

\pi(0)=\frac{1}{1+e^{.40}}\approx.401.

At x=2,

\eta(2)=-.40+.70(2)=1.00

and

\pi(2)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-1}}\approx.731.

The duration contrast changes the linear predictor by 1.4 and the completion probability by about .330 over this particular interval.


Code
x <- c(0, 2)
eta <- -.40 + .70 * x
pi <- plogis(eta)

data.frame(x = x, eta = eta, probability = pi)


Each row now has a complete response distribution. At x=0, the model assigns probability about .401 to response 1 and .599 to response 0. It does not assign probability to values between them.
crumbs: Components of a generalized linear model

title: Components of a generalized linear model
text:
Keep the two scales visible
A coefficient describes an additive change on the \eta scale. The corresponding response-scale change depends on the inverse link.
With a nonlinear inverse link, the same coefficient-sized change in \eta can produce different probability changes at different starting values.
Thus every GLM interpretation should state whether it concerns

the linear-predictor scale; or
the response-mean scale.

The distinction is particularly important for a nonlinear inverse link. The coefficient \beta_1=.70 is a constant change in \eta per duration unit. It does not say that probability increases by .70, and it does not imply one constant probability difference at every starting value.
crumbs: Components of a generalized linear model

title: Components of a generalized linear model
section: Do not omit the response distribution
text:
Do not omit the response distribution
Writing only

\pi_i=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)

describes the conditional mean but leaves the observation statement implicit. The full GLM also says that Y_i is Bernoulli given that mean. This statement supplies the conditional variance and the likelihood used for inference.
A mean equation is not a complete probability model. Omitting the response distribution makes it difficult to see whether the family matches the measurement or which variation assumptions the fit uses.
crumbs: Components of a generalized linear model

title: Components of a generalized linear model
text:
Check each part separately
These three model components suggest three checks:

Does the family assign probability only to possible observations?
Does the linear predictor contain the comparisons required by the theory?
Does the inverse link turn every possible \eta into a valid mean?

A model can pass one check and fail another. A Poisson family has count support, but a linear predictor may omit exposure. A valid inverse logit keeps probabilities bounded, but the predictor may encode an uninterpretable category contrast.
The next pages examine a common mathematical form for response families and the data summaries those families retain.






NoteCheck the ranges




Why can \eta_i remain unconstrained even when \mu_i must be a probability?
Recalculate the displayed Bernoulli prediction at x=1.
Which component of a generalized linear model supplies the mean-variance relation?
Explain why a conditional mean equation is not a complete probability model.
crumbs: Components of a generalized linear model

title: Changing conditional variance
text:
The linear-regression checks used changes in residual spread to diagnose a failure of the constant-variance assumption. The standard statistical term for such a change in conditional variance is heteroscedasticity.
Suppose a phonetic model predicts vowel duration from local articulation rate. Durations at slow rates may cluster tightly, while durations at fast rates may vary more because speakers use different reduction strategies.
The ordinary linear regression model presented earlier assumes
Y_i\mid x_i
\sim
\mathcal{N}(\mu_i,\sigma^2).
The conditional mean \mu_i may change with articulation rate, but the conditional standard deviation \sigma is fixed.
Heteroscedasticity means that the conditional variance changes across observations:
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid x_i)=\sigma_i^2.
The model is homoscedastic because one \sigma describes every predictor value. Heteroscedasticity is a mismatch between that assumption and a response whose conditional spread changes.

title: Changing conditional variance
section: Separate a mean pattern from a variance pattern
text:
Separate a mean pattern from a variance pattern
Consider two articulation-rate bands.



rate band
fitted mean duration
residual SD




slow
100 ms
10 ms


fast
70 ms
30 ms



The difference between 100 and 70 milliseconds is a mean pattern. The difference between 10 and 30 milliseconds is a variance pattern. A model can represent the first while missing the second.
The two distinctions can be reconstructed from six durations. Suppose the slow group contains 90, 100, and 110 milliseconds, while the fast group contains 40, 70, and 100 milliseconds. Their means are 100 and 70, and their sample standard deviations are 10 and 30.


Code
vowels <- data.frame(
  rate = rep(c("slow", "fast"), each = 3),
  duration = c(90, 100, 110, 40, 70, 100)
)

aggregate(
  duration ~ rate,
  data = vowels,
  FUN = function(x) c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x))
)


Pooling all six responses into one standard deviation would conceal the fact that the fast group is three times as variable on this scale.

title: Changing conditional variance
text:
Inspect residual spread directly
A residual-versus-fitted plot should be read vertically. At each fitted value, ask how wide the residual cloud is.


Code
fit <- lm(duration ~ rate, data = vowels)

plot(
  fitted(fit),
  residuals(fit),
  xlab = "fitted mean",
  ylab = "residual"
)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)


A fan shape suggests that conditional variance changes with the fitted mean. But fitted values can combine several predictors, so residuals should also be plotted against theoretically relevant predictors such as articulation rate, boundary position, or speaker group.
Group summaries provide a second view:


Code
vowels$residual <- residuals(fit)
aggregate(residual ~ rate, data = vowels, FUN = sd)


The groups are descriptive. They help locate the pattern but do not define the final variance model.
The grouping choice can create or hide a pattern. Very wide bins mix predictor values whose spreads differ. Very narrow bins contain too few observations to estimate spread reliably. A residual plot retains the continuous predictor, while grouped summaries provide an interpretable second view.

title: Changing conditional variance
text:
Understand the inferential consequence
Ordinary least-squares coefficient estimates can remain centered on the intended linear projection under some forms of heteroscedasticity. Their usual standard errors, however, rely on the constant-variance model and can be wrong.
The direction of the error depends on where response spread and predictor information occur. If the most extreme predictor values also have the widest residual distributions, the slope can be less precise than the homoscedastic calculation suggests. There is no rule that heteroscedasticity always makes every standard error too small.
The mismatch also matters for prediction. A model with one \sigma may produce intervals that are too wide for common words and too narrow for rare words.
In the vowel example, one pooled \sigma may produce intervals that are too wide for slow-rate durations and too narrow for fast-rate durations. The conditional means can be approximately correct while the predictive intervals fail in opposite directions.
An adequate mean fit does not establish an adequate response distribution. Residual checks must examine both the center and vertical spread.
Three repairs answer different questions:

heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors adjust coefficient uncertainty while leaving the variance pattern undescribed;
a response transformation changes the scale on which variance is modeled;
distributional regression models \sigma_i directly.

The next page takes the third approach.
The choice depends on the scientific target. If spread is a nuisance for slope uncertainty, an uncertainty correction may be enough. If speaker variability at fast rates is theoretically meaningful, a model for \sigma_i answers the more direct question.






NoteSeparate center from spread




Which table column describes a mean pattern, and which describes a variance pattern?
Why can one residual plot conceal a speaker-specific variance pattern?
Which repair would you choose if variation itself bears on the linguistic claim?
Why does heteroscedasticity not always move every standard error in the same direction?
Explain why an adequate conditional mean does not establish an adequate response distribution.

title: Influence
text:
The preceding page defined leverage from predictor position alone. But an unusual position need not change the fitted coefficients. Influence measures the extent to which a fitted result depends on a particular observation.
Influence asks a case-deletion question: how much would the fit change if observation i were not used? This question combines the observation’s predictor position with the mismatch between its response and the fitted conditional mean.

title: Influence
text:
Compare two edge observations
Consider predictor values

\mathbf{x}=(2,3,4,5,11).

The point at x=11 has high leverage. Now consider two possible responses for that point.
In dataset A, the responses are

\mathbf{y}_A=(6.1,6.4,6.5,6.8,8.0).

In dataset B, only the last response changes:

\mathbf{y}_B=(6.1,6.4,6.5,6.8,10.5).

The last observation has the same leverage in both datasets because the predictor values are identical. But it should affect the fitted slope much more in dataset B because its response lies farther from the relation supported by the four central observations.

title: Influence
text:
Ask the deletion question directly
We can fit each dataset with and without the edge observation:


Code
dataset_a <- data.frame(
  x = c(2, 3, 4, 5, 11),
  y = c(6.1, 6.4, 6.5, 6.8, 8.0)
)

dataset_b <- transform(
  dataset_a,
  y = c(6.1, 6.4, 6.5, 6.8, 10.5)
)

fit_a <- lm(y ~ x, data = dataset_a)
fit_b <- lm(y ~ x, data = dataset_b)

fit_a_without_edge <- lm(y ~ x, data = dataset_a[-5, ])
fit_b_without_edge <- lm(y ~ x, data = dataset_b[-5, ])

rbind(
  a_full = coef(fit_a),
  a_without_edge = coef(fit_a_without_edge),
  b_full = coef(fit_b),
  b_without_edge = coef(fit_b_without_edge)
)


Removing the edge observation changes the dataset B slope much more. This is a direct answer to the case-deletion question for one coefficient.

title: Influence
section: Summarize case deletion with Cook’s distance
text:
Summarize case deletion with Cook’s distance
Refitting a model after deleting every observation can produce many coefficient comparisons. Cook’s distance summarizes the overall change in fitted values when observation i is deleted:

D_i
=\frac{e_i^2}{p\widehat\sigma^2}
\frac{h_{ii}}{(1-h_{ii})^2},

where e_i is the residual, h_{ii} is the leverage, \widehat\sigma^2 is the fitted residual variance, and p is the number of estimated coefficients.
The formula exposes the two ingredients. A larger residual increases influence, and larger leverage increases influence. Neither ingredient alone guarantees a large Cook’s distance.


Code
cbind(
  x = dataset_a$x,
  leverage = hatvalues(fit_a),
  cooks_a = cooks.distance(fit_a),
  cooks_b = cooks.distance(fit_b)
)


The last observation has the same leverage in both columns but a different Cook’s distance. Its response determines whether the unusual predictor position substantially changes the fit.

title: Influence
section: Treat a large value as a question
text:
Treat a large value as a question
A large Cook’s distance identifies an observation that deserves investigation. It does not decide that the observation is invalid. The useful sequence is:

verify the measurement, transcription, and coding;
check whether the observation belongs to the population targeted by the study;
inspect which coefficient or fitted region changes under deletion; and
report whether the theoretical conclusion depends on the observation.

These steps answer different questions. A miscoded value can be corrected. A valid but unusual token cannot be deleted merely because it changes the result.
Deleting an observation only because it produces an inconvenient effect estimate changes the sample using information about the desired conclusion. It can make the reported uncertainty much too small.

title: Influence
text:
Connect influence to linguistic sampling
Suppose a study of a rare syntactic construction contains one verb with many tokens in an unusual frame. Row-level Cook’s distances ask about individual tokens. But the theoretical result may depend on the verb as a group. Deleting one token at a time may then make every value look modest even though deleting the verb changes the conclusion.
The diagnostic unit should match the sampling claim. If the intended generalization concerns verbs, a verb-level deletion analysis is informative. If it concerns speakers, a speaker-level analysis is informative. This principle does not require a multilevel model, though later models represent these grouped sources of variation directly.

title: Influence
text:
Report the sensitivity
An influence analysis is most useful when it reports the quantity that changes. For instance: “Deleting verb V changed the frame coefficient from .42 to .17, while deleting any other verb changed it by less than .04.” This statement lets the reader evaluate the concentration of evidence.
A statement that “no influential observations were found” is weaker unless the analysis defines the diagnostic, the unit of deletion, and the consequence that was examined.






NoteAnswer the case-deletion question




Why can two observations with the same leverage have different influence?
Which two quantities enter Cook’s distance?
Why does a large Cook’s distance not by itself license deletion?
If the scientific generalization concerns verbs, why might deleting one row at a time answer the wrong question?

title: Intraclass correlation
text: The random-intercept page showed that responses from the same group share a deviation. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) measures the resulting model-implied correlation for a linear random-intercept model with normally distributed errors and random intercepts.

title: Intraclass correlation
section: Begin with the intercept only model
text:
Begin with the intercept only model
Suppose

Y_{ij}=\beta_0+b_j+\varepsilon_{ij},

with

b_j\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau^2)

and

\varepsilon_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2).

The response has two sources of variation. The group deviation b_j is shared by every observation in group j. The residual \varepsilon_{ij} belongs to one observation.

title: Intraclass correlation
text:
Derive the shared covariance
Consider two distinct observations i and i' from group j. Their covariance is

\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{ij},Y_{i'j})
=\operatorname{Cov}(b_j+\varepsilon_{ij},
b_j+\varepsilon_{i'j}).

The residuals are independent of each other and of the group deviation under the model. The only shared term is b_j. Thus

\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{ij},Y_{i'j})=\tau^2.

Each response has variance

\operatorname{Var}(Y_{ij})
=\tau^2+\sigma^2.

Correlation is covariance divided by the product of the standard deviations. Because the two responses have the same variance, their correlation is

\operatorname{ICC}
=\frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2+\sigma^2}.

The numerator is the between-group variance. The denominator is the response variance after averaging over the random intercept. Thus the ICC is the between-group variance divided by the marginal response variance in this intercept-only model.

title: Intraclass correlation
text:
Work through a numerical value
Suppose participant variance is 100 and residual variance is 300. Then

\operatorname{ICC}
=\frac{100}{100+300}
=.25.

Two trials from the same participant have model-implied correlation .25. Equivalently, one quarter of the response variance, conditional on the fixed intercept but marginal over participant deviations, is attributed to stable participant baseline differences under this model.
If participant variance were zero, the ICC would be zero. Sharing a participant would add no response similarity. If residual variance became very small relative to participant variance, the ICC would approach one.

title: Intraclass correlation
section: Estimate it from a fitted model
text:
Estimate it from a fitted model
For a linear random-intercept model fit with lme4, the variance components can be extracted and combined:
variance_table <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit_intercepts))

participant_variance <- variance_table$vcov[
  variance_table$grp == "participant"
]

residual_variance <- sigma(fit_intercepts)^2

icc_participant <-
  participant_variance /
  (participant_variance + residual_variance)

icc_participant
In a crossed participant and item model, the denominator may include participant variance, item variance, and residual variance. The relevant numerator depends on which pair of observations is being compared. Two responses from the same participant but different items share the participant component. Two responses to the same item from different participants share the item component.

title: Intraclass correlation
text:
Keep the interpretation model specific
Adding predictors can change both \tau^2 and \sigma^2. The ICC is thus conditional on the fitted mean structure. An intercept only ICC and an ICC after condition and speaker age have been included need not match.
A model with a varying predictor association also gives pairs different covariances at different predictor values. One constant ICC no longer describes every pair. Likewise, logistic and Poisson mixed models do not have a freely estimated normally distributed residual on the response scale. Their ICC definitions require additional scale choices.
This model dependence is not a defect. It means that the ICC summarizes the particular probability model being used. Report the model and the variance components alongside the ratio.

title: Intraclass correlation
text:
Connect the ICC to replication
When the ICC is positive, repeated observations from one participant contain less independent information than the same number of observations from different participants. More trials can estimate one participant’s baseline more precisely. More participants provide replication across the participant population.
The ICC does not declare repeated trials useless. It identifies why row count and participant count answer different information questions.






NoteCheck the shared variance



Two responses share an item but not a participant in a crossed intercept model. Which variance component belongs in their covariance? Why is the full denominator larger than that component?


The next page examines the partially pooled group deviations returned by the fitted model.

title: Iteratively reweighted least squares
text:
The least-squares page derived a closed-form coefficient solution from a quadratic objective. In many generalized linear models, the conditional mean is a nonlinear function of the coefficients on the response scale, so maximum-likelihood estimation requires an iterative numerical method.
One common procedure is iteratively reweighted least squares.
The procedure replaces one nonlinear optimization with a sequence of local weighted linear problems. Each update is easy to solve, but its working responses and weights are valid only near the current coefficient values.

title: Iteratively reweighted least squares
text:
Start from provisional coefficients
Given provisional coefficients \boldsymbol\beta^{(t)}, compute the linear predictor

\boldsymbol\eta^{(t)}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta^{(t)}

and the fitted means

\boldsymbol\mu^{(t)}=g^{-1}(\boldsymbol\eta^{(t)}).

These means determine the conditional variance under the chosen response family.
The superscript (t) marks an iteration, not an exponent. Iteration 0 begins from initial coefficients, iteration 1 uses the first update, and the process continues until a declared convergence rule is met.

title: Iteratively reweighted least squares
text:
Construct a local linear problem
Near the current fitted values, approximate the nonlinear relation between the response and the linear predictor. This produces a working response

z_i
=
\eta_i^{(t)}
+
(y_i-\mu_i^{(t)})
\left.
\frac{d\eta_i}{d\mu_i}
\right|_{\mu_i^{(t)}}.

It also produces a weight for each observation. The weight depends on the variance function and the slope of the link.
The working response z_i is not a transformed linguistic measurement. It is a temporary numerical quantity constructed to approximate the log likelihood near the current fit. It changes at the next iteration.

title: Iteratively reweighted least squares
text:
Solve weighted least squares
Using the working responses and weights, update the coefficients by solving

\boldsymbol\beta^{(t+1)}
=
(\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}
\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{z}.

Then recompute the means, working responses, and weights. Continue until the likelihood or coefficient vector changes by less than a tolerance.

title: Iteratively reweighted least squares
section: Work through an intercept-only Bernoulli update
text:
Work through an intercept-only Bernoulli update
Suppose five trials produce

\mathbf y=(1,1,0,1,0).

Fit one Bernoulli probability with a logit link. The linear predictor is the intercept alone:

\eta_i=\beta_0.

Begin at

\beta_0^{(0)}=0.

The fitted probability is .5 for every observation. For logistic IRLS, the working response is

z_i
=\eta_i+
\frac{y_i-\pi_i}{\pi_i(1-\pi_i)}.

At \eta_i=0 and \pi_i=.5, a success has

z_i=0+\frac{1-.5}{.5(1-.5)}=2,

while a failure has

z_i=0+\frac{0-.5}{.5(1-.5)}=-2.

Thus

\mathbf z^{(0)}=(2,2,-2,2,-2).

Every initial weight is

w_i^{(0)}=\pi_i(1-\pi_i)=.25.

With equal weights and an intercept only, the weighted least-squares update is the mean of the working responses:

\beta_0^{(1)}
=\frac{2+2-2+2-2}{5}
=.4.

The new fitted probability is

\pi^{(1)}
=\frac{1}{1+e^{-.4}}
\approx.599.

The observed success proportion is 3/5=.6, so one update has already moved close to the maximum-likelihood probability.


Code
y <- c(1, 1, 0, 1, 0)
eta_0 <- rep(0, length(y))
pi_0 <- plogis(eta_0)
weights_0 <- pi_0 * (1 - pi_0)
z_0 <- eta_0 + (y - pi_0) / weights_0
beta_1 <- weighted.mean(z_0, weights_0)

c(
  updated_intercept = beta_1,
  updated_probability = plogis(beta_1),
  exact_intercept = qlogis(mean(y))
)


The exact maximum-likelihood intercept is

\operatorname{logit}(.6)\approx.4055.

Further IRLS steps close the small remaining gap.

title: Iteratively reweighted least squares
text:
Why the weights change
In a Bernoulli model, observations with fitted probability near zero or one have a different conditional variance from observations near one half. The local information about the coefficients thus differs across observations and across iterations. Reweighting reflects that changing information.
For the intercept-only example, all observations share a probability and thus a weight within each iteration. With predictors, fitted probabilities differ across rows, so the weights differ as well. The weighted linear problem is then local to both the current coefficients and each observation’s predictor row.

title: Iteratively reweighted least squares
text:
What convergence means
Algorithmic convergence means the updates stabilized. It does not mean the model fits the data well, that the maximum is well identified, or that the predictors answer the linguistic question. Warnings about nonconvergence, fitted probabilities at boundaries, or a nearly singular design matrix require investigation.
Numerical convergence does not establish that the fitted model is scientifically adequate. IRLS convergence addresses a numerical question. Response support, predictor coding, and predictive adequacy remain separate.
You will usually let software perform these calculations. Understanding the iteration explains why a generalized linear model can fail to converge and why the fitted result depends on both the response family and the link.
The sequence of weighted linear updates also explains why changing the family or link changes more than a label. It changes the fitted means, the conditional variances, the working responses, and the weights used at every iteration.






NoteReconstruct one local update




Why is one ordinary least squares calculation not enough for most generalized linear models?
What quantities are recomputed at each iteration?
What does algorithmic convergence fail to establish?
Starting from \pi=.5, calculate the working response for one success and one failure.
Explain why IRLS convergence does not establish scientific model adequacy.

title: Leverage
text:
The residual diagnostics ask whether responses depart from fitted means in systematic ways. Leverage instead concerns where each observation falls among the predictor values used to fit the line.
Residual size tells us whether a response lies far from its fitted conditional mean. It does not tell us whether the observation occupies an unusual position on the predictor. Leverage measures the second property.
This distinction matters because an observation at the edge of the predictor range can help determine the fitted slope even when its response lies close to the fitted line. Leverage quantifies this unusual predictor position.

title: Leverage
text:
Compare positions on one predictor
Consider five words with predictor values

\mathbf{x}=(2,3,4,5,11).

The sample mean is

\bar x=5.

The word at x=11 is six units above the mean, while the word at x=4 is one unit below it. The first word occupies a more unusual design position, regardless of its observed response.
For simple linear regression with an intercept, observation i has leverage

h_{ii}
=\frac{1}{n}
+\frac{(x_i-\bar x)^2}
{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}.

The first term gives every observation the same baseline leverage. The second term increases with squared distance from the predictor mean.
For the five predictor values,

\sum_{j=1}^5(x_j-\bar x)^2
=(-3)^2+(-2)^2+(-1)^2+0^2+6^2
=50.

The leverage at x=4 is

h
=\frac15+\frac{(-1)^2}{50}
=.22.

The leverage at x=11 is

h
=\frac15+\frac{6^2}{50}
=.92.

The edge observation has very high leverage because its predictor value is far from the center of this design.

title: Leverage
text:
Calculate every leverage value


Code
x <- c(2, 3, 4, 5, 11)
n <- length(x)

leverage_by_hand <-
  1 / n + (x - mean(x))^2 / sum((x - mean(x))^2)

data.frame(x = x, leverage = leverage_by_hand)
sum(leverage_by_hand)


With an intercept and one predictor, the leverage values sum to 2. This is the number of fitted coefficients. Their average is thus 2/n, which gives a useful reference for identifying observations far above the design’s usual leverage.
The reference is descriptive, not an automatic deletion rule. A high-leverage observation may be exactly the observation needed to study the edge of a linguistically relevant range.

title: Leverage
section: Retrieve leverage from a fitted model
text:
Retrieve leverage from a fitted model
Leverage depends only on the predictor values used to fit the model. We can attach any response values to verify the software calculation:


Code
design_example <- data.frame(
  x = x,
  y = c(6.1, 6.4, 6.5, 6.8, 8.0)
)

fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = design_example)

cbind(
  by_hand = leverage_by_hand,
  from_model = hatvalues(fit)
)


The columns agree. If we changed all five responses but kept the predictor values fixed, the leverage values would remain unchanged.

title: Leverage
text:
Separate leverage from residual size
An observation may have high leverage and a small residual. The point at x=11 could lie almost exactly on the fitted line while still anchoring its right end. In contrast, a point near x=5 could have a very unusual response and a large residual while occupying an ordinary predictor position.
This gives two separate questions:

Is the response far from its fitted conditional mean?
Is the predictor value far from the center of the observed design?

Residuals answer the first. Leverage answers the second. A large residual and high leverage are thus different properties of an observation.

title: Leverage
section: Interpret high leverage in a linguistic design
text:
Interpret high leverage in a linguistic design
Suppose the predictor is corpus frequency. A genuinely rare word may have high leverage after log frequency is entered into a small sample. Its position is not necessarily a recording error. It may instead reveal that the sample contains little information near that end of the frequency range.
The first response should be to inspect the design and the observation’s provenance. Is the value coded correctly? Does it belong to the target population? Is the edge of the range theoretically relevant? Only then should we ask how strongly it affects the fitted coefficients.
That final question is influence, which the next page introduces using case deletion.






NoteLocate the unusual design position




Calculate the leverage for x=5 in the five-value example.
Why can leverage be calculated without looking at the responses?
Construct a case with high leverage and a small residual.
Explain why residual magnitude and leverage answer different questions.

title: Link functions
text:
The preceding page showed why binary probabilities and positive expected counts cannot be represented by an unconstrained straight-line mean. The design-matrix page already introduced the real-valued linear predictor:
\eta_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i.
A conditional mean may be constrained. A Bernoulli mean must lie between zero and one, and a Poisson mean must be positive. A link function connects these two scales.
The link function performs this mapping between the conditional mean and the real-valued linear predictor. The linear predictor remains free to take any real value, while the inverse link guarantees that the resulting conditional mean lies in the range licensed by the response measurement.

title: Link functions
text:
Link and inverse link
Let

\mu_i=\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid x_i].

The link function g maps the mean to the linear predictor:

g(\mu_i)=\eta_i.

The inverse link maps back:

\mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i).

The two directions answer different computational questions. The link asks, “Which unconstrained value represents this conditional mean?” The inverse link asks, “Which conditional mean corresponds to this unconstrained value?”
Regression predictions usually travel in the second direction. Predictors and coefficients produce \eta_i, then the inverse link produces \mu_i.
For ordinary linear regression, the identity link gives g(\mu)=\mu. For logistic regression, the logit link gives

g(\pi)=\log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}.

For Poisson regression, the log link gives

g(\lambda)=\log\lambda.

Its inverse is

g^{-1}(\eta)=e^\eta.

Exponentiation maps every real value to a positive value. It can produce a conditional mean below 1, such as .3, even though an observed count must be an integer. A distributional mean need not itself be an observable response.
For a Bernoulli response, the inverse logit is

g^{-1}(\eta)
=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta}}.

This function maps the real line into (0,1). At \eta=0, it gives probability .5. Large positive values approach 1, and large negative values approach 0.

title: Link functions
text:
Build a mapping table


Code
eta <- c(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2)

data.frame(
  eta = eta,
  identity_mean = eta,
  logit_mean = plogis(eta),
  log_mean = exp(eta)
)


The identity inverse link reproduces the real-valued predictor. The inverse logit stays between zero and one. The exponential remains positive. The same linear-predictor values thus imply different mean scales under different MRMs.

title: Link functions
section: Coefficients live on the link scale
text:
Coefficients live on the link scale
If x increases by one, \eta changes by \beta_1. This is an additive statement on the link scale.
Under a log link,

\lambda(x+1)
=
\exp(\eta+\beta_1)
=
\lambda(x)\exp(\beta_1).

The response mean is multiplied by \exp(\beta_1). Under a logit link, \exp(\beta_1) instead multiplies the odds.
The response-mean difference is not generally constant. Under the inverse logit, adding 1 to \eta changes probability from .50 to about .731 when \eta starts at 0. The same addition changes probability from about .881 to .953 when \eta starts at 2. The link-scale change is 1 in both cases, while the probability changes are about .231 and .072.
A constant coefficient on the link scale does not generally produce a constant difference on the response scale. Nonlinear inverse links make the response-scale difference depend on the other predictor values.

title: Link functions
text:
Verify the two directions
For a Bernoulli mean \pi=.8, the logit link gives

\eta
=\log\frac{.8}{1-.8}
=\log4
\approx1.386.

Applying the inverse returns

\frac{1}{1+e^{-1.386}}\approx.8.

For a count mean \lambda=5, the log link gives \eta=\log5. Exponentiating returns 5. These round trips are useful checks on a coefficient interpretation.

title: Link functions
section: Keep the link separate from the response family
text:
Keep the link separate from the response family
The response family determines possible observations and a mean-variance relation. The link determines how predictors change the conditional mean. These are distinct model choices.
For instance, the Bernoulli family supplies responses 0 and 1. The logit link is one way to keep their conditional probability valid. Another monotone mapping could also stay within (0,1) while implying a different relation between \eta and probability.
The fact that a mapping has the right range is necessary but not sufficient. Its shape affects coefficient interpretation and extrapolation. The mapping should be stated and its response-scale predictions checked.

title: Link functions
text:
Compare on the response scale
With a nonlinear inverse link, a constant change in \eta does not produce a constant change in \mu. Report predicted probabilities or expected counts at meaningful predictor values. These response scale summaries are often easier to connect to a linguistic claim than a link scale coefficient alone.
A good report retains both scales. The coefficient gives the additive change in \eta. A prediction table shows what that change means for probabilities or expected counts at the predictor values relevant to the linguistic contrast.
The next page combines a link function with a response family and a linear predictor.






NoteMove between the two scales




Why can the linear predictor remain unconstrained?
What does a coefficient mean under a log link?
Apply the inverse logit to \eta=0 and \eta=2.
Explain why a constant link-scale coefficient need not produce a constant response-scale difference.
Why are the response family and link separate choices?

title: Two predictors in logistic regression
text:
The multiple-regression page introduced partial comparisons, and the logistic-regression page placed a binary response on the log-odds scale. A logistic model with several predictors combines those already introduced ideas.
Suppose an experiment records whether a referent is mentioned with a pronoun. One proposal says that a referent is pronominalized because it was the preceding subject. A second says that pronominalization depends on how recently the referent was mentioned.
These properties need not vary independently. Preceding subjects may also tend to be recent. A one predictor model for subject status can then mix grammatical prominence with recency. A one predictor model for recency can mix memory accessibility with grammatical role.
A logistic regression with multiple predictors places both comparisons in one linear predictor. Each coefficient describes one modeled contrast while the other predictors are held fixed. The partial comparison is now measured on the log-odds scale.

title: Two predictors in logistic regression
text:
Write the additive model
Let Y_i=1 mark a pronoun and Y_i=0 mark another referring expression:

Y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i).

Let subject_status equal one when the antecedent was the preceding subject and zero otherwise. Let recency count the number of intervening discourse units. The additive model is

\operatorname{logit}(\pi_i)
=\beta_0
+\beta_1\text{subject\_status}_i
+\beta_2\text{recency}_i.

The intercept \beta_0 is the pronoun log odds for a nonsubject antecedent with recency zero. The subject coefficient \beta_1 compares subject and nonsubject antecedents at the same modeled recency. The recency coefficient \beta_2 describes a one unit recency change at the same subject status.
The phrase “at the same” is the partial comparison. It comes from the additive linear predictor, not from a guarantee that the observed corpus contains many perfectly matched tokens.

title: Two predictors in logistic regression
section: Combine the coefficients for one observation
text:
Combine the coefficients for one observation
Suppose

\beta_0=-.5,
\qquad
\beta_1=1.2,
\qquad
\beta_2=-.3.

For a preceding subject with two intervening units,

\eta=-.5+1.2(1)-.3(2)=.1.

The predicted pronoun probability is

\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(.1)\approx.525.

For a nonsubject at the same recency,

\eta=-.5+1.2(0)-.3(2)=-1.1,

so the probability is approximately .250. These two profiles differ only in subject status. Their probability difference is approximately

.525-.250=.275.

Now hold subject status fixed at one and increase recency from two to three. The linear predictor falls from .1 to -.2, and the probability falls from .525 to about .450. This second profile comparison isolates the modeled recency association.

title: Two predictors in logistic regression
section: Interpret coefficients without changing scales silently
text:
Interpret coefficients without changing scales silently
The coefficient \beta_1=1.2 is a 1.2 increase in pronoun log odds. Exponentiating gives

e^{1.2}\approx3.32.

Thus subject antecedents have 3.32 times the modeled pronoun odds of nonsubject antecedents at the same recency. This is not a constant probability difference. The .275 difference above applies to the declared recency value and parameter values.
Likewise,

e^{-.3}\approx.74.

Each additional discourse unit multiplies the modeled pronoun odds by about .74 at either subject status under the additive model. Response scale predictions are still needed to show how that ratio changes probabilities at relevant profiles.

title: Two predictors in logistic regression
text:
Fit and predict in R
fit_pronoun <- glm(
  pronoun ~ subject_status + recency,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = reference_forms
)
The formula contains two additive predictor terms. No product term appears, so the model assumes that the subject status difference is constant on the log odds scale across recency.
Construct an explicit prediction grid:
profiles <- expand.grid(
  subject_status = c(0, 1),
  recency = c(0, 2, 4)
)

profiles$pronoun_probability <- predict(
  fit_pronoun,
  newdata = profiles,
  type = "response"
)

profiles
The grid does two things. First, it makes the held fixed values visible. Second, it reveals the nonlinear response scale pattern implied by an additive log odds model.

title: Two predictors in logistic regression
section: Inspect support for the partial comparison
text:
Inspect support for the partial comparison
A coefficient can be computed even when predictor combinations are sparse. Suppose nearly every subject antecedent has recency zero and nearly every nonsubject antecedent has recency four. The model can still report \beta_1, but its same recency subject comparison relies heavily on the assumed additive form because few observations directly support it.
Inspect the joint predictor distribution before treating a partial coefficient as an ordinary matched contrast:
with(reference_forms, table(subject_status, recency))
With a continuous predictor, use a plot or binned summary rather than a large sparse table. The goal is to see whether both subject status values occur across a common recency range.
Adding the second predictor does not automatically remove confounding. Unmeasured discourse status, animacy, genre, or lexical properties may still be associated with both predictors and the response. The coefficient remains conditional on the variables and functional form actually included.

title: Two predictors in logistic regression
section: Add a predictor because the theory needs its contrast
text:
Add a predictor because the theory needs its contrast
A larger formula is not automatically a better linguistic analysis. A predictor earns its place when it encodes a hypothesis, a design control, or a specific source of measurement variation.
In the dative alternation, accessibility, pronominality, animacy, and length bear on harmonic alignment. Their correlated distribution makes a joint model useful because the theory concerns their distinct directional contributions. An arbitrary identifier or convenience column does not become theoretically informative because its coefficient changes another estimate.
The additive model also makes a substantive restriction. It assumes that the subject status association is constant on the log odds scale across recency. If the theory predicts that grammatical prominence matters most for distant antecedents, the restriction is wrong. The interaction page adds a product term for that new question.






NoteCheck the partial comparison



What observations support \beta_1 if subject antecedents tend to be more recent than nonsubject antecedents? Describe the same recency comparison the model needs. Then state what sparse overlap would force the additive form to supply.








NoteProblem Set 3 connection



Problem Set 3, Task 2 uses one additive logistic model to ask whether discourse accessibility, pronominality, animacy, and relative length predict dative choice in the directions licensed by harmonic alignment. The formulas are fixed before the coefficients are inspected. This makes the task an application of partial comparisons, not an invitation to search among formulas until a preferred pattern appears.

title: Two predictors in logistic regression
text:
What multiple predictors add
A multiple-predictor logistic model assigns each coefficient a partial log odds comparison while the remaining modeled predictors are fixed. Response scale profiles show the combined nonlinear consequences of those coefficients. Joint predictor support determines how directly the data inform each partial comparison. An interaction is needed only when the linguistic hypothesis says that one association changes with another predictor.

title: Adding a second predictor
text:
The simple linear model conditions the response mean on one predictor. Multiple regression extends the same conditional mean to several predictors, so each coefficient must be read relative to the others in the model.
Suppose a word-recognition study predicts log response time from two lexical properties:
The theoretical question is whether each source of lexical structure is associated with response time when the other is held at the same modeled value.

title: Adding a second predictor
text:
Extend the mean function
With one predictor,

m(x_1)=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1.

Add the second predictor:

m(x_1,x_2)
=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2.

The ordinary multiple linear regression model is

Y_i\mid x_{i1},x_{i2}
\sim
\mathcal{N}
\left(
\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\beta_2x_{i2},
\sigma^2
\right).

title: Adding a second predictor
section: Compare observations at the same x_2
text:
Compare observations at the same x_2
Hold neighborhood density at x_2. Increase log frequency by one unit:

\begin{aligned}
m(x_1+1,x_2)-m(x_1,x_2)
&=\beta_1.
\end{aligned}

Thus \beta_1 is the frequency association among observations compared at the same modeled neighborhood density.
Likewise, \beta_2 is the neighborhood-density association among observations at the same modeled log frequency.
The coefficients are partial regression coefficients. Each describes the modeled association for one predictor while the other predictors are held fixed. It can differ from the marginal association between that predictor and the response.
The word partial indicates that other predictors are held constant. The frequency coefficient compares model predictions that differ by one frequency unit while neighborhood density is fixed. It need not equal the association obtained when neighborhood density is allowed to vary along with frequency.
Adding a predictor changes the conditioning set for the other coefficients. It does not merely improve an existing coefficient. It changes the modeled comparison that the coefficient represents.

title: Adding a second predictor
text:
Calculate one prediction
Suppose

\beta_0=6.2,
\qquad
\beta_1=-.08,
\qquad
\beta_2=.015.

For a word with centered log frequency 1 and centered neighborhood density 4,

m(1,4)
=6.2-.08(1)+.015(4)
=6.18.

Both predictor contributions are added to the same conditional mean.
The same equation gives a direct comparison. Consider two words with centered neighborhood density 4 and centered log frequencies 1 and 2. Their expected responses differ by

m(2,4)-m(1,4)
=\beta_1
=-.08.

Now keep centered log frequency at 1 and compare neighborhood densities 4 and 6:

m(1,6)-m(1,4)
=2\beta_2
=.03.

Each coefficient controls a family of comparisons in which the other predictor is held fixed in the model.

title: Adding a second predictor
text:
Fit the additive model


Code
lexical_decision <- data.frame(
  log_frequency = c(-1.5, -1, -.5, 0, .5, 1, 1.5, 2),
  neighborhood_density = c(14, 12, 13, 9, 10, 6, 7, 3),
  log_rt = c(6.540, 6.450, 6.440, 6.330, 6.315, 6.205, 6.195, 6.075)
)

fit_two <- lm(
  log_rt ~ log_frequency + neighborhood_density,
  data = lexical_decision
)

coef(fit_two)


This model assumes that the frequency slope is the same at every neighborhood density and vice versa. An interaction will later relax that assumption.
The fitted frequency coefficient is about -.066. It is the estimated log-frequency association among model comparisons with neighborhood density held fixed. The fitted neighborhood coefficient is about .020 at a fixed modeled log frequency.
The intercept is the expected response when both centered predictors equal zero. This interpretation is useful only if the centering constants have been stated.

title: Adding a second predictor
section: Compare the marginal and partial slopes
text:
Compare the marginal and partial slopes
In the constructed observations, higher-frequency words tend to have fewer phonological neighbors:


Code
cor(
  lexical_decision$log_frequency,
  lexical_decision$neighborhood_density
)


The correlation is about -.94. Thus the one-predictor frequency model compares words whose neighborhood densities also tend to differ:


Code
fit_one <- lm(log_rt ~ log_frequency, data = lexical_decision)

c(
  marginal_frequency_slope = coef(fit_one)["log_frequency"],
  partial_frequency_slope = coef(fit_two)["log_frequency"]
)


The one-predictor slope is -.125, while the two-predictor slope is about -.066. Neither is the uniquely correct description independently of a question. The first describes the frequency association as neighborhood density varies in this sample. The second describes the frequency association under a model comparison that fixes neighborhood density.
This difference follows from the change in conditioning set. It should not be narrated as the second model “correcting” the first unless the design and theory establish that the partial comparison is the intended target.

title: Adding a second predictor
section: Adding a variable changes the coefficient target
text:
Adding a variable changes the coefficient target
The frequency coefficient in the two-predictor model is not merely a more accurate version of the one-predictor coefficient. It answers a different question because it conditions on neighborhood density.
Adding every available column does not automatically isolate a causal or theoretical effect. The predictor set should follow from the comparisons the theory requires and from the design that supports them.
For instance, controlling for a variable caused by both the predictor and response can create a misleading partial association. Controlling for a noisy proxy can also leave substantial variation in the property the analysis meant to hold fixed. Regression performs the declared conditional comparison; it does not determine whether that comparison supports a causal claim.

title: Adding a second predictor
text:
Read predictions before coefficient labels
A reliable interpretation method is to choose two predictor rows, calculate their fitted means, and subtract. If only frequency changes by one unit, the difference is \beta_1. If both predictors change, the difference is

\beta_1\Delta x_1+\beta_2\Delta x_2.

This calculation prevents one coefficient from being used to describe a contrast that also changes other predictors. The model’s prediction for that contrast may involve several coefficients.






NoteCheck the conditioning set




In words, distinguish the frequency slope in log_rt ~ log_frequency from the frequency slope in log_rt ~ log_frequency + neighborhood_density.
Using the displayed coefficients, compare predictions for two words that differ by two frequency units and three neighborhood-density units.
Explain how adding a predictor changes the comparison represented by the other coefficient.
Why does adding a predictor not by itself license a causal interpretation?

title: From probabilities to log odds
text:
The link-function page used the logit to connect a Bernoulli probability to a real-valued linear predictor. This page develops the odds and log-odds quantities inside that transformation.
Let \pi be the probability of an in completion. The probability of the alternative for completion is 1-\pi.
The odds compare these two probabilities:
\operatorname{odds}(\pi)
=\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}.
The numerator corresponds to the modeled event. The denominator corresponds to its complement. If the event coding is reversed, the odds become their reciprocal. The direction of an odds comparison thus depends on which event appears in the numerator.

title: From probabilities to log odds
text:
Convert several probabilities



probability \pi
complement 1-\pi
odds \pi/(1-\pi)




.20
.80
.25


.50
.50
1


.80
.20
4



Odds of .25 mean one expected event for every four expected nonevents. Odds of 4 mean four expected events for every one expected nonevent.
Probabilities range from 0 to 1. Odds range from 0 to infinity.
Odds are not probabilities. Odds 4 correspond to probability .8, not to a probability of 4. To convert odds o back to probability, solve

o=\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}

for \pi:

\pi=\frac{o}{1+o}.

Thus odds .25 give probability .25/1.25=.20, and odds 4 give probability 4/5=.80.

title: From probabilities to log odds
text:
Take the logarithm
The log odds, or logit, are

\operatorname{logit}(\pi)
=\log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}.

For the three probabilities:



\pi
odds
log odds




.20
.25
-1.386


.50
1
0


.80
4
1.386



Log odds span the real line. Probabilities below .50 produce negative log odds, .50 produces zero, and probabilities above .50 produce positive log odds.
This range makes log odds suitable for a linear predictor.
Taking the logarithm also turns reciprocal odds into sign reversals. If the odds of in are 4, the odds of for are 1/4. Their log odds are 1.386 and -1.386. Reversing the modeled event is thus visible as a coefficient-sign reversal on the logit scale.

title: From probabilities to log odds
text:
Transform back to probability
Solve

\eta=\log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}

for \pi. The inverse logit is

\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\eta)
=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta}}.

It maps every real \eta into a probability between zero and one.
We can verify the round trip:


Code
probability <- c(.20, .50, .80)
odds <- probability / (1 - probability)
log_odds <- log(odds)
recovered_probability <- plogis(log_odds)

data.frame(
  probability = probability,
  odds = odds,
  log_odds = log_odds,
  recovered_probability = recovered_probability
)


plogis() is R’s inverse-logit function. The recovered probabilities equal the original values up to numerical precision.

title: From probabilities to log odds
text:
Interpret an additive change
Suppose log odds increase by \beta:

\log\operatorname{odds}_2
=\log\operatorname{odds}_1+\beta.

Exponentiating gives

\operatorname{odds}_2
=e^\beta\operatorname{odds}_1.

Thus adding \beta to log odds multiplies odds by e^\beta.
Suppose \beta=\log2\approx.693. Then a one-unit predictor increase doubles the odds. If the starting probability is .20, the starting odds are .25. Doubling gives odds .50, which correspond to probability

\frac{.50}{1+.50}=.333.

The probability change is about .133.
If the starting probability is .70, the starting odds are

\frac{.70}{.30}\approx2.333.

Doubling gives odds about 4.667 and probability

\frac{4.667}{1+4.667}\approx.824.

The probability change is about .124. The odds multiplier is 2 in both cases, but the probability difference depends on the starting point.

title: From probabilities to log odds
section: Distinguish an odds ratio from a probability ratio
text:
Distinguish an odds ratio from a probability ratio
For the first comparison, the probability ratio is

.333/.20\approx1.665,

while the odds ratio is 2. These are different summaries and should not be conflated.
An odds ratio can be constant across predictor values under logistic regression while probability ratios and probability differences vary. A report should state which summary it uses and provide response-scale probabilities for the linguistic profiles of interest.






NoteCheck the reference point




Convert probability .50 to odds and log odds. Why does this probability become the zero point on the logit scale?
Convert odds 3 to probability.
If an odds ratio is 2, must the probability ratio equal 2? Use one numerical case to justify the answer.
Explain how reversing the modeled event changes the odds and the odds-probability ratio substitution.









NoteProblem Set 3 connection



Problem Set 3, Task 3 converts fitted log odds into probabilities for two predeclared dative profiles. The task is included because several theoretically meaningful coefficients combine on the log odds scale, while the linguistic comparison is easier to understand on the probability scale.


Odds compare an event with its complement, while log odds place that comparison on the real line. A fixed additive change in log odds is a fixed odds multiplier, not a fixed probability change.

title: Ordinal mixed models
text:
This page combines the cumulative link introduced for ordinal regression with the group deviations introduced for generalized linear mixed models.
Suppose each participant rates several discourses on an ordered commitment scale from no through maybe to yes. Each discourse also receives judgments from several participants. The ordinal regression page represents the response order, but it does not yet represent the two repeated units.
An ordinal mixed model places random effects inside the location predictor of a cumulative link model. The response categories and cutpoints are unchanged. The new step is the same one used by a generalized linear mixed model: observations that share a participant or discourse also share a modeled deviation.

title: Ordinal mixed models
text:
Start from the cumulative link
Let Y_{ijd} be participant j’s ordered response to discourse d in condition i. For each cutpoint c, an ordinal regression has

\operatorname{logit}\Pr(Y_{ijd}\leq c)
=\kappa_c-\eta_{ijd}.

Suppose X_{ijd} represents an embedding environment. Without random effects,

\eta_{ijd}=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{ijd}.

All participants and discourses with the same predictor value receive the same location. Repeated observations are treated as independent after conditioning on that predictor.

title: Ordinal mixed models
text:
Add both repeated units
Let u_j be a participant deviation and v_d be a discourse deviation:

\eta_{ijd}
=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{ijd}+u_j+v_d,

with

u_j\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_{\text{participant}}^2)

and

v_d\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_{\text{discourse}}^2).

A positive participant deviation moves that participant toward higher response categories across represented discourses. A positive discourse deviation moves judgments of that discourse upward across participants. The two variance parameters describe different sources of heterogeneity and should not be combined into one generic error term.
The model is crossed when participants judge multiple discourses and discourses receive judgments from multiple participants. Neither unit nests inside the other. The formula should preserve that design.

title: Ordinal mixed models
section: Follow one observation through the model
text:
Follow one observation through the model
Suppose one observation has fixed predictor location .6, participant deviation .3, and discourse deviation -.4. Its complete location is

\eta=.6+.3-.4=.5.

With cutpoints \kappa_1=-.8 and \kappa_2=1, its predicted category probabilities are

\Pr(Y=\text{no})=F(-.8-.5)=F(-1.3)\approx.214,


\Pr(Y=\text{maybe})
=F(1-.5)-F(-.8-.5)
\approx.622-.214=.408,

and

\Pr(Y=\text{yes})=1-F(.5)\approx.378.

The participant deviation raises the response location, while the discourse deviation partly offsets that rise. Both operate before the inverse link converts the location into category probabilities.

title: Ordinal mixed models
text:
Fit the crossed model
judgments$commitment <- ordered(
  judgments$commitment,
  levels = c("no", "maybe", "yes")
)

fit_commitment_mixed <- ordinal::clmm(
  commitment ~ embedding_environment + discourse_status +
    (1 | participant_id) +
    (1 | discourse_id),
  data = judgments,
  link = "logit"
)
The fixed terms describe the modeled linguistic contrasts. (1 | participant_id) represents baseline response tendencies. (1 | discourse_id) represents baseline differences among the linguistic materials. The cutpoints are estimated jointly with the fixed coefficients and variance parameters.
The model can include an interaction when the linguistic theory predicts that the embedding effect changes with discourse status:
fit_commitment_interaction <- ordinal::clmm(
  commitment ~ embedding_environment * discourse_status +
    (1 | participant_id) +
    (1 | discourse_id),
  data = judgments,
  link = "logit"
)
The interaction belongs in the formula only when its contrast has been stated before fitting. The presence of several response categories does not by itself motivate a larger fixed effect structure.

title: Ordinal mixed models
section: State which groups are represented in a prediction
text:
State which groups are represented in a prediction
A prediction for an observed participant and discourse can condition on both estimated deviations. A prediction for a new participant judging an observed discourse may condition on the discourse deviation but must average over or newly draw the participant effect. A prediction for a new participant and new discourse must handle both random effect populations.
These are distinct predictive questions. Setting every random effect to zero gives a location at the center of each grouping distribution. It is not automatically the same as averaging response probabilities over those distributions because the cumulative logit inverse is nonlinear.
The target should thus be stated before predictions are generated. Otherwise the same fixed coefficient can be accompanied by several apparently conflicting probability summaries that differ only in their conditioning choices.

title: Ordinal mixed models
section: Interpret the linguistic contrast on the response scale
text:
Interpret the linguistic contrast on the response scale
An embedding coefficient remains a common shift across cumulative logits. Random effects do not turn it into a change in slider points or category numbers. Report predicted probabilities for no, maybe, and yes in the theoretically diagnostic conditions.
Participant and discourse variation also bear on the claim. A large discourse variance means that the represented materials differ substantially after the fixed predictors are included. It does not show that the fixed contrast is absent. It shows that the fixed contrast is not a complete account of discourse level commitment.
This distinction is especially important for lexical semantic predictors such as factivity. A coarse predicate category may show an average contrast while individual predicates or discourses vary widely. The model can support the average association and simultaneously block the claim that the category determines every response.

title: Ordinal mixed models
section: What a random intercept cannot repair
text:
What a random intercept cannot repair
Participant response behavior may differ in more than baseline location. Some participants may use maybe broadly, while others divide their responses between the endpoints. A location random intercept cannot represent every threshold or scale difference. Likewise, discourse variation may interact with the embedding manipulation rather than merely shifting every condition together.
These limitations should be diagnosed from response distributions and theoretically relevant contrasts. Adding a complex random effect structure without sufficient replication can make the model weakly identified. A simpler model should be described as simpler, not as proof that the omitted variation is zero.






NoteReading: de Marneffe, Simons, and Tonhauser (2019)



Read The CommitmentBank: Investigating projection in naturally occurring discourse, focusing on the response scale, embedding environments, and variation among predicates, items, and annotators. The reading is included because it shows why an average factivity contrast and substantial discourse level variation can coexist. The problem set uses a prespecified teaching model rather than reproducing every analysis in the paper.








NoteProblem Set 4 connection



Problem Set 4, Task 3 fits a seven category cumulative logit model with annotator, discourse, and predicate intercepts. Students must keep the ordered measurement and all three repeated units in one model before interpreting factivity.








NoteCheck the grouping structure



Why are participant and discourse intercepts crossed? For a new discourse prediction, which estimated deviation cannot be reused? What kind of participant response variation is not represented by a location random intercept?

title: Ordinal mixed models
text:
What the mixed model adds
An ordinal mixed model retains ordered cutpoints and cumulative logits while adding shared participant and discourse deviations to the response location. The model separates a linguistic contrast from participant and discourse variation. Its predictions must state whether each grouping unit is observed or new. Problem Set 4 applies this model to commitment judgments and then asks how far the average embedding pattern transfers across discourses.

title: Group heterogeneity and marginal dispersion
text:
The Poisson dispersion page treated excess conditional variation as a diagnosis rather than a cause. The Poisson mixed-model page supplies one possible cause: persistent rate differences across known groups.
A Poisson regression without random effects can appear overdispersed when it omits a known grouping structure. Suppose speakers differ persistently in their filled pause rates. Pooling their segments under one Poisson mean mixes low-rate and high-rate speakers, so the combined count distribution varies more than a single Poisson distribution.
This extra variation arises by marginalizing over heterogeneous groups. It is not another response distribution. It is the difference between variation conditional on a random effect and variation after that effect has been averaged over.

title: Group heterogeneity and marginal dispersion
section: Begin with the conditional Poisson claim
text:
Begin with the conditional Poisson claim
For segment i from speaker j, suppose

Y_{ij}\mid b_j
\sim
\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_{ij}(b_j)),

with

\log\lambda_{ij}(b_j)
=
\log t_{ij}+\eta_{ij}+b_j

and

b_j\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau^2).

The quantity \eta_{ij} contains the fixed intercept and predictors. Conditional on a particular value of b_j,

\operatorname{Var}(Y_{ij}\mid b_j)
=
\operatorname{E}(Y_{ij}\mid b_j)
=
\lambda_{ij}(b_j).

Thus the model is still Poisson within the conditional statement. The speaker effect does not insert a free residual variance into that Poisson distribution.

title: Group heterogeneity and marginal dispersion
text:
Average over the speaker population
Now consider a segment from a new speaker whose random effect has not been observed. Its expected count averages over the random effect distribution:

m_{ij}
=
\operatorname{E}_{b}
[\lambda_{ij}(b)].

The law of total variance separates two sources of variation:

\operatorname{Var}(Y_{ij})
=
\operatorname{E}_{b}
[\operatorname{Var}(Y_{ij}\mid b)]
+
\operatorname{Var}_{b}
[\operatorname{E}(Y_{ij}\mid b)].

Substitute the conditional Poisson mean and variance:

\operatorname{Var}(Y_{ij})
=
\operatorname{E}_{b}[\lambda_{ij}(b)]
+
\operatorname{Var}_{b}[\lambda_{ij}(b)].

The first term is the marginal mean m_{ij}. The second term records variation in expected counts across speakers. Thus

\operatorname{Var}(Y_{ij})
=
m_{ij}
+
\operatorname{Var}_{b}[\lambda_{ij}(b)].

If \tau>0, speaker baselines vary, so the second term is positive. The marginal variance then exceeds the marginal mean even though every conditional response distribution is Poisson.

title: Group heterogeneity and marginal dispersion
text:
Calculate the extra variation
The normal random intercept becomes log normal after exponentiation. For the model above,

m_{ij}
=
t_{ij}\exp(\eta_{ij})
\exp\left(\frac{\tau^2}{2}\right).

The variance of the conditional expected count is

\operatorname{Var}_{b}[\lambda_{ij}(b)]
=
m_{ij}^2
[\exp(\tau^2)-1].

The marginal count variance is thus

\operatorname{Var}(Y_{ij})
=
m_{ij}
+
m_{ij}^2[\exp(\tau^2)-1].

Suppose the marginal expected count is 3 and \tau=.6. Then

3^2[\exp(.6^2)-1]
\approx
3.90.

The marginal variance is about

3+3.90=6.90.

The extra 3.90 is not unexplained observation noise. Under this model, it arises because new speakers have different expected rates.

title: Group heterogeneity and marginal dispersion
section: See why repeated rows are associated
text:
See why repeated rows are associated
Two segments from the same speaker share b_j. If one segment indicates that the speaker has a high baseline rate, another segment from that speaker also becomes more likely to have a high count. Averaging over the unknown speaker effect thus induces positive association among the speaker’s rows.
Segments from different speakers do not share this deviation because their random effects are independent under the model. The random intercept thus explains a patterned source of variation. It increases marginal dispersion and represents which rows should vary together.
This structure distinguishes a group-level random effect from an observation-level dispersion adjustment. A negative binomial response can represent count variation beyond a Poisson distribution. But an independent observation-level adjustment does not by itself say that several segments share a persistent speaker rate. The grouping term is licensed by known repetition in the design.

title: Group heterogeneity and marginal dispersion
text:
Diagnose at the intended level
A Pearson dispersion ratio from a Poisson regression without random effects can combine at least two sources: persistent group heterogeneity and remaining variation within groups. Adding the speaker random intercept may account for the first source. It need not account for the second.
After fitting the mixed model, ask whether the represented speaker variation matches the repeated data. If counts still vary too widely among comparable segments from the same speaker, the random intercept is not a complete account. The conditional mean may omit a predictor, the speaker effect may vary with a predictor, or the count response may need another variance relation.
The narrow conclusion is that a marginally overdispersed count distribution is compatible with a conditionally Poisson mixed model. It does not follow that every instance of overdispersion should be repaired with a random intercept. The design must identify a repeated unit, and the fitted group variation must account for the pattern actually observed.






NoteCheck the conditioning level




How can the marginal variance exceed the marginal mean when the conditional distribution is Poisson?
What does the term \operatorname{Var}_{b}[\lambda_{ij}(b)] represent?
Why do two segments from the same speaker become associated after averaging over b_j?
Why does marginal overdispersion not by itself license a speaker random intercept?

title: Poisson regression for linguistic diversity
text:
The exposure-offset page separated an expected rate from the number of opportunities. This application uses the same construction for counts of languages across countries with different geographic areas.
The number of languages spoken in a country is a count. That observation may suggest a Poisson regression, but it does not yet tell us what the regression should compare. Countries differ greatly in geographic area. A large country provides more geographic opportunity for distinct language communities than a small country does. Comparing their raw language counts would mix the proposed ecological effect with this difference in opportunity.
An exposure offset separates the language count from the amount of geographic area in which languages could occur. The resulting analysis asks whether countries with different mean growing seasons have different rates of linguistic diversity after geographic area has been held fixed.

title: Poisson regression for linguistic diversity
text:
Begin with the linguistic account
Nettle proposes that ecological risk may affect the size and stability of social networks. In an environment with a longer growing season, smaller communities may be able to support themselves with less exchange across groups. That social organization may favor the maintenance of a greater number of languages. In an environment with a shorter growing season, risk sharing may encourage larger networks and reduce that tendency.
This proposal gives us a theory bearing predictor. Mean growing season is not included because it happens to be a numeric column. It represents the ecological contrast that Nettle proposes as one part of an account of linguistic diversity.
Let Y_i be the number of languages in country i, let x_i be mean growing season in months, and let A_i be geographic area. We begin with

Y_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_i).

The expected count depends on both exposure and mean growing season:

\log\lambda_i
=\log A_i+\beta_0+\beta_1x_i.

The quantity \log A_i is an offset, so its coefficient is fixed at one. The remaining coefficients describe the expected language rate at a given geographic area.

title: Poisson regression for linguistic diversity
text:
Inspect the released variables
The teaching data contain 74 countries and five columns. Langs is the number of languages, MGS is mean growing season in months, and Area is the base ten logarithm of area. Population is also stored on a base ten log scale, but it is not part of the present comparison.
nettle <- read.csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bodowinter/applied_statistics_book_data/master/nettle_1999_climate.csv"
)

dim(nettle)
head(nettle)
range(nettle$Langs)
range(nettle$MGS)
There are 74 language counts. They range from 1 to 862. Mean growing season ranges from 0 to 12 months. These summaries confirm that the response and predictor have the meanings required by the comparison, but they do not yet address the scale of exposure.

title: Poisson regression for linguistic diversity
section: Put the offset on the right log scale
text:
Put the offset on the right log scale
The model uses the natural logarithm because glm() uses the natural log link for a Poisson regression. The data file stores
