\operatorname{Area}_i=\log_{10}A_i.

Passing Area directly to offset() would place a base ten logarithm into a natural log equation. The required conversion follows from

\log A_i=\log(10)\log_{10}A_i.

Thus the correct offset is log(10) * Area.
fit <- glm(
  Langs ~ MGS + offset(log(10) * Area),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = nettle
)

coef(summary(fit))
The fitted mean growing season coefficient is about .250. Its standard error under the Poisson model is about .005. We should first interpret the coefficient on the scale of the model:

\log\lambda(x+1)-\log\lambda(x)=\beta_1.

A one month increase in mean growing season is associated with a .250 increase in the log expected language rate at equal geographic area.

title: Poisson regression for linguistic diversity
text:
Return to the response scale
Exponentiating the coefficient gives a rate ratio:
exp(coef(fit)["MGS"])
The result is about 1.284. According to this fitted conditional mean, a one month increase in mean growing season is associated with an expected language rate about 1.284 times as large when geographic area is held fixed. This is an increase of about 28 percent.
We can also compare two concrete values. Consider otherwise comparable countries with mean growing seasons of six and seven months. Their expected language rate ratio is

\frac{\lambda(7)}{\lambda(6)}
=\exp\{\beta_1(7-6)\}
=\exp(\beta_1).

This comparison has the same value, about 1.284. The offset means that we are comparing rates at equal exposure, not predicting that the two countries have equal raw counts.

title: Poisson regression for linguistic diversity
section: See why the base conversion matters
text:
See why the base conversion matters
The printed textbook analysis passes the stored Area column directly to the offset. We can fit that specification to see what the change of logarithm base alters.
fit_mismatched <- glm(
  Langs ~ MGS + offset(Area),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = nettle
)

c(
  mismatched = exp(coef(fit_mismatched)["MGS"]),
  converted = exp(coef(fit)["MGS"])
)
The mismatched specification gives a rate ratio of about 1.233, while the converted specification gives about 1.284. The qualitative association is the same, but the estimated size is not. The distinction matters because an offset is part of the model rather than a display convenience. Its units determine the comparison made by every coefficient.

title: Poisson regression for linguistic diversity
section: State what the comparison does not establish
text:
State what the comparison does not establish
The fitted association is consistent with Nettle’s predicted direction. It is not, by itself, evidence that growing season causes linguistic diversity. Countries may differ in population history, political organization, mobility, contact, and many other properties related to both climate and language counts. Countries may also be spatially or historically dependent.
The Poisson response adds another assumption: after the modeled predictors are taken into account, the conditional variance equals the conditional mean. We will learn how to check that assumption on the next page. Keeping that criticism separate lets this page answer one question: how should a Poisson regression compare language counts when countries provide different amounts of geographic exposure?






NoteCheck the comparison



Suppose two countries have the same mean growing season, but one has twice the geographic area of the other. Under this model, the larger country has twice the expected language count. Which part of the equation imposes that comparison?

title: Quasi Poisson variance
text:
The dispersion diagnostic can reveal more conditional variation than a Poisson model permits. One narrow response is to keep the Poisson mean relation while multiplying its variance by a constant. This specification is called a quasi-Poisson model.
The word quasi signals that the specification does not provide a complete probability distribution. It provides a conditional mean and a conditional variance. That distinction determines both what the model can repair and what it cannot supply.

title: Quasi Poisson variance
text:
Keep the same conditional mean
Suppose Y_i is a linguistic count and \mathbf{x}_i contains its predictors. The quasi Poisson mean uses the familiar log relation:

\operatorname{E}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i)=\mu_i,


\log\mu_i=\mathbf{x}_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\beta}.

The coefficients retain their multiplicative interpretation. If x_i increases by one unit while the other predictors remain fixed, then

\frac{\mu(x+1)}{\mu(x)}=\exp(\beta_x).

An exposure offset can also remain in the conditional mean. The quasi Poisson model does not change the research comparison encoded by the predictors or the offset.

title: Quasi Poisson variance
text:
Multiply the variance
The Poisson restriction is

\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i)=\mu_i.

The quasi Poisson model replaces it with

\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i)=\phi\mu_i,

where \phi is a dispersion multiplier. This is the quasi-Poisson variance function.
When \phi=1, the mean variance relation matches the Poisson model. When \phi>1, the response is overdispersed. When \phi<1, it is underdispersed.
Suppose a fitted conditional mean is 9 and \widehat\phi=4. The Poisson model assigns variance 9 and standard deviation 3. The quasi-Poisson model assigns

\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i)
=4\times 9=36

and standard deviation 6. The fitted mean remains 9. Only the represented spread changes.

title: Quasi Poisson variance
text:
See what changes in estimation
For the same log linked mean, the quasi Poisson coefficient estimates equal the corresponding Poisson estimates. The constant dispersion multiplier does not alter their location. It changes their estimated uncertainty.
The standard errors are multiplied by approximately \sqrt{\widehat\phi}. If a Poisson standard error is .10 and \widehat\phi=4, then

\operatorname{SE}_{\text{quasi}}
=.10\sqrt{4}
=.20.

The same coefficient is now estimated with twice the standard error. The uncertainty calculation now acknowledges that the counts vary more than the Poisson distribution predicts.
poisson_fit <- glm(
  count ~ predictor,
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = counts
)

quasi_fit <- glm(
  count ~ predictor,
  family = quasipoisson(link = "log"),
  data = counts
)

cbind(
  poisson = coef(poisson_fit),
  quasi = coef(quasi_fit)
)

c(
  poisson = coef(summary(poisson_fit))["predictor", "Std. Error"],
  quasi = coef(summary(quasi_fit))["predictor", "Std. Error"]
)
The first comparison should return the same coefficients. The second should return different standard errors whenever the estimated dispersion differs from one.

title: Quasi Poisson variance
text:
Notice what is missing
A complete response distribution assigns a probability to every possible count. The quasi-Poisson variance function does not. It states how the variance relates to the mean, but it does not specify the full shape of the count distribution.
This omission has practical consequences. There is no ordinary likelihood for the complete quasi Poisson model. Thus ordinary likelihood quantities such as AIC are unavailable, and the model does not directly provide a full predictive distribution for new counts.
The quasi-Poisson model is most useful when the conditional mean coefficients are the target and a constant variance multiplier gives an adequate uncertainty adjustment. It is less useful when the shape of the response distribution, the probability of zeros, or predictive count intervals are central to the question.

title: Quasi Poisson variance
text:
Interpret the repair narrowly
An estimated \phi greater than one says that residual variation is larger than the Poisson variance. It does not explain why. For instance, omitted predictors or unrepresented dependence can also inflate the dispersion estimate. Multiplying the variance does not recover either source.
This limit makes the dispersion multiplier a statistical adjustment rather than a linguistic account. The predictors still carry the linguistic claim. The multiplier only changes how much unstructured variation remains around that claim.






NoteCheck the repair



A Poisson fit and a quasi Poisson fit have the same predictor coefficient, but the second fit has a standard error three times as large. What does this difference imply about \widehat\phi? Which part of the scientific claim remains unchanged?

title: Group-specific estimates
text:
The partial-pooling page explained why group deviations are estimated jointly with a population distribution. A fitted multilevel model thus gives each observed group a partially pooled estimate of its deviation from the population relation. These values are often called conditional modes in a frequentist fit or group-specific estimates more generally.
They are useful summaries of the fitted group structure. They are not raw group means, independently estimated fixed coefficients, or error free rankings.

title: Group-specific estimates
text:
Build the group estimate
Suppose a random intercept model has population baseline \widehat\beta_0 and estimated speaker deviation \widehat b_j. The fitted speaker baseline is

\widehat\beta_0+\widehat b_j.

The deviation answers a conditional question: given the population coefficients, variance components, and this speaker’s observations, where does the model place the speaker relative to the population center?
The estimate is partially pooled through the shared group distribution. A speaker with an unusually high raw mean based on two noisy tokens will usually have an estimated deviation closer to zero than that raw difference. A speaker with many consistent observations receives less shrinkage.
Raw group means and partially pooled estimates differ most for groups with little information or high within-group noise.

title: Group-specific estimates
text:
Extract both kinds of quantity
With lme4, ranef() returns estimated deviations and coef() adds the population coefficients to return group-specific coefficients.
speaker_deviations <- ranef(fit_intercepts)$participant
speaker_coefficients <- coef(fit_intercepts)$participant

head(speaker_deviations)
head(speaker_coefficients)
If the model contains only a participant random intercept, the first table reports \widehat b_{0j}. The second reports \widehat\beta_0+\widehat b_{0j} and repeats any population slopes.
These tables should be interpreted with the model formula in view. A deviation of 20 ms is relative to the model’s baseline predictor values. Changing a coding reference or centering a continuous predictor changes the intercept meaning.

title: Group-specific estimates
section: Display the estimates and their uncertainty
text:
Display the estimates and their uncertainty
A caterpillar plot orders group deviations and displays their conditional uncertainty.
library(lattice)

dotplot(ranef(fit_intercepts, condVar = TRUE))
The plot can reveal groups with weak information, groups with unusual fitted deviations, and a group distribution that may not resemble the assumed shape. It is a model diagnostic and descriptive display.
The intervals are conditional on estimated population parameters in common frequentist implementations. They do not include every source of uncertainty. A Bayesian posterior for each group effect can represent parameter uncertainty more fully, but the ranks remain uncertain there as well.

title: Group-specific estimates
section: Do not turn the display into many tests
text:
Do not turn the display into many tests
The model assumes that the group deviations arise from one population distribution. Testing every speaker against zero and labeling speakers whose intervals exclude zero changes the scientific target. It treats sampled groups as a collection of separate hypotheses and creates a multiple comparison problem.
If particular speakers, dialects, or corpora are the scientific targets, their planned comparisons should be represented explicitly in the population relation. Random effects are not a substitute for declaring those targets.

title: Group-specific estimates
text:
Treat ranks as uncertain
The displayed order is based on point estimates. Neighboring groups can exchange ranks across plausible parameter values. A plot that places speaker 17 above speaker 9 does not establish a stable population ordering.
Rank uncertainty is often greatest in the middle, where many deviations are similar. Extreme estimates may also move substantially when their groups have few observations. Reporting the first and last point estimate without uncertainty can thus overstate what the data say.

title: Group-specific estimates
section: Use the estimates for appropriate questions
text:
Use the estimates for appropriate questions
Group estimates can help with three tasks:

checking whether a few groups dominate a fitted pattern;
describing the scale of modeled group variation;
generating a new, separately tested hypothesis about measured group properties.

They should not replace the population coefficient when the groups were sampled for generalization. Nor should they be correlated with a new group predictor using only the point estimates as if those estimates were observed without error. A measured group predictor belongs in the multilevel model itself.






NoteCompare raw and partially pooled group estimates



Two speakers have the same raw mean. One contributes three tokens and the other contributes three hundred. Why might their pooled deviations differ? Which additional quantities would you inspect before comparing their ranks?


The next page relaxes the common slope assumption by allowing a predictor association to vary across groups.

title: Random intercept models
text:
The partial-pooling page introduced group deviations from a shared population center. A random-intercept model places one such deviation in a regression equation.
Suppose several vowel tokens are measured for every speaker. Speakers may differ in baseline duration even after vowel category has been included as a predictor. A random-intercept model gives each speaker a partially pooled baseline deviation while keeping one population association for vowel category.

title: Random intercept models
text:
Insert one speaker deviation
For token i from speaker j, write

Y_{ij}
=\beta_0+b_{0j}+\beta_1x_{ij}+\varepsilon_{ij},

where

b_{0j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau_0^2)

and

\varepsilon_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2).

The population intercept is \beta_0. Speaker j has baseline \beta_0+b_{0j}. If b_{0j}=15 ms, that speaker’s fitted baseline is 15 ms above the population baseline at the same predictor value.
The subscript zero in b_{0j} marks an intercept deviation. It changes the vertical position of the speaker’s regression line. It does not change the association \beta_1.

title: Random intercept models
text:
Compare two speakers
Suppose \beta_0=100 ms and \beta_1=20 ms. Let speaker A have b_{0A}=-10 ms and speaker B have b_{0B}=15 ms. Their fitted means are

\widehat\mu_A(x)=90+20x

and

\widehat\mu_B(x)=115+20x.

The lines are parallel. Speaker B is predicted to have durations 25 ms longer than speaker A at every value of x. The model attributes that stable difference to their intercept deviations.
This model assumes that the predictor association is the same for every speaker. That common slope assumption is appropriate only when the modeled association can reasonably be treated as constant across speakers.

title: Random intercept models
text:
See the induced dependence
Two observations from speaker j share the same b_{0j}. Conditional on that deviation, their residuals may be independent. Before the deviation is known, the responses are associated because both contain the same speaker baseline.
For two trials i and i' from the same speaker,

Y_{ij}=\beta_0+b_{0j}+\beta_1x_{ij}+\varepsilon_{ij}

and

Y_{i'j}=\beta_0+b_{0j}+\beta_1x_{i'j}+\varepsilon_{i'j}.

Observing an unusually high response on the first trial provides information about b_{0j} and thus about the second trial. This is how the model represents the repeated speaker unit identified from the data structure.

title: Random intercept models
text:
Add a crossed item intercept
In a reading experiment, trials may share both participants and sentence items. Give participant j a deviation b_{0j} and item k a deviation c_{0k}:

Y_{ijk}
=\beta_0+b_{0j}+c_{0k}
+\beta_1x_{ijk}+\varepsilon_{ijk}.

Use separate population distributions:

b_{0j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau_{p}^{2}),


c_{0k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau_{s}^{2}).

The two standard deviations describe different populations. \tau_p measures participant baseline variation. \tau_s measures sentence item baseline variation.

title: Random intercept models
text:
Translate the equation into R
library(lme4)

fit_intercepts <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ condition +
    (1 | participant) +
    (1 | item),
  data = reading_experiment
)
condition supplies a population coefficient. (1 | participant) adds a participant intercept distribution. (1 | item) adds an item intercept distribution. The two grouping terms are crossed because participant and item identifiers occur in many combinations.
The formula does not create replication absent from the data. If each item is seen by only one participant, the design may not distinguish item and participant variation well. The grouping terms must be supported by the incidence structure.

title: Random intercept models
text:
State what remains common
The condition coefficient \beta_1 remains identical for every participant and item. The model represents different baselines, not different condition associations. This is a substantive restriction rather than a software default to accept without thought.






NoteCheck the formula



Two trials come from the same participant but different items. Which random effect do they share? Under the common slope assumption, how does their condition association compare?


The next page measures the response similarity induced by a shared random intercept.

title: Conditional means
text:
The earlier discussion of conditional expectation defined an expected value within a specified condition. Regression uses that same object while allowing the conditioning value to vary.
Suppose a self-paced reading study records reading time at each word. Let
Y_i=\text{log reading time for word }i
and let
X_i=\text{surprisal of word }i\text{ in bits}.
Surprisal measures how unexpected the word was under a specified language model. A processing account may predict that more surprising words take longer to read.

title: Conditional means
text:
Begin with one predictor value
Consider words with surprisal 4 bits. Their reading times vary, so the model should not assign one inevitable response to every such word.
Instead, we can ask for the expected response among observations with that predictor value:

\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=4].

This is a conditional mean. It is the center of the response distribution restricted to words with surprisal 4.
Now consider 5 bits:

\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=5].

If the second quantity is larger, expected log reading time increases with surprisal.

title: Conditional means
section: Treat the conditional mean as a function
text:
Treat the conditional mean as a function
Let the predictor value vary:

m(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x].

The function m maps every predictor value x to the expected response at that value.
A regression model specifies a form for this conditional distribution. Its central location may change with x, and in richer models its scale or shape may change as well.

title: Conditional means
text:
Compare conditional and marginal means
The marginal mean

\mathbb{E}[Y]

averages over words with every surprisal value. It does not describe how reading time changes across surprisal.
The conditional mean preserves that distinction. It lets us compare the response distribution at 4 bits with the distribution at 5 bits.

title: Conditional means
text:
State the regression question precisely
For this study, the question is

How does expected log reading time at a word change as that word’s surprisal changes?

Surprisal is treated as a supplied predictor. Estimating the language model that produced it is a separate inferential task.
The conditional association also need not be causal. Frequency, word length, contextual constraint, and other properties may vary with surprisal. A causal interpretation requires design and identification assumptions beyond the regression equation.






NoteCheck the target



Why does \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=4]=6 not imply that every word with surprisal 4 has log reading time 6?


The next page makes one first assumption about m(x): it is a straight line.

title: Residuals
text:
The fitting page used observed minus fitted discrepancies in the least-squares objective. We now inspect those discrepancies observation by observation.
For observation i, the fitted line supplies an estimated conditional mean
\widehat{y}_i
=\widehat{\beta}_0+\widehat{\beta}_1x_i.
The residual is the observed response minus this fitted value:
e_i=y_i-\widehat{y}_i.
The residual is an observation-level discrepancy. It records what remains after subtracting the model’s prediction for that observation.
The direction of the subtraction matters. We subtract the fitted value from the observed response, not the observed response from the fitted value. This convention makes a positive residual an observation above the fitted line.

title: Residuals
text:
Calculate three residuals
For the six constructed observations, the fitted equation is

\widehat y_i=5.629+.0714x_i.

The first three residuals are approximately:









observation
observed y_i
fitted \widehat{y}_i
residual e_i




1
5.7800
5.7714
.0086


2
5.8200
5.8429
-.0229


3
5.9300
5.9143
.0157



A positive residual places the observation above its fitted mean. A negative residual places it below.
The magnitude records how poorly the conditional mean predicts that observation on the response scale.
For observation 2,

e_2
=5.8200-5.8429
\approx-.0229.

The fitted conditional mean is about .0229 log-time units above the observed response. The residual does not say that the fitted value is wrong by the same amount for all words with 3 bits of surprisal. It describes this observation.

title: Residuals
section: Compute them from the fitted model
text:
Compute them from the fitted model


Code
reading_times <- data.frame(
  surprisal = 2:7,
  log_rt = c(5.78, 5.82, 5.93, 5.99, 6.05, 6.13)
)

fit <- lm(log_rt ~ surprisal, data = reading_times)
reading_times$residual <- residuals(fit)
reading_times


Equivalently,


Code
reading_times$log_rt - fitted(fit)


The equality of the two vectors verifies that residuals are observed responses minus fitted values. We can also attach fitted values to see all three quantities together:


Code
transform(
  reading_times,
  fitted = fitted(fit),
  reconstructed_response = fitted(fit) + residuals(fit)
)


The reconstructed response equals the observed response in every row because

y_i=\widehat y_i+e_i.

This identity holds by the definition of a residual. It does not depend on the normality assumption.

title: Residuals
text:
Residuals are not error terms
The ordinary linear regression model contains unobserved errors

\varepsilon_i=Y_i-\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid X_i].

These errors are defined relative to the unknown true conditional mean. Residuals are defined relative to the fitted mean estimated from the same sample.
Thus e_i is observable after fitting, while \varepsilon_i is a model quantity we do not directly observe. Residuals provide evidence about the error assumptions, but they are not identical to the errors.
Suppose the true conditional mean at x_i were 5.90, the fitted mean were 5.88, and the observed response were 5.94. The unobserved error would be

\varepsilon_i=5.94-5.90=.04,

while the residual would be

e_i=5.94-5.88=.06.

The two values differ because the fitted mean differs from the true mean. With more informative data and an adequate model, residual patterns may approximate error patterns more closely. They never become the same object by definition.

title: Residuals
section: A zero sum is not a fit check
text:
A zero sum is not a fit check
In ordinary least squares with an intercept,

\sum_i e_i=0.

This equality follows from the fitting procedure. It can hold even when residuals trace a strong curve or widen systematically with fitted values.
For the constructed fit:


Code
sum(residuals(fit))


The output may be a tiny nonzero value because computers approximate real-number arithmetic. A value near 10^{-16} is numerical noise, not a meaningful failure of the zero-sum property.
The zero sum also does not imply that positive and negative residuals are small. Residuals of 1, -1, 10, and -10 sum to zero while containing large observation-level discrepancies. The sum loses the sizes and their ordering across predictors.

title: Residuals
text:
Preserve the response scale
A raw residual has the response’s units. Here it is measured in log-time units. If the response were vowel duration in milliseconds, a raw residual would be in milliseconds. This makes residual size interpretable only relative to the response scale and the scientific setting.
Comparing raw residual magnitudes across models with different response transformations can thus be misleading. The numerical scale has changed. On this page, all interpretations remain on the fitted log-reading-time scale.
The next page plots residuals to reveal patterns that their sum conceals.






NoteCheck the sign




An observed log reading time is 6.20 and its fitted mean is 6.05. Calculate and interpret the residual.
If the true conditional mean were 6.00, what would the corresponding error be? Why does it differ from the residual?
Explain why a zero residual sum cannot establish that all residuals are small.
What units does a raw residual inherit?

title: Shrinking correlated coefficients
text:
The correlated-predictor page showed that nearly overlapping design-matrix columns can leave separate coefficients unstable while fitted values remain stable. Ridge regression changes the estimation rule for that setting.
Suppose a reading-time model contains lexical frequency and contextual predictability. These predictors may be strongly correlated: frequent words also tend to be more predictable. The fitted model can still predict reading time well while assigning a large positive coefficient to one predictor and a large negative coefficient to the other. A small change in the sample may reverse the allocation.
The problem is not that either predictor lacks a linguistic interpretation. The problem is that the observed data provide little information for separating their partial associations. We need an estimation rule that makes this weak separation explicit.

title: Shrinking correlated coefficients
text:
Begin with the least-squares objective
For a multiple linear regression with centered predictors, ordinary least squares chooses coefficients to minimize the residual sum of squares (RSS)

\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left(y_i-\beta_0-\sum_{j=1}^{p}x_{ij}\beta_j\right)^2.

When two columns of the design matrix are identical, many coefficient vectors can produce the same fitted values. When they are nearly identical, the minimum is unique but shallow in one direction. Coefficients can move far along that direction while changing the residual sum of squares very little.

title: Shrinking correlated coefficients
text:
Add a coefficient penalty
Ridge regression changes the estimation rule by adding the squared size of the slope coefficients to the objective:

\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\lambda}
=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\boldsymbol\beta}
\left[
\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)
+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2
\right].

The constant \lambda\geq0 is the regularization parameter. When \lambda=0, the objective is ordinary least squares. As \lambda increases, large slope coefficients become more costly.
The intercept is normally excluded from the penalty. Penalizing it would pull the response baseline toward zero in the measurement’s arbitrary units. The slopes are the terms whose unstable allocation we want to regularize.

title: Shrinking correlated coefficients
section: Work through a perfectly correlated example
text:
Work through a perfectly correlated example
Let two standardized predictors have the same values:



observation
x_1
x_2
y




1
-1
-1
-2


2
0
0
0


3
1
1
2



The intercept is zero because every column is centered. The fitted value is

\widehat y_i=(\beta_1+\beta_2)x_i.

Ordinary least squares reaches zero residual error whenever

\beta_1+\beta_2=2.

The solutions (2,0), (1,1), and (10,-8) fit the three observations equally well. The data do not distinguish them.
Now set \lambda=2. Because the predictors are interchangeable, the ridge minimum assigns them the same coefficient. Let \beta_1=\beta_2=b. The penalized objective becomes

\begin{aligned}
Q(b)
&=2(2-2b)^2+2(b^2+b^2)\\
&=8(1-b)^2+4b^2.
\end{aligned}

Differentiating and setting the result to zero gives

\begin{aligned}
Q'(b)&=-16+24b=0,\\
b&=\frac{2}{3}.
\end{aligned}

The ridge estimate is thus

\widehat\beta_1=\widehat\beta_2=\frac{2}{3}.

The coefficients sum to 4/3, so the fitted line no longer passes through all three observations. Ridge accepts some residual error on the observed points in exchange for smaller, uniquely determined coefficients.

title: Shrinking correlated coefficients
text:
Compute the estimate from matrices
Let \mathbf X contain a column of ones followed by the predictor columns. The ridge estimate is

\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\lambda}
=\left(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X+\lambda\mathbf P\right)^{-1}
\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y,

where \mathbf P has a zero for the intercept and ones for the slopes.


Code
x <- c(-1, 0, 1)
X <- cbind(intercept = 1, x1 = x, x2 = x)
y <- c(-2, 0, 2)

lambda <- 2
penalty <- diag(c(0, 1, 1))

beta_ridge <- solve(
  crossprod(X) + lambda * penalty,
  crossprod(X, y)
)

beta_ridge


The calculation returns an intercept of zero and two slope coefficients equal to 2/3. Unlike the ordinary inverse of \mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X, the penalized inverse exists in this example.

title: Shrinking correlated coefficients
text:
Put predictors on comparable scales
The penalty acts on numerical coefficient size. Suppose lexical frequency is measured once in raw token counts and once in millions of tokens. The two columns express the same information on different scales, but their coefficients differ by a factor of one million. A common penalty would then treat the parameterizations differently.
For this reason, ridge regression normally uses centered predictors divided by their training-set standard deviations:

x_{ij}^{*}
=\frac{x_{ij}-\overline{x}_j}{s_j}.

The centering and scaling constants are part of the estimation rule. Changing them changes the meaning of a one-unit coefficient and thus changes the force of the penalty. They must be reported together with \lambda.

title: Shrinking correlated coefficients
text:
Interpret shrinkage with care
Ridge changes the target of estimation. Its coefficients minimize a penalized objective, not the unpenalized residual sum of squares. They are biased toward zero under repeated sampling, and this bias is deliberate. The intended gain is lower variance when the predictors do not support stable coefficient separation.
Ridge also does not decide which correlated predictor is the linguistic cause of the response. In the perfectly correlated example, it divides the signal equally because the columns are numerically interchangeable. A different scale or correlation pattern changes that allocation. Theoretically distinct predictors remain theoretically distinct, even when regularization stabilizes a prediction rule that uses both.
The penalty strength must be declared. A value that produces small observed-data error is not automatically useful for new verbs, speakers, or texts. Later pages on predictive evaluation show how to select \lambda for the observations and population to which the prediction will be applied.

title: Shrinking correlated coefficients
section: Ridge does not identify separate coefficient meanings
text:
Ridge does not identify separate coefficient meanings
A stable prediction does not license a separate causal or theoretical interpretation for each shrunken coefficient. Ridge may stabilize the prediction by shrinking correlated slopes. It does not turn the shrunken slopes into clean estimates of separate linguistic mechanisms.
When the scientific question concerns the distinct roles of frequency and predictability, the design needs observations that separate those predictors or additional assumptions that justify the decomposition. When the question concerns prediction for new lexical items, ridge can still be useful even if the individual slopes receive a narrower interpretation.






NoteCheck the penalty




What does ridge add to the ordinary least-squares objective?
Why is the intercept usually excluded from the penalty?
In the worked example, give another ordinary least-squares solution whose coefficients sum to 2.
Why must predictors be put on comparable scales before applying one penalty?
Explain why a stable prediction does not supply separate interpretations for the two correlated linguistic predictors.



The residualization page next considers a different reparameterization of correlated predictors. It does not impose a coefficient penalty.

title: Singular mixed model fits
text:
The random-effects-correlation page represented intercept and slope deviations with a covariance matrix. A singular fit occurs when the estimated random-effects covariance matrix has lower rank than the model specification allows.
Singularity is a statement about the fitted covariance structure. It is not the same as optimizer nonconvergence.

title: Singular mixed model fits
section: Begin with a two dimensional structure
text:
Begin with a two dimensional structure
Suppose a model includes listener random intercepts and noise slopes:
log_rt ~ noise_condition +
  (1 + noise_condition | listener)
The listener covariance matrix is

\boldsymbol\Sigma
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\tau_0^2 & \rho\tau_0\tau_1\\
\rho\tau_0\tau_1 & \tau_1^2
\end{bmatrix}.

With positive intercept and slope variances and a correlation inside the interval (-1,1), the matrix has rank two. It represents two directions of group variation.
If \widehat\tau_1=0, the slope direction collapses. The model requested between-group slope variation, but the fitted covariance matrix contains none. If |\widehat\rho|=1, one deviation is a perfect linear function of the other, and the matrix again loses a dimension.
The fitted random-effect covariance matrix has then lost a dimension and is singular.

title: Singular mixed model fits
text:
Separate singularity from nonconvergence
An optimizer can converge successfully to a boundary value. In that case, the numerical search found a stable optimum, and the fitted covariance matrix is singular. Software may report convergence alongside a singularity warning.
The reverse is also possible. An estimated covariance matrix can be nonsingular even though the optimizer failed to settle at a reliable optimum. A convergence warning concerns the numerical search. A singularity warning concerns the rank of the fitted covariance matrix.
Both checks are needed:
isSingular(fit_correlated, tol = 1e-4)
summary(fit_correlated)
The first command checks the fitted covariance geometry. The summary and optimizer messages report numerical behavior.

title: Singular mixed model fits
section: Inspect the design before changing the model
text:
Inspect the design before changing the model
A random slope requires within group predictor variation. If many listeners appear in only one condition, the design cannot separate their baselines from listener specific condition associations. Few listener levels or few observations per condition can also leave the slope variance weakly informed.
The same reasoning applies to crossed item slopes. A condition that varies within listeners but not within items may support a listener slope and fail to support an item slope.
Thus a singular fit should send us back to the sources of dependence and the within-group predictor support. The first question is not which term makes a warning disappear. It is which requested population variation the design can identify.

title: Singular mixed model fits
text:
Inspect the fitted dimensions
rePCA() rotates the estimated covariance matrix into independent directions and reports their standard deviations:
rePCA(fit_correlated)
In a larger random effects structure, individual variances and correlations may not reveal the collapsed combination. The rotated representation can show that one linear combination of deviations has an estimated standard deviation near zero.
This result is especially useful when a formula has several slopes. The singularity may involve a combination of them rather than one variance component equal to zero.

title: Singular mixed model fits
Singular mixed model fits
Sufficient statistics
text:
The earlier chapter defined a likelihood as a function of a parameter with the observed data held fixed. The exponential-family page showed that data enter some likelihoods through a compact sum. Sufficiency states when such a reduction retains all likelihood information about a parameter.
Suppose we observe binary responses y_1,\ldots,y_n under one Bernoulli probability \pi. Once we know the number of successes, do the individual orderings of zeroes and ones provide additional information about \pi?

title: Sufficient statistics
text:
Factor the likelihood
The joint likelihood is

L(\pi)
=
\prod_{i=1}^{n}
\pi^{y_i}(1-\pi)^{1-y_i}.

Collecting exponents gives

L(\pi)
=
\pi^{\sum_i y_i}
(1-\pi)^{n-\sum_i y_i}.

The data affect this likelihood only through \sum_i y_i, the number of successes. The order in which the responses occurred does not matter for estimating \pi under this model.
The success count is thus a sufficient statistic for \pi.
Sufficiency allows likelihood-irrelevant detail to be omitted from inference about one parameter. The resulting reduction is lossless for inference about \pi under the stated independent, constant-probability Bernoulli model. It need not be lossless for another question.

title: Sufficient statistics
text:
Compare two ordered response sequences
Consider two sequences of six binary responses:

\mathbf y_A=(1,1,1,0,0,0)

and

\mathbf y_B=(1,0,1,0,1,0).

Both contain three successes and three failures. Under one Bernoulli probability,

L_A(\pi)=\pi^3(1-\pi)^3

and

L_B(\pi)=\pi^3(1-\pi)^3.

At \pi=.6, both likelihoods equal

.6^3(.4)^3=.013824.

The model cannot use the clustered successes in sequence A or the alternation in sequence B to distinguish values of \pi. Their sufficient statistic is the same:

T(\mathbf y_A)=T(\mathbf y_B)=3.

title: Sufficient statistics
text:
What sufficiency means
A sufficient statistic T(\mathbf{Y}) for parameter \theta is a statistic for which the conditional distribution of the full data given T(\mathbf{Y}) does not depend on \theta. Informally, after the statistic is known, the remaining details of the sample contain no additional information about that parameter under the assumed model.
The phrase “under the assumed model” is essential. The order of binary responses is irrelevant to an independent Bernoulli model. It may be informative about learning, fatigue, or sequential dependence under another model.
This gives a direct diagnostic question. If the order is scientifically meaningful, does the fitted model represent the process that could produce an ordered pattern? Sufficiency says the order is unnecessary for one parameter under one model. It does not say the order is linguistically meaningless.

title: Sufficient statistics
text:
Use the factorization criterion
A statistic T(\mathbf y) is sufficient for \theta if the likelihood can be written as

L(\theta;\mathbf y)
=h(\mathbf y)g(T(\mathbf y),\theta),

where h does not depend on \theta. For the Bernoulli sample,

h(\mathbf y)=1

and

g(T,\pi)=\pi^T(1-\pi)^{n-T}.

All dependence on \pi passes through T=\sum_i y_i. This is the factorization criterion for sufficiency.

title: Sufficient statistics
text:
A linguistic example
Suppose a speaker produces a voiced variant on 18 of 30 independent tokens with identical modeled conditions. For a one-probability Bernoulli model, the pair (18,30) contains the likelihood information about \pi.
The log likelihood is

\ell(\pi)
=18\log\pi+12\log(1-\pi).

The individual token order no longer appears. If the number of trials n is fixed and known, the success count 18 alone supplies the sample-dependent part.
If the trials differ by verb, time phrase, or trial position, collapsing to one count destroys predictor information. Sufficiency is always relative to a parameter and a model.
For instance, suppose the first 15 tokens occur phrase-medially and the last 15 occur phrase-finally. A model with separate position probabilities needs two success counts, one within each position. The overall count 18 does not say how successes were divided across the two predictor rows.
The required statistic changed because the parameterization changed. There is no model-free sufficient summary of a dataset.

title: Sufficient statistics
text:
Connection with the exponential family
In a one parameter exponential family, the data enter the likelihood through a statistic such as \sum_i y_i. This compact dependence is one reason the family supports a common fitting theory.
It does not license arbitrary aggregation. Regression gives observations different conditional means through their predictors. Two observations with different predictor rows are not interchangeable merely because their responses have the same family.

title: Sufficient statistics
section: Separate inference compression from data storage
text:
Separate inference compression from data storage
A sufficient statistic need not replace the original observations in an analysis archive. The token-level data may be needed to check independence, locate coding errors, study later hypotheses, or reconstruct grouped sampling.
The original data should not be deleted merely because one current parameter has a sufficient statistic. Sufficiency is a likelihood statement. It is not a data-management instruction.

title: Sufficient statistics
text:
Calculate the sufficient statistic


Code
y_a <- c(1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0)
y_b <- c(1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0)
pi <- .6

c(
  successes_a = sum(y_a),
  successes_b = sum(y_b),
  likelihood_a = prod(pi^y_a * (1 - pi)^(1 - y_a)),
  likelihood_b = prod(pi^y_b * (1 - pi)^(1 - y_b))
)


The equal likelihood values verify the hand calculation for this model and parameter value.






NoteIdentify the model-relative compression




Why is the number of successes sufficient for one Bernoulli probability?
When could response order contain information that this model ignores?
Why can regression data not always be reduced to one success count?
What sufficient summaries would a two-position Bernoulli model require?
Explain why a sufficient statistic does not make the original observations dispensable.

title: Variance inflation from correlated predictors
text:
The correlated-predictor page explained why a coefficient becomes uncertain when few observations separate two predictors. A variance inflation factor (VIF) measures that uncertainty increase in an ordinary linear regression.
As on the earlier standard-error page, the relevant uncertainty is repeated-sample variation in an estimator. The diagnostic asks a counterfactual precision question: how much larger is the sampling variance of coefficient j because its predictor overlaps with the other predictors in this design?

title: Variance inflation from correlated predictors
text:
Define the auxiliary regression
For predictor X_j, regress it on all other predictors and record R_j^2. Then

\operatorname{VIF}_j
=
\frac{1}{1-R_j^2}.

If the other predictors do not explain X_j, then R_j^2=0 and \operatorname{VIF}_j=1. The sampling variance is not inflated relative to the no-overlap reference.
Suppose word length is regressed on log frequency and neighborhood density, producing

R_{\text{length}}^2=.75.

Then

\operatorname{VIF}_{\text{length}}
=
\frac{1}{1-.75}=4.

Under the usual linear-model conditions, the sampling variance of the length coefficient is four times what it would be if length had the same marginal variation but were uncorrelated with the other predictors. Its standard error is multiplied by

\sqrt{4}=2.

Variance and standard error are not inflated by the same factor because standard error is the square root of variance. If VIF is 9, coefficient variance is nine times the reference and standard error is three times the reference.

title: Variance inflation from correlated predictors
section: Connect VIF to residual predictor variation
text:
Connect VIF to residual predictor variation
The auxiliary regression predicts X_j from the other predictors. When R_j^2 is large, little residual variation in X_j remains. The response model must estimate coefficient j from this remaining variation.
Since

1-R_j^2

is the proportion of predictor variation left by the auxiliary regression, VIF is its reciprocal. If 25 percent remains, VIF is 1/.25=4. If 10 percent remains, VIF is 1/.10=10.
For length and frequency, the informative observations are unusually long frequent words and unusually short rare words. A large VIF says that such comparisons are scarce. It does not say that they are linguistically irrelevant.

title: Variance inflation from correlated predictors
section: Calculate VIF from a predictor table
text:
Calculate VIF from a predictor table
Suppose a morphological study uses stem length and affix count as predictors of production duration:


Code
morphology_design <- data.frame(
  stem_length = c(2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8),
  affix_count = c(0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 2, 3),
  duration = c(310, 335, 390, 365, 430, 505, 540, 620)
)

auxiliary <- lm(stem_length ~ affix_count, data = morphology_design)
r_squared_j <- summary(auxiliary)$r.squared
vif_j <- 1 / (1 - r_squared_j)

c(r_squared = r_squared_j, vif = vif_j, se_multiplier = sqrt(vif_j))


The response duration does not enter the auxiliary regression. VIF is a property of the predictor design. Changing every duration while leaving the two predictors fixed would leave the reported VIF unchanged.
For a model with only two predictors, the auxiliary R^2 equals their squared correlation. With more predictors, R_j^2 measures how well their combination predicts X_j.

title: Variance inflation from correlated predictors
text:
Avoid a mechanical threshold
Rules such as VIF greater than 5 or 10 are conventions. The same value can have different consequences depending on sample size, predictor range, and the precision required for the scientific claim.
For instance, doubling a coefficient standard error may still leave enough precision to distinguish two substantively different hypotheses in one study. The same doubling may erase the distinction in another. The VIF quantifies a design consequence; the theory determines whether that consequence is tolerable.
Inspect coefficient intervals, predictor support, and sensitivity to reasonable specifications. Do not delete a theory-bearing predictor solely to cross a threshold.
If the car package is installed, it can retrieve VIFs from a fitted model:


Code
fit_morphology <- lm(
  duration ~ stem_length + affix_count,
  data = morphology_design
)

# car::vif(fit_morphology)


For categorical predictors represented by several columns, software may report a generalized VIF. Its definition and degrees-of-freedom adjustment must be checked before comparing it with a one-column VIF.

title: Variance inflation from correlated predictors
text:
Keep prediction and attribution separate
Collinear models can make stable predictions within the observed predictor region while assigning unstable coefficients to correlated predictors. VIF diagnoses coefficient attribution, not predictive accuracy on new responses.
VIF also does not say which predictor should be removed. Deleting stem length sets its partial coefficient to zero and changes the affix-count comparison. If both predictors express distinct hypotheses, the enlarged uncertainty may be the honest result.
Deleting a predictor based only on a VIF cutoff treats a diagnostic as a model-selection command. A VIF is more useful when paired with the support plot and the coefficient contrast the study needs.






NoteRead the variance inflation factor




What VIF results when R_j^2=.50?
What happens to the coefficient standard error when VIF equals 9?
Why is a high VIF not sufficient reason to remove a theoretical predictor?
Why can VIF be calculated without the response?
Explain why a VIF cutoff does not by itself determine whether a predictor should be deleted.

title: Why standard beta regression fails for sliders
text:
The bounded-response page distinguished the values permitted by a measurement from those permitted by a response distribution. A slider from no to yes appears to invite beta regression after its responses are rescaled to the unit interval. The scale and the likelihood differ at precisely the values that express the strongest possible answers, though: the slider includes zero and one, while an ordinary beta variable lies strictly between them.
There are two problems to follow. Standard beta regression cannot use endpoint responses as recorded, and moving those responses inward by an arbitrary amount makes that choice part of the likelihood. The derivation follows Section 1 of the supplementary material for Grove and White (2025).
crumbs: Why standard beta regression fails for sliders

title: Why standard beta regression fails for sliders
section: The scale and the likelihood have different support
text:
The scale and the likelihood have different support
Suppose an inference experiment asks participants to respond on a slider with endpoints labeled no and yes. After rescaling, the recorded response satisfies

Y_i\in[0,1].

A standard beta regression instead assumes

Y_i\mid\mu_i,\phi
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha_i,\beta_i),

where

\alpha_i=\mu_i\phi,
\qquad
\beta_i=(1-\mu_i)\phi,
\qquad
0<\mu_i<1,

and the beta density is defined for

0<Y_i<1.

Thus a response of exactly zero or one is not an extreme observation under this model. It is outside the response space. The response support is wrong, regardless of convergence or sample size.
The mismatch can matter theoretically. Consider a prompt asking whether an embedded proposition follows from a sentence containing know. A semantic model in which know is factive may supply an intended answer of exactly one. Participants may then map that answer onto the physical slider with some response error. A response model should allow us to distinguish the intended answer from error in producing a slider response. A likelihood that excludes one cannot represent the full measurement process when either the theory or the participant can use that endpoint.
crumbs: Why standard beta regression fails for sliders

title: Why standard beta regression fails for sliders
crumbs: Why standard beta regression fails for sliders

title: Why standard beta regression fails for sliders
section: Follow one endpoint through the likelihood
text:
Follow one endpoint through the likelihood
The beta density for one interior observation is

f(y_i\mid\alpha_i,\beta_i)
=\frac{y_i^{\alpha_i-1}(1-y_i)^{\beta_i-1}}
{B(\alpha_i,\beta_i)}.

Its log-density is

\log f(y_i\mid\alpha_i,\beta_i)
=(\alpha_i-1)\log y_i
+(\beta_i-1)\log(1-y_i)
-\log B(\alpha_i,\beta_i).

Now take an observed zero and replace it with \delta. Its pointwise contribution becomes

\ell_{i,0}(\delta)
=(\alpha_i-1)\log\delta
+(\beta_i-1)\log(1-\delta)
-\log B(\alpha_i,\beta_i).

For an observed one replaced with 1-\delta, the roles reverse:

\ell_{i,1}(\delta)
=(\alpha_i-1)\log(1-\delta)
+(\beta_i-1)\log\delta
-\log B(\alpha_i,\beta_i).

When \delta is small, \log(1-\delta) is close to zero. The influential term is thus \log\delta. Its value does not become negligible as the nudge becomes smaller:



\delta
\log\delta




.01
-4.605


.001
-6.908


.0001
-9.210



Every tenfold reduction in \delta changes \log\delta by about -2.303. That change enters once for every endpoint response, multiplied by \alpha_i-1 for a zero or \beta_i-1 for a one. Its direction depends on the fitted beta shape, but its magnitude grows with the number of endpoints.
A small change on the response scale can thus induce a large change on the log-likelihood scale. The two scales should not be confused.
crumbs: Why standard beta regression fails for sliders

title: Why standard beta regression fails for sliders
text:
The full endpoint contribution
Let I_0 index the observed zeros and I_1 the observed ones. The endpoint-dependent portion of the nudged log-likelihood is

\begin{aligned}
\ell_{\partial}(\delta)
= {} & \sum_{i\in I_0}
\left[(\alpha_i-1)\log\delta
+(\beta_i-1)\log(1-\delta)\right]\\
&+\sum_{i\in I_1}
\left[(\alpha_i-1)\log(1-\delta)
+(\beta_i-1)\log\delta\right].
\end{aligned}

Ignoring terms that approach zero as \delta shrinks gives the approximation

\ell_{\partial}(\delta)
\approx
\log\delta
\left[
\sum_{i\in I_0}(\alpha_i-1)
+\sum_{i\in I_1}(\beta_i-1)
\right].

This expression makes three consequences visible.

The nudge affects every endpoint, so its influence can accumulate rapidly.
It interacts with the fitted mean because \alpha_i=\mu_i\phi and \beta_i=(1-\mu_i)\phi. It can thus affect coefficient and precision estimates rather than merely adding the same constant to every model.
Two candidate models generally imply different \alpha_i and \beta_i, so changing \delta can change their likelihood difference.

That last consequence matters whenever models are compared with likelihood-based quantities. Such comparisons aggregate pointwise likelihood values. If those values depend strongly on an analyst-chosen nudge, the comparison partly measures the preprocessing choice. A sensitivity analysis may reveal the dependence, but it cannot supply a principled value of \delta.






WarningA deterministic transformation does not remove the choice



A software default or a rule based on sample size may choose \delta automatically. The endpoint contribution still contains \log\delta. Automation hides the researcher degree of freedom; it does not give the beta likelihood support at zero and one.
crumbs: Why standard beta regression fails for sliders

title: Why standard beta regression fails for sliders
section: When standard beta regression remains coherent
text:
When standard beta regression remains coherent
This support problem does not imply that beta regression is never useful. It can be coherent when the measurement process produces genuinely continuous values strictly inside (0,1). For instance, an interface whose handle cannot reach either endpoint may have open-interval support.
The absence of endpoints in one sample is weaker evidence. If the instrument permits exact endpoint responses, a future participant can still produce one. And if the endpoint labels express theoretically meaningful answers, excluding those values makes a substantive claim about the response process. That claim needs justification from the task, not merely a dataset that happened to contain no zeros or ones.
Once endpoints are possible, the analysis should use a likelihood that is defined for them and whose endpoint behavior matches the measurement story. The next page introduces one such likelihood. Other stories, such as censoring at a detection limit or a small set of ordered response categories, would require different models.
crumbs: Why standard beta regression fails for sliders

title: Why standard beta regression fails for sliders
text:
Read the model

A slider permits 0 and 100, but a particular sample contains only values from 7 through 94. Does the sample alone establish open-interval support?
Why can changing \delta affect a comparison between two beta regressions rather than adding the same constant to both log-likelihoods?
Suppose 80 observed zeros are nudged inward. For those cases, which fitted beta-shape parameter multiplies the influential \log\delta term?
crumbs: Why standard beta regression fails for sliders

title: Why standard beta regression fails for sliders
text:
What the derivation established
Standard beta regression assigns responses to (0,1), while sliders that permit endpoint selections produce values in [0,1]. Nudging endpoints inward changes the data and places \log\delta directly in every endpoint’s likelihood contribution. This dependence can accumulate across endpoints and alter parameter estimates or model comparisons. The next page introduces ordered-beta regression, which models both endpoints without an arbitrary nudge.
crumbs: Why standard beta regression fails for sliders

\[

=\sigma^2+\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat f(x))^2+\operatorname{Var}(\widehat f(x))
\]

Predict the responses in fold \(k\).

Question
Does a larger model improve maximized likelihood enough to reject the restrictions imposed by a nested smaller model?

D=2\{\ell(\widehat\theta_1)-\ell(\widehat\theta_0)\}.
\]

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data

Compute each omitted response density under the posterior that would have been obtained without that response.
\[
p(y_i\mid y_{-i})=\int p(y_i\mid\theta)p(\theta\mid y_{-i})\,d\theta
\]

Method
\[
\operatorname{elpd}_{\mathrm{waic}}
=\operatorname{lppd}
-\sum_i\operatorname{Var}_s\!\left[\log p(y_i\mid\theta^{(s)})\right]
\]
Larger values are preferred.
