title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Big Question
How well does a fitted model predict linguistic observations that did not contribute to its fit?

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Answer

Name what is omitted and what remains available.
Choose a loss whose scale matches the scientific question.
Fit every adaptive step without the held-out responses.
Interpret comparison at the linguistic unit named by the claim.

title: Comparing predictive loss
text:
The grouped-validation page returned held-out losses to the groups omitted during fitting. Comparing two procedures requires pairing their losses on those same groups. The uncertainty calculation then reuses the paired-mean procedure on group-level loss differences.
Suppose two models produce held-out predictions for the same passages. Reporting that Model B has lower aggregate RMSE than Model A gives a direction, but not the distribution of the improvement. A tiny gain concentrated in three passages supports a different claim from a modest gain observed throughout the corpus.
A paired comparison computes both models’ losses on the same held-out groups and summarizes their difference at that level. Pairing removes variation due merely to the two models being evaluated on different observations.

title: Comparing predictive loss
text:
Pointwise differences
For observation i, define

\Delta_i
=
L(y_i,\widehat{y}_{i,A})
-
L(y_i,\widehat{y}_{i,B}).

Positive \Delta_i favors Model B because it has lower loss. Negative values favor Model A. The sign convention should be stated; “difference in RMSE” is otherwise ambiguous.
If the predictive question concerns independent observations, the distribution of \Delta_i may be the relevant evidence. If it concerns passages, positions within one passage should first be aggregated:

\Delta_p
=
\frac{1}{n_p}
\sum_{i:g(i)=p}\Delta_i.

The mean \overline{\Delta} then estimates the average passage-level change in loss among the represented passages.

title: Comparing predictive loss
text:
Why not test fold means?
Computational folds do not necessarily correspond to sampling units. Ten folds may each contain positions from several passages, and their training sets overlap. A t test on ten fold means thus treats arbitrary partitions as independent replications.
Returning losses to passages yields 55 paired passage comparisons in a 55-passage corpus, regardless of whether the models were computed with five grouped folds or leave-one-passage-out evaluation. These are still not a probability sample of every possible text, but they are the units specified by the scientific claim.

title: Comparing predictive loss
text:
Direction, magnitude, and heterogeneity
A predictive comparison should report at least three quantities.

Aggregate direction and magnitude: the overall RMSE or mean loss for each model and their difference.
Improvement rate: the proportion of held-out groups with \Delta_g>0.
Variation: an interval or full plot of the group differences.

These quantities can disagree. Model B may have lower overall RMSE because it greatly improves a few difficult passages while slightly harming most others. That model could be useful for position-weighted prediction but provide weak evidence for a typical-passage improvement.
Plotting \Delta_g against group size and baseline loss can locate the source. A gain associated only with long passages may reflect weighting; a gain associated only with high-loss passages may reflect repair of one failure mode.

title: Comparing predictive loss
Comparing predictive loss
text:
Small gains and theoretical claims
A theoretically motivated predictor may have a coefficient in the expected direction yet produce little held-out improvement. This can happen because its unique contribution is small, its measurement is noisy, or the relevant pattern varies across groups. The predictive result does not erase the coefficient; it narrows the claim.
For instance, semantic and morphosyntactic predictability may be associated with shorter first fixations in the fitted corpus. But if adding those predictors does not reliably reduce passage-level loss beyond lexical cloze, the evidence for new-passage predictive contribution is limited. This is a stronger and more specific statement than “the predictors do not matter.”
The reverse pattern is also possible. A model can improve prediction through a proxy that has no theoretical interpretation. Predictive success would then justify the model for that predictive use, but not the linguistic mechanism attributed to it.

title: Comparing predictive loss
text:
Multiple comparisons
Trying many response variables, losses, split rules, transformations, and predictor sets creates many opportunities for a favorable difference. A prespecified primary predictive question, loss, and model contrast control this flexibility. Secondary analyses can examine other choices as sensitivity checks, provided they are labeled and reported together.
The model sequence should also be nested in the scientific argument. A control model establishes performance from design and lexical variables; a lexical model tests full-form predictability; a graded model tests added partial information. Comparing every possible subset would replace the theory with a model tournament.

title: Comparing predictive loss
text:
Check the comparison

If \Delta_p=L_{p,A}-L_{p,B} is positive, which model is favored?
Why should word-position losses be aggregated before uncertainty is reported for a new-passage claim?
Give a situation in which aggregate RMSE improves while fewer than half of passages improve.
What does a coefficient in the expected direction establish that a held-out loss comparison does not, and vice versa?

title: Comparing predictive loss
text:
What the comparison establishes
A paired comparison evaluates two models on the same held-out responses and returns loss differences to the groups specified by the scientific claim. Direction, magnitude, improvement rate, and group variation jointly characterize the result. PS2 applies this procedure to a theory-guided sequence of control, lexical, and graded-prediction models.

title: Grouped cross-validation
text:
The page on what must be new at prediction time distinguished omitted trials from omitted participants, items, and passages. The cross-validation page noted that random row folds can place several trials from the same participant, tokens of the same word, or positions from the same passage in both training and test data. When a complete group must be absent during fitting, this overlap contradicts the predictive question.
Grouped K-fold cross-validation assigns whole groups to folds. All observations sharing the grouping identifier receive the same fold label. The fitting and scoring algorithm remains cross-validation, while the partition ensures that a group does not appear in both training and test data.

title: Grouped cross-validation
text:
Constructing grouped folds
Let g(i) be the group containing observation i. Grouped cross-validation requires

g(i)=g(j)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{fold}(i)=\operatorname{fold}(j).

When complete passages are omitted, g(i) is the passage identifier. When complete speakers are omitted, it is the speaker identifier. A simple R construction assigns folds to unique groups and joins those assignments back to rows.


Code
groups <- unique(dat$passage_id)
set.seed(214)
group_fold <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = length(groups)))
names(group_fold) <- groups

fold <- unname(group_fold[as.character(dat$passage_id)])
stopifnot(all(tapply(fold, dat$passage_id, function(x) length(unique(x))) == 1))


The final assertion is part of the analysis. A fold variable that looks grouped can still contain a join or coercion error.

title: Grouped cross-validation
text:
Leave-one-group-out evaluation
When the number of groups is manageable, leave-one-group-out cross-validation uses each group as its own test set. With G passages, it fits G models and yields one collection of predictions for each passage.
This design has two advantages. First, every group receives a prediction from all other groups. Second, the per-group scores remain visible; a mean cannot conceal that a model helps a few passages and harms many others.
It also has limitations. If G is small, the score varies over only a small set of held-out groups. And if one group is unusual, its fitted model omits a large and distinctive part of the data. These are properties of the available evidence rather than reasons to revert to row folds.

title: Grouped cross-validation
text:
Grouped scores describe grouped populations
Suppose passage p contains n_p word positions and has mean loss

\overline{L}_p
=
\frac{1}{n_p}
\sum_{i:g(i)=p}
L(y_i,\widehat{y}_i).

A passage-weighted score is

\frac{1}{G}\sum_{p=1}^G \overline{L}_p.

Each passage receives equal weight. A position-weighted score instead pools every position before averaging. The latter may be a useful corpus summary, but its uncertainty should not treat positions from one passage as independent passage transfers.
The group is thus used twice: first to construct the split, and second to summarize the variation relevant to the claim.

title: Grouped cross-validation
text:
Crossing several grouping dimensions
Linguistic datasets often cross readers and items. Holding out readers evaluates new readers on observed items. Holding out items evaluates new items for observed readers. Holding out both requires a design in which test observations contain neither training readers nor training items.
These are not ordered versions of one procedure. They ask different questions, and the hardest question need not be the most relevant. A speech technology deployed to returning users may care about new utterances from adapted speakers. A linguistic claim about a construction may care about new speakers and new lexical items.
When groups are nested, the higher-level grouping variable controls the split. Sentence positions nest within passages, so a passage-level split automatically removes its sentences and positions. Splitting sentences across folds does not evaluate prediction for an omitted passage because other sentences from the same passage remain in training.

title: Grouped cross-validation
text:
Group leakage through derived predictors
Moving rows together does not prevent every form of group leakage. A predictor may have been estimated using responses from all groups before the split.
For instance, a word-position mean reading time computed over all readers leaks test-reader responses into an evaluation of omitted readers. A speaker-normalized acoustic measure computed from the held-out speaker’s full recordings may be permissible after adaptation but not before adaptation. An item difficulty score estimated from all judgments leaks test-participant responses into the score unless the analysis explicitly permits that external calibration.
Thus grouped folds must be applied before response-derived features are estimated. Independently collected lexical norms may be available for new passages, while reading-time summaries from those passages are not.

title: Grouped cross-validation
text:
Similar scores are possible
Grouped and random scores can be similar. This does not show that grouping was unnecessary. If the fitted relation generalizes well to omitted groups, new-group performance should be similar to performance on omitted rows from represented groups.
The grouped split earns its place because it evaluates the claimed unit. A visible performance drop is one possible result, not an acceptance criterion for the method. Conversely, a large drop may reflect genuine distribution shift, omitted group structure, or a preprocessing error. Per-group inspection is needed to distinguish them.






NoteProblem Set 3 connection



Problem Set 3, Task 4 holds out complete verb types before fitting two dative models. The response is a token headed by a verb absent from training. A random row split would retain other tokens of the held-out verb and would answer a different question about other tokens of represented verbs.








NoteProblem Set 4 connection



Problem Set 4, Task 4 evaluates factivity and embedding models with folds grouped by discourse. Rating-level leave-one-out prediction would retain sister ratings of the same discourse and evaluate another rating from a represented discourse, not a discourse absent during fitting.

title: Grouped cross-validation
text:
Check the grouping variable

Why is a sentence split insufficient when a complete passage must be absent during fitting?
In crossed participant by item data, what question is evaluated by holding out participants while retaining observed items?
Give a response-derived predictor that could leak even when all rows from a test group move together.
If grouped and random RMSE are nearly equal, what can and cannot be concluded?

title: Grouped cross-validation
text:
Before comparing models
Grouped cross-validation moves all observations from a group into the same fold. The group defines both what is withheld and the level at which predictive variation is summarized. Similar random and grouped scores may be a substantive success, but they do not make the predictive questions interchangeable. The next page compares models using paired losses for each held-out group.

title: Penalizing in-sample fit
text:
The likelihood-ratio page compared models connected by a specific parameter restriction. Information criteria address a different comparison by combining fitted likelihood with a penalty for estimated flexibility.
Suppose two models predict log reading time. One uses word length and lexical frequency. The other adds several interactions. The larger model will usually achieve at least as much maximized likelihood on the observations used to fit it, even when the added terms mostly follow sample-specific variation.
This difference is the optimism of training error: performance on the observations used to fit a procedure tends to be better than its expected performance on new observations. An information criterion estimates a correction by combining fitted likelihood with a complexity penalty. The resulting score estimates a model’s relative predictive discrepancy under a particular approximation. It is not a significance test, and its absolute value is not a measure with a standalone linguistic interpretation.
This page focuses on the Akaike information criterion (AIC). We first derive its fit and penalty terms. We then calculate and implement a small model comparison. Finally, we distinguish AIC from the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), direct cross-validation, and comparisons that use incompatible likelihoods.

title: Penalizing in-sample fit
text:
Separate fit from penalty
Let \ell be a model’s maximized log likelihood and let k be its number of estimated parameters. AIC is

\operatorname{AIC}=2k-2\ell.

The expression has two parts:

\underbrace{-2\ell}_{\text{lack of fitted likelihood}}
+
\underbrace{2k}_{\text{complexity penalty}}.

A larger maximized log likelihood makes -2\ell smaller. Adding parameters makes 2k larger. Lower AIC is preferred because the criterion places good fitted likelihood and lower estimated optimism on the same direction of the scale.
The coefficient 2 in the penalty is not an arbitrary classroom convention. Under the assumptions motivating AIC, 2k approximates how optimistic the in-sample fit is as an estimate of performance on new observations from the represented process. The approximation concerns the complete candidate model and its maximum-likelihood fit.

title: Penalizing in-sample fit
text:
Work through two candidate models
Suppose model A has

k_A=3
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\ell_A=-210.

Its AIC is

\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{AIC}_A
&=2(3)-2(-210)\\
&=6+420\\
&=426.
\end{aligned}

Now suppose model B has five parameters and a maximized log likelihood of -207:

\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{AIC}_B
&=2(5)-2(-207)\\
&=10+414\\
&=424.
\end{aligned}

The additional parameters improve log likelihood by 3. That improvement reduces the lack-of-fit term by 6, while the two additional parameters increase the penalty by 4. The improvement is thus larger than the added penalty, and model B has the lower AIC by 2.
Only this difference matters for the comparison:

\Delta_A
=
\operatorname{AIC}_A-\min_m\operatorname{AIC}_m
=
426-424
=
2.

The absolute score 424 is not an error measured in log milliseconds or words. It becomes informative only relative to AIC values computed from compatible candidate models.

title: Penalizing in-sample fit
text:
Calculate the score in R
If the maximized log likelihood and parameter count are already available, the formula is direct.


Code
candidate <- data.frame(
  model = c("A", "B"),
  parameters = c(3, 5),
  log_likelihood = c(-210, -207)
)

candidate$aic <-
  2 * candidate$parameters -
  2 * candidate$log_likelihood

candidate$delta_aic <- candidate$aic - min(candidate$aic)
candidate


For fitted R models, AIC() extracts the same ingredients from the model objects.


Code
AIC(fit_length, fit_surprisal)


This convenient call does not check the scientific comparability of the models. It is the analyst’s responsibility to verify that both objects represent the same response observations and compatible likelihoods.

title: Penalizing in-sample fit
section: Keep the response and observations fixed
text:
Keep the response and observations fixed
Information criteria compare models only when their likelihoods refer to the same observed responses. Suppose an ordinary linear regression is fit to raw reading time and another is fit to log reading time. The two likelihoods assign density to different response variables. Their AIC values are not directly comparable without accounting for the transformation.
The same problem arises when candidate models use different rows. If the richer model contains a predictor with missing values, its fitting function may silently drop more observations. Its log likelihood then summarizes a different dataset. An AIC difference would mix model specification with a change in observations.
A useful check is to compare the row identifiers used in every fit, not merely their reported sample sizes. Equal counts do not guarantee that the same tokens were included.


Code
identical(
  rownames(model.frame(fit_a)),
  rownames(model.frame(fit_b))
)


This is a mechanical check for one necessary condition. It does not establish that the likelihood families are compatible.

title: Penalizing in-sample fit
text:
Compare AIC with BIC
The BIC uses

\operatorname{BIC}=k\log n-2\ell,

where n is the sample size supplied to the approximation. Its parameter penalty grows with \log n. Thus, AIC and BIC may prefer different models, particularly in larger datasets.
BIC is not merely AIC with a stricter penalty. The criteria arise from different motivations and approximations. AIC is motivated by relative expected predictive discrepancy. BIC is motivated by an approximation connected to model evidence under additional assumptions.
Repeated linguistic data create a further difficulty for BIC because the meaning of n may be delicate. Ten thousand trials from 50 speakers do not supply 10,000 independent speakers. Treating every trial count as an unproblematic sample size can make the penalty look more decisive than the design warrants.
For current purposes, the main lesson is modest: report which criterion was used and why it matches the comparison. Do not describe BIC as a universally improved version of AIC.

title: Penalizing in-sample fit
section: Understand what AIC does not encode
text:
Understand what AIC does not encode
AIC approximates relative expected performance for the observation-level likelihood under its regularity conditions. It does not create held-out predictions. It also does not know which unit a linguistic claim requires to be new.
Suppose a reading-time model contains repeated observations from the same passages. AIC cannot distinguish another position in an observed passage from a position in a passage omitted during fitting. Grouped cross-validation can encode that distinction by changing the separation between training and test data.
This difference does not make AIC useless. It makes the scope of the score narrower. AIC can compare a fixed collection of compatible candidate likelihood models without repeatedly refitting them. Direct validation is preferable when prediction for a group absent during fitting is central to the scientific claim.

title: Penalizing in-sample fit
text:
Avoid threshold interpretation
An AIC difference of 2 is not a conventional significance threshold. The difference says that, among these candidates and under the AIC approximation, model B has a criterion value 2 units lower than model A. It does not supply a null tail probability.
The magnitude must also be interpreted alongside the candidate set and stability of the analysis. A small difference may change after a reasonable preprocessing decision. Reporting the component log likelihoods, parameter counts, and criterion differences makes the source of the comparison visible.
Thus, AIC ranks the specified candidates. It does not certify that the best-ranked candidate is an adequate account of the response process.

title: Penalizing in-sample fit
text:
Check the penalized comparison

Why can maximized likelihood alone not select among models of different sizes?
In the worked comparison, how much does model B improve log likelihood, and how much additional AIC penalty does it receive?
What does an AIC difference of 2 describe, and what does it not describe?
Why should models fit to raw and log reading time not be compared by their printed AIC values?
Why can AIC not distinguish prediction for omitted items from prediction for omitted participants?
What additional difficulty does repeated linguistic data create for the n in BIC?

title: Penalizing in-sample fit
text:
Before Bayesian pointwise criteria
AIC addresses optimism of training error by adding a parameter-count penalty to maximized likelihood. The score is relative, requires compatible responses and observations, and does not encode which groups should be absent during fitting. The next page develops a Bayesian leave-one-out approximation that averages over posterior uncertainty and retains pointwise contributions for diagnostic inspection.

title: Comparing nested likelihoods
text:
The earlier maximum-likelihood page showed how a likelihood compares parameter values within one model. A likelihood-ratio test compares two models when one is a restricted version of the other.
Suppose one ordinary linear regression predicts log reading time from word length. A second linear regression adds word surprisal. The second model can reproduce the first whenever the surprisal coefficient is zero. Thus, the two models differ by a specific, testable restriction.
One statistical model is nested within another when it can be obtained by restricting parameters in the larger model. This parameter-space relation differs from nested grouping in a sampling design, such as trials within speakers. A likelihood-ratio test (LRT) asks whether relaxing the parameter restriction improves maximized likelihood by more than would usually be expected if the restriction held in the population. It does not ask which model predicts new passages better, and it does not apply to arbitrary pairs of models.
This page develops the comparison in four steps. We first state what nesting requires. We then derive the likelihood-ratio statistic and calculate one reading-time comparison. Finally, we consider the reference distribution, the cases in which it may fail, and the narrower interpretation licensed by the test.

title: Comparing nested likelihoods
text:
State the nesting relation
Let M_0 be the word-length-only linear regression:

Y_i\sim\operatorname{Normal}(\mu_i,\sigma^2),
\qquad
\mu_i=\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{WordLength}_i.

Let M_1 add word surprisal:

Y_i\sim\operatorname{Normal}(\mu_i,\sigma^2),
\qquad
\mu_i=\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{WordLength}_i
+\beta_2\operatorname{Surprisal}_i.

Setting \beta_2=0 in M_1 gives M_0. Every parameter setting available to the smaller model is thus also available to the larger model. We write this relation as

M_0\subset M_1.

This nesting statement depends on more than the printed mean formula. The models must also use the same response observations, response distribution, variance specification, and likelihood definition. Models for raw and log reading time are not nested merely because they contain the same predictors.

title: Comparing nested likelihoods
section: Move from a likelihood ratio to a difference
text:
Move from a likelihood ratio to a difference
Let \widehat{L}_0 and \widehat{L}_1 be the maximized likelihoods under M_0 and M_1. Since the larger model can reproduce every fit available to the smaller model,

\widehat{L}_1\geq\widehat{L}_0.

The raw likelihood ratio compares the best fit under the restriction with the best unrestricted fit:

\frac{\widehat{L}_0}{\widehat{L}_1}.

This ratio lies between 0 and 1. A value near 1 means that relaxing the restriction adds little fit. A much smaller value means that the larger model assigns substantially more likelihood to the observed responses.
Log likelihood turns the ratio into a difference:

-2\log
\left(
\frac{\widehat{L}_0}{\widehat{L}_1}
\right)
=
-2\left(\log\widehat{L}_0-\log\widehat{L}_1\right)
=
2(\ell_1-\ell_0),

where \ell_0=\log\widehat{L}_0 and \ell_1=\log\widehat{L}_1. We use

\Lambda=2(\ell_1-\ell_0)

as the likelihood-ratio statistic. The factor of two gives the statistic a convenient large-sample reference distribution.

title: Comparing nested likelihoods
text:
Calculate one comparison
Suppose the word-length-only model has maximized log likelihood

\ell_0=-412.6,

and the model that adds surprisal has

\ell_1=-408.1.

The larger model improves log likelihood by

\ell_1-\ell_0
=
-408.1-(-412.6)
=
4.5.

Thus,

\Lambda
=
2(4.5)
=
9.

The larger model must improve the maximized likelihood. The inferential question is whether an improvement of this size is surprising under the restriction \beta_2=0.
If the larger model adds one regular parameter and the usual large-sample conditions hold, then

\Lambda\overset{\cdot}{\sim}\chi^2_1

under the null hypothesis. The degrees of freedom equal the difference in the number of freely estimated regular parameters. Here that difference is one.
In R, the tail probability is computed by


Code
pchisq(9, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)


The result is about 0.0027. Under the null model and the approximation just stated, a likelihood-ratio statistic at least as large as 9 would occur in about 0.27 percent of comparable samples.

title: Comparing nested likelihoods
section: Fit and compare the models in R
text:
Fit and compare the models in R
The model formulas make the restriction visible.


Code
fit_length <- lm(
  log_rt ~ word_length,
  data = reading
)

fit_surprisal <- lm(
  log_rt ~ word_length + surprisal,
  data = reading
)

ll_0 <- logLik(fit_length)
ll_1 <- logLik(fit_surprisal)

lrt <- 2 * (as.numeric(ll_1) - as.numeric(ll_0))
df <- attr(ll_1, "df") - attr(ll_0, "df")

c(
  statistic = lrt,
  df = df,
  p_value = pchisq(lrt, df = df, lower.tail = FALSE)
)


The comparison is valid only if both fits use the same rows. If surprisal is missing for some tokens, the second model may silently drop rows that the first model retains. A safe workflow first constructs the shared analysis dataset and then fits both models to that object.
The coefficient output from fit_surprisal answers a different question from the LRT. The coefficient estimates the direction and magnitude of the conditional surprisal association on the log-reading-time scale. The LRT evaluates the joint restriction represented by the model comparison. With one added coefficient these questions are closely related, but with several added coefficients the LRT tests them together.

title: Comparing nested likelihoods
text:
Interpret the null hypothesis narrowly
For this comparison, the null hypothesis is

H_0:\beta_2=0.

Rejecting that restriction suggests that surprisal improves the fitted likelihood beyond the word-length-only model, conditional on the specified response model and analysis sample. It does not show that the larger model is true. It also does not show that surprisal causes reading-time differences, since causal interpretation requires a design and assumptions beyond the likelihood comparison.
Likewise, failing to reject does not establish that \beta_2 is exactly zero. The data may provide little information about the parameter, or the predictor may be measured noisily. The test calibrates one restriction under one model family.

title: Comparing nested likelihoods
section: Know when the reference distribution may fail
text:
Know when the reference distribution may fail
The \chi^2 approximation assumes that the null value is an interior, regular point of the parameter space and that the parameters are sufficiently identified. Several linguistic models violate these conditions.
Testing whether a random-effect variance equals zero is a standard failure case. A variance cannot be negative, so zero lies on the boundary of the permitted parameter space. The usual \chi^2 reference distribution need not apply.
Mixture models present another difficulty because components can become unidentified under a null restriction. Small samples and weakly identified parameters may also make the large-sample approximation poor. In such cases, a simulation-based reference distribution or a method derived for the specific boundary problem may be needed.
Departures from the regular case do not make the likelihood difference uninformative. It remains a description of fitted improvement. What may fail is the simple claim that \Lambda follows a particular \chi^2 distribution under the null.

title: Comparing nested likelihoods
section: Do not treat the LRT as predictive validation
text:
Do not treat the LRT as predictive validation
The LRT uses the same responses to estimate the models and to compare their maximized likelihoods. It thus answers an in-sample inferential question about a nested restriction.
Cross-validation asks how the complete procedures predict responses excluded from fitting. A model may pass an LRT while producing only a small change in held-out loss. This pattern is possible when a conditional association is estimated precisely but contributes little to prediction relative to other sources of response variation.
The reverse distinction also matters. A predictor may improve held-out prediction through a stable proxy relation without supporting the theoretical mechanism attached to it. Thus, likelihood inference and predictive validation provide different pieces of evidence.

title: Comparing nested likelihoods
text:
Check the nested comparison

What parameter restriction makes the word-length-and-surprisal model reduce to the word-length-only model?
Why can the larger model never have a lower maximized likelihood than the smaller model?
If a larger model adds three regular parameters, what reference degrees of freedom would the usual LRT use?
Why might fitting the two models on different rows invalidate the comparison?
What part of the usual LRT fails when a random-effect variance is tested against zero?
Why does the reported tail probability not evaluate prediction for a new passage?

title: Comparing nested likelihoods
section: Before adding a general complexity penalty
text:
Before adding a general complexity penalty
The LRT compares models connected by a specific restriction. It measures the fitted likelihood gained by relaxing that restriction and calibrates the gain against an approximate null distribution when the regularity conditions hold. The next page considers a different comparison problem: how to penalize improved in-sample fit when candidate models need not be connected by one nested restriction.

title: Predictive loss
text:
The earlier mean-squared-error page used squared error to evaluate an estimator across repeated samples. Predictive loss uses the same algebra to evaluate predictions for held-out responses. The random object and averaging scheme differ, so the two quantities should not be conflated.
Once what must be held out is fixed, an evaluation still needs a numerical definition of error. A 20 ms mistake and a 100 ms mistake should not receive the same assessment, but there is more than one defensible way to express how much worse the second mistake is.
A loss function L(y,\widehat{y}) assigns a nonnegative cost to predicting \widehat{y} when the observed response is y. Lower loss is better, and zero loss usually occurs when prediction and observation coincide. The choice of loss states which mistakes matter for the intended use.
The predictive risk of a procedure is its expected loss on new responses from the population under study. A held-out mean loss estimates that expectation from the available data. Risk is thus an expectation over future responses, not a synonym for one observed error.

title: Predictive loss
text:
Squared loss
The squared-error loss is

L_{\mathrm{SE}}(y,\widehat{y})=(y-\widehat{y})^2.

Doubling the absolute error multiplies squared loss by four. Thus squared loss gives large errors disproportionate influence. Over N held-out predictions, the mean squared error is

\operatorname{MSE}
=
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i-\widehat{y}_i)^2.

The root mean squared error (RMSE) is the square root of mean squared error:

\operatorname{RMSE}=\sqrt{\operatorname{MSE}},

Taking the square root returns the score to the response’s units. If the response is log reading time, RMSE remains on the log scale; it is not an error in milliseconds merely because the untransformed response was measured that way.
The conditional mean is the optimal point prediction under squared loss. This connection explains why RMSE is a natural score for a regression model that estimates \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]. It does not make squared loss universally appropriate.

title: Predictive loss
text:
Absolute loss
The absolute-error loss is

L_{\mathrm{AE}}(y,\widehat{y})=|y-\widehat{y}|,

Its held-out average is the mean absolute error (MAE):

\operatorname{MAE}
=
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N |y_i-\widehat{y}_i|.

Absolute loss grows linearly with the error. A mistake of 100 units costs twice as much as a mistake of 50 units, rather than four times as much. The conditional median is the optimal point prediction under absolute loss.
RMSE and MAE can thus prefer different models. A model that is usually accurate but makes a few very large mistakes may have low MAE and high RMSE. Reporting both can reveal this pattern, but it does not remove the need to designate a primary loss. Otherwise, the preferred score may be selected after the comparison is seen.

title: Predictive loss
text:
A small linguistic example
Suppose two models predict mean log reading time for four word positions.


Code
observed <- c(5.1, 5.2, 5.0, 5.4)
model_a <- c(5.0, 5.3, 5.1, 5.3)
model_b <- c(5.1, 5.2, 5.0, 5.8)

loss <- function(prediction) {
  error <- observed - prediction
  c(
    RMSE = sqrt(mean(error^2)),
    MAE = mean(abs(error))
  )
}

rbind(A = loss(model_a), B = loss(model_b))


Model B predicts three positions exactly but badly misses the fourth. Absolute loss may reward its three exact predictions, while squared loss emphasizes the one large error. The scores disagree because they encode different consequences, not because one calculation is defective.

title: Predictive loss
text:
The unit of averaging
The formula for MSE averages over N observations. But the predictive question may concern groups. If one passage contains 100 word positions and another contains 20, a position-weighted MSE gives the first passage five times as much influence. A passage-weighted score first computes loss within each passage and then averages the passage means.
Neither weighting is neutral. Position weighting describes a randomly selected position from the corpus mixture. Passage weighting describes a randomly selected passage followed by a position within it. The predictive question should determine which is primary.
This distinction is especially important when reporting uncertainty. Thousands of position losses may be observed, but a new-passage claim varies across the number of passages. We will return to this issue after defining grouped validation.

title: Predictive loss
text:
Loss is not explanatory adequacy
A lower predictive loss does not show that a predictor is causal, that a latent component corresponds to a linguistic category, or that a model’s parameters have the interpretation assigned to them. Prediction evaluates a specified mapping from available information to responses under the stated data separation and population.
Conversely, a theoretically meaningful coefficient need not produce a practically important loss reduction. A small and stable association can be real while contributing little to prediction relative to other variation. Comparing predictive loss thus addresses an additional question rather than replacing parameter interpretation.

title: Predictive loss
text:
Check the loss

Which score, RMSE or MAE, is more sensitive to a small number of large errors? Why?
If the response is log duration, on what scale is RMSE computed?
Explain the population weighting difference between a position-weighted and passage-weighted loss.
Can a predictor have a nonzero estimated coefficient but fail to improve held-out loss? Give one reason.

title: Predictive loss
text:
Before separating the data
A loss function defines the cost of each prediction error. Squared loss targets conditional means and emphasizes large misses; absolute loss targets conditional medians and grows linearly. The averaging unit determines what receives weight. The next page explains why predictive error changes across possible training samples. Training and test data then explains why loss must be computed on responses excluded from fitting.

title: Training and test data
text:
The predictive-loss page specified the cost of an error, while the bias-and-variance page defined predictive error across repeated training samples. Separating training data from test data makes one corresponding comparison observable within a dataset.
The residuals of a fitted regression are optimized on the observations used to estimate its coefficients. A more flexible model can often reduce those residuals by adapting to idiosyncrasies that will not recur. Training fit thus cannot by itself estimate predictive loss for new observations.
The training set contains the observations used to fit the model. The test set contains observations used only to evaluate the fitted procedure. The training set determines every fitted quantity. The test set withholds responses that would be unavailable when an actual future prediction is made.

title: Training and test data
Training and test data
text:
Leakage
Data leakage occurs when information from the test set influences a fitted decision that would have been made without that information in the intended prediction setting. Directly fitting on a test response is one case, but preprocessing can leak more quietly.

Centering a predictor using the full dataset lets test predictor values affect the training transformation.
Imputing a missing test response from a full-data mean uses held-out responses.
Selecting predictors by their correlation with the full response consults the test set.
Choosing a model because it has the best test score turns the test set into training information for model selection.
Estimating a word-position mean from all readers before splitting readers carries test-reader responses into a supposedly held-out response.

Not every use of test predictors is leakage. At prediction time, the values of permitted predictors are usually known. A deterministic transformation fixed before fitting, such as taking the logarithm of word length, can be applied to both sets. The statement of what is held out must say which information is permitted.

title: Training and test data
text:
Split first, then estimate
A reliable workflow treats preprocessing as part of the fitted model.

State what must be held out and define the split rule.
Construct the training and test indices.
Estimate transformations, feature selections, and model parameters using training data.
Apply the training-set transformations to test predictors.
Predict test responses once.
Compute the prespecified loss.

Suppose a frequency predictor is standardized. The training mean \overline{x}_{\mathrm{train}} and standard deviation s_{\mathrm{train}} define

z_i=\frac{x_i-\overline{x}_{\mathrm{train}}}{s_{\mathrm{train}}}

for both training and test observations. The test set is not separately standardized, because that would place it in a different coordinate system. Nor should the full-data mean be used, because it would make the training representation depend on the held-out sample.

title: Training and test data
section: Why a single split is unstable
text:
Why a single split is unstable
A single split uses only part of the data for fitting and may produce an unusually easy or difficult test set. In a small experiment, changing a few observations can reverse a model comparison. The resulting score includes both model performance and the chance composition of one split.
Increasing the test fraction provides more evaluation observations but leaves fewer observations for fitting. Decreasing it has the opposite effect. There is no universally correct proportion. The design should reflect the data size, the observations or groups being held out, and the cost of instability.
Cross-validation, introduced next, rotates the test role so that every observation receives a held-out prediction. It reduces dependence on one arbitrary split, though it does not create more independent groups than the dataset contains.

title: Training and test data
section: A test set is not a source of repeated decisions
text:
A test set is not a source of repeated decisions
If several model variants are compared on the same test set and the best is selected, the reported score is optimistic for the selected model. The test responses have influenced a decision, even if no coefficient was directly fit to them.
One solution is a three-way separation: training data estimate parameters, validation data select among candidate specifications, and test data evaluate the selected procedure once. Another is nested cross-validation, in which each outer training set contains its own inner model-selection loop. Both enforce the same principle: every decision that can adapt to responses must occur without access to the responses used for final scoring.

title: Training and test data
text:
Check the separation

Why is a residual MSE usually smaller than a test MSE for the same fitted model?
A researcher chooses a spline degree using the test set, then refits the chosen spline on training data. Has leakage occurred?
Should test predictors be standardized using training or test moments? Explain.
What does a three-way split reserve the validation set for?

title: Training and test data
text:
Before rotating the split
Separating training and test data allows parameters to be estimated and analytical decisions to be made without using the responses on which predictive loss is computed. Preprocessing belongs inside that separation, and a test set ceases to be a test set once it guides model selection. The next page rotates this separation to obtain held-out predictions for every observation.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Big Question
What must a design do before a model can estimate the intended linguistic comparison?

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Data
An experiment compares recognition after familiar and unfamiliar accent training.
Each participant completes 40 trials.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Surprising Fact
Twenty four participants produce 960 rows, but training was assigned only 24 times.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Challenge
A model cannot create condition assignments, item balance, or retained observations that the design did not produce.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
This Module

Identify the unit and mechanism of assignment.
Choose a participant structure that preserves the manipulation.
Distribute item versions across participants.
Declare exclusions and evaluate the complete procedure by simulation.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Idea
Winter begins with repeated linguistic observations and asks which observations may count as independent evidence.
Winter 2020, Sections 14.2 and 14.3

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Units of assignment
What can independently receive a condition?

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Question
Does accent training vary across participants or across recognition trials?

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Answer
The unit of assignment is the entity that can independently receive a condition.

[Sources]
https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-4-experimental-design-and-ethics

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Answer
The unit of observation is the entity represented by one measured response.
Recall the unit of analysis.

[Sources]
https://bookdown.org/pkaldunn/Book/UnitsObsAnalysis.html

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Method
Ask what could have received a different condition under the actual procedure.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Output
Twelve trial rows from four participants contain twelve observations and four assignment units.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Question
A classroom receives one teaching method. Each student gives five responses.
What is assigned, and what is observed?

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Upshot
Additional trials may improve measurement. They do not add independent condition assignments.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Random assignment
How conditions reach assignment units

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Challenge
If participants choose the accent condition, prior accent experience may differ between conditions.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Answer
The assignment mechanism is the probability rule that selects a condition for each assignment unit.

[Sources]
https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-4-experimental-design-and-ethics

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Method
Under independent assignment with equal probabilities,
\[
P(Z_i=1)=P(Z_i=0)=.5.
\]

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Surprising Fact
A valid mechanism can produce a realized split of three participants and five participants.
Balance is an expectation, not a guarantee for one sample.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Approach
Restricted random assignment samples only from assignments that satisfy a declared balance condition.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Important Point #1
Random sampling concerns entry into the study.
Random assignment concerns allocation of conditions within the study.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Important Point #2
Save the realized assignment table and conceal future assignments from recruiters.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Within-participant designs
Each participant supplies a contrast

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Data
Participants differ in their use of a seven point acceptability scale.
Stable response habits may obscure a construction contrast.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Answer
In a within-participant design, each participant contributes observations to more than one condition.

[Sources]
https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Method
Each participant supplies a difference.
\[
D_i=Y_{i1}-Y_{i0},\qquad \bar D=\frac{1}{n}\sum_iD_i
\]
Recall paired observations.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Output
Four active minus passive differences are \(1\), \(2\), \(1\), and \(0\).
Their mean is one scale point.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Answer
A carryover effect occurs when an earlier condition changes a later response.

[Sources]
https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Question
If every active sentence precedes its passive counterpart, what two explanations are combined in the condition difference?

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Upshot
Stable participant shifts may cancel, but order and lasting effects remain part of the design.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Between-participant designs
Comparing groups

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Data
Accent training changes a listener. The original untrained state cannot be restored.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Answer
In a between-participant design, each participant contributes observations to only one condition.

[Sources]
https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Method
The comparison is between group means.
\[
\widehat\Delta=\bar Y_1-\bar Y_0
\]
Recall independent means.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Output
Familiar training mean: \(.800\)
Unfamiliar training mean: \(.715\)
Estimated difference: \(.085\)

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Challenge
Sorting two group vectors and pairing their rows invents a relation that the design never created.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Upshot
Use a between-participant design when the manipulation cannot be repeated without changing its meaning.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Counterbalancing
Distributing item versions

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Question
How can each item appear in every condition without showing every participant every version?

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Answer
Counterbalancing distributes item versions across lists so that condition is not tied to item identity.

[Sources]
https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Method



item
list 1
list 2




A
condition 1
condition 2


B
condition 2
condition 1

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Important Point #1
The list map must be assigned to participants by a recorded procedure.
A balanced file does not show that lists reached participants appropriately.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Important Point #2
Counterbalancing distributes condition versions. It does not make responses from the same participant or item independent.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Question
After exclusions, condition 1 has fewer observations for one item.
Is the collected dataset still balanced?

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Exclusion rules
Defining the analyzed set

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Data
A microphone failure and a 4,000 millisecond response both look unusual.
Only one is necessarily a missing measurement.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Approach
Let \(R_i=1\) when observation \(i\) is retained and \(R_i=0\) when it is excluded.
The retained analysis conditions on \(R_i=1\).

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Data
All five grammatical trials return responses.
Two of five ungrammatical trials time out.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Result #1
Among retained trials, the mean difference is only 10 milliseconds.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Result #2
The timeout rate is zero in one condition and forty percent in the other.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Interpretation
The retained mean describes trials that produced a response before timeout.
It does not show that the manipulation had little effect.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Method
Define rules before inspecting the desired contrast. Report participant and trial flow, reasons for removal, and exclusions by every relevant condition and group.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Upshot
Exclusion helps define the estimand. It is not merely table cleaning.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Power by simulation
Evaluating the complete planned procedure

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Question
How many participants are needed for a within-participant acceptability experiment?

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Challenge
There is no answer until we specify a data-generating process and a decision rule.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Data
For participant differences,
\[
D_i\sim\operatorname{Normal}(\delta,\sigma_D).
\]

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Method

Generate the exact planned design.
Apply the planned exclusions.
Fit the planned analysis.
Apply the planned decision rule.
Repeat the complete procedure.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Output
Estimated power is the proportion of simulated studies that meet the decision rule under the stated generating process.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Answer
A power curve shows estimated power across participant counts or effect assumptions.

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=187

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Challenge
Increasing the number of simulations reduces simulation error. It does not add participants to the planned study.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Upshot
Power is conditional on the assumed process, complete design, analysis, and decision rule.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Conclusion
Design before analysis

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Big Question
What must a design do before a model can estimate the intended linguistic comparison?

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Answer

Count assignments at the level where conditions can vary.
Match participant structure to the manipulation.
Counterbalance item versions and record list assignment.
Treat retention as part of the estimand.
Simulate the complete planned procedure.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Upshot
A statistical model begins after the design has already determined which comparisons the data can support.

title: Counterbalancing
text:
Suppose a sentence has a grammatical version and an ungrammatical version. Showing both versions of the same sentence to one participant may reveal the manipulation. Showing only one version avoids that repetition, but it creates a second problem: if every participant sees item A only in the grammatical condition, any special property of item A is inseparable from grammaticality.
Counterbalancing distributes item versions across stimulus lists so that each participant sees an item only once, while each item occurs in every condition across participants. It solves the item condition confound at the level of the complete design.

title: Counterbalancing
section: Represent the design as a condition map
text:
Represent the design as a condition map
Let C_{jl} denote the condition assigned to item j in list l. For a two condition design with two lists, a complete counterbalance requires

\{C_{j1},C_{j2}\}=\{0,1\}

for every item j. Each item must appear once in condition 0 and once in condition 1 across the two lists. Within each list, condition counts should also be balanced so that a participant encounters both conditions equally often.
This requirement is about the mapping from items to lists. Participant assignment to lists is a separate draw governed by the random assignment mechanism introduced earlier.

title: Counterbalancing
section: Build a two list design by hand
text:
Build a two list design by hand
Consider four sentence items and two conditions.



item
list 1
list 2




A
grammatical
ungrammatical


B
ungrammatical
grammatical


C
grammatical
ungrammatical


D
ungrammatical
grammatical



Read the table in two directions. Down list 1, there are two grammatical and two ungrammatical items. The same is true of list 2. Across the row for item A, both conditions occur. The same is true for B, C, and D.
This structure separates item identity from condition. If item A is unusually easy, its ease contributes to the grammatical condition in list 1 and the ungrammatical condition in list 2. Item A cannot explain a condition difference that persists across lists.
The condition map can be generated and checked in R.


Code
counterbalance <- data.frame(
  item = rep(LETTERS[1:4], each = 2),
  list = rep(c("list_1", "list_2"), times = 4),
  condition = c(
    "grammatical", "ungrammatical",
    "ungrammatical", "grammatical",
    "grammatical", "ungrammatical",
    "ungrammatical", "grammatical"
  )
)

with(counterbalance, table(item, condition))
with(counterbalance, table(list, condition))


The first table checks that every item appears in both conditions across lists. The second checks that each list contains equal condition counts. These are different margins of the design, and both matter.

title: Counterbalancing
section: Lists must reach participants by design
text:
Lists must reach participants by design
A valid condition map can still be undermined by how lists are distributed. Suppose list 1 is used during the first week and list 2 during the second. Testing week, recruitment source, or experimenter experience may then become associated with list. Because item conditions change with list, those properties may also become associated with condition.
Participants should thus be randomly assigned to lists or assigned through a recorded restricted mechanism that balances list counts. The realized assignment should be checked after missed sessions and exclusions. Planned balance does not imply realized balance.

title: Counterbalancing
text:
Counterbalancing does not remove dependence
Each participant still supplies several responses, and each item is still observed from several participants. Counterbalancing makes the item condition contrast available. It does not make the rows independent or eliminate participant and item variation.
This distinction matters because averaging over a perfectly balanced table can hide heterogeneous effects. An item may respond differently to the manipulation, and a participant may be more sensitive to the contrast. The random slope models introduced earlier can represent variation in the condition contrast across repeated units, but the model still depends on the counterbalanced design for an interpretable comparison.

title: Counterbalancing
text:
More than two factors
Several factors can require more lists. If two binary manipulations are fully crossed, each item has four possible versions. A complete design distributes all four versions across lists while showing only one version of an item to each participant.
Using only part of the crossing is possible, but omitted combinations impose assumptions about which effects can be separated. Before collection, write the item by list condition map and verify that every planned contrast changes within items across the complete design. This check is more informative than relying on a label such as Latin square without inspecting the actual assignments.

title: Counterbalancing
text:
Check balance after data collection
A design can be balanced in its plan but unbalanced in its collected observations. Missing sessions, programming errors, or unequal exclusions can produce this discrepancy. After collection, tabulate item by condition, list by condition, and participant by condition using the retained observations.
A second failure occurs when a condition is permanently attached to an item. No amount of participant balance can then distinguish the condition effect from the item. This failure must be repaired in the stimulus lists, not in the fitted model.






NoteAudit the counterbalance




Which table margin checks that every item appears in every condition?
Which table margin checks that a participant assigned to one list encounters balanced condition counts?
Why can assigning list 1 before list 2 confound list with testing time?
Does perfect counterbalancing make repeated responses independent?

title: Counterbalancing
text:
Summing up
Counterbalancing distributes item versions so that condition can vary within items across the complete design without repeating an item within a participant. The realized data must preserve both the item margin and the list margin. The next page asks which realized observations remain after applying exclusion rules.

title: Experimental design
text:
A statistical model begins after observations have been collected. By that point, however, many of the decisions that determine what the observations can tell us have already been made. Someone has chosen which speakers, sentences, recordings, or languages may enter the study. Someone has also decided which unit receives each condition, which responses are measured, and which observations will be retained. Recall from turning linguistic records into data that the unit represented by a row need not be the unit to which a claim applies. The model cannot undo those decisions.
Recall that the estimand is the population quantity the analysis is intended to estimate. The design determines whether the observed comparison can identify that quantity. If the estimand is a mean difference between two training procedures, for instance, then the design must produce comparable groups that differ systematically in training procedure. A precise model fitted to groups that differed before training does not repair a design that fails to identify the intended mean difference.

title: Experimental design
section: A design is a sequence of commitments
text:
A design is a sequence of commitments
Consider an experiment on the recognition of words in two accents. A useful design description answers seven questions in order.

What unit can independently receive an accent condition?
What procedure assigns conditions to those units?
Does each participant encounter one condition or more than one condition?
Which item versions does each participant encounter?
Which observations will enter the analysis?
What numerical comparison estimates the intended accent contrast?
Under a plausible data-generating process, how often will the planned procedure support the stated decision?

Each answer constrains the answers that follow. If accent is assigned once per participant, trials from that participant are not separate assignments. If every participant encounters both accents, the comparison is made within participants and order may matter. If failures to respond are removed more often in one accent, the retained comparison may target only trials on which a response was produced. The seven questions are thus parts of one design, even though we introduce them separately.

title: Experimental design
section: Repeated rows are not repeated designs
text:
Repeated rows are not repeated designs
Linguistic datasets often contain more than one repeated unit. Participants respond to several items, and items are presented to several participants. A table with 2,000 rows may have only 40 independently assigned participants, 50 sentence items, or some combination determined by the design. The row count says how many responses were recorded. It does not, by itself, say how many independent opportunities the study had to compare conditions.
This distinction is easy to miss because software places every response in a row. The first page thus separates the unit of assignment from the unit of observation and the unit of analysis introduced earlier. Random assignment then specifies the mechanism that connects the assigned condition to a causal comparison.

title: Experimental design
text:
How the module proceeds
After assignment, we distinguish within-participant designs, in which a participant contributes to more than one condition, from between-participant designs, in which a participant contributes to only one. Counterbalancing then distributes item versions across lists while preserving the intended contrast. Exclusion rules make the analyzed set explicit, and power by simulation evaluates the complete planned procedure under stated assumptions.
The pages introduce one design object at a time. They do not yet introduce models for grouped data. Instead, each page records the participants, items, blocks, or sites whose shared variation a later analysis must preserve. This ordering keeps the statistical method subordinate to the linguistic comparison.

title: Experimental design
text:
What this module adds
By the end of the module, we should be able to reconstruct how a condition reached each observation, state which comparisons were made possible by that procedure, and identify where exclusions or imbalance may have changed the target. These capabilities prepare us to represent repeated participants and items without pretending that a model can create experimental replication after collection.

title: Random assignment
text:
Suppose participants hear either a familiar or an unfamiliar accent and then identify words in noise. If participants choose which accent to hear, those who select the familiar accent may already have more experience with its speakers. A later difference in recognition could reflect the assigned accent, prior experience, or both.
The assignment mechanism is the probability rule that selects a condition for each assignment unit. Under random assignment, the distribution of the assigned condition is independent of characteristics measured before assignment. This design property supports a causal comparison because the procedure, rather than participant choice or experimenter judgment, determines who receives which condition.

title: Random assignment
section: State the mechanism before drawing an assignment
text:
State the mechanism before drawing an assignment
Let Z_i denote the condition assigned to participant i, with Z_i=1 for the familiar accent and Z_i=0 for the unfamiliar accent. Under independent assignment with equal probabilities,

P(Z_i=1)=P(Z_i=0)=.5.

This statement describes the procedure before assignments are drawn. It does not say that every realized sample will contain the same number of participants in each condition. With eight participants, an independent mechanism can produce a split of four and four, five and three, or even eight and zero. These outcomes have different probabilities, but they are all possible under the stated rule.
The distinction between the procedure and its realized result matters. Under repeated use of the assignment mechanism, expected group means for a preassignment characteristic are equal. Random assignment does not guarantee that age, language experience, hearing threshold, or another characteristic will have identical distributions in one finite sample.

title: Random assignment
text:
Work through one realized assignment
Suppose eight participants are assigned by eight independent fair draws, producing



participant
assigned accent




P1
unfamiliar


P2
familiar


P3
familiar


P4
unfamiliar


P5
unfamiliar


P6
unfamiliar


P7
familiar


P8
unfamiliar



The realized split is three familiar and five unfamiliar. That imbalance does not show that the mechanism failed. We would instead ask whether each participant had probability .5 of receiving either condition and whether the recorded assignments match the generated assignment table.
A reproducible implementation stores the random seed and the table it produces.


Code
set.seed(418)

assignment <- data.frame(
  participant = paste0("P", 1:8),
  accent = sample(
    c("familiar", "unfamiliar"),
    size = 8,
    replace = TRUE
  )
)

assignment
table(assignment$accent)


The vector passed to sample() gives the two possible conditions. replace = TRUE makes each draw independent, so the first participant’s assignment does not change the second participant’s condition probabilities. Saving only the seed is not enough when software versions or upstream code may change. Save the realized table as part of the study record.

title: Random assignment
text:
Restricted random assignment
Some studies require exact balance. We may want four participants in each accent condition or equal numbers in each stimulus list. The assignment can remain random if the procedure samples from the assignments satisfying that restriction.


Code
set.seed(418)

balanced_assignment <- data.frame(
  participant = paste0("P", 1:8),
  accent = sample(rep(c("familiar", "unfamiliar"), each = 4))
)

balanced_assignment
table(balanced_assignment$accent)


Here, the multiset of four familiar and four unfamiliar labels is shuffled across participants. Each participant has the same chance of receiving either condition, while the total condition counts are fixed. This is a restricted assignment mechanism, not an observational matching procedure performed after outcomes are known.

title: Random assignment
section: Random assignment is not random sampling
text:
Random assignment is not random sampling
Random assignment and random sampling answer different questions. As discussed in populations and samples, sampling concerns how units enter the study and thus which population they may represent. Assignment concerns how conditions are allocated among the recruited units and thus which condition comparisons receive a causal interpretation.
A convenience sample of university students can be randomly assigned to accent conditions. The design may support a causal comparison for the recruited students while leaving generalization to other ages or language communities uncertain. Conversely, a broad probability sample without random condition assignment may describe a population well but still leave a condition difference confounded.

title: Random assignment
text:
Conceal future assignments
Alternating familiar, unfamiliar, familiar, unfamiliar is balanced, but it is predictable. If an experimenter knows the next condition while scheduling participants, time of day, recruitment source, or a judgment about eligibility may become associated with condition. The sequence then fails to protect the comparison from allocation decisions.
Predictable assignment can allow recruiters to change who enters a condition. Allocation concealment and a complete assignment record help prevent that problem. A second failure occurs when participants are moved between conditions after assignment without recording the move. The analysis should preserve the original assignment and explain any departures from it.






NoteAudit the assignment mechanism




Does an exact four and four condition split imply that assignment was random? What additional information is required?
Which claim is supported by random assignment but not by random sampling?
Why can a realized imbalance occur under a valid independent mechanism?
What should be saved in addition to the randomization seed?

title: Random assignment
text:
Summing up
A random assignment mechanism is a probability rule for allocating conditions to assignment units. It balances prior characteristics in expectation, while the realized groups may still differ by chance. With the unit and mechanism fixed, we can now ask whether each participant contributes to more than one condition or to only one.

title: Within-participant designs
text:
Suppose an acceptability experiment asks whether a passive sentence receives a lower rating than its active counterpart. Participants differ greatly in how they use a seven point scale. One participant may avoid the endpoints, while another may use them often. Comparing different people across conditions would allow those stable response habits to obscure the construction contrast.
In a within-participant design, each participant contributes observations to more than one condition. The condition comparison can then be made inside each participant before it is averaged across participants. This is the same pairing logic introduced for paired observations, now treated as a design choice.

title: Within-participant designs
text:
Each participant supplies a contrast
Let Y_{i1} be participant i’s response in condition 1 and Y_{i0} the response in condition 0. The participant’s condition difference is

D_i=Y_{i1}-Y_{i0}.

For n participants, the estimated mean condition difference is

\bar D=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}D_i.

Stable participant characteristics appear in both Y_{i1} and Y_{i0}. If participant i tends to add a response shift a_i in both conditions, then

D_i=(\mu_1+a_i)-(\mu_0+a_i)=\mu_1-\mu_0.

The shared shift cancels. This cancellation explains why a within-participant design can estimate a condition contrast more precisely than a design that compares different groups with the same number of participants.

title: Within-participant designs
text:
Work through four participants
Consider one active and one passive rating from each of four participants.



participant
active
passive
active minus passive




P1
6

1


P2
7
5
2


P3
5
4

P4

0



The four participant differences are 1, 2, 1, and 0, so

\bar D=\frac{1+2+1+0}{4}=1.

The estimate says that these participants rated the active version one scale point higher on average than the passive version. It does not say that every participant showed a one point difference. P2 showed a two point difference, while P4 showed none.
The calculation in R follows the definition directly.


Code
ratings <- data.frame(
  participant = paste0("P", 1:4),
  active = c(6, 7, 5, 6),
  passive = c(5, 5, 4, 6)
)

ratings$difference <- ratings$active - ratings$passive
ratings
mean(ratings$difference)


If one aggregate response per participant and condition is the intended analysis, uncertainty can be computed from these participant differences using the earlier method for a paired mean difference.


Code
t.test(ratings$active, ratings$passive, paired = TRUE)


The argument paired = TRUE is not a software convenience. It tells R that the two values in each row belong to the same participant and that uncertainty should be calculated from the differences.

title: Within-participant designs
text:
Repetition creates dependence
The fact that the comparison is made within participants does not make the original responses independent. Responses from one participant share response habits, experience, fatigue, and other characteristics. If sentence items are also repeated across participants, responses to one item share lexical and structural properties.
For one response per participant and condition, the difference score carries the participant pairing into the analysis. With many trials per participant, one may first average within each participant and condition, then compare the participant averages. This simpler analysis changes what variation is retained. The earlier mixed effects model sequence introduced methods that preserve trial level responses while representing repeated participants and items.

title: Within-participant designs
text:
Represent carryover effects
A condition encountered early may change a later response. This change is a carryover effect. Participants may learn the task, become fatigued, or infer the experimental contrast.
Suppose every participant sees the active sentence before the passive sentence. A lower passive rating could reflect construction, later position, or both. Randomizing order distributes position across conditions, while counterbalancing can ensure that each condition appears equally often in relevant positions. Neither step makes carryover impossible. The study should record trial order and state whether a lasting effect is plausible.
Possible carryover does not automatically rule out a within-participant design. Short, reversible manipulations often permit repeated conditions, and the increase in precision may be substantial. But training, adaptation, or explicit instruction may change the participant in a way that cannot be reset. Those cases motivate a design in which each participant receives only one condition.






NoteAudit the within-participant contrast




Which quantity is averaged across participants, the two condition means separately or each participant’s difference?
What participant characteristic cancels if it adds the same shift in both conditions?
Why does pairing fail if the active and passive vectors are sorted independently before subtraction?
What design record is needed to diagnose a carryover effect?

title: Within-participant designs
text:
Summing up
A within-participant design turns each participant into a condition comparison. Stable participant shifts may cancel, but condition effects can still differ across participants and earlier conditions can alter later responses. When the manipulation cannot be repeated without changing its meaning, the appropriate alternative is a between-participant design.

title: Choosing a mixture with BIC
text:
A Gaussian mixture requires a component count and covariance structure. Adding components or covariance parameters usually improves maximized likelihood on the observations used to fit them. The largest fitted likelihood thus rewards flexibility even when the added structure does not recur.
The earlier page on information criteria introduced the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) as maximized likelihood plus a parameter-count penalty. This page applies that criterion to mixture specifications. We declare the candidates, calculate the penalty, and interpret what the resulting comparison can and cannot establish about linguistic categories.

title: Choosing a mixture with BIC
text:
State the candidate specifications
A mixture candidate includes more than the number of components K. It also includes the covariance restriction, feature representation, preprocessing rule, initialization policy, and fitting controls.
Write one candidate as

M
=
\langle K,\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}\rangle,

where \mathcal{C} is the covariance family and \mathcal{R} records the remaining fitting procedure. Comparing K=2 and K=3 while silently changing scaling would not isolate component count.
The candidate set should be declared before the final comparison. Searching many unreported specifications and presenting one favorable result makes the analytical search disappear from the report.

title: Choosing a mixture with BIC
section: See why fitted likelihood favors flexibility
text:
See why fitted likelihood favors flexibility
A larger mixture can often reproduce a smaller mixture by assigning negligible weight to an added component or by duplicating existing parameters. It may then improve fit by adapting the new component to a subset of observations.
Thus, maximized likelihood tends to increase as the candidate becomes more flexible. The same observations select the component parameters and reward the selected fit.
The improvement may represent a recurring distributional pattern. It may also represent a small irregular group or a nearly collapsed covariance. Fit diagnostics must rule out invalid solutions before any information criterion is interpreted.

title: Choosing a mixture with BIC
text:
Calculate BIC
For maximized likelihood L, q estimated parameters, and n observations, define

\operatorname{BIC}
=
-2\log L+q\log n.

Lower values are preferred under this definition. The first term rewards fitted likelihood. The second penalizes parameter count.
