Suppose a three-component model reduces -2\log L by 18 relative to a two-component model but introduces six parameters. With n=100, the added penalty is

6\log(100)
\approx
6(4.605)
=
27.63.

The change from the smaller model to the larger model is

\Delta\operatorname{BIC}
=
-18+27.63
=
9.63.

The larger model has a BIC about 9.63 units higher, so the smaller model is preferred under the stated definition. The likelihood improvement is not large enough to offset the additional penalty.

title: Choosing a mixture with BIC
text:
Implement the criterion directly


Code
candidate <- data.frame(
  model = c("two components", "three components"),
  minus_two_log_likelihood = c(400, 382),
  parameters = c(8, 14)
)

n_observations <- 100

candidate$bic <-
  candidate$minus_two_log_likelihood +
  candidate$parameters * log(n_observations)

candidate


Some software reports the negative of this expression and treats larger values as better. Check the package definition before comparing signs. Within one analysis, do not combine values produced under opposite conventions.

title: Choosing a mixture with BIC
text:
Interpret the sample size
BIC uses n inside the penalty. Repeated linguistic data make the meaning of that quantity important.
The Peterson and Barney table contains 1,520 vowel tokens from 76 speakers. Setting n=1520 counts observed token rows in the likelihood. It does not imply that 1,520 unrelated speakers were sampled. Each speaker contributes repeated vowel tokens.
Thus, a BIC comparison can rank fitted mixture specifications for the declared token likelihood without licensing a population claim that treats each token as an independent speaker. The criterion answers a relative model-selection question under the fitted likelihood. It does not repair a sampling design.

title: Choosing a mixture with BIC
text:
Interpret the candidate set
BIC compares only the candidates supplied to it. A two-component model preferred over a three-component model has not been preferred over every possible representation, covariance family, or component count.
Mixtures also complicate the regularity assumptions behind simple information-criterion arguments. Component labels can be permuted without changing the observation density, and parameters can become weakly identified when a component has little mass.
These concerns do not make the printed comparison meaningless. They limit the claim. Report the complete candidate definitions, convergence checks, and any near-degenerate solutions before interpreting the selected value.

title: Choosing a mixture with BIC
text:
Keep components separate from categories
Suppose the smallest BIC occurs at ten components for the ten intended Peterson and Barney vowel words. That numerical match does not show that BIC discovered the phonological inventory.
One vowel may require more than one Gaussian region because speakers differ. Several intended vowels may overlap within one component under the selected acoustic representation. Intended vowel labels should thus be used after fitting to describe alignment and uncertain tokens. They should not determine the mixture likelihood being compared.

title: Choosing a mixture with BIC
text:
Check the BIC comparison

Why does maximized likelihood tend to favor more flexible mixtures?
How is the BIC change 9.63 obtained in the worked comparison?
Which BIC sign convention is used on this page?
What belongs in a declared mixture specification besides K?
Why does n=1520 not mean that 1,520 unrelated speakers were sampled?
Why need the selected component count not equal the number of intended vowels?
What fit problems should be checked before interpreting BIC?

title: Choosing a mixture with BIC
text:
What BIC establishes
BIC ranks declared mixture specifications by combining maximized likelihood with a parameter-count penalty. The ranking remains conditional on the candidate set, response representation, likelihood, sample-size convention, and fitting validity. A preferred mixture is a supported distributional summary, not a discovered inventory of phonological categories.
The next page asks a different question by scoring predictions for observations excluded from fitting.

title: Expectation-maximization
text:
If the component label of every vowel token were observed, we could estimate each component from its assigned tokens. If the component parameters were known, we could calculate the posterior membership of every token. In a mixture model, neither side is known at the start.
The expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm fits a latent-variable model by alternating between two calculations. The expectation step forms the conditional expectation of the complete-data log likelihood under the current parameters. For a Gaussian mixture, this calculation requires the responsibilities from the preceding page. The maximization step then chooses parameters that maximize that expected complete-data log likelihood.
We first write both steps for a Gaussian mixture. We then carry out one weighted mean update by hand and in R, explain why the observed-data likelihood cannot decrease across exact updates, and identify the local-solution and collapse failures that make initialization checks necessary.

title: Expectation-maximization
text:
Begin with provisional parameters
Let the current mixture parameters be

\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}
=
\left\{
\pi_k^{(t)},
\boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{(t)},
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{(t)}
\right\}_{k=1}^{K},

where t indexes the current iteration. These values may come from random starting assignments or another declared initialization rule.
The superscript does not index data. It records the repeated algorithmic update.

title: Expectation-maximization
Expectation-maximization
section: The maximization step updates the weights

title: Expectation-maximization
text:
Update the component means
The updated mean is the responsibility-weighted average

\boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{(t+1)}
=
\frac{1}{N_k^{(t)}}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
r_{ik}^{(t)}\mathbf{x}_i.

Tokens with large responsibility for component k have greater influence on its center. Tokens with responsibility near zero contribute little.
Suppose one one-dimensional component has responsibilities 0.9, 0.6, and 0.1 for observations 2, 4, and 10. Its effective count is

N_k
=
0.9+0.6+0.1
=
1.6.

The weighted sum is

0.9(2)+0.6(4)+0.1(10)
=
1.8+2.4+1.0
=
5.2.

The updated mean is

\mu_k^{\mathrm{new}}
=
\frac{5.2}{1.6}
=
3.25.

The observation at 10 is far from the new mean, but it receives little weight because its current responsibility is only 0.1.

title: Expectation-maximization
Expectation-maximization
section: Reproduce the mean update in R
text:
Reproduce the mean update in R


Code
x <- c(2, 4, 10)
responsibility <- c(0.9, 0.6, 0.1)

effective_count <- sum(responsibility)

updated_mean <-
  sum(responsibility * x) /
  effective_count

effective_count
updated_mean


A one-dimensional covariance update follows the same weighting rule.


Code
updated_variance <-
  sum(
    responsibility *
    (x - updated_mean)^2
  ) /
  effective_count

updated_variance


These lines implement one maximization step after the responsibilities have been supplied. A complete EM implementation alternates this update with a new expectation step.

title: Expectation-maximization
text:
Alternate until the fit stabilizes
After the maximization step, recompute responsibilities using the updated parameters. Continue until the observed-data log likelihood or parameter changes fall below a declared tolerance.
The observed-data log likelihood is

\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\log
\left[
\sum_{k=1}^{K}
\pi_k
\mathcal{N}
(\mathbf{x}_i;
\boldsymbol{\mu}_k,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)
\right].

Exact EM updates do not decrease this likelihood. The expectation step constructs the expected complete-data log likelihood under the current parameters, and an exact maximization step selects parameters that maximize that objective. This is a likelihood-optimization result of the sort introduced in maximum likelihood, now applied when component labels are unobserved.
This monotonicity is an algorithmic guarantee. It is not a guarantee that the largest possible likelihood has been found.

title: Expectation-maximization
text:
Several starts are necessary
Mixture likelihoods can have several local maxima. Different provisional parameters may lead EM to different component locations or covariance structures.
The expectation-maximization algorithm can converge to different local optima from different initializations. Fit the same declared model from several starts, retain the valid solution with the largest attained likelihood, and record whether substantively different solutions recur.
A fixed random seed makes the collection of starts reproducible. It does not make one start sufficient.

title: Expectation-maximization
text:
Watch for collapsing components
EM may move one component toward a small number of observations while shrinking its covariance. The likelihood can become extremely large as the covariance approaches singularity.
This is not a meaningful discovery of a tiny vowel category. It is the likelihood singularity from the previous page appearing during fitting. The implementation should enforce appropriate covariance restrictions or regularization and flag degenerate solutions.
Retaining the fit with the largest likelihood could select the collapsed solution. This is why validity checks precede likelihood comparison. An invalid degenerate solution is not a candidate interpretation.

title: Expectation-maximization
text:
EM estimates a local representation
At convergence, the responsibilities and parameters agree under the alternating updates. The result is a local maximum or stationary solution for the declared mixture.
It does not establish the correct component count, covariance family, or linguistic category interpretation. Those are comparison and interpretation questions, not consequences of convergence.

title: Expectation-maximization
text:
Check the alternating algorithm

Which quantities are calculated in the expectation step?
Why does an observation with responsibility 0.1 still affect a component mean?
How is the updated mean 3.25 obtained in the worked calculation?
Why do updated mixing weights sum to one?
What does monotonic observed-data likelihood guarantee, and what does it not guarantee?
Why should the same mixture be fit from several initializations?
Why must a covariance-collapse fit be rejected before comparing attained likelihoods?

title: Expectation-maximization
text:
Before comparing mixture specifications
EM alternates posterior membership calculation with responsibility-weighted parameter updates. It improves the observed-data likelihood from a provisional starting point but may reach a local or degenerate solution. The next page compares component counts and covariance assumptions using BIC’s penalty for fitted flexibility.

title: Finding unobserved groups
text:
Some linguistic datasets provide measurements without a group label that should be predicted. A speaker may be represented by language-use ratings. A language may be represented by grammatical features. A vowel token may be represented by formant measurements. The unit of analysis still determines what can be grouped. We may then ask whether the represented objects form recurring groups.
The group is unobserved in the limited sense that it is not supplied as a response variable to the fitting procedure. The measurements are observed, and any later linguistic interpretation still requires evidence outside the fitted partition.

title: Finding unobserved groups
text:
Two kinds of group representation
The module develops two ways to estimate groups that are not supplied as response labels.

K-means clustering assigns every object to exactly one cluster.
A finite mixture model gives every object a model-based posterior probability for each component.

The second representation is not automatically better. It answers a different question and makes a more detailed distributional commitment.

title: Finding unobserved groups
text:
The K-means branch
We begin with representing objects, because a group can only reflect the rows and columns supplied to the analysis. Distance and scaling then define what it means for two represented objects to be close.
K-means introduces cluster assignments and derives its assignment and centroid updates. Within-cluster loss describes fitted compactness across candidate group counts. Silhouette widths compare each row with its assigned group and nearest alternative. Validation without labels then asks whether centroids fit on training rows represent rows excluded from fitting.

title: Finding unobserved groups
text:
The probabilistic-mixture branch
Gaussian mixtures replace distance to one centroid with a probability model for several component distributions. Posterior membership turns weighted component densities into membership probabilities. Expectation-maximization alternates membership and parameter updates to fit the model. Choosing a mixture with BIC penalizes fitted likelihood for parameter count. Held-out mixture validation then asks whether the fitted density transfers to new speakers.
The Peterson and Barney vowel measurements provide the sustained phonetic application for this branch. The application is useful because formant distributions overlap, speaker anatomy affects the raw representation, and intended vowel labels can be reserved for interpretation rather than supplied to the mixture.

title: Finding unobserved groups
section: What a learned group can establish
text:
What a learned group can establish
A fitted group is a summary under a declared representation, distance, or probability model. It is not automatically a phoneme, dialect, speaker type, or language type. Agreement with an external annotation may support an interpretation, but the annotation did not define the fitted objective.
The statistical object is a partition or component distribution. Interpreting it as a linguistic category requires a separate substantive claim about the process that produced the measurements.
By the end of the module, we should be able to reconstruct each fitted quantity, identify the assumptions that create the groups, and state which additional evidence would be needed to interpret them linguistically.

title: Posterior membership
text:
A Gaussian mixture assigns a density to every vowel token. We often also want to know how the weighted component contributions divide for one particular token. A token near overlapping vowel regions may be compatible with several components even when one contributes most.
The posterior probability of component membership gives the probability of each component label conditional on the observed measurements and fitted mixture parameters. It applies the Bayes’ rule introduced earlier to the weighted densities from the previous page, producing probabilities that sum to one. In mixture-model software, these conditional probabilities are often called responsibilities.
We first derive the formula from Bayes’ rule. We then finish the two-component density calculation by hand and in R, distinguish soft from hard assignment, and explain why membership probability is conditional on the fitted model rather than a probability that a phonological analysis is true.

title: Posterior membership
Posterior membership
text:
Finish the previous calculation
The two weighted component contributions were

0.048
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
0.008.

Their sum, the mixture density, was 0.056. The first posterior membership is

\begin{aligned}
r_{i1}
&=
\frac{0.048}{0.056}\\
&\approx0.857.
\end{aligned}

The second is

\begin{aligned}
r_{i2}
&=
\frac{0.008}{0.056}\\
&\approx0.143.
\end{aligned}

They sum to one:

0.857+0.143=1.

Component 1 accounts for most of the fitted density at this observation, but component 2 remains possible under the model.

title: Posterior membership
section: Why the probabilities sum to one

title: Posterior membership
text:
Calculate membership in R


Code
weighted_contribution <- c(0.048, 0.008)

responsibility <-
  weighted_contribution /
  sum(weighted_contribution)

responsibility
sum(responsibility)


For many observations, store weighted contributions in a matrix with one row per token and one column per component. Divide each row by its sum.


Code
responsibility_matrix <-
  weighted_density_matrix /
  rowSums(weighted_density_matrix)

head(responsibility_matrix)


The row normalization implements the denominator in Bayes’ rule.

title: Posterior membership
text:
Hard assignment discards uncertainty
A hard assignment chooses

\widehat{z}_i
=
\underset{k}{\operatorname{argmax}}
r_{ik}.

The worked token is assigned to component 1. But the hard label hides the difference between memberships (0.51,0.49) and (0.99,0.01). Both yield label 1 even though the first observation lies near a modeled boundary and the second does not.
For Peterson and Barney vowel tokens, retaining the complete membership vector can reveal which intended vowels occupy overlapping formant regions and which individual tokens the fitted mixture represents uncertainly.
Converting posterior membership probabilities to one hard label removes information about component overlap.

title: Posterior membership
text:
Keep assignment and uncertainty separate
A useful descriptive table contains both the most probable component and its probability.



token
assigned component
largest membership




A
1
0.98


B
1
0.54


C
2
0.91



Token B deserves inspection because its assignment is weak under the fitted model. A plot colored only by hard component would conceal this difference.
The complete probability vector is preferable when more than two components overlap. The largest probability alone does not show whether the remaining mass belongs to one close competitor or several.

title: Posterior membership
text:
Component numbers are arbitrary
If every parameter associated with component 1 is exchanged with the corresponding parameter for component 2, the mixture density is unchanged. Membership columns are exchanged as well.
This permutation nonidentifiability is known as label switching. The number attached to a component has no stable linguistic meaning. Across separate fits, component 1 may correspond to a differently numbered component with similar parameters.
Interpret a component through its mean, covariance, membership pattern, and relation to external variables. Do not interpret the integer label itself.

title: Posterior membership
section: Membership is conditional on the model
text:
Membership is conditional on the model
A posterior membership of 0.857 is not the probability that a token truly belongs to a phoneme. It is the probability of the fitted component label conditional on the measurements, component count, Gaussian form, covariance restrictions, transformations, and estimated parameters.
If the model omits a relevant formant or uses an unsuitable covariance structure, the membership may be sharply estimated under a poor representation. High numerical certainty does not validate the component interpretation.
These memberships are not arbitrary. They are exact consequences of the declared mixture. Their interpretation should retain those conditions and be checked against external phonetic information.

title: Posterior membership
text:
Check the normalized contributions

Which quantity appears in the denominator of every membership probability?
Why do the memberships for one token sum to one?
How are 0.857 and 0.143 obtained from the previous weighted densities?
What information is lost when (0.51,0.49) becomes hard label 1?
Why can component 1 in one fit correspond to component 3 in another fit?
Why is a membership of 0.99 not a 99 percent probability that a phoneme analysis is true?

title: Posterior membership
text:
Before fitting the parameters
Posterior membership normalizes weighted component densities through Bayes’ rule. It retains overlap that a hard assignment discards, while remaining conditional on the declared mixture model. The next page uses these responsibilities to alternate between membership calculation and parameter updates.

title: Silhouette widths
text:
The within-cluster sum of squares measures distance from each row to its assigned centroid. It does not ask whether that row lies just as close to another cluster. A speaker can be near one centroid and still sit on the boundary between two groups.
A silhouette width compares the row’s average distance within its assigned cluster with its average distance to the nearest alternative cluster. It is a row-level diagnostic of cohesion relative to separation.
We first define the two distances that enter the score. We then calculate positive and negative silhouettes by hand, implement the diagnostic in R, and explain why a high silhouette remains relative to the chosen distance and scaling.

title: Silhouette widths
text:
Define within-cluster cohesion
Let C(i) be the cluster containing row i. The average distance from row i to the other rows in that cluster is

a(i)
=
\frac{1}{|C(i)|-1}
\sum_{
j\in C(i),\ j\neq i
}
d(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j).

A small a(i) means that row i lies near the other rows assigned to its cluster. The quantity is the row’s mean intra-cluster distance.
The definition uses distances between rows rather than distance to the centroid. Thus, it can be applied to a declared partition even when the grouping method did not use centroids.

title: Silhouette widths
text:
Define the nearest alternative
For another cluster C, calculate row i’s average distance to all rows in that cluster:

d(i,C)
=
\frac{1}{|C|}
\sum_{j\in C}
d(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j).

The nearest alternative-cluster distance is

b(i)
=
\min_{C\neq C(i)}d(i,C).

A large b(i) means that even the closest competing cluster lies far from row i. The comparison uses the nearest alternative because a partition is only as separated as its most plausible competitor for that row.

title: Silhouette widths
text:
Combine cohesion and separation
The silhouette is

s(i)
=
\frac{b(i)-a(i)}
{\max\{a(i),b(i)\}}.

Its value lies between -1 and 1. If b(i)\geq a(i), then

s(i)
=
1-\frac{a(i)}{b(i)},

which lies between 0 and 1. If a(i)>b(i), then

s(i)
=
\frac{b(i)}{a(i)}-1,

which lies between -1 and 0.
Positive values indicate that the row is closer on average to its assigned cluster. Negative values indicate that another cluster is closer on average. Values near zero indicate an ambiguous boundary under the declared distance.

title: Silhouette widths
text:
Calculate a positive silhouette
Suppose a speaker’s average distance to the assigned cluster is

a(i)=0.8,

and the average distance to the nearest alternative cluster is

b(i)=2.0.

Since b(i) is larger, the denominator is 2.0:

\begin{aligned}
s(i)
&=
\frac{2.0-0.8}{2.0}\\
&=
\frac{1.2}{2.0}\\
&=0.60.
\end{aligned}

The speaker is substantially closer to the assigned group than to the nearest alternative under this distance.

title: Silhouette widths
text:
Calculate a negative silhouette
Now suppose

a(i)=1.5
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
b(i)=1.2.

The denominator is 1.5, so

\begin{aligned}
s(i)
&=
\frac{1.2-1.5}{1.5}\\
&=
\frac{-0.3}{1.5}\\
&=-0.20.
\end{aligned}

The negative score says that, on average, this row lies closer to another cluster than to its assigned cluster. It identifies a row for inspection. It does not automatically justify moving the row, since the fitted objective and the silhouette use different summaries.

title: Silhouette widths
text:
Compute the scores in R
The cluster package combines a declared partition with a distance matrix.


Code
distance_matrix <- dist(
  X_scaled,
  method = "euclidean"
)

sil <- cluster::silhouette(
  fit_k2$cluster,
  distance_matrix
)

head(sil)


The result stores each row’s assigned cluster, nearest alternative cluster, and silhouette width. The sample mean is


Code
mean(sil[, "sil_width"])


Plot the row-level values rather than reporting only this mean.


Code
plot(sil)


A moderate mean may hide one cluster containing many negative values. Those rows may mark overlap, an unsuitable distance, or a partition driven by a few dense regions.

title: Silhouette widths
text:
Handle singleton clusters carefully
If row i is the only member of its assigned cluster, a(i) has no other row to average. A common convention assigns silhouette zero to a singleton.
This convention should not be interpreted as evidence that the singleton lies on an ordinary boundary. It says that within-cluster cohesion is undefined from pairwise neighbors. A candidate partition with many singleton clusters may require direct inspection rather than reliance on its mean silhouette.
For a singleton cluster, the numerical convention does not create within-cluster evidence where no within-cluster pair exists.

title: Silhouette widths
section: The score depends on distance and scaling
text:
The score depends on distance and scaling
Every a(i) and b(i) is calculated from the chosen distances. Changing column scaling changes the pairwise distances and may change the nearest alternative cluster.
Suppose raw token counts dominate a language-use matrix. A high silhouette may then describe separation almost entirely along token count. Standardizing the columns may produce a different conclusion. Neither score is independent of the representation.
A high silhouette width retains a precise interpretation: rows are cohesive and separated under this particular distance and scaling. The linguistic claim should retain that condition.

title: Silhouette widths
section: Compact separation is not the only category shape
text:
Compact separation is not the only category shape
Silhouettes tend to reward compact groups separated by gaps. Linguistic categories may overlap systematically, vary in spread, or form a continuum while still supporting a useful theory.
Thus, the candidate with the largest mean silhouette is best only among the tried partitions under this score. It does not establish that the world contains exactly that number of discrete groups.
External variables can help interpret the partition, while held-out validation can ask whether the learned centers represent new rows. Neither question is answered by the fitted silhouette alone.

title: Silhouette widths
text:
Check cohesion and separation

What does a(i) average?
Why does b(i) use the nearest alternative cluster?
What does a silhouette of -0.20 suggest about the row’s average distances?
Why can a mean silhouette hide a poorly represented cluster?
How does a change in scaling alter the silhouette calculation?
Why is a singleton silhouette of zero a convention rather than evidence of ordinary boundary membership?

title: Silhouette widths
text:
Before holding out rows
A silhouette compares each row’s cohesion with its nearest alternative under a declared distance. It diagnoses the fitted partition one row at a time but remains tied to the same observations and geometry used to form the groups. The next page asks whether centroids estimated from training rows reconstruct rows excluded from fitting.

title: Validating a mixture on held-out speakers
text:
BIC penalizes maximized likelihood on the observations used for fitting. The training and test separation asks a different question: does a fitted mixture assign high predictive density to observations that did not determine its parameters?
This page develops one validation design for the Peterson and Barney vowel measurements. The target is prediction for a new speaker. Thus, every token from a held-out speaker must remain outside the fitted mixture.
crumbs: Validating a mixture on held-out speakers

title: Validating a mixture on held-out speakers
section: Apply log loss to a fitted density
text:
Apply log loss to a fitted density
Recall that predictive loss assigns a numerical cost to a prediction. For a model fit to training observations, the log loss for held-out observation i is

L_i(M)
=
-\log
p_M
(\mathbf{x}_i\mid D_{\mathrm{train}}).

Smaller loss means that the fitted mixture assigns greater density to the held-out observation. Average loss across the declared test units to compare candidates.
Suppose model A assigns density 0.04 to a held-out token and model B assigns density 0.06. Their log losses are

L_i(A)=-\log(0.04)\approx3.22

and

L_i(B)=-\log(0.06)\approx2.81.

The paired difference is

d_i
=
L_i(B)-L_i(A)
\approx
-0.41.

The negative difference favors model B for this token.
crumbs: Validating a mixture on held-out speakers

title: Validating a mixture on held-out speakers
text:
Hold out complete speakers
Peterson and Barney speakers contribute multiple vowel tokens. A token-level split would leave the same speaker’s other formant measurements in training. It would answer a new-token question for speakers partly represented during fitting.
For a new-speaker target, all tokens from one speaker must be excluded together. This is the grouped cross-validation rule applied to speakers. The fitted mixture then has no acoustic measurements from that speaker when it scores the speaker’s held-out tokens.
This grouping rule follows the linguistic claim, not the number of rows in the matrix. A model that predicts another token from a familiar speaker may be useful, but it answers a different question.
crumbs: Validating a mixture on held-out speakers

title: Validating a mixture on held-out speakers
section: Keep the complete fit inside each fold
text:
Keep the complete fit inside each fold
Every training fold must estimate scaling, mixture parameters, and specification-dependent quantities without using held-out speakers. The mixture should also use the same declared multi-start policy in every fold.


Code
# Each element of folds contains every row for one or more speakers.
for (fold in seq_along(folds)) {
  test <- folds[[fold]]
  train <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(X)), test)

  center <- colMeans(X[train, , drop = FALSE])
  spread <- apply(X[train, , drop = FALSE], 2, sd)

  X_train <- sweep(X[train, , drop = FALSE], 2, center, "-")
  X_train <- sweep(X_train, 2, spread, "/")

  X_test <- sweep(X[test, , drop = FALSE], 2, center, "-")
  X_test <- sweep(X_test, 2, spread, "/")

  fit <- fit_mixture(
    X_train,
    components = K,
    covariance = covariance_family,
    starts = 50
  )

  heldout_loss[test] <- -log(density_mixture(fit, X_test))
}


The functions are schematic because packages encode covariance families differently. The procedural requirement is exact: held-out speakers cannot affect the representation or mixture whose density scores them.
crumbs: Validating a mixture on held-out speakers

title: Validating a mixture on held-out speakers
section: State the information available for normalization
text:
State the information available for normalization
Raw formants may allocate components partly to anatomical speaker differences. A speaker-relative representation may align more closely with intended vowels, but it creates a new information question.
If the held-out speaker’s complete formant set supplies that speaker’s own means and standard deviations, the analysis evaluates an adapted representation in which the speaker’s acoustic scale is already available. It does not evaluate the first token from a speaker whose acoustic scale has never been observed.
The training-only transformation in the code above asks a stricter question. Its center and spread come only from training speakers. Neither choice is universally correct. The report must specify which measurements are available at prediction time.
crumbs: Validating a mixture on held-out speakers

title: Validating a mixture on held-out speakers
text:
Return token losses to speakers
A full comparison retains one paired model difference for each held-out token, but speakers are the groups relevant to the scientific claim. Summarize or resample the token differences at the speaker level.
Cross-validation folds share most of their training observations. Fold averages are computational summaries, not independent linguistic samples. A t test over repeated fold means would make precision depend on how often the analyst reran the partition.
Instead, calculate the relevant loss summary for each held-out speaker and describe variation across speakers. Repeated partitions can still show sensitivity to a computational choice, but they do not create new sampled speakers.
crumbs: Validating a mixture on held-out speakers

title: Validating a mixture on held-out speakers
text:
Examine stability across fits
Mixture fitting can reach different local solutions from different starting values. The preferred candidate may also change across speaker resamples or covariance restrictions.
If several specifications have similar held-out loss, the data may not support one stable partition. Report the range of supported specifications and which component interpretations persist across them.
A primary candidate may still be selected by a declared rule. The sensitivity analysis shows how much substantive weight that single selection can bear.
crumbs: Validating a mixture on held-out speakers

title: Validating a mixture on held-out speakers
text:
Check the validation design

What does held-out log loss measure?
What does a negative value of L_i(B)-L_i(A) favor?
Why must all Peterson and Barney tokens from one test speaker move together?
Which transformations must be estimated inside each training fold?
How does speaker-specific normalization change the information available at prediction time?
Why are repeated fold averages not independent linguistic samples?
What should be reported when preferred specifications change across speaker resamples?
crumbs: Validating a mixture on held-out speakers

title: Validating a mixture on held-out speakers
text:
What held-out mixture validation establishes
Held-out log loss evaluates whether a fitted mixture assigns density to observations excluded from fitting. Grouping complete speakers aligns the split with a new-speaker claim, and training-only transformations prevent held-out acoustic measurements from shaping the fitted representation. The comparison remains conditional on the stated prediction-time information and candidate set.
crumbs: Validating a mixture on held-out speakers

title: Factorization
text:
Big Question
Can several linguistic measurements be represented by a smaller number of recurring numerical patterns?

title: Factorization
text:
Data
A vowel token may have F1, F2, F3, duration, and voice quality measurements.
A verb may have frequencies for more than one hundred syntactic frames.

title: Factorization
text:
Challenge
The columns may share structure, but a lower dimensional representation is meaningful only with respect to a declared matrix and reconstruction task.

title: Factorization
text:
This Module

Define rows, columns, origins, and units.
Build one rank one pattern.
Order several patterns with the singular value decomposition.
Interpret scores, loadings, and reconstructed cells.
Select rank using held out reconstruction.
Test whether VALEX components predict MegaAcceptability profiles.

title: Factorization
text:
Represent the measurements
Rows, columns, origins, and units

title: Factorization
text:
Question
What does one cell of a linguistic data matrix measure?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
For \(\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\),
\[x_{ij}=\text{the value of variable }j\text{ for object }i.\]

title: Factorization
text:
Question
What does \(x_{31}=300\) mean?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
Token 3 has an F1 measurement of 300 Hz.
Both indices are required for that interpretation.

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #1
If rows are tokens, scores locate tokens. If rows are speakers, scores locate speakers.
Aggregation changes the represented object.

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #2
Columns define the representation.
Including duration and twice duration gives the same measurement two coordinates.

title: Factorization
text:
Method
Before factorization, record what one row represents, how rows were selected, what each column measures, which columns repeat information, and which collection the objects come from.

title: Factorization
text:
Data
PHOIBLE may contain several inventories for one language from different sources.
The row selection rule must be fixed before a language by segment matrix is interpreted.
PHOIBLE 2.0 documentation

[Sources]
PHOIBLE 2.0 download and citation page: https://phoible.org/download
PHOIBLE FAQ on multiple inventories and sources: https://phoible.org/faq

title: Factorization
text:
Question
What coordinate system should later components use?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
Centering changes a column’s origin. Scaling changes its unit.
These operations recall the earlier treatment of centering.

title: Factorization
text:
Method
\[x^c_{ij}=x_{ij}-\bar x_j\]
\[z_{ij}=\frac{x_{ij}-\bar x_j}{s_j}\]

title: Factorization
text:
Question
Durations are 100, 120, and 140 ms.
What are their standardized values?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
The mean is 120 ms and the sample standard deviation is 20 ms.
The standardized values are \(-1\), \(0\), and \(1\).

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #3
Giving every column variance one is a weighting decision.
It is not a neutral software default.

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #4
New observations must use the training means and standard deviations.
Recomputing them on evaluation observations creates data leakage.

title: Factorization
text:
Upshot
Factorization reorganizes the information supplied in a matrix. It cannot recover omitted observations or repair a theoretically inappropriate representation.

title: Factorization
text:
Build component patterns
From one outer product to an ordered decomposition

title: Factorization
text:
Question
When can one pattern reproduce every cell of a matrix?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
A nonzero matrix has rank one when it can be written as an outer product:
\[\mathbf X=\mathbf a\mathbf b^{\mathsf T}.\]

[Sources]
Penn State STAT 508, Lesson 7: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat508/Lesson07.html

title: Factorization
text:
Data
\[
\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}2&4\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}2&4\\4&8\\6&12\end{bmatrix}.
\]

title: Factorization
text:
Interpretation
The first vector varies across rows. The second gives the column pattern.
All rows and columns are proportional.

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #1
Rank is an algebraic property of the matrix.
It is not a psychological construct or a linguistic category.

title: Factorization
text:
Challenge
Most linguistic matrices are not exactly rank one.
We need an ordered set of approximate rank one patterns.

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
The singular value decomposition, or SVD, writes
\[\mathbf X=\mathbf U\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf V^{\mathsf T}.\]

[Sources]
University of Illinois CS 357, Singular Value Decomposition: https://cs357.cs.illinois.edu/textbook/notes/svd.html

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
The columns of \(\mathbf U\) are left singular vectors.
The columns of \(\mathbf V\) are right singular vectors.

[Sources]
University of Illinois CS 357, Singular Value Decomposition: https://cs357.cs.illinois.edu/textbook/notes/svd.html

title: Factorization
text:
Output
\[\mathbf X=\sum_{k=1}^r\sigma_k\mathbf u_k\mathbf v_k^{\mathsf T},\qquad \sigma_1\geq\sigma_2\geq\cdots>0.\]
Each term is rank one.

title: Factorization
text:
Interpretation
The singular value \(\sigma_k\) measures the strength of term \(k\) under squared reconstruction error.
The first term is the closest rank one approximation.

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #2
Singular vectors have arbitrary sign.
Replacing \(\mathbf u_k\) and \(\mathbf v_k\) by their negatives leaves the reconstructed matrix unchanged.

[Sources]
Palarea Albaladejo, Principal Components Analysis, sign indeterminacy: https://imae.udg.edu/~jpalarea/StatsDS/principal-components-analysis.html

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #3
Repeated singular values weaken interpretation of individual directions.
The associated subspace is identified more strongly than one orientation within it.

title: Factorization
text:
Upshot
The SVD orders rank one patterns by their contribution to squared reconstruction of the specified matrix.

title: Factorization
text:
Principal components
Directions of variation around column means

title: Factorization
text:
Question
Which direction through the measured variables has the greatest projected variation?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
Principal component analysis, or PCA, finds orthogonal directions in a centered matrix, ordered by projected variance.

[Sources]
Penn State STAT 508, Lesson 7: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat508/Lesson07.html

title: Factorization
text:
Method
Center the columns, then decompose
\[\mathbf X_c=\mathbf U\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf V^{\mathsf T}.\]

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
The columns of \(\mathbf V\) are the principal component directions.
The score matrix is
\[\mathbf Z=\mathbf X_c\mathbf V=\mathbf U\boldsymbol\Sigma.\]

[Sources]
Penn State STAT 508, Lesson 7: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat508/Lesson07.html

title: Factorization
text:
Goal
The first direction \(\mathbf v_1\) maximizes
\[\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf X_c\mathbf v)\]
subject to \(\lVert\mathbf v\rVert_2=1\).

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #1
PCA uses numerical variation in the matrix.
It does not use category labels or a theory of the response unless they were built into the representation.

title: Factorization
text:
Question
If F1 and F2 both increase together across tokens, should the first direction assign them the same sign or opposite signs?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
The same sign represents their common increase.
The complete direction may be multiplied by \(-1\) without changing the component.

title: Factorization
text:
Upshot
PCA identifies directions that reconstruct centered numerical variation. A direction does not acquire a linguistic interpretation from its rank alone.

title: Factorization
text:
Read and reconstruct components
Row coordinates, variable directions, and residual cells

title: Factorization
text:
Question
Which quantity locates an observation, and which quantity describes a component direction through variables?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
Scores locate row observations.
Loadings are the entries of unit length component directions through the original variables.

[Sources]
Penn State STAT 508, Lesson 7: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat508/Lesson07.html

title: Factorization
text:
Method
For centered row \(\mathbf x_i^c\) and component direction \(\mathbf v_k\),
\[z_{ik}=\mathbf x_i^{c\mathsf T}\mathbf v_k.\]

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #1
Join scores to linguistic metadata by stable row identifiers.
Row order alone is fragile after filtering or reshaping.

title: Factorization
text:
Interpretation
Read a loading pattern across variables and a score pattern across observations.
Do not interpret one isolated sign without its companion entries and metadata.

title: Factorization
text:
Question
What does retaining the first \(K\) components reproduce?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
A rank-\(K\) approximation is
\[\widehat{\mathbf X}_K=\sum_{k=1}^K\sigma_k\mathbf u_k\mathbf v_k^{\mathsf T}.\]

[Sources]
Penn State STAT 508, Lesson 7: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat508/Lesson07.html

title: Factorization
text:
Output
The residual matrix is
\[\mathbf E_K=\mathbf X-\widehat{\mathbf X}_K.\]
Every cell records what the retained terms did not reconstruct.

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
For centered data, the proportion of variance explained is
\[\frac{\sum_{k=1}^K\sigma_k^2}{\sum_{k=1}^r\sigma_k^2}.\]

[Sources]
Penn State STAT 508, Lesson 7: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat508/Lesson07.html

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #2
Observed variance explained is an in sample reconstruction summary.
It is not held out prediction and not a measure of linguistic information.

title: Factorization
text:
Question
How are reconstructed standardized values returned to the original units?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
Multiply each column by its training standard deviation, then add its training mean.
The inverse transformation must use the fitted coordinate system.

title: Factorization
text:
Upshot
Scores and loadings interpret the low rank coordinates. Reconstruction returns those coordinates to the cells that defined the original linguistic representation.

title: Factorization
text:
Choose the retained rank
Separate fitting, selection, and final evaluation

title: Factorization
text:
Question
How many components should be retained for a declared reconstruction task?

title: Factorization
text:
Approach
Choose the rank that minimizes reconstruction loss on validation cells that did not determine the components.

title: Factorization
text:
Implementation

Fit preprocessing and components on training data.
Evaluate fixed candidate ranks on validation data.
Select one rank using the declared loss.
Refit on training plus validation data.
Evaluate once on untouched test data.

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #1
Centering, scaling, imputation, and component directions are fitted operations.
Each must remain inside the training split.

title: Factorization
text:
Challenge
Observed reconstruction error decreases whenever rank increases.
It therefore cannot choose rank without an external criterion.

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #2
A bend in a scree plot describes the singular value sequence.
It does not directly answer which rank predicts held out cells best.

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #3
Cell weighting defines the evaluation target.
Equal cell, row, and variable weighting answer different reconstruction questions.

title: Factorization
text:
Upshot
A selected rank is conditional on the representation, split, candidate set, and loss. It is not the true number of linguistic dimensions.

title: Factorization
text:
Corpus distributions and clause selection
VALEX predictors and MegaAcceptability profiles

title: Factorization
text:
Question
Can a verb’s corpus distribution predict its acceptability across clause embedding frames?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
A verb’s selectional profile records its acceptability across syntactic frames.
White and Rawlins 2020

[Sources]
White and Rawlins, Frequency, acceptability, and selection: https://doi.org/10.5334/gjgl.1001

title: Factorization
text:
Data
MegaAcceptability supplies 50 frame judgments for each retained verb.
VALEX supplies a 109 dimensional corpus frame distribution for the same verb.
White and Rawlins 2020

[Sources]
White and Rawlins, Frequency, acceptability, and selection: https://doi.org/10.5334/gjgl.1001

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #1
VALEX counts are converted to within verb proportions.
The predictor represents allocation across complement frames, not total verb frequency.

title: Factorization
text:
Goal
Compare two theoretically distinct predictors for verbs excluded from fitting.
The direct predictor uses all VALEX frame proportions. The factor predictor uses retained PCA scores.

title: Factorization
text:
Method
Both analyses use ridge regression to predict the same 50 response columns.
Only the predictor representation changes.

title: Factorization
text:
Implementation
Outer grouped cross validation excludes complete verbs. Inner validation fits normalization, PCA, rank selection, and the ridge penalty using only the outer training verbs.

title: Factorization
text:
Question
May PCA be fitted once using all VALEX verbs because it does not use acceptability judgments?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
No. The question concerns a new verb. Its VALEX row must not determine the component directions used to represent it.

title: Factorization
text:
Output
Out of sample \(R^2\) compares each model with frame mean predictions fitted on the training verbs.
Positive values remove some baseline squared error.

title: Factorization
text:
Result #1
The direct VALEX profile obtains out of sample \(R^2=.246\) with a verb bootstrap interval of \([.224,.266]\).
Course analysis of White and Rawlins data

[Sources]
Course notes, VALEX and MegaAcceptability analysis: ../../factorization/valex-megaacceptability.html
White and Rawlins 2020: https://doi.org/10.5334/gjgl.1001

title: Factorization
text:
Result #2
The selected factor model obtains \(R^2=.239\).
Factor minus direct is \(-.0066\) with interval \([-.0100,-.0029]\).
Course analysis of White and Rawlins data

[Sources]
Course notes, VALEX and MegaAcceptability analysis: ../../factorization/valex-megaacceptability.html

title: Factorization
text:
Interpretation
PCA compression does not improve this mapping.
Inner validation selects the largest candidate rank, 50, in every outer fold.

title: Factorization
text:
Result #3
Prediction is weakest for object plus finite clause frames.
Direct \(R^2\) is .083 there, compared with .254 for matched finite clauses without an object.
Course analysis of White and Rawlins data

[Sources]
Course notes, VALEX and MegaAcceptability analysis: ../../factorization/valex-megaacceptability.html
White and Rawlins 2020: https://doi.org/10.5334/gjgl.1001

title: Factorization
text:
Upshot
Corpus distributions predict new verbs, but PCA directions of corpus variation discard a small amount of predictive information and do not repair the object frame failure.

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #2
The result rejects this predictive compression.
It does not show that clause selection lacks abstract syntactic or semantic structure.

title: Factorization
text:
Conclusion
What a component can establish

title: Factorization
text:
Big Question
Can several linguistic measurements be represented by a smaller number of recurring numerical patterns?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer

The matrix fixes the represented objects and measurements.
The coordinate system determines which variations count as large.
SVD orders rank one reconstruction patterns.
PCA applies that ordering to centered variation.
Scores, loadings, and reconstructions answer different questions.
Held out loss selects rank for a declared task.

title: Factorization
text:
Question
Which rows, columns, preprocessing choices, and evaluation loss license the proposed linguistic interpretation of a component?

title: Choosing the number of components
text:
A matrix with rank r has r nonzero singular-value terms. Keeping all of them reproduces the fitted matrix, while keeping fewer gives a lower-dimensional representation. The analysis must decide where to stop without using the same outcomes both to choose the rank and to support the final claim.
Selecting the retained rank is a model-selection problem. When the intended use is reconstruction of excluded cells or observations, validation reconstruction loss selects the rank whose fitted representation best predicts a designated validation set. A separate test set remains untouched until the rank has been fixed.
We first formalize this separation. We then select a rank from a small loss table by hand and in R. Finally, we compare held-out reconstruction with visual and observed-variance rules and examine the instability that can arise when several ranks perform similarly.

title: Choosing the number of components
text:
Separate fitting, selection, and evaluation
Let \mathcal{T} index entries available for fitting, \mathcal{V} index validation entries, and \mathcal{S} index test entries. These sets are disjoint:

\mathcal{T}\cap\mathcal{V}=\varnothing,
\qquad
\mathcal{T}\cap\mathcal{S}=\varnothing,
\qquad
\mathcal{V}\cap\mathcal{S}=\varnothing.

For each candidate rank K, fit the complete rank K reconstruction procedure using only the fitting entries. Denote its prediction for cell (i,j) by

\widehat{x}^{(\mathcal{T})}_{ij,K}.

Under squared loss, the validation risk is

\widehat{R}_{\mathcal{V}}(K)
=
\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|}
\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{V}}
\left(
x_{ij}-\widehat{x}^{(\mathcal{T})}_{ij,K}
\right)^2.

The selected rank is

\widehat{K}
=
\underset{K\in\mathcal{K}}{\operatorname{argmin}}
\widehat{R}_{\mathcal{V}}(K),

where \mathcal{K} is the candidate set fixed before inspecting the test outcomes.
Only after choosing \widehat{K} do we evaluate the selected procedure on \mathcal{S}. The test loss is not another input to rank selection.

title: Choosing the number of components
text:
Work through a validation curve
Suppose four candidate representations produce the following validation losses.



retained rank K
validation squared loss




0
0.25


1
0.18


2
0.14


3
0.16



Rank 0 is a declared baseline that uses no low-rank adjustment. Rank 1 reduces validation loss by

0.25-0.18=0.07.

Rank 2 reduces it by another

0.18-0.14=0.04.

Rank 3 has lower fitted reconstruction error than rank 2 on the training matrix, but its validation loss rises by

0.16-0.14=0.02.

The validation rule thus selects

\widehat{K}=2.

This choice does not assert that the true linguistic system has exactly two dimensions. It says that rank 2 gives the lowest estimated validation loss among these candidates for the declared reconstruction task.

title: Choosing the number of components
text:
Implement the selection in R
The rank curve can be stored in a data frame.


Code
rank_curve <- data.frame(
  rank = c(0L, 1L, 2L, 3L),
  validation_loss = c(0.25, 0.18, 0.14, 0.16)
)

selected_row <- which.min(rank_curve$validation_loss)
selected_rank <- rank_curve$rank[selected_row]

selected_rank


Plotting the complete curve makes near ties and unexpected reversals visible.


Code
plot(
  rank_curve$rank,
  rank_curve$validation_loss,
  type = "b",
  xlab = "Retained rank",
  ylab = "Validation squared loss"
)


The which.min() call implements the formal \operatorname{argmin}. The more substantial work occurs before that line: preprocessing, fitting, and reconstruction must be repeated without using validation or test values as fitting information.

title: Choosing the number of components
section: Treat preprocessing as part of the procedure
text:
Treat preprocessing as part of the procedure
Suppose the columns are centered before the decomposition. Their means must be estimated from the fitting entries available for that candidate fit. A validation or test value cannot contribute to the origin used to predict itself.
The same rule applies to scaling and any rule used to construct the candidate matrix. The procedure evaluated at rank K includes all fitted choices that produce \widehat{x}^{(\mathcal{T})}_{ij,K}.
Computing one decomposition from the complete matrix and then scoring selected entries creates data leakage. Those entries are not held out because their values already affected the column transformations and component directions.

title: Choosing the number of components
Choosing the number of components
section: Why observed reconstruction cannot select rank
text:
Why observed reconstruction cannot select rank
Observed reconstruction error weakly decreases whenever another singular-value term is added. If the only rule is to minimize error on the fitted matrix, the rule selects the largest permitted rank.
That result follows from the construction rather than from evidence that every retained direction will generalize. A later term may restore a small irregularity unique to the fitted entries. Validation asks whether retaining that term helps predict entries excluded from the fit.
This is why the selected rank may occur before the full matrix rank. Compression creates an empirical tradeoff only when evaluated away from the entries that determined the representation.

title: Choosing the number of components
section: Why a scree bend answers another question
text:
Why a scree bend answers another question
A scree plot displays d_k^2 or its proportion of total observed squared variation by component order. It can reveal whether singular values decline sharply or gradually. Looking for a bend is descriptive, but the bend may be ambiguous and does not use excluded reconstruction outcomes.
A fixed cumulative-variance threshold, such as 0.90, is reproducible but conventional. It selects the smallest K that represents a chosen proportion of fitted squared variation. It does not select the rank that best predicts the declared validation cells.
Validation need not always replace a scree plot. If the scientific aim is explicitly descriptive compression of this observed matrix, the singular-value profile may be the relevant object. But if the claim concerns reconstruction of excluded entries or new observations, validation matches that claim more directly.

title: Choosing the number of components
text:
Preserve one final evaluation
Once \widehat{K} has been selected, the test set supports one final evaluation of the selected procedure. Comparing many ranks on the test set and reporting the best turns the test outcomes into another validation set.
After selection, one may refit the rank \widehat{K} procedure using the fitting and validation information together, provided the test values remain excluded. This mirrors the training, validation, and test workflow introduced earlier. The refitting rule should be fixed before the test score is seen.
The resulting test loss evaluates the selected procedure, not the entire rank curve. Its interpretation remains tied to the cell sampling and weighting used in the test set.

title: Choosing the number of components
text:
Report rank uncertainty and sensitivity
Validation losses may be nearly tied. Suppose ranks 2 and 3 have losses 0.140 and 0.141. Selecting rank 2 is mechanically correct under the minimum rule, but the evidence does not support a strong claim that rank 2 is uniquely best.
Plot the curve and report the relevant differences. If the substantive interpretation changes sharply across nearly tied ranks, that instability is part of the result.
The selected rank may also depend on matrix construction, scaling, and the candidate set. A sensitivity analysis can repeat the declared selection procedure under a small number of theoretically defensible data decisions. It should not search a large collection of choices until one produces a preferred interpretation.






NoteProblem Set 5 connection



Problem Set 5, Task 6 chooses rank from balanced validation loss rather than a visual elbow or an observed variance threshold. Task 9 then checks whether the conclusion changes under two inventory selection rules and three rare segment thresholds. These tasks are included because rank selection and data construction are both parts of the fitted procedure.

title: Choosing the number of components
text:
Check rank selection

Which entries determine \widehat{K}, and which entries must remain untouched until final evaluation?
Why does observed reconstruction error favor the largest permitted rank?
In the worked curve, how much lower is rank 2 validation loss than rank 3 loss?
What population weighting difference separates balanced cell loss from loss averaged over all observed cells?
Why does a 0.90 variance threshold not estimate held-out reconstruction performance?
What should be reported when several ranks have nearly identical validation losses?

title: Choosing the number of components
text:
What rank selection establishes
Validation reconstruction loss chooses the retained rank for a declared held-out reconstruction task without using final test outcomes. The choice applies to the complete fitted procedure, including preprocessing and data construction, and it does not identify a true number of linguistic dimensions. With this separation in place, the factorization can support a scoped claim about reconstruction rather than a claim selected from the same cells used to evaluate it.

title: Factorization
text:
Linguistic datasets often contain several measurements of the same objects. A vowel token may have values for several formants. A verb may have counts for several syntactic frames. A language may have a binary value for every segment represented in an inventory database.
These matrices can be large even when their columns share substantial structure. If several acoustic measurements rise together, or if sets of segments tend to recur across inventories, treating every cell as unrelated may obscure the common pattern.
Matrix factorization represents recurring patterns with fewer dimensions by rewriting a data matrix as products or sums of smaller matrices. The unit of analysis introduced at the start of the course still determines what one row represents. The resulting factorization can describe observations, describe variables, and reconstruct cells, but its interpretation remains tied to the objects and measurements placed in the original matrix.

title: Factorization
text:
Three questions govern the module
We will ask three questions in order.

What do the rows, columns, origins, and units mean?
How can one or more rank one patterns reconstruct the matrix?
How many patterns should be retained for the declared reconstruction task?

The order prevents a common interpretive shortcut. A component cannot be understood before the row and column representation is fixed, and a retained dimension cannot be justified before reconstruction has been defined.

title: Factorization
text:
How the pages connect
We begin with linguistic data matrices, which fix the row objects and measurement columns. Centering and scaling then define the coordinate system used to measure variation.
Rank one structure introduces a single outer-product pattern. Singular value decomposition orders several such patterns, and principal component analysis applies that decomposition to variation around column means.
The final pages turn the representation back toward interpretation and evaluation. Scores and loadings distinguish row coordinates from column directions. Reconstruction maps retained components back to cells and measures the residuals. Choosing components selects the retained rank on validation outcomes before a separate final evaluation.

title: Factorization
text:
What factorization can establish
A successful low-rank reconstruction suggests that the chosen matrix contains recurring numerical structure. It does not by itself show that a component is a psychological variable, a universal phonological dimension, or a causal process.
This limitation is productive. It tells us what additional checks are needed: inspect the variables that define each direction, relate row scores to known sampling and provenance labels, and evaluate reconstruction on cells that did not determine the representation.
By the end of the module, we should be able to reconstruct every matrix expression from its row and column meanings, reproduce each hand calculation in R, and state exactly what a retained component does and does not license us to claim.

title: Rank one structure
text:
Suppose three speakers are measured on three speech-rate variables. The speakers differ in their overall rates, but every variable orders them in exactly the same proportional way. The nine cells may then contain only one shared pattern repeated at different strengths.
A nonzero matrix has rank one when it can be written as the outer product of one vector with an entry for each row and another vector with an entry for each column. This representation separates variation across objects from variation across variables without assigning either vector a new substantive meaning.
We first construct an outer product one cell at a time. We then derive the proportionality that defines rank one, compute the matrix in R, and distinguish the algebraic claim from a claim about an underlying linguistic process.

title: Rank one structure
Rank one structure
text:
Read the two vectors
The vector \mathbf{a} has one entry per row. In the speech-rate interpretation, it says how strongly each speaker expresses the common pattern. The entry for speaker 3 is three times the entry for speaker 1.
The vector \mathbf{b} has one entry per column. It says how each measurement participates in the pattern. The third measurement has three times the column weight of the first.
These interpretations are relative. We could multiply \mathbf{a} by 2 and divide \mathbf{b} by 2:

(2\mathbf{a})
\left(
\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{b}
\right)^{\mathsf T}
=
\mathbf{a}\mathbf{b}^{\mathsf T}.

Thus, the individual vector scales are not identified by the outer product. Their product is. Later decompositions use a normalization convention to separate direction from magnitude.

title: Rank one structure
text:
Derive proportional rows and columns
The ith row of a rank one matrix is

\mathbf{x}_i^{\mathsf T}
=
a_i\mathbf{b}^{\mathsf T}.

Every row is thus a multiple of the same row pattern \mathbf{b}^{\mathsf T}. In the worked matrix,

\mathbf{x}_2^{\mathsf T}
=
2\mathbf{x}_1^{\mathsf T}

and

\mathbf{x}_3^{\mathsf T}
=
3\mathbf{x}_1^{\mathsf T}.

The same reasoning applies to columns:

\mathbf{x}_{\cdot j}
=
b_j\mathbf{a}.

Every column is a multiple of \mathbf{a}. This double proportionality is what lets one outer product generate the complete matrix.
If two nonzero rows are not proportional, one outer product cannot represent both. The matrix then has rank greater than one.

title: Rank one structure
text:
Count what has been compressed
The 3\times 3 matrix contains nine cells. Its rank one representation uses three entries in \mathbf{a} and three entries in \mathbf{b}, subject to the scaling ambiguity just described.
The important reduction is structural rather than merely numerical. Instead of treating every cell as unrelated, the representation states that all cells arise from row strength times column participation.
For an n\times p matrix, this rule uses an n-entry row vector and a p-entry column vector. When n and p are large, one shared pattern may summarize a substantial collection of cells.

title: Rank one structure
section: Compute the outer product in R
text:
Compute the outer product in R
The function outer() implements the cell rule x_{ij}=a_i b_j.


Code
a <- c(1, 2, 3)
b <- c(1, 2, 3)

X_rank_one <- outer(a, b)
X_rank_one


Matrix multiplication gives the same result when the vector shapes are explicit.


Code
a_column <- matrix(a, ncol = 1)
b_row <- matrix(b, nrow = 1)

a_column %*% b_row


We can check the numerical rank with a QR decomposition.


Code
qr(X_rank_one)$rank


The result is one. The computation verifies the algebraic property of this matrix. It does not supply a linguistic interpretation of the vectors.

title: Rank one structure
text:
Distinguish exact structure from approximation
Real linguistic measurements will almost never satisfy exact proportionality. Suppose the bottom-right entry is measured as 9.1 rather than 9. The displayed rows are no longer exact multiples, and the numerical matrix may have rank greater than one.
This does not make rank one structure useless. It changes the question from exact representation to approximation: how much of the matrix can one outer-product pattern reconstruct, and where are the remaining errors? The next page supplies an ordered way to answer that question.
We should not use that later machinery prematurely. At this point, rank one means exactly that one outer product generates the nonzero matrix.

title: Rank one structure
section: Rank is not a psychological construct
text:
Rank is not a psychological construct
A potential interpretation is that one rank one pattern proves the existence of one mental variable. This interpretation does not follow from the algebra.
Matrix rank is a property of the observed numerical representation. A shared recording artifact could create proportional columns. A theoretical construct could produce a matrix with higher observed rank because the measurements contain additional variation. And changing the chosen columns could change the rank without changing the speakers.
A low-rank pattern may motivate a substantive hypothesis, but the factorization alone does not identify a linguistic construct or the process that generated the pattern.
Numerical rank also depends on a tolerance. Tiny rounding errors can turn an intended zero into a very small nonzero value. Software thus decides whether small directions count as effectively zero. Exact algebra and numerical computation should not be conflated.






NoteProblem Set 5 connection



Problem Set 5, Task 6 builds a reconstruction by adding rank one patterns to a segment prevalence baseline. Every added term must be interpreted as the combination of one inventory score vector and one segment loading vector.

title: Rank one structure
text:
Check the common pattern

In the worked matrix, which entries of \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{b} generate x_{32}=6?
Why is every row of \mathbf{a}\mathbf{b}^{\mathsf T} proportional to \mathbf{b}^{\mathsf T}?
What happens to the outer product if \mathbf{a} is doubled and \mathbf{b} is halved?
Why would changing one cell from 9 to 9.1 usually remove exact rank one structure?
What additional evidence would be needed to interpret the common pattern as a psychological construct?

title: Rank one structure
text:
Before ordering several patterns
A rank one matrix is generated by one vector for its rows and one vector for its columns. The outer product explains every cell through their multiplication, but it does not identify the linguistic construct that produced the pattern. The next page represents any real matrix as an ordered sum of such rank one patterns.

title: Scores and loadings
text:
A principal component analysis returns numbers for both sides of the linguistic data matrix. One set locates the row objects in the new coordinate system. The other set describes how the original measurement columns define that system. Confusing the two leads to claims about variables that were computed from observations, or claims about observations that were computed from variables.
Scores locate observations. On this page, loadings are the entries of the unit-length component directions through the original variables. The two quantities are connected by matrix multiplication, but they answer different questions.
We first derive one score from one row and one direction. We then connect the calculation to complete score and loading matrices, implement the extraction in R, and examine sign, terminology, and metadata-join failures.

title: Scores and loadings
text:
Scores locate row objects
Let \mathbf{X}_c be an n\times p centered matrix and let \mathbf{V} contain its principal component directions. The score matrix is

\mathbf{Z}
=
\mathbf{X}_c\mathbf{V}.

Entry z_{ik} is the score of observation i on component k. If \mathbf{x}_i^{\mathsf T} is centered row i and \mathbf{v}_k is direction k, then

z_{ik}
=
\mathbf{x}_i^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{v}_k
=
\sum_{j=1}^{p}x^c_{ij}v_{jk}.

Thus, a score is a weighted sum of one observation’s centered measurement values.

title: Scores and loadings
Scores and loadings
text:
Loadings describe directions
The entries in \mathbf{v}_k tell us how the original variables are combined to form component k. In the worked direction, both variables have weight 1/\sqrt{2}. They contribute equally and with the same sign.
Compare that direction with

\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}_1
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\-1
\end{bmatrix}.

The score under this second direction is

\widetilde{z}_{i1}
=
\frac{2-1}{\sqrt{2}}
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\approx0.71.

The first direction represents common movement in the two measurements. The second represents a contrast between them. Relative signs and magnitudes define this pattern.

title: Scores and loadings
section: State which quantity is called a loading
text:
State which quantity is called a loading
The word loading is used for more than one quantity. Some texts and software call the entries v_{jk} of \mathbf{V} loadings. These are unit-length direction weights.
Other sources scale those weights by the component standard deviation. Under that convention, a loading may be written

\ell_{jk}
=
v_{jk}\sqrt{\lambda_k},

where \lambda_k is the variance of component k. The two conventions answer related but nonidentical numerical questions. On this page, loading refers to v_{jk}, and scaled loading refers to \ell_{jk}. A printed value cannot be compared across analyses until the convention has been stated.

title: Scores and loadings
section: Connect scores and directions to the SVD
text:
Connect scores and directions to the SVD
Recall the singular value decomposition:

\mathbf{X}_c
=
\mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf T}.

Multiplying by \mathbf{V} gives

\mathbf{Z}
=
\mathbf{X}_c\mathbf{V}
=
\mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}.

Thus, component k has score vector

\mathbf{z}_{\cdot k}
=
d_k\mathbf{u}_k.

The singular value scales the unit-length left singular vector into observation coordinates. In contrast, the corresponding right singular vector \mathbf{v}_k remains a unit-length direction through the original columns.
This relationship explains why scores and weights have different dimensions. There is one score per row and one weight per column for every retained component.

title: Scores and loadings
text:
Extract the quantities in R
For an object returned by prcomp(), the score and direction matrices are stored separately.


Code
score_matrix <- pca_fit$x
weight_matrix <- pca_fit$rotation

dim(score_matrix)
dim(weight_matrix)

head(score_matrix)
weight_matrix


If X contains n rows and p columns, score_matrix has n rows. Its columns index components. The weight_matrix has p rows, one for each original variable.
To verify one score, multiply a centered row by the corresponding direction.


Code
X_centered <- scale(
  X,
  center = pca_fit$center,
  scale = FALSE
)

score_i1 <- X_centered[1, ] %*% weight_matrix[, 1]

c(
  from_product = score_i1,
  from_prcomp = score_matrix[1, 1]
)


If the PCA used scaling, the row must also be divided by the same stored scales before this multiplication. The score formula uses the transformed coordinates on which the component directions were fit.

title: Scores and loadings
section: Join scores to metadata by identifier
text:
Join scores to metadata by identifier
Scores inherit the row order of the matrix supplied to PCA. Linguistic labels often live in a separate table. A safe join uses a stable row identifier.


Code
score_data <- data.frame(
  token_id = rownames(score_matrix),
  PC1 = score_matrix[, 1],
  PC2 = score_matrix[, 2]
)

score_data <- merge(
  score_data,
  token_metadata,
  by = "token_id",
  all.x = TRUE,
  sort = FALSE
)


Binding labels by accidental row position may attach the wrong vowel, speaker, language, or database source to each score. The resulting plot can look persuasive because the coordinates are real even though the labels are wrong.
Check identifier uniqueness and the number of matched rows before interpreting labeled score plots. A row-order mismatch can attach scores to the wrong linguistic objects.

title: Scores and loadings
section: Interpret patterns rather than isolated signs
text:
Interpret patterns rather than isolated signs
The SVD sign indeterminacy applies to both scores and loadings. If \mathbf{v}_k changes sign, the corresponding scores also change sign. Relative positions and reconstructions remain the same.
Thus, a claim that one language has a positive score is incomplete without describing the chosen orientation. A more stable claim describes which objects lie together or on opposite sides and which variables point together or apart.
A large loading also does not mean that the variable causes the component. The direction was computed from the variables. Causal language reverses that construction and requires evidence not supplied by PCA.






NoteProblem Set 5 connection



Problem Set 5, Task 8 reads segment loadings together with inventory scores. Loadings describe a direction in the retained segment space, while scores locate selected inventories along that direction. Neither quantity by itself identifies what generated the pattern.

title: Scores and loadings
text:
Check rows and columns

Which quantity locates one observation in component space?
In the worked example, why is the first score 3/\sqrt{2}?
What pattern is represented by weights with the same sign, and what pattern is represented by opposing signs?
Why must an analysis state its loading convention?
What happens to the scores when the corresponding component direction changes sign?
Why should score metadata be joined by a stable row identifier?

title: Scores and loadings
text:
Before rebuilding the matrix
Scores locate the original row objects, while loadings describe directions through the original columns under the convention stated on this page. Their multiplication is interpretable only under a stated loading convention and a verified metadata alignment. The next page combines scores and component directions to calculate which cells a retained representation restores and which discrepancies it leaves behind.

title: Can corpus distributions predict clause selection?
text:
Clause embedding verbs differ in the complements they permit. Think occurs naturally with a declarative clause, as in Someone thought that something happened. Wonder occurs naturally with an interrogative clause, as in Someone wondered whether something happened. Persuade instead favors an object followed by an infinitive, as in Someone persuaded someone to do something.
These differences define a verb’s selectional profile. The question on this page is whether a verb’s distribution in a large corpus predicts that profile.
We will build the analysis in four stages. First, we will define the corpus predictor and acceptability response. Second, we will state two linguistic hypotheses that distinguish a complete distribution from a compressed distribution. Third, we will compare those representations on verbs excluded from fitting. Finally, we will inspect where the predictions succeed and fail.
crumbs: Can corpus distributions predict clause selection?

title: Can corpus distributions predict clause selection?
text:
Start with the linguistic observations
MegaAcceptability contains judgments for 1,000 English clause embedding verbs in 50 surface syntactic frames. Each original verb by frame cell received five judgments on a scale from 1 to 7. The frames vary several properties of the complement, including clause type, tense, the presence of an object, and the eventive or stative interpretation of an infinitive.
The intersection with the usable VALEX inventory contains 958 verbs. Restricting the raw judgments to those verbs, omitting ten missing responses, and retaining participants who reported being native speakers of American English leaves 238,917 responses from 727 participants. Every analysis below uses that fixed intersection.
Consider five cells from the dataset.








verb
frame
sentence




think
NP Ved that S
Someone thought that something happened.


persuade
NP Ved NP to VP[+eventive]
Someone persuaded someone to do something.


wonder
NP Ved whether S
Someone wondered whether something happened.


try
NP Ved to VP[+eventive]
Someone tried to do something.


promise
NP Ved to VP[+eventive]
Someone promised to do something.



The notation abstracts away from the particular nouns and embedded predicates in the stimuli. NP Ved whether S, for instance, records a past tense matrix verb followed by an interrogative clause. This makes the response matrix about complement selection rather than about one particular sentence.
Let y_{vk} denote the normalized acceptability of verb v in MegaAcceptability frame k. One row of the response matrix is then

\mathbf{y}_v
=
\begin{bmatrix}
y_{v1} & y_{v2} & \cdots & y_{v,50}
\end{bmatrix}.
