The complete response matrix \mathbf{Y} has one row for each retained verb and 50 columns. This is the object we want to predict.






TipReasoning check



If we instead placed individual ratings in the rows, would a row still represent a selectional profile?
No. A row would represent one participant’s response to one sentence. Constructing a verb profile requires us to say how those responses are combined and how participant use of the response scale is handled.
crumbs: Can corpus distributions predict clause selection?

title: Can corpus distributions predict clause selection?
text:
Interpret the normalized response scale
Participants may use the seven response categories differently. One participant may use almost the complete scale, while another may concentrate responses between 3 and 6. Treating their raw numbers as if they shared an origin and unit may preserve variation in response habits that is not part of verb selection. We will use the training based transformation developed in centering and scaling.
For a particular training set of verbs, let \bar r_{p,\mathcal T} be participant p’s mean rating and let s_{p,\mathcal T} be the corresponding standard deviation. We transform each rating using

z_{pi}
=
\frac{r_{pi}-\bar r_{p,\mathcal T}}
     {s_{p,\mathcal T}}.

We then average the transformed ratings within each verb by frame cell. A normalized value of 1 means that the responses to that cell were, on average, one participant specific standard deviation above the participants’ training means. A value of 0 marks the relevant participant baselines. It does not mark a boundary between grammatical and ungrammatical sentences.
This interpretation also explains why a difference of one normalized unit is not a difference of one point on the original response scale. The normalized scale is relative. Its origin and unit come from the training responses.
The training qualification matters. If a test verb helped determine a participant’s mean or standard deviation, its response would affect its own normalization before prediction. To avoid data leakage, fit the participant transformation on training verbs and apply those fixed values to test responses.
One participant had a zero training standard deviation in one of the 300 normalization fits used below. The prespecified fallback used the overall training mean and standard deviation for that participant. No participant lacked training responses. Thus the fallback repaired an undefined division without consulting a validation or test response.






WarningWhat this normalization does not establish



The responses are ordinal. Subtracting a mean and dividing by a standard deviation treats adjacent response categories as equally spaced for this preprocessing step. That is an approximation, not a trial level model of ordinal judgments.
White and Rawlins use a more elaborate ordinal normalization. Across the 47,900 verb by frame cells used here, the training style transformation fitted to the complete retained sample correlates 0.946 with their released normalized values. The simpler transformation tracks the released profiles closely enough for this factorization application, while allowing every fitted quantity to remain inside its training fold.
crumbs: Can corpus distributions predict clause selection?

title: Can corpus distributions predict clause selection?
text:
Construct the corpus predictor
VALEX is a corpus derived lexicon of verb subcategorization frequencies. For each verb, it records counts for syntactic patterns such as a sentential complement, an infinitival complement, an object, or no detected complement. The released analysis distinguishes 109 frame and class combinations among the verbs shared with MegaAcceptability.
Let c_{vj} be the VALEX count for verb v in corpus frame j. Raw counts mix two kinds of information: the total number of corpus occurrences for the verb and the allocation of those occurrences across frames. The analysis concerns the allocation, so we convert each count to a within verb proportion:

x_{vj}
=
\frac{c_{vj}}
     {\sum_{h=1}^{109} c_{vh}}.

The row

\mathbf{x}_v
=
\begin{bmatrix}
x_{v1} & x_{v2} & \cdots & x_{v,109}
\end{bmatrix}

is the verb’s normalized VALEX frame distribution. Its entries are nonnegative and sum to one.
The following table collapses the VALEX class distinctions only to make three profiles readable. The fitted model retains all 109 original columns.










verb
largest corpus frame
proportion
next largest corpus frame
proportion




think
sentential complement
0.501
no detected complement
0.322


persuade
infinitival complement with subject
0.533
noun phrase
0.237


try
verbal infinitive
0.646
no detected complement
0.157



These are theoretically relevant predictors. The high sentential complement proportion for think and the high infinitival proportion for try encode distributional facts that a theory of selection should connect to their acceptability profiles. The predictor is not merely verb frequency, word length, or an arbitrary vector supplied to the model.






TipReasoning check



Why not use the total VALEX count as the only predictor?
Total count measures how often a verb was observed. It does not say which complements the verb occurred with. Two verbs can have the same total count and very different distributions across sentential, infinitival, and nominal frames.
crumbs: Can corpus distributions predict clause selection?

title: Can corpus distributions predict clause selection?
text:
State the two hypotheses
The first hypothesis concerns the complete direct profile.
First, the complete 109 dimensional VALEX distribution for a verb may predict its 50 dimensional MegaAcceptability profile.
This hypothesis concerns generalization to verbs, not filling a randomly hidden cell for a verb already seen during fitting. A successful test must thus exclude complete verbs.
The second hypothesis concerns abstraction.
Second, a lower dimensional representation of the VALEX distribution may predict the MegaAcceptability profile better than the complete distribution.
The motivation for the second hypothesis is that raw corpus frames may divide evidence too finely. Several observed frames might express a shared syntactic or semantic distinction. If PCA recovers that shared structure, a small number of scores might preserve the predictive regularity while discarding frame specific noise.
Compression alone does not constitute linguistic abstraction. PCA orders directions by variation in the VALEX matrix, not by their relation to a theory of clause selection. The comparison tests whether this particular shallow abstraction improves prediction. It cannot show that the selected components are grammatical primitives.
crumbs: Can corpus distributions predict clause selection?

title: Can corpus distributions predict clause selection?
text:
Change only the predictor representation
The direct model uses the complete row \mathbf{x}_v. For each of the 50 response columns, ridge regression predicts normalized acceptability from the same 109 predictors. Writing all response columns together gives

\widehat{\mathbf{Y}}_{\mathrm{direct}}
=
\mathbf{1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_0^{\mathsf T}
+
\mathbf{X}\mathbf{B}.

This matrix expression is just 50 ridge regressions sharing a predictor matrix and penalty. It does not introduce a different response model.
The factor model changes one part of the procedure. We center the VALEX columns using the training verbs, fit PCA to those training rows, and retain the first K scores:

\mathbf{Z}_K
=
\left(
\mathbf{X}
-
\mathbf{1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal T}^{\mathsf T}
\right)
\mathbf{V}_{\mathcal T,K}.

Ridge regression then predicts the same response matrix from \mathbf{Z}_K:

\widehat{\mathbf{Y}}_{\mathrm{factor}}
=
\mathbf{1}\boldsymbol{\gamma}_0^{\mathsf T}
+
\mathbf{Z}_K\mathbf{G}.

The models have the same verbs, the same responses, the same loss, and the same type of ridge regression. Their difference is whether the ridge regression receives 109 direct proportions or K PCA scores. This isolates the comparison between the complete distribution and its lower dimensional representation.
crumbs: Can corpus distributions predict clause selection?

title: Can corpus distributions predict clause selection?
section: Keep every fitted choice inside the training data
text:
Keep every fitted choice inside the training data
The outer evaluation uses five repetitions of ten fold grouped cross validation. Each outer fold excludes complete verbs. Within its training verbs, five fold validation applies the component selection procedure to the factor model. It selects the ridge penalty for the direct model and jointly selects the retained rank and ridge penalty for the factor model.
The fitting sequence for one outer fold is:

Set aside the outer test verbs.
Split the remaining verbs into inner training and validation sets.
Fit participant normalization on the inner training responses.
Fit PCA centering and component directions on the inner training VALEX rows.
Evaluate each fixed rank and ridge candidate on the inner validation verbs.
Select the candidates with the lowest inner validation squared loss.
Refit normalization, PCA, and ridge regression on all outer training verbs.
Evaluate the selected procedures once on the outer test verbs.

The ridge candidates are 0.01, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, and 10. The rank candidates are 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50. These sets were fixed before the outer results were inspected.
Why must PCA be fitted again inside every inner split? Suppose an inner validation verb has an unusual concentration in one VALEX frame. If that row helps determine the component direction, its distribution has already influenced its own representation. The later ridge fit does not remove this data leakage.






TipReasoning check



May we compute one PCA from all 958 verbs because the PCA does not use acceptability?
No. The target is prediction for a new verb. Its VALEX row is part of the information withheld under that target. Using the row to fit the component directions gives the factor model access to the test verb before evaluation.

title: Can corpus distributions predict clause selection?
text:
Define the predictive score
The baseline predicts the training mean separately for each of the 50 MegaAcceptability frames. It knows that some frames tend to receive higher judgments than others, but it does not use the identity or VALEX profile of the test verb.
For a fitted model m, define out-of-sample R^2 relative to the frame-mean baseline as

R^2_m
=
1
-
\frac{
\sum_i (y_i-\widehat y_{m,i})^2
}{
\sum_i (y_i-\widehat y_{\mathrm{base},i})^2
}.

A value of 0 means that the model matches the frame mean baseline. A positive value means that the verb specific prediction removes some of the baseline squared error. A negative value means that it does worse than the baseline.
The difference

\Delta R^2
=
R^2_{\mathrm{factor}}
-
R^2_{\mathrm{direct}}

tests the second hypothesis. Positive values favor compression. Negative values favor the complete distribution.
Uncertainty is computed with the bootstrap by resampling verbs. Each sampled verb contributes all of its frames and all five outer predictions. This preserves the paired comparison between representations and respects the verb as the held-out unit.

Evaluate the hypotheses
Before this analysis, we decided that the first hypothesis would count as supported only if direct out-of-sample R^2 reached at least 0.20, its verb bootstrap interval lay above zero, and R^2 was positive in every repetition. We treated the difference between representations as stable if its interval excluded zero or lay completely between -0.01 and 0.01.

The factor model does not support the second hypothesis. Inner validation selected 50 components in all 50 outer folds, which is the largest permitted factor rank. Even that representation has an out-of-sample R^2 that is 0.0066 lower than the direct profile, and the difference is negative in all five repetitions. The result is small but stable.
This is an informative failure of compression. The direct corpus distribution predicts new selectional profiles, but the PCA directions with the most corpus variation do not preserve all of the information useful for that prediction.






TipReasoning check



Does selecting 50 components show that English clause selection has 50 latent dimensions?
No. It shows that 50 was the best candidate rank for this predictor, response, loss, and candidate set. Since it was also the largest candidate, the validation results suggest that additional VALEX directions may remain useful. They do not identify a true number of grammatical dimensions.

Direct out-of-sample R^2 falls from 0.254 for finite clauses without an object to 0.083 for their matched object frames. At the individual frame level, direct R^2 is 0.037 for NP Ved NP whether S, 0.061 for NP Ved NP whichNP S, and 0.109 for NP Ved NP that S. Thus the stable overall loss and the small local gain are compatible: compression discards useful information in the frames that already work, and restores very little where the direct mapping fails.
White and Rawlins connect the object pattern to communicativity. A verb such as persuade may license a finite clause after an object because the object refers to a recipient of communicated content. Corpus cooccurrence can register the surface sequence without directly representing that semantic relation. The error pattern is consistent with this proposal, though it does not isolate communicativity from animacy, discourse, or errors in automatic corpus analysis.

title: Can corpus distributions predict clause selection?
text:
What the application establishes
The analysis supports three conclusions.

VALEX complement distributions contain information about the acceptability profiles of verbs excluded from fitting.
PCA compression does not improve this mapping. Nested validation consistently retains the largest candidate rank, and the selected factor model performs slightly worse than the direct profile.
Prediction remains especially weak for an object followed by a finite clause. The error is organized by a theoretically relevant construction rather than spread uniformly across the response matrix.

These conclusions are narrower than a claim that selection reduces to frequency. VALEX is a noisy corpus measurement, MegaAcceptability is an aggregate judgment measurement, and ridge regression estimates a predictive association. The remaining object frame error may point to semantic information absent from the corpus frame inventory, but the present comparison does not identify that information.
The live question is thus more specific than whether abstraction matters. Which representation of communicativity, argument structure, or event structure predicts the object plus finite clause contrast without sacrificing the direct distributional signal in the other frames? Answering that question would require a new theoretically specified predictor and a new held-out comparison. It cannot be answered by renaming the present principal components.

Check the reasoning

What does one row of the VALEX matrix represent?
Why are VALEX counts converted to within verb proportions?
What is the held-out unit, and which linguistic claim makes that unit appropriate?
Which quantities must be refitted inside an inner training split?
What is held constant between the direct and factor models?
Why does a selected rank of 50 not identify 50 grammatical categories?
Which frame family produces the most pronounced direct prediction failure?
Does a small stable loss for PCA imply that no abstract representation could improve the mapping?

The final question is the main scope check. This analysis rejects one shallow predictive compression, not abstraction in general. A future abstraction must earn its interpretation through theoretically defined inputs, fold safe fitting, and improved prediction on verbs that did not determine it.

title: Complete case analysis
text:
Suppose an acoustic study records duration, F1, and F3 for every fricative token. F3 is absent on several long tokens because tracking was difficult. A software function that requires all three measurements may silently remove those rows. The resulting analysis runs, but it no longer describes the same set of tokens.
Complete case analysis, also called listwise deletion, retains only rows observed on every variable required by the analysis. Its apparent simplicity hides two consequences. It reduces the amount of information, and it may change the target population from all eligible observations to a selected subset.

title: Complete case analysis
text:
Define the complete case indicator
Let J be the set of variables required by an analysis. For row i, define

C_i=\prod_{j\in J}R_{ij}.

Because each R_{ij} is zero or one, C_i=1 only when every required value is observed. A complete case estimate of a mean is

\bar Y_{C=1}
=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}C_iY_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}C_i}.

This quantity is a mean over complete rows. It equals the mean over all eligible rows only under additional conditions on the missingness mechanism and the estimand.

Consider eight tokens. Duration is observed for every token, but F3 is missing for the three longest tokens.

The mean duration over all eight tokens is

\bar Y=\frac{100+110+120+130+140+150+160+170}{8}=135.

The complete case mean is

\bar Y_{C=1}=\frac{100+110+120+130+140}{5}=120.

Deletion changes the mean by 15 milliseconds because the retained tokens are shorter. The complete case mean is not arithmetically incorrect. It answers a different question: what is mean duration among tokens for which both duration and F3 were observed?

title: Complete case analysis
text:
Make deletion explicit in R


Code
acoustic <- data.frame(
  token = paste0("t", 1:8),
  duration = seq(100, 170, by = 10),
  F3 = c(2480, 2510, 2440, 2460, 2420, NA, NA, NA)
)

required <- c("duration", "F3")
acoustic$is_complete <- complete.cases(acoustic[required])

table(acoustic$is_complete)
mean(acoustic$duration)
mean(acoustic$duration[acoustic$is_complete])
aggregate(duration ~ is_complete, data = acoustic, FUN = mean)


The first mean is available here only because duration itself is observed for all rows. In a real analysis requiring F3 as a response, the missing F3 values cannot be used to calculate the full target. Comparing observed duration across complete and incomplete rows nevertheless shows that deletion selects shorter tokens.

title: Complete case analysis
text:
Several columns multiply the loss
Complete case loss can be large even when each variable is mostly observed. Suppose five required measurements are independently observed in 90 percent of rows. A row is complete only when all five values are observed, so its probability of being complete is

P(C_i=1)=.9^5\approx.59.

A dataset with 1,000 rows would retain about 590 complete rows on average. The exact retained count varies, and the independence assumption used in this calculation may fail. The hand calculation is meant to show why missingness accumulates across columns, not to predict an exact count for every dataset.

title: Complete case analysis
section: When does deletion preserve a target?
text:
When does deletion preserve a target?
Under MCAR, complete rows form a random subset with respect to the measurements, so familiar complete case estimates may remain unbiased for their full data targets. MAR does not provide this guarantee automatically. If completeness depends on an observed variable related to the response, unadjusted deletion can change the response distribution.
The relevant condition can also depend on the estimand. Missingness in a response and missingness in a predictor do not have identical consequences for every estimate. Thus, the report should state which variables define completeness and which complete row population the estimate describes.
Complete case analysis may be reasonable when missingness is rare, the retained sample remains adequate, and the selection assumptions are plausible for the target. These are substantive conditions, not properties conferred by the complete.cases() function.

title: Complete case analysis
section: Complete-case analysis can change the target population
text:
Complete-case analysis can change the target population
Complete-case analysis can change the target population from all eligible observations to observations with complete records. This change often goes unreported when software drops rows automatically and reports only the final sample size.
To diagnose it, record the number of rows before and after deletion, count missingness for every required variable, and compare observed characteristics across complete and incomplete rows. Such comparisons cannot reveal the missing values. They can show whether the retained subset differs on information that remains observed.






WarningDo not hide the analysis set



Store the complete case indicator in the analysis table. Report the variables used to define it, the number of retained rows, and the observed differences between retained and removed rows.








NoteCheck the deletion claim




Which variables belong in J for a particular analysis?
Why is the complete case duration mean 15 milliseconds below the full mean in the worked example?
If four independently observed variables are each present in 80 percent of rows, what proportion of rows is complete on average?
What does comparing observed duration across complete and incomplete rows reveal, and what can it not reveal?

title: Complete case analysis
text:
Summing up
Complete case analysis retains rows observed on every required variable. It can lose much more data than any single column suggests and may replace a full sample estimand with an estimand over selected rows. The next page considers an alternative that reconstructs missing matrix entries.

title: Missingness mechanisms
text:
Suppose an eye tracking study measures first pass reading time for words in simple and complex sentences. Some words receive no first pass fixation, so their reading times are absent. A table of missingness indicators can show whether absences are more common in complex sentences. It cannot, by itself, say whether complexity explains the absence or whether the unseen reading time still affects the probability of being observed.
A missingness mechanism states how the probability of the complete missingness-indicator pattern depends on measurements that are observed and measurements that are missing. The three mechanisms introduced below make different dependence claims. They do not describe three visual arrangements of blank cells. The scalar notation below isolates one missingness indicator so that those dependence claims can be read directly.

title: Missingness mechanisms
section: Separate the observed and missing parts
text:
Separate the observed and missing parts
Let Y denote the measurements that would exist in the complete data. For a particular pattern, write Y_{\mathrm{obs}} for the observed part and Y_{\mathrm{mis}} for the missing part. Let R=1 when the target measurement is observed and R=0 when it is missing, following the indicator convention from the preceding page.
The mechanism concerns

P(R=1\mid Y_{\mathrm{obs}},Y_{\mathrm{mis}}),

the probability of observation given the complete data. The three labels restrict which quantities this probability may depend on.

title: Missingness mechanisms
text:
Missing completely at random
Values are missing completely at random (MCAR) when the observation probability depends on neither observed nor unobserved measurements:

P(R=1\mid Y_{\mathrm{obs}},Y_{\mathrm{mis}})=P(R=1).

Imagine that a software failure deletes each trial with the same probability, regardless of sentence complexity, word identity, participant, or reading time. Under this account, observed trials are a random subset of the full trials.
MCAR is a strong claim. Failing to detect an association between missingness and an observed variable does not establish it. A finite dataset may simply provide little information about the association, and the missing values cannot be checked directly.

title: Missingness mechanisms
text:
Missing at random
Values are missing at random (MAR) when observation may depend on observed measurements but does not additionally depend on the missing value after those measurements are conditioned on:

P(R=1\mid Y_{\mathrm{obs}},Y_{\mathrm{mis}})
=P(R=1\mid Y_{\mathrm{obs}}).

Suppose skipping is more common in complex sentences, and sentence complexity is observed for every word. Under an MAR account, complexity may change the probability that reading time is absent. Among words with the same observed complexity and other relevant observed properties, however, the unseen reading time does not further change that probability.
The name is potentially misleading. MAR does not say that blanks are scattered uniformly through the table. It permits visible and systematic missingness whenever that structure is explained by observed information.

title: Missingness mechanisms
text:
Missing not at random
Values are missing not at random (MNAR) when observation still depends on the unseen value after observed measurements have been considered:

P(R=1\mid Y_{\mathrm{obs}},Y_{\mathrm{mis}})
\neq P(R=1\mid Y_{\mathrm{obs}}).

Suppose very short reading times correspond to skipped or barely fixated words that the apparatus does not record as a first pass fixation. Even among words with the same observed complexity, the missing reading time itself may affect whether a value appears. This is an MNAR account.
The observed data generally do not identify this remaining dependence. Domain knowledge about the measurement process and sensitivity analyses are needed to ask how conclusions change under plausible MNAR departures.

Consider six trials.

It is also compatible with an MNAR account in which unusually short or long reading times are difficult to record and happen to occur in complex sentences.
The pattern is not compatible with a deterministic claim that observation is unrelated to sentence complexity in these six trials. But that descriptive fact does not prove that the population mechanism depends on complexity, much less that the dependence is MAR rather than MNAR.
We can compute the visible proportions without claiming a mechanism.


Code
trials <- data.frame(
  complexity = rep(c("simple", "complex"), each = 3),
  word_length = c(4, 7, 5, 4, 7, 5),
  reading_time = c(240, 310, 270, 290, NA, NA)
)

trials$observed <- !is.na(trials$reading_time)

with(trials, table(complexity, observed))
aggregate(observed ~ complexity, data = trials, FUN = mean)


The proportions describe P(R=1\mid\text{complexity}) in this sample. They contain no direct information about the reading times in t5 and t6. Thus, the calculation can reveal a pattern relevant to MAR, but it cannot distinguish MAR from MNAR.

title: Missingness mechanisms
text:
Mechanisms can differ by level
An entire participant may be absent because recruitment failed. A session may be incomplete because the eye tracker lost calibration. An individual word may lack a first pass time because it was skipped. Assigning one label to the whole dataset can conceal these different processes.
The analysis should define the indicator and mechanism at the level where absence occurs. Participant absence, session failure, and trial absence may require different assumptions even when their blanks ultimately appear in one rectangular table.

title: Missingness mechanisms
section: A plot cannot distinguish MAR from MNAR
text:
A plot cannot distinguish MAR from MNAR
A missingness plot alone cannot diagnose MCAR, MAR, or MNAR. The plot contains R and observed measurements. The distinction between MAR and MNAR concerns dependence on Y_{\mathrm{mis}}, which the plot cannot display.
This limitation does not make pattern analysis useless. It can challenge MCAR, identify observed variables that should be retained, and guide sensitivity analyses. It cannot turn an unobserved dependence into an observed one.






NoteClassify the claim




Under MCAR, may observation depend on an observed sentence label?
Under MAR, may missingness be visibly associated with sentence complexity?
What additional dependence makes a mechanism MNAR?
Why can the six trial table not distinguish MAR from MNAR?

title: Missingness mechanisms
text:
Summing up
A missingness mechanism restricts how observation may depend on observed and unobserved measurements. MCAR removes both dependencies, MAR permits dependence on observed information, and MNAR retains dependence on unseen values. These assumptions determine what may follow when incomplete rows are deleted, which is the focus of complete case analysis.

title: Iterative PCA imputation
text:
Suppose a phonetic study measures several correlated spectral properties for every token. A tracker fails on one measurement, but the remaining measurements place the token near a well defined acoustic direction. Can the observed cells help reconstruct the missing one?
Iterative PCA imputation repeatedly uses a low rank reconstruction to update missing cells while leaving observed cells fixed. The new object on this page is the update procedure. Principal components and matrix reconstruction have already been introduced.

title: Iterative PCA imputation
Iterative PCA imputation
section: Work through a rank one matrix
text:
Work through a rank one matrix
Consider two standardized acoustic measurements with one absent value.

\mathbf{Y}=
\begin{pmatrix}
-1&-1\\
0&?\\
1&1
\end{pmatrix}.

The observed mean of the second column is (-1+1)/2=0, so column mean initialization gives

\mathbf{X}^{(0)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
-1&-1\\
0&0\\
1&1
\end{pmatrix}.

This matrix already has rank one. Its two columns are identical, and both can be represented by the score vector (-1,0,1)^\top. A rank one reconstruction returns the same matrix. The missing middle value is thus updated to zero, and a second iteration makes no change.
The imputed value has a specific interpretation. Under a one dimensional linear representation of these standardized measurements, the middle token lies at score zero, so its second measurement is reconstructed at the centered value zero. The procedure does not claim that zero was observed.

title: Iterative PCA imputation
section: Implement the iteration in base R
text:
Implement the iteration in base R
The following function implements the formal update for a centered matrix. If measurements are on incomparable scales, scaling decisions should be made before this function is called, using the principles from the prerequisite page.


Code
pca_impute <- function(x, k = 1, tolerance = 1e-8, max_iterations = 100) {
  missing <- is.na(x)
  filled <- x

  for (column in seq_len(ncol(x))) {
    filled[missing[, column], column] <- mean(x[, column], na.rm = TRUE)
  }

  for (iteration in seq_len(max_iterations)) {
    center <- colMeans(filled)
    centered <- sweep(filled, 2, center, FUN = "-")
    decomposition <- svd(centered)

    kept <- seq_len(k)
    scores <- decomposition$u[, kept, drop = FALSE]
    values <- diag(decomposition$d[kept], nrow = k, ncol = k)
    loadings <- decomposition$v[, kept, drop = FALSE]

    reconstructed_centered <- scores %*% values %*% t(loadings)
    reconstructed <- sweep(reconstructed_centered, 2, center, FUN = "+")

    updated <- filled
    updated[missing] <- reconstructed[missing]
    change <- max(abs(updated[missing] - filled[missing]))
    filled <- updated

    if (change < tolerance) {
      break
    }
  }

  filled
}


Apply the function to the hand worked matrix.


Code
acoustic <- matrix(
  c(-1, 0, 1, -1, NA, 1),
  nrow = 3,
  ncol = 2
)

completed <- pca_impute(acoustic, k = 1)
completed

completed[!is.na(acoustic)] == acoustic[!is.na(acoustic)]


The final comparison checks the defining constraint: every originally observed cell remains unchanged. A production implementation should also return the iteration count, final change, centering values, and chosen rank so that convergence and preprocessing can be audited.

title: Iterative PCA imputation
text:
The rank controls the reconstruction
The number of retained components K controls which relations can inform a missing cell. Too small a value can remove real variation by forcing the matrix into an overly simple representation. Too large a value can reproduce unstable details of the initialized matrix.
This page does not choose K from the same missing cells it reconstructs. The next page masks observed cells, fits the complete imputation without those values, and uses reconstruction error to evaluate candidate settings. The choice must be made without allowing the hidden values to influence the fitted reconstruction.

title: Iterative PCA imputation
text:
Imputed values remain estimates
A completed matrix may look indistinguishable from an observed matrix in software. The two kinds of cells are not epistemically equivalent. An observed cell contains a measurement. An imputed cell contains a prediction under a low rank assumption, a centering decision, a chosen K, and an initialization procedure.
Using one completed matrix in a later analysis treats these predictions as fixed. This generally understates the uncertainty created by not observing the values. A procedure that propagates imputation uncertainty would require additional machinery beyond the single reconstruction introduced here. The data should retain an indicator distinguishing measured and imputed cells.

title: Iterative PCA imputation
section: PCA imputation can remove unusual measurements
text:
PCA imputation can remove unusual measurements
PCA imputation can remove unusual but real measurements when they do not follow the leading linear components. A rare vowel category, a nonlinear acoustic relation, or an extreme value may be pulled toward the dominant pattern.
This failure is especially concerning when extreme values are more likely to be missing. The low rank procedure may make the completed data look regular precisely because it replaces absent extremes with central predictions. Good numerical convergence does not diagnose this substantive error.






NoteCheck the reconstruction




Which cells may change after each low rank reconstruction?
Why does the missing entry in the hand worked matrix remain zero after one update?
What assumption allows observed acoustic columns to inform a missing cell?
Why should an imputation indicator remain in the completed data?
What kind of token is most likely to be pulled toward the dominant PCA structure during imputation?

title: Iterative PCA imputation
text:
Summing up
Iterative PCA imputation alternates between low rank reconstruction and replacement of the originally missing cells. It preserves observed cells, but its predictions depend on linear low rank structure and a chosen component count. We next evaluate those predictions by masking values that are actually observed.

title: Annotations are measurements
text:
Suppose five annotators rate how likely an event is to have happened on a seven point scale. Their recorded numbers are not direct observations of the event’s semantic status. The numbers are responses produced by a prompt, a scale, an interface, and individual response behavior.
The recorded response must be distinguished from the intended linguistic property. This extends the earlier distinction between a measured response and the claim attached to it. Without that distinction, an item average can be mistaken for the semantic quantity that the instrument was designed to probe.

title: Annotations are measurements
section: Separate the response from the target
text:
Separate the response from the target
Let \theta_i denote the semantic quantity for item i, and let Y_{ij} denote annotator j’s recorded response to that item. A measurement model describes

p(Y_{ij}\mid\theta_i,\text{annotator }j,\text{instrument}).

The response Y_{ij} is observed. The quantity \theta_i is not. Its interpretation comes from the annotation question and from the assumptions connecting possible responses to values of \theta_i.
This notation does not yet specify a response distribution. The scale may be ordered, bounded, binary, or gated. The purpose of the notation is to prevent the response and target from collapsing into the same symbol before the instrument has been described.

title: Annotations are measurements
section: Work through equal means with different responses
text:
Work through equal means with different responses
Consider two items rated by four annotators.



item
annotator 1
annotator 2
annotator 3
annotator 4
mean




A
4
4
4
4
4


B
1
2
6
7
4



Both items have mean four:

\bar Y_A=\bar Y_B=4.

The response patterns differ sharply. Item A produces complete agreement at the middle of the scale. Item B produces disagreement concentrated near opposite ends. If \theta_i is intended to represent a shared item property, these patterns supply different evidence about that property even though their means coincide.
The same distinction appears in base R.


Code
ratings <- data.frame(
  item = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 4),
  annotator = rep(paste0("j", 1:4), times = 2),
  response = c(4, 4, 4, 4, 1, 2, 6, 7)
)

aggregate(response ~ item, data = ratings, FUN = mean)
aggregate(response ~ item, data = ratings, FUN = var)
with(ratings, table(item, response))


The first summary cannot distinguish the items. The variance and response table can. A measurement model fitted to raw responses may represent this disagreement, while a model fitted only to item means cannot reconstruct it.

title: Annotations are measurements
text:
Aggregation changes the available evidence
For item i with J_i responses, the item mean is

\bar Y_i=\frac{1}{J_i}\sum_{j=1}^{J_i}Y_{ij}.

This is a useful descriptive statistic. It removes the identities of the annotators, the shape of the response distribution, and the number of responses unless those quantities are stored separately. Two means can thus be numerically equal while representing different measurement records.
Aggregation is not always inappropriate. If the estimand is explicitly the mean recorded response in a fixed annotation protocol, then \bar Y_i is close to the target by definition. If the estimand is a latent semantic property that should be separated from response behavior, the raw annotations contain information the mean discards.

title: Annotations are measurements
section: Reliability and validity answer different questions
text:
Reliability and validity answer different questions
Reliability concerns the consistency of repeated measurements. Validity concerns whether the measurements support the intended interpretation of \theta_i. Annotators might agree reliably because they share a response shortcut that does not track the proposed semantic property.
A statistical model can estimate response variation and agreement under its assumptions. The linguistic argument must still connect the prompt and response scale to the construct. High agreement cannot supply that connection by itself.

title: Annotations are measurements
section: Describe the instrument before the likelihood
text:
Describe the instrument before the likelihood
An instrument description should answer the following questions in complete sentences.

What response values can be recorded?
Are scale endpoints qualitatively distinct from interior values?
Does one answer determine whether another question appears?
How is confidence recorded, if at all?
Which responses repeat within items and annotators?

These answers constrain the response model used later. A binary gate, an ordered category, and a continuous slider have different supports. Treating them as interchangeable numerical columns would obscure the measurement process.






NoteReading: White et al. (2020)



White et al., The Universal Decompositional Semantics Dataset and Decomp Toolkit.
Read the annotation sections to identify the recorded response, the semantic target, and the repeated units. The reading is included because the dataset preserves the measurement structure needed for the final custom model.

title: Annotations are measurements
section: An aggregate response is not the target construct
text:
An aggregate response is not the target construct
An aggregate response is not automatically the intended semantic property. Treating it as such removes the distinction between what the instrument records and what the analysis aims to infer.
The equal means example diagnoses the problem. If two response patterns imply different evidence about agreement or scale use, a method that receives only the means cannot recover that difference. The repair begins by retaining the raw responses and writing a generative account of how they arise.






NoteSeparate responses from the target property




Which quantity is observed, Y_{ij} or \theta_i?
What information distinguishes items A and B after their means are calculated?
Under what estimand might the item mean itself be the intended target?
Why can reliable annotations still have poor construct validity?

title: Annotations are measurements
text:
Summing up
An annotation is a measured response, while the linguistic construct is the quantity the response is intended to inform. Raw annotations preserve disagreement, scale use, and response counts that an item mean can hide. The next page orders the steps connecting the construct to the response in a data-generating process.

title: Gated annotations
text:
Suppose an annotation protocol first asks whether a described event has a particular property. Only after an affirmative response does the interface ask for the degree to which that property holds. A blank follow up is then structurally missing by design because the instrument never displayed that question. It is not a failed measurement of a displayed question and should not be analyzed as one of the stochastic missingness mechanisms.
A joint model for gated annotations represents the gate response and the conditional follow up as two parts of one observation process. It does not assign a follow up value to a trial on which the annotator was never asked the follow up question.

title: Gated annotations
section: Factor the gate and follow up
text:
Factor the gate and follow up
Let G_{ij}=1 when annotator j affirms the gate for item i, and let G_{ij}=0 otherwise. When G_{ij}=1, let Y_{ij} be the follow up response. Write \pi_{ij} for the gate probability and f_Y(y_{ij}\mid\phi_{ij}) for the conditional follow up probability or density.
The observed response contribution is defined by the two possible gate values:

p(g_{ij},y_{ij}^{\mathrm{obs}})
=
\begin{cases}
\pi_{ij}f_Y(y_{ij}\mid\phi_{ij}), & g_{ij}=1,\\
1-\pi_{ij}, & g_{ij}=0.
\end{cases}

When g_{ij}=1, the response contributes a gate probability and a follow up factor. When g_{ij}=0, it contributes only the probability of a negative gate. The second case never requires evaluating a density at an unrecorded follow up value.

title: Gated annotations
Gated annotations
section: The follow up target is conditional
text:
The follow up target is conditional
An average of observed follow up responses describes cases that passed the gate. Formally, it estimates a quantity such as

E[Y_{ij}\mid G_{ij}=1].

It does not estimate an unconditional property across all items unless the model defines what that property means when the gate fails. The conditioning is part of the linguistic target.
For instance, a temporal property may be meaningful only for events that annotators first classify as having a relevant temporal structure. Treating a negative gate as the lowest temporal rating asserts that absence of applicability and a low degree are the same semantic state. The instrument does not license that assertion automatically.

title: Gated annotations
section: Dependence still belongs in the joint model
text:
Dependence still belongs in the joint model
The gate and follow up can share item and annotator quantities introduced on the preceding pages. An item that often passes the gate may also tend to receive high conditional ratings. One annotator may affirm more gates and use higher follow up categories.
Representing such dependence is a later modeling choice within the full joint model. It requires enough affirmative gates to inform the follow up component. If very few responses pass, a rich dependence structure may be weakly identified even when the gate itself is estimated precisely.

title: Gated annotations
text:
Check the complete response process
A predictive check should reproduce the gate rate and the distribution of follow up responses among affirmative gates. It should also retain item and annotator labels so that systematic failures are not hidden by an overall histogram.
Matching only the observed follow up distribution leaves the selection step unchecked. A model could predict conditional ratings well for the small set of passed gates while badly predicting which items enter that set.

title: Gated annotations
section: A skipped response is not a zero
text:
A skipped response is not a zero
Protocol-generated blanks must not be replaced with numerical zeros. Doing so merges two events: the annotator rejected the gate, and the annotator passed the gate but selected the lowest follow up value.
Retain the gate variable and write the observed response contribution conditionally. A rectangular table can still store NA in the follow up column. The joint model, rather than the storage format, determines what that NA means.






NoteCheck the gate




Which factor contributes when g_{ij}=0?
What population does E[Y_{ij}\mid G_{ij}=1] describe?
Why is a protocol generated blank different from a recorded zero?
Which two distributions must a predictive check reproduce?
Why can a low gate rate weaken the follow up model?

title: Gated annotations
text:
Summing up
A model for gated annotations gives negative gates a gate probability and affirmative gates both a gate probability and a conditional follow up factor. It preserves the conditional meaning of the follow up rather than treating absence as a low value. Before interpreting the full model, we must check whether its parameters can be recovered from data generated under the model.

title: Custom model design
text:
Suppose several annotators judge whether an event happened, how confident they are, and which event properties apply. The recorded table contains numbers and categories, but the linguistic target is not any one cell. It may be an item level property that the responses measure only indirectly.
The models introduced earlier begin with a response distribution and ask how its parameters vary. A custom model begins one step earlier. It asks which sequence of linguistic states, annotator decisions, and instrument rules could have produced the recorded responses. Familiar probability distributions still supply the pieces. The custom part is their organization through the joint distributions and conditional independence assumptions introduced earlier.
The recorded annotation and the intended linguistic quantity are different objects. A model connects them only if every probability term corresponds to a defensible part of the annotation process. Additional latent variables do not help merely because they make the model flexible.

title: Custom model design
section: A custom model starts from the instrument
text:
A custom model starts from the instrument
Before writing a likelihood, describe the response protocol.

State which question the annotator sees.
State which responses are possible.
State whether a response controls which question appears next.
State which items and annotators contribute repeated responses.
State which linguistic quantity the response is intended to measure.

These statements constrain the model. If a follow up appears only after an affirmative gate, its blank cells are generated by the protocol. If annotators use an ordered scale differently, a single item mean may combine item structure with response behavior. The model should represent these facts rather than treating them as details of data cleaning.

title: Custom model design
text:
How the module proceeds
We begin with annotations as measurements, which separates a recorded response from the item quantity it is intended to measure. Data-generating processes then order the random steps that connect the two. Writing a joint model translates those steps into one probability term per choice.
Next, annotator effects add a stable response tendency only after the item response model is explicit. Gated annotations represent a protocol in which the availability of a follow up response depends on an earlier answer. Parameter recovery tests whether the complete fitting procedure can recover known generating quantities.
The final page combines these pieces in a UDS measurement model. Universal Decompositional Semantics is reserved for this application. Earlier pages use schematic annotation tables so that the dataset is not fitted repeatedly while each component is introduced.

title: Custom model design
section: What this module does not reteach
text:
What this module does not reteach
The joint models use response distributions, grouped variation, posterior computation, and posterior predictive checks introduced earlier in the course. Those methods are prerequisites rather than new topics here. We focus instead on which pieces belong together and what each latent quantity means for the annotation process.
This scope keeps the model subordinate to the measurement argument. The goal is not to create the most elaborate probability program. It is to write the smallest generative account that represents the recorded instrument and the linguistic target.

title: Custom model design
text:
What this module adds
By the end of the module, we should be able to distinguish an annotation from a construct, turn an instrument description into a joint distribution, represent stable annotator tendencies and gated questions, and block an interpretation when parameters cannot be recovered. We begin with the measurement distinction on which every later step depends.

title: Measuring natural parts judgments
text:
Consider two predicate instances from the Universal Decompositional Semantics data.
The event structure annotation asks whether the situation described by a predicate has natural parts. All three annotators answered no for called. All three answered yes for eat. This difference concerns the internal temporal structure of the two situations. An eating event can often be divided into smaller eating events. A particular calling event need not support the same division.
That interpretation is only a starting point. The observations are responses from particular annotators to predicate instances in context. They are not direct observations of event structure, and they do not establish a lexical distinction between call and eat. This page develops a measurement model that keeps those distinctions in view.
The analysis uses the binary response model and crossed random intercepts introduced earlier. It estimates an item propensity and an annotator response tendency from the raw binary annotations. The model introduces no conditional follow up response, confidence score, or linguistic predictor. Those additions would create new identification questions before the basic measurement has been checked.

title: Measuring natural parts judgments
text:
Begin with the recorded response
Let Y_{ij} be annotator j’s response to predicate instance i. We code yes as 1 and no as 0:

Y_{ij}\in\{0,1\}.

This is the only response variable in the model. A yes response sends the annotator to questions about the duration and similarity of the parts. A no response sends the annotator to questions about the duration and dynamicity of the whole situation. The response thus has a substantive interpretation within the annotation instrument.
The target is also narrow. We want the conditional probability of yes for one predicate instance when the annotator random intercept is set to zero. This is a location on the log-odds scale, not a probability averaged over the annotator population. We do not yet want a score for the part similarity question, because that response is available only after a yes. We also do not want to turn the released normalized value into an observed response. It is an estimate produced from the annotations.
This separation gives us three objects:

The raw annotation is Y_{ij}.
The item propensity is a latent quantity for predicate instance i.
The released normalized value is a useful external comparison.

Only the first object enters the likelihood as data.

title: Measuring natural parts judgments
text:
Inspect the released annotation design
The audit pins version 0.3.2 of the official decomp Python package. Its raw natural_parts file contains 45,965 responses to 33,106 predicate instances. Most training instances have one annotation. The development and test partitions contain 6,414 multiply annotated instances, which are the useful portion of the release for separating item and annotator variation.
The teaching extract is selected without using response values. The procedure first retains annotators with at least 140 responses in the complete multiply annotated development and test data. It then retains items connected to at least two of those annotators. A fixed hash of the item identifiers selects 1,000 items while keeping at least 50 responses for every retained annotator.

title: Measuring natural parts judgments
section: See why raw proportions are not enough
text:
See why raw proportions are not enough
For one item, the raw proportion of yes responses is

\bar Y_i=\frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}Y_{ij}.

This proportion is easy to compute. The two opening items have proportions 0 and 1. But each is based on only three responses. A proportion of 1 from three responses is not the same evidence as a proportion of 1 from thirty responses.
The annotator composition also differs across items. In the teaching extract, observed annotator yes rates range from about .02 to .43. These raw rates partly reflect which items each person saw, so they are not yet estimates of a pure annotator tendency. They do show why an item judged by three relatively affirmative annotators should not be treated as directly comparable to an item judged by three relatively negative annotators.
Pooling every response by item would remove the annotator identities. Keeping one fixed item proportion would also act as if every item had been measured equally precisely. The model should retain the individual responses and represent both sources of variation.

title: Measuring natural parts judgments
text:
Add the item propensity
Let u_i be the deviation for item i, and let \alpha be the population location. If items were the only repeated unit, we could write

Y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ij})

and

\operatorname{logit}(\pi_{ij})=\alpha+u_i.

The fitted Stan model begins with independent standard-normal variables and centers their realized values:

z_i^{\text{item}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1),
\qquad
u_i=\sigma_{\text{item}}
\left(z_i^{\text{item}}-\bar z^{\text{item}}\right).

This parameterization makes the fitted item deviations sum to zero. The parameter \sigma_{\text{item}} is their scale parameter on the log odds scale. A larger value allows stronger differences among items. Because centering makes the realized deviations dependent, \sigma_{\text{item}} is not exactly their finite-sample standard deviation.
The shared scale and standard-normal distribution produce the partial pooling developed earlier. An item with three unanimous responses can move away from zero, but its estimate remains more regularized than a raw proportion of 0 or 1. The model does not claim that all items are identical. It uses the complete collection to estimate how far a sparsely measured item can reasonably move.

title: Measuring natural parts judgments
text:
Add the annotator location
Now let a_j be annotator j’s random intercept. The model is

Y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ij}),


\operatorname{logit}(\pi_{ij})
=\alpha+u_i+a_j,


z_i^{\text{item}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1),
\qquad
u_i=\sigma_{\text{item}}
\left(z_i^{\text{item}}-\bar z^{\text{item}}\right),

and

z_j^{\text{annotator}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1),
\qquad
a_j=\sigma_{\text{annotator}}
\left(z_j^{\text{annotator}}-\bar z^{\text{annotator}}\right).

A positive a_j raises the probability of a yes response across the items seen by annotator j. A negative value lowers it. The parameter \sigma_{\text{annotator}} is the scale of stable location variation among annotators on the log odds scale.
Both sets of deviations sum to zero in the fitted model. Under this convention, \alpha is the log odds when the item and annotator deviations are zero. The conditional item probability

\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\alpha+u_i)

is the yes probability for item i with the annotator random intercept set to zero.
This probability describes a coordinate in the model. It is not the marginal probability obtained by integrating over the annotator distribution, and it does not describe a new person sampled by averaging demographic properties. It also need not equal the raw yes proportion, because the inverse logit is nonlinear and the observed responses are unevenly distributed across annotators.

title: Measuring natural parts judgments
text:
Complete the Bayesian model
The fitted model uses the following priors:

\alpha\sim\mathcal{N}(0,2.5^2),


\sigma_{\text{item}}\sim\operatorname{HalfNormal}(\text{scale}=2),

and

\sigma_{\text{annotator}}\sim\operatorname{HalfNormal}(\text{scale}=2).

These priors are regularizing on the log odds scale. They allow substantial variation while discouraging the scale parameters from drifting to implausibly large values when an item has only a few responses.
The complete Stan program is stored at research/dataset-audits/uds/uds_natural_parts.stan. Its likelihood is compact:
response ~ bernoulli_logit(
  alpha + item_effect[item] + annotator_effect[annotator]
);
The short likelihood is the endpoint of the model construction, not its beginning. Its indices encode the scientific claim that every response depends on both a predicate instance and an annotator.

title: Measuring natural parts judgments
section: Recover the quantities before fitting UDS
text:
Recover the quantities before fitting UDS
The recovery study uses the exact item and annotator incidence pattern from the teaching extract. It generates responses with

\alpha=-2.1,
\qquad
\sigma_{\text{item}}=1.6,
\qquad
\sigma_{\text{annotator}}=1.6.

These values produce an imbalanced response distribution with substantial item and annotator variation. Each of 12 simulated datasets is fit with two chains, 400 warmup iterations per chain, and 400 retained draws per chain.
Before the run, the audit set six substantive limits. The median absolute intercept error had to be at most .25. Median absolute relative error had to be at most 15 percent for the item scale and 25 percent for the annotator scale. Median recovery correlations had to reach .60 for item effects, .90 for annotator effects, and .65 for conditional item probabilities with the annotator random intercept set to zero. The diagnostic screen also required no divergent transitions and a key parameter \widehat R no greater than 1.05 in any recovery fit.

text:
Fit the released responses
Only after recovery passed did the audit fit the released responses. The real fit used four chains, 800 warmup iterations per chain, and 800 retained draws per chain. It produced no divergent transitions. The largest \widehat R among the three population parameters was 1.004, and the largest among the item and annotator effects was 1.010.

The intercept instead locates an item and annotator whose deviations are both zero. The observed average mixes different item and annotator deviations through a nonlinear link.

title: Measuring natural parts judgments
text:
Check the response process
A fitted item ordering is not enough. As in the earlier chapter on posterior predictive checks, replicated datasets should resemble the response features that motivated the model.
The observed yes rate is .223. Across 400 posterior predictive replications, the central 95 percent interval for the yes rate is [.208, .239], with median .223.
The observed proportion of items containing both a yes and a no response is .440. The corresponding predictive interval is [.412, .473], with median .442.
Both observed summaries fall inside their predictive intervals. The second result matters especially. A model could match the overall yes rate while producing too little or too much disagreement within items. The fitted model reproduces both features with separate item and annotator variation.

title: Measuring natural parts judgments
section: Compare with the released normalized values
text:
Compare with the released normalized values
The official release also supplies one normalized natural_parts value per item. Those values are not responses in the fitted binary model, so they were not used during fitting. They provide a useful comparison after fitting.
The Spearman correlation between the posterior median item probabilities and the released normalized values is .818. The two procedures thus produce similar, but not identical, item orderings.
This association is not a test in which one analysis must defeat the other. The released values use a broader normalization procedure, while the fitted analysis uses a deliberately small binary model. Agreement suggests that the binary response model captures much of the released ordering. The remaining differences show where annotator composition, shrinkage, or modeling choices can matter.

title: Measuring natural parts judgments
section: State what the model does not establish
text:
State what the model does not establish
The binary item-annotator model passed its declared recovery and predictive checks, but its scope remains limited.

The teaching extract contains 1,000 of the 6,414 multiply annotated development and test items. Its deterministic selection preserves connectivity and ignores the responses, but it is not a random sample of all UDS predicates.
Most items have three responses. Individual item probabilities remain strongly regularized, even when their posterior ordering is useful in aggregate.
The annotator term represents only a stable location shift. It does not represent differences in discrimination, response consistency, or interpretation.
The raw confidence serialization does not match the documented confidence scale. The audit excludes confidence rather than assigning it an uncertain interpretation.
The model does not estimate part similarity, duration, dynamicity, or a relation between the two branches of the annotation. Each addition would require its own response model and recovery study.
The item is a predicate instance in context. The result should not be restated as a context free property of a verb lemma.

These limits are part of the result. They identify the analysis supported by the released design and the analyses that still require work.






NoteCheck the binary response model




Why is the released normalized value not an observed response in this likelihood?
What does the connected annotator and item graph make possible?
Why can an item with three yes responses have a posterior probability below 1?
What does \sigma_{\text{annotator}} represent?
Why does recovery of the item ordering not make every item estimate precise?
Which new response would require a separate model before it could enter this analysis?

title: Measuring natural parts judgments
text:
Summing up
The model makes four distinctions explicit. First, a raw yes or no annotation is evidence about event structure rather than event structure itself. Second, predicate instances vary in their propensity to receive a yes response. Third, annotators vary in their stable response locations. Fourth, the released normalized values are a comparison for the fitted item measurements rather than inputs to their likelihood.
The parameter-recovery simulation shows that the procedure can recover the intended population scales and regularized latent orderings under the model. The released fit then reproduces both the overall yes rate and within item disagreement. This supports one narrow measurement analysis of natural parts judgments while leaving the conditional branches for a later model.
